summary: We study when compositional structure yields dimension reduction in supervised learning. We frame learning as empirical risk minimization with a function-space prior: a regularization functional selects a subset of functions with favorable approximation and metric entropy. The models are compositions $f(x)=g(Ax+\Delta h(x))$, where $A\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times d}$ is a linear base map, $\Delta h$ is a nonlinear correction, and $g$ is an outer function; that is, $f$ is an arbitrary smooth function of a $k$-dimensional representation of the input that is linear up to a correction. We prove covering-number bounds showing that the statistical complexity of this class interpolates between an intrinsic regime, parametric in the $kd$ entries of the linear map and nonparametric only in the representation dimension $k$, and an ambient $d$-dimensional nonparametric rate; the interpolation is controlled by the correction size $\varepsilon=\|\Delta h\|$. We then connect $\varepsilon$ to data geometry. If the data lie in a small tube around a $k$-dimensional manifold and the regression target depends on the input only through its nearest point on that manifold, then locally the target factorizes exactly as $g(Ax+\Delta h(x))$ with $A$ a tangent chart and a correction whose Sobolev norm scales linearly with curvature at the localization scale. Patching such local models over an atlas gives a finite-sample excess-risk bound for a least-squares estimator over a finite net of local models, whose ambient term vanishes with curvature. For a one-dimensional model problem we also prove a converse: on curved data, every affine compositional predictor faces an error floor unless its correction budget scales with curvature, while the matching curved model class attains the intrinsic rate. The correction size $\varepsilon$ is thus the effective-dimension parameter linking curvature to statistical complexity.

AI.tldr: This paper proves covering-number and excess-risk bounds for compositional function priors f(x) = g(Ax + Delta h(x)), showing how correction size links manifold curvature to effective statistical dimension.
AI.motivation: Explaining when compositional structure yields dimension reduction in supervised learning requires connecting function-space priors to the underlying geometry and curvature of data manifolds.
AI.method: The authors analyze empirical risk minimization over compositions of a linear map A, nonlinear correction Delta h, and outer function g, proving covering-number bounds, local manifold-chart factorizations, finite-sample excess-risk bounds, and a 1D lower-bound converse.
AI.result: Statistical complexity interpolates between a k-dimensional intrinsic nonparametric rate (plus kd linear parameters) and an ambient d-dimensional rate controlled by ||Delta h||, which scales linearly with manifold curvature; on curved 1D data, affine models without sufficient correction face an error floor.
AI.conclusion: The nonlinear correction norm acts as an effective-dimension parameter that directly links data-manifold curvature to the sample complexity of compositional learners.

title: Steering Bayesian Inference and Decisions through Data Poisoning
summary: Adversarial machine learning has revealed that statistical models can be manipulated through poisoned data, and Bayesian inference is no exception. Earlier work has shown that subtle poisoning attacks can drive the posterior toward a distribution of the attacker's choosing. Such posterior attraction attacks require a fully specified target posterior; however, attackers typically care about only a few posterior quantities or, more consequentially, about a downstream decision. Herein, we study how an attacker can alter Bayesian inference and decisions by deleting or replicating a few observations, chosen to minimize the maximum mean discrepancy between the resulting posterior and a target distribution. A suitable kernel lets the attacker steer selected posterior moments without specifying the rest of the target. Because Bayes actions depend on the posterior only through expected utilities, which are themselves posterior moments, the same approach can target a decision directly. We construct the attacks with a gradient-based heuristic that requires only posterior samples, and analyze its convergence. Experiments with regression and hierarchical models compare moment-based and full-posterior attacks, and illustrate how deleting a handful of observations can flip a Bayesian decision.

AI.tldr: This paper shows how an attacker can steer specific Bayesian posterior moments or downstream decisions by deleting or replicating a few data points via MMD minimization.
AI.motivation: Existing Bayesian data poisoning attacks require specifying a full target posterior, whereas attackers typically aim to manipulate only specific posterior quantities or downstream Bayes decisions.
AI.method: The authors minimize the maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) between the poisoned posterior and a target using a kernel tailored to selected posterior moments or expected utilities, solved via a gradient-based heuristic using only posterior samples.
AI.result: Convergence analysis and experiments on regression and hierarchical models compare moment-based and full-posterior attacks, demonstrating that deleting a handful of observations can flip a Bayesian decision.
AI.conclusion: Kernelized MMD poisoning enables targeted manipulation of Bayesian moments and decisions without needing to specify a complete target posterior.

title: A Geometric Understanding of Denoising Autoencoder with Applications to Image Denoising
summary: Denoising autoencoders have shown strong empirical performance in recovering clean data from their noisy observations, yet their underlying statistical behavior remains underexplored. In this paper, we study denoising autoencoders under the manifold hypothesis, assuming that clean data are supported on low-dimensional smooth manifolds embedded in a high-dimensional ambient space, while noisy observations are generated by isotropic Gaussian noise. We establish generalization guarantees in three geometric scenarios: a single manifold, a pairwise separated finite union of manifolds, and a finite union of intersecting manifolds. Using local chart representations, partitions of unity, and neural network approximation, we derive upper bounds for the expected squared reconstruction error for denoising autoencoder. In the single-manifold and separated-union scenarios, the error consists of a sample-dependent statistical term of order $n^{-2/(d+2)}\log^4 n$, a residual term of order $d\sigma^2/D$ caused by tangential noise, and an exponentially small tail term associated with failure of the manifold projection. Here $D$ is the data ambient dimension, $d$ is the intrinsic dimension of the clean-data manifold, and $\sigma^2$ is the expected squared noise magnitude. In the scenario of intersecting manifolds, we further identify an additional ambiguity term determined by the probability mass near the intersection neighborhood. Numerical experiments on synthetic manifolds and real image datasets support the predicted sample-size scaling law and illustrate the additional reconstruction ambiguity near manifold intersections.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes non-asymptotic generalization bounds for denoising autoencoders under the manifold hypothesis across single, separated, and intersecting manifold settings.
AI.motivation: Despite strong empirical success in image denoising, the statistical generalization behavior of denoising autoencoders on low-dimensional manifolds corrupted by high-dimensional isotropic Gaussian noise remains underexplored.
AI.method: Using local chart representations, partitions of unity, and neural network approximation, the authors upper-bound the expected squared reconstruction error for single manifolds, separated unions of manifolds, and intersecting manifolds.
AI.result: For single and separated manifolds, the error decomposes into a statistical term O(n^-2/(d+2) log^4 n), a tangential-noise residual O(d sigma^2 / D), and an exponentially small projection-failure tail, while intersecting manifolds incur an extra ambiguity term near intersections; synthetic and real-image experiments confirm the scaling laws.
AI.conclusion: Manifold geometry and intersection neighborhoods govern the statistical convergence rate and irreducible error floor of denoising autoencoders.

title: Minimax Estimation of Discrete Distributions under Hockey-stick Divergence
summary: We initiate the study of estimating a discrete distribution with respect to the hockey-stick divergence from independent samples. We provide non-asymptotic upper and lower bounds on the minimax expected loss in terms of the alphabet size, the number of samples, and the divergence parameter. The upper bounds are achieved by add-constant estimators, while the lower bound is derived via a Bayes risk argument. Both upper bounds and lower bounds reveal a transition between polynomial and exponential regimes as the parameters of the problem vary.

AI.tldr: This paper initiates the study of minimax discrete distribution estimation under hockey-stick divergence, proving matching upper and lower bounds that reveal polynomial-to-exponential regime transitions.
AI.motivation: Estimating discrete distributions from independent samples is fundamental in statistics, but minimax rates under the hockey-stick divergence had not been characterized.
AI.method: The authors derive non-asymptotic minimax upper bounds using add-constant estimators and matching lower bounds via a Bayes risk argument in terms of alphabet size, sample size, and the divergence parameter.
AI.result: Both upper and lower bounds establish the minimax expected loss and reveal a sharp transition between polynomial and exponential sample-complexity regimes as problem parameters vary.
AI.conclusion: Add-constant estimators achieve minimax-optimal rates for discrete distribution estimation under hockey-stick divergence, with complexity governed by a parameter-dependent phase transition.

title: Joint Learning of Factual and Counterfactual Worlds for Causal Prior-data Fitted Networks
summary: Estimating treatment effects is central to science across many disciplines and requires counterfactual reasoning about alternative worlds. In the real world, however, each unit reveals its outcome only under the factual world. Thus, the factual and counterfactual outcomes can never be jointly learned by any model trained on real data. The problem is therefore tractable only in synthetic settings, where both worlds can be generated. Recent progress on prior-data fitted networks (PFNs) has shown that models pre-trained purely on synthetic data can transfer to real-world prediction. This paradigm has since carried over to causal effect estimation. Despite this fully synthetic setup, existing causal PFNs carry the real-world constraint into their training objective, confining learning to a single world's outcome per unit. The dependence between the two worlds is thereby lost, and the density of the treatment effect relies by default on independence, which is implausible in practice. We therefore propose joint learning, a training setup in which a causal PFN learns the joint distribution of the factual and counterfactual outcomes of each unit. From the joint distribution, we obtain both the response and the individual treatment effect densities, and at inference, we apply optimal transport across units to obtain an approximation of the average treatment effect density. Ours is therefore the first causal PFN approach to provide all three densities together while accounting for the cross-world dependence. We apply joint learning and optimal transport to existing causal PFNs and evaluate it across semi-synthetic, synthetic, and real benchmarks spanning diverse causal scenarios. The jointly trained models significantly improve upon their baselines in point estimation and uncertainty quantification in most settings, indicating that joint learning is a preferable training setup for causal PFNs.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes joint learning of factual and counterfactual outcomes for causal prior-data fitted networks (PFNs), enabling coherent individual and average treatment effect density estimation.
AI.motivation: Existing causal PFNs train on only one world's outcome per synthetic unit, mirroring real-world constraints unnecessarily, which loses cross-world dependence and forces treatment effect densities to assume independence.
AI.method: The authors train causal PFNs on synthetic data to learn the joint distribution of factual and counterfactual outcomes per unit, yielding response and individual treatment effect densities, and apply optimal transport across units at inference to approximate the average treatment effect density.
AI.result: Evaluated across synthetic, semi-synthetic, and real causal benchmarks, jointly trained causal PFNs significantly improve point estimation and uncertainty quantification over single-world baselines in most settings.
AI.conclusion: Exploiting synthetic access to both factual and counterfactual worlds during PFN pre-training captures cross-world dependence and improves causal effect estimation.

title: Learning Autoregressive Neural Operators on Solver-Defined Physical Constraint Manifolds
summary: Autoregressive neural operators approximate time-dependent PDE solvers by repeatedly composing a learned transition, although the resulting states need not remain feasible under the discrete constraints of the numerical problem. We study this issue for incompressible flow, where each velocity state must satisfy solver-level incompressibility together with prescribed boundary values. We formulate autoregressive operator learning as a map between solver-defined affine feasible sets and introduce PCM-NO, a projected-residual realization of this feasible-transition principle. The neural backbone predicts a candidate state increment, a fixed tangent projection extracts its admissible component, and a metric retraction maps the advanced state to the prescribed feasible set. With exact affine constraint solves, the resulting transition is closed on the feasible set, while an affine identity separates admissible-update parameterization from state-level closure. With approximate solves, tangent-only residuals admit a cumulative upper bound, whereas per-step retraction resets feasibility to the residual achieved by the current solve. Experiments on periodic Navier--Stokes flow and lid-driven cavity flow demonstrate the superiority of PCM-NO in preserving solver-level constraints over long autoregressive rollouts and under parameter, boundary-value, and resolution shifts, while achieving lower rollout errors and better flow-specific diagnostics across both in-distribution and stress settings.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces PCM-NO, an autoregressive neural operator that preserves solver-defined physical constraints such as incompressibility and boundary conditions via tangent projection and metric retraction.
AI.motivation: Autoregressive neural operators for time-dependent PDEs often drift off the discrete feasible set of numerical constraints during long rollouts.
AI.method: PCM-NO formulates transitions between solver-defined affine feasible sets by predicting a candidate state increment, extracting its admissible component with a fixed tangent projection, and applying a metric retraction to enforce feasibility.
AI.result: Theoretical bounds characterize exact vs. approximate constraint solves, and experiments on periodic Navier-Stokes and lid-driven cavity flows show lower rollout errors, better flow diagnostics, and stronger constraint preservation under parameter, boundary, and resolution shifts.
AI.conclusion: Embedding tangent projection and metric retraction into autoregressive neural operators ensures solver-level physical feasibility over long rollouts and distribution shifts.

title: Tight Sequential Confidence Intervals for Online Kernel Regression
summary: We characterize, in the worst case over kernels, the sharp minimax width of online confidence intervals for elements of a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS). This resolves the open problem posed by Vakili et al. (2021) in its original discrete-time form. A learner observes $y_i=f(x_i)+\epsilon_i$ at adaptively chosen points, with $\|f\|_{\mathcal H_k}\le B$ and i.i.d. $R$-sub-Gaussian noise, and reports the interval $|f(x)-\mu_n(x)|\le\rho_n(\delta)\sigma_n(x)$, where $\mu_n$ and $\sigma_n$ are the posterior mean and standard deviation of a surrogate Gaussian process model with regularization parameter $\lambda$. Writing $\rho_n^*(\delta)$ for the minimax confidence width for a fixed kernel, we show that, for the sum of a linear kernel and a periodic Sobolev kernel, all sufficiently large $n$, and all $\delta\in(0,1/4]$, $\rho_n^*(\delta)\asymp B+(R/\lambda)\sqrt{\gamma_n+\log(1/\delta)}$, where $\gamma_n$ is the maximal information gain and grows polynomially in $n$. Building on Lattimore (2023), we construct an adaptive design on a fixed two-dimensional domain for which, under Gaussian noise, the normalized error at a prespecified point is $\Omega(B+(R/\lambda)\sqrt{\gamma_n})$ with constant probability. This rules out the conjectured polylogarithmic width in the worst case over kernels and online designs.

AI.tldr: This paper resolves an open problem by proving the sharp minimax width of sequential confidence intervals for online kernel regression, ruling out polylogarithmic widths in the worst case.
AI.motivation: Whether online RKHS confidence intervals could achieve polylogarithmic width in the worst case over kernels and adaptive designs (posed by Vakili et al., 2021) remained an open question.
AI.method: For a surrogate GP model with regularization lambda and maximal information gain gamma_n, the authors construct an adaptive 2D design under Gaussian noise using the sum of a linear kernel and a periodic Sobolev kernel.
AI.result: They prove the minimax confidence width scales as Theta(B + (R/lambda) sqrt(gamma_n + log(1/delta))), showing a constant-probability normalized error of Omega(B + (R/lambda) sqrt(gamma_n)) at a prespecified point where gamma_n grows polynomially in n.
AI.conclusion: Polynomial dependence on maximal information gain is unavoidable in worst-case online kernel regression confidence intervals, settling the Vakili et al. open problem.

title: Conditional Asset Pricing Transformer
summary: In this paper, we propose a conditional asset pricing transformer (CAP-T) that captures nonlinear interactions among firms through attention to forecast excess returns. In the first stage, a transformer estimates conditional expected returns, and kernel-weighted principal component analysis of its residuals estimates the local factor loading space. Projecting the conditional mean onto this space separates factor risk compensation from conditional mispricing. Then, in the second stage, separate transformers learn these two components, whose predictions are combined to forecast returns. As a result, the proposed framework decomposes returns into conditional mispricing, factor risk compensation, a centered factor component, and an unpredictable innovation. We establish approximation and generalization bounds and characterize how first-stage prediction errors propagate through local factor estimation and component learning, providing statistical guaranties for conditional mispricing, factor loadings, and factor risk premia. Finally, simulations and empirical studies demonstrate the predictive and interpretive benefits of the proposed method.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes the Conditional Asset Pricing Transformer (CAP-T), a two-stage attention framework that decomposes excess stock returns into conditional mispricing and factor risk compensation.
AI.motivation: Capturing nonlinear firm interactions while cleanly separating factor risk premia from conditional mispricing with statistical guarantees remains challenging in empirical asset pricing.
AI.method: Stage one uses a transformer to estimate conditional expected returns and applies kernel-weighted PCA to its residuals to estimate local factor loadings; stage two trains separate transformers on the projected factor risk compensation and orthogonal conditional mispricing components.
AI.result: The authors establish approximation and generalization bounds tracking stage-one error propagation to mispricing, loadings, and risk premia, and show improved predictive and interpretive performance in simulations and empirical studies.
AI.conclusion: Combining attention-based return forecasting with kernel-weighted residual PCA yields an interpretable, statistically grounded decomposition of asset returns.

title: Sharp Gaussian Approximation for Q-Learning
summary: Gaussian approximation provides a foundation for online statistical inference in reinforcement learning. We establish sharp non-asymptotic Gaussian approximation rates in Wasserstein distance for asynchronous Q-learning with Polyak-Ruppert averaging. We prove an upper bound of $\widetilde{O}(n^{-1/4})$, where $n$ is the number of iterations, together with a matching lower bound up to logarithmic factors. Q-learning is more challenging to analyze than linear stochastic approximation due to the nonlinearity of the Bellman operator. Asynchronous updates introduce further challenges due to Markovian noise. Our analysis separates the errors from Bellman nonlinearity, Markovian noise, and the finite-sample covariance discrepancy. In particular, we show that Markovian noise induces an unavoidable bias even when the Bellman operator is linear. The trade-off between this bias and the covariance discrepancy determines the convergence rate. We further extend our analysis to the synchronous setting and establish a sharp rate of $\widetilde{O}(n^{-1/2})$.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes sharp non-asymptotic Gaussian approximation rates in Wasserstein distance for asynchronous and synchronous Q-learning with Polyak-Ruppert averaging.
AI.motivation: Online statistical inference in reinforcement learning requires tight Gaussian approximation rates, which are complicated in Q-learning by Bellman operator nonlinearity and Markovian noise from asynchronous updates.
AI.method: The authors separate errors from Bellman nonlinearity, Markovian noise, and finite-sample covariance discrepancy to derive upper and matching lower bounds in Wasserstein distance for Polyak-Ruppert averaged Q-learning.
AI.result: They prove a sharp rate of O_tilde(n^-1/4) for asynchronous Q-learning (with a matching lower bound up to log factors, driven by an unavoidable Markovian-noise bias even for linear Bellman operators) and extend it to O_tilde(n^-1/2) for synchronous Q-learning.
AI.conclusion: The trade-off between Markovian-noise bias and covariance discrepancy fundamentally governs the O_tilde(n^-1/4) Gaussian approximation rate of asynchronous Q-learning.

title: Integrating Latent Block Models into Variational Autoencoders for Disentangled Representation Learning
summary: We introduce LBM-VAE, a novel framework that integrates Latent Block Models (LBMs) into Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) to jointly cluster observations and latent dimensions. Beyond its clustering capabilities, LBM-VAE provides a block-structured latent representation that naturally supports disentangled representation learning. In contrast to conventional approaches that associate each factor of variation with an individual latent dimension, our framework allows factors of variation to be encoded across groups of latent dimensions. Experimental results demonstrate the promising clustering performance of LBM-VAE, while achieving competitive results in disentangled representation learning. LBM-VAE highlights the potential of combining co-clustering and variational inference to learn structured and interpretable latent representations.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces LBM-VAE, integrating Latent Block Models into Variational Autoencoders to jointly co-cluster observations and latent dimensions for block-structured disentangled representations.
AI.motivation: Conventional disentangled VAEs tie each factor of variation to a single latent dimension, limiting their ability to represent factors distributed across groups of latent dimensions.
AI.method: LBM-VAE embeds a Latent Block Model into the VAE latent space to simultaneously cluster observations and group latent dimensions into coherent blocks.
AI.result: Experiments demonstrate promising co-clustering performance alongside competitive disentangled representation learning compared to existing approaches.
AI.conclusion: Combining co-clustering with variational inference enables VAEs to learn structured, interpretable representations where factors of variation span groups of latent dimensions.

title: The Manifold-Index Model: provably and efficiently avoiding the statistical and computational curse of dimensionality
summary: We study vector-valued regression with predictors filling a tube around an unknown $m$-dimensional manifold $\mathcal{M}$ in $\mathbb{R}^D$. In the Manifold-Index Model, the mean response is $F=f\circ\Pi_{\mathcal{M}}$, where $\Pi_{\mathcal{M}}$ is the nearest-point projection onto $\mathcal{M}$ and $f:\mathcal{M}\to\mathbb{R}^p$ is a possibly non-injective link function. Multiscale ANisotropic lOcal Regression (MANOR) estimates tangent planes by multiscale PCA of predictors with similar responses, then refines them by pooling outer products of local slopes. The neighborhoods narrow tangentially while retaining complete normal fibers. We assume a Lipschitz link differential and bounded response noise. For $p\ge m$, under our geometric and sampling conditions, $n$ independent observations give mean tangent-space error of order $n^{-2/(m+4)}$ and integrated squared prediction error at the $m$-dimensional nonparametric rate $n^{-4/(m+4)}$, up to logarithmic factors. In a scaling regime with fixed intrinsic dimension, model and scale parameters, and ratio of manifold volume to the $m$-th power of its reach, the required sample size grows polynomially in $D+p$, and computation is polynomial in $n$, $D$ and $p$. Numerical experiments on curves with non-monotone links and surfaces with vector-valued responses compare observed convergence rates with the theoretical bounds; a Langevin dynamics example tests prediction of hitting probabilities under an approximate manifold-index model.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes the Manifold-Index Model and the MANOR estimator for vector-valued regression on tubular manifold data, achieving intrinsic-dimension rates in polynomial time and sample complexity.
AI.motivation: High-dimensional regression around an unknown m-dimensional manifold suffers from the curse of dimensionality unless both statistical rates and computation scale with intrinsic rather than ambient dimension.
AI.method: Multiscale ANisotropic lOcal Regression (MANOR) estimates tangent planes via multiscale PCA on response-similar neighborhoods that narrow tangentially while retaining full normal fibers, then pools outer products of local slopes.
AI.result: Under a Lipschitz link differential and p >= m, n samples yield O(n^-2/(m+4)) tangent-space error and O(n^-4/(m+4)) integrated squared prediction error (up to log factors), with sample size and compute polynomial in D and p; experiments on curves, surfaces, and Langevin hitting probabilities confirm the rates.
AI.conclusion: Anisotropic multiscale local regression provably and efficiently circumvents the ambient curse of dimensionality in manifold-index regression.

title: Measuring Coherence in Predictive Models
summary: Many sequential decision-making procedures, such as active learning, implicitly assume that a model's current predictions agree with those it expects to make after updating on new data, a property we call coherence. Most models in use do not update by exact conditioning and are not guaranteed to be coherent, which can lead to worse decisions. Yet there is currently no general way to measure incoherence or to tell when it matters. We develop tools to measure incoherence and characterise when it affects decisions. We introduce the incoherence ratio, an MMD-based measure of how far any updating procedure departs from coherence, computed only from the procedure's own predictions and updates, and accompany it with an anytime-valid test of coherence. In Bayesian experimental design, acquisition objectives that are equivalent for coherent models choose different data under every approximate model we study, and the incoherence ratio tracks how far incoherence distorts them. We also introduce action coherence, which captures only the incoherence that changes a decision. What a resulting disagreement costs, however, is determined primarily by predictive accuracy. Sequential decisions depend on how a model updates as well as on what it predicts, so coherence, like accuracy, should be checked rather than assumed.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the incoherence ratio, an anytime-valid coherence test, and action coherence to measure when approximate predictive models disagree with their own future updates.
AI.motivation: Sequential decision procedures like active learning assume models update coherently by exact conditioning, yet approximate models violate coherence without a general way to measure it or assess its decision impact.
AI.method: The authors define the MMD-based incoherence ratio from a model's own predictions and updates, pair it with an anytime-valid test, and define action coherence to isolate incoherence that alters decisions.
AI.result: In Bayesian experimental design, equivalent acquisition objectives select different data under every tested approximate model, with distortion tracked by the incoherence ratio, while the cost of disagreement depends primarily on predictive accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Because sequential decisions depend on how a model updates as well as what it predicts, coherence should be explicitly measured and tested rather than assumed.

title: Generalized Prediction Set with Bandit Feedback
summary: In high-stakes environments where uncertainties abound, set-valued prediction offers a cautious and robust mechanism by presenting multiple potential labels as the prediction for each test instance to mitigate the potential risk associated with prediction errors. Yet, integrating this paradigm with out-of-distribution (OOD) detection remains scarcely explored in such settings as online learning with bandit feedback. The bandit feedback mechanism informs the learner about the correctness of the pulled arm/action instead of the explicit ground truth label, leaving the true class label unknown when an incorrect action is taken. To address this challenge, we introduce BanditGPS which conducts set-valued prediction with OOD detection in the bandit feedback setting, using an estimation to the ground truth of class labels. BanditGPS achieves three objectives: render small/informative prediction sets, enhance the OOD detection performance, and control the recall for all normal classes to meet prescribed requirements. Our approach is characterized by the loss function, which trades off between high OOD detection and small prediction sets. Theoretically, we prove that the convergence rate of the regret is $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(T^{-1/2})$. The empirical results further show that BanditGPS effectively controls the recalls with promising performances on OOD detection and informative prediction.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces BanditGPS, an online set-valued prediction framework with out-of-distribution (OOD) detection under bandit feedback.
AI.motivation: High-stakes online learning with bandit feedback only reveals whether a pulled arm was correct rather than the true class label, making it difficult to combine informative prediction sets, OOD detection, and class-wise recall control.
AI.method: BanditGPS estimates ground-truth class labels from bandit feedback and optimizes a loss function that trades off small prediction sets against high OOD detection while enforcing prescribed recall constraints across normal classes.
AI.result: Theoretically, BanditGPS achieves an O_tilde(T^-1/2) regret convergence rate, and empirical results confirm effective recall control alongside strong OOD detection and informative prediction sets.
AI.conclusion: Estimating class labels from bandit feedback within a constrained trade-off loss enables reliable set-valued prediction and OOD detection in online environments.

title: High-dimensional transfer learning with unaligned ordinal responses
summary: In this work, we study high-dimensional transfer learning with unaligned ordinal responses, allowing different domain-specific regression coefficients, cumulative links and thresholds. We develop the sample-split and full-target algorithms that pool source and target likelihoods and then estimate a target correction. Under suitable conditions, our algorithms achieve minimax-optimal rates for parameter estimation and excess risk. Simulations favor the full-target algorithm over the sample-split algorithm for finite-sample estimation and prediction. An application to a medical dataset further demonstrates the predictive gains of our full-target algorithm over the target-only and pooled baselines when transferring information from the five-category source data to binary hospital mortality.

AI.tldr: This paper develops minimax-optimal transfer learning algorithms for high-dimensional ordinal regression with unaligned responses, differing coefficients, and domain-specific thresholds.
AI.motivation: Transferring knowledge across ordinal response datasets is challenging when source and target domains have unaligned categories, different cumulative links, and distinct regression parameters.
AI.method: The authors propose sample-split and full-target algorithms that pool source and target likelihoods before estimating a target-specific correction.
AI.result: Both algorithms achieve minimax-optimal rates for parameter estimation and excess risk; simulations favor the full-target algorithm in finite samples, and transferring 5-category source data to binary hospital mortality improves prediction over target-only and pooled baselines.
AI.conclusion: Likelihood pooling with target correction enables minimax-optimal high-dimensional transfer learning even when ordinal response scales are unaligned across domains.

title: The Limits of Closed-Form Couplings for Few-Step Generation
summary: Few-step generators via flow models require complicated technical solutions such as a pretrained flow model or a consistency loss. While rectified flows have gained popularity for their success in few-step sampling, they pay a cost of needing a pre-trained model and sampling a large number of couplings per dataset. Yet for a finite dataset and a Gaussian probability path, the probability-flow vector field of the empirical distribution is available in closed form, so one could use this field as the teacher and skip pretraining altogether. We demonstrate that, surprisingly, this approach is impossible for problems of practical relevance. In particular, the analytic solution of the diffusion process in high dimensions becomes almost a linear transformation. The integration returns the noise vector drawn at initialisation, plus a drift that is empirically a faint copy of the data point, almost independent of the noise. The coupling therefore differs from an independent pairing only through this drift. As a result, training a model on these couplings is almost equivalent to training the model on the independent draws of the noise and the data, which does not provide a useful teacher. We highlight that this is the direct consequence of the high-dimensionality of the data, and that for low enough dimensions or large enough datasets, analytic couplings become more efficient teachers. We quantify this effect by the fraction of endpoint energy carried by the drift, which scales as $\frac{\log N}{d}$ for a dataset of size $N$ in a $d$-dimensional space. Finally, we provide an empirical study confirming all the theoretical results presented in the paper.

AI.tldr: This paper proves that using the closed-form empirical probability-flow vector field as a teacher for few-step flow models fails in high dimensions because the resulting couplings degenerate to near-independent pairings.
AI.motivation: Because the probability-flow ODE of an empirical dataset under a Gaussian path has a closed-form vector field, it could in principle replace expensive pretrained teachers in rectified-flow distillation.
AI.method: The authors analyze the high-dimensional analytic diffusion solution and quantify the drift energy fraction carried by the empirical coupling as a function of dataset size N and dimension d.
AI.result: In high dimensions, the integration returns initial noise plus a faint data drift whose energy fraction scales as (log N)/d, making training on empirical couplings nearly equivalent to training on independent noise-data pairs, as confirmed empirically.
AI.conclusion: Closed-form empirical couplings cannot serve as useful few-step teachers unless d is small or N is exponentially large, explaining why pretrained teachers or consistency losses remain necessary.

title: Compressed Simulation-Based Inference: Neural Posterior Estimation for Massive Data via Low-Dimensional Sketches
summary: Neural posterior estimation (NPE) is a popular Bayesian simulation-based inference (SBI) approach that uses neural networks trained on simulated data--parameter pairs to approximate the posterior given a user-chosen prior. For high-dimensional observations, NPE methods typically approximate the conditional density of the parameter given a user-chosen or learned summary statistic, rather than the entire dataset, due to the curse of dimensionality. However, both approaches face challenges: hand-crafting good summaries for complex models requires considerable effort from scientists, while learning them from massive datasets can be prohibitively computationally expensive. To address these challenges, we propose approximating the conditional density of a parameter given low-dimensional sketches of the data. We show that, for a model with a $p$-dimensional parameter, only $2p+1$ random sketches are needed for posterior consistency. We compare with state-of-the-art embedding networks for NPE, and we find that our method \emph{matches} the best embedding network's performance while \emph{increasing computational efficiency}.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes compressed neural posterior estimation (NPE) using 2p + 1 random low-dimensional data sketches, matching state-of-the-art embedding networks with higher computational efficiency.
AI.motivation: For massive high-dimensional datasets in simulation-based inference, hand-crafting summary statistics is labor-intensive while learning neural embedding networks is computationally expensive.
AI.method: The authors approximate the parameter posterior conditioned on random low-dimensional sketches of the data rather than learned or hand-crafted summaries.
AI.result: They prove that 2p + 1 random sketches suffice for posterior consistency in a p-dimensional parameter model, and experiments show the method matches top NPE embedding networks while improving computational efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Low-dimensional random sketches provide a theoretically grounded, computationally cheap alternative to learned summary networks in neural posterior estimation.

title: Comments on "Deep Fréchet Regression"
comment: Comment on arXiv:2407.21407 ("Deep Fréchet Regression"). This discussion comment will appear in the Journal of the American Statistical Association (JASA)
summary: We discuss the Journal of the American Statistical Association (JASA) discussion paper "Deep Fréchet Regression" and explore an alternative perspective based on conditional flow matching. We propose learning covariate-dependent transport directly within the response space, avoiding separate manifold learning and reverse mapping. This perspective offers a potentially more flexible framework for incorporating geometric structure and modeling full conditional distributions.

AI.tldr: This commentary on "Deep Frechet Regression" proposes an alternative conditional flow matching perspective that learns covariate-dependent transport directly in the response space.
AI.motivation: Separate manifold learning and reverse mapping steps in Deep Frechet Regression may limit flexibility when modeling geometric structure and full conditional distributions.
AI.method: The authors outline learning covariate-dependent transport directly within the response space via conditional flow matching.
AI.result: As a commentary paper, it presents no new experiments and instead frames conditional flow matching as an alternative to separate manifold learning and reverse mapping.
AI.conclusion: Direct response-space conditional flow matching offers a flexible geometric alternative for modeling full conditional distributions in Frechet regression settings.

title: Generative Data Augmentation Without External Data: An Empirical and Theoretical Study on Deep Networks
summary: Generative data augmentation adds samples from generative models to a classifier's training set. Many influential studies use generators pre-trained on large external datasets, and so mix the value of synthetic data with knowledge transferred through pretraining. We study the case without external data, where each generator learns only from the classifier's own training set, and ask when and why adding generated samples to that training set raises or lowers the classifier's test accuracy. We train classifiers with four backbones on six datasets, two of them medical, adding samples from four generators. We bound the excess risk of a classifier trained with synthetic data, that is, how far its population risk can lie above the minimum risk within its hypothesis class. The bound charges synthetic data for the total variation distance between the real and generated distributions and credits synthetic data for a larger training set. The gain from adding synthetic data, the fall in population risk, is at most the excess risk of the real-only classifier, which trains on the real images alone. Read through the bound, the experiments suggest that synthetic data help most when our classifiers detect only a small discrepancy between the generated and real data and the real-only classifier has room to improve, and that synthetic data help little or hurt when the detected discrepancy is large. Generators with a larger lower bound on the total variation distance, a bound that we estimate from our own classifiers, tend to help less on five of the six datasets, and on the CIFAR datasets the most accurate backbone gains the least. The bound gives these directions but not the size of the largest gains, most of which traditional augmentation also reaches at the same number of optimizer steps.

AI.tldr: This empirical and theoretical study characterizes when generative data augmentation without external data helps or hurts classifier accuracy, showing gains depend on total variation distance and real-only excess risk.
AI.motivation: Prior studies of generative data augmentation often use externally pre-trained generators, conflating the value of synthetic samples with external pretraining knowledge.
AI.method: The authors train four classifier backbones on six datasets (including two medical datasets) augmented by four generators trained solely on each classifier's own training set, and derive an excess-risk bound charging synthetic data for total variation (TV) distance to real data.
AI.result: Synthetic data help most when classifier-estimated TV lower bounds are small and real-only excess risk has room to improve, and help little or hurt when discrepancy is large; on five of six datasets larger TV bounds yield smaller gains, and traditional augmentation matches most of the largest gains at equal optimizer steps.
AI.conclusion: Without external pretraining, generative augmentation is bounded by real-only excess risk and generator-real TV discrepancy, rarely surpassing well-tuned traditional augmentation.

title: ONAM: Fitting Orthogonal Neural Additive Models for Post-Hoc Interpretability of Black-Box Predictions
summary: Modern machine learning models, such as artificial neural networks, achieve high predictive performance through increasingly complex black-box architectures, limiting their use in settings where transparency, interpretability, and fairness are required. Here we present the R package ONAM, which provides a novel and practical implementation of functional decomposition, a technique to facilitate the interpretability of black-box models through structured effect representations. ONAM implements an algorithmic framework for the post-hoc decomposition of predictions into components associated with different input features. The package is designed for usability and efficiency, including functionalities for visualization as well as quantitative measures to assess interpretability. As a model-agnostic method, it can be applied to a wide range of prediction models. We describe the mathematical foundations, algorithmic design, and software architecture of ONAM. A central result of the proposed methodology is that the resulting decomposition satisfies the condition of hierarchical orthogonality, thereby guaranteeing that all components are identifiable and uniquely defined.

AI.tldr: ONAM is an R package that implements Orthogonal Neural Additive Models for post-hoc functional decomposition and interpretability of black-box prediction models.
AI.motivation: Complex black-box machine learning models achieve high accuracy but lack transparency, interpretability, and fairness.
AI.method: ONAM provides a model-agnostic algorithmic framework for post-hoc functional decomposition into feature-associated components satisfying hierarchical orthogonality, along with visualization and quantitative interpretability tools.
AI.result: The resulting decomposition is proven to satisfy hierarchical orthogonality, guaranteeing that all components are identifiable and uniquely defined.
AI.conclusion: ONAM offers a practical, mathematically grounded R software tool for unique post-hoc interpretation of black-box predictions.

title: Stagewise Adaptive Boosting
summary: Stagewise algorithms and sparsity-inducing regularization are two influential approaches to high-dimensional modeling. Existing stagewise theory, however, largely centers on convex regularization, whereas stronger sparsity and other structural preferences are often pursued through fixed-level nonconvex optimization rather than generating an entire adaptive solution path. We develop stagewise adaptive boosting, a general framework that builds a monotone path by selecting the update consistent with structural preference. The framework can encourage sparsity along the path itself and also admits extensions that promote other properties of the solution, including group selection, similarity across models for multiple outcomes, and known priorities or prerequisite relations among predictors. We study its theoretical property as well as finite sample performance using simulations and real-data analyses. Across these studies, the proposed pathwise approach often achieves predictive performance comparable to commonly used baselines while selecting substantially smaller models. These results suggest that adaptive stagewise learning provides a practical route to stronger sparsity and richer structural control without repeatedly solving separate weighted or nonconvex optimization problems.

AI.tldr: Stagewise adaptive boosting is a general framework that constructs a monotone solution path aligned with structural preferences such as sparsity, group selection, and predictor priorities.
AI.motivation: Existing stagewise theory focuses on convex regularization, whereas stronger sparsity and structural preferences typically require solving separate fixed-level nonconvex optimizations rather than generating an adaptive path.
AI.method: The framework builds a monotone path by selecting updates consistent with structural preferences, supporting sparsity, group selection, multi-outcome similarity, and predictor prerequisite relations.
AI.result: Theoretical analysis, simulations, and real-data studies show the pathwise approach achieves predictive performance comparable to standard baselines while selecting substantially smaller models.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive stagewise learning provides a practical pathwise alternative to repeated nonconvex optimization for achieving stronger sparsity and structural control.

title: Setting Optimal Reserve Prices using Fine-Tuned Language Models
summary: Online auction houses must set reserve prices for highly differentiated products whose unstructured descriptions contain valuable demand information. Existing approaches generally require managers to specify product attributes in advance. We ask whether a language model can instead learn from listing descriptions and historical bids to set item-specific reserve prices before bidding begins. We fine-tune a pretrained text embedding language model using the structural likelihood of auction bids as its training objective. This directs representation learning toward the valuation distribution that determines the reserve decision. We show that consecutive upper bids identify the tail information needed to set an optimal reserve without observing or modeling the number of potential bidders. A split-sample estimator learns the representation on one half of the data and conducts structural estimation and inference conditional on that representation on the other. We apply the method to approximately 65,800 online used-vehicle auctions. With seller values calibrated to match the sale rate among listings, the model implies a counterfactual net increase of $165.8 million, representing a 14.6% increase above the incumbent reserve policy. The framework translates a listing description and a seller's value into an item-specific reserve recommendation without constructing a product taxonomy or requiring a bid history for the item being priced. It provides an approach to adapting language models for operational decisions in marketplaces where products are heterogeneous and demand-relevant information is recorded in text.

AI.tldr: This paper fine-tunes a pretrained text embedding language model on auction bid likelihoods to set item-specific reserve prices from unstructured product descriptions.
AI.motivation: Online auction houses must set reserve prices for differentiated products with unstructured text descriptions, whereas existing methods require pre-specified product attributes.
AI.method: The authors fine-tune a text embedding model using the structural likelihood of consecutive upper auction bids, combined with a split-sample estimator for representation learning and structural inference without observing bidder counts.
AI.result: Applied to about 65,800 online used-vehicle auctions, the model implies a counterfactual net increase of $165.8 million, or 14.6% above the incumbent reserve policy.
AI.conclusion: Structural likelihood fine-tuning adapts language models to make item-specific operational pricing decisions directly from listing text.

title: HeteroWear: Sensor-Aware Self-Supervised Learning for Heterogeneous Wearable Activity Recognition
comment: Extended version of a paper accepted at IEEE BigData 2026. Code: this https URL
summary: Self-supervised learning for wearable sensing is usually confined to a single dataset or device family, leaving open whether representations transfer across heterogeneous sensor configurations and whether gains come from pretraining rather than architecture or richer sensor input. We present HeteroWear, a sensor-aware self-supervised framework pretrained on an eight-dataset wearable corpus (173 subjects, 358,261 windows) spanning inertial and physiological signals across body locations, devices, and sampling rates. HeteroWear separates within-sensor temporal modeling from cross-sensor relational modeling using sensor-context embeddings, temporal and cross-sensor Transformers, and latent cross-attention fusion. Training combines structured sensor dropout, cross-configuration consistency, and per-axis masked sensor modeling; missing sensors are omitted rather than reconstructed. Under leave-one-dataset-out pretraining and subject-disjoint evaluation on PAMAP2, WISDM, HHAR, HARTH, and UCI-HAR, HeteroWear improves mean macro-F1 from 0.688 to 0.724 over the identical architecture trained from scratch, with the largest gain on HHAR (0.823 versus 0.741), and achieves the highest macro-F1 on four of five benchmarks relative to single-accelerometer supervised baselines. Held-out-device evaluation yields a mean +0.066 macro-F1 improvement. Under 50% test-time channel removal, HeteroWear retains 73.8% of full-channel performance versus 64.1% for the same architecture trained from scratch without sensor dropout. Ablations show that structured sensor dropout primarily drives robustness, while cross-configuration consistency and sensor-context encoding contribute to transfer.

AI.tldr: HeteroWear is a sensor-aware self-supervised learning framework pretrained on eight wearable datasets that improves activity recognition transfer and robustness across heterogeneous sensor setups.
AI.motivation: Wearable self-supervised learning is typically limited to single datasets or device families, leaving cross-configuration transfer and the true source of pretraining gains unclear.
AI.method: Pretrained on 173 subjects and 358,261 windows, HeteroWear separates within-sensor temporal modeling from cross-sensor relational modeling using sensor-context embeddings, dual Transformers, latent cross-attention fusion, structured sensor dropout, cross-configuration consistency, and per-axis masked modeling.
AI.result: Under leave-one-dataset-out evaluation on PAMAP2, WISDM, HHAR, HARTH, and UCI-HAR, HeteroWear raises mean macro-F1 from 0.688 to 0.724 over training from scratch, gains +0.066 macro-F1 on held-out devices, and retains 73.8% performance under 50% channel removal versus 64.1% without pretraining.
AI.conclusion: Separating temporal and relational modeling with structured sensor dropout enables effective self-supervised transfer and missing-channel robustness across heterogeneous wearables.

title: Log-optimal two-sample testing by betting
summary: For each standard Borel observation space, we construct a single anytime-valid two-sample procedure that is asymptotically log-optimal for every pair of unknown probability laws and every limiting ratio of diverging sample sizes, including zero and infinity. For independent balanced pairs, the optimal log-wealth rate is $2\JS(P,Q)$, where $\JS$ is the Jensen--Shannon divergence. Unequal sizes yield weighted Jensen--Shannon information and the one-sample limit $\log W(n_1,n_2)/n_2\to\KL(Q\|P)$ when $n_1/n_2\to\infty$. Refining finite partitions and logarithmic-loss learning with measurable characteristic kernels provide universal constructions. Our main contribution is the generality of our construction, and its connections to classical batch efficiency notions. Practical implementations allow continuous classifier fine-tuning, as demonstrated on finite alphabets, Gaussian data, and handwritten digits.

AI.tldr: This paper constructs an anytime-valid two-sample test by betting that is asymptotically log-optimal for any unknown probability laws and any limiting sample-size ratio on standard Borel spaces.
AI.motivation: Existing two-sample testing procedures lack a single anytime-valid construction that achieves asymptotic log-optimality universally across all distributions and sample-size ratios, including zero and infinity.
AI.method: The authors use refining finite partitions and logarithmic-loss learning with measurable characteristic kernels to build a universal betting-based test, connecting it to classical batch efficiency notions.
AI.result: For balanced pairs the optimal log-wealth rate is 2 JS(P, Q), while unequal sizes yield weighted Jensen-Shannon information and the one-sample KL(Q||P) limit; practical implementations with continuous classifier fine-tuning are demonstrated on finite alphabets, Gaussian data, and handwritten digits.
AI.conclusion: Universal betting with characteristic kernels or refining partitions unifies anytime-valid two-sample testing with asymptotic log-optimality.

title: Mean-field Token Steering
summary: We consider stochastic token steering through a deep stack of transformer layers as a mean-field control problem for an interacting particle system on the unit sphere, where interactions arise from the attention mechanism. In the mean-field limit, the token population evolves via a controlled integro-partial differential equation where the feedback control acts as a corrective vector field guiding the population toward an aggregate configuration of tokens in the representation space. We deduce the minimum effort control to accomplish this task over a fixed time horizon interpreted as normalized layer depth. We show that the resulting controlled dynamics for the token population can be understood as a mean-field Schrödinger bridge adapted to the sphere geometry. Building on this, we propose a novel generalization of the dynamic Sinkhorn recursion to compute the consistent token evolution. Numerical experiments confirm that the proposed approach achieves exact steering of the token population.

AI.tldr: This paper formulates stochastic token steering in deep transformers as a mean-field control problem on the unit sphere, solved via a generalized dynamic Sinkhorn recursion.
AI.motivation: Understanding and steering token representations through deep transformer layers requires modeling interacting particle dynamics induced by attention.
AI.method: In the mean-field limit, token populations evolve via a controlled integro-PDE on the unit sphere; the authors derive the minimum-effort control as a spherical mean-field Schrodinger bridge and propose a generalized dynamic Sinkhorn recursion to compute it.
AI.result: Numerical experiments confirm that the proposed approach achieves exact steering of the token population.
AI.conclusion: Framing transformer token steering as a spherical mean-field Schrodinger bridge provides an exact computational method for guiding representation dynamics.

title: Learning the Average Dose-Response Function with a Right-Censored Treatment
summary: This paper considers estimation and inference for the average dose-response function under right-censored treatment duration and missing outcomes for censored units. Using the duration lower bounds provided by censored records, we construct a novel multiply robust estimator through augmented local estimating equations. Under suitable regularity conditions, the estimator remains consistent when any two of the outcome regression, treatment density, and censoring survival function are consistently estimated. We establish its convergence rate and asymptotic distribution within a cross-fitting framework under appropriate conditions on nuisance estimation. To address local smoothing bias that can distort confidence interval coverage, we further develop a debiased estimator that supports asymptotically valid pointwise inference without undersmoothing. Under additional uniform conditions, we construct simultaneous confidence bands using a Gaussian multiplier bootstrap. Simulation studies evaluate estimation accuracy, the validity of pointwise and uniform inference, and robustness to nuisance model misspecification. A semi-synthetic study calibrated to NHANES illustrates the proposed methods in a setting with a known dose-response function.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a multiply robust estimator and a debiased inference procedure for the average dose-response function under right-censored treatment duration and missing outcomes.
AI.motivation: Right-censored treatment durations with missing outcomes complicate estimation and valid inference for continuous dose-response functions.
AI.method: Using duration lower bounds from censored records, the authors construct a multiply robust estimator via augmented local estimating equations with cross-fitting, add a debiased estimator for pointwise inference without undersmoothing, and use a Gaussian multiplier bootstrap for simultaneous confidence bands.
AI.result: The estimator is consistent if any two of outcome regression, treatment density, and censoring survival are consistently estimated; simulations and a semi-synthetic NHANES study validate estimation accuracy, coverage, and robustness.
AI.conclusion: Augmented local estimating equations with debiasing enable valid, multiply robust dose-response inference under right-censored treatments.

title: Efficient and Accurate Causal Validation of Training Data Attribution
summary: Causal validation of training data attribution (TDA) methods is costly, since evaluation involves retraining a model on many different subsets of the original training set. For example, the Linear Datamodeling Score (LDS), which has become a standard metric for evaluating TDA methods, measures the correlation between TDA predictions and expected retrained model outputs. In this paper, we reduce the amount of computation needed to estimate the LDS along three axes: the number of sampled training subsets, the number of retraining seeds per subset, and the number of models in the attribution ensemble. Each of these factors induces a form of bias in the LDS estimation, and removing these sources of bias significantly reduces the number of retrainings needed to match the same accuracy in LDS estimation. On ResNet-9/CIFAR-10, finite-subset debiasing achieves $3.2\%$ relative RMSE with as few as $4$ subsets, and $32$ subsets match the accuracy of ordinary Spearman using $96$ subsets, measured against a 300-subset reference. On ResNet-9/CIFAR-10, BERT/QNLI and GPT-2/WikiText-2, estimating the training-noise variance allows us to reproduce the standard five-seed LDS at the same accuracy with $2$--$5\times$ fewer retrainings.

AI.tldr: This paper reduces the retraining cost of computing the Linear Datamodeling Score (LDS) for training data attribution by removing finite-subset, retraining-seed, and ensemble-size biases.
AI.motivation: Causal validation of training data attribution via LDS is computationally expensive because it requires retraining models on many training subsets and random seeds.
AI.method: The authors identify and debias three sources of estimation bias in LDS: finite numbers of sampled training subsets, limited retraining seeds per subset, and finite attribution ensemble sizes.
AI.result: On ResNet-9/CIFAR-10, finite-subset debiasing achieves 3.2% relative RMSE with 4 subsets and matches 96-subset ordinary Spearman accuracy using 32 subsets; across ResNet-9/CIFAR-10, BERT/QNLI, and GPT-2/WikiText-2, noise-variance estimation reproduces 5-seed LDS with 2-5x fewer retrainings.
AI.conclusion: Debiasing LDS estimators substantially cuts the retraining budget required for accurate causal validation of training data attribution.

title: Interpreting Random Forests: Comparing Surrogate Models and Rule Extraction Methods
summary: Random forests (RFs) often achieve high prediction performance, but their ensemble structure can be difficult to interpret. Surrogate models and rule extraction methods offer interpretable approximations, yet guidance on selecting an appropriate method for a specific research question remains limited. We compared 12 methods for interpreting RFs, with a decision tree as a prediction-oriented reference, across 11 simulation settings and 67 benchmark datasets for regression and classification. Evaluation addressed prediction and structural similarity to the RF, model complexity, prediction performance, and runtime. Simulations additionally assessed explainability using known effect and noise variables. No method performed best across all objectives. For regression, SLIM provided the strongest general performance for prediction similarity or performance on test data, while a linear model offered a simpler global interpretation of linear effects when performance was comparable. For classification, inTrees achieved the strongest overall benchmark performance, with CTree and OC-CART providing useful alternatives. ART consistently produced the most compact representations. NH and SIRUS offered strong structural similarity for regression, while MRT most closely reproduced RF variable usage in the classification simulations, illustrating that prediction-oriented rankings do not necessarily identify the best structural explanation. Outcome-type restrictions, runtime limits, and method-specific failures reduced result availability for several approaches and should be considered alongside performance when selecting a method. Method selection should therefore be guided by the outcome type, anticipated data structure, and intended interpretability objective. Prediction similarity alone is insufficient for explaining an RF and should be considered jointly with structural similarity and model complexity.

AI.tldr: This study benchmarks 12 surrogate and rule-extraction methods for interpreting random forests across 11 simulations and 67 datasets, finding that no single method excels at all objectives.
AI.motivation: Guidance on choosing among surrogate models and rule-extraction methods for interpreting random forests remains limited.
AI.method: The authors compare 12 interpretation methods against a decision tree reference on prediction similarity, structural similarity, complexity, prediction performance, runtime, and simulation-based explainability across regression and classification tasks.
AI.result: For regression, SLIM led in prediction similarity and test performance while NH and SIRUS excelled in structural similarity; for classification, inTrees led overall benchmark performance, ART produced the most compact representations, and MRT best matched variable usage.
AI.conclusion: Selecting a random forest interpreter requires matching the method to outcome type, data structure, and interpretability goals rather than relying on prediction similarity alone.

title: Over-the-Air Semantic Alignment via Dual Stacked Intelligent Metasurfaces
summary: Semantic communications enable task-oriented information exchange, but suffer from latent-space mismatch when transmitter and receiver employ heterogeneous machine learning models. Existing semantic alignment methods rely on digital processing, introducing computational and latency overhead. This paper proposes a dual stacked intelligent metasurfaces (dual-SIM) architecture that performs semantic alignment entirely in the wave domain. By jointly exploiting programmable metasurfaces at both ends of a link and the wireless channel, the proposed architecture realizes an end-to-end linear transformation between heterogeneous latent spaces. We show phase-only multilayer SIM can approximate both supervised linear aligners and zero-shot Parseval-frame equalizers. We investigate single-SIM, disjoint asymmetric and symmetric dual-SIM, and jointly optimized dual-SIM configurations, considering channel equalization and constructive channel exploitation. For joint design, we develop an alternating projected gradient algorithm with convergence guarantees to first-order stationary points. We further introduce a deep-unrolled network that unrolls gradient-based iterations to reduce computational cost of SIM reconfiguration under channel variations. Numerical results with heterogeneous vision transformer encoders show accurate semantic alignment from moderate to high signal-to-noise ratios. The joint and symmetric disjoint dual-SIM designs achieve the highest accuracy over compact channels, the joint design leads at shallow stack depths, and the advantage over single-SIM designs diminishes at equal depth.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a dual stacked intelligent metasurfaces (dual-SIM) architecture that performs semantic alignment between heterogeneous ML models entirely in the wave domain.
AI.motivation: Existing semantic alignment methods for heterogeneous transmitter-receiver models rely on digital processing, adding computational and latency overhead.
AI.method: Dual-SIM uses programmable metasurfaces at both link ends and the wireless channel to realize end-to-end linear transformations, optimized via an alternating projected gradient algorithm and a deep-unrolled network for fast reconfiguration.
AI.result: Simulations with heterogeneous vision transformer encoders show accurate semantic alignment at moderate-to-high SNR, with joint and symmetric disjoint dual-SIM leading over compact channels and joint design leading at shallow stack depths.
AI.conclusion: Wave-domain dual-SIM architectures eliminate digital alignment overhead while achieving accurate cross-model semantic communication.

title: Bellman Residual Bracketing: Resolving the Sample Complexity of Discounted and Average-Reward RL
summary: We study the sample complexity of the empirical planning or plug-in approach for reinforcement learning (RL) with a generative model. We show the discounted plug-in approach finds an $\varepsilon$-optimal policy with $O(SA (1-\gamma)^{-3} \varepsilon^{-2} \log(SA/\delta))$ samples, where $S, A, \gamma, \delta$ are the state and action sizes, discount factor, and failure probability, respectively. In the average-reward setting, we show that discounted plug-in and direct (undiscounted) plug-in achieve $O(SAH\varepsilon^{-2}\log(SA/\delta))$ and $O(SAD\varepsilon^{-2}\log(SA/\delta))$ complexities, respectively, where $H$ upper-bounds the optimal bias span and $D$ is the diameter. Combining with our lower bounds for nonadaptive generative models, these results resolve the minimax sample complexity of discounted RL and average-reward RL --- in both the span- and diameter-based classes --- up to constant factors. Our main technical contribution is a novel Bellman residual bracketing technique which improves the efficiency of prior absorbing-MDP-based concentration analyses.

AI.tldr: This paper resolves the minimax sample complexity of discounted and average-reward reinforcement learning with a generative model up to constant factors using Bellman residual bracketing.
AI.motivation: Prior absorbing-MDP concentration analyses for plug-in RL with a generative model left gaps in tightness across discounted and average-reward settings.
AI.method: The authors introduce Bellman residual bracketing to tighten concentration bounds for empirical planning (plug-in) in both discounted and average-reward MDPs, complemented by lower bounds for nonadaptive generative models.
AI.result: Discounted plug-in achieves O(SA (1-gamma)^{-3} epsilon^{-2} log(SA/delta)) samples, while discounted and direct plug-in achieve O(SAH epsilon^{-2} log(SA/delta)) and O(SAD epsilon^{-2} log(SA/delta)) in average-reward RL, matching lower bounds up to constants.
AI.conclusion: Bellman residual bracketing settles the minimax sample complexity of plug-in generative-model RL in both discounted and span/diameter average-reward classes.

title: Certified Algorithms for Gaussian Location Mixture NPMLEs via Discretized Gradient Flows
summary: We study the computation of approximate nonparametric maximum likelihood estimators (NPMLEs) for Gaussian location mixtures in arbitrary dimension $d\ge 1$ via the Fisher-Rao gradient flow. We provide a certified algorithm based on an entropic proximal discretization of the flow which, given a sufficiently small $\varepsilon > 0$, returns an absolutely continuous mixing measure $\tilde\mu$ admitting an exact finite-dimensional representation and satisfying $\hat L_n-L_n(f_{\tilde\mu})\le\varepsilon$. For almost every dataset $X_1,\cdots, X_n \in \mathbb{R}^d$ satisfying $n>2(d+1)(m+1)^2$, where $m$ is the number of support points of the NPMLE, the algorithm requires $O(n\varepsilon^{-1}\log^{d+2}(1/\varepsilon))$ time. En route, we also establish results on the well-posedness and convergence properties of the continuous-time Fisher--Rao flow. In particular, initializing the flow at the uniform probability measure on a ball containing the convex hull of the observations, we show that $\hat L_n-L_n(f_{\mu_t})=O(\log t/t)$. We also establish that, for almost every dataset satisfying the same condition on $n$ as above, the set of global maxima of the optimal score is the same as the support of the NPMLE, and the Hessian of the optimal score is nondegenerate at these points, extending a result of (Polyanskiy-Sellke, 2025) to higher dimensions.

AI.tldr: This paper provides a certified algorithm for computing Gaussian location mixture NPMLEs in arbitrary dimension via an entropic proximal discretization of the Fisher-Rao gradient flow.
AI.motivation: Computing nonparametric maximum likelihood estimators (NPMLEs) for Gaussian location mixtures in higher dimensions lacks certified polynomial-time-in-epsilon algorithms and continuous-time convergence guarantees.
AI.method: The authors discretize the Fisher-Rao gradient flow using an entropic proximal scheme, returning an absolutely continuous mixing measure with an exact finite-dimensional representation, and analyze the continuous-time flow initialized uniformly on a ball.
AI.result: For almost every dataset with n > 2(d+1)(m+1)^2, the algorithm achieves epsilon-optimality in O(n epsilon^{-1} log^{d+2}(1/epsilon)) time; continuous-time flow converges at O(log t / t), and optimal score maxima match the NPMLE support with nondegenerate Hessians.
AI.conclusion: Discretized Fisher-Rao gradient flows yield certified, dimension-general algorithms for Gaussian location mixture NPMLEs.

title: Weighted conformal prediction under covariate shift: process limits, estimated weights and efficiency
summary: Weighted split conformal prediction handles covariate shift by reweighting calibration scores with the likelihood ratio $v=dQ_X/dP_X$; its training-conditional coverage is a functional of the self-normalized weighted empirical distribution function $\hat F_m$, and we study the process $\sqrt m(\hat F_m-F_Q)$. It converges in $\ell^\infty$ to the Gaussian process $W(G(t))-F_Q(t)W(K^2)$, with $G(t)=\mathbb{E}_Q[v\mathbf{1}\{S\le t\}]$ and $K^2=1+\chi^2(Q\|P)$, if and only if $\chi^2(Q\|P)<\infty$ (for non-degenerate scores); $\sup v$ plays no role. The limit gives the joint law of the coverage across levels, consistent bootstraps, inflations asymptotically exact uniformly in the level, and Berry-Esseen-type rates. With estimated ratios, a uniform expansion remains valid when the estimate uses the calibration covariates; the estimation error enters through a covariance term that can reduce the variance below the oracle's, and a pairs bootstrap reproduces it. When the ratio is known, the weighted conformal threshold is semiparametrically efficient if and only if the ratio and the coverage indicator are uncorrelated under the test distribution, with an explicit efficient correction otherwise. When $\chi^2(Q\|P)=\infty$, the ratio has a regularly varying tail of index $p\in(1,2)$ and the score decouples from it in the far tail, the finite-dimensional limits are $p$-stable at the rate $m^{1-1/p}$ up to a slowly varying factor.

AI.tldr: This paper characterizes the asymptotic process limits, bootstrap validity, and semiparametric efficiency of weighted split conformal prediction under covariate shift.
AI.motivation: The finite-sample and asymptotic behavior of training-conditional coverage in weighted split conformal prediction, especially with estimated likelihood ratios or unbounded chi-squared divergence, is not fully understood.
AI.method: The authors study the self-normalized weighted empirical process sqrt(m)(F_hat_m - F_Q), deriving its l^infty Gaussian process limit, uniform expansions for estimated ratios, semiparametric efficiency conditions, and p-stable limits when chi^2(Q||P) is infinite.
AI.result: Convergence to the Gaussian limit holds if and only if chi^2(Q||P) < infinity; estimating ratios from calibration covariates can reduce variance below the oracle, and known-ratio thresholds are efficient if and only if the ratio and coverage indicator are uncorrelated under Q.
AI.conclusion: Chi-squared divergence governs the asymptotic regime of weighted conformal prediction, with estimated weights offering potential efficiency gains.

title: Does Learning Order Explain Forgetting? The Lie Bracket as an Early-Warning Signal for Catastrophic Forgetting Without Old Data
comment: 14 pages, 4 figures. Code and results: this https URL
summary: A network trained on task A and then task B ends at different weights than one trained on B and then A. To leading order this gap is set by the Lie bracket of the two tasks' gradient fields, and Dherin (2023) conjectured that a non-vanishing bracket may be linked to catastrophic forgetting. I test this conjecture empirically. Across Split MNIST, Split Fashion-MNIST and Split CIFAR-10, the forgetting of A is almost exactly the difference in A's loss between the two training orders (Spearman rho = 0.96-1.00). I then ask whether the bracket can predict that forgetting early in training on B and without any of A's data, using only a small summary stored when A finishes: its gradient and its top 20 Hessian eigenpairs. When the old task is well learned and forgetting is slow (task-incremental), this stored bracket ranks forgetting with rho = 0.70-0.81, against 0.33-0.58 for the penalty of Elastic Weight Consolidation, and matches or exceeds re-evaluating A on its own data. When forgetting is fast (domain-incremental), the stored summary goes stale and the EWC penalty is as good or better. The bracket fails outright when the old task is only half learned; I trace this to a residual gradient on A an order of magnitude larger, which makes first-order (slope) damage matter. The bracket is therefore a useful early-warning signal for the quiet kind of forgetting, under a clear condition.

AI.tldr: This study tests whether the Lie bracket of task gradient fields predicts catastrophic forgetting early in training without access to old-task data.
AI.motivation: Dherin (2023) conjectured that the Lie bracket of two tasks' gradient fields links to catastrophic forgetting, but this had not been tested empirically as a data-free early-warning signal.
AI.method: Using only a stored summary of task A (its gradient and top 20 Hessian eigenpairs) after A finishes, the author evaluates the Lie bracket's ability to rank forgetting of A during early training on task B across Split MNIST, Split Fashion-MNIST, and Split CIFAR-10.
AI.result: Forgetting of A correlates strongly with the two-order loss gap (Spearman rho = 0.96-1.00); in task-incremental settings, the stored bracket ranks forgetting with rho = 0.70-0.81 versus 0.33-0.58 for EWC, though it degrades in fast domain-incremental forgetting or when A is half-learned.
AI.conclusion: The Lie bracket serves as a useful data-free early-warning signal for slow catastrophic forgetting when the prior task is well learned.

title: Decorrelation Before Variable Selection: Left and Right Transforms and Their Trade-Off
