summary: Decorrelation has two forms. A left transform keeps coefficients and changes noise; a right transform keeps noise and changes coefficients. Cholesky whitening alone keeps noise variables inactive when true ones come first; decorrelation preserving coefficients and noise loses information.

AI.tldr: This paper characterizes the trade-off between left and right decorrelation transforms prior to variable selection.
AI.motivation: Decorrelating variables before variable selection alters either the noise structure or the regression coefficients, creating a fundamental trade-off.
AI.method: The authors compare left transforms (which preserve coefficients and alter noise) against right transforms (which preserve noise and alter coefficients), including Cholesky whitening.
AI.result: Cholesky whitening alone keeps noise variables inactive when true variables appear first, whereas any decorrelation that preserves both coefficients and noise loses information.
AI.conclusion: Analysts must choose between preserving coefficients or noise during pre-selection decorrelation, as preserving both incurs information loss.

title: Calibrated Functional Prediction from Overlapping Nonlinear Observations
summary: We study prediction of nonlinear audit functionals from scalar observations of a shared hidden table state. For Schur-rational operators, local Gaussian projections yield a common sparse kernel for overlapping tasks, repeated row identities, and cross-row dependence. Shared-state residual samples extend this kernel through a positive-semidefinite feature representation. Positive matrix integration and sample-value enclosures connect the original inputs to the actual saved hybrid prediction. A sorted calibration-role perturbation bound then certifies its complete finite-pool pinball risk. Independent complete-loss selection chooses the ridge, score scale, and residual weight, while task-rank calibration supplies an upper endpoint. Evaluation uses twenty new reference contexts per dataset at two task sizes, giving 400 conditions across ten benchmark populations. The mean dataset complete-loss ratios are 0.9977 to the degree-two kernel, 0.9961 to matched complete-MC shrinkage, and 0.9911 to the retrospective minimum over 174 public configurations. The last ratio has a paired reference-bootstrap interval of [0.9898,0.9927]. On 40 profiles at coefficient tolerance $10^{-7}$, Gamma quadrature has a geometric mean cold-time ratio of .0646 to strengthened Arb/Petras integration.

AI.tldr: This paper develops calibrated functional prediction for nonlinear audit functionals from overlapping scalar observations of a shared hidden table state, with finite-pool pinball risk certificates.
AI.motivation: Predicting nonlinear audit functionals across overlapping tasks and repeated row identities requires calibrated uncertainty bounds and efficient numerical integration.
AI.method: Local Gaussian projections for Schur-rational operators yield a sparse kernel extended via shared-state residual samples, combined with positive matrix integration, sample-value enclosures, and a sorted calibration-role perturbation bound.
AI.result: Across 400 conditions on ten benchmark populations, mean complete-loss ratios are 0.9977 to the degree-two kernel, 0.9961 to matched complete-MC shrinkage, and 0.9911 (95% CI [0.9898, 0.9927]) to the retrospective minimum over 174 configurations, with Gamma quadrature achieving a 0.0646 cold-time ratio to Arb/Petras integration.
AI.conclusion: Kernel-based functional prediction with calibration-role bounds delivers tight, certified finite-pool risk and fast quadrature.

title: Enhancing Mixed Oil Length Prediction through Graph Representation Learning
summary: During the pipeline transportation of refined oil products, the inevitable formation of mixed oil segments poses considerable economic challenges to pipeline networks. Therefore, it is important to accurately predict the length of these mixed oil segments. Although previous methods have achieved relatively accurate predictions by integrating machine and deep learning algorithms, they ignore the statistical dependencies that remain among real-world mixed oil samples, which degrades model accuracy. To address this issue, we propose a novel Sample Dependencies Incorporated Graph Representation Learning (SDI-GRL) model. By representing samples and pipeline features as nodes of a graph, SDI-GRL connects dependent samples through their shared features, allowing message passing to propagate information across related samples. This graph-based framework allows our model to capture the statistical dependencies among samples absent in prior works. A case study on a mixed oil dataset demonstrates that our SDI-GRL model surpasses the strongest existing approach, reducing both the RMSE and the MAE by more than 10%.

AI.tldr: SDI-GRL is a graph representation learning model that captures statistical dependencies among mixed oil samples to improve mixed oil length prediction in pipelines.
AI.motivation: Existing machine and deep learning methods for mixed oil length prediction ignore statistical dependencies among real-world samples, degrading accuracy.
AI.method: SDI-GRL constructs a graph with samples and pipeline features as nodes, connecting dependent samples through shared features so message passing propagates information across related samples.
AI.result: In a case study on a mixed oil dataset, SDI-GRL outperforms the strongest existing baseline by reducing both RMSE and MAE by more than 10%.
AI.conclusion: Modeling sample dependencies via graph message passing significantly improves mixed oil length prediction.

title: A Convergence Analysis of the Random Feature Method for Linear PDEs
summary: The Random Feature Method (RFM) distinguishes itself among machine learning approaches to partial differential equations (PDEs) through its superior accuracy and computational efficiency. Nevertheless, the theoretical underpinnings of RFM remain incompletely elucidated. This paper provides a comprehensive analysis of RFM within the framework of kernel methods, focusing on two principal aspects: (i) approximation by finitely many random features in Sobolev norms and the PDE residual seminorm, and (ii) estimation over the induced reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) from finitely many noiseless collocation observations. We relate both problems to kernel ridge regression (KRR) and establish upper and lower bounds in terms of the eigenvalues of the associated integral operators under the respective assumptions. Combining the approximation and estimation lower bounds, we establish a lower bound under simultaneous restrictions on the numbers of random features and collocation observations. We further quantify how activation regularity affects these eigenvalues, obtaining algebraic upper bounds for finitely smooth activations and stretched-exponential upper bounds for analytic activations.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes a kernel-method convergence analysis for the Random Feature Method (RFM) on linear PDEs, deriving upper and lower bounds for approximation and estimation.
AI.motivation: Despite RFM's empirical accuracy and efficiency for solving PDEs, its theoretical foundations remain incompletely understood.
AI.method: The authors analyze RFM in terms of kernel ridge regression, studying finite random-feature approximation in Sobolev norms and PDE residual seminorms, RKHS estimation from noiseless collocation points, and eigenvalue decay for finitely smooth versus analytic activations.
AI.result: They establish upper and lower bounds in terms of integral operator eigenvalues, a joint lower bound under simultaneous feature and collocation limits, algebraic decay bounds for finitely smooth activations, and stretched-exponential bounds for analytic activations.
AI.conclusion: Connecting RFM to kernel ridge regression rigorously quantifies how activation smoothness, feature count, and collocation size govern PDE convergence.

title: FARCH: A Functional ARCH Model for Calibrated Prediction Bands
summary: Forecasting a curve, rather than a handful of scalar summaries of it, requires a notion of uncertainty that is itself functional. We propose FARCH, a functional nonlinear autoregressive model with conditional heteroscedasticity, in which the conditional mean and the conditional volatility of the next curve are forecasted jointly and nonparametrically, by reusing a single kernel weighting scheme --- built on a wavelet semi-metric between curves --- first on the curves themselves and then on their squared residuals. From this pair of estimators we derive two constructions of prediction bands: a pointwise band, obtained from marginal scenario quantiles, and a uniform, sup-norm band, calibrated for decisions that concern the entire forecasted path rather than any single instant. Applied to day-ahead forecasting of half-hourly French national electricity demand (1996--2009), and compared, under an identical protocol, against four existing prediction-interval constructions that do not model the conditional variance explicitly, the uniform FARCH band attains pointwise coverage statistically indistinguishable from its nominal target at the 80%, 90% and 95% levels, and a curve-wise coverage of 90.1%, significantly above the 70.8% reached by the best competing method, at the cost of a wider interval. Pointwise bands, in contrast, undercover regardless of whether the variance is modelled explicitly, indicating that state-dependent volatility and simultaneous calibration are two distinct ingredients that a trustworthy prediction band must combine.

AI.tldr: FARCH is a nonparametric functional ARCH model that jointly forecasts conditional mean and volatility curves to construct calibrated pointwise and uniform prediction bands.
AI.motivation: Curve forecasting requires functional uncertainty quantification, yet existing prediction-interval methods often ignore conditional heteroscedasticity or fail to calibrate simultaneously across the entire path.
AI.method: FARCH reuses a single wavelet semi-metric kernel weighting scheme on curves and their squared residuals to forecast conditional mean and volatility, yielding both marginal pointwise bands and uniform sup-norm bands.
AI.result: On day-ahead French national electricity demand (1996-2009), the uniform FARCH band hits nominal 80%, 90%, and 95% pointwise coverage and 90.1% curve-wise coverage versus 70.8% for the best competitor, albeit with wider intervals, while pointwise bands undercover.
AI.conclusion: Combining state-dependent conditional volatility with simultaneous sup-norm calibration is essential for trustworthy functional prediction bands.

title: CONGA: Compiling Gaussian Fiber Geometry for Structured Bayesian Inference
comment: Accepted to the Workshop on Geometric Distributional Deep Learning (GDDL), NeurIPS 2026
summary: In structured Bayesian models, a large latent block is often Gaussian conditional on a smaller set of parameters, yet generic inference methods relearn this geometry during warmup. We study how this structure can be used to construct transports for posterior inference. The conditional mean and precision determine exact affine maps, including symmetric Brenier and triangular Knothe-Rosenblatt maps, that separate a standard normal block from the remaining non-Gaussian core. KL and relative Fisher objectives then reduce to objectives on this core. We introduce CONGA, a compiler that identifies candidate Gaussian blocks and selects a temporal, spectral, or sparse implementation according to their structure and computational cost. Marginalization requires an identity established from the model; numerical evidence alone permits only a target-preserving change of variables, and a failed check leaves the model unchanged. On the Stock-Watson inflation model, CONGA improves minimum ESS per second by 12.5x for NUTS. It also restores convergence where the raw target fails: for WALNUTS on the same model, and for NUTS on a 6760-dimensional electricity load model reduced to 34 core coordinates. Experiments on graph-indexed fields show how coloring and fill affect the choice of map, including cases where retaining the original target is preferable. Code at this https URL

AI.tldr: CONGA is a compiler that exploits conditional Gaussian fiber geometry in structured Bayesian models to construct exact affine transports, accelerating posterior inference.
AI.motivation: Generic Bayesian samplers waste warmup relearning conditional Gaussian geometry present in large latent blocks of structured models.
AI.method: CONGA identifies candidate Gaussian blocks, selects temporal, spectral, or sparse Brenier or Knothe-Rosenblatt maps to separate a standard normal block from the non-Gaussian core, and restricts marginalization to model-verified identities.
AI.result: On the Stock-Watson inflation model, CONGA improves minimum ESS per second by 12.5x for NUTS and restores convergence for WALNUTS, and it restores NUTS convergence on a 6760-dimensional electricity load model reduced to 34 core coordinates.
AI.conclusion: Compiling conditional Gaussian fiber geometry into exact transports substantially speeds up and stabilizes structured Bayesian inference.

title: Summary Sufficiency in Simulation-Based Inference via Mutual Information
summary: Simulation-based inference (SBI) enables posterior estimation when the likelihood is intractable but data can be simulated from the model. For high-dimensional or variable-length data, SBI methods typically rely on low-dimensional summary statistics as conditioning inputs for posterior estimation, making their sufficiency crucial for accurate inference. Mutual information (MI) provides a natural information-theoretic characterization of sufficiency, quantifying how much parameter information a summary retains. However, these MI quantities are generally intractable in likelihood-free settings. Sui et al. (2026) estimate MI from a trained neural posterior using the Barber--Agakov (BA) lower bound, while discussing, but not computing, a Fisher-information upper bound. This makes the estimate ambiguous: a small lower bound may indicate either an insufficient summary or an inaccurate density estimator. We address this limitation with a tractable diagnostic that estimates the BA gap and reveals what the difference between bounds has actually measured. We extend the resulting sufficiency metric to observation-centered restricted data spaces, allowing simulations to focus on a neighborhood of the data while preserving the target posterior and enabling valid sufficiency comparisons between summaries. We illustrate the use of this diagnostic tool on a temporal epidemic-type aftershock sequence model by comparing learned and hand-crafted summary statistics for variable-length earthquake catalogs.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a tractable diagnostic for the Barber-Agakov gap to disambiguate summary sufficiency in simulation-based inference (SBI), extending it to observation-centered neighborhoods.
AI.motivation: Estimating mutual information via the Barber-Agakov (BA) lower bound alone cannot distinguish an insufficient summary statistic from an inaccurate neural density estimator.
AI.method: The authors propose a tractable diagnostic that estimates the BA gap and extend the sufficiency metric to observation-centered restricted data spaces that preserve the target posterior.
AI.result: Applied to a temporal epidemic-type aftershock sequence model, the diagnostic effectively compares learned and hand-crafted summary statistics for variable-length earthquake catalogs.
AI.conclusion: Measuring the BA gap on observation-centered neighborhoods provides an unambiguous way to evaluate summary sufficiency in likelihood-free inference.

title: Anytime-Valid PAC-Bayes Certificates for Adaptive Test-Time Scaling
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. Xiaoyu Li and Jiangxuan Long contributed equally. 31 pages, 7 figures, 15 tables
summary: Test-time scaling systems often choose how much to sample, which prompt to use, and which verifier or aggregation rule to trust after repeatedly inspecting a calibration set. Standard validation error bars are not valid after this adaptive selection. We model a test-time scaling recipe as a randomized predictor with a random cost and prove a time-uniform PAC-Bayes certificate that holds simultaneously over all calibration times, all posterior mixtures over recipes, and all data-dependent stopping rules. Thus the same event covers the recipe search that precedes deployment, not merely the fixed recipe finally reported. For a finite grid of budgets and verifiers, the penalty is the familiar $\log M/n$, which in the worst case no certificate valid after selection can avoid, while non-uniform priors and localized posterior mixtures can give sharper certificates for structured searches. We specialize the result to self-consistency and show a complementary margin law: plurality voting improves exponentially in the sample budget only on examples where the correct answer is the generator's unique mode; otherwise more compute can provably amplify errors. The same margin analysis yields an oracle water-filling law for compute allocation. A synthetic audit quantifies the optimism caused by adaptive budget selection, and a 192-example GSM8K audit using gpt-4.1-mini generations illustrates risk-cost reporting for a real inference pipeline. At scale, with two models on GSM8K and MATH-500, selected-best error bars fall below the out-of-split GSM8K risk in up to 22.5% of random splits at a nominal 5% while the certificate never does, and on the full GSM8K test split it tightens to 0.109 (held-out risk 0.039). The results give a lightweight, distribution-free way to report risk and compute claims for adaptive inference systems.

AI.tldr: This paper proves time-uniform PAC-Bayes certificates for adaptive test-time scaling that remain valid across repeated calibration inspection, recipe selection, and data-dependent stopping.
AI.motivation: Standard validation error bars become invalid when test-time scaling recipes (sample budgets, prompts, verifiers) are adaptively selected on a calibration set.
AI.method: Modeling a scaling recipe as a randomized predictor with random cost, the authors derive an anytime-valid PAC-Bayes certificate over all calibration times and posterior mixtures, plus a margin law and water-filling allocation rule for self-consistency.
AI.result: On GSM8K and MATH-500, naive selected-best error bars fall below out-of-split risk in up to 22.5% of random splits at nominal 5% while the certificate never fails, tightening to 0.109 on full GSM8K (held-out risk 0.039).
AI.conclusion: Time-uniform PAC-Bayes certificates provide distribution-free risk and compute guarantees for adaptive test-time scaling pipelines.

title: The Price of Choosing Examples: Context Overfitting in Adaptive In-Context Learning
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. Xiaoyu Li and Jiangxuan Long contributed equally. 31 pages, 8 figures, 5 tables
summary: In-context learning is usually analyzed as if the examples in the prompt were sampled before the learner is chosen. In deployed systems they are not: examples are retrieved, filtered, re-ranked, edited, and repeatedly tested after seeing the query and the data store. We formalize this gap by treating prompt construction as adaptive data analysis through a conditional stochastic-kernel calculus. Our main quantity is the context capacity, the mutual information or approximate max-information between the data store and the final prompt transcript. For any frozen in-context learner and any adaptive context pipeline with capacity $\kappa$, we prove a finite-sample context generalization bound of order $\sqrt{\kappa/k}$, where $k$ is the number of selected examples whose losses form the reported score. We prove a matching lower bound, whose constant is exact when $\log k\ll\kappa\ll k$, and derive two PAC-Bayesian retrieval rules: a first-order Gibbs rule that charges data-dependent candidate gates their prior mass, and a self-normalized second-order rule. On Banking77 with 64 retrieval recipes and two model families, the certificates hold in all 24,000 resampled selection events, and from 64 (Qwen2.5-7B) or 128 (GPT-4.1-mini) reused validation queries the Gibbs rule certifies a risk below the zero-shot error in over 99% of validation draws. Finally, we instantiate the theory for Bayesian linear in-context regression, including an order-statistics analysis of query-aligned top-$k$ Gaussian retrieval. The results separate context quality from context certification: longer or more relevant contexts improve risk only when the procedure used to choose them is stable enough for selected-context evidence to transfer.

AI.tldr: This paper formalizes context overfitting in adaptive in-context learning via context capacity and proves finite-sample generalization bounds and PAC-Bayesian retrieval rules.
AI.motivation: Deployed in-context learning pipelines adaptively retrieve, filter, and test examples after seeing the query and data store, violating standard non-adaptive prompt-sampling assumptions.
AI.method: Using a conditional stochastic-kernel calculus, the authors define context capacity (mutual or approximate max-information between data store and prompt transcript) and derive first-order Gibbs and second-order self-normalized PAC-Bayesian retrieval rules.
AI.result: They prove a sqrt(kappa/k) generalization bound with a matching lower bound; on Banking77 with 64 retrieval recipes, certificates hold in all 24,000 resampled events and certify risk below zero-shot error in over 99% of draws from 64 (Qwen2.5-7B) or 128 (GPT-4.1-mini) reused queries.
AI.conclusion: Controlling context capacity separates prompt quality from certification, ensuring selected in-context evidence transfers reliably.

title: Dimension-free spectral laws and the risk of spectral filters
summary: Spectral properties of the sample covariance are key to modern machine learning with high-dimensional data. Random matrix theory (RMT) supplies powerful tools; however, most classical results assume proportional asymptotics, where $d/n$ tends to a finite limit. In functional data analysis and kernel methods, a fixed infinite-dimensional Hilbert space is often the more natural setting for the observations, beyond the scope of proportional asymptotics. This calls for a dimension-free spectral theory for i.i.d. observations $\boldsymbol{x}_1, \dots, \boldsymbol{x}_n$ in a Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$ with trace-class population covariance $\Sigma$. Building on the dimension-free ridge regression analysis of Cheng and Montanari (2024), we establish two deterministic equivalents with explicit nonasymptotic error bounds. The first approximates the empirical spectral law $\widehat{\mu}_n$ of the sample Gram matrix by a deterministic law $\mu_n$. The second characterizes the conditional prediction risk of analytic spectral filters in linear regression. Previous sharp approximations to prediction risk in this setting have focused on ridge regression and closely-related problems. Our analysis covers a broader class of filters at the bulk scale, with an explicit user-friendly spectral stability condition to check. We apply our theory to power and critical spectral laws, and we recover the proportional regime. For prediction, we study (negative) ridge estimators, iterated ridge, and gradient flow. Mathematically, building on the idea of stochastic interpolation, we construct a deterministic backward path to interpolate the spectral parameter. The resulting bounds on resolvent and mixed-resolvent traces give mesoscopic approximations to the spectral law within the bulk and, by Cauchy's formula, deterministic equivalents for the prediction variance and squared bias of analytic spectral filters.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes dimension-free deterministic equivalents and nonasymptotic error bounds for sample Gram spectral laws and analytic spectral-filter prediction risks in infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces.
AI.motivation: Classical random matrix theory assumes proportional d/n asymptotics, which fails to capture functional data and kernel methods in fixed infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces.
AI.method: Extending Cheng and Montanari (2024) via a deterministic backward interpolation path and Cauchy's formula, the authors derive mesoscopic resolvent bounds and deterministic equivalents for empirical spectral laws and conditional prediction risks under an explicit spectral stability condition.
AI.result: The theory covers negative ridge, iterated ridge, and gradient flow, applies to power and critical spectral laws, and recovers the proportional regime.
AI.conclusion: Dimension-free backward interpolation extends sharp spectral-risk characterization beyond ridge regression to general analytic spectral filters.

title: Variance-adaptive confidence regions for fixed-benchmark binomial mixtures, with application to LLM evaluation
comment: 27 pages main text plus 57-page supplement. Code: this https URL
summary: We construct confidence intervals for linear functionals $\theta(F_m)=\int h\,dF_m$ of the empirical law $F_m$ of success probabilities $p_1,\dots,p_m$, from independent counts $c_i\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n,p_i)$, as for a language model run $n$ times per problem. Coverage is at least $1-\alpha$ for every $n$, $m$ and fixed $(p_i)$, simultaneously for all bounded $h$. The variance-adaptive (VA) region tests each candidate mixing law with the conditional variance of the tail counts it implies. This variance is linear in the law, so the region is a linear program, and cell envelopes keep it valid off-grid. Regions calibrated for iid sampling target a super-population law and are conservative for $\theta(F_m)$. With all $n$ tail counts, fixed $n$, continuous $h$ and a grid refined as $m\to\infty$, the identification part of VA's width is first-order worst-case optimal, as for any localization with the same index set. Under a rule fixed before the main comparator runs, VA was narrower than a two-stage plug-in band at every $n$ (median width ratio 0.60 at $n=128$), but not than the asymptotic, pointwise AMARI interval at $n=128$; on real rollout pools it was wider than both pointwise and Bonferroni-adjusted AMARI at $n\le128$. For $P(p>0)$ and pass@$k$ with $k\gg n$ the data support only lower bounds.

AI.tldr: This paper constructs variance-adaptive (VA) confidence regions for linear functionals of fixed-benchmark binomial mixtures, with applications to multi-rollout LLM evaluation.
AI.motivation: Confidence intervals calibrated for i.i.d. super-population sampling are conservative for fixed-benchmark empirical laws of success probabilities observed via n binomial counts per problem.
AI.method: The VA region tests candidate mixing laws using the conditional variance of implied tail counts, formulated as a linear program with cell envelopes for off-grid validity.
AI.result: Coverage is at least 1-alpha for all n, m, and fixed (p_i) simultaneously over bounded h; VA is narrower than a two-stage plug-in band at every n (median width ratio 0.60 at n=128) though wider than AMARI on real rollout pools at n<=128, and P(p>0) or pass@k (k>>n) only admit lower bounds.
AI.conclusion: Variance-adaptive linear programming yields finite-sample valid, simultaneous confidence regions tailored to fixed-benchmark LLM evaluations.

title: In-Context Estimation and Prediction for Parametric ODEs
summary: Transformers have demonstrated the ability to perform in-context learning, that is, to adapt to new tasks from a few examples without updating their parameters. Existing theory has largely focused on emulating gradient-based algorithms for convex statistical problems or establishing general function approximation guarantees without exploiting the underlying statistical structure. We study in-context parameter estimation and trajectory prediction for parametric ordinary differential equations (ODEs), where estimation is generally nonconvex. Under suitable identifiability and regularity conditions, we construct a transformer that estimates unknown system parameters from noisy trajectory observations through a two-stage approximate maximum likelihood procedure: a coarse search provides an initialization within a locally strongly convex region, followed by gradient descent with local linear contraction. For prediction, we compose this estimator with a neural approximation of the ODE solution map. We further show that, through parameter sharing, a single transformer can perform both parameter estimation and trajectory prediction simultaneously. For these constructions, we establish nonasymptotic guarantees and finite-pretraining oracle inequalities that separate errors due to finite pretraining data, finite context length, and finite-sized transformer approximation. Numerical experiments on linear and nonlinear ODEs further show that pretrained transformers can benefit from longer inference contexts without updating their weights.

AI.tldr: This paper constructs transformers that perform nonconvex in-context parameter estimation and trajectory prediction for parametric ODEs, backed by nonasymptotic oracle inequalities.
AI.motivation: Existing in-context learning theory focuses on convex problems or generic function approximation without exploiting the statistical structure of nonconvex parametric ODEs.
AI.method: The authors construct a transformer implementing a two-stage approximate MLE (coarse initialization plus local gradient descent) composed with a neural ODE solution map, and show parameter sharing enables simultaneous estimation and prediction.
AI.result: They establish nonasymptotic guarantees and finite-pretraining oracle inequalities separating pretraining data, context length, and approximation errors, and numerical experiments on linear and nonlinear ODEs confirm gains from longer inference contexts.
AI.conclusion: Transformers can provably implement structured two-stage estimation and prediction for nonconvex parametric ODEs in context.

title: High-probability Uniform Mixing via Dobrushin Contraction and Accelerated Hamiltonian Monte Carlo
summary: Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, since its invention and subsequent rise to widespread use, has been motivated by its ability to accelerate convergence to equilibrium compared to diffusive methods, both in terms of dependence on condition number and dimension. In the present work, we establish this acceleration simultaneously in both aspects for critically damped Metropolis-adjusted kinetic Langevin with persistent uniforms. More precisely, for target measures $\mu(dx)\propto e^{-U(x)}dx$ with $m$-strongly convex, $L$-gradient Lipschitz, and $L_H$-Frobenius Hessian Lipschitz potentials, we show that the method mixes to $\varepsilon$-accuracy in total variation using $\mathcal O\bigl((\kappa^{1/2}+L_H^{1/2}m^{-3/4})\,d^{1/4}\bigr)$ gradient evaluations up to logarithmic factors, both uniformly over starting points in domains of high equilibrium probability and from warm starts. The proof incorporates ideas from previous studies by Bou-Rabee and Chen et al. that show either aspect of acceleration separately, into novel coupling technology. This new coupling technology for general Markov chains extends earlier frameworks aimed at capturing fast local equilibration in the presence of slow global mixing. Specifically, via a weak-$(1,1)$ maximal inequality that follows from Hopf's maximal ergodic theorem, we uncover a stability mechanism in high-probability domains with respect to equilibrium. This enables straightforward localization to naturally arising domains of fast local mixing, and seamlessly fits broad local frameworks via Dobrushin contraction, Wasserstein contraction and local Harris' theorems. We develop the Dobrushin formulation.

AI.tldr: This paper proves that critically damped Metropolis-adjusted kinetic Langevin with persistent uniforms achieves accelerated O((kappa^{1/2} + L_H^{1/2} m^{-3/4}) d^{1/4}) mixing in both condition number and dimension.
AI.motivation: While Hamiltonian Monte Carlo is used to accelerate convergence over diffusive methods in both condition number and dimension, establishing both accelerations simultaneously remained open.
AI.method: Combining Hopf's maximal ergodic theorem with a novel coupling framework for general Markov chains, the authors localize fast local mixing via Dobrushin contraction to high-probability equilibrium domains.
AI.result: For m-strongly convex, L-gradient Lipschitz, L_H-Frobenius Hessian Lipschitz potentials, the method mixes to epsilon total variation accuracy in O((kappa^{1/2} + L_H^{1/2} m^{-3/4}) d^{1/4}) gradient evaluations up to log factors, uniformly over high-probability domains and warm starts.
AI.conclusion: Maximal-inequality localization and Dobrushin coupling rigorously establish simultaneous condition-number and dimension acceleration for kinetic Langevin Monte Carlo.

title: Nonparametric Instrumental Kernel Regression: The Well- and Misspecified Setting Under General Link Conditions
summary: We study nonparametric instrumental variable regression when the outcome takes values in a separable Hilbert space $\mathbb{Y}$, for instance a curve, a density or the kernel mean embedding of a distribution. The structural function solves an ill-posed operator equation whose conditional expectation operator need not be injective, and whose solutions need not belong to the hypothesis space. We analyse a two-stage kernel estimator that extends kernel instrumental variable regression to $\mathbb{Y}$-valued outcomes and allows spectral regularisation in both stages, including Landweber iteration and Showalter's method in the second stage. We show that the second stage is a regularisation method in the Hilbert scale generated by the inverse of the kernel integral operator. This viewpoint identifies the solution towards which the estimator converges: the minimum-norm solution in the reproducing kernel Hilbert space in the well-specified case and, in the misspecified case, the unique solution in the range of the continuous extension of the projection operator associated to the well-specified setting. Under source conditions and link conditions expressed through general index functions, we derive non-asymptotic bounds in a scale of interpolation norms that hold with high probability in terms of the first-stage error, with or without identification and in the well- and misspecified settings. For polynomial link conditions, we recover the rate of scalar kernel instrumental regression and extend it to targets outside the hypothesis space; for exponential link conditions, we obtain logarithmic rates in the severely ill-posed regime.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes two-stage nonparametric instrumental variable kernel regression for Hilbert-space-valued outcomes under general link conditions in both well- and misspecified settings.
AI.motivation: Extending kernel instrumental variable regression to function- or distribution-valued outcomes without injectivity or well-specification assumptions lacks non-asymptotic convergence guarantees.
AI.method: The authors analyze a two-stage kernel estimator allowing spectral regularization (including Landweber iteration and Showalter's method) in the second stage, framed as regularization in a Hilbert scale.
AI.result: They identify the limiting minimum-norm or projected solutions and derive high-probability non-asymptotic bounds in interpolation norms, recovering scalar rates for polynomial links and logarithmic rates for exponential links.
AI.conclusion: Hilbert-scale regularization theory provides unified non-asymptotic guarantees for infinite-dimensional instrumental kernel regression regardless of identification or misspecification.

title: Differentiable Exact Learning
summary: We introduce a framework for differentiable exact learning that couples an unbounded external environment to a state-tracking neural controller, which we train on policy-trajectory observations (PTOs): expert behavior traces that expose observations and actions while hiding internal states. In addition to the learning framework, we introduce Differentiable Finite-State Transducers (DFSTs) which use multilinear updates, support log-parallel training, and emulate arbitrary finite-state controllers, yielding computational universality through environmental interaction. From tiny training datasets, compact DFSTs achieve extreme length generalization on arithmetic and universal-simulation tasks. We replicate the success of DFSTs on RNNs and GRUs, thereby supporting a broader learning recipe: State-Tracking Controller + Unbounded External Environment + PTOs = Extreme Length Generalization. Beyond length generalization, our metric-extraction protocol recovers interpretable discrete controllers from trained DFSTs, which we prove equivalent to the target arithmetic and universal-simulation algorithms. Furthermore, for our Softmax DFST models, simply taking $\mathrm{argmax}$ over the transition probabilities yields discrete controllers which provably exactly perform universal Turing-machine simulation and binary arithmetic. Proving exact learning for the neural controllers requires assumptions, which we empirically support. We make our code, training recipes, model weights, and proof checkers publicly available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a differentiable exact learning framework that couples a state-tracking neural controller with an unbounded external environment using policy-trajectory observations (PTOs), achieving extreme length generalization and exact discrete controller extraction.
AI.motivation: Training neural controllers to perform exact algorithmic tasks with extreme length generalization and interpretable discrete equivalence remains challenging when internal states are hidden.
AI.method: The authors pair an unbounded external environment with state-tracking neural controllers trained on PTOs (expert traces exposing observations and actions while hiding internal states), and introduce Differentiable Finite-State Transducers (DFSTs) with multilinear updates and log-parallel training, alongside a metric-extraction protocol and Softmax DFST argmax discretization.
AI.result: From tiny training datasets, compact DFSTs, RNNs, and GRUs achieve extreme length generalization on arithmetic and universal-simulation tasks; extracted discrete controllers are proved equivalent to target algorithms, and Softmax DFST argmax controllers provably perform exact universal Turing-machine simulation and binary arithmetic.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a general recipe (State-Tracking Controller + Unbounded External Environment + PTOs) for extreme length generalization and provably exact, interpretable algorithm learning in neural controllers.

title: Almost Controlled: The FDR of Benjamini-Hochberg on Weighted Conformal p-Values
comment: 55 pages, 3 figures, 1 table. Main text 10 pages; full proofs in the appendices
summary: Weighted conformal p-values generalize conformal inference to cases with covariate shift. One way to use them is to pass them to the Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure, either to decide which test units to select or to detect outliers. But weighted conformal p-values may not be positively dependent, so we want to know: does BH still control the false discovery rate (FDR) in finite samples? Based on experiments, it appears to, but we prove it doesn't. We give two counterexamples, certified in exact rational arithmetic, where the FDR exceeds its target level $q$. We also identify how large the difference between the FDR and $q$ can be. With $n$ calibration points, $m$ test units and weight ratio $B$, the relative excess $\mathrm{FDR}/q-1$ is bounded by a function of $n$, $m$, $B$ and $q$ that is of order $\sqrt{Bm/(nq)}$ when $Bm/(nq)$ is small. The bound holds for every configuration with $B\le n$ and every $n$. This order can be reached when multiple non-null test units share a common threshold: in a Poisson-limit model, that configuration's excess is $c(q)\sqrt{Bm/(nq)}$ to first order as $B/n\to0$ and then $m\to\infty$. For some fixed distributions with this structure, the excess decreases only like $n^{-1/2}$ as $n$ grows. If every test unit is null, the excess is $O(B/n)$ at fixed $m$, and in certain configurations it grows linearly with $m$. To assist practitioners in judging how large the FDR can be, we turn that bound, which depends only on $n$, $m$, $q$ and $B$, into a lowered BH level with proved finite-sample control, and give a much less conservative rule of thumb that covers every worst case we were able to find but provides no guarantee.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that the Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure on weighted conformal p-values does not strictly control the finite-sample false discovery rate (FDR) under covariate shift, and bounds the worst-case excess.
AI.motivation: Weighted conformal p-values extend conformal inference to covariate shift, but because they may not be positively dependent, it was unknown whether passing them to BH still guarantees finite-sample FDR control despite apparent empirical control.
AI.method: The authors construct exact rational-arithmetic counterexamples where FDR exceeds target level q, derive finite-sample upper bounds on the relative excess FDR/q - 1 in terms of calibration size n, test units m, weight ratio B, and q, analyze a Poisson-limit model, and convert the bound into a lowered BH level with proved control plus a less conservative rule of thumb.
AI.result: For B <= n, the relative excess FDR/q - 1 is of order sqrt(Bm/(nq)) when Bm/(nq) is small, matching the Poisson-limit excess c(q)sqrt(Bm/(nq)) when multiple non-null units share a threshold; for some fixed distributions excess decreases as n^(-1/2), and when all units are null excess is O(B/n) at fixed m and can grow linearly with m.
AI.conclusion: Practitioners cannot rely on standard BH for exact finite-sample FDR control with weighted conformal p-values, and can instead use the derived lowered BH level for guaranteed control or the proposed rule of thumb for tighter practical sizing.

title: The cost of enforcing long-run coverage: a phase transition in online conformal prediction
summary: Consider an online prediction setting, where at each time, we are given a new feature vector and asked to provide a prediction interval or prediction set that will likely contain the corresponding response. In this setting, if the data points are i.i.d. (or more generally, exchangeable), conformal prediction provides a mechanism for building valid prediction sets around the output of any trained model, offering coverage probability $\geq 1-\alpha$ at each time $t$. In practice, however, issues such as distribution drift, changepoints, or other challenges may cause violations of the i.i.d. assumption. In this adversarial setting, online conformal prediction methods can still offer guarantees on long-run empirical coverage. However, there is a trade-off between these two types of goals: enforcing tight constraints on long-run empirical coverage to protect against the adversarial setting can lead to unstable oscillations in the instantaneous training-conditional coverage in the i.i.d. setting. In this work, we seek best-of-both-worlds algorithms that aim to minimize cumulative error in instantaneous training-conditional coverage when in the i.i.d. setting, while also offering long-run empirical coverage guarantees in the adversarial setting. Specifically, consider a condition that requires long-run empirical coverage to deviate from the target level $1-\alpha$ by at most $\mathcal{O}(T^{-\beta})$, for some $\beta\in[0,1]$. We prove that this family of conditions can be described with a phase transition. For $\beta\in[0,\frac{1}{2}]$, it is possible to construct algorithms satisfying such a constraint in the adversarial setting, while offering the same instantaneous coverage performance as split conformal prediction if the data is in fact i.i.d. On the other hand, for $\beta\in(\frac{1}{2},1]$, this type of condition comes at a cost, and does not achieve best-of-both-worlds behavior.

AI.tldr: The paper proves a phase transition in online conformal prediction showing that enforcing O(T^(-beta)) long-run empirical coverage in adversarial settings is compatible with optimal i.i.d. instantaneous coverage only for beta in [0, 1/2].
AI.motivation: Enforcing tight long-run empirical coverage constraints to handle distribution drift or adversarial data in online conformal prediction can cause unstable oscillations in instantaneous training-conditional coverage when the data are actually i.i.d.
AI.method: The authors analyze best-of-both-worlds online conformal prediction algorithms that minimize cumulative instantaneous training-conditional coverage error in i.i.d. settings while guaranteeing long-run empirical coverage deviations of at most O(T^(-beta)) for beta in [0, 1] in adversarial settings.
AI.result: They prove a phase transition at beta = 1/2: for beta in [0, 1/2], algorithms can satisfy the adversarial O(T^(-beta)) constraint while matching split conformal prediction's instantaneous coverage on i.i.d. data, whereas for beta in (1/2, 1], the constraint incurs a cost and precludes best-of-both-worlds behavior.
AI.conclusion: The result characterizes the exact theoretical limit on how tightly long-run adversarial coverage can be enforced without degrading instantaneous i.i.d. conformal prediction performance.

title: Optimal Autoregressive Chain-of-Thought Learning via Bagging
summary: We study how to learn an autoregressive next-token generator $f\colon\Sigma^\star\to\Sigma$ from a class $\mathcal{F}$, given chain-of-thought (CoT) demonstrations of length $T$ generated by $f$. We present a simple algorithm based on bagging, which outputs a majority vote of generators that are trained to be CoT-consistent on bootstrap samples of the training data. For binary token sets, it achieves the optimal sample complexity of $O((d_{\mathrm{VC}}+\log(1/\delta))/\epsilon)$, independent of the CoT length $T$, where $d_{\mathrm{VC}}$ is the VC dimension of $\mathcal{F}$. For finite token sets $\Sigma$, the VC dimension is replaced by a multiclass analogue, the Graph dimension $d_{\mathrm{G}}$, and the sample complexity is optimal up to a $\log|\Sigma|$ factor. The number of generators in the majority-vote ensemble is $O(\log(T/\delta))$, and we show that the ensemble can be distilled into a single generator in $\mathcal{F}$ at the expense of $n\log(nT)$ unlabeled prompts.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a bagging-based algorithm for learning an autoregressive next-token generator from chain-of-thought (CoT) demonstrations that achieves optimal sample complexity independent of CoT length T.
AI.motivation: Learning autoregressive next-token generators from long CoT demonstrations raises the question of whether sample complexity must grow with the CoT length T.
AI.method: The authors propose a bagging algorithm that trains generators to be CoT-consistent on bootstrap samples of the training data and outputs a majority-vote ensemble, which can also be distilled into a single generator using unlabeled prompts.
AI.result: For binary token sets, the algorithm achieves optimal sample complexity O((d_VC + log(1/delta))/epsilon) independent of T; for finite token sets Sigma, it replaces d_VC with the Graph dimension d_G and is optimal up to a log|Sigma| factor, using an ensemble of O(log(T/delta)) generators distillable with n log(nT) unlabeled prompts.
AI.conclusion: Bagging enables sample-efficient autoregressive CoT learning whose sample complexity does not scale with reasoning length, and the resulting ensemble can be distilled back into a single model.

title: "I Am Not a Kiddo!": Quantifying Epistemic Infantilization in Large Language Models via Multi-Metric Bias Analysis
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for tutoring and professional knowledge retrieval, yet safety evaluations still focus mainly on overt harms such as toxicity while overlooking benevolent failure modes. We study epistemic infantilization, defined as an identity-conditioned reduction in technical depth that appears when disability disclosure precedes an expert-level query. To measure this effect, we construct a counterfactual dataset of matched question-answer pairs and compare model responses across three settings: no identity context, disability disclosed in prior conversational context, and disability disclosed via a short query prefix. We introduce two composite metrics, the Infantilization Bias Index (IBI) and the Epistemic Accessibility Response Score (EARS), which capture retention of mathematical and formal content, domain terminology, reasoning coverage, and tone signals such as simplification markers and unsolicited offers to adjust the level. Across five open-weight model families, we find consistent evidence that disability disclosure reduces epistemic access by replacing formal explanations with higher-level summaries, with Physics and Mathematics most affected. Using question-clustered inference that respects the repeated-measures structure of the data, the effect remains reliable after accounting for correlated observations. These findings suggest an inclusion tax, where disabled users must request rigor more explicitly than non-disabled users. We conclude by arguing that accessibility should mean format adaptation rather than content simplification.

AI.tldr: The paper quantifies epistemic infantilization in LLMs, showing that disclosing a disability before an expert-level query causes models to replace formal technical explanations with simplified summaries.
AI.motivation: LLM safety evaluations focus on overt harms like toxicity while overlooking benevolent failure modes such as reducing technical depth when users disclose a disability.
AI.method: The authors build a counterfactual dataset of matched question-answer pairs across three settings (no identity context, prior conversational disability disclosure, and short query prefix disclosure) and introduce two composite metrics, the Infantilization Bias Index (IBI) and Epistemic Accessibility Response Score (EARS), analyzed via question-clustered inference across five open-weight model families.
AI.result: Disability disclosure consistently reduces epistemic access by replacing formal explanations with higher-level summaries, with Physics and Mathematics most affected, and the effect remains statistically reliable after accounting for repeated measures.
AI.conclusion: Disabled users face an inclusion tax requiring explicit requests for rigor, highlighting that accessibility should mean format adaptation rather than content simplification.

title: VidEngram: Agentic Long-Term Video Understanding via Structured Hierarchical Memory
comment: 10 pages, 4 figures, 4 tables. Demo video and code are linked in the paper
summary: Long-video question answering is wasteful and lossy when a multimodal model must re-encode the same video for every query: context limits force sparse sampling or truncation, and no reusable representation remains for later questions. We present VidEngram, an agentic video QA system that builds a persistent hierarchical memory once at ingest and answers later questions from that memory. VidEngram captions video and audio jointly with Qwen2.5-Omni, consolidates segment memories into episode and entity layers, and uses a text-only agentic planner with specialized retrieval tools to produce grounded answers. The web interface makes this process inspectable: users can watch memory formation, inspect retrieval traces, verify cited evidence in the video player, and explore entity relationships. On the full OmniVideoBench, VidEngram with a GPT-5-mini planner outperforms a strong single-pass Qwen2.5-Omni baseline (37.0% vs. 32.3%), with gains concentrated on longer videos where single-pass coverage becomes sparse. Because perception is paid once, subsequent queries use low-cost text-only planning.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces VidEngram, an agentic long-video QA system that builds a persistent hierarchical memory once at ingest and answers subsequent queries using a text-only planner, outperforming single-pass baselines on OmniVideoBench.
AI.motivation: Re-encoding long videos for every query is computationally wasteful and lossy due to context limits forcing sparse sampling or truncation without reusable representations.
AI.method: VidEngram jointly captions video and audio with Qwen2.5-Omni, consolidates segment memories into episode and entity layers, and uses a text-only agentic planner with retrieval tools and an inspectable web interface to answer queries from the stored memory.
AI.result: On the full OmniVideoBench, VidEngram with a GPT-5-mini planner achieves 37.0% accuracy compared to 32.3% for a single-pass Qwen2.5-Omni baseline, with gains concentrated on longer videos.
AI.conclusion: Paying perception cost once to build a structured hierarchical memory enables more accurate and lower-cost text-only querying for long-term video understanding.

title: Check Token: Real-Time Self-Verification and Precise Truncation in LLM Reasoning
summary: ECC memory embeds 8 parity bits for every 64 data bits and automatically detects and corrects errors on each read. The parity bits carry no data and only safeguard integrity, at ~12.5% overhead. Yet the reasoning chains of large language models lack such built-in self-verification: once an error occurs it propagates along the chain, and existing methods can only verify externally after generation completes. We propose the check token, establishing built-in self-verification for language model generation streams for the first time: a functional marker <CHECK> is added to the vocabulary, and the model triggers self-checking (analysis, localization, truncation, rewriting) by outputting it at any position. The check token carries no reasoning content (discarded after triggering) and only safeguards reasoning correctness, directly corresponding to the role of ECC parity bits, also at only ~13% overhead. Speculative forking further eliminates false-positive latency, and segmented reward makes trigger timing end-to-end learnable. Experiments (Qwen3-32B / Qwen3-Next) show that the check token achieves +10.8 pp improvement on HMMT25 at 1.13x overhead, with token efficiency 88x that of Best-of-8, and the precise truncation advantage monotonically increases with chain length.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes the check token (<CHECK>), a learnable vocabulary marker that enables built-in real-time self-verification and precise truncation during LLM reasoning at ~13% overhead.
AI.motivation: LLM reasoning chains lack built-in error detection like ECC memory parity bits, causing errors to propagate along the chain while existing verification methods only run externally after generation completes.
AI.method: A functional <CHECK> token is added to the vocabulary so the model can trigger self-checking (analysis, localization, truncation, rewriting) at any position, paired with speculative forking to eliminate false-positive latency and segmented rewards to learn trigger timing end-to-end.
AI.result: On Qwen3-32B and Qwen3-Next, the check token improves HMMT25 accuracy by +10.8 percentage points at 1.13x overhead with 88x the token efficiency of Best-of-8, and its precise truncation advantage grows monotonically with chain length.
AI.conclusion: Built-in check tokens provide a practical, low-overhead mechanism for real-time self-verification and error truncation inside LLM generation streams.

title: Read, Route, Patch: Robust Test-Time Evolution for LLM Agents
summary: Large Language Model (LLM)-based agents can improve long- horizon interactive decision-making through test-time evolu- tion, yet existing methods face three information bottlenecks: memory retrieval overemphasizes textual similarity, candi- date harnesses are often behaviorally redundant, and whole- harness rewriting may overwrite useful evidence or introduce cross-component inconsistency. We introduce Trident, which improves experience utilization, behavioral exploration, and harness evolution through boundary-aware memory reading, diversity-aware candidate routing, and order-aware insertion- based updating, respectively. We evaluate Trident on five benchmarks spanning text games, web interaction, and cod- ing tasks. Across qwen-32B, mistral-small-3.2-24B, and gpt- oss-20B, Trident achieves the best average performance and consistently outperforms non-learning, memory-based, reflection-based, and automated prompt optimization base- lines. Compared with the strongest baseline, APEX, Trident yields relative average gains of 30.7%, 30.8%, and 38.3% on the three backbones, respectively. Ablation and sensitivity stud- ies further show that the three designs provide complementary gains and remain robust to parameter variations.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Trident, a test-time evolution framework for LLM agents that addresses memory, redundancy, and rewriting bottlenecks to outperform existing baselines across text games, web, and coding benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing test-time evolution methods for LLM agents suffer from memory retrieval overemphasizing textual similarity, behaviorally redundant candidate harnesses, and whole-harness rewriting that overwrites useful evidence or breaks consistency.
AI.method: Trident combines boundary-aware memory reading for experience utilization, diversity-aware candidate routing for behavioral exploration, and order-aware insertion-based updating for harness evolution.
AI.result: Evaluated on five benchmarks across qwen-32B, mistral-small-3.2-24B, and gpt-oss-20B, Trident achieves the best average performance and outperforms the strongest baseline (APEX) by relative average gains of 30.7%, 30.8%, and 38.3%, respectively.
AI.conclusion: Addressing memory, diversity, and incremental harness updating together yields substantial, robust test-time evolution gains for long-horizon LLM agents.

title: Human vs Machine Translation Detection: A Cross-Model, Cross-Domain, and Low-Resource Analysis
comment: 20 pages, 6 figures, 12 tables. Accepted at the Conference on Language Modeling (COLM) 2026. Code: this https URL
summary: The growing reliance on web-crawled corpora for training large language models introduces a critical challenge: machine-translated (MT) content is often treated as human translation (HT), potentially degrading data quality and propagating synthetic artifacts, especially in low-resource settings. In this work, we study MT-HT detectability across high-resource (English, Spanish) and low-resource (Swahili, Afrikaans) languages using both decoder-only LLMs in zero-shot and few-shot settings, and fine-tuned multilingual encoders trained at the sentence level and on token-chunked inputs. We find that decoder-only models provide limited discrimination overall and exhibit a consistent class-asymmetric failure mode: they recognize human-written text reliably (high HT recall) but rarely flag fluent machine output (low MT recall). Encoder-based classifiers achieve high accuracy when evaluated on data generated by the same MT systems and translators used during training in a legislative domain, but their MT recall drops sharply on unseen translators and on unseen domains such as low-resource conversational text and medical content. To address this limitation, we evaluate models on longer inputs by chunking text into segments of up to 300 tokens, which substantially improves generalization, suggesting that sentence-level signals are insufficient for robust detection. Finally, we analyze the relationship between translation quality and detectability using COMET and BLEURT, showing that lower-quality MT is more easily identified, while high-quality MT remains difficult to distinguish from HT. Our results highlight the importance of input granularity, translator generalization, and translation quality in building robust MT detection systems across domains and languages.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates machine vs. human translation detection across high- and low-resource languages, finding that decoder-only LLMs struggle with MT recall and that chunking longer inputs improves encoder generalization across domains and unseen translators.
AI.motivation: Web-crawled corpora increasingly mix machine-translated (MT) text with human translation (HT), risking data quality degradation, especially in low-resource languages where MT-HT detectability is underexplored.
AI.method: The authors test zero-shot and few-shot decoder-only LLMs and fine-tuned multilingual encoders (at sentence level and on 300-token chunks) across English, Spanish, Swahili, and Afrikaans, and analyze quality-detectability links using COMET and BLEURT.
AI.result: Decoder-only LLMs show high HT recall but low MT recall; sentence-level encoders perform well in-domain on seen translators but drop sharply on unseen translators and domains (conversational, medical), whereas 300-token chunking substantially improves generalization, with lower-quality MT being easier to detect than high-quality MT.
AI.conclusion: Robust MT detection across languages and domains requires longer input granularities, evaluation on unseen translators, and accounting for translation quality.

title: Automating literature screening and knowledge synthesis with large language models
summary: Scientific literature is expanding rapidly, yet much of its knowledge remains difficult to organize and reuse due to the substantial workload needed to navigate large, heterogeneous literature corpora. Here, we develop a generalizable large language model (LLM)-powered framework that automates literature screening, structured information extraction, and knowledge synthesis within a unified workflow. We benchmarked 11 state-of-the-art proprietary and open-weight LLMs across three materials science screening tasks differing in scope, corpus size, and class imbalance. Seven LLMs achieved balanced accuracies above 0.90 across all tasks, with the best-performing LLM reaching 0.96--0.98, demonstrating the potential of LLMs to accurately screen large, highly imbalanced scientific corpora. The framework also substantially reduces manual effort, screening 10,000 records within four minutes compared with approximately 83 person-hours for manual screening. Beyond literature screening, the framework extracts structured information from full-text articles, enabling content-level quantification of research landscapes that extends traditional bibliometric analysis based on publication metadata. This capability reveals methodological trends and underexplored directions, as shown for machine learning in concrete materials science. We further demonstrate its utility for information and data discovery by identifying publications containing silicate glass density data that are difficult to retrieve using conventional search strategies, which can support downstream hypothesis development, research design, and data-driven scientific discovery. Overall, these results demonstrate the broad applicability of LLM-powered literature analysis across scientific domains and its potential to transform large, unstructured literature corpora into structured, analyzable knowledge at scale.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an LLM-powered framework for automated literature screening, structured extraction, and knowledge synthesis, achieving up to 0.96-0.98 balanced accuracy on materials science tasks while cutting screening time from ~83 person-hours to four minutes.
AI.motivation: Rapidly expanding scientific literature makes manual screening and structured knowledge synthesis labor-intensive and hard to scale across large, heterogeneous, and imbalanced corpora.
AI.method: The authors benchmark 11 proprietary and open-weight LLMs on three materials science screening tasks and apply full-text structured extraction to quantify research landscapes and discover specific data such as silicate glass density.
AI.result: Seven LLMs exceed 0.90 balanced accuracy across all three tasks, with the top model reaching 0.96-0.98, and the framework screens 10,000 records in four minutes compared to ~83 person-hours manually while uncovering methodological trends and hard-to-find data publications.
AI.conclusion: LLM-powered workflows can accurately and rapidly transform large unstructured scientific corpora into structured, analyzable knowledge for data-driven discovery.

title: OmniTag-LLM: Multilingual Multitask Speech Tagging
summary: Multimodal LLMs promise to replace the traditional cascade of specialist speech models with a single system that, from one audio clip, jointly transcribes and labels emotion, gender, language, and named entities. Yet most benchmarks still score these tasks in isolation, and largely in English. We introduce OmniTag-Bench, a five-language benchmark (en/de/es/fr/it) and training recipe for joint understanding: one audio clip in, one JSON object out (transcript, emotion, gender, LID, token-level NER). We evaluate ten open multimodal LLMs and a LoRA fine-tuned Qwen3-Omni on a unified prompt and scorer. Beyond aggregate scores, OmniTag-Bench reveals a systematic failure mode: several strong models often transcribe or translate non-English speech into English, inflating multilingual WER. Fine-tuning improves the base model on NER, emotion, and WER while nearly doubling accuracy on independent human-labeled emotion corpora, suggesting transferable gains beyond pseudo-label imitation. The fine-tuned model also generalizes to unseen but related languages, transferring to held-out Dutch. We release prompts, the scorer, and the labeling pipeline.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces OmniTag-Bench, a five-language benchmark and training recipe for joint speech transcription and tagging, revealing a cross-lingual English-translation failure mode and showing that LoRA fine-tuning improves accuracy and cross-lingual transfer.
AI.motivation: Most speech benchmarks evaluate transcription, emotion, gender, language ID, and NER separately and mostly in English, leaving joint multilingual multimodal LLM performance underexplored.
AI.method: The authors build OmniTag-Bench (en, de, es, fr, it) requiring one JSON output per clip (transcript, emotion, gender, LID, token-level NER) and evaluate ten open multimodal LLMs plus a LoRA fine-tuned Qwen3-Omni using a unified prompt and scorer.
AI.result: Strong models frequently transcribe or translate non-English speech into English, inflating multilingual WER; LoRA fine-tuning improves NER, emotion, and WER, nearly doubles accuracy on independent human-labeled emotion corpora, and transfers to held-out Dutch.
AI.conclusion: Joint multilingual evaluation exposes systematic cross-lingual failures in multimodal LLMs, while targeted LoRA fine-tuning yields transferable improvements across tasks and related languages.

title: Where Language Models Fail Like Aphasic Patients and Where They Don't
comment: 15 pages, 9 figures, 1 table. Supplementary information included (15 figures, 7 tables). A companion analysis comparing model scale and attention design within a single inference implementation is in preparation and will be reported in a subsequent version
summary: The computational architecture of human word production -- whether semantic-lexical retrieval and phonological encoding constitute dissociable processing stages -- has been debated for decades using hand-designed models with small vocabularies. We introduce computational architectural dissociation: using known architectural properties of vision-language models (VLMs) to derive falsifiable predictions about which patient error types should and should not align with model errors under perturbation. Because VLMs perform picture naming through learned semantic competition over full vocabularies but lack phonological encoding entirely, perturbation-induced errors should match patient patterns for semantic-stage categories but not phonological ones. Testing LLaVA 1.6 (Vicuna-13B) against 88 patients with aphasia across 175 Philadelphia Naming Test items (~37 million naming attempts, 50 perturbation seeds), we find that six of eight error categories show significant item-level alignment (Spearman $\rho$ = 0.32-0.50, all p < 0.001) while the two phonological categories -- formal errors and abstruse neologisms -- show no alignment ($\rho$ = 0.110 and 0.084, both n.s.), confirming the predicted dissociation. Spectral analysis of the output probabilities places each error type at a distinct position in a six-dimensional space, giving a mechanistic interpretability tool. The dissociation is layer-specific (peaking at L22, 55% depth), severity-independent, and stable across seeds (split-half r > 0.998). Weight perturbation of four additional 7B VLMs spanning the tested architectural combinations produced correct-rate alignment of comparable magnitude ($\rho$ = 0.21-0.27). Whether the per-category dissociation itself depends on scale or on attention design requires a comparison within a single inference implementation, which is reported separately.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces computational architectural dissociation, showing that perturbed vision-language models (VLMs) align with human aphasia errors on semantic-stage categories but not phonological categories.
AI.motivation: Whether human word production separates semantic-lexical retrieval from phonological encoding has long been debated using small-vocabulary hand-designed models.
AI.method: Because VLMs perform picture naming via semantic competition without phonological encoding, the authors perturb LLaVA 1.6 (Vicuna-13B) and four 7B VLMs across 175 Philadelphia Naming Test items and compare error patterns against 88 aphasia patients using Spearman correlation and spectral analysis.
AI.result: Six of eight error categories align significantly at the item level (rho = 0.32-0.50, p < 0.001), whereas the two phonological categories (formal errors and abstruse neologisms) show no alignment (rho = 0.110 and 0.084, n.s.); the dissociation peaks at layer 22 (55% depth) and is stable across seeds (split-half r > 0.998).
AI.conclusion: Perturbation-based comparison of VLMs against patient data provides a falsifiable, large-vocabulary computational test supporting the dissociation between semantic-lexical retrieval and phonological encoding.

title: Endogenous Preferences as Vulnerability Signals: Discovering Universal Adversarial Triggers for LLM Utility Degradation
summary: Deployed large language models must remain useful when untrusted text enters their prompt context. Adversarial prompting and red-teaming methods typically define the failures they seek through task labels, harmful targets, judge feedback, or downstream utility scores. We ask whether a frozen model's clean behavior can reveal a reusable context vulnerability when its task-level form is unknown, and downstream task feedback is withheld. To study this question, EndoUT uses a Siamese-style design that compares the same frozen victim on clean and span-modified versions of each unlabeled instruction. Without a task-level target, the clean pass supplies the victim's preferred response-onset token as an instruction-conditioned reference; Endogenous Preference Disruption (EPD) measures how insertion weakens that preference. An auxiliary generator supplies bounded-span proposals; EPD guides its update and ranks the pool without access to downstream information. The highest-scoring victim-specific span is fixed before evaluation and reused unchanged across all held-out inputs. Across four instruction-tuned models and nine benchmarks, fixed triggers reduce benign-task utility by 40.2 percentage points on average, with negative mean change on every benchmark and greater average degradation than every evaluated baseline under the reported protocols. Matched protocol ablations show stronger transfer for source-side selection followed by fixed reuse than for null-context fixed reuse or per-input generation. Transfer recurs across proposers with proposal-dependent strength; output-level analyses identify victim-specific associations between trigger families and downstream failure patterns. Thus, clean behavior can expose context vulnerabilities that transfer across inputs yet manifest through structured, victim-specific patterns of utility degradation. The code and data will be released upon acceptance.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces EndoUT, a method that discovers universal adversarial triggers for LLM utility degradation using only a frozen model's clean behavior without task labels or downstream feedback. Fixed triggers selected by EndoUT reduce benign-task utility by 40.2 percentage points on average across four instruction-tuned models and nine benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing adversarial prompting and red-teaming methods rely on task labels, harmful targets, judge feedback, or downstream utility scores. They cannot detect reusable context vulnerabilities when the task-level failure form is unknown and downstream feedback is withheld.
AI.method: EndoUT uses a Siamese-style design comparing a frozen victim model on clean and span-modified versions of unlabeled instructions. The clean pass provides the preferred response-onset token as a reference, and Endogenous Preference Disruption (EPD) measures how an inserted span weakens that preference to guide an auxiliary generator and rank candidate triggers.
AI.result: Across four instruction-tuned models and nine benchmarks, fixed triggers reduce benign-task utility by 40.2 percentage points on average, with negative mean change on every benchmark and greater degradation than all evaluated baselines. Ablations show stronger transfer for source-side selection with fixed reuse than for null-context reuse or per-input generation.
AI.conclusion: Clean model behavior can expose context vulnerabilities that transfer across inputs and manifest as structured, victim-specific patterns of utility degradation.

title: Theoretical Foundations of Computational Islamic Jurisprudence (Fiqh)
summary: This paper presents the theoretical foundations and a comprehensive formal system for Computational Islamic Jurisprudence (Fiqh). We begin by establishing six foundational principles that distinguish computational Fiqh from conventional natural language processing and general theological formalization. These principles define Islamic jurisprudence as a normative deductive science operating on empirically grounded facts, necessitating a dual inductive-deductive methodology, and requiring a logical foundation specifically engineered for Fiqh rather than adopted from existing formalisms. Based on these principles, we construct a three-layer stratified computational language, $\mathcal{F} = D \circ A \circ G$, consisting of: (1) an Arabic Morphological/Grammatical Grounding Engine that transforms fully vocalized Classical Arabic into language-independent Grounded Action Structures (GAS); (2) the Arabic Reified Action Calculus (ARAC) that normalizes these structures into canonical logical representations; and (3) a function-free Horn-clause Datalog engine for executable legal deduction. Furthermore, we introduce a bridging methodology (Algorithm $\Omega$) that dynamically generates a Fiqh-Categorized Attribute Grammar from inductively extracted Horn clauses via an Ontological Meta-Map ($\mathcal{M}_{onto}$), seamlessly connecting the inductive extraction of legal rules to their deductive application. The paper rigorously proves the system's semantic correctness, representational completeness, termination, and decidability. Crucially, by leveraging morphosyntactic inflection markers ($\delta$ modes) as structural constraints, we prove the strict unambiguity of the proposed grammar, achieving deterministic $O(n)$ linear parsing complexity. This work provides a mathematically verifiable, epistemologically grounded, and computationally tractable foundation for automated Islamic jurisprudence.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes theoretical foundations and a formal three-layer computational system for Computational Islamic Jurisprudence (Fiqh). It proves semantic correctness, representational completeness, termination, decidability, and deterministic O(n) linear parsing complexity.
AI.motivation: Computational Fiqh differs from conventional NLP and general theological formalization because it operates as a normative deductive science on empirically grounded facts, requiring a dual inductive-deductive methodology and a purpose-built logical foundation.
AI.method: The authors define six foundational principles and construct a three-layer stratified language F = D o A o G: an Arabic Morphological/Grammatical Grounding Engine producing Grounded Action Structures (GAS), the Arabic Reified Action Calculus (ARAC) for canonical logical normalization, and a function-free Horn-clause Datalog engine for legal deduction. Algorithm Omega dynamically generates a Fiqh-Categorized Attribute Grammar from inductively extracted Horn clauses via an Ontological Meta-Map.
AI.result: The paper rigorously proves the system's semantic correctness, representational completeness, termination, and decidability. Using morphosyntactic inflection markers (delta modes) as structural constraints, it proves strict grammar unambiguity and deterministic O(n) linear parsing complexity.
AI.conclusion: This work provides a mathematically verifiable, epistemologically grounded, and computationally tractable foundation for automated Islamic jurisprudence.

title: Whose Side Are You On? Measuring Stance at Scale for Reddit Discourse Analysis During the Israel-Gaza War
comment: Code is available at: this https URL
summary: Large-scale discourse analysis often requires stance labels, yet for many high-salience political events such labels are unavailable at the comment level. We introduce and validate a comment-level stance measurement instrument that assigns Pro-Israel, Pro-Palestinian, or Undefined stance using Reddit comment text. The instrument is calibrated from a small, manually annotated gold-standard dataset and scaled through large language model-assisted labeling, achieving weighted-$F_{1}=0.88$ against held-out human annotations. To enable corpus-scale measurement, we operationalize the instrument as a lightweight classifier based on DistilBERT embeddings and an RBF SVM, which achieves weighted-$F_{1}=0.7935$ on the original gold-standard set. Applying this instrument, we measure the stance of approximately 2.7 million Reddit comments posted between 2023 and 2025 during the Israel-Gaza war. We demonstrate what this measurement enables by analyzing stance-conditioned asymmetries in sentiment, toxicity, and emotional framing across political affiliations. This work shows how validated, low-cost stance measurement can support large-scale descriptive analysis of polarized discourse, without relying on network structure or prior labeled corpora.

AI.tldr: This paper develops and validates a comment-level stance measurement instrument for Reddit discourse during the Israel-Gaza war, scaling it to analyze 2.7 million comments. It reveals stance-conditioned asymmetries in sentiment, toxicity, and emotional framing across political affiliations.
AI.motivation: Large-scale discourse analysis requires comment-level stance labels, which are often unavailable for high-salience political events without relying on network structure or prior labeled corpora.
