Removing the unused vision stack and non-task vocabulary and using int8 weights or fp8 activations causes no resolved loss, whereas int4 leaves a small residual. QLoRA healing overfits its calibration domain. A Cometoid best-of-4 reranker at $T=0.3$ improves both the 8-bit and 4-bit systems under WMT25 test set. On post-submission WMT26, both remain competitive with bf16 under reference-free metrics; the small difference between the reranked variants is treated as noise.

AI.tldr: This paper compresses google/gemma-3-12b-it for three translation directions on one H100 using pruning, quantization, and Cometoid best-of-4 reranking, showing that 8-bit and 4-bit systems remain competitive with bf16 on WMT26.
AI.motivation: Compressing large language models reduces serving cost, but relying on a single automatic metric can miss quality degradation, and paired bootstrap analysis reveals metric disagreement on 4-bit quantization.
AI.method: Guided by WMT24 human meta-evaluation, the authors use MetricX24-XXL as the primary metric and CometKiwi-XXL as a cross-check, remove the unused vision stack and non-task vocabulary, apply int8 weights or fp8 activations (or int4), and add a Cometoid best-of-4 reranker at T=0.3.
AI.result: Removing the vision stack and non-task vocabulary with int8 weights or fp8 activations causes no resolved quality loss, int4 leaves a small residual, QLoRA healing overfits its calibration domain, and Cometoid best-of-4 reranking improves both 8-bit and 4-bit systems on WMT25 and keeps them competitive with bf16 on post-submission WMT26.
AI.conclusion: Combining targeted pruning, 8-bit or 4-bit quantization, and reference-free reranking yields competitive translation quality with lower serving cost while avoiding metric blind spots.

title: Skill-Latent Rewards: LLM-Guided Reward Formulation for Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning
summary: Long-horizon reinforcement learning under sparse and delayed feedback remains an open challenge. Existing return-decomposition methods redistribute episodic rewards to ease credit assignment, but they operate on raw state--action transitions and disregard the subgoal structure that governs meaningful progress in complex tasks. We propose Skill-LR, a hierarchical reinforcement learning framework in which a vision--language model identifies the agent's active subgoal at each timestep and a large language model generates a matching latent reward formulation through a two-stage prompting process. By conditioning reward signals on the currently active subgoal, Skill-LR produces stage-specific credit that evolves with the hierarchical plan, reducing temporal variance and improving sample efficiency. On multi-stage MiniGrid and BabyAI benchmarks, including DoorKey and Unlock-to-Unlock, Skill-LR converges faster and more reliably than sparse environmental rewards and strong credit-assignment baselines such as RUDDER and LaRe, demonstrating that subgoal-aligned latent rewards offer a principled path toward stable, interpretable credit assignment in long-horizon tasks.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Skill-LR, a hierarchical reinforcement learning framework that uses a vision-language model to detect active subgoals and an LLM to generate matching latent rewards, improving sample efficiency on MultiGrid and BabyAI.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon reinforcement learning suffers from sparse and delayed feedback, and existing return-decomposition methods operate on raw state-action transitions while ignoring the subgoal structure of complex tasks.
AI.method: Skill-LR uses a vision-language model to identify the agent's active subgoal at each timestep and a large language model to generate a corresponding latent reward formulation via a two-stage prompting process, conditioning reward signals on the active subgoal.
AI.result: On multi-stage MiniGrid and BabyAI benchmarks including DoorKey and Unlock-to-Unlock, Skill-LR converges faster and more reliably than sparse environmental rewards and credit-assignment baselines such as RUDDER and LaRe.
AI.conclusion: Subgoal-aligned latent rewards provide a principled approach for stable, interpretable credit assignment and improved sample efficiency in long-horizon reinforcement learning.

title: Not All Data Leakage Is Equal: A Controlled Benchmark of Evaluation Inflation in Tabular Classification
summary: Data leakage is widely recognized as a threat to trustworthy machine-learning evaluation, yet the phrase covers mechanisms with very different statistical consequences. We present a controlled empirical benchmark that measures the inflation in held-out ROC-AUC caused by five common leakage mechanisms: global standardization, global median imputation, duplicate contamination, supervised feature selection before splitting, and target encoding before splitting. The benchmark spans six public datasets and two synthetic stress tests, three model families, and five repeated stratified train/test splits, yielding 600 paired clean-versus-leaked comparisons. To avoid pseudo-replication, inference is performed on dataset-level effects with cluster bootstrap confidence intervals and Holm-corrected one-sided Wilcoxon tests. Label-dependent or direct data-reuse mechanisms produced systematic optimism: global target encoding increased ROC-AUC by 2.42 percentage points on average (95% cluster-bootstrap CI 0.62--4.89), global supervised feature selection by 1.93 points (0.63--3.39), and duplicate contamination by 1.52 points (0.40--2.80). All three remained significant after multiplicity correction. In contrast, global scaling and global median imputation had near-zero average effects under the i.i.d. settings studied here. A controlled target-encoding stress test further shows that leakage becomes sharply worse as categories become sparse. The results support a severity-aware view of leakage: evaluation pipelines should prevent all held-out-data dependence, but label-dependent transformations and observation reuse deserve especially aggressive auditing.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a controlled empirical benchmark measuring ROC-AUC inflation from five data leakage mechanisms across 600 paired comparisons, finding that label-dependent and data-reuse mechanisms cause significant optimism while global scaling and median imputation have near-zero average effects.
AI.motivation: Data leakage threatens trustworthy machine-learning evaluation, but the term covers distinct mechanisms whose statistical consequences have not been systematically compared.
AI.method: The authors benchmark global standardization, global median imputation, duplicate contamination, supervised feature selection before splitting, and target encoding before splitting across six public datasets, two synthetic stress tests, three model families, and five repeated stratified splits, using cluster bootstrap confidence intervals and Holm-corrected one-sided Wilcoxon tests.
AI.result: Global target encoding inflated ROC-AUC by 2.42 percentage points on average, global supervised feature selection by 1.93 points, and duplicate contamination by 1.52 points (all significant after multiplicity correction), whereas global scaling and global median imputation had near-zero average effects under i.i.d. settings, and sparse categories worsened target-encoding leakage.
AI.conclusion: Evaluation pipelines should prevent all held-out-data dependence, with especially aggressive auditing for label-dependent transformations and observation reuse.

title: Mechanistic Interpretability of Mambas Selective Gate in Financial Markets: A Leakage-Controlled Study
summary: Selectively gated state-space models (SSMs), notably Mamba, are increasingly used for financial time series, yet how they internally represent market regimes (bull, bear, sideways) remains opaque. This paper applies Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) to a six-layer Mamba trained on approximately twenty-one years of daily data for a point-in-time set of S&P 500 constituents plus macroeconomic and Fama-French factors, decomposing per-layer hidden states with Top-K Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs). Our central contribution is methodological and cautionary. A prior, uncontrolled configuration recovered market regimes from SAE features at F1 = 1.00. Under a controlled protocol that (i) removes the three input features that overlap the HMM label definition, (ii) disables the auxiliary regime-classification head, (iii) uses a point-in-time constituent universe, and (iv) evaluates against labels disjoint from the inputs, the same regime label is recovered at only F1 = 0.398, indistinguishable from a logistic baseline on raw inputs (0.435) and from an SAE trained on a randomly initialized, untrained Mamba (0.364). A 2x2 attribution grid shows the near-perfect result is an interaction of auxiliary supervision and label-defining inputs: neither factor alone exceeds F1 ~ 0.40. Effect sizes with block-bootstrap inference show the residual selective-gate (Delta t) regime effect is statistically detectable but economically negligible and uniform across layers rather than layer-specialized; the apparent polysemanticity gradient disappears under continuous, theory-grounded measures. We contribute a reproducible leakage-control protocol for interpretability evaluation of financial SSMs, a quantified demonstration that previously reported regime structure is a label-contamination artifact, and a modest economically grounded feature subset that genuinely survives the controls.

AI.tldr: This paper applies Mechanistic Interpretability with Top-K Sparse Autoencoders to a six-layer Mamba trained on 21 years of S&P 500 and macro data, showing that previously reported near-perfect market regime recovery is a label-contamination artifact.
AI.motivation: Selectively gated state-space models like Mamba are increasingly used for financial time series, yet how they internally represent market regimes remains opaque and prior interpretability evaluations lacked strict leakage controls.
AI.method: The authors train a six-layer Mamba on a point-in-time S&P 500 constituent universe plus macroeconomic and Fama-French factors, decompose per-layer hidden states with Top-K Sparse Autoencoders, and enforce a leakage-controlled protocol removing overlapping inputs, disabling the auxiliary regime head, and evaluating against disjoint labels.
AI.result: An uncontrolled setup recovered market regimes at F1 = 1.00, whereas under the leakage-controlled protocol recovery dropped to F1 = 0.398, indistinguishable from a logistic baseline on raw inputs (0.435) and an SAE on an untrained Mamba (0.364), with a 2x2 attribution grid confirming the artifact stems from auxiliary supervision interacting with label-defining inputs.
AI.conclusion: The study provides a reproducible leakage-control protocol for financial SSM interpretability and demonstrates that previously reported regime structure was largely a label-contamination artifact, leaving only a modest economically grounded feature subset.

title: Multimodal Fusion with Pre-trained Models for Psychotherapy Outcome Prediction from Emotional Dynamics
comment: Preprint. 18 pages, 7 figures; 6-page supplementary material as ancillary file. This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible
summary: In-session emotional dynamics are associated with psychotherapy outcomes but difficult to measure at scale. Pretrained multimodal models provide automated access to facial, vocal, and textual signals, yet clinical datasets remain small. Our research question is how pretrained multimodal representations can best support psychotherapy outcome prediction under data scarcity. Three studies use 106 sessions from 88 patients and nine session-level outcome scales (HSCL-11, EPO-1, POMS). Study 1 asks whether deep learning outperforms classical machine learning: a two-stage deep pipeline, first predicting window-level valence/arousal and then session outcomes, transferred poorly (best single configuration, $r=.078$). Study 2 asks which representation and preprocessing choices work best: statistical pooling of frozen pretrained embeddings with regularized classical models achieved average $r=.406$ across nine scales under per-scale configuration selection, up to $r=.490$ for symptom distress, with complementary modalities and no significant benefit from manual affect annotations or therapist features. Study 3 asks whether deep learning remains inferior under these choices: classical models outperformed an optimized single-stage deep model at the single-configuration level ($r=.281$ vs. $.222$) and on all nine scales under matched per-scale selection ($.406$ vs. $.252$). The results suggest that under clinical data scarcity, pretrained representations with fixed statistical pooling and regularized classical models are more reliable than learned aggregation.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates how pretrained multimodal models can predict psychotherapy outcomes under clinical data scarcity, finding that fixed statistical pooling of frozen embeddings with regularized classical models outperforms deep learning architectures.
AI.motivation: In-session emotional dynamics are linked to psychotherapy outcomes but are hard to measure at scale, and while pretrained multimodal models offer automated facial, vocal, and textual signals, clinical datasets remain small.
AI.method: Across three studies using 106 sessions from 88 patients and nine outcome scales (HSCL-11, EPO-1, POMS), the authors compare a two-stage deep pipeline, statistical pooling of frozen pretrained embeddings with regularized classical models, and an optimized single-stage deep model.
AI.result: The two-stage deep pipeline transferred poorly (best single configuration r=.078), whereas statistical pooling with regularized classical models achieved average r=.406 across nine scales (up to r=.490 for symptom distress) and outperformed the optimized single-stage deep model both at the single-configuration level (r=.281 vs. .222) and under matched per-scale selection (.406 vs. .252).
AI.conclusion: Under clinical data scarcity, frozen pretrained multimodal representations combined with fixed statistical pooling and regularized classical models are more reliable than learned deep aggregation.

title: Predictive maintenance in manufacturing: The operational value of continual machine learning
summary: Predictive maintenance in high-volume manufacturing often faces a domain-incremental learning problem: as new product configurations enter production, prediction models must learn from newly available data while preserving performance on earlier configurations that remain in operation. In this paper, we empirically study the operational value of continual machine learning methods for addressing this challenge in predictive maintenance, using real-world maintenance data from Bosch. The setting at Bosch covers 25 product configurations over five years, which creates a practical challenge for predictive maintenance models, as such models must be updated with data from newly introduced configurations without reducing performance on configurations learned earlier, a phenomenon known as "forgetting". At the same time, retaining all historical sensor data and repeatedly retraining models is often infeasible in high-volume manufacturing since industrial machines generate too large data volumes. To address this challenge, we combine continual machine learning with robust optimization to support predictive maintenance. We then compare continual machine learning with a broad set of baselines, including fine-tuning, domain-adaptation methods, online learning methods, and configuration-specific models. Across experiments, continual machine learning methods achieve stronger predictive performance and lower maintenance costs than the baselines, with a reduction of cost-related indicators of more than 40 % relative to the baselines. Our results demonstrate the operational value of continual machine learning for decision support in maintenance when product portfolios grow over time and historical manufacturing data cannot be fully retained.

AI.tldr: This paper empirically evaluates continual machine learning combined with robust optimization for predictive maintenance on five years of Bosch manufacturing data, achieving over 40% reduction in cost-related indicators compared to baselines.
AI.motivation: Predictive maintenance in high-volume manufacturing faces domain-incremental learning as new product configurations enter production, requiring models to learn new configurations without forgetting earlier ones while avoiding the infeasible storage and retraining of all historical sensor data.
AI.method: The authors combine continual machine learning with robust optimization on real-world Bosch maintenance data covering 25 product configurations over five years, and compare against fine-tuning, domain-adaptation, online learning, and configuration-specific baselines.
AI.result: Continual machine learning methods achieved stronger predictive performance and lower maintenance costs than all baselines, reducing cost-related indicators by more than 40%.
AI.conclusion: Continual machine learning provides substantial operational value for maintenance decision support when product portfolios expand and historical sensor data cannot be fully retained.

title: GRAFT: Cross-Backbone LoRA Reuse for Continual Language and Multimodal Learning
summary: In continual learning, parameter-efficient fine-tuning enables large language models to acquire new capabilities through lightweight adapters such as LoRA, yet the reuse of pretrained adapters is typically restricted to models sharing the same backbone. This limits the transfer of learned capabilities from language models to multimodal models. We propose GRAFT (Generalist Reuse of Adapters via Feature-space Transfer), a framework for cross-backbone LoRA reuse. GRAFT retrieves the most relevant pretrained LoRA adapter from a modality-aware library and maps it into the target backbone through a learned linear bridge between corresponding source and target feature spaces. We evaluate GRAFT on ten Super-NaturalInstructions text tasks, transferring Qwen2.5 LoRAs to Qwen2.5-VL, and five multimodal tasks, where Qwen2.5-VL LoRAs are directly reused. Compared with randomly initialized LoRA adapters, GRAFT improves performance on most evaluated tasks. These results show that GRAFT provides a simple and effective mechanism for reusing learned capabilities across language and multimodal models in continual learning.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes GRAFT, a framework for cross-backbone LoRA reuse that transfers adapters between language and multimodal models via a learned linear bridge, improving performance over randomly initialized LoRAs.
AI.motivation: In continual learning, reusing pretrained LoRA adapters is typically restricted to models sharing the same backbone, which prevents transferring learned capabilities from language models to multimodal models.
AI.method: GRAFT retrieves the most relevant pretrained LoRA adapter from a modality-aware library and maps it into the target backbone through a learned linear bridge between corresponding source and target feature spaces.
AI.result: Evaluated on ten Super-NaturalInstructions text tasks (transferring Qwen2.5 LoRAs to Qwen2.5-VL) and five multimodal tasks (reusing Qwen2.5-VL LoRAs), GRAFT improves performance over randomly initialized LoRA adapters on most evaluated tasks.
AI.conclusion: GRAFT offers a simple and effective mechanism for reusing learned capabilities across different language and multimodal backbones in continual learning.

title: SynthDCB: World Distillation for Scalable Device Control Benchmarking
comment: 65 pages, 7 figures, 17 tables. Details and access are available at: this https URL
summary: Scaling device-control evaluation requires scaling both the worlds agents interact with and the tasks they must solve. We introduce SynthDCB, a scalable benchmark for environment awareness and device control built through world distillation. World distillation transforms knowledge of device behaviors, interaction constraints, and environmental effects into modular executable components, which are composed into interactive worlds with explicit states, actions, and temporal dynamics. A unified capability representation connects tool discovery, world execution, and task synthesis, allowing new capabilities to enter evaluation through a shared construction pipeline. SynthDCB instantiates Home, Car, and Phone domains with 114 device classes, 1,166 functions, and 95 events, supporting five task families with 32 subtypes. The stateful design enables task validation and agent evaluation through state correctness and tool-call traces. We evaluate seven models on 2,560 test tasks; the best achieves 68.2% Pass@1. Error analysis reveals challenges in answer delivery, feasibility diagnosis, and temporal coordination. Construction experiments demonstrate scalability across domains and token efficiency: world distillation reduces token consumption by 0.9-66.0% and 46.2-92.5% relative to Codex with low and xhigh reasoning effort, respectively, while achieving broader capability coverage. SynthDCB makes executable world construction the basis of scalable device-control benchmarking, connecting an expanding space of capabilities and interactions to verifiable agent evaluation.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces SynthDCB, a scalable device-control benchmark built via world distillation across Home, Car, and Phone domains, where the best of seven evaluated models achieves 68.2% Pass@1.
AI.motivation: Scaling device-control evaluation requires scaling both interactive environments and tasks, which is difficult without a unified, verifiable construction pipeline.
AI.method: SynthDCB uses world distillation to convert device behaviors, constraints, and environmental effects into modular executable components with explicit states, actions, and temporal dynamics, instantiating 114 device classes, 1,166 functions, and 95 events across five task families and 32 subtypes.
AI.result: Across 2,560 test tasks evaluated on seven models, the best model achieves 68.2% Pass@1, with error analysis highlighting gaps in answer delivery, feasibility diagnosis, and temporal coordination; world distillation also reduces token consumption by 0.9-66.0% and 46.2-92.5% compared to Codex with low and xhigh reasoning effort, respectively.
AI.conclusion: SynthDCB grounds scalable device-control benchmarking in executable world construction, linking expanding capability spaces to verifiable agent evaluation.

title: SERAG: SEmantical and Relational approach for Anomaly detection on knowledge Graphs
summary: Knowledge graphs constructed from text can contain facts that are individually plausible yet inconsistent with their relational context. We introduce SERAG, a supervised anomaly detector that combines two complementary plausibility estimates: a semantic score computed from separately encoded subject, relation, and object labels, and a relational score obtained through a relational graph convolutional network. The scores are standardized, calibrated, and fused. We evaluate the method on a subset of ICEWS18 with vocabulary-constrained synthetic anomalies generated by an LLM, using pooled and chronological splits. At 10% anomaly prevalence, SERAG achieves test AUPRCs of 0.321 and 0.258, respectively, compared with 0.159 and 0.146 for the strongest adapted baseline. Fusion improves mean test AUPRC over either branch alone, with a larger gain in the pooled protocol and a smaller validation-selected gain in the chronological protocol. Additional anomaly supervision improves performance. These results support the complementarity of textual and relational signals for detecting synthetic anomalies under the evaluated protocols.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces SERAG, a supervised anomaly detector for knowledge graphs that fuses a text-based semantic score with an R-GCN relational score, outperforming baselines on ICEWS18.
AI.motivation: Knowledge graphs constructed from text can contain facts that appear individually plausible yet are inconsistent with their surrounding relational context.
AI.method: SERAG computes a semantic plausibility score from separately encoded subject, relation, and object labels and a relational score from a relational graph convolutional network, then standardizes, calibrates, and fuses both scores.
AI.result: On a subset of ICEWS18 with LLM-generated vocabulary-constrained synthetic anomalies at 10% prevalence, SERAG achieves test AUPRCs of 0.321 (pooled) and 0.258 (chronological), compared with 0.159 and 0.146 for the strongest adapted baseline, with fusion outperforming either branch alone.
AI.conclusion: Textual semantic signals and relational graph signals are complementary for detecting synthetic anomalies in knowledge graphs under the evaluated protocols.

title: HIMX: mixed-format matrix multiplication based on customized HIFLOAT4 representations
summary: 4-bit weight-activation quantization (W4A4) is an important approach for efficient large language model (LLM) inference. Recent hierarchical formats such as HiFloat4 (HIF4) improve the representational range of 4-bit quantization through multi-level scaling. However, the same local mantissa representation in HIF4 may not be equally suitable for weights and activations, which exhibit distinct distribution characteristics. To address this limitation, we propose HiMX, a mixed-mantissa framework built upon the hierarchical scaling structure of HIF4. Our key observation is that the two HIF4-compatible mantissa representations, S1P2 and E2M1, exhibit complementary quantization behavior: the denser S1P2 format provides higher resolution for concentrated weight distributions, while the wider-spaced E2M1 format provides complementary quantization characteristics for activation tensors. HiMX enables operand-tailored mantissa representations while converting heterogeneous mantissas into fixed-point integer operands with operand-specific widths, allowing different operand formats to share a unified integer multiply-accumulate (MAC) array. Block-level analysis on Qwen3-8B shows that HIF4-S1P2 is better suited for weights while HIF4 E2M1 is better suited for activations, and their mixed-format combination achieves lower output MSE than homogeneous configurations. Across multiple benchmarks, HiMX reduces the average end-to-end accuracy loss from 2.38 to 1.77 points on Qwen3-8B and from 2.23 to 1.85 points on Qwen3-30B-A3B, demonstrating the potential benefit of heterogeneous mantissa representations for W4A4 LLM inference.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes HiMX, a mixed-mantissa W4A4 quantization framework based on HiFloat4 that pairs S1P2 weights with E2M1 activations on a unified integer MAC array, reducing accuracy loss on Qwen3 models.
AI.motivation: In 4-bit weight-activation quantization (W4A4), hierarchical formats like HiFloat4 use the same local mantissa representation for both weights and activations despite their distinct distribution characteristics.
AI.method: HiMX assigns denser S1P2 mantissas to weights and wider-spaced E2M1 mantissas to activations within HiFloat4's hierarchical scaling structure, converting heterogeneous mantissas into fixed-point integer operands so they share a unified integer MAC array.
AI.result: Block-level analysis on Qwen3-8B confirms lower output MSE for mixed-format quantization than homogeneous configurations, and across benchmarks HiMX reduces average end-to-end accuracy loss from 2.38 to 1.77 points on Qwen3-8B and from 2.23 to 1.85 points on Qwen3-30B-A3B.
AI.conclusion: Tailoring mantissa representations separately for weights and activations improves W4A4 LLM inference accuracy while remaining hardware-compatible.

title: FedFit: Federated Dynamic Sparse Training via Fisher Information scoring
comment: The paper was accepted by ICML 2026
summary: Cross-device Federated Learning (FL) is frequently bottlenecked by the prohibitive memory and communication costs of training deep neural networks on resource-constrained edge hardware. While federated dynamic sparse training aims to alleviate these costs by adjusting sparse structures during training, existing methods rely on magnitude-based heuristics that are fundamentally ill-suited for the non-convergent, heterogeneous environments inherent to FL. To address this challenge, we propose FedFit, a federated dynamic sparse training framework that replaces simple heuristics with optimization-centric criteria for structure adjustment. By leveraging a second-order approximation of the loss landscape via the Fisher Information Matrix, FedFit enables precise and efficient structure adjustment without the overhead of explicit Hessian computation. Empirical evaluations across computer vision and natural language processing benchmarks demonstrate that FedFit significantly narrows the sparse-to-dense accuracy gap, outperforming state-of-the-art methods while maintaining high communication efficiency. Our code is available at this https URL .

AI.tldr: This paper proposes FedFit, a federated dynamic sparse training framework that uses Fisher Information Matrix scoring instead of magnitude heuristics to adjust sparse structures, narrowing the sparse-to-dense accuracy gap.
AI.motivation: Cross-device federated learning faces high memory and communication costs, and existing federated dynamic sparse training methods rely on magnitude-based heuristics that are ill-suited to non-convergent, heterogeneous FL environments.
AI.method: FedFit replaces magnitude heuristics with optimization-centric structure adjustment criteria derived from a second-order approximation of the loss landscape via the Fisher Information Matrix, avoiding explicit Hessian computation.
AI.result: Empirical evaluations across computer vision and natural language processing benchmarks show that FedFit significantly narrows the sparse-to-dense accuracy gap and outperforms state-of-the-art baselines while maintaining high communication efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Second-order Fisher Information scoring enables more accurate and communication-efficient dynamic sparse training in heterogeneous federated learning.

title: Minari: Infrastructure for Collaborative Reinforcement Learning Datasets
summary: Offline reinforcement learning (RL) depends on shared datasets, but sharing them is still hard. Each benchmark ships its own format, documentation is thin, and most datasets cannot be regenerated once the environment code moves on. We introduce Minari, an open-source Python library for creating, sharing, and loading RL datasets. Its API follows Gymnasium, so recording a dataset means wrapping an environment and stepping through it as usual. From there, users can attach metadata, filter, combine, and shuffle datasets, and publish or download them with one command through the HuggingFace Hub. Every dataset stores the environment specification, seeds, applied wrappers, and pinned package requirements needed to rebuild the environment and regenerate the data. TorchRL, AgileRL, and d3rlpy already load Minari datasets natively, so switching datasets in those libraries takes one line of code. Minari also hosts 338 reproducible datasets (350K trajectories, 55M steps) covering robotic locomotion and manipulation, maze and grid navigation, language-conditioned instruction following, Atari, and web navigation, including a full regeneration of D4RL with public generation scripts. We report baseline scores for six offline RL algorithms on the regenerated D4RL and MuJoCo datasets.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Minari, an open-source Python library and Gymnasium-compatible infrastructure for creating, sharing, and reproducing offline reinforcement learning datasets, hosting 338 reproducible datasets.
AI.motivation: Sharing offline reinforcement learning datasets is hindered by inconsistent benchmark formats, sparse documentation, and an inability to regenerate datasets once environment code evolves.
AI.method: Minari provides a Gymnasium-style wrapper API to record trajectories with metadata, filtering, combination, and one-command HuggingFace Hub publishing, while storing environment specifications, seeds, wrappers, and pinned package requirements for full regeneration.
AI.result: Minari hosts 338 reproducible datasets (350K trajectories, 55M steps) including a full regeneration of D4RL, integrates natively with TorchRL, AgileRL, and d3rlpy, and reports baseline scores for six offline RL algorithms on regenerated D4RL and MuJoCo datasets.
AI.conclusion: Minari standardizes offline RL dataset creation, provenance, and sharing, making benchmark datasets reproducible and interoperable across libraries.

title: RSIMed: Scaling Medical Foundation Models beyond Limited Clinical Data via Retrieval-Grounded Self-Evolution
summary: Rare diseases are hard to diagnose, and the labeled clinical records needed to train models for them are few, private, and slow to extend, since a specialist must read every case. A model that writes its own training tasks could learn beyond these records, but no program can check a model-written diagnosis, and a wrong answer key corrupts training. To tackle this dilemma between data scarcity and difficulty of data annotations, we introduce RSIMed, Recursive Self-Improvement in Medicine, one of the first self-evolving pipelines in which a task proposer co-evolves in context with a diagnostic solver on real clinical records. Seeded by training admissions, a frozen copy of the solver writes each clinical question from retrieved medical evidence, so its answer rests on a source, and steers topics and difficulty toward what the solver still gets wrong. On rare-disease diagnosis from MIMIC-IV admissions, the accuracy of RSIMed-27B grows linearly with training compute, while a static pool of generated tasks collapses. Without any external model, RSIMed-27B and RSIMed-9B reach 0.516 and 0.488 diagnostic accuracy, above every off-the-shelf GPT-5.6 setting, whose best reaches 0.399 at 38 times the inference cost of RSIMed-27B. Tasks written by four external teachers, including GPT-5.5, train a less accurate diagnostician than the solver's own. Trained only on diagnosis, RSIMed-RL-27B also improves on the physician-written tasks of HealthBench Professional, from 0.291 to 0.303 in adjusted score.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces RSIMed, a retrieval-grounded self-evolution pipeline for rare-disease diagnosis where a task proposer co-evolves with a diagnostic solver, enabling RSIMed-27B to outperform off-the-shelf GPT-5.6 on MIMIC-IV.
AI.motivation: Labeled clinical records for rare diseases are scarce, private, and slow to annotate, while self-generated training tasks risk corrupting training if a model-written diagnosis has an unverified or wrong answer key.
AI.method: Seeded by training admissions, RSIMed uses a frozen copy of the diagnostic solver to write clinical questions grounded in retrieved medical evidence and steers topics and difficulty toward what the solver still gets wrong.
AI.result: On MIMIC-IV rare-disease diagnosis, RSIMed-27B and RSIMed-9B reach 0.516 and 0.488 accuracy, surpassing all off-the-shelf GPT-5.6 settings (best 0.399 at 38x higher inference cost) and models trained on tasks from four external teachers including GPT-5.5; RSIMed-RL-27B also improves on HealthBench Professional from 0.291 to 0.303.
AI.conclusion: Retrieval-grounded self-evolution enables medical foundation models to scale diagnostic accuracy beyond limited labeled clinical data without relying on external teacher models.

title: Screen Before You Add: Reducing Candidate Inference in Model Ensembles
summary: As new models become available, existing ensembles must be updated to be competitive, making them intrinsically dynamic. Deciding whether to add a candidate model can require inference on an entire annotated dataset. Such a screening becomes prohibitive for models with costly inference especially when they ultimately add no value. Even under simple convex aggregation, relying on benchmark scores can be misleading as strong standalone performance does not guarantee ensemble improvement, and fitted ensemble weights can hurt test performance. In this work, we study candidate screening and show how early rejection can be achieved safely, exploiting residual geometry for stratification and rejecting the candidate when the best possible remaining predictions cannot achieve the necessary improvement. The key result that justifies this approach is that, under convex aggregation and squared or Brier loss, the population optimum improves if and only if a candidate induces a prediction change positively aligned with the residuals of the population-optimal existing ensemble. An optimistic quadratic program (QP) provides certified early rejection, while posterior-scenario sampling offers an alternative heuristic. We evaluate the approach by showing the tradeoff between saved calls and screening accuracy, which refers to recovering the same accept/reject result as for the entire annotated dataset. We assess empirically whether full-dataset decisions predict candidate usefulness on a held-out test set. On two LLM panels, stratified screening with certified QP rejection saves 21-23% of candidate calls while keeping 100% screening accuracy. In our experiments, sampling posterior scenarios further increases call savings to approximately 37%, with a loss of less than one percentage point in screening accuracy.

AI.tldr: This paper studies early candidate-model rejection for dynamic ensembles, using residual geometry and an optimistic quadratic program to save 21-23% of candidate inference calls at 100% screening accuracy.
AI.motivation: Deciding whether to add a new candidate model to an existing ensemble can require expensive inference over an entire annotated dataset, and standalone benchmark scores do not reliably predict ensemble improvement.
AI.method: Exploiting the result that convex aggregation under squared or Brier loss improves iff a candidate's prediction change aligns positively with the existing ensemble's residuals, the authors stratify candidates via residual geometry and apply an optimistic quadratic program (QP) for certified early rejection or posterior-scenario sampling as a heuristic.
AI.result: On two LLM panels, certified QP rejection saves 21-23% of candidate inference calls while maintaining 100% screening accuracy relative to full-dataset decisions, and posterior-scenario sampling increases savings to about 37% with less than one percentage point loss in screening accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Residual-guided early rejection substantially reduces the inference cost of screening candidate models for dynamic ensembles without sacrificing decision reliability.

title: Rethinking Offline On-Policy Distillation: From Scalar Advantages to Distributional Supervision
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) transfers teacher capabilities through token-level feedback on student-generated trajectories, but repeatedly evaluating fresh rollouts with the teacher is computationally expensive. Offline methods such as Lightning OPD reduce this cost by caching recorded tokens' teacher log-probabilities on fixed reference rollouts. By extending the idea to a multi-turn agentic search setup, we find that it consistently underperforms the SFT starting point trained by the same teacher. We empirically observe greater teacher--reference mismatch than in mathematical reasoning and post-training distributional flattening, and theoretically show that scalar advantage supervision on fixed rollouts admits solutions with flattened output distributions under suitable conditions. Motivated by these findings, we propose Distributional On-Policy Distillation (DistOPD), a simple yet effective offline OPD method that retains candidate-token probabilities from both reference and teacher at selected positions and aggregates the remaining parts into a residual token. On agentic search, DistOPD achieves performance comparable to online OPD while improving student--teacher alignment and using training GPU-hours comparable to Lightning OPD.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes DistOPD, an offline on-policy distillation method that retains candidate-token probabilities from both reference and teacher models plus a residual token, matching online OPD on agentic search.
AI.motivation: Online on-policy distillation is computationally expensive due to repeated teacher evaluations, while existing offline methods like Lightning OPD underperform the SFT starting point in multi-turn agentic search because scalar advantage supervision on fixed rollouts causes distributional flattening.
AI.method: DistOPD replaces scalar advantage supervision on fixed rollouts by retaining candidate-token probabilities from both the reference and teacher models at selected positions and aggregating the remaining probability mass into a residual token.
AI.result: On multi-turn agentic search, DistOPD achieves performance comparable to online OPD, improves student-teacher alignment, and uses training GPU-hours comparable to Lightning OPD.
AI.conclusion: Distributional supervision with candidate-token and residual probabilities resolves the distributional flattening of offline scalar OPD while preserving its computational efficiency.

title: Algebraic Interaction: A Recipe for Neural Architecture Generation
summary: We introduce an algebraic foundation for neural architecture design in which convolution, attention, state-space models, and equivariant layers are expressed through compositions of bilinear product operators over two structures: a position algebra governing positional routing and a feature algebra governing feature interactions. This decomposition makes routing, feature algebra, and operator composition explicit design this http URL focus on the feature-algebra axis through an Algebraic Recipe: fix the routing and operator composition of an existing architecture while replacing its feature algebra. This preserves the information-flow structure while allowing computational and symmetry properties to be modified through algebraic this http URL instantiate the recipe in linear attention, Mamba, and equivariant networks. Structure-constant and Clifford algebras improve accuracy at comparable parameter count in linear attention; structure-constant algebras yield up to $3\times$ faster training and inference in Vision Mamba at competitive accuracy; and an $\mathrm{SO}(3)$-representation algebra provides rotational equivariance by construction. These results demonstrate that feature algebra alone can control accuracy, efficiency, and symmetry without redesigning positional this http URL turns algebraic structure into an explicit design variable and reduces architecture design, within our framework, to algebraic specification.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces an algebraic foundation for neural architectures that decomposes layers into a position algebra and a feature algebra, showing that changing only the feature algebra controls accuracy, efficiency, and symmetry.
AI.motivation: Neural architectures such as convolution, attention, state-space models, and equivariant layers are typically designed separately without a unified framework isolating routing from feature interactions.
AI.method: The authors express neural layers as compositions of bilinear product operators over a position algebra (positional routing) and a feature algebra (feature interactions), and propose an Algebraic Recipe that fixes routing and operator composition while replacing the feature algebra.
AI.result: Instantiating the recipe in linear attention, Vision Mamba, and equivariant networks shows that structure-constant and Clifford algebras improve linear attention accuracy at comparable parameter counts, structure-constant algebras yield up to 3x faster training and inference in Vision Mamba, and an SO(3)-representation algebra provides rotational equivariance by construction.
AI.conclusion: Treating feature algebra as an explicit design variable reduces architecture design within this framework to algebraic specification.

title: MeltKV: Memory-Aligned KV Cache Compression via Variable-Bit Packed Vector Quantization for Long-Context LLMs
comment: 9 pages, 10 figures, 5 tables. To appear in the IEEE/ACM International Conference on Computer-Aided Design (ICCAD 2026)
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly rely on long contexts, making Key-Value (KV) caches dominate memory usage and inference latency. Existing vector quantization (VQ) methods effectively compress KV caches to sub-4-bit levels but often overlook inefficiencies in memory alignment and decoding speed. This work introduces MeltKV, a memory-latency co-optimized KV cache quantization framework for long-context LLM serving. MeltKV employs a memory-aligned variable-bit index packing scheme that adaptively assigns bit-widths to grouped key channels and compactly stores indices within standard data-types, eliminating redundant bits. Additionally, head-wise codebook sharing reduces the total codebook size while maintaining accuracy. Experiments demonstrate that MeltKV effectively compresses KV representations to sub-4-bit levels down to 1 bit and, at comparable perplexity, achieves 48.1% lower memory usage and 52.9% lower latency than state-of-the-art VQ methods.

AI.tldr: This paper presents MeltKV, a memory-latency co-optimized KV cache vector quantization framework that uses memory-aligned variable-bit index packing and head-wise codebook sharing to cut memory by 48.1% and latency by 52.9%.
AI.motivation: Long-context LLM serving is bottlenecked by KV cache memory and latency, and existing sub-4-bit vector quantization methods overlook memory alignment and decoding speed inefficiencies.
AI.method: MeltKV adaptively assigns bit-widths to grouped key channels, compactly packs indices within standard data types to eliminate redundant bits, and shares codebooks head-wise to reduce total codebook size.
AI.result: Experiments show MeltKV compresses KV caches down to 1 bit and, at comparable perplexity, achieves 48.1% lower memory usage and 52.9% lower latency than state-of-the-art vector quantization methods.
AI.conclusion: Co-optimizing index packing for memory alignment with head-wise codebook sharing makes sub-4-bit KV cache vector quantization practical for fast long-context LLM serving.

title: Earth World Model: Physics-constrained latent dynamics for forecasting and environmental scenario analysis
comment: 20 pages, 5 figures, 11 tables; includes Supplementary Information
summary: World models have been widely applied to multi-agent planning and forecasting, but exogenous environmental changes are rarely incorporated as replaceable drivers in a unified state-evolution process. This limits assessment of whether environmental perturbations propagate through physical systems with faithful dynamics. We propose the Earth World Model (EWM), an Earth-centred forecasting framework that compresses heterogeneous multi-source observations into a reusable low-dimensional latent state representing the system's history and current condition. Given explicit exogenous drivers, a shared transition operator recursively updates the latent state, and physics-constrained decoding produces multi-step forecasts. Replacing the drivers enables environmental scenario analysis and evaluation of dynamic-response fidelity. We evaluated EWM for power forecasting and environmental-perturbation response at six photovoltaic sites and one wind-power site. Across four photovoltaic sites and three forecast horizons, three independent training runs yielded mean $R^2$ values of 0.8578-0.9095. In a separate six-site decoder ablation, the mean net per-unit response $\rho$ under the prescribed irradiance intervention increased from 0.180 with a multilayer perceptron decoder to 0.922 with an analytic physical decoder, close to site- and horizon-specific analytic references. The wind model achieved an injection elasticity of $0.9990 \pm 0.0006$, while pre-intervention outputs remained unchanged. These results show that forecast fit and intervention response should be evaluated separately and that the tested EWM configurations preserved response amplitude and temporal boundaries under the prescribed interventions.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes the Earth World Model (EWM), a physics-constrained latent dynamics framework with replaceable exogenous drivers for environmental forecasting and scenario analysis, validated on photovoltaic and wind-power sites.
AI.motivation: Existing world models rarely incorporate exogenous environmental changes as replaceable drivers in a unified state-evolution process, limiting assessment of whether environmental perturbations propagate with faithful physical dynamics.
AI.method: EWM compresses multi-source observations into a low-dimensional latent state, recursively updates it via a shared transition operator given explicit exogenous drivers, and uses physics-constrained decoding for multi-step forecasts and counterfactual driver interventions.
AI.result: Across four photovoltaic sites and three horizons, EWM achieved mean R^2 of 0.8578-0.9095; in a six-site decoder ablation under irradiance intervention, an analytic physical decoder raised mean net per-unit response rho from 0.180 (MLP decoder) to 0.922, and the wind model achieved an injection elasticity of 0.9990 +/- 0.0006.
AI.conclusion: Evaluating forecast fit separately from intervention response confirms that physics-constrained EWM configurations preserve response amplitude and temporal boundaries under environmental perturbations.

title: Beveridge: Open Weight System One Decision Models with Calibrated Probabilities
comment: 23 pages, 11 figures, 8 tables. Models: this https URL, this https URL, this https URL. Code: this https URL
summary: Many production systems need a model to make a narrow decision about a document (route a ticket, check a limit, refuse a request, pick the next step of a browser agent) rather than to write text about it. We present Beveridge, a family of open weight System One decision models that take a document and up to 15 typed questions (yes/no, choice among described options, or a level on an ordered scale) and return, in one forward pass without generating text, an answer with a calibrated probability for every option. Beveridge-Large-C (398M parameters) adds a 3.5M parameter decision network to ModernBERT-large: typed number and date features in the input, exact facts from a rule engine, question-to-document evidence attention, a three-step recursive core with learned halting and an exact yes/no path. Beveridge-Pro-C adapts Gemma 4 26B-A4B with LoRA to score option letters, and Beveridge-Pro-C-Web extends it to the next step of a browser agent. On held-out tests the 0.4B model reaches 93.0% on our operations-document benchmark against 91.1% for the best of five general LLMs (31B-675B) and 87.9% for a commercial System One API, and, because its confidences are calibrated (ECE 0.029 on that benchmark), it can hand over 76% of decisions automatically at 95% accuracy, where no general LLM we tested can hand over any. It answers in 4.9 ms per decision on one NVIDIA H200 GPU and 60 ms on the 14 core CPU of an Apple M4 Pro laptop. Beveridge-Pro-C-Web raises next-step accuracy on web pages from unseen site types from 49.4% to 98.2% and completes live browsing tasks without losing document accuracy. We describe the models, the training recipes and an evaluation on 19 held-out test sets against a commercial System One API and five general LLMs, including where the models are weak. Weights and inference code are released under Apache 2.0.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Beveridge, a family of open-weight System One decision models (398M and 26B-A4B) that return calibrated probabilities for typed document questions in a single forward pass, outperforming larger LLMs and a commercial API.
AI.motivation: Production systems often need fast, narrow, calibrated decisions about documents or browser-agent steps rather than free-form text generation.
AI.method: Beveridge-Large-C (398M) adds a 3.5M-parameter decision network with typed number/date features, rule-engine facts, question-to-document attention, and a three-step recursive core with learned halting to ModernBERT-large, while Beveridge-Pro-C and Beveridge-Pro-C-Web adapt Gemma 4 26B-A4B with LoRA.
AI.result: On an operations-document benchmark, Beveridge-Large-C reaches 93.0% accuracy (vs. 91.1% for the best of five 31B-675B LLMs and 87.9% for a commercial System One API) with ECE 0.029, enabling 76% automatic handover at 95% accuracy in 4.9 ms on an H200 GPU; Beveridge-Pro-C-Web raises unseen-site next-step web accuracy from 49.4% to 98.2%.
AI.conclusion: Open-weight single-forward-pass decision models with calibrated probabilities offer substantial accuracy, latency, and automation-handover advantages over general LLMs for narrow operational decisions.

title: ECOD: Experience-Calibrated On-Policy Distillation for Multi-Turn Agents
summary: Sparse and delayed rewards make reinforcement learning challenging for long-horizon language agents. On-policy distillation (OPD) complements environmental rewards with dense teacher feedback on student-generated contexts. Standard OPD can misalign supervision with relative teacher competence, student trajectory outcomes, and the temporal structure of task execution. Recent variants adjust guidance through divergence-based weighting and temporal schedules, while joint calibration from task-completion experience remains underexplored. We introduce Experience-Calibrated On-Policy Distillation (ECOD), which allocates teacher supervision at the task, trajectory, and turn levels. ECOD compares teacher and student success-rate posteriors under matched task conditions, restricts direct supervision to failed student trajectories, and derives a temporal prior from successful teacher lengths. The resulting weight applies to teacher losses or teacher-derived advantages. We evaluate ECOD on ALFWorld and WebShop with Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. Under matched teacher settings, ECOD improves standard OPD by up to 4.06% in relative ALFWorld unseen success. Across both model scales, ECOD-assisted SOD, TCOD-F2B, and ATOD configurations yield average paired relative gains of 6.20% on ALFWorld unseen and 7.05% on WebShop, with WebShop gains ranging from 2.29% to 21.60%. These results support experience-calibrated supervision allocation as a reusable mechanism across distinct distillation objectives.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes ECOD, an experience-calibrated on-policy distillation method that allocates teacher supervision at task, trajectory, and turn levels, improving ALFWorld and WebShop agent performance.
AI.motivation: Standard on-policy distillation for long-horizon language agents can misalign teacher supervision with relative teacher competence, student trajectory outcomes, and task execution structure.
AI.method: ECOD compares teacher and student success-rate posteriors under matched task conditions, restricts direct supervision to failed student trajectories, and derives a temporal prior from successful teacher trajectory lengths to weight teacher losses or advantages.
AI.result: On ALFWorld and WebShop with Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, ECOD improves standard OPD by up to 4.06% in relative ALFWorld unseen success, and ECOD-assisted SOD, TCOD-F2B, and ATOD configurations yield average paired relative gains of 6.20% on ALFWorld unseen and 7.05% on WebShop.
AI.conclusion: Experience-calibrated supervision allocation is an effective, reusable mechanism across distinct on-policy distillation objectives for multi-turn agents.

title: SART: Sign-Absolute Reformulation Theory for Binary Variable Reduction in Neural Network Verification
summary: Complete formal verification of neural networks is crucial for their deployment in safety-critical domains. A key bottleneck stems from encoding complexity: traditional methods assign one binary variable per unstable ReLU neuron. We propose the Sign-Absolute Reformulation Theory (SART), which fundamentally breaks the conventional one-to-one mapping between unstable neurons and binary variables by establishing formal reducibility criteria. This allows for finer-grained modeling, where each unstable neuron corresponds on average to fewer than one binary variable, thereby reducing verification complexity at its source. Based on SART, we derive a theoretical lower bound on the number of binary variables required for complete verification and, under the assumption that $P \neq NP$, prove that variables in the final layer can be compressed by 50\%, while the number of variables in intermediate layers cannot be further reduced. To overcome the apparent ``last-layer-only'' limitation, we recast verification as a sequential process and, crucially, show that the gain lifts to the entire network: LayerABS, a SART-based progressive tightening verifier, iteratively treats intermediate layers as temporary final layers and propagates tight bounds that shrink the global search space and binary-variable counts. Furthermore, we reveal a structural law influencing verification complexity: when the signs of weights of unstable neurons satisfy numerical symmetry, with positive and negative weights equal or differing by at most one, the worst-case verification complexity achieves the theoretical optimum, offering theoretical guidance for the design of verification-friendly architectures. As a general-purpose underlying encoding, the value of SART is independent of specific algorithms.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Sign-Absolute Reformulation Theory (SART) and the LayerABS verifier, breaking the one-to-one mapping between unstable ReLU neurons and binary variables in complete neural network verification.
AI.motivation: Complete formal verification of neural networks is bottlenecked by encoding complexity because traditional methods assign one binary variable per unstable ReLU neuron.
AI.method: SART establishes formal reducibility criteria to model unstable neurons with fewer than one binary variable on average, proves a 50% final-layer variable reduction lower bound under P != NP, and introduces LayerABS, which iteratively treats intermediate layers as temporary final layers to propagate tight bounds across the whole network.
AI.result: Theoretical analysis shows that intermediate-layer variables cannot be directly reduced without sequential tightening, LayerABS lifts the 50% compression gain across the network, and numerical symmetry between positive and negative weights of unstable neurons achieves the theoretical optimum for worst-case verification complexity.
AI.conclusion: SART provides an algorithm-independent encoding theory and architectural symmetry guidance for reducing complete neural network verification complexity.

title: Rethinking the Verification of Machine Unlearning
summary: Machine unlearning claims require evidence that a model has removed the influence of specified training data. Yet widely deployable post hoc verifiers. infer unlearning largely from predictive behavior, the final model response that remains under the provider's control. We make this limitation concrete through Output-Level Deceptive Response (ODR), an attack that produces responses accepted by output based verifiers while preserving the original representation state. By separating output conformity from internal unlearning, ODR motivates a rethinking of machine unlearning verification, shifting the audit target from what the model returns to what changes inside it. We operationalize this shift through Representation Unlearning Verification (RUV), a gray box verifier that compares intermediate forward representations in the original and unlearned models. RUV traces a four-stage response through activation reorganization, representation displacement, neighborhood disruption, and loss of manifold support. Matched retained controls distinguish target specific responses from global model drift, while joint permutation calibration combines the four evidence views into an adaptive decision. Experiments spanning exact and approximate unlearning, class and sample level requests, multiple datasets, and diverse architectures show mean ODR deception success rates of $97.0\%$ and $97.7\%$, respectively. RUV achieves mean verification accuracies of $98.9\%$ and $94.9\%$, while rejecting $99.5\%$ and $99.8\%$ of the corresponding ODR submissions.

AI.tldr: This paper exposes a flaw in output-based machine unlearning verifiers via the Output-Level Deceptive Response (ODR) attack and proposes Representation Unlearning Verification (RUV), a gray-box verifier that achieves 94.9-98.9% accuracy and rejects over 99.5% of ODR attacks.
AI.motivation: Widely deployable post hoc machine unlearning verifiers infer unlearning from predictive outputs under the provider's control, which can be spoofed without removing the underlying data representation.
AI.method: The authors introduce ODR to produce compliant outputs while preserving original representations, and propose RUV, a gray-box verifier comparing intermediate forward representations between original and unlearned models across activation reorganization, representation displacement, neighborhood disruption, and loss of manifold support with matched retained controls and joint permutation calibration.
AI.result: Across exact and approximate unlearning, class and sample requests, and diverse architectures, ODR achieves 97.0% and 97.7% mean deception success against output-based verifiers, while RUV attains 98.9% and 94.9% mean verification accuracy and rejects 99.5% and 99.8% of ODR submissions.
AI.conclusion: Reliable machine unlearning verification requires auditing internal representation changes rather than relying solely on model outputs.

title: Can a Vision-Language Model Tune Clustering In Context?
summary: Clustering is a widely used unsupervised learning method, but selecting an appropriate algorithm and set of hyperparameters for a specific dataset can require many possible configurations and evaluations. In this work, we investigate whether a Vision-Language Model can instead visually evaluate clustering results and use those decisions to then tune an explicit clustering algorithm. We study this through three progressive experiments using Qwen3.5-27B and five controlled synthetic clustering scenarios. First, we test whether the VLM can distinguish the best clustering result from a pair of plots. Second, we test whether it can assign numerical scores to those plots where a higher score represents a better result. Finally, we use these judgments within an agentic loop in which the VLM scores a k-means clustering and proposes updated hyperparameters that may result in better clustering. Our exploratory results show that the VLM performs well when clear cluster structure is present, while struggling on more ambiguous and noisy settings. In the full agentic experiment, the VLM produces clustering configurations with silhouette scores relatively close to those of grid search and Bayesian optimization, while terminating in much fewer iterations. Overall, these results provide an initial proof of concept that VLM-based visual feedback can be used to autonomously tune an explicit clustering algorithm.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether a Vision-Language Model (Qwen3.5-27B) can visually evaluate clustering plots and tune k-means hyperparameters in an agentic loop, achieving silhouette scores close to grid search and Bayesian optimization in fewer iterations.
AI.motivation: Selecting an appropriate clustering algorithm and hyperparameters typically requires evaluating many configurations, and it is unclear whether VLMs can replace exhaustive search using visual feedback.
AI.method: Using Qwen3.5-27B and five synthetic clustering scenarios, the authors test pairwise plot comparison, numerical plot scoring, and an agentic loop where the VLM scores k-means plots and proposes updated hyperparameters.
AI.result: The VLM performs well on clear cluster structures while struggling on ambiguous or noisy settings, and in the agentic loop it reaches silhouette scores relatively close to grid search and Bayesian optimization while terminating in much fewer iterations.
AI.conclusion: VLM-based visual feedback provides a promising proof of concept for autonomously tuning explicit clustering algorithms with reduced search iterations.

title: Gradient-Guided Hardware-Native MIXFP4
summary: Blackwell tensor cores support native inference with 4-bit weights and activations (W4A4), but NVFP4 leaves a perplexity (PPL) gap to BF16. Choosing a format for each 16-element block can improve accuracy, but current matrix multiply instructions cannot execute choices this fine. Applying these rules at hardware-compatible tiles loses most of their benefit. We introduce FlipQuant, which selects E2M1 or E0M3 for each MMA weight tile. It keeps both quantized weight candidates fixed and learns a binary format map from end-to-end gradients of a bucketed KL loss to a BF16 teacher, re-evaluating them after each update. Native kernels execute 16 x 64 tiles on SM120 and 256 x 64 tiles on SM100 with median GEMM overheads of 1.9% and 1.7%, respectively. Across six language models and two corpora, FlipQuant at 16 x 64 closes 42.5% of NVFP4's PPL gap to BF16 on average, compared with 13.3% for FourOverSix. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces FlipQuant, a gradient-guided hardware-native MIXFP4 quantization method for Blackwell tensor cores that learns a binary E2M1/E0M3 format map per MMA weight tile, closing 42.5% of NVFP4's perplexity gap to BF16.
AI.motivation: Blackwell tensor cores support native W4A4 inference, but NVFP4 leaves a perplexity gap to BF16, and fine-grained 16-element block format choices cannot be executed natively by current matrix multiply instructions.
AI.method: FlipQuant keeps both E2M1 and E0M3 quantized weight candidates fixed per MMA weight tile and learns a binary format map using end-to-end gradients from a bucketed KL loss to a BF16 teacher, executed via native 16x64 (SM120) and 256x64 (SM100) kernels.
AI.result: Native kernels incur only 1.9% (SM120) and 1.7% (SM100) median GEMM overhead, and across six language models and two corpora, FlipQuant at 16x64 closes 42.5% of NVFP4's perplexity gap to BF16 on average, compared to 13.3% for FourOverSix.
AI.conclusion: Learning tile-level binary format maps aligns mixed-format 4-bit quantization with Blackwell hardware constraints while substantially improving language model perplexity.

title: Hybrid Compression for Memory-Efficient Matrix-Vector Multiplication
summary: Iterative machine-learning algorithms repeatedly access large real-valued matrices through matrix-vector products, and their performance is limited by memory bandwidth rather than arithmetic throughput. Lossless compression schemes that support computation directly over the compressed data reduce both the data moved and the memory footprint of these workloads. The mm-RePair framework [11] follows this approach by applying the RePair grammar compressor to the Compressed Sparse Row/Value (CSRV) representation of a matrix and performing matrix-vector multiplications directly on the compressed data. Its effectiveness, however, degrades on matrices that are dense or contain many distinct values. In this paper we present a hybrid strategy for the mm-RePair framework that combines grammar and entropy compression. The CSRV sequence is partitioned into a grammar-compressible component, formed by the entries that mm-RePair can compress effectively, and an entropy-compressible component holding the remaining entries, which is encoded with the ans-fold coder [24]. Compression improves further by sorting and delta encoding the entries of each row in the CSRV representation, and by remapping the alphabet to a contiguous range. Experiments on real-valued machine-learning matrices, including word embeddings and transformer hidden states, show that our hybrid strategy is more compact than the original \mmRepair on every input and reduces the peak memory of multiplication, with the largest gains on dense matrices with many distinct values, at competitive multiplication times. It also outperforms the column-reordering variant of \mmRepair on most of the matrices, and combining the two is even more compact on the sparse ones, at the cost of a much longer compression time. Finally, our strategy scales with the number of threads as well as the original \mmRepair does.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a hybrid grammar-and-entropy compression strategy for mm-RePair matrix-vector multiplication, reducing compressed size and peak memory across real-valued ML matrices at competitive multiplication speeds.
AI.motivation: The mm-RePair framework compresses sparse matrices for direct matrix-vector multiplication, but its compression degrades on dense matrices or matrices with many distinct values.
AI.method: The authors partition the CSRV sequence into a grammar-compressible component (compressed with mm-RePair) and an entropy-compressible component (encoded with ans-fold), enhanced by row-wise sorting, delta encoding, and contiguous alphabet remapping.
AI.result: On real-valued ML matrices including word embeddings and transformer hidden states, the hybrid strategy is more compact than original mm-RePair on every input, reduces peak multiplication memory especially on dense matrices with many distinct values, maintains competitive multiplication times, and scales similarly with thread count.
AI.conclusion: Combining grammar and entropy compression overcomes mm-RePair's limitations on dense, high-cardinality matrices while preserving direct compressed-domain matrix-vector multiplication.

title: Actuarial-Informed Neural Networks: Constrained Deep Learning for Sex-Specific Multi-Population Longevity Forecasting
summary: We introduce Actuarial-Informed Neural Networks (AINN), a constrained deep learning framework for sex-specific multi-population longevity forecasting that embeds actuarial knowledge into LSTM training through differentiable penalty terms. Applied to a high-longevity 6-country cluster (Switzerland, Sweden, Norway, West Germany, Netherlands, Japan; 1956-2020), the framework is a challenger to the Li-Lee benchmark and unconstrained neural approaches. Our central finding is that monotonicity constraint intensity lambda functions as a continuous governance dial with a quantifiable accuracy-stability trade-off. At lambda = 0.01, 30-year forecast confidence intervals narrow by 6.5% at zero RMSE cost. At lambda = 0.1, they narrow by 25% at only +0.84% RMSE cost. This trade-off is invisible to standard hyperparameter optimizers, which select lambda by minimizing one-step RMSE, the wrong metric for structural constraints in recursive forecasting. The framework adds three contributions: (i) residual-calibrated process noise that eliminates double-counting in the dual uncertainty framework, reducing confidence intervals by 53-60%; (ii) a 5-seed model ensemble with a coefficient of variation of 1.06%; and (iii) a time-varying credibility weight Z(t) = exp(-alpha t) connecting to Buhlmann credibility theory for blending neural and actuarial predictions. A 10-year out-of-sample backtest (trained on 1956-2010, validated against observed HMD life expectancy for 2011-2020) yields a mean absolute error of 0.38 years, with 11 of 12 country x sex combinations within the 90% confidence interval. The model produces regulatory-grade outputs including Solvency Capital Requirements under the Swiss Solvency Test (ES 99.0%: +1.91 years, CHE Male) and Solvency II, reverse stress testing, and model-based stability verification (amplification ratio 1.02x).

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Actuarial-Informed Neural Networks (AINN), a constrained LSTM framework for sex-specific multi-population longevity forecasting that achieves a 0.38-year MAE on a 10-year backtest and quantifies a monotonicity-driven accuracy-stability trade-off.
AI.motivation: Unconstrained neural longevity models can violate actuarial monotonicity and underestimate or miscalibrate multi-horizon uncertainty, which standard one-step RMSE hyperparameter tuning fails to detect.
AI.method: AINN embeds differentiable monotonicity penalties into LSTM training on a 6-country dataset (1956-2020), adds residual-calibrated process noise, a 5-seed ensemble, and a time-varying Buhlmann credibility weight Z(t)=exp(-alpha t) blending neural and actuarial forecasts.
AI.result: Monotonicity intensity lambda acts as a governance dial (narrowing 30-year CIs by 6.5% at zero RMSE cost for lambda=0.01, and by 25% at +0.84% RMSE for lambda=0.1), residual calibration reduces CIs by 53-60%, and a 10-year out-of-sample backtest (2011-2020) yields 0.38-year MAE with 11 of 12 country-sex combinations inside the 90% CI.
AI.conclusion: Embedding actuarial constraints and calibrated uncertainty into deep learning produces regulatory-grade longevity forecasts and capital requirement outputs.

title: Clustering-Based Artificial Tree Ensembles for Random Forest Approximation
summary: Random Forests (RFs) offer strong prediction performance but are difficult to interpret. Most representative trees (MRTs) and artificial representative trees (ARTs) provide surrogate explanations, but a single tree may miss patterns within a forest. We investigate benefits and limitations of clustering-based representative tree ensembles for RF surrogate modeling and assess the contribution of similarity-based clustering relative to random tree partitions. Using linear and nonlinear simulations and regression benchmarks, we evaluate fidelity, prediction accuracy, complexity, and prediction stability against equally sized ensembles of top-ranked MRTs and randomly selected trees. Increasing ensemble size generally improves fidelity, accuracy, and prediction stability. ART ensembles show higher fidelity in simulations and often greater prediction stability for small ensembles. Compared with random tree partitions, similarity-based clustering generally improves ART fidelity in simulations and often on benchmarks. On benchmark datasets, MRT-based ensembles generally achieve higher fidelity and prediction accuracy, whereas ART ensembles have fewer terminal nodes. ART ensembles provide compact surrogates when reduced complexity matters and their fidelity and prediction accuracy meet application requirements. These findings clarify both the trade-offs of representative tree ensembles as RF surrogates and the contribution of similarity-based clustering beyond random clustering.

AI.tldr: This paper compares clustering-based artificial representative tree (ART) ensembles against most representative tree (MRT) and random tree ensembles as Random Forest surrogates, clarifying trade-offs between fidelity and tree compactness.
AI.motivation: Single representative trees can miss patterns inside a Random Forest, yet the benefits of clustering-based representative tree ensembles over random partitions or MRT ensembles were not well characterized.
AI.method: Using linear/nonlinear simulations and regression benchmarks, the authors evaluate fidelity, prediction accuracy, complexity, and prediction stability of similarity-clustered ART ensembles against equally sized MRT ensembles and randomly selected trees.
AI.result: Increasing ensemble size improves fidelity, accuracy, and stability; similarity-based clustering improves ART fidelity over random partitions; ART ensembles achieve higher fidelity in simulations and have fewer terminal nodes on benchmarks, while MRT ensembles generally achieve higher fidelity and accuracy on benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: ART ensembles serve as compact Random Forest surrogates when reduced complexity is prioritized, whereas MRT ensembles offer higher fidelity and accuracy on benchmark datasets.

title: Recovered or Memorized? Investigating Dynamical Consistency and Faithfulness in World Model Latents
comment: NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Interpretability for Discovery (Interp4Discovery)
summary: World models develop internal simulators that can learn the structure and dynamics of an environment. It has been demonstrated that their internal representations are both meaningful and causal, but are these representations faithful to the governing dynamics of the environment they are learning? We introduce Anchored Recovery Certification (ARC), a procedure that utilizes a discrete Fréchet distance calculation with ground truth to evaluate dynamical consistency on candidate world models up to an affine gauge. We use the procedure on TD-MPC2 (decoder-free world model) that has learned the pendulum swing on an observation lift under varying hyperparameters at k = 5, 10, 25 steps. The model is then steered within a PCA-derived intervention subspace and compared against a ground-truth simulator using relative error to investigate dynamical faithfulness. ARC sufficiency held for TD-MPC2 most consistently at k = 10, with six of seven constraints statistically significant after Holm-Bonferroni correction, while the relative error between the simulator and the causal latent remained substantial. Further research could be conducted with decoder world models such as DreamerV3 (reconstruction loss) to investigate whether the results differ.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Anchored Recovery Certification (ARC) using discrete Fréchet distance to test dynamical consistency and faithfulness in TD-MPC2 world model latents, finding consistency at k=10 steps but substantial intervention error.
AI.motivation: While world model latents are known to be meaningful and causal, it remains unclear whether their internal dynamics are truly faithful to the governing dynamics of the environment.
AI.method: The authors propose ARC to measure dynamical consistency up to an affine gauge via discrete Fréchet distance against ground truth, apply it to a decoder-free TD-MPC2 model on pendulum swing at k=5, 10, 25 steps, and steer latents within a PCA-derived intervention subspace to measure relative error against a ground-truth simulator.
AI.result: ARC sufficiency held most consistently for TD-MPC2 at k=10 (with six of seven constraints statistically significant after Holm-Bonferroni correction), whereas the relative error between the ground-truth simulator and the causal latent under intervention remained substantial.
AI.conclusion: TD-MPC2 latents exhibit statistical dynamical consistency over moderate horizons but still lack full dynamical faithfulness under latent interventions.

title: LEAP-LLM: Preserving lead-time structure for question-conditioned ECG interpretation
summary: The electrocardiogram (ECG) records cardiac electrical activity across multiple leads and is used for detecting cardiac abnormalities. Recent ECG-language models enable large language models (LLMs) to interpret cardiac signals and answer clinically relevant questions. However, existing ECG-language models typically encode the ECG independently of the clinical question, forcing the ECG representation to retain broad and potentially irrelevant signal information. Moreover, these models often aggregate information across leads which can obscure lead-specific details needed for a particular question. To tackle these limitations, we introduce LEAP-LLM, an ECG-LLM architecture for Lead-aware ECG Alignment with Prompt conditioning.
