AI.conclusion: Machine interpreting is competitive on meaning in planned speech but remains limited in spontaneous discourse and target-language quality, highlighting key targets for MI development and interpreter training.

title: EfficientSkill: Learning Skills for Token-Efficient Multi-Turn Agents
summary: Reflective skill optimizers improve multi-turn LLM agents by revising instructions from failed and successful rollouts, yet accumulating edge-case rules bloats prompts, inflates token use, and pushes agents into long, error-prone loops. We introduce EfficientSkill, a two-step framework that first discovers a reliable skill without token penalties, and then warm-starts accuracy-guarded pruning from that skill to compress instructions, bound agent turns, and offload reusable code into workspace utilities with zero implementation prompt cost. Across four frontier, mid-tier, and open-weight models on MATH-500, ALFWorld, and SpreadsheetBench, EfficientSkill cuts output tokens over unconstrained EvoSkill on 11 of 12 configurations (by up to 80%) while raising mean accuracy on every benchmark, including +14.3 and +17.5 percentage-point gains on SpreadsheetBench with Gemini 3.8 Flash and Grok 4.1 Fast by replacing stalled loops with compact workflows. By shrinking both generated tokens and replayed history, EfficientSkill lowers total token usage and serving cost across every evaluated configuration, with or without full-prefix KV caching.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces EfficientSkill, a two-step skill-optimization framework for multi-turn LLM agents that cuts output tokens by up to 80% while improving accuracy across benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Reflective skill optimizers accumulate edge-case rules that bloat prompts, inflate token usage, and push multi-turn agents into long, error-prone loops.
AI.method: EfficientSkill first discovers a reliable skill without token penalties and then performs warm-started, accuracy-guarded pruning to compress instructions, bound agent turns, and offload reusable code into workspace utilities with zero implementation prompt cost.
AI.result: Across four frontier, mid-tier, and open-weight models on MATH-500, ALFWorld, and SpreadsheetBench, EfficientSkill reduces output tokens over unconstrained EvoSkill in 11 of 12 configurations (by up to 80%) while raising mean accuracy on every benchmark, including +14.3 and +17.5 percentage-point gains on SpreadsheetBench with Gemini 3.8 Flash and Grok 4.1 Fast.
AI.conclusion: Accuracy-guarded pruning and code offloading replace stalled agent loops with compact workflows, lowering total token usage and serving cost across evaluated settings.

title: Grounding Language Models in Speech Does Not Fix "AI Flavor": Calibrated LLM Judges, Goodhart Traps, and a Preference-Tuning Fix
comment: 11 pages, 2 tables. Code and data: this https URL
summary: Chinese outputs of large language models carry a perceptible "AI flavor": formulaic sentence frames, stacked written-register connectives, repetition loops, and layout leakage. A popular hypothesis blames text-only training for the missing inner-speech layer of human writing; injecting speech or prosody signals should therefore reduce it. We test it with controlled interventions on a 0.6B model; all three fail: (i) phoneme-interleaved continued pretraining yields no spokenness gain under text-matched controls while raising repetition (+0.13 [+0.03, +0.23]); (ii) prosody-plan conditional generation reaches an adherence of only 0.257 against a pre-registered 0.50 gate; (iii) a rule-based reward built on TTS prosody-feature distance is imperceptible in double-blind evaluation by both humans (8/16) and a calibrated LLM judge (9/16). A root cause is evaluation: single-rater blind evaluation at n~20 only detects extreme (>=85%) preferences. We therefore build a calibrated LLM-judge protocol: the judge passes catch trials on known-answer pairs (16/16; single-text 22/24, same-topic pairs 24/24, versus 0.75 for the human rater), then annotates with two independent judges under A/B swapping, counting disagreement as a tie. Using the judge's agree labels directly as DPO pairs (no reward model), we obtain the first positive result: held-out blind win rate 0.833 [0.699, 0.972], repetition 0.114 to 0.000, unchanged MMLU. We further identify a Goodhart channel: the judge's length preference transduces into output-length collapse via pairwise DPO (median 75 chars vs a 300-char prompt); an SFT-anchor repairs it (w is a style knob: w=0.1 preserves gains, w=0.3 does not). Scaling preference data from 89 to 240 pairs yields no additional judge-visible gain. We release RA-Eval v0.1: a three-layer Chinese AI-flavor evaluation framework with 382 judge-annotated preference pairs.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that speech/prosody interventions fail to remove Chinese "AI flavor" from LLMs, whereas DPO using a calibrated LLM-judge protocol achieves an 83.3% blind win rate when paired with an SFT anchor to prevent length collapse.
AI.motivation: Chinese LLM outputs exhibit a perceptible "AI flavor" of formulaic frames and repetition, and it is unclear whether grounding models in speech or prosody fixes it or how to evaluate subtle style changes reliably.
AI.method: The authors test three speech/prosody interventions on a 0.6B model, build a calibrated dual-LLM-judge protocol with catch trials and A/B swapping, apply DPO directly on judge-agreed pairs, and add an SFT anchor to counter judge-induced length collapse, releasing RA-Eval v0.1 with 382 preference pairs.
AI.result: All three speech interventions fail (phoneme pretraining raises repetition by +0.13, prosody-plan adherence reaches 0.257 vs. a 0.50 gate, and TTS prosody reward is imperceptible at 8/16 human and 9/16 judge preference), whereas calibrated-judge DPO achieves a 0.833 held-out blind win rate, drops repetition from 0.114 to 0.000 without hurting MMLU, and an SFT anchor (w=0.1) prevents median output length from collapsing to 75 characters.
AI.conclusion: Calibrated LLM-judge preference tuning with an SFT anchor effectively removes Chinese AI flavor, whereas speech-grounding hypotheses and unanchored pairwise DPO fail or trigger Goodhart length collapse.

title: NoLBERT-Calls: Reading Earnings Calls Without Hindsight
summary: Language models are now a standard tool for measuring what managers say on earnings calls, but the encoders behind these measures were usually pretrained on text from the same years a backtest covers. Holding out a test period does not remove that hindsight, because it sits in the features. We adapt NoLBERT, an encoder pretrained only on text published between 1976 and 1995, to earnings calls without letting it read anything dated after 31 December 2023. The calls supply the training signal themselves: every analyst question is followed by management's answer, and the model learns to pick that answer out from the other answers of the same call. We test on every US call from January 2025 to October 2026 (20,323 calls, 254,575 questions) and make every modeling choice on calls from 2024. The adapted model, NoLBERT-Calls-2023, ranks the true answer first for 78.0% of questions (95% interval 77.8-78.2; chance 8.0%), against 26.3% before adaptation. It is 1.0 point ahead of a call-adapted ChronoBERT, 3.4 points ahead of a call-adapted FinBERT, and 18.7 and 19.8 points ahead of the best off-the-shelf retriever and BM25. A year-by-year test over 2013-2026 finds no look-ahead premium: relative to a model adapted only through 2012, the released model does no better on the years it was trained on than on years it never saw. The price of the cutoff is compute: under one shared 150-minute recipe NoLBERT adapts least well of four encoders, and its lead comes from a longer, staged adaptation of about 13 GPU-hours.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces NoLBERT-Calls-2023, an earnings-call encoder adapted from a 1976-1995 pretrained model without post-2023 data, achieving 78.0% rank-1 answer matching on 2025-2026 calls with no look-ahead premium.
AI.motivation: Standard language models used to analyze earnings calls are pretrained on text from the backtest period itself, leaving hindsight embedded in their features even when test periods are held out.
AI.method: The authors adapt NoLBERT (pretrained only on 1976-1995 text) using earnings calls dated up to 31 December 2023 by training it to match each analyst question to management's answer among other answers in the same call, using a staged adaptation of about 13 GPU-hours.
AI.result: On 20,323 US calls (254,575 questions) from January 2025 to October 2026, NoLBERT-Calls-2023 ranks the true answer first for 78.0% of questions (vs. 26.3% before adaptation, 8.0% chance), outperforming call-adapted ChronoBERT by 1.0 point, FinBERT by 3.4 points, and the best off-the-shelf retriever and BM25 by 18.7 and 19.8 points, with no look-ahead premium across 2013-2026.
AI.conclusion: Self-supervised question-answer matching on historical calls enables hindsight-free financial encoders that match or exceed modern-pretrained baselines given sufficient adaptation compute.

title: Bridging the Terminology Gap: A Data-Centric Alignment Framework for Multilingual Translation in Cross-Border Corporation
summary: As globalization accelerates the demand for seamless cross-border enterprise collaboration, multilingual translation remains bottlenecked by insufficient domain-specific terminology, rigid terminology translation, weak instruction-following capabilities, and high inference latency in long-instruction scenarios. To overcome these barriers, we propose Bridging the Terminology Gap (BTG), a data-centric framework. First, BTG mines cross-lingual term alignments from domain documents and leverages LLMs to synthesize terminology-rich parallel corpora. Second, a hybrid filtering strategy combining heuristics and XCOMET scoring ensures high data fidelity. Third, a two-stage training paradigm employs supervised fine-tuning (SFT) for targeted terminology injection, followed by reinforcement learning (RL) to refine output preferences, effectively balancing domain knowledge integration with model reliability. Extensive offline evaluations (e.g., XCOMET, GEMBA, Acc@T) and online human assessments demonstrate significant improvements in terminology accuracy and instruction-following capabilities, validating the effectiveness of our framework, which is now deployed on our cross-border collaboration platform.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Bridging the Terminology Gap (BTG), a data-centric SFT-plus-RL framework that improves domain terminology accuracy and instruction following in enterprise multilingual translation.
AI.motivation: Cross-border enterprise translation is bottlenecked by insufficient domain terminology, rigid term translation, weak instruction following, and high latency in long-instruction scenarios.
AI.method: BTG mines cross-lingual term alignments from domain documents, uses LLMs to synthesize terminology-rich parallel corpora, applies hybrid heuristic and XCOMET filtering, and trains models via supervised fine-tuning (SFT) for terminology injection followed by reinforcement learning (RL) for output preference refinement.
AI.result: Offline evaluations (XCOMET, GEMBA, Acc@T) and online human assessments show significant gains in terminology accuracy and instruction-following capabilities, leading to deployment on the authors' cross-border collaboration platform.
AI.conclusion: Combining LLM-synthesized terminology data, quality filtering, and two-stage SFT+RL alignment effectively addresses enterprise translation bottlenecks in production.

title: Bioformer-RetroMAE: retrieval-oriented pretraining of a compact biomedical language model for literature search
summary: Dense retrieval is increasingly used for biomedical literature search and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Most biomedical bi-encoders are built on BERTBase-sized encoders pretrained with masked language modeling (MLM). These encoders are costly for corpus-scale indexing and latency-sensitive query encoding, and MLM does not explicitly train the [CLS] vector that a bi-encoder uses to represent a whole text. We present Bioformer-RetroMAE, a compact (43M-parameter) retrieval-oriented biomedical encoder obtained by continually pretraining Bioformer8L} with RetroMAE on approximately 32 million PubMed titles and abstracts. After bi-encoder fine-tuning with BM25 hard negatives, we evaluated it on BioASQ Task 12B test questions by retrieving from all PubMed abstracts. Bioformer-RetroMAE outperformed BioBERT and PubMedBERT bi-encoders fine-tuned under identical settings on all metrics, despite having about 40% of their parameters and producing 512-dimensional rather than 768-dimensional vectors. Compared with PubMedBERT, it improved mean average precision (MAP) by 37.0% and Recall@100 by 29.1%. Compared with the original Bioformer8L}, RetroMAE pretraining improved MAP by 53.6% and Recall@100 by 32.8% without changing model size or inference cost. In hybrid retrieval, fusing Bioformer-RetroMAE with BM25 through weighted reciprocal rank fusion improved MAP and NDCG@10 over BM25 alone by 4.9% and 4.6%, respectively, larger gains than those obtained by fusing BM25 with PubMedBERT or BioBERT.

AI.tldr: This paper presents Bioformer-RetroMAE, a 43M-parameter biomedical encoder continually pretrained with RetroMAE on 32M PubMed abstracts that outperforms BioBERT and PubMedBERT bi-encoders on BioASQ Task 12B.
AI.motivation: Standard BERTBase-sized biomedical bi-encoders are expensive for corpus-scale indexing and low-latency query encoding, and masked language modeling does not explicitly train the [CLS] vector used in dense retrieval.
AI.method: The authors continually pretrain Bioformer8L with RetroMAE on roughly 32 million PubMed titles and abstracts, then fine-tune it as a 512-dimensional bi-encoder using BM25 hard negatives.
AI.result: Evaluated on BioASQ Task 12B across all PubMed abstracts, Bioformer-RetroMAE outperforms BioBERT and PubMedBERT despite having ~40% of their parameters, improving MAP by 37.0% and Recall@100 by 29.1% over PubMedBERT and by 53.6% MAP and 32.8% Recall@100 over original Bioformer8L, while hybrid fusion with BM25 improves MAP by 4.9% and NDCG@10 by 4.6% over BM25 alone.
AI.conclusion: Retrieval-oriented RetroMAE pretraining makes compact biomedical encoders both faster to index and substantially more accurate than larger MLM-pretrained baselines.

title: Attribute or Abstain: Evaluating Evidence-Grounded Retrieval on the Low-Resource African Business Web
summary: Retrieval-augmented systems that research companies are judged by how much they find, yet in markets where public evidence is sparse, a confident answer without support costs more than no answer. We introduce AfriBizClaims, a benchmark of 150 company-research queries across six African markets in English, French and Portuguese, including queries about fictitious companies that a correct system must decline. Each claim a system makes is judged against the page it cites by an AI judge, checked against a second AI judge from another model family and against two human annotators, and abstentions are scored against answerability labels. We compare BM25 over a pooled corpus, standard web retrieval-augmented generation, and a multi-step agent pipeline (Konexium V1), all using the same language model. The two simple baselines are well attributed: 98% of their judged claims are supported by the page they cite, and they decline every field of every fictitious company. Counting claims about a company other than the one asked about as errors, the agent pipeline's per-query precision is 68%, and it never answers a question about a named company correctly: it substitutes other firms, including for 5 of the 24 fictitious names, and it is the least stable between runs and the most expensive. In the pipeline we evaluated, more steps between the query and the evidence did not buy more grounded answers. We will release the queries, system outputs, labels and short evidence excerpts.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces AfriBizClaims, a 150-query benchmark for African company research, showing that simple BM25 and web RAG baselines achieve 98% attribution and full abstention on fictitious firms, whereas a multi-step agent pipeline fails on 100% of named-company queries.
AI.motivation: In low-resource markets with sparse public evidence, retrieval-augmented systems that hallucinate or misattribute company facts are worse than abstaining, yet multi-step agent pipelines are rarely evaluated for attribution and abstention.
AI.method: The authors build AfriBizClaims across six African markets in English, French, and Portuguese (including 24 fictitious companies), evaluate claims against cited pages using dual AI judges and two human annotators, and compare BM25, standard web RAG, and a multi-step agent pipeline (Konexium V1) using the same LLM.
AI.result: Both simple baselines achieve 98% claim support and decline every field for all fictitious companies, whereas the agent pipeline achieves 68% per-query precision, never answers a named-company query correctly (substituting other firms, including for 5 of 24 fictitious names), and is the least stable and most expensive.
AI.conclusion: Adding multi-step agentic complexity between query and evidence can degrade grounding and abstention in sparse-evidence settings compared to simpler retrieval baselines.

title: The Vocabulary Tax: Safely Trimming Unused Tokens from LLMs for On-Device Use
comment: 23 pages, 8 figures, 16 tables. Code: this https URL ; Data: this https URL
summary: Open large language models (LLMs) and speech models ship vocabularies of up to 262k tokens, and every user downloads the tables those tokens index (the input embedding, an untied output head and, in recent on-device models, per-layer embeddings), whatever languages they need. We call the bytes in rows a deployment never uses the vocabulary tax and measure it, without downloading weights, for 1,244 generative and speech-recognition models on the Hugging Face Hub. For a Thai and English deployment it is a median 4.4% of model bytes below 0.5B parameters and 2.1% above 8B, and 1.93 GB in Gemma 4 E2B: it falls hardest on the small models that edge devices run. Keeping only the rows of the deployment's writing systems is exact. Keeping the tokens seen in the user's own text removes much more, a median 29.0% below 0.5B, but the usual way of doing it breaks BPE tokenizers: it drops the intermediate tokens that merges build on, so new text is split differently 1.9 times as often as the standard check reports. We repair this with merge closure, at a cost of 5.9% more rows, and add a trim certificate: a Good-Turing estimate, from the trimming text alone, of how much new text the trimmed tokenizer will split differently (correlation 0.996 over 300 settings in 22 languages) and of how much more text a target needs. Without test data our method never exceeds a 2% target, while prior keep rules checked on test data exceed it in 9-13 of 44 settings. On six models of 270M to 3B parameters in 11 languages, trimmed models keep their predictions: where the certificate passes, a median 89.7% of rows is removed and bits per character rise by at most 2.0%. The census, the trimming and the certificate are released as an open Python package, and the per-model tax for 41 languages as an open dataset.

AI.tldr: This paper quantifies the "vocabulary tax" across 1,244 models and introduces a merge-closure BPE trimming method with a Good-Turing certificate that removes a median 89.7% of rows while keeping predictions intact.
AI.motivation: Open LLMs and speech models ship large vocabularies (up to 262k tokens) that bloat edge-device memory, while naive token trimming breaks BPE merge chains and distorts tokenization on unseen text.
AI.method: The authors measure unused vocabulary bytes across 1,244 Hugging Face models, repair BPE trimming with merge closure, and introduce a Good-Turing trim certificate computed solely from trimming text to bound tokenization divergence.
AI.result: For Thai and English, unused rows account for a median 4.4% of bytes below 0.5B parameters and 1.93 GB in Gemma 4 E2B; merge closure costs 5.9% more rows while the Good-Turing certificate correlates at 0.996 with actual split divergence across 300 settings in 22 languages and never exceeds a 2% target, removing a median 89.7% of rows on 270M-3B models with at most 2.0% bits-per-character increase.
AI.conclusion: Merge-closure trimming with a Good-Turing certificate enables safe, substantial vocabulary reduction for on-device LLMs without requiring test data, and is released as an open Python package and 41-language dataset.

title: Anatomy of an Agent Harness: Decisions, Invariants and Corner Cases
summary: An agent harness is the program around a language model that turns its replies into actions: it builds each request, runs the tools the model asks for, decides what the model may do without asking, stores the conversation, recovers from failures, and shows a person what happened. Most of these decisions are made in code and rarely written down, so each harness meets the same corner cases again. This paper writes them down as invariants to test. It gives a system model with trust boundaries; 30 decision cards in six groups, each with options and costs, an invariant, the corner cases that break it, a test and an evidence tag; six cause classes for failures; a test method built on scripted providers, recorded behaviour and planted changes; and a checklist. The cards come from building one desktop harness, Crewroom, the author's own, and from manually testing ten other harnesses and studying open-source harnesses as reference; some patterns in the cards were adopted from those, so the catalogue is not independent of them. Of the 83 invariant clauses, 56 are tagged Tested, 12 Believed and 15 Open. The checklist is applied to the author's harness as one worked example, by its builder with no second rater: of its 30 items, 11 hold, 14 do not and 5 were not tested. It is not a ranking. The paper makes no claims about answer quality or cost or other platforms, and does not evaluate or rank other harnesses.

AI.tldr: This paper formalizes the design of LLM agent harnesses into a system model, 30 decision cards, 83 invariant clauses, and a testing checklist derived from building and inspecting 11 harnesses.
AI.motivation: Agent harnesses make critical decisions around tool execution, permissions, state storage, and failure recovery in code without written specifications, causing repeated corner-case bugs.
AI.method: Drawing on building Crewroom and manually testing or studying ten other harnesses, the authors construct a system model with trust boundaries, 30 decision cards across six groups, 83 invariant clauses (56 tested, 12 believed, 15 open), six failure cause classes, and a scripted-provider test method, applying the 30-item checklist to Crewroom.
AI.result: Applying the checklist to Crewroom shows 11 items hold, 14 do not hold, and 5 were not tested, illustrating how the catalogue surfaces concrete harness gaps without ranking platforms.
AI.conclusion: Writing down harness decisions as testable invariants provides a structured engineering checklist for catching corner cases in agentic systems.

title: The novelty exposed: ablation, reproducibility and transparency in 40 technical reports of open-weight large language models (LLMs)
comment: Empirical study with an original dataset: 40 LLM technical reports coded by two independent model coders with script-verified quotes, plus a code-level comparison of open-weight architectures in Hugging Face transformers. 20 pages, 2 figures, 2 tables. Data, coding protocol and scripts in the ancillary files
summary: In 2025 alone, 48 new large language model (LLM) architectures were added to the Hugging Face transformers library, and many of them arrive with a technical report that presents the model as new. What is actually new in these models, and is it tested? We put this question to LLM technical reports. We look at three things: what the reference code shows about how new open-weight architectures differ from earlier ones; what 40 randomly sampled technical reports claim as new and whether they support it with ablation studies; and what they disclose for reproducibility and transparency. In the library, 39 of the 48 architectures added in 2025 take at least two of their three core blocks from another model, most often Llama, although part of this reflects how the library writes code. In the reports, 19 of 73 architectural or training novelty claims come with a controlled with/without comparison; 4 of 40 reports state more than one training run; 8 rerun the models they compare against under one setup; and 1 discloses data mixture, token count, and compute together. We also looked for known components given new names: none of five candidate cases hid its origin, though we did not study model names. We propose seven reporting rules for LLM release reports and apply them to two reports. We do not judge model quality, and an untested claim may still be true.

AI.tldr: This paper audits 48 LLM architectures added to Hugging Face transformers in 2025 and 40 technical reports, finding widespread component reuse and sparse ablation or reproducibility disclosures.
AI.motivation: Many open-weight LLMs arrive with technical reports claiming architectural or training novelty, but it is unclear how much is genuinely new, ablated, or reproducible.
AI.method: The authors inspect reference code for 48 architectures added in 2025, analyze 73 novelty claims across 40 randomly sampled technical reports, audit reproducibility disclosures, and propose seven reporting rules.
AI.result: In code, 39 of 48 architectures take at least two of three core blocks from another model (most often Llama); in reports, only 19 of 73 novelty claims include a controlled with/without ablation, 4 of 40 reports state more than one training run, 8 rerun baselines under one setup, and 1 discloses data mixture, token count, and compute together.
AI.conclusion: Open-weight LLM technical reports frequently omit controlled ablations and core reproducibility details, motivating standardized reporting rules.

title: Offline-First Quantized AI: Design and Evaluation of an On-Device Maternal-Health Assistant for Low-Connectivity Environments
summary: Offline language models could extend access to maternal-health information where internet connectivity is unreliable, but deployment requires both clinically appropriate responses and feasible local execution. This study presents an offline Android assistant integrating ready-made quantized language models, a clinically validated local knowledge package, conversational context, and model-initiated local retrieval. Gemma 4 E2B and Qwen3.5 0.8B were compared across 45 conversations and 312 turns per configuration, including a dedicated offline agentic benchmark. Gemma achieved higher response-quality, context-retention, and safety scores; Qwen offered faster generation and lower memory use. Clinician assessment of 150 Gemma responses across nine clinical domains yielded a mean quality score of 3.80/4, with 147 responses meeting the acceptance criterion. A paired RAG-on/off experiment evaluated 74 questions: retrieval improved 11 responses, left 56 neutral, produced four adverse response changes, and left three pairs unassessable. RAG-on had descriptively higher mean usefulness, safety, correctness, and actionability in the conditional 70-pair subset excluding the four flagged pairs from both conditions. Physical-device testing demonstrated offline responses on a 6 GB Android handset, with a 14.3 s median latency, alongside successful reconnection synchronization in the integrated application. Together, the findings document clinical response quality and practical performance of the integrated offline maternal-health assistant.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an offline Android maternal-health assistant using quantized LLMs and local RAG, achieving a 3.80/4 clinician quality score and 14.3 s median latency on a 6 GB handset.
AI.motivation: Offline language models could expand maternal-health access in low-connectivity areas, but require both clinically safe responses and feasible execution on modest mobile hardware.
AI.method: The authors integrate quantized Gemma 4 E2B and Qwen3.5 0.8B with a clinically validated local knowledge package and model-initiated retrieval, evaluating them across 45 conversations (312 turns), clinician ratings of 150 Gemma responses, and a 74-question paired RAG-on/off study on a 6 GB Android phone.
AI.result: Gemma outperforms Qwen on response quality, context retention, and safety (while Qwen is faster with lower memory), earning a mean clinician score of 3.80/4 with 147/150 responses accepted; local RAG improves 11 of 74 responses, leaves 56 neutral, and causes 4 adverse changes, while physical-device latency is 14.3 s median with working reconnection sync.
AI.conclusion: Quantized on-device LLMs with validated local knowledge can deliver clinically acceptable maternal-health guidance offline on consumer 6 GB Android devices.

title: A Dataset for Misogyny Detection in Polish Social Media: Transferability of Hateful Speech Detection from General to Specific Types of Hate
summary: Harmful language detection is commonly evaluated on broadly defined hate speech and toxicity benchmarks, yet it remains unclear whether models that successfully detect harmful language in general can transfer this capability to more specific forms of hate. We investigate this problem for misogyny detection in Polish, an area for which dedicated resources remain scarce. We introduce a new dataset of Polish social media comments annotated for misogyny, gender-directed hateful speech. Using this resource, we first assess the reliability of LLM-assisted annotation and then evaluate general-to-specific transfer by comparing models trained on general harmful language data, safety-specialized models, and models fine-tuned directly for misogyny detection. Our results show that strong performance on general harmful language detection does not transfer uniformly to misogyny; safety-specialized models demonstrate substantially stronger generalization ability. The study contributes a new Polish resource for gender-directed harmful language and demonstrates that the scope and granularity of prior safety training are important factors in transferring harmful language detection from general to specific forms of hate.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a Polish social-media dataset for misogyny detection and shows that general harmful-language models transfer unevenly to misogyny, whereas safety-specialized models generalize substantially better.
AI.motivation: Harmful-language detectors are typically evaluated on broad toxicity benchmarks, leaving it unclear whether they transfer to specific hate forms like misogyny in under-resourced languages such as Polish.
AI.method: The authors annotate Polish social media comments for misogyny, assess LLM-assisted annotation reliability, and compare general harmful-language models, safety-specialized models, and directly fine-tuned misogyny models.
AI.result: Strong performance on general harmful-language detection does not transfer uniformly to Polish misogyny, whereas safety-specialized models demonstrate substantially stronger generalization.
AI.conclusion: The scope and granularity of prior safety training strongly govern general-to-specific hate-speech transfer, and the new Polish dataset supports future research on gender-directed hate.

title: Mandarin Wh-Indefinites Follow Nonveridicality in Multilingual LLMs, Unlike English any
summary: Multilingual LLMs learn mostly from English. Do they carry English polarity licensing over to other languages? English any is licensed by downward-entailing (DE) contexts, Mandarin wh-indefinites such as shenme 'what/something' by nonveridical ones, and the two classes come apart: perhaps licenses shenme but not any, while only licenses any but entails existence. We test this dissociation in a pre-registered study of twelve open LLMs (0.5B-9B, four families), using 48 matched bilingual frames in 21 contexts and a log-probability difference-in-differences normalised by negation. All 11 models that pass the measurement gate license Mandarin wh-indefinites under possibility, necessity and evidential adverbs, at 0.42-2.33 times the strength of negation, while English any gets nothing in the same contexts. An exploratory extension to Qwen2.5-32B shows the same. The English side is weaker: any under only, first and regret is licensed but at a fraction of negation, so only 3 models show the full double dissociation in sentence probabilities. When prompted to choose between sentences, most gated models show it. In exploratory directional ablations, a direction that carries English licensing, held-out classes included, does not reach Mandarin licensing in most models. The models do not simply apply the English rule to Mandarin.

AI.tldr: This paper tests polarity licensing across 12 open LLMs and finds that they license Mandarin wh-indefinites under nonveridical contexts rather than simply transferring English downward-entailing rules.
AI.motivation: Because multilingual LLMs train mostly on English, it is unclear whether they apply English downward-entailing licensing of "any" to Mandarin wh-indefinites like "shenme", which are licensed by nonveridicality.
AI.method: In a pre-registered study of 12 open LLMs (0.5B-9B, four families) plus Qwen2.5-32B, the authors use 48 matched bilingual frames across 21 contexts, measure negation-normalized log-probability difference-in-differences, and run directional ablations.
AI.result: All 11 gated models license Mandarin wh-indefinites under possibility, necessity, and evidential adverbs at 0.42-2.33 times negation strength while English "any" receives no licensing there; directional ablations show that the direction carrying English licensing fails to reach Mandarin licensing in most models.
AI.conclusion: Multilingual LLMs develop distinct, language-appropriate licensing mechanisms for Mandarin nonveridicality rather than blindly projecting English polarity rules.

title: The Silent Cost of Conversation History in LLM Reasoning
summary: Large language models (LLMs) in multi-turn information systems accumulate their own earlier replies and a growing task state. We asked whether this conversation history lowers accuracy, and whether process-level quality metrics warn before it does. Each analysis was fixed before its outcomes were computed. In Study 1, on 48 sharded math tasks, retaining its replies lowered final success by 0.21 for GPT-4o-mini and 0.29 for Mistral-7B (Holm-adjusted p = 0.026 and 0.004); Llama-4 Scout showed the same direction, not significant. Study 2 introduces CDR-Stream, 100-turn state-tracking dialogues with an exact answer per turn and per-model difficulty calibration. With the full history, accuracy fell from about 0.6 to 0.1 within twenty turns at matched difficulty, whereas a solver-verified state summary kept it 0.52-0.59 higher (Holm-adjusted p less than 0.001). Consistency and logical coherence fell far less than accuracy, and stability rose. None of these metrics, a paired readiness measure or calibrated single-stream drift detectors gave robust, model-general early warning, although in Study 2 the repeat-based metrics were complete only for GPT-4o-mini. In the monitors we tested, a single 100-turn stream had power only for very large drops. Systems built on LLMs should keep task state outside the transcript and monitor across sessions.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that retaining conversation history degrades multi-turn LLM reasoning accuracy by 0.21-0.59 while standard process-level metrics fail to provide reliable early warning.
AI.motivation: Multi-turn LLM systems accumulate prior replies and growing task state, but it is unclear how severely this history hurts accuracy or whether drift/consistency metrics can warn before failure.
AI.method: In two pre-registered studies, the authors test 48 sharded math tasks (Study 1) and introduce CDR-Stream, 100-turn state-tracking dialogues comparing full history against solver-verified state summaries (Study 2), evaluating consistency, coherence, stability, and drift detectors.
AI.result: Retaining replies lowers math success by 0.21 for GPT-4o-mini (p=0.026) and 0.29 for Mistral-7B (p=0.004); in CDR-Stream, full-history accuracy drops from ~0.6 to 0.1 within 20 turns while a solver-verified state summary keeps accuracy 0.52-0.59 higher (p<0.001), and none of the tested process metrics or single-stream detectors give robust early warning.
AI.conclusion: LLM systems should store task state outside the conversation transcript and monitor performance across sessions rather than relying on single-stream process metrics.

title: FRAAC: A French Multimodal Large Language Model and Dataset forPictogram-Based Augmentative and Alternative Communication
summary: Pictograms are a core modality in augmentative and alternative communication (AAC), yet recent multimodal large language models (MLLMs) cannot reliably interpret or produce pictogram sequences. Two obstacles explain this gap: the absence of a standardized pictogram grammar and the scarcity of parallel text-pictogram data. We introduce Retrieval-Augmented Pictogram Selection (RAPS), an annotation method that refines a rule-based transcription system's output with LLM-based concept extraction and retrieval over a pictogram vocabulary, handling cases where hand-written rules fail (named entities, numbers, polysemous words) without requiring new rules. Applied to French, RAPS yields a synthetic corpus of 1.4 million parallel pairs, of which 300k are publicly released. In a human ranking study where annotators order four pictogram transcriptions of the same sentence, RAPS outperforms the rule-based state of the art. Moreover, we show that standard reference-based metrics separate systems of clearly different quality but fail to rank strong systems against each other. Finally, we build an instruction-tuned model that supports interaction in several AAC modalities: it accepts pictogram or text input and answers in pictograms, speech, or text.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces RAPS, an LLM-assisted pictogram retrieval method used to build a 1.4M-pair French text-pictogram corpus (300k public), and trains a multimodal model for AAC interaction.
AI.motivation: Recent MLLMs cannot reliably interpret or generate pictogram sequences for augmentative and alternative communication (AAC) due to the lack of standardized pictogram grammar and parallel text-pictogram data.
AI.method: Retrieval-Augmented Pictogram Selection (RAPS) refines rule-based transcriptions using LLM concept extraction and pictogram-vocabulary retrieval to handle named entities, numbers, and polysemy; the authors generate 1.4M French pairs and instruction-tune a multimodal model supporting pictogram, text, and speech modalities.
AI.result: In human ranking studies, RAPS outperforms the rule-based state of the art, while standard reference-based metrics fail to distinguish strong systems from one another.
AI.conclusion: RAPS enables scalable parallel data generation and multimodal instruction tuning for pictogram-based AAC, with 300k French pairs released publicly.

title: A Corpus-Driven SentencePiece Unigram Tokenizer for Sindhi: Design and Benchmark Against Fourteen Existing Tokenizers
summary: Sindhi is a low-resource Indo-Aryan language written mainly in an extended Perso-Arabic script. Several Sindhi tokenizers have been released on public model hubs, but they have not been compared with one another on shared data. We train SentencePiece Unigram tokenizers with byte fallback at four vocabulary sizes (32k to 150k) on about 1.10 million Sindhi sentences and a smaller, repeated Urdu, Persian and Arabic slice, from four public sources, and compare them with fourteen existing tokenizers on four evaluation sets: FLORES+, Sindhi Wikipedia, a news-derived sentiment corpus, and a contemporary news corpus. The metrics are fertility, single-token retention, UNK rate, byte-fallback rate, and round-trip character loss. At 64k, our tokenizer averages 1.147 tokens per word, against 1.208 for the best existing tokenizer and 1.512 for XLM-RoBERTa, and keeps 88.6% of words as single tokens. On fertility, single-token retention and UNK rate it is best or tied for best in all four evaluation sets at 64k and above; at 32k it trails one baseline on FLORES+. Margins over the best Sindhi-adapted baselines are small (0.002 fertility on FLORES+ at 64k), and we report no significance tests. A round-trip check finds no character loss for our tokenizer and silent character deletion (up to 0.85% of characters) in two existing ones; seven others lose less than 0.1%. We evaluate intrinsic metrics only, so effects on downstream tasks remain untested. Code and tokenizer files are public (DOI: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23962474).

AI.tldr: This paper trains corpus-driven SentencePiece Unigram tokenizers for Sindhi and benchmarks them against 14 existing tokenizers, achieving top fertility (1.147 tokens/word at 64k) and zero round-trip character loss.
AI.motivation: Multiple Sindhi tokenizers exist on public hubs, but they have never been benchmarked against each other on shared data or checked for character-level fidelity.
AI.method: The authors train byte-fallback SentencePiece Unigram tokenizers (32k-150k vocabularies) on ~1.10M Sindhi sentences plus Urdu, Persian, and Arabic data, comparing them against 14 baselines on FLORES+, Sindhi Wikipedia, sentiment, and news corpora.
AI.result: At 64k vocabulary, the tokenizer averages 1.147 tokens/word (vs. 1.208 for the best baseline and 1.512 for XLM-RoBERTa), retains 88.6% single-token words, ranks best or tied on fertility, retention, and UNK rate at 64k+ across all four sets, and has zero round-trip character loss whereas two existing tokenizers silently delete up to 0.85% of characters.
AI.conclusion: The public corpus-driven tokenizer improves intrinsic tokenization efficiency and eliminates silent character loss for Sindhi, though downstream task effects remain untested.

title: Can decision models extract clinical data from cancer pathology reports? An evaluation of accuracy, calibration, and failure modes
summary: Decision models are a new class of language model that, instead of generating text, choose one option per question from a fixed list and return a probability for every option. They have not yet been evaluated on clinical text. We evaluated two open-weights decision models, Nimble 9B and Tev1 4B, for extracting 25 fields from 1,113 oral cavity cancer pathology reports from a single centre, against a prospectively maintained clinical database. We compared them with two generative models: Qwen3.5 9B, run locally, and GLM-5.3-flash, run through a cloud API. Tev1 reached a mean field accuracy of 0.917 (95% CI 0.913 to 0.920), the same as Qwen3.5 9B (0.918; p = 0.26), and was four times faster (15 s against 61 s per report). Nimble reached 0.862 and GLM-5.3-flash 0.986. Both decision models matched GLM-5.3-flash on simple dichotomous categories. They were weak on measurements binned into categories, on fields whose correct answer was not reported, and on some complex decisions (e.g. involved margins). We found that the main cause of the inferior performance of Nimble's came from asking 25 questions in one request: with two questions per request, its accuracy improved. Pooled over fields, the returned probabilities were well calibrated (expected calibration error 0.022 and 0.026), but they did not flag systematic errors within single fields. A simulated strategy of sending answers with a probability below 0.94 to GLM-5.3-flash raised Tev1's accuracy to 0.982, with 38% of answers escalated. Decision models can extract explicitly stated findings from pathology reports quickly on local hardware and return useful probabilities. They should be validated in the configuration in which they will be used, restricted to the fields in which they are reliable, and combined with other methods for numeric values.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates two local open-weights decision models (Tev1 4B and Nimble 9B) on 1,113 cancer pathology reports, finding that Tev1 matches local Qwen3.5 9B accuracy (0.917) at 4x the speed and reaches 0.982 via confidence-based escalation.
AI.motivation: Decision models output calibrated option probabilities instead of generating text, but their accuracy, calibration, and failure modes have not been evaluated on clinical pathology extraction.
AI.method: The authors extract 25 fields from 1,113 oral cavity cancer pathology reports using Nimble 9B and Tev1 4B, comparing against local Qwen3.5 9B and cloud GLM-5.3-flash, analyzing calibration (ECE) and simulated confidence-based escalation.
AI.result: Tev1 achieves 0.917 mean field accuracy (matching Qwen3.5 9B's 0.918, p=0.26) four times faster (15s vs. 61s per report), while Nimble reaches 0.862 (improving when asked 2 questions per request instead of 25) and GLM-5.3-flash reaches 0.986; probabilities are well calibrated globally (ECE 0.022-0.026) and escalating predictions below 0.94 confidence to GLM-5.3-flash raises Tev1 accuracy to 0.982 (escalating 38% of answers).
AI.conclusion: Local decision models provide fast, well-calibrated extraction of explicit clinical findings when restricted to suitable fields and paired with escalation for uncertain or numeric items.

title: Rank, Don't Regress: A 279M Text Ranker Beats 2B and 7B VLMs on Referential Urdu GUI Grounding
summary: UI grounding asks a model to find the screen element that a user instruction refers to. Most current systems use a vision-language model (VLM) that reads a screenshot and outputs pixel coordinates. We study this task on Urdu mobile web pages, a setting with no published UI grounding results. Instead of regressing coordinates, we take the candidate elements from the page DOM and train a 279M-parameter cross-encoder (mDeBERTa-v3-base) to pick one. The click point is the centre of the picked element's box, so it is exact whenever the right element is picked. We built a frozen test set of 304 instructions from six Urdu news sites; 149 of them (49%) are referential and never quote the full target text. Test domains were banned from training data before collection started. The ranker scores 73.4% point-in-box accuracy, against 29.6% for UI-TARS-2B and 23.7% for Qwen2.5-VL-7B, both zero-shot. On the referential slice the ranker scores 65.8%, against 30.2% for a string-matching baseline that needs no training. In a controlled comparison at small scale, with training data drawn from the same pages, a coordinate-regression model of similar size scores 1.6%. Adding element geometry as input tokens gives the best variant, at 75.7%. The ranker's errors concentrate in two places: elements that share identical text, and ordinal instructions such as "the fourth link".

AI.tldr: This paper shows that a 279M-parameter DOM text cross-encoder (mDeBERTa-v3-base) achieves 73.4% accuracy on Urdu mobile web UI grounding, beating zero-shot 2B and 7B VLMs by over 43 percentage points.
AI.motivation: UI grounding usually relies on VLMs regressing pixel coordinates from screenshots, which performs poorly on low-resource languages like Urdu where no grounding benchmarks exist.
AI.method: Instead of pixel regression, the authors extract candidate DOM elements, train a 279M mDeBERTa-v3-base cross-encoder to rank them (clicking the selected box center), and evaluate on a frozen 304-instruction test set from six Urdu news sites (49% referential).
AI.result: The ranker achieves 73.4% point-in-box accuracy (75.7% with element geometry tokens), versus 29.6% for UI-TARS-2B, 23.7% for Qwen2.5-VL-7B, 1.6% for small-scale coordinate regression, and 65.8% vs. 30.2% string-matching on the referential slice, with errors concentrated on duplicate-text elements and ordinal instructions.
AI.conclusion: DOM-based text ranking offers a dramatically more accurate and compact alternative to VLM coordinate regression for low-resource mobile web grounding.

title: Centered Ablation: Why Last-Layer Directional Ablation Under-Fires or Collapses, and a Closed-Form Fix
summary: Directional ablation removes a hidden state's component along a "behaviour direction" while a language model runs. It is the standard way to switch a behaviour such as refusal off, but it is erratic: on some models it barely fires, on others the text collapses into repetition. We show why, and fix it. At the last residual stream, ablation is exactly a logit bias: a fixed vocabulary footprint scaled by a gate, the cosine between the hidden state and the direction. The gate is measured from the origin, but last-layer states share a large common mode far from it, so a direction that overlaps the common mode fires on benign text and under-fires on its targets. Centered Ablation (CA) projects the common mode out of the direction, in closed form. Across 8 models, CA raises attack success by 29 and 46 points where the standard recipe under-fires, cuts collapse on Gemma-2-9B from 50\% to 1\%, and preserves 12 to 40 points more benign answers on high-overlap models, 39 to 46 more than the affine offset of prior work. Two numbers computed before generation predict, on models the analysis had not seen, which gain faithfulness and which gain attack success, and a collapse index marks when text degenerates. We also show that two standard safety judges score collapsed text in opposite directions, which can fabricate a 46-point effect.

AI.tldr: This paper explains why last-layer directional ablation under-fires or collapses text and introduces Centered Ablation (CA), a closed-form fix that projects out the residual stream's common mode.
AI.motivation: Directional ablation is the standard way to disable behaviors like refusal, but it erratically under-fires on some models and causes repetitive text collapse on others.
AI.method: The authors show that last-layer ablation acts as a cosine-gated logit bias whose origin-measured gate is corrupted by a large shared common mode, and propose Centered Ablation (CA) to project out that common mode in closed form.
AI.result: Across 8 models, CA raises attack success by 29 and 46 points where standard ablation under-fires, cuts collapse on Gemma-2-9B from 50% to 1%, preserves 12-40 points more benign answers (39-46 more than affine offsets), and reveals that two standard safety judges score collapsed text in opposite directions, fabricating a 46-point effect.
AI.conclusion: Centering behavior directions around the residual stream's common mode resolves ablation instability and exposes judge artifacts on collapsed outputs.

title: Risk-certified prompt optimization for LLM-as-a-judge guardrails
summary: LLM-as-a-judge guardrails are often controlled primarily through system prompts, yet standard prompt optimization methods target average performance rather than explicit safety constraints. This paper studies system-prompt selection as a constrained optimization problem: maximize benign pass rate while keeping the missed-attack rate below a user-specified level {\alpha} with finite-sample statistical control. The framework combines LLM-based judging, automatic prompt generation, and distribution-free risk certification. This work instantiates it in two procedures: CPS and CRISP. CPS generates a fixed pool of prompts from training data, then certifies candidates on a held-out evaluation set using simultaneous upper confidence bounds and selects the certified prompt with the highest benign utility. CRISP instead integrates risk feedback into an adaptive search, using hard example-guided rewriting and a reusable-holdout interface to steer generation toward the feasible utility frontier. Experiments on four datasets covering prompt injection, system-prompt leakage, and sensitive-information disclosure show that risk-certified selection consistently respects the target missed-attack level on heldout tests, while utility improves as the permitted risk is relaxed. CRISP is especially useful when fixed-pool search fails to produce certifiable high-utility candidates.

AI.tldr: This paper formulates guardrail system-prompt optimization as risk-certified constrained optimization and introduces CPS and CRISP to maximize benign utility while bounding missed-attack rate.
AI.motivation: Standard prompt optimization for LLM-as-a-judge guardrails targets average performance rather than providing finite-sample statistical guarantees on missed-attack risk.
AI.method: The authors propose two distribution-free risk-certification procedures: CPS, which certifies a fixed prompt pool via simultaneous upper confidence bounds, and CRISP, which integrates risk feedback into adaptive hard-example rewriting using a reusable holdout.
AI.result: Across four datasets covering prompt injection, system-prompt leakage, and sensitive-information disclosure, both methods consistently respect the target missed-attack rate on held-out tests while improving benign utility as risk tolerance relaxes, with CRISP excelling when fixed pools lack certifiable high-utility prompts.
AI.conclusion: Risk-certified prompt optimization provides finite-sample safety guarantees for LLM-as-a-judge guardrails without sacrificing benign utility.

title: Who Can You Hide Behind? Author-Conditioned Style Transfer and the Evasion of a Commercial AI-Text Detector
summary: AI-text detectors can be sensitive to changes in writing style. We examined this sensitivity by rewriting 991 AI-generated answers with Gemini, using prompts that included a writing sample from one of 55 named authors. We scored each original and its rewrite with the QuillBot AI detector. The median score fell from 100% to 0%, and the mean fell from 67.9% to 11.2%. Of the rewrites, 66% received a score of exactly 0%. Among the 699 originals scored at least 50%, 71% of rewrites scored below 10% (paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p-value below 1e-100). Scores varied across the authors used in the prompts. All rewrites associated with 10 authors scored 0%, whereas the mean score remained above 50% for six authors (Kruskal-Wallis test, p-value below 1e-80). Greater reuse of five-word sequences from the author sample was associated with lower scores, although rewrites with less than 5% reuse still averaged 15.2%. These results describe one detector and one rewriting system, not detectors in general. The study lacks a generic-rewrite baseline, did not measure preservation of meaning, and produced rewrites that were substantially longer than the originals.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that Gemini-based author-conditioned style transfer drops QuillBot AI-detector median scores from 100% to 0% across 991 AI-generated answers, with strong variation across target authors.
AI.motivation: AI-text detectors are known to be sensitive to writing style, but the extent to which author-conditioned rewriting evades a commercial detector has not been systematically quantified.
AI.method: The authors rewrite 991 AI-generated answers using Gemini prompted with writing samples from 55 named authors and score both originals and rewrites with the QuillBot AI detector.
AI.result: Median detection scores fall from 100% to 0% (mean 67.9% to 11.2%), with 66% of rewrites scoring 0% and 71% of high-scoring originals dropping below 10% (p < 1e-100); scores vary significantly by author (p < 1e-80), with 10 authors yielding 0% on all rewrites and 6 averaging above 50%.
AI.conclusion: Author-conditioned style transfer can substantially evade a commercial AI-text detector, though findings are limited to one detector, one rewriter, and longer rewrites without meaning-preservation checks.

title: Do We Still Need Fine-Tuned Classifiers? Swapping Typed Decision Models into 24 ACL-Venue Papers
summary: Typed Decision Models such as TypeSafe's Jev, also called System One or System 1 models, answer typed questions about an input with a probability for each option, and they need no training. Many NLP papers still fine-tune a task-specific classifier, and prompted large language models (LLMs) trail such classifiers on most text classification benchmarks. We ask how many of these fine-tuned classifiers a Typed Decision Model can replace under each paper's own evaluation, and what is needed where it cannot. We swap the predictors of 24 ACL-venue papers for Jev, keep each paper's splits, label definitions and metric, and check the results with Cloudflare's Clef, Microsoft-Decision-1 and OpenAI's GPT-6 Luna Decisions. The resulting 46 English test sets, with their questions and published scores, form the TDM-Gauntlet benchmark. With a zero-shot prompt, Jev directly replaced the paper's predictor on 12 of the 46 test sets, mostly single judgments with plain labels, but rarely where the paper's method was trained on its labels. Where Jev scored lower, we most often attributed the shortfall to an annotation convention that the label name does not state. With 500 training labels plus validation and no user-managed GPU, calibration and GEPA-style prompt optimization closed a median 72% of the gap to the paper's method, about twice what off-the-shelf GEPA closed, for a median $1.66 per search. On the same labels, fine-tuned encoders such as RoBERTa and DeBERTa closed 59%, and LoRA fine-tuning of the open LLM Qwen3.8-27B closed 97%. Fine-tuning remains the most accurate option, but a zero-shot prompt is often enough for plain labels, and prompt optimization closes most of the remaining gap.

AI.tldr: This paper swaps Typed Decision Models (Jev) into 24 ACL-venue papers (46 test sets, TDM-Gauntlet), finding that zero-shot prompts replace 12 classifiers and prompt optimization closes a median 72% of the remaining gap.
AI.motivation: Many NLP papers still fine-tune task-specific classifiers, and it is unclear how many can be replaced by training-free Typed Decision Models that output calibrated option probabilities.
AI.method: The authors build TDM-Gauntlet from 46 English test sets across 24 ACL papers, evaluate Jev zero-shot (cross-checked with Clef, Microsoft-Decision-1, and GPT-6 Luna Decisions), and test calibration plus GEPA-style prompt optimization on 500 training labels without user-managed GPUs.
AI.result: Zero-shot Jev directly replaces the paper's classifier on 12 of 46 test sets (mostly plain-label single judgments); with 500 labels, calibration and GEPA-style optimization close a median 72% of the gap (for $1.66 median per search), versus 59% for fine-tuned RoBERTa/DeBERTa and 97% for LoRA Qwen3.8-27B.
AI.conclusion: Fine-tuning remains most accurate overall, but zero-shot Typed Decision Models suffice for plain labels and prompt optimization bridges most of the gap without GPU management.

title: FIDEL: Abugida-Aware Pre-tokenization for Ethiopic Languages
summary: Subword tokenizers assume that meaningful linguistic units can be recovered by splitting text at learned boundaries, an assumption better suited to concatenative morphology than to Semitic root-and-pattern systems. The challenge is acute for the Ethiopic languages, whose abugida script encodes consonant-vowel units as single characters and hides consonantal structure. We introduce FIDEL (FIdäl DEcomposition and Linearization), a family of reversible abugida-aware pre-tokenization schemes that expose consonant and vowel-order structure, extend SPLINTER reductions from abjad scripts to the Ethiopic abugida, and evaluate them on three Ethiopic languages under controlled conditions, holding corpus, architecture, budget and protocol fixed so that tokenization is the only variable. We report intrinsic tokenizer statistics for BPE and UnigramLM across vocabulary sizes alongside downstream NLP tasks, including transfer scenarios. We find that FIDEL reduction improves news classification consistently and named-entity recognition at larger capacity, while sentiment analysis performance declines under the more aggressive schemes, and extractive question answering performance is preserved.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces FIDEL, a family of reversible abugida-aware pre-tokenization schemes for Ethiopic languages, improving news classification and large-capacity NER while preserving QA performance.
AI.motivation: Subword tokenizers split text at learned boundaries suited to concatenative morphology, hiding the consonantal root-and-pattern structure encoded in Ethiopic abugida characters.
AI.method: The authors propose FIDEL (FIdäl DEcomposition and Linearization) to reversibly expose consonant and vowel-order structure, extending SPLINTER reductions to three Ethiopic languages under controlled BPE and UnigramLM comparisons.
AI.result: FIDEL consistently improves news classification and improves named-entity recognition at larger model capacity, preserves extractive QA performance, and reduces sentiment analysis accuracy under more aggressive decomposition schemes.
AI.conclusion: Abugida-aware pre-tokenization benefits structure-sensitive Ethiopic tasks like classification and NER, though aggressive decomposition can hurt sentiment analysis.

title: Hochschild Cocycle and Universality of Merge
summary: The Hopf algebra Markov chain dynamical system, on the Hopf algebra of non-planar binary forests, that models the action of Merge on workspaces in Chomsky's Minimalist Model of syntax, satisfies a universal property, determined by the fact that the Merge operation is a Hochschild 1-cocycle. This universal property has an interpretation in terms of models of the syntax-semantics interface, as it shows that, if the side of semantics possesses a sufficiently rich compositional structure, then that structure is uniquely induced by the syntactic Merge, once the semantic values of lexical items and syntactic features are assigned. We illustrate how this universality works by showing, in particular, full compatibility of this Hopf algebraic formulation with Heim-Kratzer semantics.

AI.tldr: This paper proves that the Hopf-algebraic Merge operation in Chomsky's Minimalist syntax is a Hochschild 1-cocycle, inducing a universal property that uniquely determines compositional semantics.
AI.motivation: Formalizing the syntax-semantics interface in Minimalist syntax requires understanding how syntactic Merge constrains and induces semantic composition.
AI.method: The authors analyze the Hopf algebra Markov chain dynamical system on non-planar binary forests modeling Merge and establish its universal property via the Hochschild 1-cocycle condition, demonstrating compatibility with Heim-Kratzer semantics.
AI.result: Once lexical semantic values and syntactic features are assigned, any sufficiently rich compositional semantic structure is uniquely induced by syntactic Merge.
AI.conclusion: The Hochschild 1-cocycle property provides a rigorous algebraic foundation for the universality of Merge at the syntax-semantics interface.

title: When Should Decision Models Compare Candidates?
summary: Language-model agents frequently select among candidate actions, such as tools and web elements. Should decision models score candidates independently or allow their scores to depend on other candidates? We investigate this question by comparing three approaches: Pointwise scoring, Setwise scoring, and Candidate Attention. Across five agent-decision benchmarks, Pointwise scoring remains competitive, while Setwise scoring performs better on some tool-selection and binary-decision tasks. Candidate Attention does not consistently improve upon Pointwise scoring, despite allowing cross-candidate interaction. Using two controlled synthetic tasks, we further examine whether models learn to use candidate-set information. With targeted relational training, Setwise models learn candidate dependencies and generalize to shifted inputs, while Candidate Attention shows weaker transfer. Our results show that access to other candidates does not guarantee effective comparison, and that its benefits depend on both task requirements and training.

AI.tldr: This paper compares Pointwise, Setwise, and Candidate Attention scoring for LLM-agent decision models, finding that Pointwise remains competitive while Setwise excels on relational tasks only with targeted training.
AI.motivation: Agent decision models must select among candidate actions or web elements, but it is unclear when cross-candidate comparison actually helps over independent scoring.
AI.method: The authors compare Pointwise scoring, Setwise scoring, and Candidate Attention across five agent-decision benchmarks and two controlled synthetic tasks testing relational generalization.
AI.result: Pointwise scoring remains competitive across the five benchmarks, Setwise scoring wins on some tool-selection and binary-decision tasks, and Candidate Attention fails to consistently beat Pointwise; on synthetic tasks, Setwise generalizes to shifted inputs after targeted relational training whereas Candidate Attention transfers poorly.
AI.conclusion: Giving decision models access to other candidates does not automatically yield effective comparison; gains depend on both task structure and relational training.

title: Refusal Register is Causally Steerable: Decomposing the Refusal Direction into Category-Aligned Components in Gemma-2-9B-IT
comment: 10 pages, 7 figures. Code: this https URL
summary: Prior work shows that refusal in instruction-tuned language models can be ablated by intervening on a single residual-stream direction (Arditi et al., 2024), and more recent work finds multiple refusal-mediating directions and concept cones (Wollschläger et al., 2025). We ask a different question: do refusal-related directions carry information about the register of refusal language - how the model refuses - and not only whether it refuses? In Gemma-2-9B-IT we identify two SVM-derived linear directions (B1 for harmful-content vs. neutral, B2 for self-reference vs. neutral) at layer 20 with cos(B1, B2) = 0.252 (about 75 degrees, substantially non-parallel). Adding the harmful-vs-neutral difference-of-means direction (cosine 0.68 with B1) to the residual stream of self-reference prompts at alpha = 2.0 shifts content-safety vocabulary from 2.55 to 10.37 hits per 100 tokens, while a magnitude-matched random direction produces 1.13-2.16; the model continues to refuse but switches register from meta-style ("as a language model...") to content-style ("this would be harmful"). The same register-injection effect reproduces qualitatively in Gemma-2-2B-IT at layer 12 (content vocabulary 1.72 -> 6.37 at alpha = 1.0, vs. random control 1.35), with a narrower coherent-injection window than in 9B. The two directions are not symmetric: the B2 -> harmful intervention produces a much smaller register effect, and across ablation, sufficiency, and injection B1's causal effects are consistently larger than B2's. We frame this asymmetry as part of the finding: B1 appears to encode both category detection and refusal-vocabulary information, while B2 encodes primarily category detection. We frame the contribution as identifying category-aligned components related to the Arditi-style difference-of-means direction that play distinct functional roles in refusal register.

AI.tldr: This paper decomposes refusal in Gemma-2-9B-IT into two non-parallel directions (harmful-content vs. self-reference) that causally steer refusal register between meta-style and content-safety vocabulary.
AI.motivation: Prior work showed that single or multiple directions mediate whether a model refuses, but not whether those directions encode how the model refuses (its linguistic register).
AI.method: The authors extract two SVM directions at layer 20 of Gemma-2-9B-IT—B1 (harmful vs. neutral) and B2 (self-reference vs. neutral)—and perform activation injection, ablation, and sufficiency tests, replicating in Gemma-2-2B-IT.
AI.result: B1 and B2 are nearly orthogonal (cos = 0.252); injecting the harmful-vs-neutral difference-of-means direction into self-reference prompts shifts content-safety vocabulary from 2.55 to 10.37 hits per 100 tokens (vs. 1.13-2.16 random), switching register from meta-style to content-style while preserving refusal, with B1 showing consistently stronger causal effects than B2.
AI.conclusion: Category-aligned refusal directions play asymmetric functional roles, encoding both category detection and the linguistic register of refusal.

title: Augmenting Pretrained Language Models with N-gram Embeddings through Incremental Training
summary: As a new scaling technique for large language models, the n-gram embedding improves the base ability of a model while adding almost no inference cost. Mainstream research realizes it through joint training of the n-gram embedding with the backbone, which severely restricts the settings in which an n-gram embedding can be used. We therefore propose training an n-gram embedding onto an existing model through incremental training, to extend where the technique can deliver value. Specifically, we explore several settings of the n-gram embedding under incremental training---the learning rate of the embedding, the vocabulary size, and the injection position---and train an n-gram embedding onto the existing model under the best configuration. Experiments show that the best configuration under incremental training does not fully coincide with that under pretraining; moreover, the incrementally trained knowledge is written predominantly into the n-gram embedding, while the general ability of the backbone is retained throughout this training process.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes incremental training of n-gram embeddings onto existing pretrained LLMs, showing that optimal hyperparameters differ from pretraining and knowledge is stored in the n-gram table without degrading backbone abilities.
AI.motivation: N-gram embeddings improve LLM capabilities at near-zero inference cost, but standard joint pretraining restricts their adoption on already-trained models.
AI.method: The authors incrementally train n-gram embeddings onto an existing pretrained model while varying embedding learning rate, vocabulary size, and injection position.
AI.result: Optimal configurations under incremental training differ from pretraining setups, and incrementally learned knowledge is written predominantly into the n-gram embedding while preserving the backbone's general capabilities.
AI.conclusion: Incremental n-gram embedding training offers a practical way to augment existing pretrained LLMs without forgetting or inference overhead.

title: Abstention Direction in Large Language Models: Mechanistic Interpretability of Abstention Across Query Ambiguity, Knowledge Limits, and Safety Alignment
summary: Abstention, the withholding of a response by a large language model (LLM) under uncertainty or safety risks, is essential for trustworthy models. The causes of abstention fall into three perspectives: ambiguity in the Query (Q), limits of Model Knowledge (MK), and misalignment with Human Values (HV). However, prior analyses of internal representations have focused on HV, using a refusal direction computed from harmful and harmless queries. No study has analyzed the three perspectives jointly. We therefore extend the refusal direction framework to all three perspectives. Specifically, for each perspective, we construct counterfactual pairs that share a template and differ only in the abstention-inducing factor, and compute an abstention direction by normalizing the difference in mean activations between the two polarities. Activation steering experiments show that intervening in middle layers increases or decreases abstention across all three perspectives. Moreover, steering yields cross-perspective effects, indicating that the abstention directions share a common directional component.

AI.tldr: This paper extends refusal-direction interpretability to abstention across query ambiguity, model knowledge limits, and human values, finding that middle-layer steering works across all three via a shared directional component.
AI.motivation: Prior mechanistic interpretability of abstention focused solely on human-value safety alignment, leaving query ambiguity and knowledge-limit abstention unexamined.
AI.method: The authors construct template-matched counterfactual pairs for each of the three abstention perspectives, compute normalized difference-in-means abstention directions, and perform middle-layer activation steering experiments.
AI.result: Intervening in middle layers increases or decreases abstention across all three perspectives and produces cross-perspective steering effects, demonstrating a shared directional component.
AI.conclusion: Abstention across ambiguity, knowledge limits, and safety alignment shares a common mechanistic representation in middle layers of LLMs.

title: Weight-Space Programming Changes How an LLM Uses Python for Computational Biology
comment: 16 pages, 3 figures, 6 main tables, and 1 supplementary table
summary: Weight-space programming allows a language model to edit another model's weights without gradient-based training. We used Claude Opus 5.5 to edit Qwen3.5-0.8B and investigated how the edits changed its use of Python on computational biology problems. We compared four initial edited checkpoints with the original model on 50 test problems across three test seeds, yielding 600 paired evaluations. Strictly correct answers increased from 44 to 77, and technically correct answers, which included correct final values rejected for formatting, increased from 64 to 100. Repeated Python calls decreased from 1,834 to 1,044. Among the 64 pairs in which only the edited response was technically correct, the original model had already computed the correct value in 36 but did not submit a technically correct final answer. The edited model corrected the computation in 13 of the 64 pairs. With six additional checkpoints on the same 50 problems, technically correct answers rose from 96 to 154 across 900 pairs. We explored three selected problems with ten test seeds for each of ten checkpoints. On the melting-temperature problem, correct Python outputs decreased from 60 to 22 while technically correct final answers increased from 0 to 18. Weight editing changed both the calculations Qwen ran and whether it submitted a correct answer.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that weight-space programming (editing Qwen3.5-0.8B weights using Claude Opus 5.5) alters both Python computation and answer submission on computational biology problems, raising technically correct answers from 64 to 100.
AI.motivation: Weight-space programming enables one LLM to edit another model's weights without gradient training, but how such edits change tool-use behavior like Python execution is poorly understood.
AI.method: The authors use Claude Opus 5.5 to edit Qwen3.5-0.8B weights and evaluate four initial and six additional checkpoints across 50 computational biology problems (600 and 900 paired evaluations).
AI.result: Strictly correct answers rise from 44 to 77 and technically correct answers from 64 to 100 (and 96 to 154 across 900 pairs) while repeated Python calls drop from 1,834 to 1,044; in 36 of 64 newly solved pairs the original model had already computed the right value but failed to submit it, and on a melting-temperature problem correct Python outputs fell (60 to 22) even as final answers rose (0 to 18).
AI.conclusion: Non-gradient weight-space edits reshape both internal tool-use computations and final-answer formatting/submission behavior.

title: Language Models Meet Vibration Testing for LEO Constellation Satellites with Calibrated Response Prediction from Few-show Sweeps
summary: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly drive engineering analysis end to end, turning textual records into the inputs of numerical programs, but a plausible and wrong value can pass silently into a decision. We propose deterministic validation gates for LLM-driven engineering analysis, a general paradigm in which a typed configuration produced by LLMs is consumed only after it passes deterministic checks on units, physical consistency, verbatim quotes, agreement between independent models, consistency with measurement exports and the applicability of trained models. The gates target hallucinations from two directions, since quote checking catches fabricated content while agreement between models catches errors of omission that quote checking misses. We instantiate the paradigm on sine vibration acceptance testing for low Earth orbit mega-constellation satellites, where DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and Qwen-plus read Chinese test records and extract a configuration of 76 fields. Fact-level F1 ranged from 0.98 to 1.0 on five input variants, with all repairs frozen on development inputs and evaluated on held-out inputs. With all gates, 20 of 20 configurations produced notching results bit for bit identical to the gold run, and all 17 real and injected errors in consumed fields were stopped, of which 16 would have run without gates. Retraining the bound model on a dataset built from an LLM configuration reproduced its results within GPU nondeterminism. We also report a negative result of practical value. Direct LLM curve forecasting only matches linear extrapolation, whereas a small physics-structured network reduces the over-notched bandwidth by 86% to 89% at calibrated coverage c = 0.90, which delineates where direct LLM prediction should give way to a trained model.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces deterministic validation gates for LLM-driven engineering analysis, stopping all 17 real and injected errors in 76-field satellite vibration-testing configurations while showing physics-structured networks beat direct LLM curve forecasting.
AI.motivation: LLMs extracting numerical-program inputs from engineering text can silently pass plausible but wrong values into safety-critical decisions.
AI.method: The authors require LLM-extracted typed configurations to pass deterministic checks on units, physical consistency, verbatim quotes, cross-model agreement (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and Qwen-plus), export consistency, and model applicability on Chinese LEO satellite sine-vibration test records.
AI.result: Extraction achieves 0.98-1.0 fact-level F1, 20/20 gated configurations produce bit-identical notching results to gold runs, and all 17 errors are blocked (16 would have run without gates); for curve forecasting, direct LLM prediction only matches linear extrapolation whereas a small physics-structured network cuts over-notched bandwidth by 86-89% at 0.90 calibrated coverage.
AI.conclusion: Deterministic validation gates make LLM-driven engineering extraction reliable, while specialized physics-structured models remain necessary for numerical curve forecasting.

title: Invariant-Aware Harness Enforcement to Protect LLM Agents from Silent API Failures
comment: 26 pages, 7 figures. Code: this https URL . Data: this https URL
summary: LLM agents answer questions by calling APIs and trusting the results. An API can fail silently. It ignores part of a request, such as a misnamed filter, yet returns HTTP 200 and a plausible but wrong result. Current fixes, such as checklists, reviewer models and LLM judges, ask the model to catch it. But models often see the problem and answer anyway. We present SilentGuard, which moves the decision from the model to the harness running tool calls. It tests each result against invariants that any correct API must satisfy and withholds values that break one.
