Our experiments reveal an important requirement for planning representations: they must separate invariant spatial task structure from appearance.

AI.tldr: Through controlled visual-factor evaluations in ProcTHOR ObjectNav, the paper shows that surface material changes most strongly impair navigation, and that planning representations must separate invariant spatial task structure from visual appearance.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of visual generalization in navigation change multiple factors simultaneously, making it hard to identify which visual variations cause failures.
AI.method: The authors evaluate model-free RL, model-based RL, and agents with frozen pretrained visual features on ProcTHOR ObjectNav where floor plans, object locations, goals, and start states are held fixed while visual factors (surface materials, clutter, lighting, goal appearance) are varied individually or together.
AI.result: Surface material changes account for most of the drop in success, whereas clutter and lighting have little effect; global image statistics do not reliably predict performance, and a model-based agent planning over frozen DINOv2 features achieves the highest success (0.83) under full shift while remaining sensitive to surface appearance.
AI.conclusion: Effective planning representations must separate invariant spatial task structure from visual appearance.

title: Where slide-level foundation-model classifiers fail on atypical breast lesions
summary: Whether a ductal breast lesion is called atypical hyperplasia or low-grade carcinoma in situ increasingly determines surgery. However, slide-level classifiers built on pathology foundation models (PFMs) perform worst on these lesions. Using four PFMs, cross-validation on BRACS and preregistered hypotheses, we studied where the classification of atypia fails. Because slides are labelled with their most severe lesion, only 39% of the slides with annotated atypical ductal hyperplasia (ADH) were labelled ADH. Attention ranked the lesion high but rarely first, and showing the model only the lesion helped little, whereas classifiers trained per decision with lesion-level labels improved all four atypical boundaries. ADH regions inserted into benign slides raised the probability of malignancy more than that of atypia. In a hospital with pathologist-labelled single-subtype slides and in HISTAI, benign slides were scored closer to lesions and triage specificity fell from 0.48-0.53 to 0.00-0.07 and 0.22.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates why slide-level pathology foundation-model (PFM) classifiers fail on atypical breast lesions, finding that slide-level max-severity labelling and attention misranking cause severe drops in triage specificity.
AI.motivation: Distinguishing atypical ductal hyperplasia (ADH) from low-grade carcinoma in situ increasingly determines surgery, yet slide-level PFM classifiers perform worst on these atypical lesions.
AI.method: Using four PFMs, cross-validation on BRACS, and preregistered hypotheses, the authors analyze slide-level vs. lesion-level labels, attention ranking, region insertion into benign slides, and external validation on hospital single-subtype slides and HISTAI.
AI.result: Only 39% of slides with annotated ADH were labelled ADH due to max-severity labelling; attention rarely ranked ADH first, lesion-level labels improved all four atypical boundaries, inserting ADH into benign slides raised malignancy probability more than atypia, and triage specificity fell from 0.48–0.53 to 0.00–0.07 (hospital) and 0.22 (HISTAI).
AI.conclusion: Slide-level max-severity labels and global aggregation obscure atypical lesions, highlighting the need for lesion-level supervision in pathology foundation models.

title: Floorplan-Context-Aware Cross-Environment Human Activity Recognition from mmWave Radar Point Clouds
summary: Human activity recognition (HAR) models based on mmWave radar point clouds and trained in controlled open spaces often experience performance degradation when deployed in furnished rooms. We propose a Floorplan-Context-Aware (FCA) HAR enhancement method that augments the input with subject-furniture relative position information to improve cross-environment performance. Because existing mmWave point-cloud datasets lack registered floorplans, we introduce a pseudo-landmark augmentation strategy for training the FCA model. In cross-environment evaluation on the mm-ADL-Home dataset, FCA achieves 77.70% accuracy and 65.49% macro-F1, improving upon the point-cloud-only direct-transfer baseline by 10.73 and 10.05 percentage points, respectively, and exceeding the strongest evaluated adaptation baseline by 7.37 and 6.27 percentage points. At deployment, FCA requires only a one-time registration of furniture landmarks, with no target-domain activity annotations or model weight updates.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Floorplan-Context-Aware (FCA) human activity recognition from mmWave radar point clouds, using pseudo-landmark augmentation during training to improve cross-environment generalization in furnished rooms.
AI.motivation: mmWave radar HAR models trained in open spaces degrade significantly when deployed in furnished rooms, and existing datasets lack registered floorplans.
AI.method: FCA augments radar point-cloud inputs with subject-furniture relative position information and introduces a pseudo-landmark augmentation strategy for training; deployment requires only a one-time registration of furniture landmarks without target-domain activity labels or weight updates.
AI.result: On the mm-ADL-Home dataset in cross-environment evaluation, FCA achieves 77.70% accuracy and 65.49% macro-F1, outperforming the point-cloud-only direct-transfer baseline by 10.73 and 10.05 percentage points and the strongest adaptation baseline by 7.37 and 6.27 percentage points.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating floorplan-context landmarks via pseudo-landmark training substantially improves cross-environment mmWave HAR without target-domain retraining.

title: Beyond the Training Cameras: Coverage-Controlled Probes of Viewing Direction in Frozen Vision Models
summary: Vision models are trained on 2D images of a 3D world. Do their hidden features encode the direction from which the camera views a scene, and if so, in what form? We study the relative viewing direction $\alpha$ of two objects in rendered scenes where both object centres stay at fixed pixels while the camera moves, so that perspective, shading and shadows change but the projected layout does not. In eight pretrained models, from diffusion models to self-supervised and image-text encoders, $\alpha$ is encoded in a strikingly simple form: a single two-dimensional plane in the hidden space, shared across scenes, in which the difference between the two objects' features traces $(\cos\alpha, \sin\alpha)$. The plane keeps its orientation when lighting, colours, floors and object shapes change. This encoding is more than a summary of a few visible measurements: readouts fitted on one set of camera paths stay accurate at camera positions outside their range in seven of the eight models, whereas decoders of the measured object and shadow geometry, equally accurate within that range, fail there. In the diffusion transformer PixArt-$\alpha$, the plane forms abruptly at a single block and carries direction information to later blocks, yet editing it changes the objects rather than the generated viewpoint. We also examine how this encoding carries over to scanned real objects.

AI.tldr: Probing eight frozen vision models on rendered scenes with fixed object pixel centres, the paper discovers that relative viewing direction is encoded in a single shared 2D plane that generalizes beyond the training camera paths.
AI.motivation: Vision models are trained on 2D images of a 3D world, but it is unclear whether and in what form their hidden features encode camera viewing direction.
AI.method: The authors render scenes where two object centres remain at fixed pixels while the camera moves (changing perspective, shading, and shadows) and probe eight pretrained models (diffusion, self-supervised, and image-text encoders) for relative viewing direction α.
AI.result: Across all eight models, the difference between the two objects' features traces (cos α, sin α) in a single shared 2D plane invariant to lighting, colours, floors, and shapes; readouts generalize outside training camera paths in 7 of 8 models (unlike geometry/shadow decoders), and in PixArt-α the plane forms abruptly at one block though editing it alters objects rather than viewpoint.
AI.conclusion: Frozen vision models naturally encode relative camera viewing direction as a simple, generalizable 2D circular subspace.

title: From Cloud to Edge: A Fully Local Pipeline for Pothole Risk Assessment and Driver Warning Generation
comment: 23 pages, 8 figures, 7 tables. And submitted to MDPI Sensors
summary: Vision-language models can turn road images into clear, geometry-aware pothole warnings, but current systems depend on commercial cloud services. Our earlier five-stage pipeline needed two cloud calls per scene, taking about 20 s and USD 0.105, and could not run offline. We rebuild every stage to run on a single local GPU and evaluate it with the same data, prompts, and protocol. Segmentation keeps the original Segment Anything weights but runs them in half precision with graph compilation, which makes it 2.7x faster without changing any downstream risk class; five lightweight variants could not match its masks on small road defects. Severity is graded by six ConvNeXt students distilled from 3092 cloud labels. They reach Cohen's kappa = 0.268 against human consensus at 28 ms per pothole, close to the cloud model's 0.321, within the camera setup they were trained for. A local 8-billion-parameter vision-language model writes the warnings under a grammar that admits only in-lane maneuvers. Three blind, independent raters scored these warnings safer than the cloud warnings (4.18 vs. 3.65 of 5; p = 0.001; 50 scenes) and equally clear, whereas an automated LLM judge ranked them the other way. The complete pipeline runs at 1.27 s per scene, 16x faster than the cloud system, offline and at no per-scene cost.

AI.tldr: The paper rebuilds a cloud-based five-stage pothole risk assessment and driver warning pipeline to run completely locally on a single GPU, achieving 16x faster inference (1.27 s/scene) at zero per-scene cost.
AI.motivation: Existing geometry-aware pothole warning pipelines depend on commercial cloud services, taking about 20 s and USD 0.105 per scene and failing to operate offline.
AI.method: The authors run Segment Anything in half precision with graph compilation (2.7x faster), distill severity grading into six ConvNeXt students from 3,092 cloud labels, and use a local 8B vision-language model constrained by a grammar admitting only in-lane maneuvers.
AI.result: The ConvNeXt students reach Cohen's kappa = 0.268 against human consensus at 28 ms/pothole (vs. 0.321 for cloud); three blind raters scored local warnings safer than cloud warnings (4.18 vs. 3.65 of 5, p = 0.001, 50 scenes) and equally clear, while the full pipeline runs in 1.27 s/scene (16x faster).
AI.conclusion: A fully local, grammar-constrained VLM and distilled perception pipeline can match or exceed cloud warning safety offline at zero per-scene cost.

title: TIVS: Mapping the Sensitivity Landscape of Visual Token Transformations in MLLMs
summary: Recent efforts to improve the efficiency of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have explored visual token pruning, quantization, and feature compression. However, the properties that determine whether transformed visual tokens remain usable by a frozen decoder are not well characterized. We introduce \textbf{TIVS (Token Identity Versus Statistics)}, a training-free intervention framework that separately studies sequence permutation, token retention, numerical precision, and statistical replacement under controlled conditions. On 192 POPE questions, three token permutations change TinyLLaVA accuracy by only $-0.17$ percentage points on average, while changing 4.69\% of individual predictions. Diagonal and rank-64 Gaussian replacements decrease accuracy by 25.0 and 28.1 points on the same subset. Further experiments with exact moment constraints, quantization error, token retention, and additional visual tasks reveal how strongly the effects depend on the original feature values and the evaluation setting. These findings provide an empirical basis for assessing visual token transformations in frozen MLLMs and designing more reliable multimodal interfaces.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces TIVS, a training-free intervention framework that maps how visual token permutation, retention, quantization, and statistical replacement affect frozen MLLM decoders.
AI.motivation: Visual token pruning, quantization, and compression are widely used to speed up MLLMs, but it is poorly understood which token properties determine whether transformed tokens remain usable by a frozen decoder.
AI.method: TIVS (Token Identity Versus Statistics) independently intervenes on sequence permutation, token retention, numerical precision, and statistical replacement (such as diagonal and rank-64 Gaussian replacements and exact moment constraints) under controlled conditions.
AI.result: On 192 POPE questions, three token permutations change TinyLLaVA accuracy by only -0.17 percentage points on average (altering 4.69% of individual predictions), whereas diagonal and rank-64 Gaussian replacements drop accuracy by 25.0 and 28.1 points.
AI.conclusion: TIVS provides an empirical basis for understanding and designing reliable visual token transformations in frozen MLLMs.

title: Event-based object detection under adverse lighting and motion: lessons for construction sites
summary: Vision-based monitoring on construction sites fails at night, at dawn and dusk, in tunnels and under floodlights, when conventional RGB cameras under- or over-expose. Event cameras record per-pixel brightness changes with microsecond latency and over 120 dB of dynamic range, but their benefit for site-relevant object detection has not been quantified on real data. We compare three recent event-based detectors (SMamba, SATE and EvRT-DETR) with an RGB detector trained on the same data, using the pixel-aligned PEOD dataset. On low-light frames (70% of the test set) the best event detector reaches 27.2 AP against 21.3 AP for RGB, and a training-free late fusion of both sensors is the best option in every lighting condition (33.3 AP). An object-level analysis of 53,091 objects shows that brightness has little effect on event detectors, whereas fast motion matters: above 20 pixels per frame RGB finds 11-19% of medium-size objects and EvRT-DETR 39-60%. Activation patching locates the damage caused by losing events at the 1/16-resolution features, with small objects depending on the finest scale, and shows that event detectors fail when few signal events meet added noise. A model-agnostic pruning study keeps about 95% of accuracy with 60% of the input but halves small-object recall. On rendered construction sites, used zero-shot, dimming the floodlights drops RGB to near zero while the event detector keeps most of its AP50. We close with camera-placement guidance for construction sites.

AI.tldr: Evaluating three event-based detectors against an RGB detector on the PEOD dataset, the paper quantifies event-camera benefits under adverse lighting and fast motion for construction sites and shows that training-free late fusion performs best.
AI.motivation: Conventional RGB monitoring on construction sites fails under low light, tunnels, floodlights, and fast motion, while the quantitative benefit of high-dynamic-range event cameras on real site data remained unmeasured.
AI.method: The authors compare SMamba, SATE, and EvRT-DETR against an RGB detector on the pixel-aligned PEOD dataset, perform object-level analysis across 53,091 objects, apply activation patching and input pruning, and test zero-shot on rendered sites.
AI.result: On low-light frames (70% of test set), the best event detector reaches 27.2 AP vs. 21.3 AP for RGB, and training-free late fusion achieves 33.3 AP across all lighting conditions; above 20 px/frame motion, EvRT-DETR finds 39–60% of medium objects vs. 11–19% for RGB, and 60% input pruning retains ~95% accuracy while halving small-object recall.
AI.conclusion: Event cameras paired with training-free RGB late fusion substantially improve construction-site object detection under adverse lighting and fast motion.

title: How Far Is Too Far? Object Recognition Declines Monotonically with Semantic Distance
summary: Vision models are sensitive to object-background context, yet it remains unclear how recognition changes as the semantic distance between objects and backgrounds increases. We introduce ImageNet-OOC1k, a benchmark enabling graded control of object-background relationships along a continuous consensus visual-semantic dissimilarity axis. This formulation reveals a highly consistent monotonic decline in recognition accuracy across 35 models spanning convolutional neural networks, Vision Transformers, and vision-language models. Internal analyses of Vision Transformers reveal patterns consistent with aggregation failure, where object evidence is present at the patch level but not consolidated into the final prediction. Using this characterization as a diagnostic probe, a simple spatial re-ranking strategy recovers a subset of these errors and improves in-sample accuracy by up to 5.7 percentage points. These results establish context sensitivity as a continuous and predictable property of modern vision systems, with Vision Transformer analyses suggesting that aggregation limitations may contribute to some failure types even when object evidence remains available.

AI.tldr: Using a new benchmark ImageNet-OOC1k, the paper shows that object recognition accuracy declines monotonically with object-background semantic distance across 35 vision models due to Vision Transformer aggregation failures.
AI.motivation: Vision models are sensitive to object-background context, but how recognition degrades as semantic distance between objects and backgrounds increases continuously has remained unclear.
AI.method: The authors introduce ImageNet-OOC1k, which controls object-background relationships along a continuous visual-semantic dissimilarity axis, evaluate 35 CNN, ViT, and VLM models, analyze internal ViT patch representations, and test a spatial re-ranking probe.
AI.result: All 35 models exhibit a consistent monotonic decline in accuracy with increasing semantic distance; internal ViT analyses show object evidence is present at the patch level but fails to consolidate into the final prediction, and spatial re-ranking recovers up to 5.7 percentage points in-sample accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Context sensitivity is a continuous, predictable property of modern vision systems, driven in part by ViT aggregation limitations even when patch-level object evidence remains intact.

title: SEAT: Sign-Type Evidence-Audited Transport for Multi-Label Tongue Diagnosis
summary: Automated tongue-sign recognition can improve the consistency of non-invasive examinations that otherwise rely on subjective visual judgment. A single tongue image often exhibits multiple coexisting signs characterized by heterogeneous evidence, including localized morphology, global chromaticity, and inter-label dependence. However, existing methods typically rely on shared representations and uniform multi-label heads, making it difficult to verify whether predictions stem from clinically relevant evidence rather than spurious visual correlations. We propose SEAT, an evidence-audited framework that matches distinct evidence types with dedicated prediction and evaluation mechanisms. Built on frozen DINOv2 patch features, SEAT couples mask-guided sign-specific attention for localized morphology, a semi-relaxed optimal transport pathway over LAB/HSV color prototypes to enhance pale-tongue recognition, and a co-occurrence-aware transport regularizer to shape the batch-level predicted label marginal. These components are evaluated through audits matched to their evidence types. On the TongueDx benchmark, SEAT achieves a mean macro-F1 of 72.59 with a standard deviation of 1.04 across six random seeds, with a six-model ensemble reaching 74.15. The ensemble outperforms a backbone-matched baseline and a larger, domain-specialized vision-language model by 8.06 and 2.99 percentage points, respectively. Our results demonstrate that aligning dedicated prediction pathways and audits with sign-specific characteristics improves multi-label accuracy while offering more targeted evidential grounding than uniform post-hoc spatial explanations. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes SEAT, an evidence-audited framework built on frozen DINOv2 features that pairs sign-specific morphology, color transport, and label co-occurrence pathways for multi-label tongue diagnosis.
AI.motivation: Tongue images exhibit coexisting signs with heterogeneous evidence (localized morphology, global chromaticity, inter-label dependence), whereas existing shared-representation multi-label heads cannot verify whether predictions rely on clinically relevant evidence.
AI.method: On frozen DINOv2 patch features, SEAT combines mask-guided sign-specific attention for morphology, a semi-relaxed optimal transport pathway over LAB/HSV color prototypes for pale-tongue recognition, and a co-occurrence-aware transport regularizer, each evaluated with matched audits.
AI.result: On TongueDx, SEAT achieves 72.59 ± 1.04 mean macro-F1 across six seeds, and a six-model ensemble reaches 74.15, outperforming a backbone-matched baseline by 8.06 percentage points and a larger domain-specialized VLM by 2.99 points.
AI.conclusion: Aligning dedicated prediction pathways and audits with sign-specific evidence types improves both multi-label tongue diagnosis accuracy and evidential grounding.

title: Input-Space versus Feature-Level Conditioning for Robust Facial Expression Recognition
summary: Facial expression recognition (FER) degrades sharply when illumination, exposure or resolution departs from the training distribution. Two remedies dominate practice: enriching the input signal, or conditioning intermediate features on an estimated image quality. The two are rarely compared under matched backbones, training budgets and condition annotations, and their cost is seldom reported. We present a controlled comparison on RAF-DB. Input-space conditioning uses four deterministic, label-free views (logarithmic stretching, inverse-logarithmic stretching, down-up resampling and identity), each processed by a shared backbone with a branch-specific BatchNorm and linear head, with the branch logits averaged. Feature-space conditioning is implemented as FiLM and Conditional BatchNorm under an identical protocol. Across six backbone architectures the input-space variant improves top-1 accuracy on every one (mean +0.94 percentage points; bootstrap interval [0.51, 1.63]; sign test p = 0.016), with a seed-controlled estimate of +0.42 percentage points on ResNet-18, whereas feature-level conditioning yields +0.10 and +0.03 percentage points. We attribute the gap to the information content of the heuristic condition label rather than to the conditioning mechanism. The gain costs 4.00x FLOPs, 4.18x latency and 3.79x training time, i.e. 0.26 percentage points per additional GFLOP, and we state an explicit rule for when the trade is worth making.

AI.tldr: In a controlled comparison on RAF-DB, the paper shows that input-space conditioning consistently outperforms feature-level conditioning for facial expression recognition across six backbones, at a 4x compute cost.
AI.motivation: Facial expression recognition degrades under shifts in illumination, exposure, or resolution, but input-space enrichment and feature-level conditioning have rarely been compared under matched backbones, budgets, and annotations.
AI.method: The authors compare input-space conditioning (four deterministic, label-free views processed by a shared backbone with branch-specific BatchNorm and linear heads, averaging logits) against feature-space conditioning (FiLM and Conditional BatchNorm) on RAF-DB under an identical protocol.
AI.result: Across six backbones, input-space conditioning improves top-1 accuracy on every one (mean +0.94 percentage points, sign test p = 0.016; +0.42 on ResNet-18) vs. +0.10 and +0.03 for feature-level conditioning, at a cost of 4.00x FLOPs, 4.18x latency, and 3.79x training time (0.26 pp/GFLOP).
AI.conclusion: Input-space conditioning provides more reliable robustness gains than heuristic feature-level conditioning, subject to an explicit accuracy-versus-compute trade-off.

title: Drift-Conditioned Structural Replay for Continual Cardiac Ultrasound Segmentation
summary: Conventional experience replay typically applies fixed preservation constraints to historical exemplars, overlooking variations in how learned representations, predictions, and anatomical structures change during sequential training. To address this limitation, we propose Drift-Conditioned Structural Replay Loss (DCSRL), an exemplar-adaptive supervision mechanism that regulates anatomical preservation according to source-referenced knowledge drift. DCSRL operates within a reliability-guided replay framework that selects informative historical exemplars using anatomical content and boundary characteristics while adaptively regulating replay during training. For each retained exemplar, DCSRL constructs a frozen source-task reference signature and subsequently measures changes in feature representations, class probabilities, boundary responses, and predicted anatomical structures. These complementary drift measurements are aggregated and normalized to generate bounded, exemplar-specific coefficients that dynamically adjust boundary and structural replay losses without modifying the underlying memory-selection policy. We evaluate DCSRL under sequential learning across CAMUS, CardiacNet, and EchoNet-Dynamic, comparing its performance with regularization-, distillation-, and replay-based continual-learning approaches. Experimental findings indicate that DCSRL improves overall final segmentation performance and anatomical boundary preservation, particularly under heterogeneous imaging conditions, although trade-offs remain in knowledge transfer across tasks. These findings suggest that source-referenced multidimensional drift conditioning offers a promising direction for adaptive anatomical knowledge preservation in continual cardiac ultrasound segmentation.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Drift-Conditioned Structural Replay Loss (DCSRL), which adapts boundary and structural replay losses per exemplar based on multidimensional source-referenced knowledge drift in continual cardiac ultrasound segmentation.
AI.motivation: Conventional experience replay applies fixed preservation constraints to historical exemplars, ignoring how learned representations, predictions, and anatomical structures drift differently during sequential training.
AI.method: For each retained exemplar, DCSRL constructs a frozen source-task reference signature and measures drift in feature representations, class probabilities, boundary responses, and predicted structures, normalizing these into bounded coefficients that dynamically weight boundary and structural replay losses.
AI.result: Evaluated on sequential learning across CAMUS, CardiacNet, and EchoNet-Dynamic against regularization, distillation, and replay baselines, DCSRL improves overall final segmentation performance and anatomical boundary preservation, especially under heterogeneous imaging conditions.
AI.conclusion: Source-referenced multidimensional drift conditioning enables adaptive anatomical knowledge preservation in continual cardiac ultrasound segmentation.

title: Spatiotemporal Reconstruction of Auroral Precipitations with Neural Fields
comment: Accepted to the IEEE/CVF Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision (WACV 2027). Camera-ready version with supplementary material. 17 pages, 15 figures
summary: Auroras provide remote optical observations of energetic electrons precipitating into the upper atmosphere, and whose energy distribution encodes key information about large scale magnetospheric processes. Recovering the underlying electron precipitation field from ground-based camera images of auroras remains a challenging inverse problem. Existing auroral tomography techniques are often limited to simplified static settings, discrete spatial and energy grids, or strong assumptions on the electron energy spectrum. We propose to model the dynamic auroral electron precipitation field via a temporally conditioned neural network. The state of the precipitation field at each frame is represented by a per-frame latent code driven by learned discrete dynamics. A shared decoder maps horizontal positions and latent states to electron energy spectra. The predicted flux is converted to multi-wavelength volume emission rates and rendered into camera images accounting for delayed emissions. We evaluate the method on synthetic dynamic auroral sequences and real multi-view auroral videos, showing that the proposed representation produces temporally coherent precipitation reconstructions and image projections consistent with the observations.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a temporally conditioned neural field to reconstruct dynamic auroral electron precipitation fields from ground-based multi-view auroral videos.
AI.motivation: Existing auroral tomography methods are limited to static settings, discrete spatial/energy grids, or strong assumptions on the electron energy spectrum.
AI.method: A per-frame latent code driven by learned discrete dynamics represents the precipitation field state, a shared decoder maps horizontal positions and latent states to electron energy spectra, and predicted flux is converted to multi-wavelength volume emission rates and rendered into camera images accounting for delayed emissions.
AI.result: Evaluated on synthetic dynamic auroral sequences and real multi-view auroral videos, the method produces temporally coherent precipitation reconstructions and image projections consistent with observations.
AI.conclusion: Temporally conditioned neural fields overcome static and grid limitations to enable physically consistent spatiotemporal reconstruction of auroral precipitations.

title: SemLite-GS: Semantic-Selective Parallel Gaussian Splatting for Lightweight Building Reconstruction from UAV Oblique Imagery
summary: Lightweight 3D building models support urban spatial analysis, but their production often requires dense scene reconstruction, building extraction, and mesh simplification. Although 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) is more efficient than conventional multi-view stereo, existing large-scale methods lack semantic selection and parallel instance-level training. We present SemLite-GS, a building-centric framework that reconstructs lightweight building meshes from large-scale UAV oblique imagery. First, an orthographic reference map establishes globally consistent building identities, which are propagated to oblique views to form camera-instance pairs and regions of interest. Second, semantic-selective parallel PGSR training jointly processes multiple pairs within relevant image regions while updating only target Gaussians; contextual Gaussians remain fixed to preserve visibility. Third, architectural planes extracted from rendered depth, opacity, and normal maps guide signed distance field optimization, producing meshes with adaptive polygon allocation and well-defined structural boundaries. Experiments on multiple large-scale UAV datasets demonstrate that our SemLite-GS substantially reduces building reconstruction time compared with representative full-scene 3DGS methods. With comparable polygon budgets, SemLite-GS achieves superior preservation of dominant planar structures and sharp architectural transitions compared with conventional dense reconstruction followed by mesh decimation. The source code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper presents SemLite-GS, a building-centric Gaussian splatting and SDF optimization framework that reconstructs lightweight building meshes from large-scale UAV oblique imagery faster and with sharper structural boundaries.
AI.motivation: Existing large-scale 3D Gaussian Splatting methods lack semantic selection and parallel instance-level training, requiring dense scene reconstruction followed by mesh decimation to produce lightweight building models.
AI.method: SemLite-GS propagates building identities from an orthographic reference map to oblique views, performs semantic-selective parallel PGSR training updating only target Gaussians while keeping contextual Gaussians fixed, and uses extracted architectural planes to guide SDF optimization for adaptive-polygon meshing.
AI.result: On multiple large-scale UAV datasets, SemLite-GS substantially reduces reconstruction time compared with full-scene 3DGS methods and preserves dominant planar structures and sharp architectural transitions better than dense reconstruction plus decimation at comparable polygon budgets.
AI.conclusion: Semantic-selective parallel Gaussian splatting paired with plane-guided SDF meshing enables fast, lightweight, and structurally sharp 3D building reconstruction.

title: When Backdoors Can Be Switched Off: Suppression-Aware Backdoor Attacks on Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models map visual observations, robot states, and natural-language instructions to robotic actions, but their multimodal interfaces introduce new security risks. Existing VLA backdoor attacks primarily study trigger-based activation and stealthy action manipulation, leaving conditional suppression of malicious behavior underexplored. We investigate suppression-aware backdoors, which combine conjunctive trigger activation with instruction-conditioned suppression. We instantiate this design through three variants: Cross-Modal Trigger, combining robot-state and spatially separated visual triggers; Self-Suppressing Trigger, requiring a state trigger and a [DISRUPT] instruction token for activation, with [RESTORE] token suppressing the attack; and Multi-Trigger, additionally requiring a visual trigger while retaining suppression even when physical triggers persist. We evaluate these attacks using SmolVLA on two SO-100 manipulation datasets against four baselines: State Backdoor, BadVLA, TabVLA, and SilentDrift. Self-Suppressing and Multi-Trigger reduce Isolation Forest detection from 96--98% to 1--18% and action-space l divergence by 10--14X, achieving 63--71% attack success rates with perfect clean-task performance. Experiments with OpenVLA on LIBERO further show that the attacks transfer to a 7B-parameter policy, evading STRIP and action-distribution-shift detection. Our findings establish conditional suppression as an important dimension for evaluating backdoor threats in VLA policies.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates suppression-aware backdoor attacks on Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, showing that conditional suppression variants evade existing defenses while maintaining high attack success and clean performance.
AI.motivation: Existing VLA backdoor attacks focus on trigger-based activation and stealthy action manipulation, leaving conditional suppression of malicious behavior underexplored.
AI.method: The authors introduce three variants—Cross-Modal Trigger, Self-Suppressing Trigger ([DISRUPT] activates, [RESTORE] suppresses), and Multi-Trigger—and evaluate them on SmolVLA (SO-100 datasets) and OpenVLA (7B, LIBERO) against four baselines (State Backdoor, BadVLA, TabVLA, SilentDrift).
AI.result: Self-Suppressing and Multi-Trigger reduce Isolation Forest detection from 96–98% to 1–18% and action-space divergence by 10–14x, achieving 63–71% attack success rates with perfect clean-task performance, and transfer to 7B OpenVLA evading STRIP and distribution-shift detection.
AI.conclusion: Conditional suppression represents a critical, underexplored dimension for evaluating and defending against backdoor threats in VLA policies.

title: A Threshold-Free Visual-Semantic Matching Metric for Evaluating Consistency in Subject-Driven Image Generation
summary: In subject-driven text-to-image generation, quantitatively evaluating localized visual consistency across varying poses and environments remains a major challenge. Existing metrics either rely on global image embeddings (CLIP, DINO) and Vision-Language Models (VLMs) that pool spatial representations and miss fine-grained textural artifacts, or depend on scalar threshold-gated dense metrics such as Visual-Semantic Matching (VSM) that suffer from point-alignment dropouts, severe threshold sensitivity, and score instability. To overcome these limitations, we propose TF-VSM, a fully continuous, threshold-free visual-consistency metric paired with an extended feature-disentanglement retraining schedule for dual-branch ResNet feature-aggregation networks. Rather than enforcing rigid binary cutoffs $(T_s,T_v)$, TF-VSM weights every object point by a non-linear semantic match confidence $w_j=ReLU(\hat{s}_j)^2$ and continuously integrates visual similarity over all consistency levels $r\in[0,1]$, yielding a closed-form confidence-weighted score without any hand-tuned hyperparameters. On a controlled 100-pair benchmark with ground-truth inpainting oracles, TF-VSM attains Pearson $0.638$ and Spearman $0.674$ oracle correlation, improving over the pretrained VSM baseline ($0.454/0.589$) by $+0.171/+0.116$ after retraining, and drastically outperforming CLIP ($-0.052/-0.004$), DINO ($0.087/0.121$), and VLMs ($0.096/0.003$). Six diagnostic ablations confirm that smooth confidence weighting is the right mechanism, that hard semantic gating is brittle (dropping to $0.533$ Pearson at $T_s{=}0.8$), and that the threshold-free metric is essentially invariant to the training-time loss balance $\alpha$ that the thresholded metric still depends on.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes TF-VSM, a continuous, threshold-free visual-semantic matching metric with feature-disentanglement retraining that achieves much higher oracle correlation than CLIP, DINO, VLMs, and thresholded VSM.
AI.motivation: Existing subject-driven generation metrics either pool spatial features (CLIP, DINO, VLMs) and miss fine-grained artifacts, or use threshold-gated dense metrics (VSM) that suffer from alignment dropouts, threshold sensitivity, and score instability.
AI.method: TF-VSM replaces rigid binary cutoffs with smooth confidence weighting w_j = ReLU(s_j)^2 and continuously integrates visual similarity over all consistency levels r in [0, 1], paired with an extended feature-disentanglement retraining schedule for dual-branch ResNet networks.
AI.result: On a 100-pair benchmark with inpainting oracles, TF-VSM reaches 0.638 Pearson and 0.674 Spearman correlation, improving over pretrained VSM (0.454/0.589) by +0.171/+0.116 after retraining and outperforming CLIP (-0.052/-0.004), DINO (0.087/0.121), and VLMs (0.096/0.003), while remaining invariant to loss balance α.
AI.conclusion: Smooth confidence weighting and continuous integration eliminate threshold brittleness, yielding a stable and accurate metric for localized visual consistency.

title: Fine-Grained RLAIF for Visual Safety: Learning to Zoom into Hazards for Multimodal Safety Alignment
summary: Recent multimodal safety alignment heavily relies on a text-centric paradigm, assuming risks are explicit in language or globally prominent in images. However, real-world hazards are often visually subtle or peripheral, causing existing models to fail due to their reliance on coarse, global visual representations. In this work, we study fine-grained visual safety alignment and introduce a challenging 1,200-sample benchmark across four domains, where hazards necessitate localized inspection. To address this, we propose Fine-Grained RLAIF (FGR), a reinforcement learning framework that casts image zoom-in as a learnable perception policy. FGR employs a decomposed reward design to jointly align three core safety behaviors: (i) where to look via a visual evidence reward, (ii) when to act via a tool-formatting constraint, and (iii) how to reason via visually grounded safety explanations. FGR achieves accuracy ranging from 86.71% to 93.00%, consistently outperforming strong multimodal and agent-based baselines.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a 1,200-sample fine-grained visual safety benchmark and proposes Fine-Grained RLAIF (FGR), an RL framework that learns an image zoom-in perception policy, achieving 86.71%–93.00% accuracy.
AI.motivation: Recent multimodal safety alignment relies on text-centric paradigms or coarse global visual representations, causing models to miss subtle or peripheral real-world visual hazards.
AI.method: FGR casts image zoom-in as a learnable perception policy trained with a decomposed reward aligning where to look (visual evidence reward), when to act (tool-formatting constraint), and how to reason (visually grounded safety explanations).
AI.result: On the new 1,200-sample benchmark across four domains, FGR achieves 86.71% to 93.00% accuracy, consistently outperforming strong multimodal and agent-based baselines.
AI.conclusion: Learning a targeted zoom-in perception policy via decomposed RLAIF rewards enables accurate, visually grounded detection of subtle multimodal safety hazards.

title: Pros4D: Modeling Evolving 4D Worlds in Latent Space for Dynamic Spatial Reasoning
summary: Dynamic spatial reasoning from monocular video enables vision-language models (VLMs) to understand how 3D environments evolve over time, supporting physical world understanding and embodied intelligence. Existing efforts primarily address observed-dynamics understanding, whereas agents in dynamic environments also require future-dynamics prediction beyond the observation boundary. Moreover, external geometric processing and textual descriptions can increase inference complexity or lose information when representing continuous dynamics. These limitations motivate a shared internal state that preserves observed dynamics and remains predictive beyond the input video. Accordingly, we present Pros4D, a framework for modeling evolving 4D worlds in latent space that unifies retrospective understanding of observed-dynamics with prospective reasoning for future-dynamics prediction. Specifically, Pros4D-Engine derives geometry-grounded supervision and constructs paired examples for both tasks, while Pros4D-Bench evaluates them across eight spatial task categories spanning dynamic cameras, objects, and scenes. At the model level, Pros4D compresses observed dynamics into latent observed states and autoregressively rolls them forward into latent future states. 4D Latent Alignment (4DLA) grounds these states through complementary visual-semantic and geometric supervision, while joint language supervision connects them to task reasoning. Experiments across benchmarks show consistent improvements over strong baselines in both capabilities.

AI.tldr: The paper presents Pros4D, a framework that unifies observed-dynamics understanding and future-dynamics prediction in latent space, alongside Pros4D-Engine and Pros4D-Bench.
AI.motivation: Existing dynamic spatial reasoning methods focus on observed dynamics and often rely on external geometric processing or text descriptions, whereas embodied agents also need future-dynamics prediction beyond the observation boundary.
AI.method: Pros4D compresses observed monocular video dynamics into latent observed states and autoregressively rolls them forward into latent future states, grounded via 4D Latent Alignment (4DLA) with visual-semantic, geometric, and language supervision; Pros4D-Engine generates paired supervision and Pros4D-Bench evaluates eight dynamic spatial categories.
AI.result: Experiments across benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over strong baselines in both retrospective observed-dynamics understanding and prospective future-dynamics prediction.
AI.conclusion: Modeling evolving 4D worlds in a unified, geometry-grounded latent space bridges retrospective spatial understanding and prospective future prediction for VLMs.

title: The Flip Test: Video World Models Fail to Learn the World State
summary: Video world models promise to predict the future of a scene from its present. Do current models keep this promise? We probe this question counterfactually. When a small change to the present flips the future, such as a box resting a few millimeters before or past a table edge, a model that tracks the state of the world must flip its prediction too. We build FlipTest, a three-level hierarchy of increasingly strict tests over 1,680 initial frames from 10 simulated and 15 real-world tasks. At the base, visual minimal pairs, two nearly identical frames whose true futures differ, test whether predictions change across the boundary; matched controls go further and test whether they change only where the future does; and dense sweeps, the strictest level, locate exactly where they change. All 11 video world models we evaluate fall short. The best averages 18.3% pair accuracy over real and simulated scenes, below the 25% of random guessing. Models flip as often on steps that leave the future unchanged as on steps that change it, and their response stays flat across the sweeps. On the same frames, a vision-language model is selective and traces a near S-shaped curve near the boundary, and a coding agent that measures the image comes close to the true boundary. This implies that the deciding information is in the frame, and video models just miss it. We therefore urge the community to rethink world modeling as pure video prediction. Next-frame prediction must do more than draw plausible pixels; it must also identify the causal states that control future dynamics.

AI.tldr: Using a counterfactual benchmark (FlipTest) of 1,680 initial frames, the paper shows that all 11 evaluated video world models fail to track causal world states, scoring below random guessing (best 18.3% vs. 25%).
AI.motivation: Video world models promise to predict scene futures from the present, but it is unclear whether they actually track the underlying causal world state rather than just generating plausible pixels.
AI.method: The authors build FlipTest, a three-level counterfactual hierarchy (visual minimal pairs, matched controls, and dense sweeps) over 1,680 frames from 10 simulated and 15 real-world tasks where small present changes flip the true future, and evaluate 11 video world models, a VLM, and a coding agent.
AI.result: All 11 video world models fail, with the best averaging 18.3% pair accuracy (below 25% random guessing) and flat responses across sweeps, whereas a VLM traces a near S-shaped boundary curve and a coding agent closely locates the true boundary.
AI.conclusion: Deciding state information is present in the frame but missed by video world models, urging a shift from pure pixel prediction to identifying causal states.

title: When Does Reusing Layers Help Multimodal Embeddings?
summary: We ask whether a compact universal multimodal embedding models can produce better search embeddings by running the same layers again. Looped transformers add computation with nearly unchanged model size, making them an appealing alternative to a larger encoder. Their success in language-model reasoning and recent use for retrieval motivate the idea, but higher retrieval scores alone do not reveal what an extra pass contributes. We study eleven loop designs and training variants on three checkpoints of one vision-language architecture. Our protocol distinguishes whether a model uses its extra pass, whether its image states respond to the query, and whether those updates improve retrieval. We prove that an image placed before the query remains query-independent through repeated layers when information only travels forward. We then open a query-to-image path in three ways, including order-alternating recurrence, which places the query first on the next pass. Each path produces query-sensitive image states. For bidirectional attention and order alternation, freezing later visual updates does not lower accuracy. On all 78 datasets of the Massive Multimodal Embedding Benchmark version 2 (MMEB-V2), a standard added loop loses 0.46 points against its trained control; an intermediate generative stage changes the effect to +0.36. A model pretrained with recurrence gains +4.23 points over its own loop-removed control and benefits from query-conditioned image updates when answering visual questions or locating objects from text.

AI.tldr: Studying 11 looped-transformer designs on MMEB-V2, the paper shows that reusing layers only helps multimodal embeddings when a query-to-image path is opened and the model is pretrained with recurrence.
AI.motivation: Looped transformers add compute without increasing model size, but higher retrieval scores alone do not reveal whether extra passes actually update image states in response to the query.
AI.method: The authors prove that an image placed before a query stays query-independent under forward-only recurrence, and test three ways to open a query-to-image path (including order-alternating recurrence) across 11 loop designs and training variants on three checkpoints.
AI.result: Across all 78 MMEB-V2 datasets, a standard added loop loses 0.46 points vs. its control, an intermediate generative stage shifts this to +0.36, and a model pretrained with recurrence gains +4.23 points over its loop-removed control while benefiting from query-conditioned image updates.
AI.conclusion: Layer reuse improves multimodal embeddings only when recurrence is paired with query-to-image information flow and recurrence-aware pretraining.

title: PRISM: Primitive-Integrated Separable Modulation with Priority Visual Memory Queue for Compositional Zero-Shot Learning
summary: Compositional Zero-Shot Learning (CZSL) recognizes unseen attribute--object pairs by recombining primitives from seen compositions. Existing methods stop sharing evidence at deployment: fixed prototypes cannot exploit unlabeled test streams, while composition-wise refinement cannot propagate corrections across pairs sharing a primitive. We introduce PRISM, an online CZSL framework that extends primitive sharing to test-time adaptation. Its Hierarchical Knowledge Accumulation Module (HiKAM) factorizes prototype migration into composition-, attribute-, and object-level residual banks. A Priority Visual Memory Queue (PVMQ), initialized by Prototype Queue Initialization (PQI), grounds text updates with bounded visual evidence. The same adaptive core supports exhaustive Full PRISM and recall-calibrated Adaptive PRISM-Lite, which selects candidate budgets from held-out ranks. Comprehensive closed- and open-world experiments on UT-Zappos, MIT-States, and C-GQA demonstrate the state of the art, with Full PRISM achieving the best open-world AUC and harmonic mean on all three benchmarks and the best closed-world results on UT-Zappos and C-GQA. Fine-grained long-tail and non-stationary primitive-block evaluations reveal gains on under-supported concepts and stable adaptation under prolonged skew. Adaptive PRISM-Lite further delivers substantial efficiency gains in the full open-world space with only a small accuracy cost. PRISM thus combines primitive-shared online adaptation, multimodal grounding, and candidate-aware inference.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces PRISM, an online Compositional Zero-Shot Learning (CZSL) framework that extends primitive sharing to test-time adaptation via factorized residual banks and a priority visual memory queue.
AI.motivation: Existing CZSL methods stop sharing primitive evidence at deployment: fixed prototypes cannot use unlabeled test streams, and composition-wise refinement cannot propagate corrections across pairs sharing a primitive.
AI.method: PRISM's Hierarchical Knowledge Accumulation Module (HiKAM) factorizes prototype migration into composition-, attribute-, and object-level residual banks, while a Priority Visual Memory Queue (PVMQ) grounds text updates with bounded visual evidence; Adaptive PRISM-Lite selects candidate budgets from held-out ranks.
AI.result: On UT-Zappos, MIT-States, and C-GQA, Full PRISM achieves state-of-the-art open-world AUC and harmonic mean on all three benchmarks and best closed-world results on UT-Zappos and C-GQA, with Adaptive PRISM-Lite delivering large efficiency gains at a small accuracy cost.
AI.conclusion: Combining primitive-shared online adaptation, multimodal grounding, and candidate-aware inference advances both accuracy and efficiency in open-world CZSL.

title: Beyond Vehicle-Centric Data: Scaling Autonomous Driving through Roadside-to-Vehicle Generation
summary: Training autonomous driving models requires large and diverse datasets, collected primarily by vehicles. Scaling them entails investment in fleet operation, data processing and annotation. Road infrastructure records traffic and multi-vehicle interactions, yet the viewpoint gap between roadside and onboard sensors limits its direct use for training. Here we introduce AnyR2V, a framework that transforms multimodal roadside observations into seven-camera surround-view videos for different vehicle perspectives. It aggregates sequential observations into a shared scene representation of geometry and road-user motion, then renders appearance, depth and layout conditions along target-vehicle trajectories. Supervised by spatiotemporally aligned roadside-vehicle pairs, AnyR2V generates surround-view videos guided by scene structure and road-user motion. Existing roadside 3D bounding boxes are transformed into target-vehicle coordinates and paired with generated images, allowing one traffic recording and its annotations to yield training data from multiple vehicle perspectives. We construct R2V360, a dataset of 89 real traffic sequences at an urban intersection, with aligned multimodal roadside data and onboard surround-view videos. AnyR2V outperforms six scene reconstruction methods in image fidelity and in depth and semantic agreement between generated and real onboard images. We further evaluate generated videos along other vehicles' trajectories by adding them to real training data. Adding generated frames equal to 50% of the original real training frame count improves mean average precision (mAP) by 3.3-3.4 AP-points across three 3D object detectors on the real onboard test set, relative to real-data-only baselines. These results demonstrate that roadside traffic records can provide training data from multiple vehicle perspectives, offering a new data source for autonomous driving.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces AnyR2V, a framework that converts roadside multimodal observations into seven-camera surround-view vehicle videos, and R2V360, a dataset of 89 aligned roadside-vehicle sequences, improving 3D object detection mAP by 3.3–3.4 points.
AI.motivation: Scaling autonomous driving datasets via vehicle fleets is costly, while abundant roadside infrastructure recordings cannot be directly used for onboard training due to the viewpoint gap.
AI.method: AnyR2V aggregates sequential roadside observations into a shared geometry and motion representation, renders appearance, depth, and layout conditions along target-vehicle trajectories, and transforms roadside 3D bounding boxes into target-vehicle coordinates to generate surround-view training videos.
AI.result: AnyR2V outperforms six scene reconstruction methods in fidelity, depth, and semantic agreement on R2V360; adding generated frames equal to 50% of real training frames improves mAP by 3.3–3.4 AP points across three 3D object detectors on real onboard test sets.
AI.conclusion: Roadside-to-vehicle video generation provides an effective, scalable new source of multi-perspective training data for autonomous driving.

title: AGPF: Dynamic Source Selection for Feature Pyramid Fusion
summary: Feature pyramids provide dense predictors with features at several spatial resolutions. However, it remains largely unexplored which pyramid levels each output location should aggregate information from. We investigate this question by allowing each output location to attend to features from every pyramid level and measuring how attention is distributed across scales. Surprisingly, locations on the finest output grid allocate approximately 75\% of their attention to features two levels coarser, rather than to the current or adjacent levels. Even on the same output grid, the balance shifts toward coarser features as object size increases. These observations motivate Asymmetric Global Pyramid Fusion (AGPF), a neck that preserves the original output grids while allowing each location to dynamically select its contextual sources across scales. Each location interacts with a multiscale memory whose features are aligned in image coordinates, enabling flexible cross-scale aggregation without altering prediction resolutions. Compared with FPN, AGPF improves all 19 object detection and all seven instance segmentation configurations evaluated on COCO. A single fusion block improves Cascade Mask R-CNN by 1.7 box AP and 2.3 mask AP, and the gains consistently transfer to semantic and panoptic segmentation.

AI.tldr: Finding that fine-grid locations attend ~75% to features two pyramid levels coarser, the paper proposes Asymmetric Global Pyramid Fusion (AGPF), which improves all 19 object detection and 7 instance segmentation configurations on COCO.
AI.motivation: Feature pyramids provide multi-resolution features for dense prediction, yet it remains poorly understood which pyramid levels each output location should aggregate from.
AI.method: The authors measure cross-scale attention across pyramid levels and propose AGPF, a neck that preserves original output grids while allowing each location to dynamically attend to a multiscale memory aligned in image coordinates.
AI.result: Compared with FPN, AGPF improves all 19 object detection and all 7 instance segmentation configurations on COCO; a single fusion block boosts Cascade Mask R-CNN by 1.7 box AP and 2.3 mask AP, with gains transferring to semantic and panoptic segmentation.
AI.conclusion: Allowing each output location to dynamically select contextual sources across scales via a coordinate-aligned multiscale memory consistently outperforms standard FPN.

title: Passable for Whom? Few-Shot Personal Calibration of Sidewalk Accessibility Perception
summary: Whether a sidewalk is passable depends on who is trying to pass: people who use the same mobility aid disagree about the same image, so one label per scene, or per aid, is wrong for many of them. We introduce few-shot personal accessibility perception: from K answers of a person never seen before, predict their judgment of sidewalk scenes never seen before. PassCal separates a shared description of the scene from the person's interpretation of it. The description comes from the internal state of a frozen vision-language model (VLM) and from barrier type, severity and context properties predicted by a detector trained on 14.9k public audits; the interpretation, a calibration of the person's response style and a weighting of the properties, is fit from their answers. On 8,883 judgments in which each of 135 verified mobility-aid users rated the same 50 sidewalk scenes, with people and scenes both held out, eight answers lower the Brier score from 0.550 to 0.479. The same VLM prompted with those answers reaches 0.562, and the same calibration without the scene 0.521. Conformal risk control turns predictions into passable, blocked or "depends on you" statements with a bounded expected rate of wrong statements over people; at 5%, eight answers raise the share of decisive scenes from 27% to 42%. Audit-supervised properties improve all sixteen vision and VLM encoders we test and outperform attributes from a sidewalk navigation VLM.

AI.tldr: PassCal predicts individual mobility-aid users' sidewalk passability judgments from a few examples by separating a shared scene representation from user-specific calibration, improving Brier score and decisive-scene coverage.
AI.motivation: People using the same mobility aid often disagree on whether a sidewalk is passable, making single-label-per-scene or per-aid predictions inaccurate for many users.
AI.method: PassCal combines a frozen VLM's internal state and barrier type, severity, and context properties from a detector trained on 14.9k public audits into a shared scene description, then fits per-user response-style calibration and property weights from K user answers, using conformal risk control to output passable, blocked, or "depends on you".
AI.result: On 8,883 judgments from 135 mobility-aid users across 50 scenes with both users and scenes held out, eight answers reduce Brier score from 0.550 to 0.479 (vs. 0.562 for prompting the VLM and 0.521 for scene-free calibration) and raise decisive scenes at 5% risk from 27% to 42%; audit-supervised properties improve all 16 tested vision and VLM encoders.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling shared audit-grounded scene properties from few-shot personal calibration enables accurate, risk-controlled personalized accessibility perception.

title: PanDWM: Panoramic 4D Driving World Models
comment: Code: this https URL, Website: this https URL
summary: Driving world models usually generate videos from six pinhole cameras with separate optical centres and small overlaps, and must learn to keep these views consistent. We present PanDWM, which stitches them into one $360^\circ$ panoramic band. Camera boundaries then fall inside one image, so keeping the views consistent means keeping the image continuous, and each pixel still records its camera ray. Conditioned on layouts, a causal student generates the band window by window in four steps; it is distilled from a causal teacher and trained on its own rollouts. A feed-forward decoder lifts each frame along these rays into 3D Gaussians, and static Gaussians from neighbouring frames complete them into 4D scenes. On nuScenes, scored in one stitched $360^\circ$ view, PanDWM has lower FID and FVD than the multi-camera baselines at $8$-$46\times$ their speed, and keeps its 50-step teacher's FID while lowering FVD by 22-25%.

AI.tldr: PanDWM stitches six driving camera views into a continuous 360-degree panoramic band for 4D driving world modeling, achieving lower FID and FVD than multi-camera baselines at 8x to 46x their speed.
AI.motivation: Existing driving world models generate six separate pinhole camera videos with small overlaps and must learn cross-view consistency explicitly.
AI.method: PanDWM stitches the six views into a single 360-degree panoramic band where camera rays are preserved per pixel, trains a layout-conditioned causal student in four steps via distillation from a causal teacher and self-rollouts, and lifts frames along rays into 3D Gaussians completed with static neighbor Gaussians into 4D scenes.
AI.result: On nuScenes evaluated in the stitched 360-degree view, PanDWM achieves lower FID and FVD than multi-camera baselines at 8x-46x higher speed, and matches its 50-step teacher's FID while reducing FVD by 22%-25%.
AI.conclusion: Representing multi-camera driving scenes as a continuous panoramic band simplifies cross-view consistency and enables fast, high-quality 4D world generation.

title: Do Pretraining Optimizer Gains Transfer to KL Distillation?
summary: Matrix-structured optimizers can improve language-model pretraining, but it is unclear whether these gains transfer to short-horizon KL distillation from an instruction-tuned initialization. We compare AdamW and diagonal AdaGrad with two tractable Shampoo reductions, SOAP, and All-2D Muon across four dense Qwen student-teacher pairs under a common forward-KL objective and fixed training budget. Across scales, none of the evaluated matrix-structured recipes consistently improves the quality versus trainer-time trade-off over the elementwise references: AdamW generally attains the lowest validation KL, while AdaGrad can be slightly faster at larger scale. SOAP often tracks AdamW in KL but incurs substantial trainer-time overhead, and the two Shampoo reductions reverse ordering across model pairs, showing that conclusions depend on the feasible recipe. These results suggest that pretraining optimizer gains do not transfer automatically to KL distillation and should be re-established for the target objective and systems regime.

AI.tldr: An empirical comparison of optimizers for short-horizon KL distillation on Qwen models finds that matrix-structured optimizers do not consistently outperform elementwise AdamW or AdaGrad in quality versus trainer-time trade-off.
AI.motivation: Matrix-structured optimizers improve language-model pretraining, but it is unknown whether those gains transfer to short-horizon forward-KL distillation from instruction-tuned initializations.
AI.method: The authors compare AdamW and diagonal AdaGrad against two tractable Shampoo reductions, SOAP, and All-2D Muon across four dense Qwen student-teacher pairs under a shared forward-KL objective and fixed training budget.
AI.result: AdamW generally achieves the lowest validation KL, AdaGrad is slightly faster at larger scale, SOAP matches AdamW's KL with substantial trainer-time overhead, and the two Shampoo reductions reverse ordering across model pairs.
AI.conclusion: Pretraining optimizer gains do not automatically transfer to KL distillation and must be re-evaluated for the specific objective and systems regime.

title: Federated versus Centralized PV Capacity-Factor Forecasting: A Non-Inferiority Study Across Seven Stations in North Macedonia
comment: Submitted to Energy, Sustainability and Society
summary: Background: Photovoltaic (PV) forecasts inform energy commitments by PV operators and aggregators and guide charge-discharge scheduling in solar-plus-storage systems. Federated learning enables collaborative model training through model updates when local operators cannot pool raw operational data. This study evaluated whether federated training was non-inferior to centralized training for PV capacity-factor prediction across seven stations in North Macedonia. A common multilayer perceptron was used in an offline forecasting comparison with a 24-hour timestamp lag. Exploratory validation compared local, centralized, Federated Averaging, and Federated Proximal (FedProx) training. FedProx (E = 1, mu = 1) was selected for a confirmatory comparison under a protocol fixed before test evaluation. The comparison used past-only offline inputs, five paired training seeds, macro-averaged mean absolute error (MAE), a prespecified non-inferiority margin of 0.005, and a paired day bootstrap with 10,000 repetitions over 49 test dates. Results: FedProx achieved a macro-MAE of 0.128397, compared with 0.133405 for centralized training. The paired difference (FedProx minus centralized) was -0.005008 (95% confidence interval: [-0.009926, -0.000537]). The upper confidence bound was below the prespecified margin, satisfying the non-inferiority criterion. All five seed-specific differences favored FedProx, and its mean MAE was lower at six of the seven stations. Post hoc calendar sensitivity analyses did not change the conclusion. Conclusions: These findings support further evaluation of federated forecasting for collaboration under data-pooling constraints. The study demonstrates predictive non-inferiority within the evaluated setting. Benefits for energy commitments and battery scheduling remain potential applications requiring operational evaluation.

AI.tldr: A confirmatory non-inferiority study across seven PV stations in North Macedonia shows that FedProx federated forecasting is non-inferior to centralized training for 24-hour-lagged PV capacity-factor prediction.
AI.motivation: Local PV operators and aggregators often cannot pool raw operational data, raising the question of whether federated learning can match centralized forecasting accuracy.
AI.method: Using a common multilayer perceptron with 24-hour-lagged past-only inputs, the authors select FedProx (E = 1, mu = 1) from exploratory validation and compare it against centralized training across five paired seeds, macro-MAE, a 0.005 non-inferiority margin, and a 10,000-repetition paired day bootstrap over 49 test dates.
AI.result: FedProx achieves a macro-MAE of 0.128397 versus 0.133405 for centralized training, with a paired difference of -0.005008 (95% CI [-0.009926, -0.000537]) below the 0.005 margin, outperforming centralized training on all five seeds and six of seven stations.
AI.conclusion: Federated forecasting with FedProx provides non-inferior predictive accuracy under data-pooling constraints, supporting further operational evaluation for energy commitments and battery scheduling.

title: Architectures and KV Replay for Depth-Recurrent Language Models
summary: Depth recurrence increases effective model depth by repeatedly applying a fixed computation block. However, sharing attention parameters does not share the key-value (KV) states generated at different recurrence iterations, which causes memory growth with recurrence depth during autoregressive decoding. We study how to reduce this memory cost through architectural and cache-sharing approaches within a common depth-recurrent framework. We first study a looped hybrid that repeats a stack of Transformer layers, with recurrent mLSTM or Gated DeltaNet blocks replacing most attention layers and periodic Transformer attention anchors retained. We then restrict recurrence to a dedicated recurrent workspace in a Parcae-style architecture and test its stabilising adapter as a wrapper for the looped hybrid. Finally, we train a looped Transformer with recurrent KV replay, where only selected recurrence iterations write KV states that later iterations reuse. This trains the model to operate with the same shared KV topology used during inference. We find that looped hybrids require sufficiently frequent attention anchors, with performance depending strongly on the recurrent mixer. For cross-iteration KV sharing, recurrent KV replay allows multiple recurrence iterations to reuse the same KV states while retaining performance close to the full looped Transformer with separate KV caches for each iteration.

AI.tldr: This paper studies looped hybrid architectures and recurrent KV replay to reduce the decoding memory growth of depth-recurrent language models while preserving performance.
AI.motivation: Depth-recurrent models reuse attention parameters across iterations, but still accumulate separate KV states at each recurrence depth, increasing decoding memory.
AI.method: The authors evaluate looped hybrids replacing most attention layers with mLSTM or Gated DeltaNet blocks while keeping periodic attention anchors, test a Parcae-style recurrent workspace with a stabilizing adapter, and train a looped Transformer with recurrent KV replay where only selected iterations write KV states reused by later iterations.
AI.result: Looped hybrids require sufficiently frequent attention anchors and depend strongly on the recurrent mixer, while recurrent KV replay enables cross-iteration KV sharing with performance close to a full looped Transformer with separate per-iteration KV caches.
AI.conclusion: Architectural hybridization and recurrent KV replay offer practical ways to curb KV-cache memory growth in depth-recurrent language models.

title: Successive Convexification in Learned World Models for Safe Offline Planning
comment: 28 pages, 13 figures. Under review at L4DC 2027
summary: World models learned from offline data allow an agent to plan without further interaction with the environment, but the sampling-based planners used with them handle safety constraints only by scoring or rejecting sampled action sequences. We instead pose safe planning in the latent space of a learned world model as a successive convex program (SCP), in which a learned discrete-time control barrier function is imposed as a constraint at every step of the horizon. SCP requires smooth dynamics, so we build the networks from smoothed MaxMin activations and spectrally normalised layers, and bound the resulting linearisation error in terms of the Lipschitz bound and the smoothing width. As SCP is a local method, we start it from a sampled plan. On two Safety-Gymnasium navigation tasks with offline data, this planner has fewer violations than MPPI and CEM drawing 128 times as many samples at equal wall-clock time in our main comparison, though not significantly, and earns greater return at longer horizons, and is much safer than SCP without a sampled start. SCP converged more often on Lipschitz-bounded models. Unlike sampling, it also reports at each step whether its plan is a feasible, first-order optimal KKT point of the planning problem in the model, or that no feasible plan was found nearby. Our implementation is publicly available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The authors formulate safe offline planning in learned world models as a successive convex program (SCP) with learned discrete-time control barrier function constraints, improving safety and long-horizon return over sampling-based planners.
AI.motivation: Sampling-based planners in offline learned world models only handle safety by scoring or rejecting sampled action sequences rather than enforcing constraints directly.
AI.method: They build smooth world models using smoothed MaxMin activations and spectrally normalized layers with bounded linearization error, initialize SCP from a sampled plan, and enforce a learned discrete-time control barrier function at every horizon step.
AI.result: On two Safety-Gymnasium offline navigation tasks, the SCP planner achieves fewer safety violations than MPPI and CEM using 128x more samples at equal wall-clock time (though not statistically significant), higher return at longer horizons, better safety than uninitialized SCP, higher convergence on Lipschitz-bounded models, and explicit KKT feasibility reporting.
AI.conclusion: Successive convexification with Lipschitz-bounded world models and control barrier constraints provides a principled, certifiable alternative to pure sampling for safe offline planning.

title: Grokking Can Be Steered: Selecting Desirable Solutions By Choice Of Learning Rule
summary: During grokking, a network transitions from memorization to generalization, yet what shapes the neural implementation (circuit) of the generalizing solution and specifically the number of participating neurons (its size) remains unclear. We find that the learning rule, the combination of credit assignment algorithm and optimizer, controls this: On modular addition, every learning rule we study that groks recovers the same Fourier-based algorithm, yet implemented by circuits that differ in size. Why? A neuron stays in use when its credit is large relative to the non-gradient term of its own update, and this single condition unifies three routes to unused neurons: the coupled weight decay, Adam's $\epsilon$ and the decay of a trainable per-neuron gain. Equalizing the magnitude of credit assigned to each neuron, or scaling each neuron's weight decay by its credit, expands the effective circuit size, measured from the outgoing weights, from 60% to 99% of the layer's neurons at similar training and test accuracy. We vary which neurons share one equalization factor, from the whole layer to individual neurons, and find that the circuit stays concentrated for groups of eight or more and fully distributes only when every neuron has its own factor. Credit magnitudes are usually set by the normalization of standard optimizers: Nero, which normalizes per neuron, distributes the computation, whereas Adam and seven others, including RMSProp, Muon, and Shampoo, use other normalization schemes and retain small, concentrated circuits. Distributed circuits tolerate neuron deletion better, while concentrated circuits can be pruned further and transfer about twice as fast to a task that recombines the same features, largely by recruiting their unused neurons. Learning rule choice thus steers circuit size, trading robustness against compressibility and transfer speed without changing the learned algorithm.

AI.tldr: The choice of learning rule controls the number of participating neurons in grokking circuits on modular addition, trading off deletion robustness against compressibility and transfer speed without changing the underlying algorithm.
AI.motivation: While grokking transitions from memorization to generalization, what determines the size and sparsity of the resulting neural circuit has remained unclear.
AI.method: The authors analyze credit assignment and optimizer normalization on modular addition, unifying coupled weight decay, Adam's epsilon, and trainable gain decay under a single neuron-survival condition, and vary credit-equalization grouping from layer-wide to per-neuron.
AI.result: All grokking rules recover the same Fourier-based algorithm, but equalizing per-neuron credit or scaling weight decay by credit expands active circuit size from 60% to 99% at similar accuracy; Nero (per-neuron normalization) distributes computation whereas Adam, RMSProp, Muon, and Shampoo keep circuits concentrated, yielding ~2x faster transfer and better pruning at the cost of lower robustness to neuron deletion.
AI.conclusion: Learning-rule normalization directly steers neural circuit concentration, creating a controllable trade-off between robustness, prunability, and transfer speed.

title: Probing SAM Perturbations Through Statistical Replay
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 Workshop: AXIOM - Foundations of Efficient Deep Learning
summary: Sharpness Aware Minimization (SAM) updates model parameters using gradients evaluated at adversarially perturbed weights, but it remains unclear which aspects of this procedure are sufficient to reproduce its generalization behavior. In our ResNet 18 experiments on CIFAR 10, simple curvature regularizers based on the Hessian trace and largest eigenvalue remain below SAM in validation accuracy, motivating a direct examination of its perturbations. We introduce statistical replay, a diagnostic that summarizes perturbations from reference SAM trajectories using elementwise means and standard deviations over local windows and constructs new perturbations during independent SGD training. Pure replay uses only these summaries, whereas mixed replay adds isotropic Gaussian noise. Pure replay does not reproduce SAM's validation behavior, while mixed replay and pure isotropic perturbations can approach its validation performance at selected scales without reproducing its training dynamics. An equal radius random direction within SAM performs similarly to SGD, and source, temporal, and layer interventions further suggest that replay behavior depends on perturbation construction. Together, these preliminary results weaken several simple explanations of SAM while leaving an important part of its mechanism unexplained.

AI.tldr: Using statistical replay of Sharpness Aware Minimization (SAM) perturbations, this study shows that simple summary statistics of SAM perturbations do not reproduce SAM's validation accuracy or training dynamics.
AI.motivation: It remains unclear which properties of SAM's adversarial weight perturbations are sufficient to explain its generalization benefits over SGD.
