AI.method: On ResNet-18 and CIFAR-10, the authors compare Hessian-based curvature regularizers against SAM and introduce statistical replay, which records elementwise means and standard deviations of SAM perturbations over local windows and replays them (purely or mixed with isotropic Gaussian noise) during independent SGD training.
AI.result: Hessian regularizers underperform SAM; pure statistical replay fails to match SAM's validation accuracy; mixed replay and pure isotropic noise approach SAM's validation accuracy at selected scales without matching its training dynamics; and equal-radius random directions within SAM perform similarly to SGD.
AI.conclusion: Simple statistical summaries and isotropic noise fail to capture SAM's full mechanism, leaving key aspects of how SAM perturbations drive generalization unexplained.

title: Func-JEPA: Learning a Sobolev Space of Functions as Latent Vectors
comment: 42 pages, 16 figures, 30 tables. Code: this https URL. Model and data: this https URL
summary: Pretraining an encoder once and reusing it across tasks is a widespread approach in vision and language. However, neural symbolic mathematics still trains a dedicated sequence-to-sequence model for each task, so that no representation of a function is shared. In this work, we propose the Function Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (Func-JEPA, abbreviated f-JEPA): an encoder of mathematical functions, pretrained on their symbolic form, whose latent space imitates the Sobolev space H^1 and in which differentiation is a learned latent operator. The norm of a latent is computed exactly from the function, whereas its direction is learned to match Sobolev angles. The frozen encoder is then reused by lightweight modules for decoding, composition, integration, and regression from samples. The representation and four downstream tasks are evaluated within and outside the pretraining distribution. f-JEPA recovers exact formulas from noisy samples more often than the compared symbolic-regression methods, whereas computer algebra and task-specific models remain stronger on standard integration and differential-equation benchmarks.

AI.tldr: Func-JEPA (f-JEPA) pretrains a shared symbolic function encoder whose latent space imitates the Sobolev space H^1 with a learned differentiation operator, enabling reuse across decoding, composition, integration, and noisy symbolic regression.
AI.motivation: Unlike vision and language, neural symbolic mathematics typically trains separate sequence-to-sequence models per task without sharing a reusable function representation.
AI.method: f-JEPA encodes symbolic functions into latent vectors with exact norms and directions learned to match Sobolev H^1 angles, models differentiation as a learned latent operator, and freezes the encoder for lightweight downstream modules.
AI.result: Evaluated in- and out-of-distribution across four tasks, f-JEPA recovers exact formulas from noisy samples more often than compared symbolic-regression methods, while computer algebra systems and task-specific models remain stronger on standard integration and differential-equation benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Learning a Sobolev-structured latent function space provides a reusable representation that excels at noisy symbolic regression.

title: Random Cut Forests, Games and Diffusion over Approximately Nested Anisotropic Local Geometry
summary: Just as the data in a dynamic stream changes, questions asked of the stream also change in intent: what to hold constant, which counterfactuals to consider, and so forth. Energy-based learning has been celebrated for its uniform approach to losses and estimation, but interpretability remains challenging. Tree-based methods, on the other hand, offer high interpretability but often rely on bespoke, disjointed estimators. Neither paradigm readily supports changing questions on streaming data. In this paper we take a step towards combining energy, interpretability, and streaming. Random cut forests retain an evolving geometry of the data. We study this geometry as the basis for diffusion dynamics, prediction, explanation, and games. We show that several existing scores are escape probabilities of random walks on the trees. The induced affinity is realized exactly by a sparse electrical network on each tree, giving a single energy calculus, a Hamiltonian, maintained along one path per update. This connects an estimate, its supporting evidence, and the response to intervention through the same boxes, gaps, masses, and paths. Different questions correspond to different clamp decisions on the energy. Fixing observed values gives harmonic prediction with Gaussian uncertainty. Fixing a partition gives normalized cuts whose cost is attributed exactly to oriented faces. Releasing clamps gives coalition games, in which collusive displacement measures the field response. With noise, the same energy gives diffusion dynamics whose relaxation rates are read from the boxes. Axis-parallel cuts localize at a rate set by affine rather than ambient dimension, and this control passes to the averaged energy. Across a forest the boxes are only approximately nested; common reference observations align the trees. A rotating star with added noise illustrates the measurements.

AI.tldr: This paper unifies random cut forests with a sparse electrical-network energy calculus (Hamiltonian) to support streaming prediction, explanation, normalized cuts, coalition games, and diffusion over evolving local geometry.
AI.motivation: Existing energy-based and tree-based methods struggle to combine interpretability, unified estimation, and support for changing queries on streaming data.
AI.method: The authors map each tree's evolving box geometry to a sparse electrical network with a single Hamiltonian maintained along one path per update, where clamping observed values, partitions, or releasing clamps yields harmonic prediction, normalized cuts, coalition games, and diffusion dynamics.
AI.result: Axis-parallel cuts localize at a rate governed by affine rather than ambient dimension, common reference observations align approximately nested boxes across a forest, and a noisy rotating-star experiment illustrates the resulting measurements.
AI.conclusion: Framing random cut forests as an electrical-network energy calculus bridges interpretable tree geometry with unified energy-based inference and game-theoretic attribution on streams.

title: Read, Then Shade? How Visual Evidence Changes Incentive-Driven Misreporting in Vision-Language Advisors
comment: 45 pages, 5 figures. This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) increasingly read a scene and report it to someone who acts on the report, sometimes under objectives that differ from that person's. We ask whether a stated incentive moves what a VLM reports, and whether this changes when the value must be read from pixels rather than given as text. In seeded synthetic scenes, a model reads the position of a target on a labelled axis and reports one integer to a fixed receiver; it is paid, in simulation, for accuracy or for a report a few units to one side, and every scene is also presented with the true value as text. Across a pilot and three follow-up studies with hash-frozen protocols, four small open VLMs from three families, and 15,170 held-out trials, a stated payoff moved reports in both modalities, and exact compliance at three units was significantly lower with the image than with text for three of four models; Qwen2.5-VL 7B showed no reliable difference. Adding the true value as text to the image prompt removed the gap in every model. For InternVL3 the gap vanished on scenes it read correctly when it wrote its reading first; for Gemma 3 it persisted. For Qwen2.5-VL 3B, which read every scene correctly, the gap held in four of five payoff paraphrases, nearly vanished when the model wrote its reading before its report or when the prompt stated that the client wants the truth, vanished with an unpaid goal, and persisted when the model reported before stating its reading; how often it shaded at all, even with text, depended strongly on the wording. When told that the client wants the true value, three of four models still shaded every text report. Visual input did not make these advisors reliably more truthful; it made compliance with a stated incentive depend on whether the read value is made explicit and on output order, a dependence that text-only evaluations and mean-shift metrics do not reveal.

AI.tldr: Experiments with four small open VLMs show that visual input does not make models more truthful under stated incentives; instead, incentive compliance depends on whether the read value is stated explicitly and on output order.
AI.motivation: As VLMs act as advisors reporting visual scenes under potentially misaligned incentives, it is unclear whether reading values from pixels rather than text changes incentive-driven misreporting.
AI.method: Across 15,170 held-out trials on synthetic scenes with a target on a labelled axis, four small open VLMs report an integer under accuracy or shifted-report payoffs, comparing pixel inputs, text inputs, image-plus-text inputs, and different output orderings.
AI.result: Stated payoffs shift reports in both modalities, with three of four models showing lower exact 3-unit compliance on images than text (Qwen2.5-VL 7B shows no reliable difference); adding the true value as text removes the gap, while writing the reading before the report removes or nearly removes the gap in InternVL3 and Qwen2.5-VL 3B (but not Gemma 3), and three of four models still shade text reports even when told the client wants the truth.
AI.conclusion: Visual evidence alters incentive compliance through reading explicitness and output ordering, revealing failure modes missed by text-only evaluations and mean-shift metrics.

title: Sharp First-Hit Identification from Finite Depth Samples
comment: 36 pages, 9 figures. This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible
summary: Which depths in a new camera view are determined by finitely many source-depth measurements? Pointwise uncertainty bounds do not answer this question: unobserved geometry between samples can change which surface is encountered first. We study a bounded Lipschitz class of continuous source inverse-depth fields with interval observations and known camera pose. Building on classical Lipschitz envelopes, we characterize the exact set of attainable first-hit depths and construct a globally admissible scene for every value in that set. The set can be disconnected. We also give a necessary and sufficient test for several proposed depths to be first hits of one shared scene. An epipolar reduction uses scalar cone inequalities without enumerating surfaces. In a rectified model with source spacing $h$, interval half-width $\varepsilon$, baseline $b$, and slope bound $L$, we prove a sharp worst-case inverse-depth diameter of $\max\{Lh+2\varepsilon,2\varepsilon/(1-bL)\}$ when $bL<1$, subject to sufficient depth and domain range for attainment. Exact samples still give the sharp bound $Lh$ at $bL=1$, while above this threshold ambiguity need not vanish as sampling becomes arbitrarily dense. Any positive measurement uncertainty can destroy uniform stability at the critical threshold. We provide constructive examples, an exact rational validation oracle, and a frozen ten-scene evaluation using reference, stereo, and learned-depth observations. The experiments separate solver correctness under the scene assumptions from failure of those assumptions: fixed learned-depth bands often yield narrow but incorrect sets. The results identify what a specified scene class permits; they do not infer a continuum regularity or physical-scene guarantee from sampled predictions.

AI.tldr: This paper characterizes the exact set of attainable first-hit depths in a novel camera view from finitely many bounded-Lipschitz interval depth samples, proving sharp worst-case diameter bounds and a stability threshold.
AI.motivation: Pointwise uncertainty bounds on depth samples cannot determine which surface is hit first in a new view because unobserved geometry between samples can alter occlusion.
AI.method: Using classical Lipschitz envelopes and an epipolar reduction with scalar cone inequalities, the authors characterize all attainable first-hit depths (which can be disconnected), provide a multi-depth consistency test, and construct globally admissible scenes.
AI.result: In a rectified model with spacing h, half-width epsilon, baseline b, and slope bound L, the sharp worst-case inverse-depth diameter is max(Lh + 2*epsilon, 2*epsilon / (1 - bL)) for bL < 1, Lh at bL = 1 with exact samples, and potentially non-vanishing above bL = 1; experiments on 10 frozen scenes with an exact rational oracle show fixed learned-depth bands often produce narrow but incorrect sets.
AI.conclusion: The results establish exact geometric limits on first-hit depth identifiability from finite samples and distinguish solver correctness from violated scene assumptions.

title: Spectral Steering: Local Inverse Geometry for Frozen Diffusion Generators
summary: A frozen diffusion generator may need to change several output properties while preserving others. We study when guidance faithfully realizes such a structured request and whether local inverse correction improves its direction. Our account links this benefit to the interaction between the request and the objective-specific remaining-sampler Jacobian: conditioning alone is insufficient. Spectral steering combines a request-specific cosine-gain predictor with damped inverse correction and fixed-time relinearization for finite edits. Scalar nulls and matched-movement controls test the predicted mechanism. Across 8,923 instances in a retrospectively identified local regime, predicted and realized gains correlate at Spearman 0.79, versus -0.11 for condition number. Experiments span images, audio, robotics, and control and planning, including complex character motion generation. On 50 paired inpainting cases, four corrections improve unobserved-pixel PSNR over Adam by 3.25 dB at equal total derivative traversals. Together, the analysis and controls connect request-dependent geometry to directional gains and establish where these gains translate into downstream performance.

AI.tldr: Spectral steering improves multi-property guidance of frozen diffusion generators by combining a request-specific cosine-gain predictor with damped inverse Jacobian correction and fixed-time relinearization.
AI.motivation: Guiding a frozen diffusion generator to change some properties while preserving others often fails when the request interacts poorly with the remaining-sampler Jacobian, and condition number alone does not predict success.
AI.method: The method uses a request-specific cosine-gain predictor alongside damped inverse correction and fixed-time relinearization for finite edits, tested against scalar nulls and matched-movement controls.
AI.result: Across 8,923 local-regime instances, predicted and realized gains correlate at Spearman 0.79 versus -0.11 for condition number; on 50 paired inpainting cases, four corrections outperform Adam by 3.25 dB unobserved-pixel PSNR at equal derivative traversals, with gains demonstrated across images, audio, robotics, and control.
AI.conclusion: Accounting for request-dependent local inverse geometry enables more faithful, directional multi-property steering in frozen diffusion models.

title: Risk-Averse Decision-Focused Learning: Minimizing CVaR of Regret
summary: Many combinatorial optimization (CO) problems involve parameters that are uncertain when the problem must be solved. In such settings, the parameters have to be predicted from correlated contextual information before a solution can be computed. \emph{Decision-focused learning} (DFL) addresses this by training the predictive model to produce predictions that optimize downstream decision quality. Most existing DFL methods are risk-neutral and minimize the expected regret. In high-stakes applications this can lead to undesirable outcomes, because decision-makers must also account for the tail risk of decision quality. Prior risk-sensitive approaches typically model uncertainty explicitly and solve a stochastic or robust optimization problem at inference time, which increases computational complexity. We instead propose a DFL framework that achieves risk-sensitive behavior while retaining point predictions and deterministic optimization at inference time. Starting from the dual representation of the Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) and adding entropy regularization, we derive a smooth surrogate for the CVaR of regret. Its gradient induces an instance-dependent reweighting within each minibatch that emphasizes high-risk outcomes, so the approach can turn existing surrogate-loss DFL methods, including the SPO+ loss, into risk-sensitive variants. When instantiated with SPO+, the resulting objective admits a generalization bound on the CVaR of the true regret. Experiments on knapsack, portfolio, shortest-path, and energy-aware scheduling problems show substantial reductions in tail regret when the uncertain parameters exhibit heterogeneous tail behavior.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a risk-averse decision-focused learning framework that minimizes a smooth entropy-regularized CVaR surrogate of regret while keeping point predictions and deterministic optimization at inference time.
AI.motivation: Standard decision-focused learning minimizes expected regret and ignores tail risk, whereas prior risk-sensitive methods require costly stochastic or robust optimization at inference time.
AI.method: Starting from the dual representation of CVaR with entropy regularization, the authors derive a smooth regret surrogate whose gradient reweights minibatch instances toward high-risk outcomes, compatible with existing DFL surrogates like SPO+ and backed by a CVaR generalization bound.
AI.result: Experiments on knapsack, portfolio, shortest-path, and energy-aware scheduling problems demonstrate substantial reductions in tail regret when uncertain parameters exhibit heterogeneous tail behavior.
AI.conclusion: Minibatch reweighting via a smooth dual CVaR surrogate brings risk sensitivity to decision-focused learning without adding inference-time optimization overhead.

title: SLiDE: Structured Linear Dynamics for Forecasting with Exogenous Inputs
summary: Accurate time series forecasting with exogenous inputs is critical across domains, including energy and retail, yet modern deep learning models often overfit to correlations that do not generalize under shifts in these inputs. We propose SLiDE, a Koopman-inspired architecture for forecasting with exogenous inputs that imposes structure on latent temporal dynamics. SLiDE approximates nonlinear system evolution using a learned linear operator in a latent space, combining (i) a history encoder that reconstructs the current latent state from past targets and inputs with (ii) a shared linear rollout driven by future exogenous variables. By enforcing a common linear recurrence across encoding and prediction, SLiDE aligns how past information is encoded with how future states evolve, reducing parameterization and preventing reliance on spurious correlations in the input history. Empirically, SLiDE achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on real-world benchmarks, including electricity price forecasting and retail demand, while maintaining a computational footprint comparable to lightweight MLP architectures. SLiDE is especially effective at generalizing to shifted exogenous inputs, reducing MSE by 20% on electricity price samples with out-of-range exogenous values and MAE by 30% in a synthetic transfer setting where the same dynamical system is driven by an unseen exogenous process. Ablations confirm the importance of both the structured history encoder and the linear latent rollout, suggesting that structured latent linear dynamics provide a useful inductive bias for forecasting with exogenous inputs.

AI.tldr: SLiDE is a Koopman-inspired forecasting architecture that models latent temporal dynamics with a shared linear operator driven by exogenous inputs, improving out-of-distribution generalization at lightweight MLP cost.
AI.motivation: Deep forecasting models often overfit to spurious correlations in historical inputs and fail to generalize when exogenous inputs shift.
AI.method: SLiDE pairs a history encoder reconstructing the current latent state with a shared linear rollout driven by future exogenous variables, enforcing a common linear recurrence across encoding and prediction.
AI.result: SLiDE achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on electricity price and retail demand benchmarks with MLP-level compute, reducing MSE by 20% on out-of-range electricity price exogenous values and MAE by 30% on a synthetic unseen-exogenous transfer task.
AI.conclusion: Enforcing a shared structured linear latent dynamics model provides an effective inductive bias for generalizing under exogenous input shifts.

title: Explicit Regularization for Flow Matching
comment: 40 pages (main text pp. 1-24, references pp. 24-26, appendices A-C pp. 27-40), 4 figures, 11 tables
summary: Learning the underlying probability distribution from samples is a core problem in statistics and applied mathematics. Generative models based on diffusion and flow matching learn a velocity field whose flow transports a known distribution to the data distribution. They produce novel, realistic samples, although the empirical learning problem is ill posed near the data distribution. Its minimizer transports the samples onto the training data, and small perturbations of the data change the velocity field strongly near the end of the flow. The observed generalization is often attributed to implicit regularization by the network parameterization, early stopping of the training, and the time integration during sampling. Explicit regularization has advanced the theory and computation of many inverse problems and has recently been proposed to prevent memorization in generative models. With a regularizer on the magnitude of the velocity, however, the field approaches the memorizing velocity unless the regularization parameter grows to infinity fast enough, and it then stays bounded by a constant that is small only for large parameters. We show that penalizing the derivatives of order $k$ of the velocity renders the $D$-dimensional empirical problem well posed uniformly in time if $2k > D$ and the training points are in general position. Our experiments in one and two dimensions discretize the velocity with splines and use direct solvers for the regularized least-squares problems to exclude optimization error. Refining the discretization in space and time changes the error of the Hessian-regularized flows only marginally, whereas without the regularizer the error tends to that of memorization. These flows generalize, with errors comparable to or lower than those of well-tuned kernel density estimates.

AI.tldr: Penalizing k-th order derivatives of the velocity field in flow matching makes the D-dimensional empirical learning problem uniformly well posed in time when 2k > D, preventing memorization.
AI.motivation: Empirical flow matching is ill posed near the data distribution, causing minimizers to memorize training points unless regularized, and simple velocity-magnitude penalties fail without extreme regularization weights.
AI.method: The authors analyze higher-order derivative penalties on the velocity field and validate them in 1D and 2D using spline-discretized velocities solved via direct regularized least-squares.
AI.result: When 2k > D and training points are in general position, the empirical problem is uniformly well posed in time; Hessian-regularized flows remain stable under space-time refinement and generalize with errors comparable to or lower than well-tuned kernel density estimates, unlike unregularized flows that converge to memorization.
AI.conclusion: Higher-order velocity derivative regularization provides a theoretically grounded, discretization-stable mechanism to prevent memorization in flow matching.

title: PBit1: One Programmable P-Bit per Parameter - A Finite-Control Representation of Pretrained Networks
comment: 7-page main paper with 3 figures, plus a 12-page supplement
summary: We introduce PBit1, a finite-control representation of pretrained neural networks that assigns one programmable p-bit to each learned parameter. A 12-bit command sets its probability, a shared affine range maps that probability to the weight domain, and temporal observations reconstruct the weight for inference. Operator-aware range grouping and sensitivity-based sampling allocation adapt the representation to the network. Across five independent weight draws at 32,768 observations per scalar, selected configurations preserve task quality in GPT-2, DistilBERT, and LFM3-1.7B with every learned scalar converted and no fine-tuning. GPT-2 and LFM3 perplexity increase by approximately 0.66% and 0.26%, respectively, while DistilBERT accuracy changes from 87.51% to 87.49%. A sensitivity-based policy reduces GPT-2 reconstruction observations by 41.7% while retaining the quality criterion. Complete-model evaluations reuse reconstructed weights in BF16 inference, and THRML operator experiments examine native sampling and spatial-temporal tradeoffs. Together, these results establish PBit1 as a concrete construction for studying finite-control weight representation and temporal reconstruction in pretrained networks.

AI.tldr: PBit1 represents each learned parameter of a pretrained neural network as a single programmable p-bit with a 12-bit probability command and shared affine range, preserving task quality without fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Exploring finite-control probabilistic hardware representations for pretrained networks requires mapping continuous weights to programmable p-bits without degrading model quality.
AI.method: PBit1 assigns one p-bit per parameter using a 12-bit probability command, maps probabilities to weights via operator-aware affine range grouping, and reconstructs weights from temporal observations using sensitivity-based sampling allocation.
AI.result: Across five draws at 32,768 observations per scalar without fine-tuning, GPT-2 and LFM3-1.7B perplexity increase by ~0.66% and 0.26% respectively, DistilBERT accuracy shifts from 87.51% to 87.49%, and sensitivity-based allocation cuts GPT-2 observations by 41.7% while preserving quality.
AI.conclusion: PBit1 establishes a concrete finite-control p-bit weight representation and temporal reconstruction scheme for pretrained language models.

title: Synthetic Neurosymbolic Task Generation with Controlled Constraint Complexity
summary: We introduce NeSySy, a synthetic generator for neurosymbolic learning tasks that jointly produces logical constraints and consistent datasets. Unlike existing benchmarks, NeSySy provides fine-grained control over key properties such as constraint structure, tightness, input dependence, and data generation and alignment strategies. In particular, it allows the use of rich constraints over infinite domains, and uses solvers to ensure that the constraints are meaningful and that generated samples satisfy the constraints. We design NeSySy to support both learning with declarative constraints and learning from distant supervision. Across a range of constraint families, we provide evidence that its parameters induce systematic and largely independent effects on task difficulty. Using NeSySy, we study constraint-aware learning methods, identifying regimes where explicit constraint enforcement is beneficial and where expressive unconstrained models can instead learn constraint structure directly from data. Our results establish NeSySy as a controlled testbed for analysing the interaction between learning and logical structure. NeSySy is built around a pipeline that incorporates solvers. Satisfiability checkers (CNFgen and Z3) generate and certify constraints. Constrained optimizers (RC2 for MaxSAT, Z3 for OMT) compute optimal repairs that guarantee every generated sample is consistent.

AI.tldr: NeSySy is a solver-backed synthetic generator for neurosymbolic learning tasks that jointly produces logical constraints and consistent datasets with fine-grained control over constraint complexity.
AI.motivation: Existing neurosymbolic benchmarks lack systematic control over constraint structure, tightness, input dependence, and alignment, limiting controlled analysis of learning under logical structure.
AI.method: NeSySy integrates satisfiability checkers (CNFgen, Z3) to generate and certify constraints, including over infinite domains, and constrained optimizers (RC2 for MaxSAT, Z3 for OMT) to compute optimal repairs ensuring sample consistency for both declarative-constraint and distant-supervision settings.
AI.result: Experiments across constraint families show that NeSySy's parameters independently control task difficulty and reveal regimes where explicit constraint enforcement helps versus where unconstrained models learn constraints from data.
AI.conclusion: NeSySy provides a rigorous, solver-certified testbed for studying how neural learning interacts with logical constraints.

title: Before the Word: Name Information in Description-Derived States of Small Language Models, With and Without Naming Failure
comment: 22 pages, 9 tables. Code and data: this https URL
summary: The tip-of-the-tongue (TOT) state, knowing an object but not its name, motivates this study as an analogy only. We ask whether small language models form a name-predictive state from a name-free description, and whether it differs when naming fails but description selection succeeds. In an internally pre-registered study (a frozen document, no external registry) of Qwen2-0.5B, SmolLM2-1.7B and Phi-3-mini with 200 items, we combine a similarity read-out, a Patchscopes-style read-out and activation patching with matched controls. H1 (name information in the state) was supported in all nine model-by-description-type combinations; the agreement rule was met by the similarity measure together with patching, while Patchscopes stayed near chance. Post-hoc robustness checks after internal review (logit lens, single-position patch, manipulation check) temper this reading: name information in middle layers is clearest under the multi-position patch and the similarity measure, and weak under single-position patching at 50% depth. H2' (description-paraphrase consistency of name-free states not lower in failure items) is mixed: the SmolLM2 deficit test is significant under the pre-registered specification but not robust; Phi-3 non-inferiority holds across margins and a word-overlap covariate, although its bootstrap interval includes zero; Qwen2-0.5B is inconclusive. A capacity explanation remains untested. We report vehicle-level signals only, not meaning.

AI.tldr: An internally pre-registered study of three small language models finds name-predictive information in middle-layer states derived from name-free descriptions, though robustness varies across readouts and failure-consistency results are mixed.
AI.motivation: Inspired by the tip-of-the-tongue analogy, the authors investigate whether small language models form name-predictive internal states from name-free descriptions and whether these states differ when naming fails.
AI.method: Testing Qwen2-0.5B, SmolLM2-1.7B, and Phi-3-mini on 200 items, they combine similarity readouts, Patchscopes readouts, and activation patching with matched controls, followed by post-hoc logit-lens and single-position patching checks.
AI.result: Name information is detected across all nine model-by-description combinations via similarity and multi-position patching (while Patchscopes stays near chance and 50%-depth single-position patching is weak); paraphrase consistency during naming failure is mixed across models (non-robust deficit in SmolLM2, non-inferiority in Phi-3, inconclusive in Qwen2-0.5B).
AI.conclusion: Small language models encode vehicle-level name-predictive signals in middle layers from name-free descriptions, but sensitivity depends on readout method and failure-state consistency remains model-dependent.

title: Well-Log Reconstruction with Pre-trained Geological Knowledge: A Knowledge-Conditioned Large-Language-Model Generative Agent
summary: Missing well-log intervals make subsurface reconstruction ill-posed. Existing numerical regression models lack geological prior knowledge to constrain ambiguous inverse mappings. We propose GeoLog-Agent, a knowledge-conditioned generative agent using pre-trained large language models (LLMs) as a source of geological priors. A universal Geo-Harness translates LLM stratigraphic reasoning into formation-anchored petrophysical trajectories, feature-wise linear modulation, and conditional adversarial constraints. On the Norwegian North Sea benchmark, GeoLog-Agent achieves a mean $R^2$ of 0.9307 and a peak $R^2$ of 0.9713. It exceeds the nine-baseline average $R^2$ of 0.8387 by 0.0920, with a 30.97% average RMSE reduction, and exceeds the strongest baseline by 0.0274--0.0498 in $R^2$, with 16.25%--24.05% lower RMSE. Ablations confirm the effectiveness and synergy of geological prior reasoning, multi-scale dilated generation, and conditional adversarial modules. Transferring the coupling mechanism to six conventional deep learning models improves their $R^2$ by 0.0162--0.0789 with cross-well stability. These results demonstrate how foundation-model domain reasoning can constrain deep generative reconstruction of missing petrophysical measurements.

AI.tldr: GeoLog-Agent uses pre-trained LLMs as geological priors via a Geo-Harness to condition deep generative reconstruction of missing well-log intervals, outperforming nine baselines on the Norwegian North Sea benchmark.
AI.motivation: Missing well-log intervals make subsurface reconstruction ill-posed, and purely numerical regression models lack geological prior knowledge to constrain ambiguous inverse mappings.
AI.method: A universal Geo-Harness translates LLM stratigraphic reasoning into formation-anchored petrophysical trajectories, feature-wise linear modulation, and conditional adversarial constraints within a multi-scale dilated generator.
AI.result: On the Norwegian North Sea benchmark, GeoLog-Agent achieves 0.9307 mean R^2 (0.9713 peak), exceeding the nine-baseline average by 0.0920 R^2 (30.97% lower RMSE) and the strongest baseline by 0.0274-0.0498 R^2 (16.25%-24.05% lower RMSE), while transferring the coupling to six conventional models improves their R^2 by 0.0162-0.0789.
AI.conclusion: Conditioning deep generative models on LLM-derived geological priors substantially improves cross-well accuracy and stability in petrophysical log reconstruction.

title: Robust Well-Log Reconstruction Across Point Gaps and Whole Wells via Boundary-Gated Soft-Thresholding Kalman Fusion
summary: Missing wireline logs hinder subsurface characterization. Deep reconstruction networks suffer from gap-boundary steps and cross-basin shifts, while interpolation and Gaussian smoothers struggle with long intervals and outliers. We propose boundary-gated soft-thresholding Kalman fusion (ST-KF), unifying multiresolution wavelet shrinkage, distance-gated residual prior learning, and closed-form robust Kalman smoothing with learning--inference decoupling. Across two public benchmarks totaling 263 wells in the Norwegian North Sea and New Zealand's Taranaki Basin, ST-KF ranks first over 0.15--100-m anchored gaps with 0.09% parameter overhead. Against the strongest of nine baselines, pooled RMSE falls by 5.0%--8.3% for bulk density and 6.4%--15.6% for compressional slowness; against the four strongest baselines, reductions are 0.7%--4.1% for neutron porosity and 1.3%--2.9% for photoelectric factor. Ablations and sensitivity analyses confirm operator synergy and stable performance: removing state-space fusion increases short-gap errors by up to 58.8%, while zero-shot transfer cuts anchored errors by 14%--68%. The results show that local borehole continuity transfers across basins whereas cross-property mappings shift with regional geology, supporting measurement-guided log reconstruction.

AI.tldr: Boundary-gated soft-thresholding Kalman fusion (ST-KF) unifies wavelet shrinkage, distance-gated residual priors, and robust Kalman smoothing to reconstruct missing well logs across point gaps and whole wells.
AI.motivation: Deep well-log reconstruction models suffer from gap-boundary discontinuities and cross-basin domain shifts, while classical smoothers struggle with long gaps and outliers.
AI.method: ST-KF decouples learning and inference by combining multiresolution wavelet shrinkage, distance-gated residual prior learning, and closed-form robust Kalman smoothing.
AI.result: Across 263 wells in the Norwegian North Sea and Taranaki Basin, ST-KF ranks first over 0.15-100 m anchored gaps with 0.09% parameter overhead, cutting pooled RMSE against the strongest baseline by 5.0%-8.3% for bulk density and 6.4%-15.6% for compressional slowness; removing state-space fusion raises short-gap errors by up to 58.8%, and zero-shot transfer cuts anchored errors by 14%-68%.
AI.conclusion: Local borehole continuity transfers reliably across basins, making measurement-guided state-space fusion effective for robust well-log reconstruction.

title: Multi-Objective Causal Bandits: Minimal Intervention Space and Policy-Level Learning
comment: To appear in Proceedings of NeurIPS 26
summary: Many decision-making problems involve multiple objectives, where actions affect several performance metrics, fairness criteria, or safety constraints. We study multi-objective causal bandits with multiple reward nodes, where actions correspond to interventions on subsets of variables in a causal graph and performance is evaluated through Pareto optimality. Existing approaches to multi-objective bandits often rely on pairwise Pareto dominance or optimize a fixed scalarization. However, pairwise comparisons alone can fail to identify actions dominated by randomized policies, whose expected reward vectors lie in the convex hull of action-level rewards. Thus, an intervention may be suboptimal even if no single intervention dominates it, because it can be dominated by a randomized policy over other interventions. We formalize this policy-level phenomenon and show that it has consequences for both causal action-space reduction and online learning. First, we provide a necessary-and-sufficient graphical characterization of possibly Pareto- optimal minimal intervention sets. Our characterization yields a minimal, sound, and complete candidate intervention family from the graph alone, correcting prior formulations that may include intervention sets that are never Pareto-optimal under any compatible structural causal model. Second, over this reduced intervention space, we design an online UCB-style algorithm that eliminates actions using dominance tests against convex combinations of other actions, and prove logarithmic gap-dependent Pareto regret. Finally, we study constrained multi-objective causal bandits, where feasibility and optimality may be realized only with randomized policies, and develop an online UCB-style constrained bandit algorithm with sublinear regret and constraint-violation guarantees.

AI.tldr: This paper formalizes policy-level Pareto dominance in multi-objective causal bandits, provides a sound and complete graphical characterization of minimal candidate interventions, and designs UCB-style algorithms with logarithmic Pareto regret.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-objective bandit methods rely on pairwise dominance or fixed scalarizations, missing actions that are dominated by randomized policies over other interventions.
AI.method: The authors derive a necessary-and-sufficient graphical criterion for possibly Pareto-optimal minimal intervention sets, then design an online UCB-style algorithm that eliminates actions via convex-combination dominance tests, plus a constrained variant for randomized-policy feasibility.
AI.result: The graphical characterization corrects prior formulations by excluding never-optimal intervention sets, the unconstrained UCB algorithm achieves logarithmic gap-dependent Pareto regret, and the constrained algorithm achieves sublinear regret and constraint-violation guarantees.
AI.conclusion: Accounting for randomized-policy dominance yields tighter causal action-space reduction and provably efficient online learning in multi-objective causal bandits.

title: LoopFill: Pipelined Multi-Token Speculative Decoding for Looped Transformers
summary: Looped Transformers improve parameter efficiency by repeatedly applying the same Transformer layers. During autoregressive decoding, however, generating each token requires several sequential passes through these layers, leading to high decoding latency. Pipelined self-speculative methods use shallow-loop predictions to process tokens at different loops in the same batch, but each token must reach the drafting depth before the next can enter the pipeline. We introduce LoopFill, a training-free speculative decoding algorithm for looped LLM that combines multi-token suffix drafts with shallow-loop predictions in a single draft tree. Both drafters contribute to one tree, so a suffix lookup can immediately extend a shallow prediction and several future tokens can enter the pipeline together. The shared block computes the highest-scoring draft candidates at different loop depths in one batch, and full-depth verification preserves the model's autoregressive output distribution. Across seven benchmarks, LoopFill's average speedup over greedy autoregressive decoding is $5.85\times$ on Ouro-2.6B and $5.13\times$ on Huginn-3.5B. The speedups exceed those of LoopAhead, the strongest baseline, by \(40\%\) on Ouro-2.6B and \(25\%\) on Huginn-3.5B.

AI.tldr: LoopFill is a training-free speculative decoding algorithm for looped Transformers that combines multi-token suffix drafts with shallow-loop predictions in one draft tree, achieving 5.13x-5.85x speedups.
AI.motivation: Looped Transformers reduce parameters by repeating layers, but sequential passes per token create high autoregressive decoding latency, and prior pipelined methods stall until each token reaches drafting depth.
AI.method: LoopFill merges multi-token suffix lookups and shallow-loop predictions into a single draft tree so suffix matches immediately extend shallow drafts, evaluates top candidates across loop depths in one batch, and verifies at full depth to preserve the exact output distribution.
AI.result: Across seven benchmarks, LoopFill achieves average speedups over greedy decoding of 5.85x on Ouro-2.6B and 5.13x on Huginn-3.5B, outperforming the strongest baseline LoopAhead by 40% and 25% respectively.
AI.conclusion: Combining suffix drafting with shallow-loop pipelining in a unified draft tree substantially accelerates looped LLM inference without training or distribution shift.

title: With the Right Representation, Classical Machine Learning Rivals Deep Models for Olfactory Mixture Similarity
summary: Modeling olfactory mixtures remains a critical challenge in machine olfaction because the task requires reasoning over relationships between sets of odorants rather than over individual molecules in isolation. However, prior comparisons between deep and classical approaches also varied how the relationship between the two mixtures was represented, since the classical baselines primarily relied on weak representations that described each mixture independently and provided little direct signal about how the mixtures differed. In this work, we revisit classical learning using explicit symmetric comparison features on unordered pairs of mixtures, evaluating these representations with XGBoost and kernel ridge regression (KRR). We find that XGBoost with explicit comparison features achieves performance competitive with specialized deep mixture models on the main benchmark. Ablation studies show that coordinate-wise absolute differences alone provide strong predictive performance, while combining them with sums and products yields further improvements. KRR also benefits substantially from explicit comparison features, with further gains from appropriate kernel choice and preprocessing. Overall, these results suggest that explicitly encoding how two mixtures differ is an important ingredient for classical machine learning in low-data olfactory mixture prediction.

AI.tldr: With explicit symmetric comparison features on unordered pairs of mixtures, classical models like XGBoost rival specialized deep learning models on olfactory mixture similarity prediction.
AI.motivation: Prior comparisons between deep and classical models for olfactory mixtures gave classical baselines independent per-mixture features that lacked direct relational signals.
AI.method: The authors evaluate XGBoost and kernel ridge regression (KRR) using explicit symmetric comparison features—coordinate-wise absolute differences, sums, and products—over unordered mixture pairs.
AI.result: XGBoost with explicit comparison features matches specialized deep mixture models on the main benchmark; absolute differences alone perform strongly, adding sums and products improves results further, and KRR also gains substantially with appropriate kernels and preprocessing.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly encoding pairwise mixture differences is a key ingredient that enables classical ML to compete with deep models in low-data olfaction.

title: BadGCL: Towards Persistent Backdoor Attack on Graph Continual Learning Systems
summary: Backdoor attacks pose a persistent security threat to machine learning systems, yet their behavior under graph continual learning (GCL) remains underexplored. Conventional graph backdoor attacks often lose effectiveness as models are updated across successive tasks, creating the impression that continual updates naturally weaken malicious associations. This work reveals a contrasting vulnerability: knowledge-preservation mechanisms in GCL can also preserve early injected backdoors when the poisoned update is compatible with the clean-task signal being retained. For graph data, this risk is amplified by structural triggers, which are embedded into the message-passing paths of graph neural networks (GNNs) and can induce stable representation shifts across tasks. To expose this risk, we propose BadGCL, a model-agnostic framework for persistent backdoor attacks under a strict early-stage intervention setting. BadGCL learns topology-aware structural triggers using a gradient mutual-information objective that couples poisoned gradients with clean-task optimization signals, together with a propagation consistency objective that stabilizes trigger-induced effects through graph message passing. We provide theoretical analysis showing that gradient compatibility and propagation stability jointly support long-term backdoor persistence under benign continual updates. Extensive experiments across task-IL and class-IL protocols, four GCL benchmarks, and diverse victim systems show that BadGCL achieves persistent attack effectiveness with limited clean-utility degradation, substantially outperforming graph and continual-learning backdoor baselines and remaining robust against representative defenses.

AI.tldr: BadGCL is a model-agnostic backdoor attack on graph continual learning that learns topology-aware structural triggers to persist across sequential tasks without degrading clean accuracy.
AI.motivation: Conventional graph backdoor attacks fade under continual updates, leaving open whether graph continual learning's knowledge-preservation mechanisms can inadvertently preserve early-injected backdoors.
AI.method: BadGCL optimizes topology-aware structural triggers using a gradient mutual-information objective (aligning poisoned gradients with clean-task signals) and a propagation consistency objective (stabilizing trigger effects through GNN message passing), supported by theoretical persistence analysis.
AI.result: Across task-IL and class-IL protocols on four GCL benchmarks and diverse victim models, BadGCL maintains persistent attack effectiveness with minimal clean-utility loss, outperforming graph and continual-learning backdoor baselines and resisting representative defenses.
AI.conclusion: Knowledge-preservation mechanisms in GCL can amplify structural backdoor persistence when triggers align with clean-task optimization and message passing.

title: Mesoscale Neural Operators: Learning Nonlinear Constitutive Laws from Molecular Dynamics for Scalable Fracture Predictions
summary: Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations can capture the nanoscale physics of fracture at the atomistic level, but their computational cost prohibits predictions at the length scales and time scales needed for many applications. Machine learning approaches, on the other hand, have been proposed as heuristic surrogates for material fracture, yet they cannot guarantee the physical consistency of the predicted response. To address this shortcoming, we propose the mesoscale neural operator (MNO): a data-driven nonlocal constitutive model that is learned directly from MD loading and displacement data. After training, it can be used in continuum fracture simulations on much larger domains and grid sizes. The key idea of the MNO is to exploit the built-in characteristic length of a nonlocal model, called the horizon, to travel across scales. Physical consistency across scales is obtained by building two structural ingredients into the MNO: a normalized kernel that renders the strain energy density invariant under horizon rescaling, and a rescaled critical bond stretch that keeps the energy release rate consistent across scales. Through tests on synthetic data, we show that the MNO and its learning workflow indeed discover the nonlocal continuum multiscale model in the form of the nonlocal kernel and the nonlinear constitutive relation. We then apply the framework to coarse-grained MD data and find that in a test problem, the learned model matches the MD strain energy density and critical energy release rate within 3%. It also predicts the peak transmitted forces within 6% in out-of-distribution tension tests. As a further demonstration, the model is applied to a plate with 4000 times the area of the training specimens and containing an initial defect. In this problem, the model reproduces the main features of dynamic brittle fracture, including branch and cascading branch networks.

AI.tldr: Mesoscale Neural Operators (MNOs) learn physically consistent nonlocal constitutive laws from molecular dynamics data, enabling scalable continuum fracture simulations on domains 4,000x larger than training specimens.
AI.motivation: Molecular dynamics captures nanoscale fracture physics but cannot scale to macroscopic domains, while heuristic ML surrogates lack physical consistency across scales.
AI.method: MNOs embed a nonlocal horizon length scale using a normalized kernel that keeps strain energy density invariant under horizon rescaling and a rescaled critical bond stretch that preserves energy release rate across scales.
AI.result: On coarse-grained MD data, MNOs match strain energy density and critical energy release rate within 3%, predict peak transmitted forces within 6% in out-of-distribution tension tests, and reproduce dynamic brittle branching fracture on a plate 4,000x the training area.
AI.conclusion: Building scale-invariant nonlocal physics into neural operators bridges atomistic fracture data and large-scale continuum simulations.

title: Score-Based Stochastic Closure Modeling via Offline Indirect Learning and Online Data Assimilation
summary: Stochastic closure modeling is an emerging area in reduced-order modeling of large and complex (e.g., multiscale, multi-physics) systems, for which the computationally affordable reduced-order physical descriptions (e.g., digital twins for additive manufacturing, world models for AI agents) in numerical simulations inevitably lead to information losses that cannot be well addressed by classical deterministic closures. However, learning stochastic closures typically requires closure data that are difficult to obtain from measurements or often prohibitively expensive to compute using first-principles simulations. In this work, we develop a stochastic closure modeling framework that builds on score-based diffusion models, leveraging indirect offline training and online data assimilation without requiring the direct data of closures. Numerical experiments on two-dimensional turbulent flows demonstrate that indirect offline learning captures key closure statistics and improves predictions of system state. In addition, combining the learned closure with known physical dynamics leads to better generalization capability across different regimes than purely data-driven models that directly predict system state. Compared to standard data assimilation methods with a Gaussian assumption, the posterior-score assimilation better represents non-Gaussian features of the learned closure, and its combination with state-level data assimilation further improves prediction of the system state. The proposed framework enables stochastic closure modeling in realistic and challenging scenarios of complex dynamical systems in mechanics and engineering problems, where non-Gaussian statistics of model-form uncertainties are non-negligible (e.g., due to the nonlinearities of the system dynamics and/or the observations) and true closure data are not available, for both offline learning and online assimilation.

AI.tldr: This work develops a score-based diffusion framework for stochastic closure modeling using indirect offline learning and online posterior-score data assimilation, without requiring direct closure data.
AI.motivation: Reduced-order models of complex multiscale systems lose information that deterministic closures cannot capture, yet direct closure data for training stochastic closures are rarely available.
AI.method: The framework trains score-based diffusion closures indirectly offline from system observations and couples them with physical dynamics via online posterior-score data assimilation.
AI.result: On 2D turbulent flows, indirect offline learning captures key closure statistics, combining learned closures with physical dynamics generalizes better across regimes than purely data-driven state predictors, and posterior-score assimilation captures non-Gaussian features better than Gaussian assimilation.
AI.conclusion: Score-based indirect learning and assimilation enable practical stochastic closure modeling for nonlinear, non-Gaussian dynamical systems without ground-truth closure data.

title: RIFT: Reward Improvement Field Transfer for Cross-Domain Offline RL
comment: 39 pages, 4 figures, 17 tables (10 pages main text; remainder references and appendices)
summary: Learning from limited target data is a central challenge in cross-domain offline reinforcement learning. Abundant source data can help, but dynamics differences can make direct transition reuse unreliable. We propose Reward Improvement Field Transfer (RIFT), which instead learns how low- and high-reward source transitions differ. RIFT encodes source and target transitions in a shared latent space, pairs low- and high-reward source transitions using optimal transport, and fits an affine field to their displacements. It applies this field to low-reward target anchors and decodes the results to augment the target dataset. The approach builds on the hypothesis that related domains can share useful low-to-high reward structure despite different dynamics. We bound synthesis error under shared class geometry, identify conditions favoring target anchoring over source-high transplant, and derive a conditional connection to downstream return. Experiments on dense-reward locomotion tasks under gravity, morphology, and friction shifts show improved aggregate performance over existing baselines.

AI.tldr: RIFT improves cross-domain offline RL by learning an affine reward-improvement field from optimal-transport-paired source transitions and applying it to low-reward target anchors to augment target data.
AI.motivation: Cross-domain offline RL suffers from scarce target data, and dynamics mismatches make direct reuse of source transitions unreliable.
AI.method: RIFT embeds source and target transitions into a shared latent space, pairs low- and high-reward source transitions via optimal transport, fits an affine displacement field, and applies it to low-reward target anchors before decoding into augmented target transitions.
AI.result: Backed by synthesis-error bounds and return connections, RIFT outperforms existing baselines in aggregate performance on dense-reward locomotion tasks under gravity, morphology, and friction shifts.
AI.conclusion: Transferring relational reward-improvement structure rather than raw transitions provides a more robust way to augment scarce target data in cross-domain offline RL.

title: Elicited Adaptation: Auditable Localized Fairness via Pairwise Queries
summary: How much must a predictor's scores change when a community's elicited fairness standard changes? Similarity and tolerance judgments define protected comparisons and acceptable score gaps. We study minimum uniform score movement on a fixed pool of $n$ profiles. For scores satisfying a source standard, we characterize the exact cost of retaining that standard during adaptation: runs of consecutive target constraints along shortest paths determine the optimal amplification factor. Its sharp worst case is $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$, and a full cost curve describes finite target-only repair budgets. Committing before the target is known can cost $n-1$ times the worst repair after revelation, even within one fixed convex ball of two-dimensional Mahalanobis metrics. Positive edge-budget floors cap both factors; bounded geometry also limits the commitment cost. At two interior targets of the construction attaining the $n-1$ bound, similarity queries alone yield a feasible $2$-approximate repair for tolerance $\eps\le1/[2(n-1)]$, reducing movement relative to common repair by a factor linear in $n$. Feasible $(1+\alpha)$-optimal repair on this family has worst-case tolerance-query complexity $\Theta(\alpha^{-2}n^2\log(1/\delta))$ under a fixed-slope logistic model. The analysis separates the information needed for a substantial adaptation benefit from the precision needed for nearly optimal movement. Elicitation studies and training comparisons examine tolerance choice and the relation between numerical compliance and predictive utility.

AI.tldr: This paper characterizes the exact movement cost and query complexity of adapting a predictor's scores to elicited local fairness standards via pairwise similarity and tolerance queries.
AI.motivation: When a community's fairness standard changes, it is unclear how much a predictor's scores must move to satisfy new local constraints while optionally preserving prior standards.
AI.method: Analyzing minimum uniform score movement on n profiles, the authors derive shortest-path amplification factors for retaining source standards, compare pre-revelation commitment against post-revelation repair, and analyze similarity and tolerance query complexity under a logistic model.
AI.result: Retaining a source standard has a sharp worst-case amplification factor of floor(n/2); committing before target revelation can cost n - 1 times post-revelation repair; similarity queries alone yield a 2-approximate repair for small tolerances, while (1 + alpha)-optimal repair requires Theta(alpha^-2 * n^2 * log(1/delta)) tolerance queries.
AI.conclusion: The analysis separates the coarse information needed for substantial adaptation gains from the query precision required for near-optimal fairness repair.

title: MathaMAGICal: Validating Trajectory Data Attribution During Capability Acquisition
summary: Influence-function-based methods like MAGIC provide exact first-order scores for trajectory data attribution, yet only retraining indicates whether those scores accurately predict data removal. We evaluate MAGIC on $86$M- and $152$M-parameter GPT-2-style models learning multistep arithmetic from scratch on filtered web text and four synthetic math families. Full-run attribution at $86$M suffers from numerical overflow, and even with metagradient clipping, scores correlate near chance with retraining (linear datamodeling score, LDS, $0.17$--$0.22$). In contrast, short checkpoint windows yield stable, accurate predictions at both scales (LDS $0.86$--$0.99$ across four $100$-step windows at $152$M), whereas a single-checkpoint gradient-dot baseline shows near-zero correlation. Rankings of individual training blocks predict retraining only within that single run and do not transfer across seeds or hyperparameters ($\rho \le 0.09$), whereas format-level patterns replicate across runs. Two data families, worked examples and primitive facts, occupy $2.1$--$2.6\times$ their corpus share in both the helpful and harmful $5\%$ score tails, reflecting strong bidirectional local sensitivity distinct from net benefit under multi-epoch family deletion. These results show that trajectory attribution is reliable within short, validated windows and yields family-level insights that generalize across runs.

AI.tldr: Evaluating MAGIC trajectory data attribution on 86M and 152M models learning arithmetic shows that full-run attribution fails, whereas short checkpoint windows yield accurate, stable predictions and transferable format-level insights.
AI.motivation: Influence-based trajectory attribution methods like MAGIC provide exact first-order scores, but their actual agreement with retraining during capability acquisition is unverified.
AI.method: The authors evaluate MAGIC against retraining on 86M and 152M GPT-2-style models trained from scratch on filtered web text and four synthetic math families across full runs and 100-step checkpoint windows.
AI.result: Full-run attribution at 86M overflows and correlates near chance with retraining (LDS 0.17-0.22), whereas 100-step windows at 152M achieve LDS 0.86-0.99 (vs. near-zero for single-checkpoint gradient-dot); block rankings do not transfer across seeds (rho <= 0.09), but worked examples and primitive facts consistently occupy 2.1x-2.6x their corpus share in both 5% score tails.
AI.conclusion: Trajectory data attribution is reliable within short validated windows and reveals family-level sensitivity patterns that generalize across runs.

title: Data Attribution Should Steer Pretraining
comment: Accepted to the 3rd Workshop on Attributing Model Behavior at Scale: Data Attribution and Provenance (ATTRIB 2026) at NeurIPS 2026, Idea Track. 4 pages main text, 13 pages total, 1 figure, 2 tables
summary: Pretraining data curation decides what a model learns from, yet what makes a document worth learning from depends on what the model already knows. Influence-driven selectors already rank documents to improve one run; we argue that training-data attribution should steer pretraining by identifying testable data properties that become reusable curation criteria, evaluated on new data against cheaper selectors at matched total cost, discovery included. A document ranking is consumed by the run it was computed for, whereas an explained data property can be tested across corpora and checkpoints, especially where familiar quality signals diverge from measured usefulness. Because historical contribution, an understandable explanation, and future data value require distinct evidence, we specify a feedback loop that interprets attributed sources, tests candidate data changes, and states for five claim types what evidence each requires and what none establishes. We close with a falsifiable comparison against perplexity, classifier, and mixing baselines at equal total compute.

AI.tldr: This position paper argues that training-data attribution should steer pretraining by distilling attributed sources into testable, reusable curation criteria evaluated at matched total compute.
AI.motivation: Current influence-driven selectors produce one-off document rankings tied to a single run rather than generalizable properties that can guide future pretraining curation.
AI.method: The authors propose a feedback loop that interprets attributed sources, formulates testable data-property hypotheses, and specifies distinct evidence requirements across five claim types, evaluated against perplexity, classifier, and mixing baselines at equal total compute.
AI.result: The paper outlines a falsifiable evaluation protocol distinguishing historical contribution, understandable explanation, and future data value, rather than reporting new empirical runs.
AI.conclusion: Turning attribution into reusable, compute-matched curation criteria offers a principled path for data-centric pretraining.

title: Where Should LLM Agents Adapt at Test Time? In Context, in Weights, or Both
summary: LLM agents operating repeatedly in the same environment, such as a code repository, a database, or an application suite, encounter tasks that share latent structure. Experience can reveal this structure, allowing agents to reuse environment knowledge and learn from environmental feedback. Agents can adapt at test-time using this experience through two channels: retaining it in context and updating their weights. These channels are usually studied separately, leaving unclear what each contributes and when they complement each other. We compare in-context learning (ICL), reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards using GRPO, and self-distillation using SDPO, alone and in combination, using a shared online protocol and modular framework. Agents encounter matched task streams, are evaluated on each task before adapting to it, and learn only from their own attempts and environment feedback. We evaluate 14 adaptation mechanisms and a stateless baseline with Qwen3.5-9B on 109 tasks from four environments drawn from SWE-bench Verified, AppWorld, ScienceWorld, and BIRD-Critic-SQLite, using five task orders per environment. ICL provides the largest standalone gain: its best policy raises mean success across environments from 28.8% to 49.4%. Adding GRPO to this policy achieves the highest mean success, 51.6%. While adding GRPO improves the overall mean under every ICL policy, SDPO has mixed effects. Trace analyses show fewer lookups and shorter attempts under ICL, consistent with reusing knowledge of the shared structure. However, ICL also frequently skips inspection and verification for the current task. Adding GRPO to ICL helps restore these behaviors while preserving its reduced environment lookups. These observations suggest that reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards can refine how agents use retained experience, motivating the joint study of context management and weight updates.

AI.tldr: Comparing 14 test-time adaptation mechanisms on Qwen3.5-9B across four agentic environments shows that in-context learning (ICL) provides the largest standalone gain, and adding GRPO achieves the highest overall success.
AI.motivation: LLM agents can adapt at test time via in-context experience or weight updates, but their individual contributions and interactions on repeated-environment tasks remain unclear.
AI.method: Using a shared online protocol on 109 tasks across SWE-bench Verified, AppWorld, ScienceWorld, and BIRD-Critic-SQLite (five task orders each), the authors evaluate ICL, GRPO, and SDPO alone and in combination.
AI.result: The best ICL policy raises mean success from 28.8% to 49.4%, and adding GRPO reaches 51.6% (improving every ICL policy, whereas SDPO is mixed); trace analysis shows ICL reduces lookups and attempt length but skips verification, which GRPO helps restore.
AI.conclusion: Combining in-context experience retention with verifiable-reward RL (GRPO) yields complementary gains for test-time agent adaptation.

title: Multiaccuracy as an Error Benchmark for Learning with Distribution Shift
summary: Agnostic learning has a well-developed theory of computational and statistical complexity. For learning with distribution shift, even the choice of an appropriate error benchmark remains challenging. Testable learning with distribution shift (TDS) was introduced to develop computational foundations for this setting: using labeled training data and unlabeled test data, the learner must either produce a predictor with low test error or detect distribution shift. However, standard agnostic TDS guarantees allow a constant-factor amplification of the optimum error even when the training and test distributions coincide. They therefore do not directly recover the guarantee of classical agnostic learning. We introduce shift multiaccuracy, a stronger error benchmark inspired by multiaccuracy from algorithmic fairness. This yields a TDS formulation that becomes equivalent to multiaccuracy when there is no shift. Using a recent nontrivial reduction from agnostic learning to multiaccurate prediction from prior work, we obtain the first TDS framework that formally generalizes agnostic learning through an efficient reduction preserving the training marginal. The framework retains existing algorithmic upper bounds and inherits computational lower bounds from agnostic learning. Moreover, we establish a direct connection between our model and identity testing, yielding the first statistical characterization of agnostic TDS learning, in terms of Rademacher complexity. More broadly, we argue that shift multiaccuracy might be of independent interest in unsupervised domain adaptation, as it leads to sharper out-of-distribution generalization guarantees, and can be minimized directly, since its definition does not involve the unobserved test labels.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces shift multiaccuracy as a stronger error benchmark for testable learning with distribution shift (TDS), yielding the first TDS framework that formally generalizes classical agnostic learning.
AI.motivation: Standard agnostic TDS guarantees suffer from constant-factor error amplification even when training and test distributions match, failing to recover classical agnostic learning.
AI.method: Drawing on algorithmic fairness, the authors define shift multiaccuracy, apply a reduction from agnostic learning to multiaccurate prediction that preserves the training marginal, and connect the model to identity testing.
AI.result: The resulting TDS framework formally generalizes agnostic learning while retaining existing algorithmic upper bounds, inheriting computational lower bounds, and providing the first Rademacher-complexity statistical characterization of agnostic TDS learning.
AI.conclusion: Shift multiaccuracy bridges testable distribution-shift learning and classical agnostic learning, offering sharper out-of-distribution guarantees.

title: Sample-Efficient Ensemble Reinforcement Learning at Scale
summary: Ensemble methods such as MeanQ have been shown to improve the sample efficiency of relatively small model-free deep reinforcement learning (RL) architectures, including DQN and similarly sized variants such as Rainbow. However, to our knowledge, the effects of ensembling on large-scale architectures such as Bigger Better Faster (BBF) have not been studied. In this work, we present MeanQ-BBF, a hybrid model-free algorithm that combines the principles of MeanQ and BBF. Through statistically rigorous evaluation on the Atari 100K benchmark, we show that in contrast to naive scaling of the network size of BBF, which degrades performance, MeanQ-BBF is able to leverage the increase in model capacity to improve performance over BBF. Moreover, MeanQ-BBF does this in a computationally efficient way by organizing the added parameters into largely independent learners. Finally, we discuss the performance-cost tradeoff in the context of practical sample-efficient RL.

AI.tldr: MeanQ-BBF combines MeanQ ensembling with the large-scale Bigger Better Faster (BBF) RL architecture, improving Atari 100K performance where naive BBF scaling degrades.
AI.motivation: Ensembling improves sample efficiency in small model-free RL agents like DQN and Rainbow, but its effect on large-scale architectures like BBF has not been studied.
AI.method: The authors integrate MeanQ into BBF by organizing added parameters into largely independent ensemble learners and evaluate on the Atari 100K benchmark.
AI.result: Unlike naive network scaling of BBF—which degrades performance—MeanQ-BBF leverages increased capacity to outperform BBF on Atari 100K in a computationally efficient manner.
AI.conclusion: Structuring additional capacity as independent ensemble learners unlocks scaling gains for sample-efficient model-free RL.

title: Exploration of Reinforcement Learning in Generative Recommendation Models
summary: Traditional cascaded recommender systems balance accuracy and efficiency over large item spaces, but misaligned stage-wise objectives hinder end-to-end optimization. Generative recommendation unifies these stages in an autoregressive framework, providing a natural interface for reinforcement learning (RL) to optimize the entire generation process. However, directly applying RL often leads to unstable optimization and degraded recommendation quality. We revisit Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) and other ratio-based objectives through a unified logit-gradient view. We identify three issues: (i) clipped surrogates create dead-gradient regions, under-utilizing samples; (ii) negative-advantage updates can become effectively unbounded as importance ratios grow, allowing a small subset of negatives to dominate optimization; and (iii) ratio-based control lacks sensitivity to absolute policy confidence, so updates on high-confidence cases may fail to vanish. Motivated by this diagnosis, we propose \emph{Gradient-Bounded Policy Optimization} (GBPO), a simple objective with stop-gradient normalization that is simultaneously (a) fully gradient-active, (b) sign-symmetrically bounded for both positive and negative updates, and (c) explicitly confidence-weighted under current policy probabilities. This ensures that updates gracefully vanish for $\pi\!\to\!1$ positives and $\pi\!\to\!0$ negatives. Across the evaluated settings, GBPO achieves competitive recommendation performance with more stable training than competing RL methods.

AI.tldr: Gradient-Bounded Policy Optimization (GBPO) replaces clipped ratio objectives in generative recommendation RL with stop-gradient normalization, yielding bounded, confidence-weighted updates and more stable training.
AI.motivation: Applying ratio-based RL like GRPO to autoregressive generative recommendation suffers from dead-gradient clipping regions, unbounded negative-advantage updates, and lack of sensitivity to policy confidence.
AI.method: Based on a unified logit-gradient analysis, GBPO uses stop-gradient normalization so updates are fully gradient-active, sign-symmetrically bounded for positives and negatives, and explicitly vanish as policy confidence approaches 1 for positives or 0 for negatives.
AI.result: Across evaluated generative recommendation settings, GBPO achieves competitive recommendation quality with more stable optimization than competing RL methods.
AI.conclusion: Bounding and confidence-weighting logit gradients via stop-gradient normalization stabilizes RL fine-tuning for generative recommenders.

title: When Does an AUROC Comparison Survive a Change in Population Mix?
comment: 30 pages, 5 figures. This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible
summary: Does an AUROC comparison survive a change in the proportions of tasks, populations, or image corruptions? A pooled-AUROC ranking of failure detectors or uncertainty scores describes one particular mix of groups. We study two fixed scores for a common binary target under mixtures of fixed group-conditional laws. Using the cross-group AUC decomposition, we prove that every rational symmetric quadratic comparison geometry is realizable by finite scalar-score distributions. Universal dominance is thus coNP-hard, and even exhaustive checks of every mixture on fewer than $K$ groups can miss a $K$-group reversal. A grid bound gives a dimension-uniform approximation certificate with sharp $1/m$ order. Common score marginals across groups make the comparison numerator linear, with an error envelope for imperfect alignment. These results yield exact finite-bank audits, explicit reversal mixtures and distances, and simultaneous population statements. For failure detection with a frozen ResNet-50 on ImageNet-C, 15 of 18 confidence-score comparisons win in every corruption family on a discovery split, and all 15 are finite-bank certified over all family mixtures on a held-out split; over all 15 corruption types, of 14 discovery winners the corrected grid certifies 10, leaves 3 unresolved, and finds one confirmation reversal of at least 0.05 AUROC. An audit of all 11,019 released Stable LM 2 12B outputs and 35 uncertainty methods finds 66 confirmation-set comparisons that win within all four tasks yet reverse under mixing. Discovery-fitted marginal rank alignment removes all 66; an alignment-error envelope certifies 83 comparisons. Label checks also change several selected reversals. The findings distinguish robustness of frozen scores from robustness after calibration; they do not establish human-error detection, robustness to unseen corruptions, or generalization beyond the evaluated banks.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes the hardness of universal AUROC dominance under changing group mixtures and provides finite-bank certification, grid bounds, and marginal rank alignment methods validated on ImageNet-C and Stable LM 2 12B.
AI.motivation: Pooled AUROC comparisons depend on the specific mix of groups, tasks, or corruptions, and can reverse when population proportions change.
AI.method: Using cross-group AUC decomposition, the authors prove universal dominance is coNP-hard, derive dimension-uniform grid certificates of order 1/m, and introduce marginal rank alignment with error envelopes.
AI.result: On ImageNet-C (ResNet-50), all 15 discovery winners across corruption families are certified over family mixtures, while across 15 corruption types 10 of 14 are certified, 3 unresolved, and 1 reverses by at least 0.05 AUROC; on 11,019 Stable LM 2 12B outputs, 66 within-task winners reverse under mixing, and marginal rank alignment removes all 66 while certifying 83 comparisons.
AI.conclusion: Mixture-aware certification and marginal rank alignment are essential to prevent spurious AUROC rankings under shifting population or task mixes.

title: PISG: Constraint-Aligned Signal Amplification for Diffusion-Based Combinatorial Optimization
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 (poster). 32 pages. Code: this https URL
summary: Diffusion-based solvers have become a prominent approach to neural combinatorial optimization. At inference time, they assign each decision variable a prediction score. A greedy decoder ranks candidates by these scores and checks hard constraints to ensure feasibility.
