The proposed model is evaluated in SUMO against three baselines: a model that observes only the neighbouring vehicles, a model that encodes the global traffic information, and the rule-based SUMO model. The results show that our model achieves the highest traffic flow, safety and smoothness. Furthermore, in a four-hour simulation with dynamic traffic demand, our model successfully avoids traffic jams, while other baseline models fail at high traffic flow. We also show that our model remains effective when human-driven vehicles are present. We further show that our model, trained in ideal communication conditions, can still remain collision-free and maintain throughput under realistic V2I communication errors. Finally, we visualise the relevance weights that an ego vehicle assigns to other vehicles in multiple traffic situations.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an infrastructure-based transformer MARL controller that uses attention over global traffic states to coordinate connected autonomous vehicles during highway on-ramp merging.
AI.motivation: In dense highway merging, observing only neighboring vehicles yields locally optimal decisions while observing all vehicles introduces irrelevant clutter.
AI.method: A roadside infrastructure controller collects CAV states via V2I communication and uses an attention-based observation encoder to filter relevant vehicles from the global traffic state before issuing control commands.
AI.result: Evaluated in SUMO against neighbor-only, global-state, and rule-based baselines, the proposed model achieves the highest traffic flow, safety, and smoothness, avoids traffic jams in a four-hour dynamic-demand simulation, and remains effective with human-driven vehicles and under realistic V2I communication errors.
AI.conclusion: Attention-based global-state filtering from roadside infrastructure enables safe, high-throughput cooperative highway merging even under mixed traffic and imperfect communication.

title: MT-RGCN-DTI: A Multi-Task Relational Graph Convolutional Network for Drug-Target Interaction Prediction
summary: Prediction of drug-target interaction (DTI) has become a very crucial part of drug discovery. With the increase in the data volume, it has become very important to improve prediction accuracy by integrating multiple data sources. In this regard, utilising multiple resources in the form of heterogeneous information network to address DTI prediction can be rewarding. In this work, we propose a heterogeneous information network based multi-task DTI prediction model which leverages the advantages of relation graph convolutional network (RGCN). To achieve this, the model employs drug-target interaction network, drug-drug similarity network and protein-protein similarity network to construct a heterogeneous information network. Moreover, we use a knowledge graph embedding scoring functions to model interactions between drug and targets, specifically DistMult and ComplEx as decoders over the learned node representations. We performed extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets and compared with state-of-the-art methods. We observed that the proposed model shows competitive performance, thereby confirming the effectiveness of our approach. The codes and datasets are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes MT-RGCN-DTI, a multi-task relational graph convolutional network over a heterogeneous drug-target information network for drug-target interaction prediction.
AI.motivation: Improving drug-target interaction prediction accuracy requires integrating multiple heterogeneous biological data sources rather than relying on isolated networks.
AI.method: The authors construct a heterogeneous information network from drug-target interactions, drug-drug similarity, and protein-protein similarity, encode nodes with an RGCN, and decode interactions using DistMult and ComplEx knowledge graph embedding scoring functions.
AI.result: Across multiple benchmark datasets, MT-RGCN-DTI achieves competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art drug-target interaction prediction methods.
AI.conclusion: Combining relational graph convolutions with knowledge graph embedding decoders on heterogeneous similarity and interaction networks effectively predicts drug-target interactions.

title: CECAR: Cache & Expert Co-Aware Routing Accelerates On-Device Inference of MoE LLMs
comment: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026. 24 pages, 5 figures, 19 tables
summary: Despite growing interest in on-device LLM deployment, large-scale Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models remain impractical on resource-constrained devices, as sparse expert activation still requires all expert weights to be memory-resident. To address this, we identify three key observations for on-device MoE inference: (a) cache hit rates are fundamentally bounded even under Belady's optimal policy; (b) these bounds are insufficient for low-latency on-device inference; and (c) prior cache-aware routing based on binary cache presence can induce routing instability. Based on these insights, we propose CECAR (Cache & Expert Co-Aware Routing), a MoE inference system that jointly considers expert routing and cache management. Unlike prior cache-aware routing methods, CECAR uses an ML-based cache policy to predict the expected reuse distance of each expert and prioritizes routing and execution toward experts with smaller predicted reuse distances. On the Qwen3-30B-A3B model, CECAR achieves 12.5 tokens/s on a consumer-grade GPU with only 16 GB of VRAM, where non-resident experts are fetched from SSD, delivering a 4.5x speedup over conventional MoE inference and exceeding the decode speed of baselines that keep the entire model fully resident in DRAM. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces CECAR, an on-device MoE inference system that uses ML-predicted expert reuse distances to jointly guide expert routing and cache management.
AI.motivation: Sparse Mixture-of-Experts LLMs are impractical on memory-constrained devices because cache hit rates are bounded even under Belady's optimal policy and binary cache-aware routing causes routing instability.
AI.method: CECAR trains an ML-based cache policy to predict each expert's expected reuse distance and prioritizes routing and execution toward experts with smaller predicted reuse distances, fetching non-resident experts from SSD.
AI.result: On Qwen3-30B-A3B using a consumer GPU with 16 GB VRAM, CECAR achieves 12.5 tokens/s, delivering a 4.5x speedup over conventional MoE inference and exceeding the decode speed of baselines that keep the full model in DRAM.
AI.conclusion: Co-designing expert routing with reuse-distance cache prediction makes large MoE LLM inference practical on consumer-grade, VRAM-limited hardware.

title: QA-CMIF:Accurate and Lightweight Cross-Modal Latent Imputation and Fusion for Fault-Tolerant sEMG-Inertial Hand Gesture Recognition
summary: Fusing surface electromyography (sEMG) with inertial measurements is widely used for myoelectric prosthesis control and wearable human-machine interfaces. In daily wear, however, socket micro-displacement, electrode lift-off, and wire failures often corrupt an unknown subset of sEMG channels through burst artifacts, lift-off shocks, or open-circuit dropouts. Existing fusion networks mix all channels in the first convolutional layer, so a few corrupted electrodes contaminate the entire latent representation, whereas gate-only attenuation of corrupted channels discards the co-activation cues needed to separate fine-grained gestures. We propose QA-CMIF, a quality-aware cross-modal latent imputation and fusion framework that encodes each sEMG channel independently, scores its reliability with a soft gate, and protects intact channels via a confidence-weighted residual bypass, while a cross-attention imputer repairs degraded channels in latent space using the inertial stream and remaining reliable sEMG channels under a bad-channel alignment loss. Across within-subject evaluations on 29 participants from Ninapro DB3, DB2, and DB5 spanning 17-52 gesture classes, QA-CMIF outperformed the gate-only baseline under 50% channel corruption by 1.29-2.65 percentage points, denoted pp, across all three 17-class cohorts with paired-t Holm-adjusted p<0.002, widened this margin to 2.59-4.15 pp on the 40- and 52-class tasks, and surpassed corruption-augmented conventional fusion by 4.61-19.85 pp. Requiring only 0.175-0.185M parameters and 2.45-2.63M multiply-accumulate operations across the 2000 Hz and 200 Hz setups, QA-CMIF saves 46%-55% in parameters and 72%-81% in compute over recent baselines with a 1.44 ms 99th-percentile single-thread CPU latency.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes QA-CMIF, a lightweight quality-aware cross-modal latent imputation and fusion framework for fault-tolerant sEMG and inertial hand gesture recognition.
AI.motivation: In wearable myoelectric interfaces, electrode lift-off, micro-displacement, and wire failures corrupt subsets of sEMG channels, contaminating standard early-fusion networks while gate-only attenuation discards fine-grained co-activation cues.
AI.method: QA-CMIF encodes each sEMG channel independently, scores channel reliability with a soft gate, preserves intact channels via a confidence-weighted residual bypass, and repairs degraded channels in latent space using cross-attention with the inertial stream and reliable sEMG channels under a bad-channel alignment loss.
AI.result: Across 29 participants from Ninapro DB3, DB2, and DB5 (17-52 classes) under 50% channel corruption, QA-CMIF outperforms the gate-only baseline by 1.29-2.65 pp on 17-class cohorts (p<0.002) and 2.59-4.15 pp on 40- and 52-class tasks, and beats corruption-augmented conventional fusion by 4.61-19.85 pp while using 0.175-0.185M parameters, 2.45-2.63M MACs, and 1.44 ms p99 single-thread CPU latency.
AI.conclusion: Per-channel reliability gating paired with cross-modal latent imputation enables accurate, fault-tolerant, and lightweight wearable gesture recognition.

title: Symmetry Fingerprinting with Geometric Learnable Invariants Transformers
summary: Geometric deep learning has made available a large variety of structurally equivariant neural network architectures, meaning a particular transformation of their input causes a predictable transformation of their output. But structural equivariance is a very strong inductive bias that can limit performance if chosen poorly. In contrast, choosing an architecture with low geometric bias necessitates data augmentation to obtain correct behavior; extending the training process. We propose a novel neural network architecture that is soft equivariant; we select a set of symmetry groups and during training the network will become equivariant only to those symmetry groups that are appropriate given the training data. After training we can inspect the network to obtain a symmetry fingerprint that will tell us exactly which symmetries ended up being relevant and to what degree. We show how our architecture and the fingerprinting process work in the case of an image classification task.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a soft-equivariant neural network architecture that learns from training data which symmetry groups to become equivariant to and produces an inspectable symmetry fingerprint.
AI.motivation: Hard-coded structural equivariance can hurt performance if mismatched to the data, whereas low-bias architectures require extensive data augmentation.
AI.method: Given a candidate set of symmetry groups, the proposed architecture softly learns equivariance during training only to the groups supported by the data, allowing post-training inspection of a symmetry fingerprint showing which symmetries were learned and to what degree.
AI.result: The authors demonstrate the soft-equivariant architecture and symmetry fingerprinting process on an image classification task.
AI.conclusion: Soft equivariance avoids rigid inductive biases while revealing data-driven symmetry structure through interpretable fingerprints.

title: Weights & Caches: LLMs Can Program Tabular Foundation Models
summary: Neural networks are typically programmed through optimization, rather than by explicitly specifying their computations. Recent work on weight-space programming suggests that large language models (LLMs) can instead reason about and manipulate neural-network weights directly. In this work, we show that LLMs can directly program statistical computations in tabular foundation models (TFMs), whose parameters enable inference across different datasets. We investigate three complementary settings using GPT-6 Astra, without gradient-based optimization. First, Astra directly programs nanoTabPFN from zero-initialized weights, achieving a mean ROC AUC of 0.849 across 20 TabArena datasets, compared to 0.876 for a pretrained baseline. Second, Astra diagnoses and repairs a signed-product regression failure in pretrained TabPFN-3.5, restoring near-perfect predictions on held-out synthetic datasets while preserving performance on TabArena-Lite, with only a 0.08% average relative increase in error. Third, it writes KV-cache-editing programs that steer TabPFN-3.5's predictions on unseen synthetic datasets, demonstrating transformations such as reversing linear trends and converting sine waves into approximate square waves, without modifying model weights. Together, our findings suggest that LLM-driven programming could complement gradient-based optimization across TFMs' development and usage, while offering a new way to investigate and intervene in their internal computations.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that LLMs can directly program weights and KV caches of tabular foundation models without gradient-based optimization to initialize, repair, and steer predictions.
AI.motivation: Neural networks are normally programmed via gradient optimization, raising the question of whether LLMs can explicitly reason about and program statistical computations directly in tabular foundation model weights.
AI.method: Using GPT-6 Astra without gradient optimization, the authors program nanoTabPFN from zero-initialized weights, diagnose and repair a signed-product regression failure in pretrained TabPFN-3.5, and write KV-cache-editing programs to steer TabPFN-3.5 predictions.
AI.result: Astra-programmed nanoTabPFN achieves 0.849 mean ROC AUC across 20 TabArena datasets versus 0.876 for a pretrained baseline; repairing TabPFN-3.5 restores near-perfect synthetic predictions with only a 0.08% average relative error increase on TabArena-Lite; and KV-cache programs reverse linear trends and convert sine waves into approximate square waves without weight edits.
AI.conclusion: LLM-driven weight and KV-cache programming offers a viable complement to gradient-based optimization for developing, debugging, and intervening in tabular foundation models.

title: UrbanROI: Causal Modeling for Regional ROI Forecasting under POI Entry
summary: As urban commercial environments continue to evolve rapidly, accurately modeling the economic impact of point of interest (POI) entry is essential for supporting data-driven advertising allocation, merchant onboarding, and regional business decision-making. Existing return on investment (ROI) prediction methods mainly focus on individual ads or merchants, overlooking the interaction effects among POIs and failing to capture the causal influence of structural changes in urban commercial ecosystems. In this paper, we introduce a novel research problem -- regional ROI forecasting under POI entry, which aims to predict the future ROI trajectory of a commercial region after the introduction of a new POI by modeling temporal ROI evolution and competition-driven interactions among surrounding POIs. To address these challenges, we propose UrbanROI, an intervention-aware causal forecasting framework for region-level economic outcome prediction. UrbanROI leverages an Interaction-aware Regional Graph Module to explicitly model competitive relationships among POIs based on user request contexts, spatial proximity, and request-level commercial signals, and constructs structurally aligned treatment and control graphs to simulate factual and counterfactual regional states. Extensive experiments on large-scale real-world POI and advertising datasets demonstrate that UrbanROI consistently outperforms strong baselines in post-entry regional ROI forecasting. The results demonstrate its effectiveness in temporal economic modeling, inter-POI interaction representation, and intervention-aware forecasting, providing support for regional economic analysis and business decision-making in dynamic urban commercial systems.

AI.tldr: This paper defines regional ROI forecasting under POI entry and proposes UrbanROI, an intervention-aware causal graph forecasting framework to predict post-entry regional economic outcomes.
AI.motivation: Existing ROI prediction models focus on individual ads or merchants, ignoring inter-POI competition and the causal impact of new POI entries on surrounding urban commercial ecosystems.
AI.method: UrbanROI uses an Interaction-aware Regional Graph Module to model POI competition from user request contexts, spatial proximity, and commercial signals, and constructs structurally aligned treatment and control graphs to simulate factual and counterfactual regional states.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on large-scale real-world POI and advertising datasets show that UrbanROI consistently outperforms strong baselines in post-entry regional ROI forecasting.
AI.conclusion: Modeling inter-POI interactions with aligned treatment-control graphs enables accurate causal forecasting of regional economic impacts after POI entry.

title: Deep Sequence Model for Genome Wide Discovery of Coding and Regulatory Element Signatures
comment: 4 pages, 3 figures, 1 table. Accepted at CVIS 2025. A shorter 3-page version was published in the Journal of Computational Vision and Imaging Systems, Vol. 11, No. 1 (2026)
summary: Interpreting deep neural networks for genomic sequence classification remains challenging despite strong predictive performance. We develop a lightweight CNN with post-training gradient-based analysis to identify which sequence positions drive coding versus intergenomic classification. Applied to the standardized demo_coding_vs_intergenomic_seqs dataset, our model achieves 91.87% validation accuracy while revealing interpretable patterns: nine hot spots with consistently high importance, clear class-specific separation at positions 20-100 (coding) and 150-190 (intergenomic), and a strong mean-variance correlation (r = 0.530) indicating robust discriminative features. Gradient-based importance analysis shows that the model implicitly learns biologically meaningful sequence distinctions without explicit annotations. This work demonstrates that neural network interpretability and accuracy can coexist, providing a framework for understanding genomic sequence classification and enabling biology-driven hypothesis generation.

AI.tldr: This paper combines a lightweight CNN with post-training gradient-based importance analysis to classify genomic sequences and identify biologically meaningful coding and intergenomic signatures.
AI.motivation: Interpreting deep neural networks for genomic sequence classification remains difficult even when predictive accuracy is high.
AI.method: The authors train a lightweight CNN on genomic sequences and apply post-training gradient-based importance analysis to pinpoint sequence positions driving classification decisions.
AI.result: On the demo_coding_vs_intergenomic_seqs dataset, the model achieves 91.87% validation accuracy and reveals nine high-importance hot spots, class-specific separation at positions 20-100 (coding) and 150-190 (intergenomic), and a mean-variance correlation of r = 0.530.
AI.conclusion: Lightweight CNNs paired with gradient-based attribution can achieve high genomic classification accuracy while uncovering interpretable sequence signatures without explicit annotations.

title: Microfitting: Continual Learning via Cached Test-Time Training
summary: Continual learning is a promising approach to specialize language models to an organization's private data. However, current methods exhibit a number of drawbacks including catastrophic forgetting, where new training updates overwrite prior knowledge. We present microfitting, which trains and caches a small adapter for each document. Each adapter is trained once, offline, on synthetic questions targeted at demonstrated base-model shortcomings and reused whenever that document is queried. This method borrows from test-time learning literature and sidesteps the problem of continual learning through parameter isolation, allowing the system to specialize on new data without overwriting prior knowledge. The process that generates adapter training data also improves over time, revising its recipe from previous outcomes and fresh examples of the target workload. On DeepSeek V4 Flash, microfitting substantially improves accuracy over the base model. In Enterprise Document Operations (EDO), an open-book Q&A environment over real-world enterprise documents, our method achieves a 38.2% relative improvement over base-model performance. Microfitting makes continual specialization practical and cost-efficient: a frozen model can adapt to an evolving private corpus overnight on local hardware, without modifying the base model or previously cached adapters.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces microfitting, a continual learning method that trains and caches a small adapter per document offline on targeted synthetic questions to specialize LLMs without catastrophic forgetting.
AI.motivation: Continual learning on private organizational data often suffers from catastrophic forgetting, where new updates overwrite previously learned knowledge.
AI.method: Microfitting trains a small adapter once offline for each document using synthetic questions targeting base-model shortcomings, caches it via parameter isolation for reuse at query time, and iteratively refines its data-generation recipe from prior outcomes.
AI.result: On DeepSeek V4 Flash in the Enterprise Document Operations (EDO) open-book Q&A environment over real-world enterprise documents, microfitting achieves a 38.2% relative improvement over base-model performance.
AI.conclusion: Document-level cached test-time adapters enable practical, forgetting-free overnight specialization of frozen LLMs on evolving private corpora.

title: Scaling large language model-assisted line-of-therapy adjudication with human-in-the-loop evidence-calibrated selection
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have enabled the ability to scale clinical adjudication tasks traditionally dependent on exhaustive manual review. Line-of-therapy (LoT) adjudication, a major bottleneck in oncology cohort construction, is a prime example. Line boundaries must be inferred from longitudinal treatment histories according to nuanced, study-specific definitions, at every regimen transition for every patient. LLMs can apply this adjudication at scale, but their reliability varies across patients. Treatment histories differ in complexity, and ambiguous or atypical patterns depend on expert clinical judgment. Reliable automation thus requires verified support for model assignments and the ability to identify cases that warrant manual review. Here, we present evidence-calibrated selection (ECS), a human-in-the-loop framework for scaling LLM-assisted LoT adjudication. ECS derives confidence from observed clinician adjudications, prioritizes patients with the least-supported assignments for follow-up review, and returns completed adjudications to the model as precedent. As the evidence base grows, ECS continuously calibrates confidence to estimate residual error, thus enabling more efficient use of clinician time. In simulations on 136 clinician adjudicated patients with multiple myeloma, ECS achieved a residual error of 5% after review of 44.6% of patients, compared to 62.2% when review was directed by LLM self-reported confidence and 81.9% under random sampling. These results support a scalable approach to study-specific LoT adjudication, using clinician evidence to inform automated predictions, minimize error, and reduce review burden.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes evidence-calibrated selection (ECS), a human-in-the-loop framework that calibrates LLM confidence from clinician adjudications to scale oncology line-of-therapy adjudication.
AI.motivation: LLMs can scale clinical line-of-therapy adjudication, but their reliability varies on complex treatment histories, requiring principled identification of cases that need manual clinician review.
AI.method: ECS derives confidence from observed clinician adjudications, prioritizes patients with the least-supported assignments for follow-up review, and feeds completed adjudications back to the model as precedent while estimating residual error.
AI.result: In simulations on 136 clinician-adjudicated multiple myeloma patients, ECS reaches a 5% residual error after reviewing 44.6% of patients, compared to 62.2% under LLM self-reported confidence and 81.9% under random sampling.
AI.conclusion: Grounding selection confidence in accumulating clinician evidence substantially reduces manual review burden while controlling residual error in clinical adjudication.

title: Estimating Outpatient Visit Prices from Hospital Price Transparency Data using Large Language Models
summary: Objective: Hospital care prices in the United States have increased substantially, yet patients lack effective tools to access and compare costs. We aimed to develop and evaluate an LLM-based approach for improving access to and use of hospital price transparency (PT) data. Materials and Methods: To estimate visit prices, we used a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) framework to analyze PT files from three major hospitals in Maryland and the surrounding region. We compared BM25, OpenAI embedding models, and a GPT-BM25 hybrid against a no-RAG baseline for cost estimation of individual procedures and procedure groups, then evaluated the best approach for symptom-based visit cost estimation using synthetic simulations. Results: Across hospitals, the GPT-BM25 retriever achieved the best performance, with average price MAPE of 19.44% for individual procedures and 4.90% for groups, compared with 147.98% and 82.82%, respectively, for the no-RAG baseline. In simulations, our framework correctly identified approximately 50% of reference procedures and reduced MAPE relative to the LLM-only baseline at two of the three hospitals, while achieving comparable performance at the third. Discussion: Our framework uses RAG to improve care price estimation in real-world settings. Compared with the no-RAG baseline, it substantially improved cost estimates for both individual procedures and procedure groups. Improvements were smaller in synthetic simulations, likely because inferring procedures from clinical information is more complex. Practical challenges remain, including heterogeneous PT file formats, unexplained duplicate entries, and limited availability of insurer-negotiated rates. Conclusion: LLMs that effectively integrate PT data show strong potential to provide patients with more accessible and accurate healthcare cost estimates.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) framework for estimating outpatient visit prices from hospital price transparency files using LLMs.
AI.motivation: Patients lack effective tools to access and compare rising U.S. hospital care prices despite available hospital price transparency (PT) data.
AI.method: The authors compare BM25, OpenAI embeddings, and a GPT-BM25 hybrid retriever against a no-RAG baseline on PT files from three major Maryland-area hospitals for individual procedures, procedure groups, and synthetic symptom-based visit simulations.
AI.result: The GPT-BM25 hybrid retriever achieves the lowest average price MAPE of 19.44% for individual procedures and 4.90% for procedure groups, versus 147.98% and 82.82% for no-RAG, and identifies about 50% of reference procedures in synthetic simulations while reducing MAPE at two of three hospitals.
AI.conclusion: Integrating hospital price transparency files with hybrid RAG substantially improves LLM-based healthcare cost estimation, though heterogeneous file formats and missing negotiated rates remain challenges.

title: GNN-Based Deep Reinforcement Learning for Coastal Emergency Response under Extreme Water Levels
comment: 6 pages, 1 figure, 1 table. Accepted at the Tackling Climate Change with Machine Learning workshop at NeurIPS 2026. Code: this https URL
summary: When a storm surge approaches a coastal town, the emergency plan must be put into action quickly using water-level forecasts, flood extent, road access, vulnerable residents and shelters. Bringing this information together under time pressure is slow and depends on the duty officer's expertise. This paper is one step in a wider research line from data to safe decisions: machine learning to understand the hazard, reinforcement learning and planning to choose actions, large language models (LLMs) to explain and cross-check them, and an assurance layer that keeps people in charge. Here we address the action step on a real place. We ask whether a policy can learn the timing of emergency actions from decades of real events. Lido di Venezia is represented as a heterogeneous graph built from public elevation, road, building and census data and driven by hourly tide-gauge records from 1983 to 2024, with seven actions taken from the municipal emergency plan. A PPO policy is trained on this graph and compared, on storm windows unseen in training, with a rule-based system simulating the officer's discretionary decisions. On 18 historical test scenarios, PPO achieves a similar reduction in population exposure to the rule. With uncertain forecasts and limited protection it again performs similarly but does not outperform the tuned rule, and removing graph message passing does not substantially reduce performance. PPO therefore learns an effective protective response from an outcome-based reward alone: it is given the plan's actions and when each is allowed, but not the thresholds that tell the comparator when to act. Next steps test harder edge cases, move closer to a digital twin of the territory, and replace the simulated officer with assessment by emergency-management stakeholders, supported by LLM-based interpretation of each recommendation.

AI.tldr: This paper trains a GNN-based PPO agent on a heterogeneous graph of Lido di Venezia using four decades of tide-gauge records to learn coastal emergency response timing.
AI.motivation: Activating coastal emergency plans under storm surge pressure is slow and reliant on duty-officer expertise when integrating forecasts, flood extent, roads, and shelter data.
AI.method: The authors represent Lido di Venezia as a heterogeneous graph from public elevation, road, building, and census data driven by hourly tide-gauge records (1983-2024), and train a PPO policy over seven municipal emergency actions using outcome-based rewards.
AI.result: Across 18 unseen historical storm scenarios, PPO achieves population exposure reductions similar to a rule-based system simulating officer decisions, performs comparably under uncertain forecasts without outperforming the tuned rule, and shows little performance drop when graph message passing is removed.
AI.conclusion: Outcome-based RL can learn effective emergency action timing without explicit decision thresholds, though further testing on harder edge cases and stakeholder validation is needed.

title: Protecting Safety during Reasoning Training with Low-Rank Fisher Regularisation
summary: Large language models are trained to have safety guardrails, but these can be compromised while fine-tuning for new capabilities, such as reasoning. One way to mitigate this degradation is to modify the fine-tuning objective to preserve safety behaviour, but doing so effectively and efficiently remains challenging. We revisit Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC), which penalises parameter updates based on sensitivity estimates from the diagonal of the Fisher information matrix (FIM). While EWC provides some protection, the diagonal approximation ignores interactions between parameters. We address this limitation by exploiting recent findings that safety-relevant behaviour is located in a low-rank subspace within models. Our method, Subspace-Projected Elastic Weight Consolidation (SP-EWC), projects gradients onto this subspace to capture non-diagonal curvature efficiently. We investigate three different ways of identifying the safety subspace: through safety fine-tuning updates (LoRA), safety-related activations (ActSVD), and contrastive representations of safety and utility data (cPCA). We find that this choice substantially affects performance, with SP-EWC using cPCA comparing favourably against existing methods by better maintaining safety guardrails without introducing excessive over-refusal.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Subspace-Projected Elastic Weight Consolidation (SP-EWC), which projects gradients onto a low-rank safety subspace to preserve LLM safety guardrails during reasoning fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Fine-tuning LLMs for new capabilities like reasoning can degrade safety guardrails, while standard EWC's diagonal Fisher approximation ignores parameter interactions.
AI.method: SP-EWC projects parameter updates onto a low-rank safety-relevant subspace to capture non-diagonal curvature, comparing three subspace identification methods: safety fine-tuning updates (LoRA), safety-related activations (ActSVD), and contrastive safety-utility representations (cPCA).
AI.result: The choice of subspace identification substantially affects performance, with SP-EWC using cPCA comparing favorably against existing methods by preserving safety guardrails without inducing excessive over-refusal.
AI.conclusion: Projecting Fisher regularization onto a contrastively identified low-rank safety subspace effectively protects LLM alignment during capability fine-tuning.

title: LENS: Replacing LayerNorm and Softmax in Transformers with Learnable Normalization States
comment: Source code is available at: this https URL
summary: LayerNorm and attention Softmax are critical operations in Transformers. However, they cannot be efficiently mapped to General Matrix Multiplication (GEMM) computations on hardware. Therefore, modern hardware accelerator designs, such as NPUs on ASIC/FPGA, consume a large amount of hardware resources or chip area to implement their specific arithmetic units. Building on previous work about LayerNorm, Softmax, and their alternatives, we introduce Learnable Normalization States (LENS), a framework that reformulates LayerNorm as tiny MLPs by abstracting a common structure from related methods and extends this method to Softmax, which moves more of the computation in Transformers to GEMM as a hardware-friendly architecture. We evaluate LENS on image classification with Vision Transformers (ViT) and autoregressive language modeling with Pythia models, including generalization tests on WikiText and LAMBADA. Across these tasks, LENS matches or exceeds baseline performance in several vision settings and retains most of the baseline performance in the remaining vision and language experiments. These findings may suggest that hand-designed normalization and attention functions are not the only choice as alternatives to LayerNorm and Softmax. LENS also provides a basis for exploring Transformer architectures for resource-limited accelerators.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Learnable Normalization States (LENS), replacing hardware-unfriendly LayerNorm and attention Softmax in Transformers with tiny MLPs to shift computation toward GEMM.
AI.motivation: LayerNorm and Softmax cannot be efficiently mapped to General Matrix Multiplication (GEMM), forcing NPUs on ASICs and FPGAs to dedicate substantial chip area and resources to specialized arithmetic units.
AI.method: LENS reformulates LayerNorm as tiny MLPs and extends this formulation to Softmax, moving more Transformer operations onto GEMM-friendly hardware paths.
AI.result: Evaluated on Vision Transformers for image classification and Pythia models for autoregressive language modeling (including WikiText and LAMBADA generalization), LENS matches or exceeds baselines in several vision settings and retains most baseline performance in the remaining vision and language tests.
AI.conclusion: Learnable MLP-based normalization and attention alternatives offer a viable path toward GEMM-centric Transformer architectures for resource-limited hardware accelerators.

title: Residual-Tail-Informed Flow Matching for Time Series Anomaly Detection
comment: IEEE International Conference on Big Data 2026 (December)
summary: Time series anomaly detection (TSAD) models are often trained on nominal data using average-risk objectives, which emphasize dominant normal patterns. However, real time series can contain rare but valid nominal regimes that are underrepresented in the training distribution. We show that data-space flow matching can over-penalize such rare-normal windows and assign them anomaly scores comparable to those of true anomalies. To address this, we propose Residual-Tail-Informed Flow Matching (RT-FM), an unsupervised framework that uses a temporal variational autoencoder to estimate residual latent tailness and converts it into bounded, warmup-annealed weights for training a data-space flow matching model. Experiments on seven TSAD benchmarks show that RT-FM improves rare-normal coverage while preserving strong anomaly discrimination, substantially reducing false alarms on such windows and resulting in improved aggregate detection performance. The code is available at: this https URL

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Residual-Tail-Informed Flow Matching (RT-FM) to prevent data-space flow matching from over-penalizing rare but valid normal regimes in time series anomaly detection.
AI.motivation: Unsupervised time series anomaly detection models trained with average-risk objectives often assign high anomaly scores to rare-normal regimes that are underrepresented in training data.
AI.method: RT-FM uses a temporal variational autoencoder to estimate residual latent tailness and converts it into bounded, warmup-annealed sample weights for training a data-space flow matching model.
AI.result: Across seven time series anomaly detection benchmarks, RT-FM improves rare-normal coverage, substantially reduces false alarms on rare-normal windows, and improves aggregate anomaly detection performance.
AI.conclusion: Reweighting flow matching training by residual latent tailness balances rare-normal coverage and anomaly discrimination in time series anomaly detection.

title: EPI-SST: Renewal-Structured State-Space Transformers for Epidemic Forecasting
summary: Epidemic forecasting supports public health decisions ranging from capacity planning to intervention timing, for which both point accuracy and calibrated uncertainty are essential. Although neural models have advanced point forecasting, producing reliable probabilistic predictions over multiple future horizons remains challenging. Renewal models encode epidemic propagation, while neural forecasters learn flexible multi-horizon representations; integrating these strengths within a probabilistic future rollout remains underexplored. We propose EPI-SST (Epidemic State Space Transformer), a probabilistic forecaster centered on an evidence-driven renewal transition. At each horizon, neural evidence produces a bounded update to an internal multiplier and advances a finite-memory renewal state that generates the future mean trajectory. A separate heteroscedastic Gaussian head controls predictive scale using a validation-selected log-variance penalty. Across four epidemic surveillance benchmarks, EPI-SST achieves the lowest pooled RMSE on every dataset, reducing RMSE by up to 14.2 percent relative to the strongest baseline. It also achieves the lowest continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) at horizons h = 4, 5, 6 on every dataset, with reductions of up to 43 percent relative to the strongest probabilistic baseline. During the abnormal 2019-2020 influenza season, EPI-SST reduces CRPS by 16.9 percent and calibration error by 78.9 percent; a three-seed replication preserves its distributional lead. Ablation studies and frozen-path interventions show that the renewal transition, attention conditioning, horizon coupling, and uncertainty-scale control make complementary contributions to predictive performance.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes EPI-SST, a renewal-structured state-space transformer for probabilistic epidemic forecasting that reduces RMSE by up to 14.2% and CRPS by up to 43% across four surveillance benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Neural epidemic forecasters struggle to produce calibrated multi-horizon probabilistic predictions, while integrating mechanistic renewal models with neural rollouts remains underexplored.
AI.method: EPI-SST uses neural evidence at each horizon to apply a bounded update to an internal multiplier advancing a finite-memory renewal state for the mean trajectory, paired with a heteroscedastic Gaussian head trained with a validation-selected log-variance penalty.
AI.result: Across four epidemic surveillance benchmarks, EPI-SST achieves the lowest pooled RMSE (up to 14.2% reduction) and lowest CRPS at horizons 4-6 (up to 43% reduction), and during the abnormal 2019-2020 influenza season cuts CRPS by 16.9% and calibration error by 78.9%.
AI.conclusion: Embedding a mechanistic renewal transition inside a state-space transformer with controlled uncertainty scaling yields more accurate and better-calibrated multi-horizon epidemic forecasts.

title: Flow Matching for Sampled-Data Control of Angular Distributions
summary: Synchronization and clustering in oscillator networks depend on the joint distribution of the phases. Flow Matching can steer this distribution by learning an angular velocity field from shortest arcs between paired configurations. Each arc is traversed at constant speed, yet the resulting field can vary along its own trajectories. In this article, we study how to control angular transport on the circle and product torus when each controller evaluation selects a rate to hold until the next update. Using the same local velocity samples, Flow Matching learns the instantaneous angular rate and MeanFlow learns its average along the reference trajectory over the control interval. Under direct angular actuation, holding the exact average gives the reference displacement. We relate the displacement error of holding the instantaneous rate and the training residual of MeanFlow to the conditional covariance of the teacher velocities. Experiments with 100 phases show that endpoint pairing affects the comparison. MeanFlow gives smaller one-step errors under minibatch pairing, while permutation alignment reverses the ranking for exchangeable phase clusters.

AI.tldr: The paper compares Flow Matching and MeanFlow for sampled-data angular distribution control on the circle and product torus, showing that endpoint pairing determines which method achieves lower one-step displacement error.
AI.motivation: When controlling oscillator networks under sampled-data updates where a selected angular rate is held over each interval, instantaneous velocity fields from Flow Matching can incur displacement errors along curved trajectories.
AI.method: Using the same local velocity samples, the authors compare Flow Matching (learning instantaneous angular rate) against MeanFlow (learning the trajectory-averaged rate over the control interval) and relate displacement error and training residuals to teacher-velocity conditional covariance.
AI.result: In experiments with 100 phases, MeanFlow achieves smaller one-step errors under minibatch pairing, whereas permutation alignment reverses the ranking for exchangeable phase clusters.
AI.conclusion: Selecting between instantaneous Flow Matching and averaged MeanFlow for sampled-data angular control depends on the endpoint pairing scheme used during training.

title: HoloGene: Learning to Lift Sliced Spatial Transcriptomics to Holistic 3D Gene Fields
summary: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) provides spatially resolved gene expression measurements, but most 3D ST datasets are acquired as independently processed 2D sections. Computational approaches span slice registration and integration, explicit or generative interpolation, and coordinate-field modeling. Within the last family, implicit neural representations (INRs) offer a continuous, coordinate-queryable parameterization, but standard isotropic coordinate encodings do not explicitly reflect that serial-section measurements are dense in-plane and sparse along the axial direction. We present HoloGene, an anisotropic conditional INR framework for estimating continuous 3D gene-expression fields from pre-registered ST sections. Its central contribution is an acquisition-aware factorization that couples dense in-plane synthesis with sparse axial evolution using established GAE, FiLM, pseudo-label supervision, and CORAL components. HoloGene compresses high-dimensional expression profiles into a graph-autoencoder latent manifold, uses pseudo-label-derived signature conditioning to provide coarse intra-section context, and applies depth-dependent FiLM modulation to model axial variation. A signature-stratified correlation-alignment regularizer encourages cross-slice covariance alignment in latent features. Using held-out measured sections as cross-sectional references, HoloGene improves reconstruction accuracy and biological preservation metrics compared with general-purpose INRs and adapted spatial-transcriptomics baselines. These results support anisotropic conditional modeling as a practical strategy for estimating 3D expression fields from discontinuous ST sections. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper presents HoloGene, an anisotropic conditional implicit neural representation (INR) framework that lifts pre-registered 2D spatial transcriptomics slices into continuous 3D gene-expression fields.
AI.motivation: Most 3D spatial transcriptomics datasets consist of independently processed 2D sections that are dense in-plane but sparse axially, which standard isotropic INRs fail to model explicitly.
AI.method: HoloGene factorizes dense in-plane synthesis and sparse axial evolution by compressing expression profiles into a graph-autoencoder latent manifold, conditioning on pseudo-label signatures, applying depth-dependent FiLM modulation, and regularizing cross-slice covariance with signature-stratified CORAL alignment.
AI.result: Evaluated on held-out measured sections as cross-sectional references, HoloGene outperforms general-purpose INRs and adapted spatial-transcriptomics baselines on reconstruction accuracy and biological preservation metrics.
AI.conclusion: Acquisition-aware anisotropic conditional INRs provide a practical and effective way to reconstruct continuous 3D gene-expression fields from discontinuous 2D sections.

title: Pretty Linear Liars: Unregularized Probes Favor Intervention-Unfaithful Features
comment: 13 pages, 9 figures. Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Interpretability as a Science (InterpScience)
summary: Linear probing is a common technique in mechanistic interpretability despite the fact that the decodability of a given feature does not necessarily imply the network uses that feature. Intervention faithfulness, not merely decodability, is the appropriate criterion for whether a feature serves a defined active role in the model. Meanwhile, probe regularization has been used for feature discovery, but the impact of regularization on feature causality remains unclear. We study probe regularization systematically, starting with unregularized ordinary least squares (OLS) regression and considering increasing amounts of regularization via ridge regression. We show theoretically that OLS probes amplify low-variance directions in activation space that have spurious correlations with the target feature, whereas regularization reduces influence from these directions. Empirically, we find in a toy transformer and Llama-2-7B that intervention faithfulness increases up to a point, and then decreases again, and that the optimal regularization strength leads to features bearing striking similarity (in both direction and variance) to those learned by optimizing for intervention outcomes directly. Together, these results provide mechanistic justification for regularizing regression probes.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that unregularized OLS linear probes amplify low-variance spurious directions in activation space, whereas ridge regularization improves intervention faithfulness up to an optimal point.
AI.motivation: Linear probing is widely used in mechanistic interpretability, yet decodability does not imply causal intervention faithfulness, and the effect of probe regularization on feature causality has been unclear.
AI.method: The authors theoretically analyze unregularized OLS versus ridge-regularized regression probes and empirically evaluate intervention faithfulness across regularization strengths in a toy transformer and Llama-2-7B.
AI.result: Theory shows OLS amplifies low-variance directions with spurious target correlations while ridge regularization suppresses them; empirically, intervention faithfulness rises with regularization to an optimum—recovering features closely matching those optimized directly for intervention outcomes—before declining at excessive regularization.
AI.conclusion: Regularizing regression probes is mechanistically justified for discovering causally faithful features rather than mere spurious correlations.

title: Halting in Recurrent Sequence Models
comment: 16 pages, 7 figures, 2 tables. Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Interpretability as a Science
summary: Recurrent sequence models, such as recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and state space models (SSMs), are often trained to emit an end-of-sequence (EOS) token when their output sequence is complete. During training, EOS is treated as another token without a special loss term or incentive. Although this training paradigm is widely used, it is not understood how models decide to output EOS. We study a minimal version of the EOS halting problem in which networks are trained to emit a given input sequence an instructed number of times, followed by EOS. We train tanh RNNs and linear SSMs on this task, finding that the RNNs encode the number of tokens left to copy in a linear subspace, of which two principal components capture most of the variation. Hidden states with the same remaining count converge to a shared representation regardless of their instructed repeat count. By modulating the hidden state using an affine transformation at the boundary between copied sequences, we shift the RNN's state to the representation shared by states with one fewer copy remaining. The unchanged network emits EOS one copy earlier while reproducing the shortened target sequence in 94.4% of new sequences, revealing that this representation causally determines the stopping time. In the SSMs, the difference between trajectories with different repeat counts is separated across two-dimensional rotation planes whose contributions to the EOS comparison cancel during copying and align near the stopping time. Rotating the planes independently removes most of the intended stopping while preserving the copied content, which shows that the stopping time depends on the planes' relative phases. These results identify two candidate primitives of EOS halting in recurrent models: a shared encoding of the number of remaining tokens in tanh RNNs and phase alignment across fixed rotations in linear SSMs.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates how recurrent sequence models decide to emit an end-of-sequence (EOS) token, identifying remaining-token linear subspaces in tanh RNNs and phase alignment across rotation planes in linear SSMs.
AI.motivation: Although RNNs and state space models (SSMs) are routinely trained to emit EOS tokens without special loss terms, the internal mechanisms governing when they halt are poorly understood.
AI.method: The authors train tanh RNNs and linear SSMs to copy an input sequence an instructed number of times before emitting EOS, then analyze and causally intervene on hidden states and rotation planes.
AI.result: Tanh RNNs encode remaining tokens in a low-dimensional linear subspace where affine shifts at sequence boundaries cause EOS emission one copy earlier while reproducing shortened targets in 94.4% of new sequences; linear SSMs separate repeat counts across 2D rotation planes whose phase alignment triggers halting, and independent plane rotation disrupts stopping while preserving copied content.
AI.conclusion: Recurrent models implement EOS halting via distinct, causally verifiable primitives: remaining-count linear encodings in tanh RNNs and relative phase alignment in linear SSMs.

title: Does the Voice Matter? Evaluating Frustration Detection on Deployed Clinical Voice-Agent Calls
comment: Accepted to Ml4H 2026 Accepted to GenAI4H workshop @ Neurips 2026
summary: Autonomous voice agents now conduct routine clinical follow-up calls, so some automated triage is unavoidable. A patient becoming frustrated is one thing that triage should catch. These systems typically read only the transcript the speech-to-text stage produces, not the voice, and whether that is enough is largely untested on real clinical speech. We study per-turn frustration detection on real patient calls from a deployed clinical voice agent: 150 turns from six calls labelled by three annotators, with a length-matched acted corpus as a control, and 714 turns from 30 calls. Patient turns are overwhelmingly short: across the deployed calls, roughly 59% are one or two words, against 13% in the full acted corpus, and a corpus accuracy gap remains even after the acted set is length-matched. On one-word turns, transcript-only detection does not exclude chance. Across five audio-capable language models, the transcript flags 3 or 4 of the 39 frustrated one-word turns in the 30 calls, and a classifier given only the word count reaches 57.3%. Whether audio helps depends on the model and on the instruction. Asked to attend to delivery, two Gemini 2.5 models gain 3.0 pp over the transcript across 30 calls (-1.0 to 7.5 pp). Of the turns they confidently clear, 6.9% were in fact frustrated for audio against 13.0% for the transcript, a difference of 6.1 pp (2.2 to 10.4 pp). Across the 30 calls, given one prompt identical for both inputs, no model's audio-text interval excludes zero. Under the input-specific prompts, a newer Gemini model and two smaller open models do worse with audio than with the transcript (-3.5, -8.6 and -10.6 pp). A WavLM probe trained on the clinical calls matches the best prompted model overall (71.6%) but misses every frustrated one-word turn in the 24 added calls. When a patient's turn is short, the transcript alone is not enough to rule out frustration.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates per-turn frustration detection on real deployed clinical voice-agent calls, finding that transcripts alone fail on short one-word turns and that adding audio helps only for specific models and prompts.
AI.motivation: Clinical voice-agent triage systems typically rely only on speech-to-text transcripts to detect patient frustration, but whether transcripts suffice on real clinical speech—where turns are often very short—was largely untested.
AI.method: The authors evaluate five audio-capable language models and a trained WavLM probe on real patient calls (150 turns from 6 calls and 714 turns from 30 calls) alongside a length-matched acted control corpus, comparing transcript-only and audio inputs.
AI.result: Roughly 59% of deployed patient turns are one or two words, where transcript-only detection is near chance (flagging 3-4 of 39 frustrated one-word turns); two Gemini 2.5 models gain 3.0 pp with audio when instructed to attend to delivery (reducing false clearances from 13.0% to 6.9%), whereas a newer Gemini model and two smaller open models perform worse with audio (-3.5 to -10.6 pp), and a WavLM probe matches overall accuracy (71.6%) but misses all frustrated one-word turns in 24 added calls.
AI.conclusion: Transcripts alone cannot reliably rule out frustration on short clinical patient turns, and effective audio-based detection depends heavily on model choice and delivery-focused prompting.

title: MemDoctor: Stage-wise Error Attribution and Repair for MLLM Agent Memory
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) now assist users across sessions of images and text, carried by an external memory of what was said and shown. When such an assistant answers wrongly, the failure usually began earlier, in how a record was written, updated or retrieved, and the answer alone does not say where. We formalize multimodal memory as four stages, Write, Update, Retrieve and Answer, and define nine error types across them. A stage-resolved analysis on Mem-Gallery traces most failures to a source stage, and most of those lie before the answer. Injecting known errors against fact-preserving control edits, we then follow each tainted record downstream. Early errors survive to the answer as apparent evidence, and hurt most when no other record holds the fact. A diagnosis that trusts the quoted evidence therefore blames the stage where the error surfaces, not the one where it began. We propose MemDoctor, in which the MLLM that built the memory diagnoses its own failures. It traces each needed fact backward through the four stages, accepts a diagnosis only when the cited evidence is found in memory, and repairs that stage before answering again. On a 4B backbone, MemDoctor improves accuracy on both Mem-Gallery and MemLens, outperforming all evaluated 8B baselines, and the same loop also improves MuRAG and A-Mem.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces MemDoctor, a self-diagnosis and repair framework for MLLM agent memory that traces failures backward across Write, Update, Retrieve, and Answer stages to outperform 8B baselines using a 4B model.
AI.motivation: When memory-augmented MLLMs answer wrongly, errors usually originate earlier during memory writing, updating, or retrieval, and trusting quoted evidence at the answer stage misattributes the failure's source.
AI.method: The authors formalize multimodal memory into four stages (Write, Update, Retrieve, Answer) with nine error types, and propose MemDoctor, where the MLLM traces needed facts backward through the stages, accepts a diagnosis only when cited evidence exists in memory, and repairs the faulty stage before re-answering.
AI.result: On a 4B backbone, MemDoctor improves accuracy on Mem-Gallery and MemLens, outperforming all evaluated 8B baselines, and the same diagnostic repair loop also improves MuRAG and A-Mem.
AI.conclusion: Stage-wise backward error attribution and evidence-verified repair enable smaller MLLMs to achieve superior multimodal memory accuracy.

title: Evaluation-Free Recursive Self-Improvement for Coding Agents
summary: Recent self-improving coding agents have achieved strong benchmark performance by iteratively modifying their own executable implementations. A common pattern uses downstream task-derived evidence to decide which candidates or lineages continue evolving, which we term evaluate-and-select. Obtaining this signal requires repeatedly executing evolved agents on downstream tasks, so broader exploration incurs increasing evaluation cost, while repeated optimization against a fixed evaluation distribution may encourage benchmark-specific adaptation. We ask: can coding agents self-improve without downstream task evaluation inside the evolution loop? We introduce Explore-then-Integrate (ELITE), which integrates implementation mechanisms rather than selecting a single exploratory child to continue the lineage. At each generation, ELITE proposes diverse focused improvements, implements them independently from the same parent, and inspects the resulting programs to identify complementary, redundant, and conflicting mechanisms before reimplementing a compatible subset as one coherent descendant. No downstream task outcomes or task-solving trajectories of evolved candidates are used to guide evolution; only deterministic checks of structural and operational validity are used inside the loop. On SWE-bench Pro, ELITE improves the initial agent from 60.0% to 85.6%, compared with 86.7% for the Darwin Godel Machine (DGM) and 88.3% for the Huxley-Godel Machine (HGM), while using zero candidate task evaluations and reducing observed wall-clock evolution time by 8.8x and 3.2x, respectively, under the evaluated configurations. In cross-benchmark transfer without further adaptation, ELITE averages 73.3% on SWE-bench Verified and 69.3% on Polyglot. Together, these results demonstrate the feasibility of coding-agent self-improvement without downstream candidate task evaluation in our setting.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Explore-then-Integrate (ELITE), an evaluation-free recursive self-improvement method for coding agents that achieves 85.6% on SWE-bench Pro without running candidate task evaluations during evolution.
AI.motivation: Existing self-improving coding agents rely on evaluate-and-select loops that repeatedly run evolved candidates on downstream tasks, incurring high evaluation cost and risking benchmark-specific overfitting.
AI.method: ELITE proposes diverse focused improvements, implements them independently from the same parent, and inspects the resulting programs to synthesize a compatible subset into one coherent descendant using only deterministic structural and operational validity checks, with zero downstream task evaluations inside the loop.
AI.result: On SWE-bench Pro, ELITE improves the initial agent from 60.0% to 85.6% (versus 86.7% for DGM and 88.3% for HGM) while reducing observed wall-clock evolution time by 8.8x and 3.2x, and transfers without adaptation to average 73.3% on SWE-bench Verified and 69.3% on Polyglot.
AI.conclusion: Coding agents can recursively self-improve effectively and much faster without downstream candidate task evaluation inside the evolution loop.

title: SWE-WhatIf: Simulating Real Users of Coding Agents from Recorded Session
summary: Recorded sessions between users and coding agents offer a way to evaluate how agents complete real-world tasks and interact with users. However, these sessions cannot simply be replayed with new agents, because recorded user replies may no longer apply when an agent takes a different trajectory. We introduce SWE-WhatIf, which replays recorded sessions with new agents by modeling the user's intents, the criteria for satisfying them, and the conditions under which they arise. Using this model, a user simulator generates replies that adapt to unseen agent turns while remaining grounded in the recording. Across 89 real-world sessions, SWE-WhatIf generated the replies most similar to those of real users and matched the strongest baseline when sessions were rewritten. To test adaptation, we replay sessions with agents instructed to avoid or repeat actions that the recorded user pushed back on. SWE-WhatIf produced the highest win rate for avoiding these actions (66.3%), significantly above chance. We further demonstrate its utility by ranking five LLMs as coding agents, where the highest-ranked model depended on how users specified and developed their intents, and a study with 16 users, where replaying their own sessions changed 14 participants' rankings and informed their future agent use.

AI.tldr: The paper presents SWE-WhatIf, a user simulator that replays recorded coding-agent sessions with new agents by modeling user intents, satisfaction criteria, and triggering conditions.
AI.motivation: Recorded coding-agent sessions cannot be naively replayed with new agents because static user replies become invalid when a new agent takes a different trajectory.
AI.method: SWE-WhatIf models the recorded user's intents, satisfaction criteria, and arising conditions so a simulator can generate adaptive replies grounded in the original recording.
AI.result: Across 89 real-world sessions, SWE-WhatIf generates the most human-like replies, achieves a 66.3% win rate in avoiding actions the recorded user pushed back on, and in a 16-user study changes 14 participants' agent rankings when replaying their own sessions.
AI.conclusion: Intent-grounded user simulation enables realistic, trajectory-adaptive evaluation of coding agents from recorded sessions.

title: From Repositories to Training Environments: Scaling Long-Horizon Coding Agents with Environment Evolution Loop
summary: Training coding agents for long-horizon tasks requires environments with verifiable feedback. Existing pipelines often follow a linear process that ends with validation, establishing usability but providing little guidance on improving training value. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) often requires model rollouts or model training followed by downstream evaluation, with costs and feedback delays amplified on long-horizon tasks. How can we use timely, reliable proxy signals to improve training value and synthesize environments at scale? We present RepoFactory, an automated pipeline that converts real repositories into verifiable environments where agents build complete projects from scratch given a language specification. Its Environment Evolution Loop optimizes a multiplicative objective combining validity, structural coupling, and implementation scope through proxy feedback. RepoFactory produces 10,159 environments across 17 software domains. Training Qwen3.5-35B-A3B on these environments yields RepoHorizen-35B-A3B, which achieves gains of 22.6 percentage points on NL2Repo-Bench and 8.5 points on average across five benchmarks covering long-horizon coding and agentic tasks in real-world production settings, compared with 17.5 and 6.4 points without environment evolution. These results highlight the training value of RepoFactory environments and the additional gains from the Environment Evolution Loop.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces RepoFactory and its Environment Evolution Loop to convert real repositories into 10,159 verifiable long-horizon coding environments, boosting Qwen3.5-35B-A3B by 22.6 percentage points on NL2Repo-Bench.
AI.motivation: Scaling long-horizon coding-agent training requires verifiable environments, yet linear conversion pipelines offer little guidance on improving training value and rollout-based self-improvement is too slow and costly.
AI.method: RepoFactory converts real repositories into scratch-build environments from language specifications and uses an Environment Evolution Loop optimizing a multiplicative proxy objective combining validity, structural coupling, and implementation scope.
AI.result: RepoFactory synthesizes 10,159 environments across 17 software domains; training Qwen3.5-35B-A3B yields RepoHorizen-35B-A3B, gaining 22.6 percentage points on NL2Repo-Bench and 8.5 points on average across five long-horizon benchmarks (versus 17.5 and 6.4 points without environment evolution).
AI.conclusion: Proxy-guided environment evolution provides a scalable, effective way to synthesize high-value training environments for long-horizon coding agents.

title: Edit Recommendation: Can LLMs Anticipate Edit Requests from Users, and When?
comment: Blog: this https URL, Code: this https URL
summary: After a large language model (LLM) agent generates an artifact, users often send edit requests for it. This paper studies whether an LLM can anticipate these requests before they are sent. Such anticipation is useful in practice because it reduces the effort of user review and feedback. We formalize this task as edit recommendation and build EditRecBench, a benchmark for evaluating the performance of LLMs on this task, from real-world conversation logs in WildChat-4.8M. Through benchmarking and failure analysis, we identify a practical challenge that some cases are inherently difficult to predict in real-world settings. To address this, we introduce decision model-based gating to filter out cases where predictions are unlikely to be correct before they are presented to the user. Our trained model outperforms existing decision models and raises pass@5 among shown suggestions by 12--25 points at a gating threshold. Our code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper formalizes edit recommendation—anticipating user edit requests for LLM-generated artifacts—introduces EditRecBench from WildChat-4.8M, and uses decision-model gating to raise pass@5 by 12-25 points.
AI.motivation: Users frequently send edit requests after an LLM generates an artifact, and anticipating those requests beforehand could reduce review effort, though many real-world cases are inherently hard to predict.
AI.method: The authors build EditRecBench from real conversation logs in WildChat-4.8M and introduce decision-model-based gating to filter out low-confidence predictions before showing suggestions to the user.
AI.result: The trained gating model outperforms existing decision models and raises pass@5 among shown edit suggestions by 12 to 25 points at a chosen gating threshold.
AI.conclusion: Combining edit recommendation with confidence gating makes proactive edit suggestions practical by surfacing predictions only when they are likely to be useful.

title: PlainPairs: A Corpus Pairing the Prescriber and Patient Texts of U.S. Prescription Medicine Labels
summary: A prescription medicine in the United States comes with labeling written for prescribers, and many medicines also carry a text written for patients: a Medication Guide or a patient package insert. The two texts describe the same medicine for two readers, yet public resources rarely hold them side by side. I present PlainPairs, an open corpus built from the openFDA drug label files. Version 0.1.0 holds 35,177 prescription labels that carry a patient text, 21,416 distinct patient texts, 250,829 patient-text segments matched to prescriber sections through their regulatory headings, reading-level measures on both sides, and rule-based counts of plain-language wording. A second source, the National Cancer Institute's cancer information summaries, adds 756 summaries in health-professional and patient versions, in English and Spanish. Measured on the structure of the label, the median Medication Guide reads at grade 8.7 by Flesch-Kincaid and at grade 11.1 by SMOG. The same guides measured on the flattened text that the bulk files serve read about two grades higher, a difference that comes from lost list and heading boundaries. Patient texts address the reader in 41 of every 100 sentences, against 0.2 in prescriber sections. A blind hand check of 100 pairs supports the heading-based alignment for seven of ten heading types. The corpus, its code and its documents are public, and the release keeps texts that show a company copyright mark out of the text tables.

AI.tldr: The paper releases PlainPairs v0.1.0, an open corpus pairing U.S. prescription medicine prescriber labels with patient Medication Guides/inserts and NCI cancer summaries, along with readability and alignment analyses.
AI.motivation: Prescription medicines carry both prescriber-oriented labeling and patient-oriented guides, yet public resources rarely align them side by side for plain-language and readability research.
AI.method: Built from openFDA drug label files and National Cancer Institute (NCI) summaries (English and Spanish), PlainPairs aligns patient segments to prescriber sections via regulatory headings and computes Flesch-Kincaid, SMOG, and rule-based plain-language counts.
AI.result: Version 0.1.0 contains 35,177 labels with patient texts (21,416 distinct), 250,829 aligned segments, and 756 NCI summaries; structured Medication Guides read at median grade 8.7 (Flesch-Kincaid) and 11.1 (SMOG)—about two grades lower than flattened bulk text—and address the reader in 41 per 100 sentences versus 0.2 in prescriber sections, with blind hand-checking supporting alignment for 7 of 10 heading types.
AI.conclusion: PlainPairs provides a large-scale, publicly available parallel resource for studying and improving patient-facing medical communication.

title: Seeing Isn't Resolving: Visual and Linguistic Disambiguation with Conversational Grounding
summary: Visual grounding benchmarks usually do not consider the contextual uncertainty of real-world scenarios. In this study, we construct a novel benchmark, the Japanese evaluation for Ambiguous visual Grounding with Dialogue (JAG-D) dataset. It consists of human-robot conversational multimodal interactions covering different types of ambiguity, arising from visual and linguistic categories. We evaluate the capabilities of different state-of-the-art Visual Language Models (VLMs) for ambiguity recognition and resolution. We compare dialogue context grounding performance for visual and linguistic ambiguity resolution. Our experiments show that VLMs can substantially improve the resolution of linguistic ambiguity, especially Japanese zero anaphora, by using dialogue context. We further conduct a comparative analysis to understand whether grounding improvements arise from the semantic content of the dialogue or from its conversational structure.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces JAG-D, a Japanese human-robot multimodal dialogue benchmark for visual and linguistic disambiguation, showing that dialogue context substantially helps VLMs resolve linguistic ambiguity such as zero anaphora.
AI.motivation: Existing visual grounding benchmarks largely ignore contextual uncertainty and conversational disambiguation needed in real-world human-robot interactions.
AI.method: The authors construct the JAG-D dataset covering visual and linguistic ambiguities in multimodal human-robot dialogues, evaluate state-of-the-art VLMs on ambiguity recognition and resolution, and compare semantic content versus conversational structure.
AI.result: Dialogue context substantially improves VLM resolution of linguistic ambiguity, particularly Japanese zero anaphora, compared to visual-only or context-free grounding.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating conversational grounding is essential for resolving linguistic ambiguities in real-world multimodal human-robot interaction.

title: Validating LLM-Based Essay Scorers: A Comparative Analysis in Critical Online Reasoning in Medical Education
summary: Automated essay scorers (AES) based on large language models (LLMs) promise human-level accuracy. However, training, fine-tuning, and evaluating LLMs for specific assessment tasks is costly. In particular, the question arises whether these AES should be trained for specific domains or whether models based on generic LLMs might be sufficient. Human annotations, by contrast, are often more valid but far more expensive. This study evaluates whether ensembles of AES systems based on general-purpose LLMs can approximate human ratings of medical-education writing tasks by leveraging encoded linguistic and conceptual knowledge. The goal is to assess whether general-purpose models are applicable for assisting or potentially replacing human annotation in this domain. We experiment with 11 AES systems and 8 different LLMs and evaluate 668 student responses to 12 tasks, using \numprint{2076} evaluations by 7 human annotators. These ratings are aggregated to create consistent performance levels that can be used as target classes for classifiers trained on AES outputs. Our results show that learner classes based on human ratings can be accurately reconstructed using a linear SVM trained on a small set of AES features. A single classifier generalized well across tasks and domains, with reasoning and content features being most predictive. This suggests that out-of-the-box LLMs, even without domain-specific fine-tuning, can support automatic essay grading in medical education. While individual AES systems are insufficient alone, their combination approximates human evaluators, pointing to a reduced need for manual scoring or its supplementation with automated methods.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that a linear SVM trained on features from an ensemble of general-purpose LLM-based automated essay scorers (AES) accurately reconstructs human-rated learner levels in medical education without domain-specific fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Fine-tuning LLMs for domain-specific automated essay scoring is expensive, raising the question of whether ensembles of out-of-the-box general-purpose LLMs can approximate human ratings.
AI.method: The authors evaluate 11 AES systems and 8 LLMs on 668 student responses across 12 medical-education tasks (2,076 ratings from 7 human annotators) and train a linear SVM on a small set of AES features to predict aggregated human performance classes.
AI.result: While individual AES systems are insufficient alone, a single linear SVM on combined AES features—with reasoning and content features most predictive—accurately reconstructs human-based learner classes and generalizes across tasks and domains.
AI.conclusion: Ensembles of generic, out-of-the-box LLMs can effectively support or supplement human essay grading in medical education without costly domain-specific fine-tuning.

title: Teaching Language Models to Adapt Answer Granularity to Their Confidence
summary: When precise details are uncertain, a coarser answer can retain useful information without guessing or abstaining. We investigate whether language models can learn this behavior through model-conditioned supervision derived from consistency across sampled responses and recognition of answers at different granularity levels. We evaluate LFM2.5-1.2B, Ministral~3~3B, Qwen3.5-9B, and Gemma~4~31B on temporal and geographic questions and three generalization datasets. In several in-domain settings, fine-tuning improves the balance of correctness and informativeness beyond coarsening base answers to the best fixed level. Across generalization datasets, all four models produce coarser answers more often at low than high base-model confidence. The three smaller models' answers are also preferred over base responses on held-out relations when correctness and granularity are considered jointly. These findings demonstrate learnable confidence-related granularity adaptation, with benefits varying by model.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that language models can learn to adapt answer granularity to their confidence via model-conditioned supervision, producing coarser answers when uncertain without guessing or abstaining.
AI.motivation: When precise details are uncertain, providing a coarser answer preserves useful information without hallucinating or abstaining, but it was unclear whether models can learn this confidence-dependent adaptation.
AI.method: The authors derive model-conditioned supervision from consistency across sampled responses and multi-granularity answer recognition, fine-tuning LFM2.5-1.2B, Ministral 3 3B, Qwen3.5-9B, and Gemma 4 31B on temporal and geographic questions plus three generalization datasets.
AI.result: In several in-domain settings, fine-tuning improves the correctness-informativeness balance beyond fixed coarsening; across generalization datasets, all four models output coarser answers more often at low confidence, and the three smaller models are preferred over base responses on held-out relations.
