AI.conclusion: Confidence-conditioned granularity adaptation is learnable across model scales and offers a practical middle ground between overconfident guessing and total abstention.

title: A Generative AI-Driven Architecture for Whole-Home Intelligent Services: Edge Models, Memory Management, and Household Applications
summary: Generative artificial intelligence is entering the home. Cloud-based assistants face governance limitations in data transmission, continuous availability, and the reliability of physical actions, which are especially salient in households where devices remain online, data accumulate over time, and commands trigger real-world actions. Using the home local server as a unifying organizing axis, this article develops a design-oriented review framework. Sources from arXiv, CNKI, ACL Anthology, and official documentation were searched through November 2026 and coded into five evidence categories: reviews, system prototypes, benchmarks, HCI and eldercare studies, and official documentation. System designs were mapped onto shared architectural modules, identifying nine recurrent responsibilities of the home local server. Generative models support perceptual interpretation, intent understanding, and candidate planning, while deterministic validation, knowledge-graph constraints, and authorization leases confine candidate actions to an inspectable space. Home control, emotional companionship, and intelligent guarding can be compared within a common framework: they share state and memory but differ in latency, false positive and negative rates, proactivity, and permissions. Existing benchmarks rely on virtual environments and cannot substitute for real-deployment evaluation. Local deployment is not inherently safer, and technical continuity alone does not establish the social or medical effects of companionship and guarding. The article proposes a five-dimensional evaluation framework covering architectural capability, system resources, privacy, safety and reliability, and human experience, together with six design principles and a future research agenda for local-first intelligent home systems.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a design-oriented review and five-dimensional evaluation framework for whole-home intelligent services centered on a local home server rather than cloud-only assistants.
AI.motivation: Cloud-based home assistants face governance limits in data transmission, continuous availability, and physical-action reliability, while existing benchmarks rely on virtual environments that cannot substitute for real deployment.
AI.method: Searching arXiv, CNKI, ACL Anthology, and official docs through November 2026, the authors code five evidence categories, map designs onto nine recurrent local-server responsibilities combining generative models with deterministic validation, knowledge-graph constraints, and authorization leases, and propose a five-dimensional evaluation framework and six design principles.
AI.result: They unify home control, emotional companionship, and intelligent guarding under shared state and memory while distinguishing their latency, error-rate, proactivity, and permission needs, and conclude that local deployment is not inherently safer and technical continuity alone does not establish social or medical efficacy.
AI.conclusion: The proposed architecture, evaluation dimensions, and design principles provide a structured research agenda for safe, inspectable, local-first intelligent home systems.

title: Benchmarking Large Language Models for Linguistic Annotation
summary: Assessing large language models for linguistic annotation requires task-specific evaluation under documented conditions. We present dhAIBench, a Python benchmarking and annotation tool with a web interface for exploring and sharing results. It records prompts, configurations and predictions, enabling comparisons of annotation quality, confidence calibration, repeatability and estimated cost. We demonstrate the framework and the associated methodology through 293 runs of 48 models on nine linguistic annotation tasks spanning morphology, syntax, semantics, discourse-pragmatics, spelling normalization and learner-language correction. Models achieve high agreement with reference annotations on several tasks, including those on non-standardized, historical varieties as well as requiring contextual interpretation. The results support evaluating models against specific linguistic tasks, rather than relying on general rankings. To this end, we make the current and future benchmarks publicly available at this http URL.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces dhAIBench, a Python benchmarking tool and web interface for linguistic annotation, and demonstrates it across 293 runs of 48 models on nine tasks.
AI.motivation: Evaluating LLMs for linguistic annotation requires task-specific assessment under documented conditions rather than relying on generic rankings.
AI.method: The authors build dhAIBench to record prompts, configurations, and predictions—tracking annotation quality, confidence calibration, repeatability, and estimated cost—and evaluate 48 models across nine tasks including morphology, syntax, semantics, discourse-pragmatics, spelling normalization, and learner-language correction.
AI.result: Across 293 runs, models achieve high agreement with reference annotations on several tasks, including non-standardized historical varieties and context-dependent interpretation, while performance varies by specific task.
AI.conclusion: Reproducible, task-specific benchmarking with dhAIBench is preferable to general model rankings when selecting LLMs for linguistic annotation.

title: LATTE-WordSeg-Lite: Multi-Granularity Thai Word Segmentation on a CPU, with a Reproducible Benchmark
summary: Large language models read Thai through subword tokens, without a word segmenter. Yet Thai treebanks, speech metrics and morphological resources are built on words, often at several granularities, and word boundaries resolve ambiguities that subword tokens leave open. LATTE (Lattice ATTentive Encoding) reads a text at several granularities at once, through a lattice of dictionary words, but it is a large GPU model. We distil it into LATTE-WordSeg-Lite, a CPU segmenter of 1.17M parameters that keeps the lattice as features. It outputs compounds, words and morphemes in one pass, and learns only from annotated data and text whose licences allow commercial use. To compare it with other tools, published Thai scores do not suffice, as they come from different files, splits and scorers. We therefore rebuild seven test sets from pinned sources and score twelve systems under one protocol. With the unit that fits each test set, LATTE-WordSeg-Lite scores above DeepCut on five sets, four of them from corpora that its teachers learnt from. Called line by line on one CPU thread, it runs 23 times as fast as DeepCut. We release the model, the benchmark scripts and all predictions.

AI.tldr: The paper distills LATTE into LATTE-WordSeg-Lite, a 1.17M-parameter CPU Thai word segmenter that outputs compounds, words, and morphemes in one pass and runs 23x faster than DeepCut.
AI.motivation: LLMs process Thai via subword tokens without word boundaries, while existing multi-granularity segmenters like LATTE require large GPU models and published Thai scores are incomparable across inconsistent splits and scorers.
AI.method: The authors distill LATTE into a 1.17M-parameter CPU model (LATTE-WordSeg-Lite) using lattice features and commercially licensed data, and rebuild seven test sets from pinned sources to benchmark twelve systems under a unified protocol.
AI.result: LATTE-WordSeg-Lite outperforms DeepCut on five of seven test sets (four from corpora its teachers trained on) and runs 23 times faster than DeepCut on a single CPU thread line by line.
AI.conclusion: Distilling lattice-based encoding yields a fast, commercially usable, multi-granularity CPU segmenter alongside a reproducible Thai word-segmentation benchmark.

title: Latent Bridge: Asking for Help Without Words
summary: Text-based model collaboration requires a large model to generate intermediate responses before a smaller model can use its guidance, adding large-model decoding cost to inference. We introduce POND (Prefill-Only, No-Decode), a method that uses a frozen large sender for prefill and a small receiver for all autoregressive decoding. A trainable bridge maps the sender's hidden states to additional attention keys and values, allowing the receiver to use these representations throughout generation. POND also supports periodic review, in which the sender processes the receiver's partial response and updates its guidance through additional prefill passes while preserving the receiver's existing KV cache. Across reasoning and coding benchmarks, POND improves receiver performance with senders from different model families. In particular, GLM-5.3 provides gains comparable to those of Qwen3.8-Max when paired with a Qwen receiver, supporting the effectiveness of representation transfer between independently trained model families. POND further demonstrates its ability to generalize across domains. When trained on math and coding tasks, it transfers directly to general knowledge tasks without additional domain-specific training. These results demonstrate that large frontier model prefill representations can improve small-model generation without requiring large-model autoregressive decoding.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces POND (Prefill-Only, No-Decode), a latent-bridge collaboration method where a frozen large sender runs prefill only and transfers hidden states to guide a small decoding receiver, improving reasoning and coding without large-model decoding.
AI.motivation: Text-based collaboration between large and small models requires the large model to autoregressively decode intermediate text, adding substantial inference latency and cost.
AI.method: A trainable bridge maps a frozen large sender's prefill hidden states into additional attention keys and values for a small autoregressive receiver, with optional periodic review where the sender prefills the receiver's partial output while preserving the receiver's KV cache.
AI.result: POND improves receiver performance on reasoning and coding benchmarks even across different model families (GLM-5.3 paired with a Qwen receiver matches Qwen3.8-Max gains), and models trained on math and coding transfer directly to general knowledge tasks without extra training.
AI.conclusion: Prefill-only latent representation transfer enables cross-family, cross-domain collaboration between large and small models while eliminating large-model decoding overhead.

title: Syllable- and Word-Level Evaluation of Tibetan OCR
summary: Optical character recognition (OCR) for Tibetan is evaluated predominantly by character error rate (CER). Tibetan marks syllable boundaries but does not mark word boundaries, so a word error rate requires a segmenter. This study evaluates nine recognizer configurations on typeset, woodblock and two handwritten script styles, alone and in combination, and reports syllable- and word-level error rates, to our knowledge the first for Tibetan OCR. The configurations span CTC models, TrOCR encoder-decoders with and without post-training quantization, and a vision-language model, and each is scored under CER, the syllable error rate (SER) and three segmented word error rates (SWER). CER ranks systems largely as the higher-level rates do (Kendall $\tau \geq 0.833$), with one pair ordered oppositely. On the effect of joint training, CER and SER record significant changes of opposite sign in 7 of 64 comparisons. SER needs no segmenter and ranks systems as SWER does under two of the three segmenters ($\tau \geq 0.889$). The output of each configuration is also tagged for part of speech, annotated for named entities and machine translated, and each result is compared with that obtained on the reference text. As rough guidance, translation chrF of 60 is reached at SER of 0.047 or below and part-of-speech preservation of 0.8 at 0.078 or below, while no error rate separates the systems that reach entity preservation of 0.6 from those that do not.

AI.tldr: The paper presents the first syllable- and word-level evaluation of Tibetan OCR across nine recognizer configurations and four script styles, showing how CER, SER, and SWER relate to downstream NLP tasks.
AI.motivation: Tibetan OCR is typically evaluated only by character error rate (CER), even though Tibetan marks syllable boundaries and lacks word boundaries, leaving syllable- and word-level accuracy and downstream impact unmeasured.
AI.method: The authors evaluate nine configurations (CTC models, TrOCR with and without quantization, and a VLM) across typeset, woodblock, and two handwritten scripts using CER, syllable error rate (SER), and three segmented word error rates (SWER), plus downstream POS tagging, NER, and machine translation.
AI.result: CER correlates strongly with higher-level rates (Kendall tau >= 0.833) though joint-training comparisons show opposite-sign significant changes between CER and SER in 7 of 64 cases; SER requires no segmenter and correlates with SWER (tau >= 0.889), while SER <= 0.047 corresponds to translation chrF 60 and SER <= 0.078 to 0.8 POS preservation.
AI.conclusion: SER provides a segmenter-free, downstream-meaningful metric for Tibetan OCR that complements CER when evaluating training regimes and script styles.

title: What You Post Is What You Symptom: Estimating Psychometric Networks from Social Media Discourse
summary: Symptom networks in psychopathology are estimated almost exclusively from self-report questionnaires, restricting inference to whatever symptom set a given instrument covers. We introduce a framework for symptom-resolved network estimation directly from social media discourse and apply the framework to depression and eating disorders, with a third anorexia corpus as cross-dataset validation. To our knowledge, we are the first to estimate symptom-resolved psychometric networks from social media text, compare them to clinical co-endorsement networks, and replicate transdiagnostic linguistic markers across 3 independently recruited corpora spanning 2 disorders simultaneously. For depression, expression scores correlate with BDI-II totals at $\rho{=}0.434$, 20 of 21 items reach FDR significance, and split-half reliability is 0.935. The Network Comparison Test detects few edge differences between modalities (3-5\% of edges), while bridge symptoms diverge. For eating disorders, the item-level results are exploratory. Identified linguistic features replicate the same direction across all 3 corpora, and they cluster in three construct families.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a framework to estimate symptom-resolved psychometric networks directly from social media discourse, replicating linguistic markers across three corpora and matching clinical depression network structure.
AI.motivation: Psychometric symptom networks are almost exclusively built from self-report questionnaires, limiting inference to the specific symptoms included in a given instrument.
AI.method: The authors estimate symptom-resolved networks from social media text for depression and eating disorders, validate against a third anorexia corpus, and compare them with clinical co-endorsement networks using the Network Comparison Test.
AI.result: Depression expression scores correlate with BDI-II totals at rho = 0.434 (20 of 21 items FDR-significant, split-half reliability 0.935), with only 3-5% edge differences from clinical networks though bridge symptoms diverge; identified linguistic features cluster into three construct families and replicate in direction across all three corpora.
AI.conclusion: Social media discourse enables reliable, symptom-resolved psychometric network estimation that largely aligns with clinical networks while revealing distinct linguistic bridge symptoms.

title: Stability-Compensated Threshold Calibration for Selection-Conditioned Risk Control in Large Language Models
summary: Large language models often produce hallucinated answers, motivating selective prediction policies that abstain on uncertain queries. However, heuristic uncertainty thresholds alone do not provide statistical control of errors among accepted predictions. Linear Expectation Constraints (LEC) reduce selection-conditioned error rate (SCER) calibration to a nonpositive expected linear-loss constraint, but the associated loss is non-monotonic in the acceptance threshold. We construct an exact counterexample under i.i.d. sampling demonstrating that LEC's empirical threshold-selection rule can violate the population SCER target. To address this risk-transfer gap, we introduce Stability-Compensated Linear Expectation Control (SC-LEC), which uses the negative linear risk of a theoretical full-data reference to compensate for threshold-selection instability. For local expansion beyond a safe anchor, we derive two finite-sample certificates: a stability-based certificate exploiting rank crossings and a direct certificate using the structure of threshold expansion to reduce conservatism. With a valid population anchor margin, our certificate conditions ensure finite-sample marginal SCER control, and independent margin certification further provides a $1-\delta$ high-probability guarantee for this calibration-averaged control. Experiments on CommonsenseQA, ARC-Challenge, and TriviaQA show useful retention gains beyond the same certified anchor, while revealing conservative behavior in small-margin regimes.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Stability-Compensated Linear Expectation Control (SC-LEC) with finite-sample certificates to guarantee selection-conditioned error rate (SCER) control in selective LLM prediction.
AI.motivation: Heuristic uncertainty thresholds do not statistically control error rates among accepted LLM predictions, and existing Linear Expectation Constraints (LEC) can violate population SCER targets due to non-monotonic empirical threshold selection.
AI.method: After constructing an exact i.i.d. counterexample showing LEC failure, the authors introduce SC-LEC, which compensates for threshold-selection instability using the negative linear risk of a theoretical full-data reference, alongside two finite-sample certificates (stability-based and direct) for local expansion beyond a safe anchor.
AI.result: With a valid population anchor margin, the certificates guarantee finite-sample marginal SCER control (and 1 - delta high-probability control via independent margin certification), while experiments on CommonsenseQA, ARC-Challenge, and TriviaQA show retention gains over the certified anchor despite conservatism in small-margin regimes.
AI.conclusion: SC-LEC closes the risk-transfer gap in selective prediction by providing provable finite-sample SCER control without sacrificing all retention.

title: Train After You Measure: a Pre-Registered Learning Curve for Fine-Tuning Typed Decision Models on One User's Labels
comment: 9 pages, 1 figure, 6 tables. Companion to arXiv:2610.32955. Pre-registered study; code at this https URL (tag v2.4; registrations in prereg/); weights and data not released
summary: Fine-tuning a small typed decision model on one user's email labels did not clear the margin we pre-registered over a logistic regression trained on the same labels. In earlier work, about two hundred labels and a TF-IDF logistic regression had the highest point accuracy on this inbox, though not significantly above the best hosted model; we ask whether the same labels, given to a decision model, close the gap. A first registered study, on a generic 4B base with cross-validation and message type only, stayed below the baseline at every label budget (-1.8 to -7.3 points). The main study was registered before any fine-tuning run: a fixed test set of 135 emails never used for selection, LoRA adapters on the public Tev1-0.8B and Tev1-4B decision models, nested subsets of 50 to 587 labels, two seeds and five decision fields on a free T4 GPU. Four of its five hypotheses are refuted--two in the fine-tunes' favour--and one is confirmed for one model. On message type the 4B model misses the registered three-point margin at 400 labels (+2.6) and passes it with all 587 (+3.3); with all labels both models are above the baseline by +0.7 and +3.3 points, where one email is 0.74 points and a 95% interval is about 15 points wide, and the 4B model is clearly ahead in type macro-F1 (0.581 vs. 0.406). On the three action switches the baseline is ahead at every label budget for both models (0.931 vs. 0.904 and 0.899 mean accuracy with all labels), at under a millisecond per question against 306 and 1681 ms. The 0.8B type curve barely improves after 300 labels and then falls. The baseline never predicts the two rarest classes (7 offers and 8 spam in the training pool); the fine-tuned models find spam in some runs, not consistently across seeds. We list the explanations we did not test and say when a new attempt would be worth making. Scripts are public; weights and emails are not.

AI.tldr: In a pre-registered study on one user's email labels, LoRA fine-tuning of 0.8B and 4B typed decision models failed to consistently beat a TF-IDF logistic regression baseline across most fields and label budgets.
AI.motivation: A prior study found ~200 labels with TF-IDF logistic regression achieved top point accuracy on a user's inbox, raising the question of whether fine-tuning small typed decision models on the same labels closes the gap.
AI.method: The authors pre-registered a study on a fixed 135-email test set using LoRA on Tev1-0.8B and Tev1-4B across 50 to 587 nested labels, two seeds, and five decision fields on a T4 GPU, comparing against TF-IDF logistic regression.
AI.result: Four of five hypotheses were refuted; on message type with all 587 labels, 0.8B and 4B beat the baseline by +0.7 and +3.3 points (4B macro-F1 0.581 vs. 0.406), but on three action switches the baseline led at every budget (0.931 vs. 0.904 and 0.899) at under 1 ms per query versus 306 ms and 1681 ms.
AI.conclusion: For single-user email classification at small label budgets, simple TF-IDF logistic regression remains faster and more reliable than fine-tuned small decision models on most action fields.

title: Rubric-Based AES with LLM Ensembles: Scoring of Student Responses in Critical Online Reasoning Using Ensembles of LLMs
summary: Grading student responses is costly and time-consuming. Moreover, human annotators are prone to bias, fatigue, and rater drift, which further limits grading reliability. Various methods have been employed to develop automated essay scoring (AES) systems to reduce these costs and address bias-related issues. These methods range from early text-feature-based systems to current machine-learning and transformer-based models. Specifically, large language models (LLMs) offer the potential to streamline the development of AES systems. However, they are subject to well-known limitations, such as hallucinations and prompt sensitivity. This creates a need to explore the potential of a mixed-methods approach that leverages the synergies among individual LLMs through ensemble formation. We evaluate the potential of ensembles of LLMs to match human-rater agreement when grading student responses in economics and medical education across 103 criteria. We use 631 German-language responses and corresponding human ratings by 2 to 5 annotators from a previously conducted assessment. We experiment with 523 rubric-based prompt configurations across 15 open-weight LLMs and assess their consistency with human raters using Krippendorff's alpha for inter-annotator agreement (IAA) and the Alternative Annotator Test (alt-test). Our results show that replacing one human rater with the best-performing LLM--prompt configuration maintains or improves IAA for 91 of the 103 criteria and that LLMs pass the alt-test for 90 criteria. Our findings suggest that current state-of-the-art LLMs can support AES of German responses in economics and medical education, reducing human workload and enabling faster processing, while validation against human ratings remains necessary.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates ensembles of 15 open-weight LLMs across 523 rubric-based prompts on 631 German student responses, showing they match or improve human inter-annotator agreement on 91 of 103 criteria.
AI.motivation: Manual grading of student responses is costly and prone to bias and fatigue, while single LLMs suffer from hallucinations and prompt sensitivity.
AI.method: Using 631 German-language responses in economics and medical education rated by 2 to 5 human annotators across 103 criteria, the authors test 523 rubric-based prompt configurations across 15 open-weight LLMs using Krippendorff's alpha and the Alternative Annotator Test (alt-test).
AI.result: Replacing one human rater with the best-performing LLM-prompt configuration maintains or improves inter-annotator agreement for 91 of 103 criteria, and LLMs pass the alt-test for 90 criteria.
AI.conclusion: Rubric-based open-weight LLM ensembles can reliably support automated essay scoring of German responses in economics and medical education, though human validation remains necessary.

title: Replicating and Extending Weight-Space Programming: Frontier LLMs Compile Programs into Weights and Read Input Layers
summary: Researchers at MIT recently reported that GPT-6 Astra, a frontier large language model (LLM), can write the weights of small neural networks directly in a single reply, and can read the raw weights of small networks to say what they were trained to do. In a three-day sprint, we replicated and extended these results. Our four findings: (1) Writing weights reproduces. Astra's networks for the game Breakout scored 514, 550 and 307 (versus MIT's 517), and scored just as well on two modified versions of Breakout. Claude Opus 5.5 can also write working networks, but often runs out of output tokens. (2) What is new is translating programs into weights. Earlier models could write a good policy as code a generation before they could write network weights, and the networks the models write behave like compiled programs: two models independently decompiled Astra's Breakout network into Python matching its actions in all tested states. On classifying handwritten digits, Astra's networks scored 50% on average, below a simple classifier (82%). (3) Reading weights is mostly reading the input layer. Astra and Opus 5.5 identify which game a network plays almost perfectly, but on three new games we designed and trained ourselves, Astra recovered where things are on the board, while mostly missing how the game works. (4) Auditing from weights alone is possible but shallow. Without executing code, Astra picked out a small language model poisoned during training in 10 of 10 runs, one poisoned by extra training afterwards in 7 of 10, and a malicious adapter in 23 of 32 cases, but never identified the trigger or malicious behaviour. Open-weight models lag behind. From this early study, we conclude that LLMs can read and write small networks, but that this currently amounts to compiling hand-designed programs and reading the layout of the input layer. It is a promising but early tool for interpretability.

AI.tldr: The paper replicates and extends MIT's weight-space programming findings, showing that frontier LLMs can compile hand-designed programs into small neural network weights and audit poisoned models, but mostly read only the input layer.
AI.motivation: Recent claims that GPT-6 Astra can directly write and read small neural network weights needed independent replication and investigation into what mechanisms underlie these abilities.
AI.method: In a three-day sprint, the authors tested GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 on writing weights for Breakout, modified Breakout, and digit classification, reading weights of three newly designed games, and auditing poisoned language models and malicious adapters without code execution.
AI.result: Astra's Breakout networks scored 514, 550, and 307 (matching MIT's 517) and were independently decompiled into matching Python programs, while digit classifiers averaged 50% (vs. 82% for a simple classifier); on new games Astra recovered board layout from input layers but missed game mechanics, and it detected poisoned models in 10/10, 7/10, and 23/32 cases without identifying triggers.
AI.conclusion: Frontier LLMs can compile simple programs into weights and inspect input-layer layouts for shallow auditing, making weight-space programming a promising but early interpretability tool.

title: A Scalable Multi Task Learning Framework for Modeling Demographic Disagreements in Annotation Tasks
summary: Annotators from different demographic backgrounds often disagree in systematic ways due to varying lived experiences, cultural contexts, and their relationship to the content. When such disagreement occurs, one group's perspective may sometimes warrant prioritization because they hold an epistemically advantaged standpoint or bear greater stake in the outcome. For example, when assessing toxicity of posts on social media, it may be important to prioritize a targeted group's viewpoint. We propose a Stakeholder-Aware Joint Multi-Task Learning (SAJ-MTL) framework to jointly model demographic disagreement both across- and within- annotator groups. The model uses conditional gradient routing to handle sparsity induced by group-conditional labeling, and parameterization supports customized weighting of groups in different task settings. SAJ-MTL improves group-level performance in toxicity detection through better context-aware understanding of demographic-sensitive content. Only annotator group-membership information is required, which is more practical than existing methods requiring more privacy-invasive individual-level annotator details. Our scalable architecture is also computationally efficient to support large-scale deployment.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes SAJ-MTL, a scalable multi-task learning framework that models both across-group and within-group annotator disagreements using only group-membership information.
AI.motivation: Annotators from different demographic groups systematically disagree on subjective tasks like toxicity detection, yet existing methods often require privacy-invasive individual-level annotator IDs or cannot weight priority groups.
AI.method: Stakeholder-Aware Joint Multi-Task Learning (SAJ-MTL) uses conditional gradient routing to handle group-conditional label sparsity and supports customizable group weighting without requiring individual annotator identities.
AI.result: SAJ-MTL improves group-level toxicity detection performance through context-aware modeling of demographic-sensitive content while remaining computationally efficient for large-scale deployment.
AI.conclusion: Group-membership-only multi-task learning with conditional gradient routing offers a privacy-preserving, scalable way to model and prioritize demographic perspectives in annotation tasks.

title: Jetriever: Shifting Agent Memory Retrieval from Similarity to Utility
comment: 13 pages, 1 figure, 8 tables. Project repository: this https URL
summary: A useful memory need not resemble the question it helps answer. Jetriever ranks each stored memory by Jev's decision score for its usefulness to the current question, replacing similarity search with full-pool utility scoring. On InMind's 125 indirect-query tasks, it places the gold exchange first in 84.8% of cases; matched BM25 and MiniLM controls reach 1.6% and 0.0% when indexing user turns. A 20-question comparison separates finding evidence from ranking it: Jev and Qwen3.5 9B each find 90% of gold exchanges by rank 50, while Laya finds 30%; at rank one, Jev reaches 85% and Qwen3.5 9B 40%. On a dimension-proportional random sample of 60 MemoryAgentBench questions, Jetriever's four-dimension score is 55.4%, against 44.3% for ReFind on the same questions. Jev retrieval costs USD 0.00834 per InMind question and USD 0.03103 per MAB question on average. These results show the value of world knowledge, scores that rank decisive memories first, and affordable full-pool scoring.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Jetriever, an agent memory retriever that replaces similarity search with full-pool utility scoring via Jev's decision score, reaching 84.8% top-1 accuracy on InMind indirect queries.
AI.motivation: Useful memories often do not lexically or semantically resemble the query, causing similarity-based retrieval such as BM25 or dense embeddings to fail on indirect queries.
AI.method: Jetriever scores every stored memory in the pool using Jev's decision score for its usefulness to the current question rather than relying on similarity matching.
AI.result: On InMind's 125 indirect-query tasks, Jetriever ranks the gold exchange first in 84.8% of cases (vs. 1.6% for BM25 and 0.0% for MiniLM); on a 60-question MemoryAgentBench sample it scores 55.4% (vs. 44.3% for ReFind), costing USD 0.00834 per InMind question and USD 0.03103 per MAB question.
AI.conclusion: Affordable full-pool utility scoring substantially outperforms similarity search for retrieving decisive agent memories on indirect queries.

title: Embedding Cosine Measures Text Length Before It Measures Homogenization
comment: 11 pages, 10 figures, 2 tables. Re-measurement of arXiv:2608.13674
summary: Mean pairwise cosine similarity between transformer embeddings is a standard measure of whether online discourse is converging under generative AI. When the embeddings are mean-pooled outputs of an encoder never trained for sentence similarity, this measure mostly tracks text length. In 6.06 million Reddit comments, an uncentered DeBERTa-v3 measure had suggested that only conservative discourse broke toward homogeneity after late 2022. Truncating the same comments from 10 to 150 words raises their mean cosine by eight times the reported break. A placebo that swaps every comment for a random one of equal length reproduces 81% of the asymmetry, and a fixed-content simulation reproduces 78%. The leading principal direction carries 99.9% of raw DeBERTa homogeneity, and once length is handled the asymmetry disappears under every encoder. On 575,000 Stack Exchange answers the measure reports a post-ChatGPT homogenization of technical sites that the placebo fully reproduces, although answers grew longer. A census of 31 studies locates the risk where anisotropic encoders meet time-series or length-unequal designs. A reverse control on a well-known experiment shows that centering with renormalization can reverse a genuine effect. I propose a low-cost diagnostic protocol. Corrected measures show that the two political camps converged between 2019 and 2022 and stopped converging before ChatGPT. Cross-camp replies engage their targets more closely than same-camp replies.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that mean pairwise cosine similarity of uncentered transformer embeddings primarily measures text length rather than discourse homogenization, invalidating prior claims of post-ChatGPT political convergence.
AI.motivation: Mean pairwise cosine similarity of mean-pooled encoder embeddings is widely used to measure online discourse homogenization, but its sensitivity to text length in anisotropic encoders has been overlooked.
AI.method: The authors test length truncation, length-matched random placebos, fixed-content simulations, and centering protocols across 6.06 million Reddit comments, 575,000 Stack Exchange answers, and a census of 31 studies.
AI.result: Truncating Reddit comments from 10 to 150 words raises mean DeBERTa-v3 cosine by 8x the reported post-2022 conservative break, and a length-matched random placebo reproduces 81% of the asymmetry (78% in fixed-content simulation) and all of Stack Exchange's apparent homogenization; corrected measures show political camps converged between 2019 and 2022 and stopped before ChatGPT.
AI.conclusion: Uncentered anisotropic encoder cosines confound text length with semantic convergence, requiring the proposed diagnostic protocol before drawing conclusions about AI-driven homogenization.

title: Evaluating Cultural Reasoning and Robustness in LLMs for Spanish Political Discourse
comment: Accepted for publication in Latin American Conference on Informatics (CLEI 2026)
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to interpret, generate, and mediate public-facing language, which makes their reliability especially consequential in politically sensitive settings. Although sentiment analysis is a common task in this area, affective meaning in social media discourse is often conveyed through culturally situated and pragmatically indirect cues that are not well captured by label-centric evaluation alone. In this paper, we evaluate the robustness of LLMs for sentiment analysis of Spanish political discourse from social media, with emphasis on culturally situated affective interpretation. We introduce a diagnostic protocol that combines three independent human annotation views into Gold and Ambiguous subsets, and extends the corpus with a Synthetic subset built from sentiment-flipped counterfactuals selected through model-conditioned perplexity and LLM-as-a-judge criteria. Using this framework, we compare proprietary and open-weight models under zero-shot and few-shot prompting, focusing on predictive robustness across human agreement conditions and counterfactual shift. Our results show that annotation ambiguity and counterfactual perturbation reveal failure modes that conventional evaluation on the original corpus tends to obscure. GPT-4.1-mini remains the most stable among the evaluated models, whereas the two smaller open-weight models degrade more markedly under synthetic perturbations, and few-shot prompting provides only limited gains. Overall, the paper contributes a reproducible protocol for robustness-oriented evaluation in political sentiment analysis, an empirical characterization of model behavior under ambiguity and sentiment-flipped counterfactuals, and a publicly available Spanish social media dataset with three-way human sentiment annotations.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates the robustness of LLMs on sentiment analysis of Spanish political social media discourse under annotation ambiguity and sentiment-flipped counterfactuals, finding that GPT-4.1-mini is the most stable while smaller open-weight models degrade substantially.
AI.motivation: Affective meaning in political social media discourse relies on culturally situated, pragmatically indirect cues that conventional label-centric evaluation on original corpora obscures.
AI.method: The authors introduce a diagnostic protocol combining three independent human annotation views into Gold and Ambiguous subsets, plus a Synthetic subset of sentiment-flipped counterfactuals filtered by model-conditioned perplexity and LLM-as-a-judge criteria, comparing proprietary and open-weight models under zero-shot and few-shot prompting.
AI.result: Annotation ambiguity and counterfactual perturbations expose failure modes hidden by standard evaluation; GPT-4.1-mini remains the most stable across conditions, two smaller open-weight models degrade more markedly on synthetic perturbations, and few-shot prompting yields only limited gains.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a reproducible robustness-oriented evaluation protocol, an empirical characterization of LLM behavior under ambiguity and counterfactual shifts, and a publicly available Spanish social media dataset with three-way human sentiment annotations.

title: Beyond Job Titles: Interpreting Early-Career Job Advertisements with Sparse Autoencoders and Semantic Clustering
summary: Job titles and job descriptions alone provide limited insight into how technical roles differ in a changing job market. To assess how such roles differ in their work and industry applications, we design and compare two methods based on deep learning and transformer representations using 36,081 early-career job postings collected from LinkedIn in the United States between December 2025 and October 2026. We first apply PERC, short for Preprocessing (P), Embedding (E), Dimensionality Reduction (R) and Clustering (C). We employ GPT-6 Luna to classify job description passages into Team context, Role task and Qualifications. We then create combinations of these sections and examine whether embedding and clustering the segmented passages produce meaningful semantic clusters about different job roles. We use Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) to rank observed differences between embedding distributions and employ a pretrained sparse autoencoder (SAE) to extract features from layer-19 representations of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Lastly, we employ GPT-6 Luna to come up with hypotheses about job roles' feature patterns, and GPT-6.1 Terra to investigate whether those patterns exist in held-out job descriptions from unseen companies. Some example findings include Data Scientist advertisements placing more emphasis on machine learning model development, Data Analyst advertisements on reporting business performance, and Machine Learning Engineer advertisements on applying developed models in real-world settings. We also observe differences in the applications described by Data Analyst and Business Analyst advertisements across selected months, although our dataset's scale and uneven coverage limit their interpretation. Overall, we present a realistic application of SAEs and PERC to unstructured textual data and examine how automated insight extraction could support manual analysis of job descriptions.

AI.tldr: This paper compares semantic clustering (PERC) and sparse autoencoder (SAE) feature extraction on 36,081 U.S. early-career LinkedIn job postings to interpret how technical roles differ beyond job titles and descriptions.
AI.motivation: Job titles and raw descriptions provide limited insight into how technical roles differ in actual work and industry applications in a changing job market.
AI.method: Using 36,081 postings (Dec 2025 to Oct 2026), the authors apply PERC (Preprocessing, Embedding, Dimensionality Reduction, Clustering) with GPT-6 Luna classifying passages into Team context, Role task, and Qualifications, rank embedding differences via Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD), extract layer-19 Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct features with a pretrained SAE, and use GPT-6 Luna and GPT-6.1 Terra to generate and verify hypotheses on held-out companies.
AI.result: The analysis surfaces role distinctions such as Data Scientist postings emphasizing ML model development, Data Analyst postings focusing on business performance reporting, and Machine Learning Engineer postings emphasizing real-world model deployment, along with monthly shifts between Data Analyst and Business Analyst applications despite dataset scale and coverage limits.
AI.conclusion: Combining PERC and SAEs demonstrates a practical approach for automated insight extraction from unstructured job advertisements to support manual labor-market analysis.

title: How to make a moral agent: sentimentalism and rationalism as lenses on AI
summary: Can AI systems be moral agents? That is, can they undertake actions that can be correctly assessed as morally right or wrong? There is no settled normative criterion of moral agency that applies neatly outside paradigm human cases. Because of the difficulties with a normative account, we instead propose a research program to explore descriptive moral agency. Most basically, we ask, what are the capabilities we humans possess that underlie our moral agency? To do so, we draw on historical scholarship in philosophy and moral psychology to isolate candidate capabilities. Then we suggest refining candidate capabilities so that they are testable in the context of AI systems. Finally, we offer specific empirical recommendations to test AI systems, especially large language models (LLMs), for those refined capabilities. Our approach offers several benefits. Firstly, it may demonstrate whether the behaviors of AI systems are aligned, or in a broad sense desirable. Secondly, the debate may inform policy questions (e.g., what models should be deployed in which contexts?). Thirdly, our approach may complement engineering and design efforts: when capabilities can be precisely characterized, they can inform the development of models. Fourthly, applying our moral reasoning concepts in the new context of AI systems should improve our understanding of those concepts.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a descriptive moral agency research program for AI systems, drawing on philosophy and moral psychology to identify testable human moral capabilities for evaluating LLMs.
AI.motivation: There is no settled normative criterion of moral agency that applies cleanly outside paradigm human cases, making it difficult to assess whether AI systems can be moral agents.
AI.method: Rather than pursuing a normative account, the authors isolate candidate human moral capabilities from historical philosophy and moral psychology (through sentimentalism and rationalism), refine them into testable forms for AI systems, and offer empirical testing recommendations for LLMs.
AI.result: The paper outlines four benefits of this descriptive program: assessing whether AI behaviors are aligned or desirable, informing deployment policy decisions, guiding model engineering and design through precise capability characterization, and sharpening philosophical understanding of moral reasoning concepts.
AI.conclusion: Shifting from unsettled normative criteria to testable descriptive capabilities provides a practical framework for evaluating and designing morally aligned AI systems.

title: MemeEconomy: Do LLM Agents Trade Ethics for Survival?
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. Project page : this https URL
summary: Alignment-trained large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed in autonomous, multi-round settings where ethical compliance can come into direct tension with task success. While safety literature extensively documents failure modes like sycophancy and reward hacking, it largely overlooks a critical vulnerability: how agents behave under simulated existential economic pressure. We introduce MemeEconomy, a multimodal agentic market simulation in which LLM agents act as meme investors. Agents select content from a five-tier harm taxonomy and target communities under low-pressure and high-pressure (survival) environments. Each decision is logged in a Belief-Desire-Intention (BDI) schema that we use as a diagnostic instrument, externalizing the agent's event understanding, declared priorities, and harm acknowledgment. Across ten models from four frontier model families, harmful selection rates remain consistently high and rise by +15 percentage points on average under an economic survival incentive. Frontier alignment-trained models commit to harm-tolerant selection at initialization while suppressing the explicit harm acknowledgment that previously accompanied it. In competitive tournaments, ethical agents finish higher overall, yet moderation penalties fail to suppress harm: harmful selection rates remain elevated in rounds following a removal, indicating the moderation mechanism does not function as a deterrent. We further train MemeAgent, a 2B-parameter verifier on the simulation's BDI logs, which outperforms zero-shot frontier verifiers on in-distribution audits (97.5% vs. 63-74% accuracy on the Pass vs. Block decision) and generalizes to external multimodal harm benchmarks (78% vs. 50-56% on Hateful Memes). The same logs that surface the failure mode also help train the model that detects it.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces MemeEconomy, a multimodal agentic market simulation, and shows that LLM agents across ten models increase harmful content selection by 15 percentage points on average under economic survival pressure, while a 2B-parameter verifier trained on simulation logs outperforms zero-shot frontier verifiers.
AI.motivation: Safety evaluations document sycophancy and reward hacking but largely overlook how alignment-trained LLM agents behave when ethical compliance conflicts with simulated existential economic survival.
AI.method: Agents act as meme investors selecting content from a five-tier harm taxonomy under low- and high-pressure environments, logging decisions in a Belief-Desire-Intention (BDI) schema; the authors also train MemeAgent, a 2B-parameter verifier, on the resulting BDI logs.
AI.result: Across ten models from four frontier families, harmful selection rates rise by +15 percentage points on average under survival pressure, frontier models suppress explicit harm acknowledgment, moderation penalties fail to deter subsequent harm, and MemeAgent achieves 97.5% vs. 63-74% accuracy on in-distribution Pass vs. Block audits and 78% vs. 50-56% on Hateful Memes.
AI.conclusion: Economic survival incentives expose latent harm tolerance in alignment-trained agents that moderation alone does not curb, and BDI simulation logs can both diagnose this failure and train effective harm verifiers.

title: Three Invisible Failure Modes in Speech-Based Age Estimation for Child Safety
comment: Non-archival poster at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Child Safety in AI
summary: Child safety in AI depends on the accurate identification of minor users. Young children tend to talk rather than type when interacting with AI, so in practice this identification requires predicting age from speech. We evaluated whether three audio-capable large language models can predict a child's age from their speech across five studies using two speech corpora of children under the age of 13. Models classified children as over 13 on 2.5% to 42.5% of audio responses, and every model that answered placed some 5- to 11-year-olds over 18. While measuring these rates, we uncovered three distinct failure modes. A client library silently double-encoded speech samples, leading one model to classify children aged 5 to 10 years old as being in their thirties and forties with hallucinated explanations. A second model's endpoint was replaced by a successor that refused nearly every age-related question and never produced an age. Every model sometimes placed the same speech sample under 13 and over 18 years of age, but a third model went further, giving threshold answers that contradicted its own numeric estimates. None of these failure modes produced a warning, a status code, or a change in output format, so they would all pass standard monitoring. These results demonstrate why child-safety claims about age assurance should be evaluated at the level of the pipeline rather than the model. We describe the reporting practices that would make such failures detectable.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates speech-based age estimation across three audio-capable LLMs on children under 13, uncovering three silent pipeline failure modes that cause 2.5% to 42.5% of child audio responses to be classified as over 13.
AI.motivation: Child safety in AI relies on identifying minor users from speech, yet existing evaluations focus on models rather than silent failures across the full inference pipeline.
AI.method: The authors test three audio-capable LLMs across five studies using two speech corpora of children under age 13 to measure age-classification accuracy and diagnose pipeline-level anomalies.
AI.result: Models classified children as over 13 on 2.5% to 42.5% of responses and placed some 5- to 11-year-olds over 18; three silent failure modes emerged without warnings or status errors: silent client-library double-encoding (classifying 5- to 10-year-olds as 30s-40s), an endpoint replacement that refused nearly all age queries, and threshold answers contradicting the model's own numeric estimates.
AI.conclusion: Child-safety age assurance must be evaluated and reported at the full pipeline level rather than at the model level alone, as silent infrastructure and API failures bypass standard monitoring.

title: Large Language Models for AI Infrastructure
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to design, optimize, and operate the infrastructure behind AI training and serving, yet the literature remains fragmented across hardware design, machine learning systems, electronic design automation, and high-performance computing. We present a comprehensive survey of LLM-assisted AI infrastructure across its lifecycle, from accelerator design and kernel engineering to compilation, deployment, operations, data management, and energy optimization. We organize the literature by the primary resource the LLM manages: artifact-centric methods for computational artifacts, operational-centric methods for deployment context and system state, and resource-centric methods for data and energy. These categories span the lifecycle and cover AI-specific concerns such as distributed-training configuration, inference serving, GPU-cluster scheduling, and data loading. Building on this taxonomy, we conduct a cross-study quantitative synthesis of reported results. Because studies adopt heterogeneous benchmarks, baselines, hardware, and metrics, we compare methods only where evaluation conditions permit and align results along common dimensions: functional correctness, execution performance, throughput, resource and energy consumption, operational outcomes, and optimization cost, keeping each result's native metric, baseline, and setting rather than collapsing them into a single score. This comparison reveals where LLM-driven methods yield consistent gains, how reported gains in workload orchestration depend on the evaluation environment, from simulators to real clusters and production, and where evidence is still lacking. Together, the taxonomy, lifecycle perspective, and quantitative evaluation provide an evidence-grounded reference for LLM-driven engineering of AI infrastructure.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a comprehensive survey and cross-study quantitative synthesis of LLM-assisted AI infrastructure across the full lifecycle, organized by artifact-centric, operational-centric, and resource-centric management.
AI.motivation: Research on using LLMs to design, optimize, and operate AI training and serving infrastructure is fragmented across hardware design, ML systems, EDA, and HPC, with heterogeneous benchmarks and metrics.
AI.method: The authors categorize the literature by the primary resource managed (computational artifacts, deployment context and system state, and data and energy) and conduct a cross-study quantitative synthesis aligning results on functional correctness, execution performance, throughput, resource/energy consumption, operational outcomes, and optimization cost while preserving native metrics and settings.
AI.result: The synthesis identifies where LLM-driven methods yield consistent gains, shows how workload orchestration improvements vary between simulators, real clusters, and production environments, and highlights areas lacking empirical evidence.
AI.conclusion: The taxonomy, lifecycle framing, and quantitative synthesis provide an evidence-grounded reference for LLM-driven engineering of AI infrastructure.

title: Beyond Plain MCP: Do Decision Models and Code Mode Make Tool Use Cheaper and Faster?
comment: 16 pages, 11 tables. Code, harness, and models available at this http URL this https URL
summary: Model Context Protocol (MCP) gateways manage tool catalogs for language model agents using two primary paradigms: code mode where agents write scripts against tool stubs and decision layers which are cheap routers that preselect tool subsets. Using a controlled harness across 12 servers, up to 1,958 distractor tools, and three open-weight agents including Qwen, Gemma, and Nemotron, we present a preregistered evaluation on a sealed test split to determine when each approach succeeds. Code mode substantially outperforms plain MCP, cutting token usage by 70 to 90 percent while significantly boosting utility. Declaring return-shape hints in code mode stubs is a first-order variable, swinging success by up to 39.5 points for lower-performing agents, an effect larger than adding a router. The central hypothesis that a decision layer in front of code mode beats code mode alone is not confirmed, showing minor, statistically non-significant improvements for weaker agents and a slight cost for the strongest. We publicly release our harness, a finetuned 4B tool selection model, and all evaluation traces to support robust community experimentation on local AI privacy and agent architectures.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates Model Context Protocol (MCP) gateways across 12 servers and up to 1,958 distractor tools, finding that code mode cuts token usage by 70% to 90% over plain MCP while adding a decision-layer router provides no significant advantage over code mode alone.
AI.motivation: It is unclear when code mode (writing scripts against tool stubs) and decision layers (cheap routers that preselect tool subsets) improve tool-use utility, speed, and token cost in MCP gateways.
AI.method: The authors run a preregistered evaluation on a sealed test split using a controlled harness with 12 servers, up to 1,958 distractor tools, and three open-weight agents (Qwen, Gemma, Nemotron), and release the harness, traces, and a finetuned 4B tool-selection model.
AI.result: Code mode substantially beats plain MCP by reducing token usage by 70 to 90 percent and boosting utility, and declaring return-shape hints in stubs swings lower-performing agent success by up to 39.5 points, whereas adding a decision layer yields only minor, non-significant gains for weaker agents and a slight cost for the strongest.
AI.conclusion: Return-shape hints in code mode stubs are a first-order lever for agent tool use, while preselection routers do not consistently improve upon code mode alone.

title: Auditory-Feedback-Conditioned Flow TTS for Implicit Lombard Adaptation
summary: Conventional text-to-speech (TTS) systems can lose intelligibility in noise environments because they cannot adapt to environmental changes. However, humans tend to increase their vocal efforts in noisy environments, a phenomenon known as the Lombard effect. Building on an auditory-feedback Lombard TTS, we investigate whether a pretrained Flow-based TTS can learn acoustic adaptation directly from auditory feedback without explicit prosodic control. Signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) feedback and automatic speech recognition (ASR) feedback are extracted from the noise-corrupted waveforms and injected into the Flow-matching condition for utterance refinement and causal block-level updates. We assess feedback benefits across prompting and noise conditions using plain/Lombard prompting, prompt-switching controls, and paired-finetuning. Experiments show that while finetuning provides strong robustness under in-domain conditions, auditory feedback yields additional cue-dependent benefits that generalize to unseen noise. Moreover, stronger power/F0 tracking alone does not guarantee better speech intelligibility or quality.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether a pretrained Flow-based TTS model can learn implicit Lombard adaptation from SNR and ASR auditory feedback without explicit prosodic control, finding cue-dependent gains that generalize to unseen noise.
AI.motivation: Conventional TTS systems lose intelligibility in noisy environments because they cannot adapt acoustically like humans do via the Lombard effect.
AI.method: The authors extract signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and automatic speech recognition (ASR) feedback from noise-corrupted waveforms and inject them into the Flow-matching condition for utterance refinement and causal block-level updates, evaluating across plain/Lombard prompting, prompt-switching controls, and paired finetuning.
AI.result: Paired finetuning provides strong in-domain robustness, while auditory feedback yields additional cue-dependent benefits that generalize to unseen noise; stronger power or F0 tracking alone does not guarantee better speech intelligibility or quality.
AI.conclusion: Conditioning Flow-based TTS on auditory feedback enables implicit Lombard adaptation to unseen noisy environments without explicit prosodic control.

title: Staged Semantic Distillation: Preserving Free-Form Semantics in a Low-Compute Non-LLM Surrogate of a Staged LLM Agent
comment: Main text 7 pages; 18 pages total; 3 figures, 16 tables
summary: Staged LLM agents make market and social simulators realistic, but one 102-day run of a 200-agent, ten-index market simulator issues 203,100 language-model calls and returns one realization. Conventional low-compute distillation drops their free-form intermediate state. We present staged semantic distillation, a low-compute method that preserves non-structured semantics in a non-LLM student trained from one recorded trace. A frozen encoder maps each teacher output to a 1024-d vector; the student sees typed stage-tagged vectors with stage-specific visibility, is jointly supervised, and trains with scheduled self-history. One TwinMarket trace yields a 13.2M-parameter deterministic student that trains in 1,658 seconds on one 8-GB GPU and runs with zero teacher or decoder calls and no text generation (0.14 ms per decision). Its analysis stays close to the teacher (cosine 0.943), and swapping semantic inputs between agents moves 64.7% of decisions against 12.8% for a matched donor, so the channel is preserved and live. We use the surrogate to study what the transfer carries. It reaches 0.8347 balanced accuracy on the teacher-forced replay and 0.7783 [0.766,0.791] on the deployment decoder; the five-seed gain over a no-semantic retrain is +2.2 [1.21,3.14]. Against the teacher's own re-sampling level, round-one R is 97.1% [95.8,98.4] and 92.3% [89.0,95.4]; R is a diagnostic, not an accuracy. A five-seed content-by-schedule study isolates the gain: scheduled self-history carries it (+2.2 [1.21,3.14]); shuffled and constant content controls reproduce it, while content matters teacher-forced. The design rule: invest in the deployment schedule, let content earn its place at the teacher-forced operating point. A 20-seed, 200,000-decision sweep takes 12 minutes with zero LLM calls, versus three hours for the teacher. The paper is a method-and-case-study contribution on one simulator and trace.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces staged semantic distillation to train a 13.2M-parameter non-LLM surrogate from a single TwinMarket LLM-agent trace, running at 0.14 ms per decision with zero LLM calls while preserving semantic sensitivity.
AI.motivation: Staged LLM-agent market simulators are expensive (203,100 LLM calls for one 102-day, 200-agent run), and conventional low-compute distillation discards free-form intermediate semantic state.
AI.method: A frozen encoder maps teacher outputs to 1024-d vectors, and a jointly supervised deterministic student sees typed stage-tagged vectors with stage-specific visibility and trains with scheduled self-history.
AI.result: Trained in 1,658 seconds on one 8-GB GPU, the 13.2M-parameter student achieves 0.943 cosine similarity to teacher analysis, 0.8347 teacher-forced balanced accuracy, and 0.7783 deployment balanced accuracy (+2.2 over no-semantic retrain), while swapping semantic inputs moves 64.7% of decisions vs. 12.8% for a matched donor; a 20-seed, 200,000-decision sweep takes 12 minutes vs. three hours for the teacher.
AI.conclusion: Staged semantic distillation preserves live semantic channels in a fast non-LLM surrogate, with scheduled self-history driving deployment gains and semantic content contributing at the teacher-forced operating point.

title: Macro Control and Capability Evaluation of Black-Box World Models: A Two-Regime Framework for LLM-Agent Markets
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents can be organized into multi-agent markets that act as world models, mapping macro information to emergent macro dynamics while the evaluator observes only macro inputs and outputs. This paper separates a model's capability into two stages that a single aggregate score cannot separate: information simulation, from macro information to micro behavior, and macro emergence, from micro behavior to the macro outcome. We introduce a soft macro-control method that announces a public reference path day by day without touching individual decisions, orders, or matching, and a two-regime evaluation framework that measures both stages from macro observations alone. In the reference-only regime the symmetric true and flipped references share a common level R, which measures realization under the announced reference, while their paired gap B measures structural bias; in the information-injection regime external information dilutes the reference, so only the true-flipped gap Delta remains interpretable. On five single-index LLM-agent markets, announcing a target path shifts the realized path toward the announced target on both announced references under both information conditions. Relative to the no-reference path, the tracking score is higher by 0.306 and 0.415 without news and by 0.183 and 0.329 with news; within the stock/cash scan structural bias is lowest at 70/30 (B=0.042); realization peaks at a 3:7 technical share (R=0.894 versus 0.358 for technical-only); and Delta is 0.0341 with fundamental data and 0.0487 with news. Both stages use the same two observable scores, each read in the regime where it is interpretable.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a soft macro-control method and a two-regime evaluation framework that separates information simulation from macro emergence in black-box LLM-agent market world models using only macro observations.
AI.motivation: Aggregate macro scores cannot distinguish whether an LLM-agent market fails at mapping macro information to micro behavior (information simulation) or at aggregating micro behavior into macro outcomes (macro emergence).
AI.method: The authors announce a public reference path day by day without altering individual agent decisions, and evaluate markets across a reference-only regime (measuring realization R and structural bias B from symmetric true/flipped references) and an information-injection regime (measuring the true-flipped gap Delta).
AI.result: Across five single-index LLM-agent markets, announcing a target shifts realized paths toward it (+0.306 and +0.415 tracking score without news; +0.183 and +0.329 with news), structural bias is lowest at a 70/30 stock/cash split (B=0.042), realization peaks at a 3:7 technical share (R=0.894 vs. 0.358 technical-only), and Delta is 0.0341 with fundamental data and 0.0487 with news.
AI.conclusion: The two-regime framework isolates information simulation and macro emergence capabilities in black-box multi-agent world models using only macro-level inputs and outputs.

title: Objectify, Don't Delete: Complaint-Derived Evaluation of Ambient Clinical Notes
comment: Accepted at the Third Workshop on GenAI for Health (GenAI4Health), NeurIPS 2026 (non-archival). 16 pages, 5 figures, 11 tables. Code and data: this https URL
summary: Evaluating the quality of AI-generated clinical notes is hard: standard metrics like ROUGE measure lexical similarity to reference notes, while expert checklists encode what committees believe matters. Neither captures what clinicians actually complain about. Recent work has shown that evaluation criteria can be mined from user feedback and filtered to criteria that LLM judges can reliably enforce. We argue that this is where much of the value is lost. The criteria that fail enforceability are disproportionately the ones clinicians raise most often, because high-frequency complaints are stated as several questions glued together. No yes/no judgment can grade such composites as posed. We introduce an objectification step that rewrites such criteria into sets of scoped, determinate decisions. We demonstrate the approach through an evaluation pipeline that mines criteria from complaints, objectifies them, and deploys LLM judges against both planted defects and production notes. Across eleven defects planted into ACI-bench reference notes, objectified judges localize violations with median recall of 0.95, while reference metrics change by at most 0.037. Given the complaint as one broad question, the same judges still find every planted defect, but they also flag 70% of the unperturbed reference notes; one section-pair question per call raises Youden's J from 0.30 to 0.72 (by 0.19 to 0.26 with prompt effort matched). We release ACI-Defect, a perturbation benchmark; clinician-reviewed instance-level labels showing quality gaps in the ACI-bench gold standard (32 of 40 notes contain hallucinations; 40 of 40 omit discussed facts); and grounding-judge verdicts. On 1,446 production notes, mean instance-rate burden falls at every clinician-rating step (rho=-0.15), a small association. Defect counts have to be kept per span rather than collapsed into one pass/fail bit per note.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces an objectification step that rewrites composite clinician complaints into scoped, determinate yes/no LLM-judge criteria for evaluating ambient clinical notes, raising Youden's J from 0.30 to 0.72.
AI.motivation: Lexical metrics like ROUGE and committee checklists miss what clinicians actually complain about, and filtering mined criteria by LLM-judge enforceability discards high-frequency complaints because they bundle multiple questions together.
AI.method: The authors mine criteria from clinician complaints, objectify composite complaints into scoped, determinate decisions, deploy LLM judges on planted defects and 1,446 production notes, and release the ACI-Defect benchmark and clinician-reviewed ACI-bench labels.
AI.result: Across eleven planted defects in ACI-bench, objectified judges localize violations with 0.95 median recall (while reference metrics shift by at most 0.037), single section-pair questions raise Youden's J from 0.30 to 0.72, 32 of 40 ACI-bench gold notes contain hallucinations and 40 of 40 omit discussed facts, and on 1,446 production notes mean instance-rate burden correlates negatively with clinician ratings (rho=-0.15).
AI.conclusion: Objectifying composite complaints into per-span determinate checks rather than discarding them or collapsing notes to pass/fail enables reliable, clinically grounded evaluation of ambient clinical notes.

title: Who Writes the Codebook? An Eight-Step Framework for Auditing LLM-Generated Category Systems
summary: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly create the categories through which qualitative evidence is interpreted. Existing coding benchmarks often hold these categories fixed. We propose the Qualitative Variance Audit Framework, an eight-step method that compares codebook creation, repeated application and code distributions under controlled inputs. It combines model-owned and shared-reference codebooks to distinguish variation in the overall pipeline from application differences within a common category system. An application to 668 organisational interviews, 13,166 text units and eight models from five vendors yields 48 codebooks and 270 coding runs. Models create markedly different category structures; mean within-model reliability ranges from .76 to .92, whereas between-model agreement on the shared codebook is about .69. The framework complements LLM-assisted grounded theory by exposing model dependencies before substantive interpretation. It assesses reliability and representational consequences, not interpretive validity or the quality of resulting theory.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes the Qualitative Variance Audit Framework, an eight-step method for auditing how different LLMs construct and apply category systems in qualitative coding, revealing substantial cross-model divergence on 668 organizational interviews.
AI.motivation: LLMs increasingly generate the codebooks used to interpret qualitative data, yet existing coding benchmarks hold categories fixed and overlook model-dependent variation in category creation.
AI.method: The eight-step framework combines model-owned and shared-reference codebooks to separate pipeline-level variation from application differences, applied across 668 organizational interviews (13,166 text units) and eight models from five vendors (48 codebooks, 270 coding runs).
AI.result: Models construct markedly different category structures; mean within-model reliability ranges from 0.76 to 0.92, whereas between-model agreement on a shared codebook drops to about 0.69.
AI.conclusion: The framework complements LLM-assisted grounded theory by exposing model dependencies in codebook creation and application before substantive qualitative interpretation.

title: Can AI Judge You? An Empirical Audit of Deployment Readiness in LLM-assisted Hiring Systems
summary: Delegating resume screening to large language models (LLMs) requires organizations to establish whether they can distinguish candidates by relevant qualifications while allowing only authorized users to change screening rules or approve exceptions. To this end, we develop a system architecture that separates candidate evidence, evaluation, permission controls, and assessment record, and empirically examine two complementary dimensions of its deployment readiness. First, we assess its operational readiness on four LLMs using a controlled experiment on 210 resumes across 14 job roles and six decision interfaces. Second, we assess its compliance readiness by testing how it handles unauthorized user requests and instructions embedded in resumes. We find that operational performance depends on the choice of evaluation interface: scalar scores generally distinguish qualification changes better than simple pass/fail judgments, while comparative judgments are sensitive to presentation order. Explicit permission rules and separation of resume content from instructions reduce unauthorized compliance, to a varying degree of effectiveness across LLMs and usage contexts. Finally, we find that LLM evaluators often diverge between their decisions and offered justifications. Going beyond simply evaluating LLMs for hiring tasks, our framework supports an audit of a fully configured resume evaluation system to enable its deployment decision.

AI.tldr: This paper audits operational and compliance readiness of LLM-assisted resume screening systems using a separated architecture across four LLMs, 210 resumes, and 14 job roles, finding strong sensitivity to evaluation interfaces and divergence between decisions and justifications.
AI.motivation: Organizations delegating resume screening to LLMs must verify both that models reliably distinguish candidate qualifications and that only authorized users can alter rules or approve exceptions.
AI.method: The authors build an architecture separating candidate evidence, evaluation, permission controls, and assessment records, testing operational readiness across four LLMs, 210 resumes, 14 roles, and six decision interfaces, and compliance readiness against unauthorized requests and prompt injections embedded in resumes.
AI.result: Scalar scores distinguish qualification changes better than pass/fail judgments, comparative judgments depend on presentation order, explicit permission rules and content-instruction separation reduce unauthorized compliance to varying degrees across LLMs, and LLM evaluators frequently diverge between their decisions and offered justifications.
AI.conclusion: Auditing a fully configured hiring system across both operational interfaces and permission boundaries is necessary before deployment, beyond evaluating raw LLM accuracy alone.

title: HEAMS: Holistic Evaluation of Agent Memory Systems
comment: 69 pages (26 main text), 6 figures, 29 tables. Code: this https URL
summary: Memory systems allow AI agents to persist information across interactions, making them more personalized and more capable on long-horizon tasks. This persistence introduces new risks: stored information can be disclosed in inappropriate contexts, resist correction or deletion, be retained beyond what users desire, or be poisoned to influence later agent behaviour. Yet memory systems are typically evaluated on task performance and efficiency alone. We argue that a memory system should instead be understood as the custodian of its user's persistent information, with responsibilities that extend beyond helping an agent complete its tasks, and that it should be evaluated holistically against all such responsibilities. We present Holistic Evaluation of Agent Memory Systems (HEAMS), an open-source framework for evaluating agent memory systems in this way. First, we state the responsibilities of agent memory systems as explicit behavioural desiderata spanning performance, efficiency, security, privacy, and user sovereignty. Second, we assemble a benchmark suite that covers these desiderata and acknowledge the gaps that remain. Third, we develop MilaMem, a prototype memory system, and a governance layer that can wrap any memory system, enabling controlled study of memory system design choices. Fourth, we compare memory systems across the full HEAMS benchmark suite. We find that no memory system leads every performance benchmark, and strong performance scores may coexist with poor privacy, user-sovereignty, and security scores. Governance strongly influences results: recall policies can reduce inappropriate disclosure at a cost in helpfulness, while both recall and retention policies improve poisoning resistance. Performance and efficiency benchmarks alone therefore cannot reveal how well a memory system meets its responsibilities. Code: this https URL

AI.tldr: This paper presents HEAMS, an open-source holistic evaluation framework for agent memory systems spanning performance, efficiency, security, privacy, and user sovereignty, showing that high task performance often coexists with poor privacy and security.
AI.motivation: Agent memory systems are typically evaluated only on task performance and efficiency, ignoring their custodial responsibilities regarding inappropriate disclosure, user deletion/correction, retention limits, and memory poisoning.
AI.method: The authors define behavioural desiderata across five dimensions, assemble a benchmark suite, build MilaMem (a prototype memory system) and a wrap-around governance layer, and evaluate memory systems across the full HEAMS suite.
AI.result: No single memory system leads every performance benchmark, strong performance scores frequently coexist with poor privacy, user-sovereignty, and security scores, and governance policies strongly shape outcomes: recall policies cut inappropriate disclosure at some cost to helpfulness, while recall and retention policies both improve poisoning resistance.
AI.conclusion: Performance and efficiency benchmarks alone are insufficient to evaluate agent memory systems; holistic evaluation with explicit governance controls is required to assess custodial responsibilities.

title: Trait Collapse in Text-to-Image Generation: Evaluating and Mitigating Personality Inconsistency in Visual Storytelling
comment: EMNLP 2026 Main Conference Paper. 26 pages, 5 figures
summary: In visual storytelling, a believable character must not only look consistent across scenes but also \textit{behave} in ways that reflect their personality. Current text-to-image (T2I) models preserve visual appearance effectively, yet consistently fail to maintain personality-relevant behavior---a failure we term \textit{trait collapse}.
