Large Language Models and Vision Language Models have demonstrated strong capabilities in tasks such as image interpretation, report generation, and question answering by effectively learning from multimodal data-images paired with associated text often with minimal supervision. In the healthcare domain, this ability to align visual and textual information reduces the reliance on extensive manual annotations, as models can leverage existing clinical reports and imaging data to learn meaningful representations. This integration holds promise for improving diagnostic support, treatment planning, and overall patient care, even in data constrained settings. In this review, we provide a definitive taxonomy of the medical VLM landscape, tracing the evolution from early Contrastive Alignment and Generative MLLMs to the cutting edge frontiers of Dense Pixel Grounding, Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE), and Reasoning Incentivized (RL) architectures. We critically examine the "medical bottleneck" identifying the persistent challenges of data scarcity, the "hallucination" risks in generative diagnostics, the computational strain of 3D volumetric processing, and the lack of standardized, clinically grounded evaluation metrics.

AI.tldr: This review surveys Vision-Language Foundation Models in healthcare, providing a taxonomy from early contrastive and generative MLLMs to recent dense pixel grounding, sparse MoE, and RL-based reasoning architectures, while examining key clinical bottlenecks.
AI.motivation: Although multimodal foundation models reduce reliance on manual annotations by aligning clinical reports and medical images, their real-world medical deployment faces persistent technical and clinical challenges.
AI.method: The authors present a taxonomy tracing the evolution of medical VLMs across Contrastive Alignment, Generative MLLMs, Dense Pixel Grounding, Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE), and Reasoning Incentivized (RL) architectures, and critically analyze the "medical bottleneck."
AI.result: The review identifies four core bottlenecks: data scarcity, hallucination risks in generative diagnostics, computational strain of 3D volumetric processing, and the lack of standardized, clinically grounded evaluation metrics.
AI.conclusion: Addressing data, hallucination, 3D computation, and clinical evaluation challenges is essential for translating medical vision-language foundation models into safe and effective patient care.

title: CreaTrace: Video Creative Plagiarism Detection and Evidence Tracing
summary: Video creative plagiarism refers to the unauthorized reproduction of creative ideas across videos despite substantial differences in visual appearance, posing a new challenge to video copyright protection. However, existing video copy detection methods primarily focus on visual content similarity, struggling to capture abstract creative that are entangled with specific visual realizations. To address this issue, we introduce a novel task, named Video Creative Plagiarism Detection (VCPD), and propose an iterative creative evidence tracing framework, termed CreaTrace, to verify creative similarity and accurately localize the corresponding evidence segments. Specifically, we design a Multimodal Semantic Event Segmentation strategy to divide similar long videos into coherent narrative events, facilitating event-level dataset construction and retrieving similar segments. Based on these events, CreaTrace employs Coarse Creative Matching to identify candidate event pairs through narrative semantics and camera language. Then CreaTrace presents Creative Decoupling to disentangle abstract creative patterns from specific visual realizations. Meanwhile, Creative Swap Contrastive Learning is devised to enhance creative consistency through cross-realization feature swapping. Benefiting from the above designs, our CreaTrace enables accurate creative similarity detection and temporal localization, while providing interpretable evidence report. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of CreaTrace across diverse creative plagiarism scenarios.

AI.tldr: The paper defines Video Creative Plagiarism Detection (VCPD) and proposes CreaTrace, an iterative evidence tracing framework that disentangles abstract creative patterns from visual realizations to detect and localize creative plagiarism.
AI.motivation: Existing video copy detection methods focus on visual content similarity and struggle to capture abstract creative ideas reproduced across videos with substantially different visual appearances.
AI.method: CreaTrace uses Multimodal Semantic Event Segmentation to split long videos into narrative events, Coarse Creative Matching using narrative semantics and camera language, Creative Decoupling to separate abstract creative patterns from visual realizations, and Creative Swap Contrastive Learning to enhance creative consistency via cross-realization feature swapping.
AI.result: Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of CreaTrace across diverse creative plagiarism scenarios, enabling accurate creative similarity detection, temporal localization, and interpretable evidence reports.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling abstract creative structure from specific visual realizations provides an effective foundation for detecting and tracing creative plagiarism in videos.

title: Morphology-Decoupled Segmentation for Multiple Tunnel Defects Under Complex Environments
summary: Automated tunnel-lining inspection must segment different defect geometries: cracks are thin, elongated, and connectivity-sensitive, whereas leakage, lining falling off, and segment damage are spatially extensive and context-dependent. Existing approaches generally apply a common decoder across defect classes or introduce boundary, topology, and directional mechanisms as isolated enhancements. This paper introduces Morphology-Decoupled Segmentation (MDS), in which defect morphology becomes the organising principle for feature routing, decoding, and interaction. A supervised routing module partitions multiscale encoder features into complementary linear and areal streams. The linear stream employs Deformable Strip Attention with image-conditioned direction hypotheses to preserve crack continuity without assuming fixed horizontal or vertical orientations, while the areal stream combines Pyramid Pooling with feature-pyramid fusion to capture diffuse boundaries and regional context. The representations are coupled through gated cross-morphology attention, allowing complementary information exchange while retaining morphology-specific features. A resolution-adaptive tiling and probability-blending pipeline preserves fine defects across variable-resolution imagery. MDS achieves 81.17% mIoU on the internal validation set and improves foreground image-level recognition over a backbone-matched SegDINO model, primarily for areal defects. Controlled ablations demonstrate the complementary contributions of routing supervision and cross-stream interaction while revealing a trade-off between areal-class performance and crack specialisation. The submitted model achieved 67.55% mIoU on an organiser-controlled hidden test, and the team placed second. Selective dynamic INT8 quantisation reduced model storage by 2.83 times with negligible accuracy loss.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Morphology-Decoupled Segmentation (MDS) for tunnel-lining inspection, which routes features into specialized linear and areal streams and achieves 81.17% mIoU on internal validation and second place (67.55% mIoU) on a hidden competition test.
AI.motivation: Tunnel-lining defects have distinct geometries, such as thin, connectivity-sensitive cracks versus spatially extensive areal defects like leakage or lining falling off, which existing methods handle poorly using a common decoder or isolated enhancements.
AI.method: MDS uses a supervised routing module to split multiscale encoder features into a linear stream (Deformable Strip Attention with image-conditioned direction hypotheses) and an areal stream (Pyramid Pooling with feature-pyramid fusion), coupled via gated cross-morphology attention and paired with resolution-adaptive tiling and probability blending.
AI.result: MDS achieves 81.17% mIoU on the internal validation set, outperforms a backbone-matched SegDINO model in foreground image-level recognition, reaches 67.55% mIoU to place second on an organiser-controlled hidden test, and retains accuracy with 2.83x storage reduction under selective dynamic INT8 quantisation.
AI.conclusion: Organizing feature routing, decoding, and cross-stream interaction around defect morphology improves multi-defect tunnel inspection while remaining amenable to compact quantized deployment.

title: KneeFS-Net: A Lightweight Deep Learning Model for Knee Osteoarthritis Severity Assessment with Cross-Domain External Validation
summary: Knee osteoarthritis (OA) grading from radiographs using the Kellgren-Lawrence (KL) scale requires expertise that may be scarce. We present KneeFS-Net, a lightweight ordinal grader (0.8 million parameters; 0.33 GFLOPs) combining spatial, Fourier and state-space features with landmark-guided attention. On the Osteoarthritis Initiative (OAI) test set, KneeFS-Net achieved a quadratic weighted kappa (QWK) of 0.863, mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.325 and 97.2% within-one-grade accuracy, comparable to models with 9-35-fold more parameters. We evaluated cross-population generalization on two Bangladeshi cohorts, a single-center hospital cohort and a multi-center teleradiology cohort. Without further training or adaptation, the OAI-trained model achieved QWK 0.803, MAE 0.339 and 98.2% within-one-grade accuracy on its hospital cohort, declining to QWK 0.656 and MAE 0.522 on multi-center teleradiology images. Self-supervised pretraining on 6,092 unlabeled radiographs followed by joint fine-tuning achieved QWK 0.823, MAE 0.329 and 99.7% within-one-grade accuracy in cross-validation. These findings demonstrate accurate, efficient KL grading and potential adaptation to new populations with limited annotation.

AI.tldr: The authors present KneeFS-Net, a lightweight 0.8M-parameter model for knee osteoarthritis Kellgren-Lawrence grading that matches much larger models on OAI (QWK 0.863) and adapts effectively to external Bangladeshi cohorts.
AI.motivation: Automated Kellgren-Lawrence (KL) grading of knee radiographs is needed where clinical expertise is scarce, but existing models are often heavy and their cross-population generalization across diverse clinical settings is limited.
AI.method: KneeFS-Net (0.8M parameters, 0.33 GFLOPs) combines spatial, Fourier, and state-space features with landmark-guided attention, and is further adapted to external cohorts via self-supervised pretraining on 6,092 unlabeled radiographs followed by joint fine-tuning.
AI.result: On the OAI test set, KneeFS-Net achieves a QWK of 0.863, MAE of 0.325, and 97.2% within-one-grade accuracy, comparable to models with 9-35x more parameters; without adaptation on two Bangladeshi cohorts, it achieves QWK 0.803 (hospital) and 0.656 (multi-center teleradiology), which improves to QWK 0.823, MAE 0.329, and 99.7% within-one-grade accuracy after self-supervised pretraining and joint fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: KneeFS-Net demonstrates that compact architectures combined with self-supervised pretraining can deliver accurate, efficient knee OA grading and adapt to new populations with limited annotations.

title: What Matters for Cross-Modal Alignment
summary: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis posits that models trained on different modalities converge toward a shared representation. Related work aligns frozen image and text encoders on natural images without paired data. We test zero-pair alignment on five datasets across four modalities: natural images, environmental audio, chest radiographs, and 3D computed tomography (CT). It succeeds only on COCO and fails on the other four. We analyze the failures and find that alignment must first locate the subspace where the modalities co-vary and then orient the mapping within it. Consistent with previous studies, medical imaging is the hardest case: its shared subspace carries the smallest fraction of the variance. When this fraction is small, alignment needs image-text pairs, and random-matrix theory predicts how many pairs are needed. These findings motivate LightAlign: a few pairs let a ridge regression between two frozen encoders locate and orient the mapping simultaneously, and a classifier fitted only on report text then predicts findings from the mapped images. On 3D CT, LightAlign surpasses models trained end to end on image-report pairs without finding-level labels: with only 200 pairs, LightAlign outperforms CT-CLIP on CT-RATE (0.754 vs. 0.733 AUROC), and with only 100 CT-RATE pairs, it does so on RAD-ChestCT, an out-of-distribution dataset from a different hospital. On CheXpert, it reaches 0.862 mean AUROC with only about 5% as many pairs as models trained on MIMIC-CXR.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates when zero-pair cross-modal alignment fails across five datasets and four modalities, and introduces LightAlign, a few-pair ridge regression method that outperforms end-to-end CT-CLIP on 3D CT with only 100-200 pairs.
AI.motivation: While zero-pair alignment works on natural images (COCO), it fails on other modalities such as audio, chest radiographs, and 3D CT, and the underlying geometric reasons and pair requirements are poorly understood.
AI.method: The authors show theoretically and empirically that alignment must first locate the shared co-varying subspace and then orient the mapping within it; motivated by this, LightAlign fits a ridge regression between two frozen encoders using a few image-text pairs and trains a classifier solely on report text to predict findings from mapped images.
AI.result: Zero-pair alignment succeeds only on COCO and fails on the other four datasets; with only 200 pairs on 3D CT, LightAlign outperforms end-to-end CT-CLIP on CT-RATE (0.754 vs. 0.733 AUROC), outperforms it on out-of-distribution RAD-ChestCT with 100 pairs, and reaches 0.862 mean AUROC on CheXpert using roughly 5% as many pairs as MIMIC-CXR models.
AI.conclusion: When the shared cross-modal subspace carries a small fraction of variance, as in medical imaging, a few paired examples suffice for a simple ridge regression to outperform large-scale end-to-end training.

title: Glance, then Select: Evidence-Tempered Visual Token Selection for Extremely Compressed Multimodal LLMs
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) encode a high-resolution image into thousands of visual tokens, which dominate the cost of the prefill stage. Visual token reduction removes most of these tokens, but two problems remain at extreme budgets. The vision encoder still processes every patch of the image, and the few surviving tokens often miss the small regions that hold the answer. In this paper, we propose Glance-ETD, a two-stage token reduction framework guided by a lightweight question-conditioned scorer. In the first stage, a glance encoder views the image at low resolution and re-encodes only the question-relevant regions at native resolution. In the second stage, Evidence-Tempered Diversity (ETD) selects the final tokens by combining diversity with the evidence predicted by the scorer, so that the kept tokens cover the scene and retain the answer. A single-rollout self-distillation recipe trains the MLLM with the glance encoder. With only 5% of the visual tokens, Glance-ETD retains 91.6% of the full-token performance of Qwen3.5-4B across fourteen benchmarks and outperforms the strongest prior method, LT-OPD, by 17.3 points and the same training recipe with DivPrune by 6.0. It also speeds up the time to first token on 4K images by 3.1x and generalizes to three other MLLMs and to high-resolution document benchmarks, with the largest gains on text-rich tasks.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Glance-ETD, a two-stage visual token reduction framework for MLLMs that retains 91.6% of Qwen3.5-4B's full-token performance across 14 benchmarks using only 5% of visual tokens while speeding up 4K TTFT by 3.1x.
AI.motivation: Existing visual token reduction methods still require the vision encoder to process every high-resolution patch and often discard small, answer-relevant regions at extreme token budgets.
AI.method: Glance-ETD uses a lightweight question-conditioned scorer: Stage 1 employs a glance encoder at low resolution to re-encode only question-relevant regions at native resolution, Stage 2 applies Evidence-Tempered Diversity (ETD) to balance scene coverage and evidence retention, and the MLLM is trained via single-rollout self-distillation.
AI.result: With 5% of visual tokens, Glance-ETD retains 91.6% of Qwen3.5-4B full-token performance across 14 benchmarks, outperforming LT-OPD by 17.3 points and DivPrune by 6.0 points, speeds up time to first token on 4K images by 3.1x, and generalizes to three other MLLMs and high-resolution document benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Combining question-conditioned region re-encoding with evidence-tempered diversity selection enables extreme visual token compression with minimal accuracy loss and substantial prefill speedups.

title: ReactBench-AD: Do Driving VLAs and World-Action Models React to Imminent Hazards in Their Path?
summary: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) and World-Action Models (WAMs) have emerged in autonomous driving with the promise of strong generalization to long-tail scenarios. Although these models achieve state-of-the-art results on autonomous driving benchmarks, most existing benchmarks are dominated by nominal scenarios and therefore cannot test this promise. To test one such long-tail capability that is critical for safety, we introduce ReactBench-AD, a benchmark that measures how driving models react to objects that appear in the ego vehicle's path. Built on real NAVSIM and PhysicalAI-Autonomous-Vehicles scenes, ReactBench-AD composites a crossing pedestrian, a standing pedestrian, or a stationary car consistently across all camera views and history frames. Each edited scene thus forms an exact, pixel-level counterfactual pair with its original, which allows us to isolate the causal effect of the inserted object on the predicted trajectory. Evaluating four VLAs and two WAMs, we find that they react weakly, often barely at all. Finally, we test how easily one of the evaluated VLAs, ReCogDrive, can be taught to brake hard for imminent hazards: a short fine-tuning stage on edited scenes substantially improves its reactions, with the learned behavior generalizing to unseen objects and fully real scenes, at minimal cost to nominal driving. These results call into question the out-of-the-box long-tail capabilities of these models, but suggest that they can be a strong foundation for acquiring them with little additional training, highlighting the value of real or synthetic data that demonstrates the long-tail behaviors nominal datasets rarely contain. Code and data will be made publicly available.

AI.tldr: The authors introduce ReactBench-AD, a counterfactual benchmark for testing whether driving VLAs and World-Action Models react to imminent hazards, finding that six evaluated models barely react out of the box but can be quickly fine-tuned to brake.
AI.motivation: Existing autonomous driving benchmarks are dominated by nominal scenarios and fail to evaluate whether Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) and World-Action Models (WAMs) generalize to safety-critical long-tail hazards.
AI.method: Built on real NAVSIM and PhysicalAI-Autonomous-Vehicles scenes, ReactBench-AD composites a crossing pedestrian, standing pedestrian, or stationary car consistently across all camera views and history frames to form pixel-level counterfactual pairs, and tests four VLAs, two WAMs, and short fine-tuning of ReCogDrive on edited scenes.
AI.result: Evaluated VLAs and WAMs react weakly or barely at all to inserted hazards; however, a short fine-tuning stage on edited scenes substantially improves ReCogDrive's braking reactions and generalizes to unseen objects and real scenes at minimal cost to nominal driving.
AI.conclusion: Current driving VLAs and WAMs lack reliable out-of-the-box long-tail hazard reactions, but they provide a strong foundation that can acquire safety-critical behaviors with targeted synthetic or real counterexamples.

title: FastGRN: Few-Step Generative Refinement Networks
summary: Generative Refinement Networks (GRN) generate an image by repeatedly re-predicting and refining every token of a discrete latent. They reach high fidelity, but need dozens of Markov steps. We therefore train few-step GRNs on the distribution of their own samples. We use its own uniform-state corruption to perform distribution matching on discrete tokens, which lets a discrete generator learn by backpropagation, and we pair noise with samples in the manner of rectified flow. We find that the steps of a few-step GRN do not carry the same amount of information or the same repair load. We therefore exploit its discrete refinement during training and build few-step GRNs in three parts. Oversampling samples the student with more steps than it was trained for and refines its judge on these samples. Non-uniform sampling trains only the last step and hands it most of the information at sampling time. Refinement confidence keeping holds on to the tokens the student is already sure of. We train a fast class-conditional generator on ImageNet 256 and, with the same method, a 2B text-to-image model. On ImageNet 256, the 3-step FastGRN beats the FID of GRN. On a 2B binary-token text-to-image GRN, a 4-step student also nearly matches the GenEval of GRN-T2I 2B.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes FastGRN, a few-step distillation method for Generative Refinement Networks (GRNs) that matches or beats many-step GRNs on ImageNet 256 in 3 steps and on 2B text-to-image generation in 4 steps.
AI.motivation: Generative Refinement Networks achieve high image fidelity by iteratively re-predicting discrete latent tokens, but they require dozens of Markov steps at inference time.
AI.method: FastGRN trains few-step students via distribution matching on discrete tokens using uniform-state corruption and rectified-flow-style noise-sample pairing, combined with oversampling, non-uniform sampling that trains only the last step, and refinement confidence keeping to preserve already-confident tokens.
AI.result: On ImageNet 256, a 3-step FastGRN beats the FID of the full GRN, and on a 2B binary-token text-to-image model, a 4-step FastGRN student nearly matches the GenEval score of GRN-T2I 2B.
AI.conclusion: Exploiting the asymmetric repair load across discrete refinement steps enables GRNs to be distilled into high-fidelity 3- to 4-step generators.

title: acuSimNet: Multi-View Self-Occlusion-Awared Visibility Learning for Cranio-Cervical Acupuncture Points
summary: The localization of acupuncture points (acupoints) in Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) presents unique challenges since they are defined by abstract principles rather than distinct anatomical landmarks. Existing approaches are typically constrained to single view or rely on indirect calculations of relative positions with respect to other landmarks, thereby overlooking human anatomical variations. Furthermore, acupoint visibility assessment, which determins whether points are occluded by human itself, hair, clothing, or other objects, has received limited attention in practical applications. Acupoint localization itself does not require 3D reconstruction, but inferring their occlusion relationships with anatomical surfaces does, which adds computational cost and limits real-time inference. In this work, we introduce acuSimNet, an efficient hierarchical multi-task learning architecture for multi-view, self-occlusion-aware visibility prediction of acupoints, achieving 99.97% accuracy on the validation set. Our approach also addresses the challenges of high-dimensional classification (174 acupoints in cervicocranial region), negative convergence issues for visible acupoints, and inter-task scheduling optimization, resulting in substantially accelerated convergence. We improved the training efficiency from the exisiting methods of 3000 epochs to achieve 99% validation accuracy, to our optimized framework achieving 90% accuracy in 39 epochs and 99% accuracy in 86 epochs. This architecture overcomes the limitations of existing methods, could enable practical applications in acupoints detection and visualization, advancing the automation of TCM.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces acuSimNet, a hierarchical multi-task learning architecture for multi-view, self-occlusion-aware visibility prediction of 174 cranio-cervical acupuncture points, achieving 99.97% validation accuracy with vastly faster convergence.
AI.motivation: Acupoint localization in Traditional Chinese Medicine is challenged by abstract anatomical definitions, single-view constraints, and the high computational cost of 3D reconstruction needed to infer self-occlusion from hair, clothing, or body surfaces.
AI.method: acuSimNet uses an efficient hierarchical multi-task architecture to predict multi-view self-occlusion visibility across 174 cervicocranial acupoints, addressing high-dimensional classification, negative convergence for visible points, and inter-task scheduling optimization.
AI.result: acuSimNet achieves 99.97% validation accuracy and reaches 90% accuracy in 39 epochs and 99% in 86 epochs, compared to 3,000 epochs required by existing methods to reach 99% accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Hierarchical multi-task visibility learning eliminates expensive 3D reconstruction while dramatically accelerating convergence, enabling practical real-time acupoint detection and visualization.

title: MARLIN: Multiscale And Directional Sparse Representation Learning for Imbalanced SAR Ship Classification
summary: Despite recent progress in SAR maritime monitoring, ship classification remains challenging due to limited labeled data, class imbalance, large intra-class variability, fine-grained inter-class similarity, and variations in target scale, orientation, and backscattering structure. To address these challenges, this paper proposes MARLIN, a class-frequency-aware framework with directional sparse and hierarchical multi-scale feature extraction for ship type classification in SAR images. The proposed architecture first constructs two complementary representations of each input image, where each views are processed by parallel encoder branches. Each branch begins with a directional sparse convolutional stem designed to capture elongated and orientation-dependent ship scattering patterns, followed by customized hierarchical multiscale feature extraction blocks. To improve learning under imbalanced class distributions, we introduce a class-frequency aware objective. The proposed objective combines margin-based classification with class-frequency-weighted prototype compactness and class-pair frequency weighted margin separation. This formulation shapes the embedding space by encouraging samples from the same class to form compact clusters while enforcing stronger separation for class pairs involving underrepresented ship categories. Extensive experiments on three complementary datasets demonstrate that in addition to being lightweight and parameter efficient, MARLIN improves both overall accuracy and class-balanced metrics, confirming its effectiveness for robust SAR ship-type classification under limited and imbalanced training conditions. The codes are available at this http URL.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes MARLIN, a lightweight dual-branch framework with directional sparse convolutions and a class-frequency-aware objective for imbalanced SAR ship classification, improving both overall and class-balanced accuracy across three datasets.
AI.motivation: SAR ship classification is hindered by limited labeled data, severe class imbalance, large intra-class variation, fine-grained inter-class similarity, and variations in target scale, orientation, and scattering structure.
AI.method: MARLIN constructs two complementary input views processed by parallel encoders with directional sparse convolutional stems and hierarchical multiscale blocks, trained with a class-frequency-aware objective combining margin-based classification, class-frequency-weighted prototype compactness, and class-pair frequency-weighted margin separation.
AI.result: Experiments on three complementary SAR datasets show that MARLIN is lightweight and parameter-efficient while improving both overall accuracy and class-balanced metrics under limited and imbalanced training data.
AI.conclusion: Combining directional sparse multiscale features with class-frequency-aware margin and prototype learning provides robust, efficient SAR ship-type classification under class imbalance.

title: SGIP: Learning Scene-Grounded Interaction Priors for Scene-Aware Human Motion Prediction
comment: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026. Project page: this https URL
summary: Human motion prediction (HMP) aims to forecast future movement from an observed motion sequence, and recent methods have incorporated 3D scene geometry and object semantics to improve long-term plausibility. However, the destination of future motion remains ambiguous in cluttered scenes: the same observed motion can lead to different interaction targets or navigation modes. Existing methods either handle this ambiguity implicitly or rely on auxiliary signals like gaze that are hard to obtain in practice. To address this, we propose SGIP, which explicitly predicts where in the scene future motion will be grounded across both objects and open navigation regions, and uses it to condition future trajectory and full-body pose prediction. This scene-grounded interaction prior is learned via intent distillation: at training time only, a teacher model scores candidate scene regions by combining an LLM prompted with a textual description of the person's intent with geometric motion-scene features. A student model learns to reproduce these scores from only the observed motion and 3D scene, making intent and LLM unnecessary at test time. Across multiple benchmark datasets, SGIP outperforms prior scene-aware baselines on both trajectory and pose accuracy in a realistic deployment setting where neither gaze nor intent is available at inference, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed framework. The project page is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes SGIP, a human motion prediction framework that distills scene-grounded interaction priors from an LLM-assisted teacher during training so that no intent or gaze is needed at inference, outperforming baselines on trajectory and pose accuracy.
AI.motivation: Predicting human motion in cluttered 3D scenes is ambiguous because identical observed motions can lead to different targets, and existing methods either model this implicitly or rely on hard-to-obtain auxiliary signals like gaze at test time.
AI.method: SGIP explicitly predicts where future motion will be grounded across objects and open navigation regions via intent distillation: a training-time teacher scores candidate regions using an LLM prompted with textual intent plus geometric features, and a student learns to reproduce these scores solely from observed motion and 3D scene geometry.
AI.result: Across multiple benchmark datasets in a realistic setting without gaze or intent at inference, SGIP outperforms prior scene-aware baselines on both trajectory and full-body pose accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Distilling LLM-guided scene-grounded interaction priors into a geometry-and-motion student resolves destination ambiguity in human motion prediction without requiring auxiliary inputs at deployment.

title: See the Lives of Stars in a Handful of Light
summary: Galaxies evolve over hundreds of millions of years, and no telescope has ever watched one move. Cosmological simulations make this evolution visible as a sequence of multi-view images, inviting the question of whether a galaxy can be recovered in four dimensions from its images. This setting defeats existing dynamic scene methods, since millions of stars span only a few pixels each, faint populations blend into diffuse light, and free deformations reproduce the images without obeying gravity. We present Cosmos4D, which rests on two components. Gravitational 4D Gaussian Splatting represents each star as a self-luminous Gaussian whose motion is integrated through a gravitational potential and a low-dimensional force field shared by all stars. Luminosity-stratified dynamics give bright stars individual orbits supervised across image scales and carry faint populations with a velocity field estimated from optical flow. We further build a 4D dataset of eight galaxies from four cosmological simulations, on which Cosmos4D outperforms dynamic Gaussian baselines in both photometric quality and physical accuracy. With these advancements, we glimpse eight hundred million years of a galaxy's life in ninety-six frames.

AI.tldr: The authors present Cosmos4D, a gravitational 4D Gaussian Splatting method with luminosity-stratified dynamics that reconstructs evolving galaxies from multi-view simulation images, outperforming dynamic Gaussian baselines on a new 8-galaxy dataset.
AI.motivation: Reconstructing 4D galaxy evolution from multi-view images defeats standard dynamic scene methods because millions of stars span only a few pixels, faint populations blend into diffuse light, and unconstrained deformations violate gravity.
AI.method: Cosmos4D models each star as a self-luminous Gaussian integrated through a gravitational potential and a shared low-dimensional force field, using luminosity-stratified dynamics that give bright stars individual multi-scale-supervised orbits while advecting faint populations with an optical-flow velocity field.
AI.result: On a newly constructed 4D dataset of eight galaxies from four cosmological simulations, Cosmos4D outperforms dynamic Gaussian baselines in both photometric quality and physical accuracy, capturing 800 million years of evolution in 96 frames.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating gravitational physics and luminosity-stratified dynamics into 4D Gaussian Splatting enables physically faithful 4D reconstruction of astronomical simulations from images alone.

title: Latent World Modeling for Point-Cloud Video Pretraining
summary: Masked modeling is the dominant self-supervised paradigm for point-cloud videos. However, it leaks the information it is meant to predict, whether it reconstructs masked points as in MAE-style methods or predicts their latent features. Because point-cloud tokens are anchored at points sampled from each frame, querying a target at its own position reveals where its geometry has moved, in reconstruction and latent prediction alike. For latent predictors, random spatio-temporal masks introduce a further shortcut, as visible frames on both sides of each target allow interpolation rather than forecasting. The pretext task thus reduces to completion. Once the target positions are withheld, a masked latent predictor performs only slightly better than copying the last frame. To remove this leakage, we propose PointWM, a latent world model that turns completion into forecasting by predicting the features and geometry of future frames from strictly earlier context. Each target is queried only with its last-seen position and timestamp, while a latent action learned without annotations is meant to capture the part of the future that the past leaves undetermined. On HOI4D action segmentation with a P4Transformer backbone, PointWM improves F1@50 over training from scratch by 24.9 offline and 29.1 under strictly causal inference. These results show the promise of latent world models as a leakage-free pretraining paradigm for point-cloud this http URL code is publicly available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies spatial and temporal information leakage in masked point-cloud video pretraining and proposes PointWM, a leakage-free latent world model that improves HOI4D action segmentation F1@50 by 24.9 offline and 29.1 causally over training from scratch.
AI.motivation: Existing masked modeling methods for point-cloud videos leak target geometry by querying tokens at their future positions and allow temporal interpolation shortcuts via random spatio-temporal masking, reducing the pretext task to completion.
AI.method: PointWM turns completion into forecasting by predicting future frame features and geometry strictly from earlier context, querying each target only with its last-seen position and timestamp while learning an annotation-free latent action to capture undetermined future variations.
AI.result: On HOI4D action segmentation with a P4Transformer backbone, PointWM improves F1@50 over training from scratch by 24.9 points offline and 29.1 points under strictly causal inference.
AI.conclusion: Removing spatio-temporal target leakage through causal latent world modeling establishes a stronger self-supervised pretraining paradigm for point-cloud videos.

title: Geo2Gcode: From 3D Geometry to CNC Programs through Structured Machining Primitives
summary: Turning a 3D shape into a Computer Numerical Control (CNC) program is still largely manual. For every part, a machinist chooses setups, tools, step-downs, and toolpath patterns. We present Geo2Gcode, which converts a target mesh directly into standard G-code through structured machining primitives. Each primitive couples an indexed machining direction, a closed per-view reconstruction of the target, and explicit tool-radius, layer-height, and clearing-pattern parameters, and compiles deterministically into layerwise toolpaths via signed-distance queries. Most of the fidelity comes from this compiler. A lightweight selector trained with a voxel stock simulator fills in primitive parameters without per-part manual settings, approaching the finest fixed setting at about a quarter of its toolpath length. In simulation on ABC parts, Geo2Gcode reaches roughing fidelity comparable to an expert-tuned commercial CAM setup with a moderately longer toolpath, and clearly improves on a default CAM configuration. Generated programs run in a commercial G-code simulator, and one part is machined on a physical CNC mill. These results demonstrate that roughing programs can be generated directly from geometry without per-part CAM tuning.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Geo2Gcode, which compiles 3D meshes directly into CNC G-code via structured machining primitives and a learned parameter selector, matching expert-tuned commercial CAM roughing fidelity on ABC parts and succeeding on a physical CNC mill.
AI.motivation: Converting 3D geometry into CNC machining programs remains largely manual, requiring machinists to select setups, tools, step-downs, and toolpath patterns for every individual part.
AI.method: Geo2Gcode represents operations as structured machining primitives pairing an indexed machining direction, a closed per-view target reconstruction, and explicit tool-radius, layer-height, and clearing-pattern parameters, compiling them deterministically via signed-distance queries while a lightweight selector trained with a voxel stock simulator predicts parameters.
AI.result: On ABC parts, Geo2Gcode approaches the finest fixed setting at about a quarter of its toolpath length, matches expert-tuned commercial CAM roughing fidelity (with a moderately longer toolpath), clearly outperforms default CAM, runs in a commercial G-code simulator, and successfully machines a part on a physical CNC mill.
AI.conclusion: Structured machining primitives paired with a learned parameter selector enable automated, per-part-tuning-free generation of valid CNC roughing programs directly from 3D geometry.

title: Trading Parameters for Accuracy in MambaVision for Chest Radiograph Classification
comment: 10 pages, 4 figures, 9 tables. Submitted to an IEEE journal
summary: MambaVision, a hybrid state-space and attention backbone, places most of its parameters in its widest, fourth stage. We quantified what that stage contributes to multi-label chest radiograph classification. The fourth stage was replaced with lighter single-scan state-space blocks adapted from Spatial-Mamba, with multi-scale dilated depthwise convolutions applied to the scan output; the first three stages were retained. Tiny, Small, and Base models were evaluated across nine dataset-scale combinations drawn from two source cohorts: the National Institutes of Health ChestX-ray14 archive (full ChestMNIST and a high-resolution subset) and Indiana University Open-i. At the Tiny scale, replacement reduced parameter count by 35.7% and increased graphics processing unit throughput by 19.3%; the savings came from the stage's dense projections, not from removing quadratic attention. Without distillation, the mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve on ChestMNIST was 0.004 lower than the baseline (95% bootstrap confidence interval, 0.002 to 0.006), and 0.003 to 0.006 lower across all nine combinations. Knowledge distillation from an unreplaced teacher narrowed the gap to the undistilled baseline to 0.001-0.002 and met the equivalence criterion on ChestMNIST, but distilling the baseline with the same recipe improved it by 0.001-0.003, so a gap of 0.002-0.005 persisted under symmetric training. At the Base scale, the unreplaced Small model was both smaller and more accurate. Fourth-stage replacement is a useful trade-off only for Tiny and Small models. These measurements let developers of chest radiograph screening tools weigh model size and speed against a quantified loss of diagnostic discrimination.

AI.tldr: This study quantifies the accuracy-efficiency trade-off of replacing MambaVision's parameter-heavy fourth stage with lighter Spatial-Mamba blocks for multi-label chest radiograph classification across nine dataset-scale combinations.
AI.motivation: MambaVision concentrates most of its parameters in its fourth stage, raising the question of how much that stage contributes to diagnostic performance versus model size and speed in medical imaging.
AI.method: The authors replace MambaVision's fourth stage with single-scan Spatial-Mamba blocks using multi-scale dilated depthwise convolutions, evaluating Tiny, Small, and Base variants across nine dataset-scale combinations from NIH ChestX-ray14 (ChestMNIST and high-res) and Indiana University Open-i, with and without knowledge distillation.
AI.result: At Tiny scale, replacement cuts parameters by 35.7% and boosts GPU throughput by 19.3% (driven by removing dense projections), while lowering mean AUROC by 0.004 on ChestMNIST (0.003-0.006 overall); symmetric knowledge distillation leaves a 0.002-0.005 gap, and at Base scale the unreplaced Small model is both smaller and more accurate.
AI.conclusion: Replacing MambaVision's fourth stage offers a practical size-speed trade-off for Tiny and Small chest radiograph models, whereas larger scales are better served by using a smaller unreplaced model.

title: Aerial Person Detection under Edge Constraints: Held-Out Evaluation and Edge-Ground Verification
comment: 14 pages, 1 figure, 8 tables. Code, truth registers and result files: this https URL
summary: A search drone sees a missing person as a few pixels, carries a small computer, and shares a narrow radio link. We study person detection under those limits; the primary evaluations were declared before they ran, and later analyses are marked exploratory. In an exploratory comparison, holding out recording blocks inferred from thermal frame identifiers cut recall at a fixed false-alarm target from 32.7% to 12.3%. With nothing tuned on test blocks, a 46,000-parameter detector gated by a contrast cue finds 10.4% of people against 5.7% for the same network applied everywhere. A standard detector, YOLO11n, trained under the same folds finds 54.5% at a similar false-alarm rate for about eleven times the arithmetic, and on our 4K field footage at 117 m has a walking person among its top 16 detections in up to 92% of frames against 74% for our board. Run alone, YOLO11n's thresholds set at one location overshot their false-alarm target 1.7 to 3.4 times at new locations, and its best configuration at altitude cost 4 to 24 standard passes per frame. Re-scoring its 16 best crops (154 KB per frame) with an 842,000-parameter ground model, thresholds frozen on a validation location, raised recall from 44.9% to 53.7% against the same 16 crops with YOLO's own scores; in a post hoc paired analysis over 15 test locations the gain was +8.8 points [+2.4, +12.5]. Pooled false detections fell from 0.86 to 0.64 per frame, but that paired change was not distinguishable from zero. Coverage of a still person in earth tones was very low for both detectors in the clips we flew.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates aerial person detection under edge and bandwidth constraints using held-out recording blocks, showing that a contrast-gated 46K-parameter detector and edge-ground verification with YOLO11n improve recall over standalone edge inference.
AI.motivation: Search-and-rescue drones must detect tiny, few-pixel people under tight onboard compute and narrow radio-link limits, where standard detectors suffer from threshold miscalibration across locations.
AI.method: The authors evaluate a 46,000-parameter detector gated by a contrast cue, YOLO11n trained under block-held-out folds, and an edge-ground verification pipeline that transmits YOLO11n's top 16 crops (154 KB/frame) to an 842,000-parameter ground model for re-scoring.
AI.result: Holding out recording blocks drops recall from 32.7% to 12.3%; the contrast-gated 46K model finds 10.4% vs. 5.7% ungated, while YOLO11n finds 54.5% (and 92% top-16 frame recall on 4K 117m footage vs. 74% for the edge board) but overshoots false-alarm targets 1.7-3.4x at new locations; ground re-scoring raises recall from 44.9% to 53.7% (+8.8 points across 15 test locations).
AI.conclusion: Block-held-out evaluation reveals severe cross-location calibration drift in aerial detectors, which edge-ground crop verification effectively mitigates within narrow bandwidth budgets.

title: GeoReVis: Learning Selective Revision and Evidence Consolidation for Remote Sensing Segmentation
summary: Recent methods try to inspect and revise masks to mitigate referential ambiguity and localization errors caused by complex spatial relations in language-guided remote sensing segmentation. However, these solutions often lead to Revision Degradation: revising missing regions may introduce errors into previously correct ones. Even a globally better mask can omit correct regions found in inferior masks. We term this Evidence Fragmentation: correct target evidence is scattered across imperfect masks. All masks generated by the model at this time are suboptimal. We propose GeoReVis, which unifies revision guided by execution feedback, Candidate Selection, and Cross-Mask Evidence Consolidation. It learns fine-grained revision from real actions that improve segmentation when executed and learns to select a better mask through quality comparisons between actual candidates, reducing the risk of degradation during revision. The selected whole mask can still discard useful regions. GeoReVis therefore retains all candidates across rounds, partitions their spatial disagreements into composable regions, and jointly reconstructs regions conditioned on the full instruction and context. This makes complementary and fragmentary evidence reusable regardless of its source candidate's overall quality, yielding improved segmentation. We further build a data pipeline to generate fine-grained multi-round segmentation trajectories and derive supervision for revision actions, candidate selection, and region composition from the model's own outputs, extending training beyond whole-mask IoU supervision. We also propose ReVis-Eval, a benchmark protocol evaluating multi-round revision and cross-round evidence consolidation accuracy. Experiments on ReVis-Eval and 5 benchmarks for remote sensing reasoning and referring segmentation demonstrate the effectiveness of GeoReVis.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes GeoReVis and the ReVis-Eval protocol for language-guided remote sensing segmentation, unifying execution-feedback revision, candidate selection, and cross-mask evidence consolidation to outperform baselines on six benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing iterative mask revision methods for remote sensing segmentation suffer from Revision Degradation (fixing missed areas breaks correct ones) and Evidence Fragmentation (correct regions are scattered across suboptimal candidate masks).
AI.method: GeoReVis learns fine-grained revision from execution feedback and candidate selection via quality comparisons, retains all round candidates, partitions their spatial disagreements into composable regions, and jointly reconstructs them conditioned on the full instruction using a multi-round trajectory data pipeline.
AI.result: Experiments on the newly proposed ReVis-Eval protocol and five existing remote sensing reasoning and referring segmentation benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of GeoReVis over prior methods.
AI.conclusion: Consolidating fragmentary spatial evidence across candidate masks rather than relying on a single revised mask overcomes revision degradation in complex remote sensing segmentation.

title: GlyphAtlas: Disentangling Stroke Detail from Layout for Scene Text Synthesis
summary: Scene text synthesis requires stroke-accurate characters rendered in a specified layout, as well as visual coherence with the surrounding scene. To achieve this, existing methods commonly pre-render the target text at its intended locations to form a glyph image that jointly specifies layout and glyph structure. However, this representation ties the resolution of each glyph to its target region, limiting fine-grained stroke guidance for small, densely packed, or structurally complex text. To tackle this, we propose GlyphAtlas, a scene text synthesis framework that retains the glyph image as a spatial anchor and supplies fine-grained stroke references through a dedicated glyph atlas. The atlas renders and encodes each character or word in a separate cell, decoupling reference resolution from target-region size. We further introduce atlas-anchored attention, which lets each text region retrieve stroke detail only from its corresponding atlas cells to refine the coarse glyph structure provided by the glyph image. This coarse-to-fine conditioning simplifies stroke rendering while preserving explicit layout correspondence. We optimize GlyphAtlas with a mask-weighted flow matching objective and a timestep-weighted text perceptual loss for writing accuracy and background consistency. Random resolution augmentation of atlas cells supports adjustable atlas budgets at inference. Extensive experiments demonstrate that GlyphAtlas achieves stroke-accurate synthesis of small, dense, and structurally complex text, zero-shot transfer to languages unseen during task-specific training, and leading performance in scenes with many text regions. project page: this https URL

AI.tldr: The authors present GlyphAtlas, a scene text synthesis framework that decouples stroke detail from spatial layout via a dedicated glyph atlas and atlas-anchored attention, achieving strong performance on small, dense, and unseen-language text.
AI.motivation: Standard scene text synthesis methods pre-render target text into a glyph image that couples layout and stroke resolution, degrading fine-grained stroke guidance for small, densely packed, or complex characters.
AI.method: GlyphAtlas retains the glyph image as a spatial anchor while encoding each character or word in separate cells of a glyph atlas, using atlas-anchored attention to retrieve fine stroke details, trained with a mask-weighted flow matching objective, a timestep-weighted text perceptual loss, and random resolution augmentation.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show that GlyphAtlas achieves stroke-accurate synthesis of small, dense, and structurally complex text, zero-shot transfer to languages unseen during task-specific training, and leading performance in scenes with many text regions.
AI.conclusion: Separating character stroke references into a resolution-decoupled atlas enables accurate, scalable scene text synthesis and zero-shot cross-lingual transfer.

title: DoF-Query Transformer for Adaptive Fusion of Egocentric Vision and Forearm HD-sEMG in Continuous Hand Kinematics
summary: Continuous and accurate estimation of human hand kinematics is important not only for intuitive human-machine interaction, but also for capturing fine-grained human manipulation demonstrations that can provide action supervision for embodied-intelligence datasets and dexterous robot learning. However, individual sensing modalities may be insufficient for reliable estimation under varying operating conditions. We present a finger-unencumbered multimodal framework for continuous regression of 20 hand joint angles from egocentric RGB images and 128-channel forearm high-density surface electromyography (HD-sEMG). The framework combines a Vision Transformer-based visual encoder, a Transformer-based EMG encoder, and a degree of freedom (DoF) query Transformer fusion decoder. To account for the varying informativeness of visual and EMG cues across joint DoFs and input conditions, the decoder assigns a separate learnable query to each DoF, enabling DoF-specific and context-adaptive fusion of the two modalities. The framework was evaluated on synchronized multimodal data from 10 participants. Averaged across participants, the proposed fusion model achieved a mean coefficient of determination ($R^2$) of $0.88$ and a mean absolute error (MAE) of $2.80^\circ$, compared with $0.82$ and $3.21^\circ$ for the vision-only model and $0.68$ and $5.13^\circ$ for the EMG-only model. It also outperformed the evaluated representative unimodal baselines and alternative fusion designs. DoF-wise analyses showed larger fusion gains for visually ambiguous joints and viewing conditions, while synthetic visual occlusion demonstrated greater robustness than vision-only estimation. These results highlight the complementary value of egocentric vision and forearm HD-sEMG for capturing fine-grained human hand kinematics, with potential applications in human demonstration acquisition and dexterous robot learning.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a DoF-Query Transformer that adaptively fuses egocentric RGB images and 128-channel forearm HD-sEMG to regress 20 hand joint angles, achieving 0.88 R^2 and 2.80 degrees MAE across 10 participants.
AI.motivation: Relying solely on egocentric vision or surface electromyography (HD-sEMG) for continuous hand kinematics estimation fails under visual occlusion or varying operating conditions.
AI.method: The framework pairs a ViT visual encoder and a Transformer EMG encoder with a degree-of-freedom (DoF) query Transformer fusion decoder that assigns a dedicated learnable query to each of the 20 DoFs for context-adaptive multimodal fusion.
AI.result: Evaluated on synchronized data from 10 participants, the fusion model achieves a mean R^2 of 0.88 and MAE of 2.80 degrees, outperforming vision-only (0.82 R^2, 3.21 degrees MAE), EMG-only (0.68 R^2, 5.13 degrees MAE), and alternative fusion baselines, with greater robustness under synthetic visual occlusion.
AI.conclusion: Per-DoF query fusion effectively exploits the complementary strengths of egocentric vision and forearm HD-sEMG for finger-unencumbered hand kinematics capture.

title: Radar Panoptic Transformer: Semantic-Guided Mask Queries for Dynamic Scene Understanding
summary: Automotive radar provides long-range sensing and direct Doppler velocity measurements, but its sparse and non-uniformly sampled point clouds pose significant challenges for panoptic segmentation. Dynamic objects often yield only a few detections amid a dominant static background, providing limiting the geometric cues for separating object instances. We propose \emph{Radar Panoptic Transformer (RPT)}, an end-to-end point-based network that incorporates radar-adaptive feature extraction with semantic-guided mask prediction. Its backbone aggregates pose-aligned temporal context through grouped vector attention and learns per-point neighborhood radii conditioned on range, azimuth, and radar cross section (RCS). Point-wise semantic predictions initialize queries at likely foreground detections and guide masked cross-attention through query-point class agreement, producing instance masks without geometric clustering. An auxiliary RCS-consistency loss matches instance-level statistics between predicted and annotated instances. RPT achieves state-of-the-art performance on RadarScenes with $71.6\%$ mIoU and $82.2\%$ PQ. We further evaluate RPT on MAN TruckScenes, where it outperforms the evaluated baselines in a long-range, full-surround radar setting with sensing ranges up to $230\,\mathrm{m}$. RPT achieves real-time end-to-end inference at $31$\,Hz on RadarScenes, exceeding the sensor frame rate.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Radar Panoptic Transformer (RPT), an end-to-end point-based network for automotive radar panoptic segmentation that achieves state-of-the-art 71.6% mIoU and 82.2% PQ on RadarScenes at 31 Hz.
AI.motivation: Automotive radar point clouds are sparse and non-uniform, leaving dynamic objects with few detections against a dominant static background and limiting geometric cues for clustering-based instance separation.
AI.method: RPT aggregates pose-aligned temporal context via grouped vector attention with learned per-point neighborhood radii (conditioned on range, azimuth, and RCS), initializes queries from point-wise semantic predictions for masked cross-attention without geometric clustering, and applies an auxiliary RCS-consistency loss.
AI.result: RPT achieves state-of-the-art 71.6% mIoU and 82.2% PQ on RadarScenes at 31 Hz (exceeding sensor frame rate), and outperforms evaluated baselines on long-range (up to 230 m) full-surround radar data in MAN TruckScenes.
AI.conclusion: Integrating radar-adaptive neighborhood learning with semantic-guided mask queries enables real-time, clustering-free panoptic segmentation on sparse automotive radar.

title: AstroPIE-53: Towards Understanding Failure Modes of Human Pose Estimation in Space
comment: 4 pages + references, 4 figures. Published in the Proceedings of SPAICE 2026 and i-SAIRAS 2026
summary: Reliable monitoring of astronauts is essential for safety, situational awareness, and autonomous assistance in space missions. While modern computer vision enables accurate human detection and pose estimation on Earth, its robustness in space environments remains largely unquantified due to limited data availability. We present AstroPIE-53, a pilot dataset of 53 annotated astronaut videos collected from publicly available mission footage. To respect copyright restrictions, we release video identifiers, reconstruction scripts, and dense annotations rather than raw videos. The dataset includes bounding boxes, challenge classes, and human-annotated pose failure tags. We benchmark state-of-the-art person detection and pose estimation models under realistic zero-shot deployment conditions and perform the first systematic failure analysis for astronaut monitoring. Our results reveal substantial performance degradation caused by occlusions, unusual body orientations, low contrast, and microgravity motion patterns.

AI.tldr: The authors introduce AstroPIE-53, a pilot dataset of 53 annotated astronaut mission videos, and benchmark zero-shot person detection and pose estimation models, revealing severe degradation in space environments.
AI.motivation: While human pose estimation excels on Earth, its robustness in spaceflight environments remains largely unquantified due to the lack of annotated astronaut video data.
AI.method: AstroPIE-53 provides video identifiers, reconstruction scripts, bounding boxes, challenge classes, and human-annotated pose failure tags for 53 public astronaut mission videos, used to benchmark state-of-the-art detection and pose models under zero-shot deployment.
AI.result: Systematic failure analysis reveals substantial performance degradation in current models caused by occlusions, unusual body orientations, low contrast, and microgravity motion patterns.
AI.conclusion: AstroPIE-53 establishes an initial benchmark and failure taxonomy to guide the development of more robust human pose estimation systems for spaceflight safety and autonomous assistance.

title: Ocular Recognition: Interoperability, Multi-Resolution, and Spectrum Challenges
comment: Paper submitted to IEEE journal in revision process. Abstract reduces to 1920 characteres
summary: Ocular recognition is typically developed under controlled acquisition conditions, limiting its use in semi-controlled and on-the-move scenarios. A key obstacle is the lack of representative data spanning real-world capture conditions. At a border checkpoint, for example, images may range from low-resolution visible-light periocular crops (RGB) to high-resolution near-infrared iris images (NIR). Using this heterogeneous evidence raises three questions: whether resolution-specific processing improves recognition, how to compare templates from different processing routes, and how to allocate training data across resolution specialists. We investigate resolution-specific processing and parameter sharing using three AdaFace-based architecture families: fixed-resolution specialists; Independent Backbones with Shared Heads (IBSH); and models with resolution-specific front-ends for 40x40, 80x80, and 160x160 inputs, followed by a shared identity trunk and embedding projection. We evaluate each architecture with route-specific training subsets and with a full-pool strategy, in which every specialist uses the complete selected training set. Results reveal a trade-off among same-resolution specialization, cross-resolution interoperability, and common-route re-extraction. Route-specific training produces distinct performance profiles across routes, whereas full-pool training makes route performance more uniform and primarily benefits the 160x160 route. Thus, adding training data does not improve all resolution routes equally.

AI.tldr: This study evaluates three AdaFace-based architecture families and two training-data allocation strategies for multi-resolution, cross-spectrum ocular recognition, revealing a trade-off between specialization and cross-resolution interoperability.
AI.motivation: Real-world ocular recognition (e.g., at border checkpoints) must handle heterogeneous inputs ranging from low-resolution visible-light periocular crops to high-resolution near-infrared iris images, raising questions about resolution-specific processing and data allocation.
AI.method: The authors compare fixed-resolution specialists, Independent Backbones with Shared Heads (IBSH), and models with resolution-specific front-ends (40x40, 80x80, 160x160) plus a shared trunk, evaluated under route-specific versus full-pool training strategies.
AI.result: Route-specific training yields distinct performance profiles across resolution routes, whereas full-pool training produces more uniform performance and primarily benefits the 160x160 route, exposing a trade-off among same-resolution specialization, cross-resolution interoperability, and common-route re-extraction.
AI.conclusion: Adding training data does not benefit all ocular resolution routes equally, requiring careful architectural and data-allocation choices to balance specialization against cross-resolution interoperability.

title: EvoMem3D: Adaptive-Depth Temporal Representation Memory for Multi-Camera 3D Detection
summary: Modern multi-camera 3D detectors increasingly rely on large Vision Transformer (ViT) image encoders, making repeated full-depth encoding a dominant inference cost even though adjacent driving frames are highly redundant. We present EvoMem3D, an adaptive-depth temporal framework that caches the most recent full-depth detector-interface appearance representation as a read-only anchor and combines it with policy-selected partial features from the current frame. A lightweight pre-encoding controller chooses among semantic encoder exits before image processing, allocating shallow computation to stable frames and deeper computation when the visual state changes. To reuse appearance without carrying stale geometry, we decouple temporal appearance from geometric alignment: current-frame calibration defines the decoder geometry at every timestamp, while a motion-conditioned positional adapter accounts for anchor-to-current ego motion. On nuScenes, EvoMem3D achieves 61.50 NDS and 52.76 mAP while reducing end-to-end latency from 364.4 to 168.7 ms (x2.16) relative to standard dense DETR3D. With StreamPETR, it reaches 61.36 NDS and 52.55 mAP at a x1.92 speedup. Controlled studies isolate the effects of current evidence, temporal reuse, memory correction, and adaptive routing, while our audit confirms that the policy learns to distinguish semantic driving regimes.

AI.tldr: The paper presents EvoMem3D, an adaptive-depth temporal memory framework for multi-camera 3D detection that speeds up DETR3D by 2.16x (61.50 NDS) and StreamPETR by 1.92x (61.36 NDS) on nuScenes.
AI.motivation: Modern multi-camera 3D detectors incur high inference latency by repeatedly running full-depth Vision Transformer encoders on every frame despite strong temporal redundancy across adjacent driving frames.
AI.method: EvoMem3D caches the most recent full-depth appearance representation as a read-only anchor, uses a lightweight pre-encoding controller to select shallow or deep semantic encoder exits per frame, and decouples appearance from geometry via current-frame calibration and a motion-conditioned positional adapter.
AI.result: On nuScenes, EvoMem3D achieves 61.50 NDS and 52.76 mAP while cutting DETR3D latency from 364.4 to 168.7 ms (2.16x speedup), and reaches 61.36 NDS and 52.55 mAP with StreamPETR at a 1.92x speedup.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive-depth encoding combined with motion-aligned appearance caching substantially reduces multi-camera 3D detection latency without sacrificing accuracy.

title: Self-supervised learning for zebrafish embryo phenotype evaluation: Systematic comparison of algorithms, label-efficient classification, and transfer learning
summary: Zebrafish embryos are a prominent model organism for image-based phenotyping and especially suited for large-scale imaging studies, for which machine learning (ML) models can automate evaluation. However, training ML models usually requires large labeled datasets, and differences in imaging conditions often impede reuse across laboratories. Self-supervised learning (SSL) addresses both constraints by learning transferable representations from unlabeled images. Yet central aspects like the choice of algorithm remain underexplored for domain-specific applications. To close this gap, we benchmark popular SSL algorithms on the public EmbryoNet dataset, explore label-efficient learning, and test transfer to an unseen setting. Using representations from our strongest model, a ResNet50 network trained with SwAV, a simple linear classifier reaches 86.4% accuracy and a non-linear classifier 87.1%, rivaling the fully supervised EmbryoNet model (87.1%). The SwAV model decisively outperforms supervised training from scratch when labels are scarce (70.2% vs. 45.7% accuracy with 5% of labels). On a three-class problem (normal, dead, falsely cropped) with a small, previously unseen zebrafish toxicity dataset, recorded in a different setting, our model reaches 81.3% accuracy without retraining, while EmbryoNet achieves 75.9%. Overall, self-supervised models for zebrafish embryos seem to mostly facilitate label-efficiency and transfer to new settings rather than improving supervised results.

AI.tldr: This paper benchmarks self-supervised learning (SSL) algorithms for zebrafish embryo phenotyping on EmbryoNet, showing that SwAV-pretrained ResNet50 matches supervised accuracy (87.1%) and excels in low-label (70.2% vs. 45.7%) and cross-lab transfer (81.3% vs. 75.9%) settings.
AI.motivation: Automated zebrafish embryo phenotyping typically requires large labeled datasets and struggles to generalize across laboratories due to differing imaging conditions, while domain-specific SSL algorithm choices remain underexplored.
AI.method: The authors benchmark popular SSL algorithms on the public EmbryoNet dataset, evaluating linear and non-linear classifiers, label-efficient regimes (5% labels), and zero-shot transfer to an unseen three-class zebrafish toxicity dataset recorded in a different setting.
AI.result: A ResNet50 trained with SwAV reaches 86.4% linear and 87.1% non-linear accuracy (matching the 87.1% supervised EmbryoNet model), outperforms training from scratch with 5% labels (70.2% vs. 45.7%), and achieves 81.3% accuracy without retraining on the unseen toxicity dataset versus 75.9% for EmbryoNet.
AI.conclusion: Self-supervised learning for zebrafish embryo phenotyping primarily boosts label efficiency and cross-laboratory transferability rather than surpassing fully supervised in-domain accuracy.

title: Visual Marking as a Native Reasoning Capability for Multimodal LLMs
summary: Visual reasoning often requires maintaining intermediate spatial states that are difficult to express in text. Existing approaches either rely on external drawing tools or image generators, or encode these states in latent tokens without explicit spatial correspondence to the input image. We introduce SelfMark, which enables MLLMs to construct and use visual marks directly in their native visual feature space. By treating the visual token grid as a canvas, SelfMark establishes explicit spatial correspondence between marks and images. This is achieved through a locate-mark-read procedure, where the model identifies relevant locations, constructs task-dependent mark features, and reads the resulting visual features to guide its reasoning. We jointly train a single model on spatial planning, dense counting, high-resolution VQA, and line tracing. Across six benchmarks, SelfMark outperforms state-of-the-art MLLM-based methods specialized for individual tasks. These improvements also persist with a stronger backbone, demonstrating the effectiveness of visual marking across different model capabilities. Overall, SelfMark provides a unified approach to visual reasoning by integrating spatially grounded marks directly into the visual feature space of MLLMs.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SelfMark, which enables MLLMs to construct and read visual marks directly in their native visual feature space via a locate-mark-read procedure, outperforming task-specialized MLLM baselines across six benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Visual reasoning often requires maintaining intermediate spatial states that text cannot easily express, yet existing methods rely on external drawing tools or latent tokens lacking explicit spatial correspondence to the image.
AI.method: SelfMark treats the visual token grid as a canvas and uses a locate-mark-read procedure to identify relevant locations, construct task-dependent mark features in the native visual feature space, and read them to guide reasoning, jointly trained on spatial planning, dense counting, high-resolution VQA, and line tracing.
AI.result: Across six benchmarks, a single jointly trained SelfMark model outperforms state-of-the-art MLLM methods specialized for individual tasks, and these gains persist with a stronger backbone.
AI.conclusion: Integrating spatially grounded visual marking directly into an MLLM's native visual feature space provides a unified, effective mechanism for spatial visual reasoning.

title: PoCoAttn: Position-Content Collaborative Sparse Attention for Fast and High-Fidelity Video Generation
comment: 21 pages, 15 figures, 13 tables. Project page: this https URL
summary: Video diffusion transformers rely on 3D full attention over tens of thousands of spatiotemporal tokens, and its quadratic cost dominates inference latency. Sparse attention reduces this cost, but existing methods face a dilemma: static methods apply predefined masks and cannot capture input-dependent attention, whereas dynamic methods reconstruct the sparse mask repeatedly, paying online to rediscover positional structure that is largely stable across inputs. To this end, we propose PoCoAttn, a training-free sparse attention framework that separates input-stable from input-dependent attention and resolves the former offline and the latter online. PoCoAttn features: (1) A relative-offset analysis of 3D query-key pairs, which shows that video attention decomposes into an input-stable positional prior that carries most of the attention mass and a small content-dependent residual. (2) A position-content collaborative sparse attention mechanism, which retrieves positional keys from offline-calibrated tables, selects content keys online with a head-adaptive ratio between the two sources, and compensates for the discarded keys to approximate full attention. (3) A step-adaptive budget allocation algorithm, which models how early-step sparse attention errors are amplified along the denoising trajectory and derives the optimal sparsity budget per step. Extensive experiments across four video diffusion models and three tasks show that PoCoAttn consistently achieves a better speed-fidelity Pareto frontier than state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods, improving PSNR by 1.9 to 5.0 dB over baselines and delivering up to 4.1$\times$ attention and 2.0$\times$ denoising speedups over dense FlashAttention-3 attention.

AI.tldr: The authors propose PoCoAttn, a training-free sparse attention framework for video diffusion transformers that separates offline positional priors from online content selection, achieving up to 4.1x attention speedup and 1.9-5.0 dB PSNR gains over SOTA baselines.
AI.motivation: Video diffusion transformers face quadratic 3D attention costs, and existing sparse attention methods either use rigid static masks that miss input-dependent patterns or repeatedly recompute dynamic masks online for positional structures that are largely input-invariant.
AI.method: PoCoAttn combines offline-calibrated positional key tables with online content-key selection using a head-adaptive ratio and compensation for discarded keys, alongside a step-adaptive budget allocation algorithm that models error amplification along the denoising trajectory.
AI.result: Across four video diffusion models and three tasks, PoCoAttn achieves a superior speed-fidelity Pareto frontier, improving PSNR by 1.9 to 5.0 dB over state-of-the-art baselines and delivering up to 4.1x attention and 2.0x denoising speedups over dense FlashAttention-3.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling stable positional priors from dynamic content attention with trajectory-aware budget allocation enables fast, high-fidelity video diffusion inference without retraining.

title: Unreasonable Confidence from Simulator Misspecification: Directional Robustness on the SPEED+ Sim-to-Real Benchmark
comment: 22 pages, 5 figures, 20 tables. Extended version of a paper at the Sim2Science workshop, NeurIPS 2026. Code, per-image predictions and pre-registration record: this https URL
summary: Vision-based navigation systems for orbit must be trained almost entirely on synthetic imagery, because real labelled images of a given spacecraft in flight rarely exist. Benchmarks like SPEED+ are built for that situation: the training set comes from a simulator, and the test sets are real images of a satellite mockup under two kinds of lighting. That simulator approximates how light reflects off mylar and aluminium, and like every scientific simulator it is misspecified. Its error is radiometric, since it misses the specular highlights, hard shadows and sensor saturation common in real images. We probe the resulting synthetic-to-real gap, the central risk for such systems, with a deliberately simple monocular pose estimator. In a 2x2 study of backbone adaptation and photometric augmentation, trained on synthetic images and tested on both real hardware-in-the-loop domains, we find three things. (1) The model does not know it is failing: regions conformally calibrated to 90% on synthetic data cover only 9-15% of rotation errors on sunlamp and 21-38% on lightbox, so a wrong pose carries the confidence of a correct one. (2) Transfer is asymmetric: scaling data and features improved synthetic rotation error from 1.65 to 1.03 rad but moved the harshly lit sunlamp domain by only 0.05 rad, under twice its seed s.d., whereas adapting the backbone's last stage carried 63-83% of its extra synthetic gain to both real domains. (3) Once the backbone adapts, augmentation helps only in the direction it models: our photometric stack improved the diffusely lit lightbox domain from 1.17 to 0.99 rad on every seed but moved sunlamp no more than seed-to-seed variation, while with the backbone frozen it helped sunlamp more. Every post-review experiment was pre-registered, and the code, per-image predictions and pre-registration record are at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Using a 2x2 study on the SPEED+ spacecraft pose benchmark, this paper shows that simulator radiometric misspecification causes severe overconfidence (9-15% vs. 90% nominal coverage) and asymmetric sim-to-real transfer depending on backbone adaptation and augmentation.
AI.motivation: Orbit navigation models trained on synthetic imagery suffer from radiometric simulator misspecification (missing specular highlights, hard shadows, and saturation), creating poorly understood sim-to-real failure and calibration risks.
AI.method: The authors conduct a pre-registered 2x2 study of backbone last-stage adaptation and photometric augmentation using a simple monocular pose estimator trained on SPEED+ synthetic images and tested on real sunlamp and lightbox hardware-in-the-loop domains.
AI.result: Regions conformally calibrated to 90% on synthetic data cover only 9-15% of rotation errors on sunlamp and 21-38% on lightbox; scaling synthetic data/features cuts synthetic error from 1.65 to 1.03 rad but moves sunlamp by only 0.05 rad, whereas last-stage backbone adaptation transfers 63-83% of extra synthetic gains; photometric augmentation improves lightbox (1.17 to 0.99 rad) after adaptation but barely affects sunlamp.
AI.conclusion: Simulator misspecification breaks conformal uncertainty calibration and produces asymmetric domain transfer, meaning synthetic-data scaling alone cannot reliably fix harsh real-world lighting gaps.

title: Words Speak Louder? Exploring the Language Shortcut of LLM-Driven Incomplete Multimodal Learning
comment: 19 pages, 7 figures, 14 tables. Project page: this https URL
summary: Is a face or a voice still heard once the words are known? Incomplete multimodal learning increasingly uses large language models (LLMs) as fusion engines: modality features enter as token blocks and missing modalities become placeholders. We find that LLM-driven fusion can override non-verbal evidence it can read. Contrasting its full-input prediction with counterfactual views, the same model shown one modality or no content, we identify language shortcuts. We build MR-Bench: MR-Bench-A types every test sample of four sentiment benchmarks; MR-Bench-H contains 900 human-validated clips (620 language-shortcut, LS; 280 non-verbal-shortcut, NS) from seven sources, and every model is scored on all of them.
