Zero-shot MLLMs solve at most 32.7% of the LS clips; adding the transcript to the muted video lowers vision-language accuracy by 46.1-53.1 points. Yet inverting a text-only model's answers solves 94.4%, so LS accuracy alone cannot establish use of non-verbal evidence. Inside the fusion LLM, fused states align increasingly with the text view late in the decoder. Counterfactual-View Reliability learning (CoVeR) trains views as unimodal judges and withholds fused supervision where they disagree. It achieves state-of-the-art results on five benchmarks without extra inference cost in accuracy mode. On MR-Bench-H, it reaches 61.7% LS and 93.6% NS accuracy; robust mode raises LS accuracy to 63.0% while lowering NS accuracy to 84.8%. Among LS clips solved without text, adding text causes errors on 30.1% with CoVeR versus 32.2% with LLM-Fusion. Project page: this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper uncovers language shortcuts in LLM-driven incomplete multimodal learning, introduces the MR-Bench benchmark, and proposes CoVeR, which trains unimodal judges and withholds conflicting fused supervision to reach state-of-the-art results on five benchmarks.
AI.motivation: When LLMs fuse multimodal token blocks, they can override readable non-verbal cues in favor of text, creating language shortcuts that go undetected by standard sentiment benchmarks.
AI.method: The authors build MR-Bench (including 900 human-validated clips in MR-Bench-H split into 620 language-shortcut and 280 non-verbal-shortcut cases) and propose Counterfactual-View Reliability learning (CoVeR), which trains counterfactual unimodal views as judges and withholds fused supervision where they disagree.
AI.result: Zero-shot MLLMs solve at most 32.7% of language-shortcut clips (with transcripts dropping vision-language accuracy by 46.1-53.1 points); CoVeR achieves state-of-the-art results on five benchmarks with no extra inference cost in accuracy mode, reaching 61.7% LS and 93.6% NS accuracy on MR-Bench-H (63.0% LS / 84.8% NS in robust mode).
AI.conclusion: Counterfactual unimodal reliability supervision mitigates text dominance in LLM-based multimodal fusion without adding inference overhead.

title: BlockAlign: Preference Optimization for Trajectory-Distilled Video Generation
summary: Directly aligning trajectory-distilled video generators slashes rollout costs and optimizes the deployed few-step model without teacher fine-tuning or re-distillation. However, conventional flow-matching preference objectives assume single-head local velocity supervision, mismatching the finite-interval, block-average transition interface of trajectory-distilled generators such as Parallel Decoding Distillation (PDD) and Parametric Trajectory Distillation (PTD). Naively supervising only the primary initial-subinterval velocity sub-head rather than the fused block-average velocity at block starts (DirectAlign) induces a severe training--inference mismatch that degrades quality below the unaligned baseline. We introduce BlockAlign, an interface-consistent preference optimization framework that constructs states at valid block boundaries, queries the fused block-level velocity predictor, and supervises span-normalized transition residuals-seamlessly supporting DPO-, NFT-, and rollout-style objectives while preserving the native few-step sampler. We further build a unified post-training pipeline integrating offline pairs, reward-free semi-online continuations, and online rollouts with hierarchical preference selection and objective-aware block scheduling. Experiments on multi-reference video generation across MiniMax-H3 Ref2VA and an in-house model RefVid-V4 show that BlockAlign consistently outperforms unaligned distilled models and DirectAlign in structural plausibility, reference consistency, and visual quality. Notably, our approach unlocks PDD's 5x few-step rollout speedup for 3x faster end-to-end online training, achieving statistically significant human preference gains over PDD baselines (54.0% vs. 33.3% wins/losses, or 61.8% non-tie win rate on RefVid-V4; 51.3% vs. 34.7%, or 59.7% non-tie win rate on MiniMax-H3) and up to an 82.7% win rate against DirectAlign.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes BlockAlign, an interface-consistent preference optimization framework for trajectory-distilled video generators that unlocks 5x few-step rollout speedups for 3x faster online training and achieves up to 82.7% win rate over DirectAlign.
AI.motivation: Standard flow-matching preference objectives supervise single-head local velocities, causing a severe training-inference mismatch when applied naively to trajectory-distilled generators (e.g., PDD, PTD) that predict finite-interval block-average transitions.
AI.method: BlockAlign constructs states at valid block boundaries, queries the fused block-level velocity predictor, and supervises span-normalized transition residuals across DPO-, NFT-, and rollout-style objectives, integrated into a pipeline combining offline pairs, semi-online continuations, and online rollouts with hierarchical preference selection.
AI.result: On multi-reference video generation (MiniMax-H3 Ref2VA and RefVid-V4), BlockAlign unlocks PDD's 5x few-step rollout speedup for 3x faster end-to-end online training, achieving 61.8% non-tie human preference win rate over PDD on RefVid-V4, 59.7% on MiniMax-H3, and up to 82.7% against DirectAlign.
AI.conclusion: Aligning preference supervision with the block-average transition interface of trajectory-distilled generators enables fast, stable post-training without degrading few-step sampling quality.

title: Structure-Guided Multi-Granularity Spatiotemporal Transformer for Efficient Monocular 3D Human Pose Estimation
summary: Existing multi-granularity methods for monocular 3D human pose estimation emphasize spatial joint features while underusing skeletal structure, including global connectivity and temporal continuity. Moreover, modeling entire frame sequences incurs high computational costs. We propose a Structure-Aware Multi-Granularity Spatiotemporal Transformer that integrates structural priors across spatial and temporal representations for accurate and efficient pose estimation. A three-level feature extractor captures human topology at the joint, bone, and limb levels. Gated Adaptive Spatial Attention (GASA) embeds structural constraints into spatial attention, while Multi-Granularity Feature Enhancement (MGFE) uses hierarchical pooling and fusion to strengthen local details and global semantics. Temporal Segment Fusion (TSF) aligns temporal contexts across granularities to capture both short- and long-range motion patterns. Hierarchical Cross-Attention (HCA) promotes spatiotemporal interaction between granularities, and Keyframe Attention (KFA) selects informative motion segments to reduce redundancy and computational cost. Experiments demonstrate improved accuracy and efficiency over conventional Transformer-based approaches, highlighting the effectiveness of structure-aware multi-granularity modeling for monocular 3D human pose estimation.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a Structure-Aware Multi-Granularity Spatiotemporal Transformer for monocular 3D human pose estimation that models joint, bone, and limb topologies while reducing temporal redundancy via Keyframe Attention.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-granularity 3D human pose estimators underuse global skeletal connectivity and temporal continuity, while processing entire frame sequences incurs high computational cost.
AI.method: The model extracts three-level features (joint, bone, limb), embeds structural constraints via Gated Adaptive Spatial Attention (GASA) and Multi-Granularity Feature Enhancement (MGFE), aligns temporal contexts with Temporal Segment Fusion (TSF) and Hierarchical Cross-Attention (HCA), and uses Keyframe Attention (KFA) to select informative motion segments.
AI.result: Experiments demonstrate improved accuracy and computational efficiency over conventional Transformer-based monocular 3D human pose estimation approaches.
AI.conclusion: Integrating hierarchical skeletal structure priors with keyframe-based temporal selection improves both accuracy and efficiency in monocular 3D human pose estimation.

title: VisDrone-ReID: A Unified Multi-Category Object Re-Identification Benchmark
summary: Object re-identification (Re-ID) benchmarks remain predominantly confined to single-category evaluations, limiting the development of unified systems capable of operating across diverse object types. This paper presents VisDrone-ReID, a unified multi-category Re-ID benchmark derived from the VisDrone2019-MOT dataset through a principled conversion pipeline. The pipeline resolves structural incompatibilities between multi-object tracking annotations and Re-ID evaluation requirements, addressing sequence-scoped identity collision, temporal redundancy, and the absence of a principled identity-level train/test split. The resulting benchmark comprises 9,516 identities and 150,016 images across ten object categories - pedestrian, people, bicycle, car, van, truck, tricycle, awning-tricycle, bus, and motor, sourced from 80 unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) sequences captured across urban environments. A leave-one-out (LOO) evaluation protocol is adopted to provide a comprehensive assessment. Baseline experiments across four representative Re-ID models spanning CNN and transformer architectures establish the first systematic performance reference on this benchmark. Results reveal a consistent Rank-1 to mAP gap across all models, suggesting that VisDrone-ReID presents a genuine retrieval challenge beyond nearest-neighbour matching. Per-category analysis identifies pedestrian as the most challenging category and reveals that vision-language pretraining provides a measurable advantage on semantically distinctive categories. VisDrone-ReID provides a consistent platform for studying multi-category object re-identification under the scale variation, viewpoint challenges, and category diversity characteristic of real-world surveillance scenarios.

AI.tldr: The authors introduce VisDrone-ReID, a unified multi-category object Re-ID benchmark of 9,516 identities and 150,016 images across 10 categories from 80 UAV sequences, and establish baselines across four CNN and transformer models.
AI.motivation: Existing object re-identification benchmarks are largely restricted to single categories, hindering the development of unified Re-ID systems for diverse real-world surveillance targets.
AI.method: VisDrone-ReID converts VisDrone2019-MOT into a Re-ID benchmark by resolving sequence-scoped identity collisions, temporal redundancy, and identity-level train/test splits, adopting a leave-one-out evaluation protocol across 10 object categories and benchmarking four CNN and transformer Re-ID models.
AI.result: Baseline experiments show a consistent Rank-1 to mAP gap across all four models (indicating retrieval difficulty beyond nearest-neighbor matching), identify pedestrian as the hardest category, and show that vision-language pretraining aids semantically distinctive categories.
AI.conclusion: VisDrone-ReID provides a standardized multi-category aerial benchmark for studying unified object re-identification under scale, viewpoint, and category diversity.

title: Signs of Wear: Evaluating Intelligent Speed Assistance Under Synthetic Adverse Conditions
summary: Intelligent Speed Assistance (ISA) systems rely on cameras to recognize speed-limit signs, yet existing benchmarks underrepresent the weathered, dirty, and overgrown signs commonly encountered on rural roads. We use generative image editing to introduce different forms of wear into real street-level images of speed-limit signs. The resulting ISA-Wear dataset contains paired original and edited images. Guided by text instructions, a multimodal image-editing model adds snow, rust, vegetation, faded paint, or mud to the speed-limit sign in a street-level frame at three severity levels. Where appropriate, the surrounding scene is adapted as well, and the viewpoint is kept. Every edited frame has an unedited counterpart, and we only evaluate frames whose original is recognized correctly, so any failure can be attributed to the wear. Since the model alters the sign's geometry in 21\% of the edits, all edits are filtered by a geometric check and a manual review. Severity is measured as the LPIPS distance between the original and the edited sign plate. On 716 worn frames, we find that in detect-then-read pipelines, wear breaks detection before it breaks reading. The detector finds only 62\% of the worn signs, even though it finds every one of them in the original frames. Missed detections account for 78--87\% of failed reads, a pattern that a zero-shot detector shares. Given the annotated sign box, as in the crop-based benchmarks, a classifier still reads 78\% of the worn signs, but only 56\% when it has to rely on the detector

AI.tldr: This paper introduces ISA-Wear, a dataset of 716 real and generatively edited worn speed-limit signs, showing that wear breaks sign detection (62% recall) before classification (78% crop accuracy, dropping to 56% end-to-end).
AI.motivation: Intelligent Speed Assistance (ISA) benchmarks underrepresent weathered, dirty, and overgrown speed-limit signs common on rural roads, leaving real-world failure modes poorly understood.
AI.method: Using a multimodal image-editing model guided by text instructions, the authors add snow, rust, vegetation, faded paint, or mud at three severity levels (measured by LPIPS) to street-level frames whose originals are recognized correctly, filtering out the 21% of edits that alter sign geometry via geometric checks and manual review.
AI.result: On 716 worn frames, the detector finds only 62% of worn signs (versus 100% of originals), with missed detections accounting for 78-87% of failed reads; a classifier reads 78% of worn signs given ground-truth crops, but drops to 56% when relying on the detector.
AI.conclusion: In detect-then-read ISA pipelines, physical sign wear primarily degrades the detection stage rather than character recognition, highlighting the need for wear-robust sign detectors.

title: DominoBench: Evaluating Multi-Step Physical Reasoning from Still Images
comment: DominoBench dataset, evaluation harnesses, and benchmarks available at this https URL
summary: Can a vision-language model look at a picture of a chain reaction and tell what will happen? Recent multimodal models describe scenes fluently and solve textbook physics problems, which suggests they should also predict how a scene of ramps, ledges, pendulums, seesaws and dominoes plays out once a ball is pushed. We tested this claim on 30 models from 10 families and reached a clear conclusion: unaided, no model predicts the outcome reliably. We built DominoBench, a benchmark of still images of 2D rigid-body scenes whose outcome a physics simulator computes. It holds 854 items in 427 minimal pairs, in which a change of one to three grid steps in one quantity decides whether one person survives, and every item comes with a four-rung hint ladder ending in the exact calculation that decides the outcome. Unaided, frontier models from Anthropic, Google and OpenAI are right about the person whose fate flips in at most 72% of items and answer both twins of a pair correctly in at most 34%. Pointing at the deciding step helps little, and exact geometry given as text barely helps, yet once the deciding calculation and the quantities it needs, including speeds that a still image cannot show, are written out, the same models reach 82-92% on the deciding person, while small open-weight models stay near chance. Physical prediction from a still image therefore fails at the quantitative step: the strongest models use the deciding quantity when they are given it, but do not produce it on their own. For models that plan or act in the physical world, a fluent account of a scene is thus no evidence of a correct prediction: such models must find and compute the deciding quantity unprompted, and DominoBench tests whether they do.

AI.tldr: The authors introduce DominoBench, an 854-item benchmark of 2D rigid-body chain-reaction scenes, finding that 30 evaluated VLMs fail unaided (at most 72% accuracy, 34% on minimal pairs) because they cannot perform the deciding quantitative calculation on their own.
AI.motivation: Although frontier VLMs fluently describe scenes and solve textbook physics problems, it is unclear whether they can predict physical outcomes of multi-step chain reactions from still images.
AI.method: DominoBench comprises 854 still-image items in 427 minimal pairs (where a 1-3 grid-step change flips a person's survival) simulated by a physics engine, paired with a four-rung hint ladder ending in the exact deciding calculation, used to evaluate 30 models across 10 families.
AI.result: Unaided, frontier models from Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI achieve at most 72% accuracy on the deciding person and at most 34% on both twins of a minimal pair; pointing to the deciding step or giving exact text geometry barely helps, whereas providing the explicit deciding calculation and quantities raises frontier accuracy to 82-92% while small open-weight models remain near chance.
AI.conclusion: Fluent scene description does not translate into physical prediction because VLMs fail to identify and compute the deciding quantitative step unprompted.

title: Training-Free Anonymization of Driving Data with Promptable Segmentation and 3D Human Mesh Recovery
summary: Camera recordings for autonomous driving contain faces and license plates that should be anonymized before labeling, sharing, or training. Dedicated detectors can miss small plates and faces behind vehicle glass. We present FM-Anonymize, a training-free anonymization pipeline that combines promptable segmentation, 3D human mesh recovery, and generative replacement. SAM 3 locates people, faces, and vehicles and searches zoomed vehicle crops for plates, occupants, and windows. SAM 3D Body assesses face visibility from head orientation and projects head regions for blurring. Optional diffusion inpainting replaces eligible blurred heads with synthetic faces, guided by estimated pose and keypoints. On PP4AV, the blur pipeline protects 97.8% of faces and 95.5% of plates, the highest privacy recall of all compared methods at their default settings. On our recordings, where the localization thresholds were set, it protects 97.1% of faces and 93.4% of plates, compared with 93.7%/73.0% for UrbanAnonymizer, 42.7%/40.7% for EgoBlur, and 96.6% of faces for deface. Synthetic replacement raises full-body keypoint average precision over blurring from 54.1% to 79.6% on our recordings and from 39.9% to 68.3% on PP4AV. Code and configurations are available on this https URL

AI.tldr: The paper presents FM-Anonymize, a training-free driving-data anonymization pipeline combining SAM 3, SAM 3D Body, and optional diffusion replacement, achieving 97.8% face and 95.5% plate privacy recall on PP4AV while boosting keypoint AP from 39.9% to 68.3%.
AI.motivation: Dedicated detectors used to anonymize autonomous driving footage often miss small license plates and faces occluded behind vehicle glass, while simple blurring degrades downstream pose utility.
AI.method: FM-Anonymize uses SAM 3 to locate people, faces, vehicles, and zoomed vehicle crops (plates, occupants, windows), SAM 3D Body to assess face visibility from head orientation for blurring, and optional pose-guided diffusion inpainting to replace blurred heads with synthetic faces.
AI.result: On PP4AV, the blur pipeline protects 97.8% of faces and 95.5% of plates (highest privacy recall among compared methods), and on in-house recordings it protects 97.1% of faces and 93.4% of plates (vs. 93.7%/73.0% for UrbanAnonymizer and 42.7%/40.7% for EgoBlur); synthetic replacement raises full-body keypoint AP over blurring from 54.1% to 79.6% on in-house data and 39.9% to 68.3% on PP4AV.
AI.conclusion: Combining promptable segmentation, 3D human mesh recovery, and generative face replacement delivers high-recall driving-data anonymization while preserving downstream human-pose utility.

title: InterRSGaussian: Interactive Multi-view Instance Segmentation for 3D Remote Sensing Scenes
summary: Remote sensing image segmentation plays a critical role in various applications. Interactive instance segmentation, a specialized task within image segmentation, aims to generate precise segmentation results for target objects based on user input prompts. However, previous studies on interactive instance segmentation primarily focus on single-view images, limiting their ability to comprehensively understand complex 3D remote sensing scenes. In this study, we extend interactive instance segmentation from a single-view to a multi-view framework, which can also be easily converted to a 3D segmentation format, thus achieving more accurate and comprehensive 3D remote sensing scene perception across multiple views. First, we construct a multi-view interactive instance segmentation dataset for remote sensing, comprising five distinct scenes, each captured from about one hundred different views. Second, we propose InterRSGaussian, a novel instance segmentation method based on 3D Gaussians. InterRSGaussian enables users to provide point clicks on target objects from any arbitrary view and generates view-consistent instance segmentation results across all input views without requiring manual annotations. The resulting multi-view segmentation can further be projected onto 3D point clouds for 3D segmentation. To improve training efficiency and segmentation performance, we introduce a prior distillation network for initialization. Overall, this study extends traditional 2D remote sensing scene perception into a 3D multi-view framework, enabling a more comprehensive understanding of target objects in complex environments with user interactivity.

AI.tldr: This paper extends interactive instance segmentation to 3D remote sensing scenes by introducing a multi-view dataset and InterRSGaussian, a 3D Gaussian Splatting method with prior distillation initialization.
AI.motivation: Existing interactive instance segmentation methods focus on single-view images, limiting their ability to produce view-consistent 3D segmentations for complex remote sensing scenes.
AI.method: The authors construct a multi-view remote sensing dataset of five scenes (~100 views each) and propose InterRSGaussian, which initializes 3D Gaussians via a prior distillation network and propagates user point clicks from any view into view-consistent multi-view masks that can be projected onto 3D point clouds.
AI.result: InterRSGaussian generates view-consistent instance segmentations across all input views from arbitrary single-view clicks without manual multi-view annotations, while prior distillation improves training efficiency and segmentation performance.
AI.conclusion: Lifting interactive point-click segmentation into 3D Gaussian representations enables accurate, view-consistent 3D remote sensing perception with minimal user effort.

title: UrbanTwin Sim2Real LiDAR Challenge 2026: Site-Calibrated Synthetic Data and Multi-Detector Fusion for Roadside 3D Detection
summary: This report summarizes the work submitted by team arnav007 (submission ID 1054222) for the UrbanTwin Sim2Real LiDAR Challenge (V2X-Real track) at the IEEE BigData Cup 2026. The primary objective is to train 3D detectors for vehicles, pedestrians, and trucks using only synthetic roadside LiDAR data, and to generate synthetic scans that are realistic enough to be indistinguishable from real ones. A CARLA based pipeline is developed and calibrated to the fixed sensor site, accurately modeling the range image, including no-return beams, based on unlabelled real development scans. A combined inference detector, using multiple 3D detectors (VoxelNeXt, PV-RCNN, and SECOND) trained exclusively on synthetic data, is also proposed. Each scan is aligned to the synthetic ground plane and processed through the detectors at multiple ground heights. The resulting bounding boxes are fused using bird's-eye view (BEV) clustering, followed by class-specific post-processing to refine heading, box size, and filter low-confidence detections. The final submission achieved a combined score of 0.8947. The ablation study shows that per-scan ground leveling more than doubled the real-scan mAP, while fusing boxes across different heights and models further improved performance.

AI.tldr: This report details team arnav007's 0.8947-score submission to the UrbanTwin Sim2Real LiDAR Challenge 2026, using site-calibrated CARLA synthetic scans, per-scan ground leveling, and multi-detector BEV fusion.
AI.motivation: Training roadside 3D LiDAR detectors for vehicles, pedestrians, and trucks using only synthetic data requires bridging the sim-to-real gap in sensor geometry, no-return beams, and ground-plane alignment.
AI.method: The team calibrates a CARLA pipeline to the fixed sensor site using unlabelled real development scans (including no-return beams), trains VoxelNeXt, PV-RCNN, and SECOND exclusively on synthetic data, and fuses detections across models and multiple ground-leveled heights via BEV clustering and class-specific post-processing.
AI.result: The final submission achieved a combined score of 0.8947 on the V2X-Real track, with ablations showing that per-scan ground leveling more than doubled real-scan mAP and multi-height, multi-model box fusion further improved performance.
AI.conclusion: Site-calibrated synthetic range-image simulation combined with ground-plane leveling and multi-detector BEV fusion enables strong sim-to-real roadside 3D LiDAR detection.

title: ReScene: Incremental Scene Chronology from Sparse Revisits
summary: Scene chronology aims to reconstruct a scene across visits separated by hours or days, during which objects may change in position, presence or shape. Such reconstruction must retain every earlier state, yet each revisit often provides only a few images. Storing a complete model for each visit duplicates the unchanged scene, whereas updating a single shared model alters earlier states. We present ReScene, which stores each visit as an immutable compact update, so that any earlier visit can be recovered exactly by applying the stored updates in order, without retaining past images. To localise each update, ReScene attributes the disagreement between the preceding reconstruction and the new images to individual Gaussians through their compositing weights. This attribution guides the suppression of outdated Gaussians and the refinement of persistent ones, while newly visible surfaces are initialised from learned multi-view depth. We also introduce Multi-State, a benchmark of non-rigid deformation and partial material removal, including synthetic scenes with ground-truth geometry. ReScene achieves quality higher than sequential 3DGS checkpointing with 2.5--4.8$\times$ less uncompressed history storage. At comparable PSNR, it also reduces foreground depth error by 3.2$\times$ relative to sequential ChronoGS, showing that accurate rendering does not necessarily imply accurate geometry. Code and benchmark are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ReScene, which reconstructs scene chronologies from sparse revisits by storing immutable per-visit updates, achieving higher quality than sequential 3DGS checkpointing with 2.5-4.8x less storage and 3.2x lower depth error than ChronoGS.
AI.motivation: Reconstructing scenes across sparse revisits requires preserving every past state, but storing full per-visit models duplicates static geometry while updating a single model overwrites earlier states.
AI.method: ReScene stores each revisit as an immutable compact update so any past state can be recovered in order without old images; it attributes image-reconstruction disagreements to individual Gaussians via compositing weights to suppress outdated Gaussians, refine persistent ones, and initialize new surfaces from learned multi-view depth.
AI.result: On the newly introduced Multi-State benchmark, ReScene outperforms sequential 3DGS checkpointing with 2.5-4.8x less uncompressed history storage and reduces foreground depth error by 3.2x relative to sequential ChronoGS at comparable PSNR.
AI.conclusion: Attributing per-visit disagreements to individual Gaussians for immutable incremental updates enables compact, geometrically accurate 4D scene chronology reconstruction.

title: LEDGE: Separating Critic and Editor Failures in Text-to-Image Self-Correction
summary: Text-to-image (T2I) self-correction combines a vision-language model (VLM) critic that diagnoses errors and proposes instructions with an image editor that executes them. End-to-end evaluation obscures whether failures arise from incorrect diagnoses or an editor unable to execute valid instructions. We introduce LEDGE (Learning Error Diagnosis in Generation and Editing), a framework that separates these bottlenecks. LEDGE compiles oracle edit instructions from GenEval while holding the generated images and the editor fixed, isolating the editor's correction capability from the critic's diagnostic accuracy. On Stable Diffusion 3.5 Large, oracle instructions raise GenEval from 72.0% to 81.2%, versus 74.1% for the baseline VLM critic. Yet 435 of 644 failed images remain unrepaired, exposing a substantial editor gap. We also use oracle labels from disjoint training prompts to supervise the critic. Oracle supervision raises exact diagnosis from 33.3% (the same VLM with our structured output, untrained) to 70.8%. With the same editor, the resulting critic improves GenEval from 42.2% (uncorrected) to 59.4% on Stable Diffusion 1.5, against 50.9% for the baseline critic, and from 72.0% to 76.0% on Stable Diffusion 3.5 Large, despite training only on Stable Diffusion 1.5. Improvements transfer to unseen object classes, a second editor, and independent T2I-CompBench judges and prompts. A small human evaluation confirms the ranking in estimated net corrections but suggests a smaller gain than detector-based evaluation. LEDGE thus distinguishes two limits of self-correction: knowing what to fix and being able to fix it.

AI.tldr: LEDGE decouples critic diagnosis from editor execution in text-to-image self-correction and shows that both components limit performance, while oracle supervision improves critic accuracy and downstream generation.
AI.motivation: End-to-end evaluation of text-to-image self-correction conflates errors from the VLM critic's diagnosis with failures of the image editor to execute valid edit instructions.
AI.method: LEDGE compiles oracle edit instructions from GenEval while holding generated images and the editor fixed to isolate editor capability, and uses oracle labels from disjoint prompts to supervise the VLM critic.
AI.result: On Stable Diffusion 3.5 Large, oracle instructions raise GenEval from 72.0% to 81.2% versus 74.1% for the baseline critic, yet 435 of 644 failed images remain unrepaired; oracle supervision raises exact diagnosis from 33.3% to 70.8% and improves GenEval to 59.4% on SD 1.5 and 76.0% on SD 3.5 Large, transferring across object classes, a second editor, and T2I-CompBench.
AI.conclusion: Separating diagnostic accuracy from editing capability clarifies the two distinct bottlenecks in text-to-image self-correction.

title: VISTA: A Framework for Vision-Informed Semantic Traffic Awareness
comment: 8 pages, 4 figures, Accepted for publication in IEEE Internet of Things Magazine, 2026
summary: The Internet of Things (IoT) is transforming intelligent transportation systems by connecting roadside cameras, edge computing units, vehicles, and traffic infrastructure into a shared sensing and decision-making ecosystem. However, transmitting raw traffic video over vehicle-to-everything (V2X) links is bandwidth-intensive, while deploying large multimodal models directly on resource-constrained vehicles is often impractical. To address these limitations, this article proposes VISTA (Vision-Informed Semantic Traffic Awareness), a multimodal vision-language edge-intelligence framework that combines predictive video representation learning with lightweight language-based reasoning to provide communication-efficient traffic situational awareness. In the proposed architecture, roadside surveillance units employ the Video Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (V-JEPA) and an attentive-pooler module to convert traffic video clips into compact future-scene embeddings. These embeddings are transmitted through V2X links to vehicle-mounted systems, where a TinyLlama small language model, enhanced with a custom visual adapter, interprets the embeddings alongside natural-language (NL) traffic queries. VISTA enables vehicles to obtain interpretable traffic information, reason about upcoming scene dynamics, and identify potential collision risks without receiving raw video streams. Experimental results in a digital-twin urban traffic environment show that VISTA achieves 97.77% accuracy and an 89% F1 score for future collision prediction while reducing the communication payload by several orders of magnitude compared with raw RGB video transmission. These results demonstrate the feasibility of embedding-based multimodal intelligence for low-latency, communication-efficient, and safety-oriented IoT-enabled transportation systems.

AI.tldr: VISTA is a multimodal edge-intelligence framework that transmits compact V-JEPA future-scene embeddings over V2X links to a vehicle-mounted TinyLlama model for communication-efficient traffic awareness and collision prediction.
AI.motivation: Transmitting raw traffic video over V2X links consumes excessive bandwidth, while deploying large multimodal models directly on resource-constrained vehicles is impractical.
AI.method: Roadside units use V-JEPA with an attentive-pooler module to encode traffic video clips into compact future-scene embeddings, which are sent over V2X to a TinyLlama model equipped with a custom visual adapter to answer natural-language traffic queries.
AI.result: In a digital-twin urban traffic environment, VISTA achieves 97.77% accuracy and an 89% F1 score for future collision prediction while reducing communication payload by several orders of magnitude compared with raw RGB video.
AI.conclusion: Embedding-based multimodal intelligence enables low-latency, bandwidth-efficient, and safety-oriented situational awareness in IoT-enabled transportation systems.

title: LiveView: Real-Time Camera-Controlled Re-filming of Streaming Videos
summary: Real-time camera-controlled video re-filming aims to synthesize target views from a streaming source video under online user-specified camera trajectories. This task poses two key challenges: maintaining synchronization and content consistency across views, and achieving low-latency rendering with long-horizon stability. Existing approaches are predominantly designed for offline full-sequence processing and rely on bidirectional attention or costly depth-based geometric preprocessing, making them unsuitable for low-latency streaming scenarios. To address these limitations, we develop a teacher-to-student framework that distills a high-fidelity bidirectional re-filming teacher into a few-step causal autoregressive student. We introduce Cross-Frame Injection to interleave each incoming source frame with its synchronized target latent, thereby establishing direct cross-view correspondence and improving content consistency. To ensure stable long-horizon generation, we further propose Shared Relative RoPE, which bounds temporal indices within the pretrained range, and Cycle Streaming Tuning, which exposes the student to extended cyclic trajectories during streaming training. These designs enable low-latency online video re-filming with precise camera control and sustained spatiotemporal consistency over long streaming rollouts.

AI.tldr: LiveView distills a bidirectional video re-filming teacher into a causal autoregressive student for real-time, camera-controlled re-filming of streaming videos with long-horizon stability.
AI.motivation: Existing camera-controlled video re-filming methods rely on offline bidirectional attention or costly depth preprocessing, making them unsuitable for low-latency streaming and long-horizon rollouts.
AI.method: LiveView uses teacher-to-student distillation into a few-step causal autoregressive student, combining Cross-Frame Injection to interleave source frames with synchronized target latents, Shared Relative RoPE to bound temporal indices, and Cycle Streaming Tuning on cyclic trajectories.
AI.result: The proposed designs achieve low-latency online video re-filming with precise camera control and sustained spatiotemporal consistency over long streaming rollouts.
AI.conclusion: Causal autoregressive distillation with cross-frame injection and bounded temporal encodings enables real-time camera-controlled re-filming of streaming video.

title: Improving X-Ray Baggage Instance Segmentation with Shared Point-Based Mask Refinement
summary: Overlapping projections and complex object contours make prohibited items difficult to delineate in X-ray baggage images. This study investigates shared point-based mask refinement to improve instance segmentation within Cascade Mask R-CNN. The framework combines a ResNet-101 backbone with an attention-based feature pyramid and progressively updates uncertain mask locations, increasing mask resolution from $28 \times 28$ to $112 \times 112$. A single refinement module is shared across cascade stages and refinement levels, with transformer and multilayer perceptron (MLP) variants used to examine the role of interactions among selected points. Ten configurations were evaluated on the official PIXray split across three training seeds using the original target-instance annotations for evaluation. The transformer and MLP refiners achieved mean mask average precision (AP) of 71.79 and 72.47, respectively, compared with 70.50 for the unrefined detector, yielding gains of 1.29 and 1.97 AP points. The MLP achieved the highest mean mask AP among the evaluated configurations. Both variants also improved boundary agreement on commonly detected objects, supporting improved mask delineation, while detection diagnostics did not establish a corresponding positive gain. These findings demonstrate that shared point-based refinement can improve segmentation quality in the tested cascade architecture using existing target-mask annotations, without additional occluder supervision. Evaluation on independent X-ray datasets is needed to determine how well these improvements generalize.

AI.tldr: Shared point-based mask refinement within Cascade Mask R-CNN improves instance segmentation of prohibited items in X-ray baggage images on the PIXray dataset without extra occluder supervision.
AI.motivation: Overlapping projections and complex object contours make prohibited items difficult to delineate in X-ray baggage images.
AI.method: The framework pairs a ResNet-101 backbone and attention-based feature pyramid with a single point-based refinement module (transformer or MLP) shared across cascade stages and refinement levels to progressively update uncertain mask locations from 28x28 to 112x112 resolution.
AI.result: Across three seeds on the official PIXray split, the transformer and MLP refiners achieve 71.79 and 72.47 mean mask AP compared with 70.50 for the unrefined detector, improving boundary agreement on commonly detected objects without a corresponding positive detection gain.
AI.conclusion: Shared point-based mask refinement enhances segmentation delineation in cascade X-ray detectors using existing target-mask annotations, though generalization to independent X-ray datasets remains to be tested.

title: Beyond Seeing: Fine-Grained Preference Validation and Severity-Aware Alignment for Mitigating Visual Hallucinations in Vision-Language Models
comment: 9 pages, 2 figures, 6 tables. Includes a 4-page supplementary appendix with experimental details, equations, prompt templates, and additional comparisons
summary: Large vision-language models can produce fluent responses containing objects, attributes, or relations unsupported by the image. We study an implemented alignment pipeline that normalizes released fine-grained hallucination supervision, validates chosen-rejected preference pairs with vision-language judges, repairs rejected chosen responses, and trains LLaVA adapters with standard or severity-aware direct preference optimization. The study uses 16,143 normalized feedback records and 8,386 released preference pairs, comparing direct training with zero-shot and two-shot judged severity-margin variants. The zero-shot variant reduces Object HalBench CHAIRs from 53.00 to 36.00 and CHAIRi from 15.72 to 10.41. Across aligned models, AMBER-Hal decreases from 35.90 to 25.10-26.90, accompanied by reduced visual coverage. In contrast, the base model retains the highest valid POPE adversarial F1, 84.18 versus 83.87-83.91 after alignment. These results support benchmark-dependent reductions in generative hallucination rather than uniform superiority of severity-aware alignment. We distinguish implemented pipeline components from the preference paths used in the reported experiments and discuss the limits of attributing gains to judging, repair, or the training objective individually.

AI.tldr: This study evaluates a preference-validation and severity-aware direct preference optimization pipeline for mitigating visual hallucinations in LLaVA models, finding benchmark-dependent reductions rather than uniform gains.
AI.motivation: Large vision-language models frequently generate fluent responses containing objects, attributes, or relations unsupported by the input image.
AI.method: The pipeline normalizes 16,143 fine-grained hallucination feedback records, validates 8,386 chosen-rejected preference pairs with vision-language judges, repairs rejected chosen responses, and trains LLaVA adapters using standard or zero-shot/two-shot judged severity-margin direct preference optimization.
AI.result: The zero-shot variant reduces Object HalBench CHAIRs from 53.00 to 36.00 and CHAIRi from 15.72 to 10.41, and AMBER-Hal drops from 35.90 to 25.10-26.90 with reduced visual coverage, whereas the base model retains the highest valid POPE adversarial F1 at 84.18 versus 83.87-83.91.
AI.conclusion: Fine-grained preference alignment yields benchmark-dependent reductions in generative hallucination rather than uniform superiority for severity-aware objectives.

title: How Reliable Is Visual Token Selection? Rethinking Pruning in Multimodal LLMs
comment: Accepted to Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EACL 2027
summary: Visual token pruning improves the efficiency of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) by removing redundant visual tokens, yet the reliability of existing selection signals has not been systematically examined. We analyze token selection under semantics-preserving perturbations and across representative pruning criteria, revealing two limitations. First, attention-based importance shifts non-uniformly under perturbations, so magnitude alone cannot distinguish stable evidence from unstable saliency (local instability). Second, attention- and diversity-based methods select substantially different subsets despite comparable performance, showing that useful evidence is not confined to a unique subset (global inconsistency). These findings motivate reliable token-set construction. We instantiate this perspective in CoRePruner, a training-free framework combining instruction-aware diversity with reliability-aware attention. Across image benchmarks, multiple MLLM architectures, and token budgets, CoRePruner improves performance, especially under aggressive pruning, and remains competitive on video benchmarks. Our results establish reliability as a central consideration in visual token selection.

AI.tldr: CoRePruner is a training-free visual token pruning framework for multimodal LLMs that combines instruction-aware diversity with reliability-aware attention to address instability and inconsistency in token selection.
AI.motivation: Existing visual token pruning methods have not systematically examined selection reliability, suffering from local instability under semantics-preserving perturbations and global inconsistency across different selection criteria.
AI.method: CoRePruner constructs reliable token sets without training by integrating instruction-aware diversity with reliability-aware attention based on the observed sensitivity of attention importance.
AI.result: Across image benchmarks, multiple MLLM architectures, and token budgets, CoRePruner improves performance, particularly under aggressive pruning, while remaining competitive on video benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Accounting for token-selection reliability is critical for effective visual token pruning in multimodal large language models.

title: VoxSAOR: Semantic-Aware Occupancy Robustification via Aleatoric Uncertainty Modeling
comment: The source code will be made publicly available at this https URL
summary: Vision-based 3D occupancy prediction provides a dense semantic representation of scenes for autonomous driving and embodied perception, yet remains vulnerable to occlusion, depth ambiguity, and projection errors that induce spatially varying reliability in voxel features. Existing methods typically map voxel representations to semantic predictions without explicitly modeling such observation-induced feature variations. To address this limitation, we propose VoxSAOR, a semantic-aware occupancy robustification framework that models aleatoric uncertainty through feature-space proxies. It first quantifies Local Semantic Consistency (LSC) to derive a voxel-wise structural stability prior and uses cross-view semantic consensus to filter unreliable semantic correspondences. Within each semantic category, spatially matched stable and ambiguous voxels form stable-to-ambiguous feature transitions, which are modeled by a class-conditional diagonal Gaussian distribution, capturing both feature displacement and dispersion. Guided by these proxy distributions, Aleatoric Regime Ensemble Learning (AREL) trains independently parameterized prediction heads using feature perturbations at progressively increasing scales, with perturbation strength modulated by structural reliability. At inference, proxy modeling and sampling are disabled, and all heads process the same observed features; their output probabilities are then averaged to produce a deterministic consensus prediction without requiring sampling. Experiments across multiple datasets and occupancy backbones demonstrate the effectiveness of VoxSAOR in improving semantic occupancy prediction, long-tail recognition, and predictive calibration. The source code will be made publicly available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: VoxSAOR models aleatoric uncertainty in vision-based 3D occupancy prediction via feature-space proxies and ensemble training, improving semantic accuracy, long-tail recognition, and calibration without inference-time sampling.
AI.motivation: Vision-based 3D occupancy prediction suffers from occlusion, depth ambiguity, and projection errors that cause spatially varying voxel feature reliability, which existing deterministic mappings do not explicitly model.
AI.method: VoxSAOR quantifies Local Semantic Consistency and cross-view consensus to build class-conditional diagonal Gaussian proxy distributions over stable-to-ambiguous voxel transitions, then trains independent prediction heads with Aleatoric Regime Ensemble Learning under reliability-modulated perturbations and averages their outputs deterministically at inference.
AI.result: Experiments across multiple datasets and occupancy backbones show that VoxSAOR improves semantic occupancy prediction, long-tail recognition, and predictive calibration.
AI.conclusion: Proxy-based aleatoric uncertainty modeling and ensemble training enhance 3D occupancy robustness without adding sampling overhead at inference.

title: What the Averages Hide: Monocular Metric Depth Models Still Fail in Everyday Scenes, Mostly on Scale
summary: Zero-shot monocular metric depth models are evaluated by averaging metric and scale-aligned scores across datasets. Averages cannot show how many images still have severely wrong metric depth, whether depth is under- or overestimated, or whether different models fail on the same images. We propose an evaluation built on per-image results: the failure rate (metric $\delta_1$ < 0.5); scale-aligned metrics for structure, and the bias, dispersion and absolute error of the alignment scale for scale; and a cross-model comparison that separates shared from model-specific failures. We apply it to 11 recent architectures with and without ground-truth intrinsics (18 model evaluations) on the 7 everyday-scene benchmarks (4,406 images) used by MoGe-2. Metric depth estimation is not solved in everyday scenes, and the remaining difficulty is mainly scale: the best of the 18 evaluations still has a failure rate of 7.7% (datasets weighted equally); pooled over all failures, 78.8% have intact structure, and after scale correction 98.3% no longer fail. Images failed by at least 6 architectures make up 7.3% of the data, concentrated on HAMMER and DIODE; even when selected only by architectures of other families, they hold 34% to 40% of the error of the top 6 models, against 14% to 18% for as many random images from the same datasets. Adding objects reduces the scale error of most models; ground-truth intrinsics and, in most families, larger models reduce the failures but do not remove them. We recommend reporting failure rates, structure and scale separately, and results stratified by how many models fail. We will release the code, the per-image results with shared-failure labels, and two diagnostic sets built from TUM RGB-D.

AI.tldr: A per-image evaluation of 11 zero-shot monocular metric depth architectures across 7 everyday-scene benchmarks reveals that models still fail on at least 7.7% of images, primarily due to scale errors rather than structure.
AI.motivation: Averaging metric and scale-aligned scores across datasets hides how often monocular metric depth models fail severely, whether depth is systematically biased, and whether failures are shared across architectures.
AI.method: The authors evaluate 18 model configurations (with and without ground-truth intrinsics) on 4,406 images from 7 MoGe-2 benchmarks using per-image failure rate (metric delta_1 < 0.5), scale-aligned structure metrics, alignment-scale bias and error, and cross-model failure overlap.
AI.result: The best configuration still has a 7.7% failure rate; across all failures, 78.8% preserve intact structure and 98.3% pass after scale correction, while 7.3% of images (concentrated on HAMMER and DIODE) fail for at least 6 architectures and account for 34% to 40% of the top 6 models' error.
AI.conclusion: Monocular metric depth estimation remains unsolved in everyday scenes due to scale failures, warranting per-image failure reporting and separate structure and scale evaluation.

title: AFRNet: Adaptive Frequency Redistribution Network for Image Deraining
summary: Image deraining aims to recover rain-free images from rain-degraded observations. Recent frequency-aware deraining methods have demonstrated promising performance by removing rain artifacts in the spectral domain. However, since rain artifacts and background textures often appear in several correlated subbands, prior frequency-domain deraining models still enhance frequency subbands separately. Such band-wise processing limits information exchange across subbands. Without context from other subbands, rain and clean content that appear together in one subband cannot be separated. This leads to either residual rain streaks or over-smoothing of fine details. To address this limitation, we propose AFRNet, an Adaptive Frequency Redistribution Network for image deraining. First, we introduce an Adaptive Frequency Recombination Module (AFRM) that performs cross-band modulation among wavelet subbands, enabling information interaction and adaptive recombination of degraded frequency components. We then develop a Subband Compensation Block (SCB) that compensates for decoder subband degradation by leveraging encoder subband features through inter-subband attention in the wavelet domain, alleviating detail loss during reconstruction. Extensive experiments demonstrate that AFRNet achieves competitive performance and consistent results across diverse deraining benchmarks.

AI.tldr: AFRNet is a wavelet-domain image deraining network that enables cross-band feature modulation and encoder-decoder subband compensation to remove rain streaks without over-smoothing details.
AI.motivation: Existing frequency-aware deraining methods enhance wavelet subbands independently, preventing cross-band context exchange needed to separate rain artifacts from background textures.
AI.method: AFRNet introduces an Adaptive Frequency Recombination Module for cross-band modulation among wavelet subbands and a Subband Compensation Block that uses inter-subband attention to transfer encoder subband features to the decoder.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across diverse deraining benchmarks show that AFRNet achieves competitive and consistent restoration performance.
AI.conclusion: Cross-band modulation and inter-subband compensation in the wavelet domain improve the separation of rain streaks from fine background textures.

title: SmoothShift: Disrupting Visual Adversarial Attacks on LVLMs at Test Time
summary: Visual adversarial perturbations can substantially impair large vision-language models (LVLMs) despite introducing only subtle input changes. To understand how these small changes cause substantial errors, we investigate their optimization and propagation through the model, revealing two key findings. First, stronger attacks rely on finer iterative optimization, while subtle input perturbations induce representation discrepancies that are amplified layer by layer through the vision encoder and persist in the language model. Second, disrupting the alignment between within-patch input patterns and the model's computation reduces clean-adversarial representation discrepancies and substantially weakens attacks. Together, these findings suggest that adversarial effectiveness depends on both fine-grained perturbation patterns and their coupling with the model's computation. Motivated by these findings, we propose SmoothShift, a lightweight, training-free defense that combines local smoothing and spatial transformations. Smoothing weakens fine-grained perturbation patterns, while spatial transformations disrupt their alignment with the encoder's patch grid. SmoothShift requires no model updates, auxiliary networks, or additional model inference. Experiments cover three LVLM families on four datasets and robustly fine-tuned Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP) models on eight classification datasets. Evaluations across eight attack methods and multiple perturbation budgets demonstrate improved robustness while largely preserving clean performance. SmoothShift also provides robustness gains under defense-aware attacks using mixed-gradient BPDA with EOT.

AI.tldr: SmoothShift is a lightweight, training-free test-time defense that disrupts visual adversarial attacks on LVLMs and CLIP models using local smoothing and spatial transformations.
AI.motivation: Subtle visual adversarial perturbations amplify layer by layer through LVLM vision encoders and persist in the language model by exploiting fine-grained patterns aligned with patch-grid computation.
AI.method: SmoothShift applies local smoothing to weaken fine-grained perturbation patterns and spatial transformations to break their alignment with the vision encoder's patch grid, requiring no model updates, auxiliary networks, or extra inference.
AI.result: Evaluated across three LVLM families on four datasets and robustly fine-tuned CLIP models on eight classification datasets under eight attack methods, SmoothShift improves robustness while largely preserving clean performance, including under defense-aware BPDA+EOT attacks.
AI.conclusion: Disrupting perturbation-patch alignment and fine-grained patterns at test time provides an effective, zero-training defense against visual adversarial attacks.

title: Learning a Task-Adaptive Low-Dimensional Semantic Space for Improved Visual Classification
summary: Semantic visual classification commonly aligns visual embeddings with semantic spaces induced by pretrained text encoders. However, such spaces are typically high-dimensional, weakly aligned with visual feature geometry, and insufficiently discriminative for downstream classification tasks. We propose TaSS, a framework for learning a task-adaptive low-dimensional semantic space that preserves semantic structure while explicitly optimizing class separability. TaSS is constructed through a parameterized geometry transformation of pretrained text embeddings that enlarges inter-class margins via distance reshaping and improves intra-class compactness through prototype-preserving semantic constraints. The resulting semantic space maintains meaningful semantic relationships while producing a discriminative geometry tailored for classification. Frozen visual encoder features are subsequently aligned to TaSS using a lightweight MLP, enabling improved discriminative learning without fine-tuning pretrained backbones. We further provide theoretical analysis showing that TaSS preserves semantic consistency while enforcing enhanced inter-class separation and controlled intra-class variance. Extensive experiments on skeleton-based human action recognition, video classification, and image classification benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over existing semantic alignment approaches, with gains exceeding 3 percentage points on average and up to 8.5 points on challenging datasets.

AI.tldr: TaSS learns a task-adaptive, low-dimensional semantic space from pretrained text embeddings to improve visual classification with frozen visual backbones.
AI.motivation: Semantic spaces from pretrained text encoders are high-dimensional, weakly aligned with visual feature geometry, and insufficiently discriminative for downstream visual classification.
AI.method: TaSS applies a parameterized geometric transformation to pretrained text embeddings that enlarges inter-class margins via distance reshaping and enforces intra-class compactness via prototype-preserving constraints, then aligns frozen visual features to this space with a lightweight MLP.
AI.result: Across skeleton-based action recognition, video classification, and image classification benchmarks, TaSS outperforms existing semantic alignment methods by over 3 percentage points on average and up to 8.5 points on challenging datasets.
AI.conclusion: Reshaping text-induced semantic spaces for task-specific discriminability enables stronger visual classification without fine-tuning pretrained visual backbones.

title: PerturbJEPA: Joint-Embedding Predictive Learning of Cellular Perturbation Responses
comment: 23 pages, 6 figures, 14 tables. Code: this https URL
summary: Identifying the drug and dose that produced a cellular response requires preserving treatment effects within each cellular background. A joint-embedding predictor can match its targets while ignoring the intervention if its encoder preserves differences across backgrounds but erases differences between treated and control populations within each one. We call this failure interventional contrast collapse. PerturbJEPA encodes the difference in mean gene expression between treated and control populations as an effect vector. It aligns the displacement between their latent centroids with this vector and regularizes the vectors to preserve variation across population pairs. We show that the measured displacements cannot all coincide within a batch when effect-vector variation exceeds the root-mean-square alignment error. Trained with separate drug and dose ranking objectives, the model predicts candidate responses from a common control population and matches them to the observed response without cell pairing or expression reconstruction. We evaluate 3,592 Tahoe-100M queries on held-out combinations of known interventions and cellular backgrounds, each with over 700 drug-dose candidates in a fixed, background-specific catalog. PerturbJEPA achieves 91.46% macro joint drug-dose Recall@1, exceeding STATE by 3.40 percentage points (95% drug-cluster bootstrap interval of 1.72 to 5.07 points). Controlled diagnostics show that treatment-control differences can shrink even when representations remain globally dispersed. With the drug ranking objective fixed, adding effect-vector regularization to alignment raises joint Recall@1 from 18.57% to 87.47%.

AI.tldr: PerturbJEPA is a joint-embedding predictive learning framework that prevents interventional contrast collapse and achieves 91.46% macro joint drug-dose Recall@1 on held-out Tahoe-100M cellular perturbation queries.
AI.motivation: Joint-embedding predictors can suffer from interventional contrast collapse, preserving cellular background differences while erasing treatment-versus-control differences within each background.
AI.method: PerturbJEPA encodes mean gene-expression differences between treated and control populations as effect vectors, aligns latent centroid displacements to these vectors, regularizes effect-vector variation across population pairs, and trains with separate drug and dose ranking objectives without cell pairing or reconstruction.
AI.result: On 3,592 held-out Tahoe-100M queries with over 700 drug-dose candidates each, PerturbJEPA reaches 91.46% macro joint drug-dose Recall@1, outperforming STATE by 3.40 percentage points, while adding effect-vector regularization raises joint Recall@1 from 18.57% to 87.47%.
AI.conclusion: Explicit effect-vector alignment and regularization prevent contrast collapse and enable accurate zero-pairing prediction of cellular perturbation responses.

title: SCoRe: Support-Calibrated Role Fusion for Training-Free Cross-Domain Few-Shot Segmentation
summary: We present SCoRe (Support-Calibrated Role fusion), a framework to utilize two complementary vision foundation model-based (VFM) segmenters for training-free cross-domain few-shot segmentation (CD-FSS). Our approach is based on the observation that current VFMs for CD-FSS possess capabilities where one model locates the correct object, while another model computes the better contour. Our approach uses: 1. a method to identify a VFM segmenter to lead Few-Shot Segmentation (FSS) task for a given concept, 2. a novel deterministic boundary correction method using bands of near- and far-pixels at the lead segmenter's predicted boundary of an object, and 3. a region correction mechanism for the other segmenter to conservatively prune components, fill holes, and bridge short gaps on the lead segmenter's predicted masks to improve accuracy. We evaluate SCoRe using RSRM and FSS-SAM3 across 3,314 matched five-shot episodes from 10 datasets. SCoRe achieves 72.738% foreground mIoU averaged across datasets, a gain of 5.210 percentage points over RSRM (paired 95% CI [4.618, 5.972]), with per-dataset gains up to 8.461 points over the strongest standalone method and the best point estimate on 7 of 10 datasets.

AI.tldr: SCoRe is a training-free cross-domain few-shot segmentation framework that fuses complementary vision foundation model segmenters via role selection, boundary correction, and region refinement.
AI.motivation: Existing vision foundation model segmenters for cross-domain few-shot segmentation exhibit complementary strengths, where one model locates the target object better while another produces sharper contours.
AI.method: SCoRe selects a lead segmenter per concept, applies deterministic boundary correction using near- and far-pixel bands around the predicted boundary, and uses the secondary segmenter for conservative region pruning, hole filling, and gap bridging.
AI.result: Evaluated with RSRM and FSS-SAM3 across 3,314 five-shot episodes from 10 datasets, SCoRe achieves 72.738% average foreground mIoU, outperforming RSRM by 5.210 percentage points and achieving the best point estimate on 7 of 10 datasets.
AI.conclusion: Calibrated role fusion between complementary foundation-model segmenters substantially improves training-free cross-domain few-shot segmentation.

title: From Joint Risk to Decision Invariance: Decision-Preserving Regularization for Exemplar-Free Class-Incremental Learning
summary: Exemplar-free continual learning seeks to minimize joint risk over all seen tasks, yet historical data are unavailable for direct optimization. We observe that, for classification, preserving the model's decisions on previously learned classes helps retain old knowledge. This motivates Decision-Preserving Regularization (DPR). Penalizing changes in all pairwise old-class logit margins reduces algebraically to a centered relative-logit penalty. We further apply spectral whitening to remove the classifier's spectral scale bias. Because the global classifier supplies the decision constraints for the next stage, it must remain calibrated across all seen classes despite the drift of stored old-class statistics during representation updates. We therefore fit a closed-form affine map from paired current-task features to transport old-class Gaussian means and covariances into the updated feature space, then calibrate the global classifier using these distributions and current-task features. Across CIFAR-100, Tiny-ImageNet, ImageNet-Subset, and ImageNet-1K under cold-start protocols, comparisons with state-of-the-art methods show that DPR achieves higher accuracy in most settings while remaining highly efficient. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Decision-Preserving Regularization (DPR) mitigates forgetting in exemplar-free class-incremental learning by preserving relative old-class logit margins and transporting old-class Gaussian statistics via a closed-form affine map.
AI.motivation: Exemplar-free continual learning must minimize joint risk without historical data, while representation drift invalidates stored old-class statistics and uncalibrated classifiers degrade prior decisions.
AI.method: DPR penalizes changes in pairwise old-class logit margins (which reduces to a centered relative-logit penalty), applies spectral whitening to remove classifier scale bias, and fits a closed-form affine map from paired current-task features to transport old-class means and covariances for global classifier calibration.
AI.result: Under cold-start protocols on CIFAR-100, Tiny-ImageNet, ImageNet-Subset, and ImageNet-1K, DPR achieves higher accuracy than state-of-the-art baselines in most settings while remaining highly efficient.
AI.conclusion: Preserving relative decision margins and transporting drifted class statistics enables effective, efficient exemplar-free class-incremental learning.

title: Example-Based Spatial Guidance for Training-Free Concept Erasure in Diffusion Models
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 (poster). 51 pages, including references, checklist, and appendix
summary: Text-to-image (T2I) diffusion models often synthesize policy-violating content, necessitating robust safeguards and rigorous evaluation frameworks. However, current approaches remain largely monolithic in both execution and evaluation, limited to coarse-grained categorization within broad unsafe concepts. Such approaches fail to account for the specific constituent factors of a violation, resulting in weak learning signals and allowing model collapse to bypass safety checks. To overcome these limitations, we propose Example-Based Spatial Guidance (EBSG), a training-free method that utilizes user-editable exemplar packs to provide granular spatial guidance for precise concept steering. Unlike existing methods that coarsely steer the entire image away from a broad concept, EBSG decomposes these categories into specific sub-concepts via exemplar text-image pairs, providing explicit, localized steering signals for more robust safety control. Furthermore, we introduce a vision language model (VLM)-based evaluation protocol that provides a fine-grained assessment, avoiding the pitfall of conventional binary evaluators that permit model collapse to bypass safety checks. Empirically, EBSG achieves state-of-the-art erasure performance across diverse safety datasets and concept categories, spanning four nudity benchmarks, seven I2P harmful-concept slices, and four MJA metaphor categories, while supporting multi-concept removal and transferring to a modern backbone, SD3.

AI.tldr: Example-Based Spatial Guidance (EBSG) is a training-free diffusion concept-erasure method that uses user-editable exemplar packs for localized spatial steering, paired with a fine-grained VLM evaluation protocol.
AI.motivation: Existing concept-erasure methods rely on coarse, monolithic steering and binary evaluators, resulting in weak learning signals and vulnerability to model collapse that bypasses safety checks.
AI.method: EBSG decomposes broad unsafe concepts into specific sub-concepts using exemplar text-image pairs to provide localized spatial guidance during generation, and introduces a VLM-based evaluation protocol to assess fine-grained safety without binary-evaluator loopholes.
AI.result: EBSG achieves state-of-the-art erasure across four nudity benchmarks, seven I2P harmful-concept slices, and four MJA metaphor categories, while supporting multi-concept removal and transferring to SD3.
AI.conclusion: Granular, exemplar-driven spatial guidance and VLM-based evaluation provide more robust and controllable concept erasure in text-to-image diffusion models.

title: ASCG: Adaptive Spatial Classifier Guidance for Surgical Concept Suppression in Diffusion Models
comment: 9 pages, including references and supplementary material
summary: While text-to-image (T2I) diffusion models achieve remarkable quality, they risk producing harmful content. Existing safety mechanisms often rely on indiscriminate, global interventions that induce unintended semantic drift and degrade image quality. To address this, we propose Adaptive Spatial Classifier Guidance (ASCG), a necessity-driven framework that employs probabilistic monitoring to activate guidance selectively upon harm detection. By leveraging Grad-CAM for localized suppression, ASCG effectively removes harmful concepts while preserving superior semantic fidelity compared to conventional methods. Furthermore, we overcome the limitations of traditional metrics like NudeNet---which fails to assess semantic integrity---by introducing a VLM-based evaluation framework to provide a fine-grained, robust analysis of both safety and context preservation. Our results demonstrate that ASCG not only balances safety and fidelity but also exhibits remarkable plug-and-play synergy with existing frameworks to establish state-of-the-art performance.

AI.tldr: ASCG is a necessity-driven diffusion safety framework that uses probabilistic harm detection and Grad-CAM spatial guidance to suppress harmful concepts while preserving semantic fidelity.
AI.motivation: Indiscriminate global safety interventions in text-to-image diffusion models cause unintended semantic drift and degrade image quality, while metrics like NudeNet fail to measure semantic integrity.
AI.method: ASCG monitors generation probabilistically to activate guidance only when harm is detected, uses Grad-CAM for localized concept suppression, and introduces a VLM-based evaluation framework to jointly assess safety and context preservation.
AI.result: Experiments show that ASCG balances safety and semantic fidelity and integrates in a plug-and-play manner with existing frameworks to achieve state-of-the-art performance.
AI.conclusion: Selective, spatially localized classifier guidance removes harmful diffusion content without sacrificing benign image semantics.

title: PixelBench: Evaluating Language Models for Pixel-Art Creation
summary: Pixel art is widely used in games and digital content creation, requiring readable forms, coherent spatial relationships, and harmonious colors under limited resolution and palette constraints. Language models show growing promise in visual creation, yet their pixel art creation capabilities lack systematic evaluation. We introduce PixelBench, formalizing text-to-image generation and instruction-guided editing for pixel art and providing a benchmark for these tasks. We further present a creation environment in which language model agents invoke drawing tools through code to generate and edit pixel art. We assess the quality of generated artwork through human evaluation and employ a multimodal large language model as a judge, validating the agreement between its automated assessments and human preferences. We compare language models and configurations across diverse subjects and canvas sizes. In our experiments, GPT-6 Astra achieves both the highest average judge score and the best average human rank, highlighting the potential of general-purpose language models for pixel art creation. We release the tasks, all artworks, the human rankings, and the judge protocol.

AI.tldr: PixelBench is a benchmark and code-driven drawing environment for evaluating language models on text-to-image pixel-art generation and instruction-guided editing.
AI.motivation: Although language models show promise in visual creation, their ability to produce readable, palette-constrained pixel art has lacked systematic evaluation.
AI.method: PixelBench formalizes text-to-image generation and instruction-guided editing for pixel art in an environment where LM agents invoke drawing tools via code, evaluated through both human rankings and a validated multimodal LLM judge.
AI.result: Across diverse subjects and canvas sizes, GPT-6 Astra achieves both the highest average judge score and the best average human rank.
AI.conclusion: PixelBench establishes a standardized testbed and dataset for evaluating and advancing code-based pixel-art creation by language models.

title: Event-Guided Stereo Video Super-Resolution
summary: Stereo Video Super-Resolution (SVSR) aims to reconstruct high-resolution stereo videos by exploiting temporal cues across consecutive frames and complementary spatial cues between stereo views. However, existing methods struggle to recover high-frequency texture details under rapid motion and complex illumination, compromising reconstruction quality and stereo consistency. Event cameras provide valuable motion and texture cues with high temporal resolution and wide dynamic range, yet their potential for SVSR remains underexplored. To bridge this gap, we present the first investigation of event-guided SVSR and propose a novel framework. Specifically, we develop an Event-Guided Texture Enhancement (EGTE) module that combines bidirectional temporal feature propagation with event-guided texture refinement to restore high-frequency details in complex motion regions. Subsequently, we introduce a Cross-View Texture Interaction (CVTI) module to model cross-view spatial correspondences and aggregate cross-view complementary texture information. With this design, our method effectively integrates event-driven motion and texture information, inter-frame temporal dependencies, and cross-view spatial relationships to recover motion-affected details and maintain stereo consistency. Extensive experiments on both real-world and synthetic datasets demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms existing super-resolution methods in reconstruction quality and stereo consistency. Project Page: this https URL

AI.tldr: This paper introduces an event-guided stereo video super-resolution framework that combines event-driven texture enhancement with cross-view interaction to restore high-frequency details under rapid motion.
AI.motivation: Existing stereo video super-resolution methods struggle to recover high-frequency textures under rapid motion and complex illumination, degrading both visual quality and stereo consistency.
AI.method: The framework uses an Event-Guided Texture Enhancement (EGTE) module combining bidirectional temporal propagation with event-guided refinement, followed by a Cross-View Texture Interaction (CVTI) module to aggregate complementary spatial cues across stereo views.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on real-world and synthetic datasets show that the method consistently outperforms existing super-resolution approaches in reconstruction quality and stereo consistency.
AI.conclusion: Integrating high-temporal-resolution event cues with cross-view interaction effectively resolves motion blur and preserves stereo consistency in video super-resolution.

title: Instructions Before Actions: Prospective and Retrospective Language Supervision for Driving Vision-Language-Action Data
summary: Driving vision-language-action (VLA) models can accept navigation instructions, yet predicting a driver's trajectory does not establish that a model follows the instruction. We study how driving-language supervision is collected and evaluated, distinguishing prospective instructions issued before an action from retrospective labels written after observing it. We develop ADVLAT-Engine to synchronize spoken instructions, road-scene video, and vehicle trajectories, and compare three navigation apps on 48 replayed routes. On 87 maneuvers announced by both Google Maps and a passenger, the passenger uses more scene-dependent language. We evaluate four open driving VLAs before and after fine-tuning on prospective navigation-app drives. Fine-tuning reduces passenger-drive trajectory error by 23-59%, but instruction effects remain inconsistent. At real intersections, counterfactual instructions reveal stronger responsiveness: fine-tuned Alpamayo~2 Super gains 31 and 18 accuracy points at 15 and 5~m, while Qwen-Drive follows alternative maneuvers more reliably with a discrete command than with a sentence. We additionally collected retrospective annotations from four people for the driving recordings and describe controlled comparisons of annotation content, timing, and downstream learning; those analyses are pending. Our findings separate maneuver prediction from instruction-following and establish a framework for comparing prospective and retrospective supervision.

AI.tldr: This study introduces ADVLAT-Engine and compares prospective navigation instructions against retrospective labels for driving VLAs, showing that fine-tuning reduces trajectory error but leaves counterfactual instruction-following inconsistent.
AI.motivation: Predicting a driver's trajectory does not prove that a driving vision-language-action (VLA) model actually follows navigation instructions, and the distinction between prospective instructions and retrospective labels is underexplored.
AI.method: The authors build ADVLAT-Engine to synchronize spoken instructions, road video, and trajectories across 48 replayed routes, compare three navigation apps and passenger instructions on 87 maneuvers, and evaluate four open driving VLAs before and after fine-tuning using counterfactual intersection tests.
AI.result: Fine-tuning on prospective drives cuts passenger-drive trajectory error by 23-59% with inconsistent instruction effects; on counterfactual intersections, fine-tuned Alpamayo 2 Super gains 31 and 18 accuracy points at 15 and 5 m, while Qwen-Drive follows discrete commands more reliably than full sentences.
