AI.conclusion: Separating maneuver prediction from counterfactual instruction-following is essential for evaluating language supervision in driving VLAs.

title: Counterfactual Feature Steering for Adjacency-Preserving Identity Unlearning
summary: Identity unlearning in text-to-image diffusion models is increasingly important for privacy, safety, and ethical deployment, as it aims to remove the model's ability to generate specific individuals. In this work, we study identity unlearning with \emph{adjacency preservation}, where the goal is to remove a target individual's identity while preserving related non-target identities. We propose Counterfactual Feature Steering (CFS), a method requiring one-time SAE training that performs bounded inference-time concept editing in the latent space of a sparse autoencoder attached to the text encoder. CFS derives a target direction by contrasting forget and retain distributions, then applies a per-token projection proportional to each token's current alignment with this direction, yielding counterfactual representations that suppress the target while limiting collateral damage. To evaluate adjacency preservation, we introduce the Adjacency-Weighted Unlearning Score (AWUS), which measures the tradeoff between target erasure and collateral damage, and extend it to face-specific identity similarity using ArcFace. Across 4,000 prompts derived from Celeb-100, spanning 100 celebrity identities, CFS achieves the strongest evaluated tradeoff between identity erasure of target identities and preservation of adjacent and generic concepts, while remaining stable across intervention strengths where other steering-based methods degrade. Independent ArcFace evaluation and a 10,000-caption COCO study further examine identity and general preservation. Quantitative nudity-suppression benchmarks and qualitative artistic-style examples provide evidence of transfer beyond identities on SD~1.4.

AI.tldr: Counterfactual Feature Steering (CFS) performs bounded inference-time identity unlearning in text-to-image diffusion models via a sparse autoencoder, achieving strong erasure while preserving adjacent identities.
AI.motivation: Identity unlearning in diffusion models often causes collateral damage to related non-target identities, requiring methods that balance target erasure with adjacency preservation.
AI.method: CFS trains a sparse autoencoder once on the text encoder, derives a target direction by contrasting forget and retain distributions, and applies a per-token projection proportional to each token's alignment with that direction; the authors also introduce the Adjacency-Weighted Unlearning Score (AWUS) and an ArcFace extension.
AI.result: Across 4,000 Celeb-100 prompts spanning 100 identities, CFS achieves the strongest evaluated tradeoff between target erasure and preservation of adjacent and generic concepts, remains stable across intervention strengths, and transfers to nudity suppression and artistic styles on SD 1.4.
AI.conclusion: Bounded counterfactual steering in sparse autoencoder latent space enables targeted identity unlearning with minimal collateral damage.

title: Defect-Aware Masked Autoencoders for Unsupervised Clustering of Steel Surface Defects
summary: Reliable recognition of steel surface defects is essential for automated quality inspection, but supervised methods require manually annotated images that are costly to produce. This creates a need for methods that can learn useful defect representations directly from unlabelled surface images. This work presents Defect aware MAE, a label free masked autoencoder for clustering steel surface defects. Each image is divided into 196 patches, with 147 masked and 49 processed by a Vision Transformer encoder. Texture energy based masking preferentially hides structurally informative patches, while a shallow decoder reconstructs HOG descriptors that capture local texture and edge orientation. Strong augmentation and an intermediate layer readout are used to form the final image features. Pretraining uses no class labels, bounding boxes, detection branch, or contrastive loss. On the held out NEU DET split, UMAP followed by Ward clustering achieves 98.6% Hungarian matched accuracy, 0.968 NMI, 0.967 ARI, and 0.838 silhouette score. Under an identical encoder and training schedule, it exceeds a SimCLR contrastive baseline in accuracy, NMI, ARI and silhouette scores across 5 seeds.

AI.tldr: Defect-aware MAE is an unsupervised masked autoencoder that uses texture-energy masking and HOG reconstruction to cluster steel surface defects, achieving 98.6% accuracy on NEU-DET.
AI.motivation: Supervised steel defect inspection requires costly manual annotations, creating a need for label-free representation learning directly from unlabelled surface images.
AI.method: Each image is split into 196 patches with 147 masked via texture-energy-based sampling to hide informative regions, while a ViT encoder and shallow decoder reconstruct local HOG descriptors without labels, bounding boxes, or contrastive loss, followed by UMAP and Ward clustering.
AI.result: On the held-out NEU-DET split, Defect-aware MAE achieves 98.6% Hungarian-matched accuracy, 0.968 NMI, 0.967 ARI, and 0.838 silhouette score, outperforming a SimCLR baseline across 5 seeds under an identical encoder and schedule.
AI.conclusion: Texture-energy masking paired with HOG reconstruction learns highly discriminative, label-free representations for steel surface defect clustering.

title: Competent Autonomous Driving Through Fine Tuning Vision Language Action Models with Symbolic Traffic Rules
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models offer a unified approach to perception, reasoning, and control for autonomous driving, but accurate action prediction alone does not establish compliance with traffic regulations. This paper presents a rule-guided VLA framework that incorporates symbolic traffic-rule feedback into policy optimisation. The framework combines supervised fine-tuning on expert demonstrations with reinforcement learning (RL) refinement using a reward that encourages encoded-rule compliance while penalising deviations from expert actions. Selected provisions of the United Kingdom Highway Code are formalised as executable first-order logic rules using PyReason, covering speed adaptation, following distance, and road-user priority. A frozen vision-language model extracts scene predicates, which are combined with vehicle-state information to assess the projected consequences of candidate control actions. Offline evaluation on held-out data collected in the CARLA simulator compares three group-based RL methods. The results show improvements in both action prediction accuracy and encoded-rule compliance over the supervised baseline. The best-performing variant increases the overall rule pass rate from 92.9% to 97.6%, with zero observed violations of the encoded road-user-priority check in the evaluated samples. These findings support symbolic rule feedback as a means of improving VLA policy alignment with explicit traffic-rule criteria.

AI.tldr: Fine-tuning driving vision-language-action (VLA) models with reinforcement learning guided by symbolic UK Highway Code rules improves both action accuracy and traffic-rule compliance in CARLA.
AI.motivation: Accurate imitation of expert trajectories does not guarantee that driving VLA models comply with explicit traffic regulations.
AI.method: The framework combines supervised fine-tuning with group-based RL refinement using a reward that penalizes expert-action deviations and rewards compliance with UK Highway Code rules formalized in first-order logic via PyReason over frozen-VLM scene predicates and vehicle state.
AI.result: In offline CARLA evaluations across three group-based RL methods, the best variant improves both action accuracy and overall rule pass rate (from 92.9% to 97.6%), with zero observed violations of the encoded road-user-priority rule.
AI.conclusion: Symbolic traffic-rule feedback during RL fine-tuning effectively aligns driving VLA policies with explicit regulatory criteria.

title: Room for Supervision: Training-Free Dataset Distillation for Object Detection
summary: Dataset distillation (DD) reduces storage and training costs by compressing large datasets into small collections. Most existing methods focus on image classification, where each image typically has a single category label. In contrast, object detection requires accurate category and bounding box annotations for multiple objects, together with visual content consistent with those annotations. Existing detection distillation pipelines rely on learned models and can alter the spatial relationships between objects and their backgrounds. We introduce GRASP, which packs dense native supervision into limited pixels without network training or inference. GRASP jointly searches over image selections and spatial layouts using convex allocation subproblems that penalize insufficient object resolution, excessive image compression, and padding that source context cannot fill. During composition, each selected image is cropped around all annotated objects and expanded into surrounding context without reducing object scale. The resized regions are then combined into distilled images, preserving the spatial layout within each region and retaining all original class labels and bounding box annotations. We evaluate GRASP on MS COCO and PASCAL VOC with compression ratios ranging from 0.25\% to 2\%. GRASP constructs the 1\% MS COCO dataset in under two minutes. Under a common training protocol using hard labels, GRASP achieves the state of the art with both CNN and ViT backbones. Code is available at this https URL

AI.tldr: GRASP is a training-free dataset distillation method for object detection that packs cropped, context-expanded native images into distilled canvases via convex allocation, achieving state-of-the-art performance under hard labels.
AI.motivation: Existing dataset distillation methods for object detection rely on learned models and can distort spatial relationships between objects and their backgrounds.
AI.method: GRASP jointly optimizes image selection and spatial layout using convex allocation subproblems that penalize low object resolution, excessive compression, and unfillable padding, then crops and context-expands selected regions without shrinking object scale while preserving all original bounding boxes and labels.
AI.result: Evaluated on MS COCO and PASCAL VOC at 0.25% to 2% compression ratios, GRASP constructs the 1% MS COCO dataset in under two minutes and achieves state-of-the-art accuracy with both CNN and ViT backbones under hard-label training.
AI.conclusion: Training-free convex layout packing preserves native object-background supervision and enables fast, state-of-the-art dataset distillation for object detection.

title: STARS: Stage-Adaptive Responsibility Separation for Shadow Removal in Remote Sensing Images
summary: Shadows are a ubiquitous radiative attenuation phenomenon in remote sensing images and can severely affect high-resolution remote sensing interpretation tasks. In shadow removal, although introducing a mask prior provides explicit positional information for the restoration network, it also causes non-shadow regions to be modulated by the shadow prior, producing a systematic brightness shift; notably, this phenomenon is independent of whether the mask is accurate. In remote sensing images, non-shadow regions usually occupy a larger proportion, so a small shift over these regions incurs a much higher cost on whole-image metrics than an equal gain in shadow regions. Adopting a task-decoupling perspective, we therefore decompose shadow removal into two tasks, shadow-region restoration and non-shadow-region identity, within a cascaded architecture, and handle them sequentially. Based on this insight, we propose STARS, a cascaded shadow removal framework that separates regional responsibilities across stages. The method retains the advantages of the shadow mask while resolving the degradation of non-shadow regions, without requiring a complex parallel dual-branch structure. Meanwhile, to introduce large-model prior knowledge into remote sensing tasks, we further design a Feature Selection and Fusion Adapter (FSFA). We conduct extensive experiments on three benchmark datasets, UAV-SC+, ISTD+ and WSRD+ 2026, demonstrating the superiority of STARS. The framework shows that decoupling regional responsibilities can resolve the intrinsic contradiction of mask priors, providing a new direction for image restoration with region heterogeneity.

AI.tldr: STARS is a cascaded shadow-removal framework for remote sensing images that separates shadow-region restoration from non-shadow-region identity preservation to eliminate mask-induced brightness shifts.
AI.motivation: Introducing shadow mask priors into restoration networks modulates non-shadow regions and causes systematic brightness shifts, which heavily penalizes whole-image metrics in remote sensing images where non-shadow areas dominate.
AI.method: STARS decouples shadow removal into sequential stages of shadow-region restoration and non-shadow-region identity preservation within a cascaded architecture, augmented by a Feature Selection and Fusion Adapter (FSFA) to inject large-model priors.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on UAV-SC+, ISTD+, and WSRD+ 2026 demonstrate that STARS outperforms existing methods.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling regional responsibilities across cascade stages resolves the brightness-shift trade-off of mask priors in remote sensing shadow removal.

title: Architectural Principles for Parameter-Efficient Unitary Transformations in Coherent Optical Neural Networks
summary: Coherent optical neural networks based on interferometric architectures offer a promising route toward high-throughput, energy-efficient computation by exploiting the multiple degrees of freedom of light, including spatial, temporal, and spectral modes. However, practical implementations are constrained by the number of tunable parameters due to fabrication complexity, device footprint, and control overhead. In such parameter-constrained settings, achieving high expressive power remains a central challenge. We identify two key architectural requirements for maintaining high expressive power under these constraints: (i) statistical uniformity in the implemented transformations and (ii) strong mixing capability per parameter, which enables rapid and unbiased redistribution of information across modes. To realize these requirements, we develop a logarithmic-depth butterfly-topology architecture whose fundamental building block is a single phase-shifter--beam-splitter pair, in contrast to conventional rectangular mesh architectures based on Mach-Zehnder interferometers. Computational evaluations show that, particularly at restricted parameter counts, the proposed architecture achieves lower matrix-reconstruction errors and higher classification accuracies than conventional meshes in both feedforward and recurrent networks. We further quantify these design principles using graph-theoretic measures, expected squared moduli of transformation-matrix entries, and matrix-reconstruction error. The resulting framework provides a quantitative and physically interpretable basis for parameter-efficient optical neural networks.

AI.tldr: A logarithmic-depth butterfly-topology coherent optical neural network built from single phase-shifter and beam-splitter pairs achieves higher expressivity and lower reconstruction error than conventional rectangular meshes under tight parameter budgets.
AI.motivation: Coherent optical neural networks face strict tunable-parameter limits due to fabrication complexity, device footprint, and control overhead, making high expressivity per parameter critical.
AI.method: Identifying statistical uniformity and strong per-parameter mixing as key principles, the authors design a logarithmic-depth butterfly-topology architecture using single phase-shifter and beam-splitter building blocks instead of Mach-Zehnder interferometer meshes.
AI.result: Computational evaluations in feedforward and recurrent networks show lower matrix-reconstruction errors and higher classification accuracies than conventional rectangular meshes, particularly at restricted parameter counts, supported by graph-theoretic and matrix-entry analyses.
AI.conclusion: Butterfly-topology interferometric architectures provide a physically interpretable, parameter-efficient foundation for coherent optical neural networks.

title: Attention Sinks as Spectral Spikes: A Mechanism Analysis of Gated Attention
comment: The 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)
summary: Transformer attention exhibits attention sinks, where a small subset of source tokens absorbs disproportionate attention mass across layers. Recent work shows that post-SDPA output gating strongly reduces attention-sink behavior, while separate studies link attention sinks to gradient sinks and massive activations through backward training dynamics. Yet how the same gate affects forward sink structure, backward gradient concentration, and training-time representation signatures remains unclear. We address this gap by formulating attention sinks as sink-induced low-rank modes in token-space covariance, with directions aligned to high-mass attention columns. Under this view, post-SDPA gating acts as a mode-dependent contraction: it attenuates sink-induced spectral energy in the forward pass and locally reduces value-path gradients routed through sink columns in the backward pass. Empirically, random-matrix diagnostics show that gating reduces outlier mass, weakens sink-subspace alignment, and increases effective rank, while backward analyses show active-gate attenuation of first-token value gradients. Training-time diagnostics further show that gating suppresses the co-emergence of attention concentration, value-gradient amplification, and representation dominance.

AI.tldr: Post-SDPA output gating suppresses attention sinks by acting as a mode-dependent contraction that attenuates sink-induced low-rank spectral modes in the forward pass and value-path gradients in the backward pass.
AI.motivation: While post-SDPA gating is known to reduce attention sinks, its mechanistic effects on forward sink structure, backward gradient concentration, and training-time representations were unclear.
AI.method: The authors formulate attention sinks as sink-induced low-rank modes in token-space covariance and analyze how post-SDPA gating contracts these modes and attenuates value-path gradients using random-matrix and training-time diagnostics.
AI.result: Empirically, gating reduces outlier mass, weakens sink-subspace alignment, increases effective rank, attenuates first-token value gradients, and suppresses the co-emergence of attention concentration, gradient amplification, and representation dominance.
AI.conclusion: Formulating attention sinks as spectral spikes explains how post-SDPA gating jointly stabilizes forward representations and backward gradient dynamics.

title: Latent Feedback Is a Compute and Data Amplifier
summary: When high-quality data runs out, a common practice is to train on it for several epochs, but each repeat is worth less than the last. Latent feedback, which feeds each token's top-layer state into the next token's input, is another way to spend that compute, yet it has not been tested against a vanilla Transformer that spends the same compute on more epochs. We run this test across a ladder of model sizes, unique data and epochs, tuning both models at every size and amount of unique data. Latent feedback makes every FLOP and every token count for more except when unique data is scarce relative to model size, a regime that today's models are far from. We find that latent feedback serves as an amplifier: with unique data fixed, it reaches a Transformer's loss with less compute; with epochs fixed, it reaches that loss with less unique data. Furthermore, both savings grow with unique data per parameter and with repetition, and downstream tasks agree. To go beyond our grid, we fit one scaling law to both models, in which latent feedback enters as a Transformer with more parameters; it predicts that both savings keep growing with unique data and repetition. Fitted on models from 60M to 271M parameters, the law predicts the losses at a held-out 778M size to within 0.3% and the gap between the two models to within 0.05%. At most, latent feedback saves 48% of the compute and 47% of the unique data. When data, not compute, is the limit, latent feedback is the better use of a FLOP for a model of a given size.

AI.tldr: Latent feedback acts as a compute and data amplifier over vanilla Transformers, saving up to 48% compute and 47% unique data across model sizes and repetition regimes.
AI.motivation: Repeating scarce high-quality training data yields diminishing returns in vanilla Transformers, and it was unknown whether spending that compute on latent feedback (feeding top-layer states into the next token's input) is more effective.
AI.method: The authors compare tuned vanilla Transformers and latent-feedback models across a grid of model sizes (60M to 271M, plus a held-out 778M test), unique data amounts, and epochs, and fit a unified scaling law.
AI.result: Latent feedback reaches equivalent loss with less compute or less unique data (up to 48% compute and 47% unique data saved), with savings growing with unique data per parameter and repetition; the scaling law predicts held-out 778M losses within 0.3% and model gaps within 0.05%.
AI.conclusion: When data rather than compute is the bottleneck, latent feedback is a strictly more efficient use of FLOPs than multi-epoch repetition.

title: Reasoning Again with a Quarter of the Experts: Retry First, Then Train
summary: Removing three quarters of the routed experts from a 122B-parameter reasoning mixture-of-experts model makes it fit in a 12 GiB file, and breaks it in a specific way: on LiveCodeBench it enters verbatim reasoning loops that run to the token limit on 44 of 120 development problems, where the unpruned model at the same 2-bit quantization loops on none. We study how much of that loss can be recovered without changing the kept experts' quantized bytes, in three steps of increasing cost. On development problems, a sampling penalty recovers part of it. Stopping a reply when it starts to loop and drawing again recovers more on top of it, with no weight change. Our method, B, adds rank-8 trained corrections to the kept experts, loaded as an adapter, and restores two experts per layer; it is fitted layer by layer to the unpruned model's expert block on the pruned model's own activations. In a pre-registered comparison on 130 easy and medium LiveCodeBench problems that no part of the study had touched, with both arms given the same sampling penalty and the same stop-and-redraw policy, B solves 116 problems against 104 (+9.2 pp, 95% CI [+3.1, +15.4]; 15 problems gained, 3 lost). A training-free weight edit aimed at the loops, tested the same way earlier, did not help. B removes more wrong answers than loops, and costs 1.7x the wall time. On two older benchmarks used as regression checks, B stays inside a pre-set 2 pp tolerance but shows no gain (HumanEval+ +0.6 pp, MBPP+ -1.9 pp). The evidence is one model, one quantization and one benchmark family; we state what it does and does not show.

AI.tldr: Removing 75% of routed experts in a 122B-parameter 2-bit MoE model causes verbatim reasoning loops on LiveCodeBench, which can be substantially recovered via stop-and-redraw sampling and rank-8 adapter corrections.
AI.motivation: Aggressive expert pruning (75% removed) shrinks a 122B MoE model into 12 GiB but induces verbatim reasoning loops to the token limit on 44 of 120 LiveCodeBench development problems.
AI.method: The authors test three recovery steps without altering kept quantized bytes: a sampling penalty, stopping and redrawing upon loop detection, and method B, which adds rank-8 trained adapter corrections and restores two experts per layer fitted to the unpruned expert block.
AI.result: On 130 held-out LiveCodeBench problems with identical sampling and redraw policies, method B solves 116 versus 104 (+9.2 pp, 95% CI [+3.1, +15.4]) at 1.7x wall time, while staying within a 2 pp tolerance on HumanEval+ (+0.6 pp) and MBPP+ (-1.9 pp).
AI.conclusion: Combining loop-aware redrawing with lightweight layer-wise adapter corrections recovers reasoning capability in heavily pruned quantized MoE models.

title: Fuzzy Explainable Continual Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning for Robotic Navigation
summary: Continual robot navigation requires reinforcement learning policies to continuously adapt to new environments while retaining previously acquired knowledge. Meanwhile, explainable reinforcement learning aims to learn meaningful behavioral representations through policy interaction. However, these objectives are inherently conflicting, as continual learning emphasizes policy stability whereas explainable behavior learning requires adaptive exploration. Existing methods rarely address both simultaneously. To resolve this issue, this paper proposes a Fuzzy Explainable Continual Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning (FECHRL) method. A two-stage behavior cloning strategy is introduced to balance rapid policy adaptation and explainable behavior evolution by progressively transitioning from strong imitation guidance to autonomous reinforcement learning. Furthermore, a fuzzy critic based on a Takagi--Sugeno fuzzy inference system is proposed to alleviate value extrapolation errors during the transition between imitation-guided learning and autonomous exploration, thereby improving continual training stability. Experimental results on sequential multi-scenario navigation tasks demonstrate that the proposed method effectively unifies continual learning capability and policy explainability within a single reinforcement learning framework, achieving stable knowledge retention and meaningful behavioral explanation.

AI.tldr: FECHRL unifies continual learning and policy explainability in robotic navigation using a two-stage behavior-cloning schedule and a Takagi-Sugeno fuzzy critic.
AI.motivation: Continual robotic navigation requires policy stability to retain prior knowledge, which conflicts with the adaptive exploration needed for explainable reinforcement learning.
AI.method: FECHRL introduces a two-stage behavior-cloning strategy that transitions progressively from strong imitation guidance to autonomous RL, paired with a Takagi-Sugeno fuzzy inference critic to reduce value extrapolation errors during the transition.
AI.result: Experiments on sequential multi-scenario navigation tasks show that FECHRL achieves stable knowledge retention alongside meaningful behavioral explanations.
AI.conclusion: Combining progressive imitation-to-RL scheduling with a fuzzy critic resolves the stability-exploration trade-off in explainable continual robot navigation.

title: iEEG Can Help EEG: Improving Clinical Scalp EEG Analysis through Intracranial Priors
summary: Scalp electroencephalography (EEG) is a cornerstone of clinical brain monitoring, making the quality of its signal fundamental to downstream tasks and models. However, that signal is heavily contaminated by non-neural interference and blurred by volume conduction. Existing methods operate almost exclusively within the scalp modality, so they inherit the contamination they would need to overcome. In practice, intracranial EEG (iEEG) observes the neural activity with far higher fidelity, yet it is invasive and therefore scarce, and the two modalities are rarely recorded as pairs at scale, share no common channel space, and offer no clean ground truth to directly supervise a mapping. Motivated by the neuronal synchronization mechanism shared by the two modalities, we propose a reprogramming approach that fits a signal-to-signal model on iEEG alone and freezes it as a cross-modal prior. We introduce ReBrain, a framework to transfer an iEEG-learned prior to scalp EEG, which re-expresses any scalp signal through that prior and can be inserted upstream of any downstream model with no pairing or fine-tuning. ReBrain consistently improves host models across recordings from multiple hospitals and across architecture families, and our analysis traces this gain to genuine neural structure carried by iEEG rather than to the architecture itself. This work provides evidence that a scarce clean modality can serve as a transferable prior for an abundant noisy one, offering a general recipe for cross-modal transfer among biosignals. Our code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: ReBrain transfers a signal-to-signal prior learned solely from scarce invasive intracranial EEG (iEEG) to denoise abundant, noisy scalp EEG without paired data or fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Clinical scalp EEG is heavily contaminated by non-neural interference and volume conduction, while cleaner iEEG is invasive, scarce, and rarely recorded simultaneously with scalp EEG.
AI.method: ReBrain fits a signal-to-signal model on iEEG alone, freezes it as a cross-modal neural prior, and inserts it upstream of any downstream scalp EEG model to re-express scalp signals without pairing or fine-tuning.
AI.result: ReBrain consistently improves downstream host models across multi-hospital recordings and diverse architecture families, with analyses attributing gains to genuine neural structure from iEEG.
AI.conclusion: A scarce, high-fidelity biosignal modality can serve as a transferable, zero-pairing prior to enhance abundant, noisy clinical recordings.

title: Explainable Federated Learning via Global-Local Attribution Alignment
comment: 26 pages, 2 figures, 9 tables. Published in Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2026)
summary: Federated learning enables on-device training without centralizing data, yet existing systems still struggle to provide explanations that are both locally faithful and globally consistent under strict privacy and bandwidth constraints. Prior approaches either keep explanations siloed across clients, transmit heavy or sensitive artifacts, or replace expressive task models with interpretable surrogates that sacrifice accuracy. We propose xFedAlign, a model-agnostic framework that decouples task optimization in parameter space from explanation coordination in a compact group space. Each client distills a lightweight surrogate to produce private, per-class top-k attribution artifacts, which are robustly aggregated by the server into a Global Explanation Prior that softly aligns client explanations without constraining task learning. Across image, text, and tabular benchmarks with IID and non-IID partitions, xFedAlign matches FedAvg accuracy while consistently reducing explanation drift and improving deletion and insertion AUC relative to Local-XAI, FedAttr-Agg, and Fed-XAI, with only a few kilobytes of additional communication per round. Privacy and robustness evaluations further demonstrate reduced membership inference advantage and increased resistance to attribution poisoning, enabling consistent and trustworthy explanations in federated learning.

AI.tldr: xFedAlign is a model-agnostic federated learning framework that aligns local client explanations via a server-aggregated Global Explanation Prior, matching FedAvg accuracy with minimal communication overhead.
AI.motivation: Federated learning struggles to produce explanations that are both locally faithful and globally consistent under privacy and bandwidth constraints without sacrificing task accuracy.
AI.method: Each client distills a lightweight surrogate to generate private per-class top-k attribution artifacts, which the server robustly aggregates into a Global Explanation Prior to softly align client explanations independently of parameter-space task optimization.
AI.result: Across image, text, and tabular benchmarks (IID and non-IID), xFedAlign matches FedAvg accuracy, reduces explanation drift, improves deletion and insertion AUC over Local-XAI, FedAttr-Agg, and Fed-XAI with only a few kilobytes per round, and improves resistance to membership inference and attribution poisoning.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling explanation alignment from task optimization enables consistent, private, and communication-efficient explainability in federated learning.

title: Generative AI-Driven Parametric Design Optimization Framework for Vehicle Closure Systems
summary: This study presents a generative AI-driven parametric design optimization framework integrating performance-oriented generation with editable computer-aided design (CAD) and downstream computer-aided engineering (CAE) analysis for industrial vehicle closure systems. The framework is demonstrated on an automotive tailgate assembly with complex geometry, coupled components, and competing performance and feasibility requirements. A production-oriented CATIA model is restructured into a reference-based parametric template with a 13-dimensional design representation. An automated CAD/CAE workflow generates parametric models, performs structural analysis, and constructs a database of mass, maximum displacement, and maximum von Mises stress. Gaussian process regression surrogates predict performance, while diffusion and flow matching models generate design candidates. The design problem minimizes mass and maximum displacement, with stress assessed as an engineering feasibility constraint. Performance-guided generation using surrogate guidance and performance-aware training using a performance-aware loss incorporate engineering objectives, with sensitivity to guidance scale and loss weight evaluated. Generative search is compared with NSGA-II under matched evaluation budgets using a common surrogate model. Selected Pareto-region candidates are reconstructed in CATIA and re-evaluated through native CAE; all verified candidates are successfully regenerated and analyzed. Relative to the baseline, the knee-point design reduces mass by 7.1% and maximum displacement by 29.4%, while extreme verified solutions achieve maximum reductions of 10.3% and 37.3%, respectively. The results demonstrate performance-oriented multi-objective design exploration compatible with editable industrial CAD and native engineering verification.

AI.tldr: A generative AI-driven parametric design framework combines Gaussian process surrogates, diffusion and flow-matching models, and automated CATIA/CAE workflows to optimize automotive tailgate closure systems.
AI.motivation: Industrial vehicle closure design involves complex coupled geometries and competing mass, displacement, and stress constraints that are expensive to explore with traditional CAD/CAE loops.
AI.method: A CATIA tailgate model is parameterized into 13 dimensions to build an automated CAD/CAE database; Gaussian process surrogates guide diffusion and flow-matching models via surrogate guidance and performance-aware loss, with Pareto candidates reconstructed in CATIA for native CAE verification.
AI.result: Compared with NSGA-II under matched budgets, all verified generative candidates regenerate in CATIA, with the knee-point design reducing mass by 7.1% and maximum displacement by 29.4%, and extreme solutions achieving up to 10.3% and 37.3% reductions.
AI.conclusion: Surrogate-guided generative models integrate directly with editable industrial CAD/CAE pipelines for multi-objective structural optimization.

title: AdaModalX: Synchronization-Free MFM Inference for Distributed Multimodal Mobile Sensing via Progressive Data Orchestration
summary: Multimodal foundation models (MFMs) support generalizable inference in distributed mobile sensing applications by integrating heterogeneous data streams. However, existing MFM inference pipelines typically require complete and synchronized multimodal inputs, whereas mobile sensing streams arrive asynchronously due to network variability and heterogeneous data volumes across modalities. Waiting for all modalities increases end-to-end latency, while inference with incomplete inputs can reduce accuracy. We argue that multimodal inference should depend on the utility of available information rather than modality completeness. Based on this principle, we propose AdaModalX, a progressive multimodal inference framework that decouples inference execution from modality synchronization through runtime utility-aware orchestration. At each device, importance-aware data uploading uses a lightweight probe distilled from the edge-side MFM to allow reliable samples to exit locally while uncertain samples continue uploading. At the edge, on-demand MFM activation constructs candidates from fully received samples and, when needed, imputed features derived from partially received delayed inputs. A lightweight contribution assessor built on frozen MFM encoders estimates candidate utility and activates the MFM once the candidate meets its corresponding utility threshold. Experiments on four mobile sensing applications show that AdaModalX improves the accuracy-latency trade-off, achieving up to 26.97% accuracy improvement and up to 64.75% end-to-end latency reduction.

AI.tldr: AdaModalX is a synchronization-free multimodal inference framework for distributed mobile sensing that uses utility-aware progressive data orchestration to improve accuracy by up to 26.97% and cut latency by up to 64.75%.
AI.motivation: Asynchronous arrival of mobile sensing streams forces existing multimodal foundation model (MFM) pipelines to either wait for all modalities (high latency) or run on incomplete inputs (low accuracy).
AI.method: AdaModalX uses a distilled lightweight probe on devices to exit reliable samples locally while uploading uncertain ones, and an edge-side contribution assessor on frozen MFM encoders to activate the MFM once combined complete and imputed delayed features meet a utility threshold.
AI.result: Across four mobile sensing applications, AdaModalX improves the accuracy-latency trade-off, achieving up to 26.97% higher accuracy and up to 64.75% lower end-to-end latency.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling multimodal inference from strict modality synchronization via runtime utility assessment enables fast, accurate distributed mobile sensing.

title: On the Applicability of $p$-adic Numbers in Computational Modules for Neural Networks
summary: The applicability of $p$-adic arithmetic as an intermediate computational module in an otherwise unchanged machine-learning pipeline is investigated. A one-feature linear regression on the scikit-learn Diabetes dataset serves as the test model. The fitted coefficients are represented in $\mathbb{Q}_p$, predictions are computed in that field, and rational reconstruction is applied to the outputs. In the pyAdic experiments, rational reconstruction either returns no result or produces values that differ from the baseline predictions; changing computational precision can change both the magnitude and sign of the reconstructed value. In SageMath, forward conversions succeed, but the reconstructed predictions differ from the baseline. An alternative representation based on digit reversal fails to preserve ordinary addition because of carry propagation. Under the tested settings, none of the test predictions is reconstructed correctly. These results show that the tested conversion and reconstruction procedures do not provide a compatible intermediate module even for linear regression. Models defined directly over $p$-adic data and operations offer a direction for further investigation.

AI.tldr: Testing p-adic arithmetic as an intermediate module in a standard linear regression pipeline fails to reconstruct any test predictions accurately, showing incompatibility with standard ML pipelines.
AI.motivation: Whether p-adic numbers can serve as a drop-in intermediate computational module inside an otherwise unchanged machine-learning pipeline had not been verified.
AI.method: The authors fit a one-feature linear regression on the scikit-learn Diabetes dataset, convert coefficients to Q_p, compute predictions in p-adic arithmetic using pyAdic, SageMath, and digit reversal, and apply rational reconstruction.
AI.result: In pyAdic, rational reconstruction returns no result or wrong values whose magnitude and sign shift with precision; SageMath forward conversions succeed but yield wrong reconstructions, and digit reversal breaks addition via carry propagation, with zero test predictions reconstructed correctly.
AI.conclusion: Standard conversion and rational reconstruction procedures cannot support p-adic intermediate modules even for linear regression, pointing instead toward models defined natively over p-adic operations.

title: Tabular Foundation Models as Emulators for Forecasting Terrestrial Ecosystem Dynamics
summary: Process-based terrestrial biosphere models such as the Ecosystem Demography (ED) model underpin global carbon budgets, but their cost limits global, high-resolution and scenario-rich simulation. Deep emulators such as DeepED reduce that cost but require task-specific architectures and training. Tabular foundation models offer a different route: TabPFN predicts new rows by in-context learning, without being trained on the task. We compare TabPFN-3.5 with two DeepED baselines, $DeepED_{LSTM}$ and $DeepED_{Transformer}$, on CarbonGlobe's overall evaluation, which trains on a uniform 1/16 sample of sites and tests on the other 50,779, predicting the 40-year state of all seven ED outputs. We then test every model, trained on present-day data only, on ED runs forced by SSP1-2.6 and SSP5-8.5 for 2021--2060 in six continental forest regions. With no training, TabPFN-3.5 has the lowest present-day height error of the three models and is within 4% of $DeepED_{LSTM}$ for soil carbon, but is less accurate for AGB, LAI and the carbon fluxes. In 2060, errors are several times larger than at the same sites under present-day forcing, and every model underestimates the biomass that ED gains. Under SSP5-8.5, TabPFN-3.5 is the most accurate model for height, AGB, soil carbon and LAI, with the lowest AGB error in all six regions, although, unlike ED, it predicts no larger biomass gain than under SSP1-2.6. Under SSP1-2.6, no model is best overall.

AI.tldr: TabPFN-3.5, used via in-context learning without task-specific training, is competitive with DeepED emulators on present-day ecosystem states and achieves the lowest error on key variables under high-emissions 2060 forcing.
AI.motivation: Process-based terrestrial biosphere models like Ecosystem Demography (ED) are too costly for high-resolution global simulations, while deep emulators require task-specific architectures and training.
AI.method: The authors compare zero-training TabPFN-3.5 against DeepED_LSTM and DeepED_Transformer trained on a 1/16 sample of CarbonGlobe sites, evaluating 40-year predictions across 50,779 test sites and 2021-2060 projections under SSP1-2.6 and SSP5-8.5 in six forest regions.
AI.result: On present-day data, TabPFN-3.5 achieves the lowest height error and is within 4% of DeepED_LSTM on soil carbon; by 2060 all models underestimate ED biomass gains, but under SSP5-8.5 TabPFN-3.5 is most accurate for height, AGB (lowest error in all six regions), soil carbon, and LAI.
AI.conclusion: Tabular foundation models offer a viable zero-training alternative for ecosystem emulation, though extrapolating future biomass responses under climate forcing remains challenging.

title: Model Immunization Beyond Condition Numbers: The Importance of Plateau Regions
summary: Harmful fine-tuning can rapidly compromise safety alignment in Large Language Models, underscoring the vulnerability of deployed models to post-release modification. While prior work motivates model immunization by inducing ill-conditioned curvature to slow harmful optimization, this approach is not scalable due to the high computational cost of Hessian estimation. We refine this paradigm by extending the theoretical framework to prioritize plateau regions alongside curvature. We further introduce an immunization algorithm based on efficient Hessian estimation and bounds on the extremal singular values of the Hessian. We demonstrate the proposed immunization framework in three applications: (i) Fine-tuning-as-a-service settings where benign user data may be mixed with poisoned harmful data, (ii) open-weight settings where an adversary can fine-tune on harmful-only data with varied training dynamics, and (iii) robust unlearning, where immunized models better resist relearning attacks after unlearning. Extensive experiments confirm that our approach achieves robust defense against adversarial fine-tuning while largely maintaining general utility and downstream trainability. Our code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Extending LLM immunization to prioritize plateau regions alongside Hessian curvature yields a scalable defense against harmful fine-tuning and relearning attacks while preserving general utility.
AI.motivation: Prior model immunization methods induce ill-conditioned curvature to slow harmful fine-tuning, but high Hessian estimation costs limit their scalability.
AI.method: The authors extend immunization theory to prioritize plateau regions alongside curvature and introduce a scalable algorithm using efficient Hessian estimation and bounds on extremal Hessian singular values.
AI.result: Across fine-tuning-as-a-service with poisoned data, open-weight harmful-only fine-tuning, and robust unlearning against relearning attacks, the method provides strong defense while largely maintaining general utility and downstream trainability.
AI.conclusion: Targeting plateau regions with efficient Hessian bounds makes LLM immunization practical and robust across diverse post-release threat models.

title: A Temporal Convolutional Network with Multi-Head Attention Model: A Surrogate for Parallel DEVS Semiconductor Fab Simulation
summary: Semiconductor factories process many kinds of wafers organized into lots of various sizes and configurations. Different kinds of machines, each with its own operations, process wafers for hours to days, and the wafers undergo many incremental fabrication steps (with re-entry) and flows spanning days to weeks across connected machines. Fast and accurate predictions of throughput ($TH$) and turnaround time ($TA$) dynamics for individual machines and their combinations are essential for factory operations. To use machine learning methods for this purpose, this paper presents a Temporal Convolutional Network with Multi-head Attention (TCNA) architecture. It uses simulated datasets from a benchmark Parallel DEVS (PDEVS) semiconductor fabrication factory model. The factory processes configurable wafer lots with uniform and sinusoidal wafer arrival profiles and may undergo preventive maintenance. The wafer lot size, arrival profile, and factory maintenance policy are used as static covariates. TCNA is applied to a selected set of simulated discrete-event throughput and turnaround time trajectories. The $TH$ and $TA$ time series predicted by TCNA, evaluated with the common $MAPE$, $MSE$, and $R^2$ measures, show comparable or higher accuracy relative to other model architectures, with similar parameter counts and epoch times; the TCNA model size and execution time are similar to those of other architectures such as the Temporal Fusion Transformer. Although time series predictions are less accurate than high-resolution simulations, they can be deployed at a much lower computational cost. The TCNA achieves orders-of-magnitude speedup over PDEVS simulation with an acceptable loss of accuracy, enabling frequent product scheduling, capacity planning, and maintenance planning.

AI.tldr: A Temporal Convolutional Network with Multi-Head Attention (TCNA) serves as a fast surrogate for Parallel DEVS semiconductor fab simulations, achieving orders-of-magnitude speedup with comparable accuracy.
AI.motivation: High-resolution discrete-event simulations of semiconductor fabs are too computationally expensive for frequent product scheduling, capacity planning, and maintenance planning.
AI.method: TCNA combines temporal convolutions with multi-head attention and incorporates static covariates (wafer lot size, arrival profile, and maintenance policy) to predict throughput and turnaround time trajectories generated by a benchmark Parallel DEVS fab model.
AI.result: Evaluated via MAPE, MSE, and R^2, TCNA matches or exceeds competing architectures such as Temporal Fusion Transformer at similar parameter counts and epoch times, while delivering orders-of-magnitude speedup over PDEVS simulation.
AI.conclusion: TCNA provides an accurate, computationally efficient surrogate for discrete-event semiconductor fabrication simulations in operational planning.

title: LINK: Lightweight and Inductive Node-to-Node Propagation Rule Learning for Traffic Kriging
summary: Spatio-temporal traffic kriging aims to reconstruct traffic time series at unobserved locations with no historical traffic observations by leveraging spatial and temporal dependencies across the road network. Existing Graph Neural Network (GNN)-based approaches primarily rely on neighborhood aggregation to capture spatial dependencies, thereby modeling traffic interactions implicitly and making it difficult to accurately recover traffic magnitudes at locations without historical observations. To address this limitation, we propose LINK, a Lightweight and Inductive Node-to-node propagation rule learning paradigm for traffic Kriging. LINK introduces three key designs: 1) a propagation-centric traffic kriging paradigm that explicitly learns a shared node-to-node transition rule; 2) a context-aware Spectral Propagation Network that performs traffic-state propagation in both the spectral and time domains; and 3) TraffiKrig, a realistic traffic kriging benchmark that preserves heterogeneous road-segment characteristics and road-specific metadata while enabling systematic comparison of representative kriging methods under a unified metadata-enhanced setting. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LINK achieves strong reconstruction accuracy and computational efficiency. Compared with the strongest baseline on each subset, LINK achieves an average MAE reduction of 54.7% over original baselines. LINK also achieves substantial efficiency improvements, reducing training time by 66.5% and inference time by 86.6% compared with the fastest competing methods. Zero-shot experiments further demonstrate the transferability of the learned propagation rule across regions.

AI.tldr: LINK is a lightweight, inductive traffic kriging framework that learns a shared node-to-node propagation rule in spectral and time domains, cutting MAE by 54.7% and inference time by 86.6% over baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing GNN-based traffic kriging methods rely on implicit neighborhood aggregation, struggling to accurately reconstruct traffic magnitudes at unobserved road locations without historical data.
AI.method: LINK learns an explicit, shared node-to-node transition rule using a context-aware Spectral Propagation Network in both spectral and time domains, and introduces TraffiKrig, a metadata-preserving traffic kriging benchmark.
AI.result: Compared with the strongest baselines on each subset, LINK reduces average MAE by 54.7%, training time by 66.5%, and inference time by 86.6%, while transferring zero-shot across regions.
AI.conclusion: Explicit node-to-node propagation rule learning enables accurate, fast, and regionally transferable spatio-temporal traffic kriging.

title: RoShift: Lazy Shift and Weight-aware Rotation for Activation Sparsity in LLM Inference
summary: Activation sparsity accelerates LLM decoding by skipping unnecessary weight reads and computation. However, SiLU-based LLMs exhibit little natural sparsity, and imposing high sparsity can substantially degrade accuracy. We propose RoShift, a training-free method that transforms activations into sparsity-friendly representations. RoShift introduces lazy shift, which recenters SiLU activation distributions around zero and defers correction to the end of the FFN to obtain additional sparsity. It also reduces sparsification-induced output error through rotation that jointly accounts for activation and weight information. By fusing the corrections required for shifting and rotation, RoShift translates these gains into decoding speedup. At 50% and 60% sparsity, RoShift improves average accuracy over TEAL by 1.60 and 3.29 percentage points, respectively, across five models. It achieves up to $1.72\times$ decoding speedup over the dense model on an RTX 5090 at 50% sparsity and yields a better accuracy-speedup Pareto frontier than TEAL. Code is available at this https URL

AI.tldr: RoShift is a training-free method combining lazy activation shifting and weight-aware rotation to induce sparsity in SiLU-based LLMs, achieving up to 1.72x decoding speedup on an RTX 5090.
AI.motivation: SiLU-based LLMs exhibit little natural activation sparsity, and enforcing high sparsity degrades accuracy unless activations are transformed into sparsity-friendly distributions.
AI.method: RoShift introduces lazy shift to recenter SiLU activations around zero while deferring correction to the end of the FFN, pairs it with rotation accounting for both activations and weights, and fuses the shift and rotation corrections.
AI.result: Across five models, RoShift outperforms TEAL by 1.60 and 3.29 percentage points in average accuracy at 50% and 60% sparsity, respectively, achieving up to 1.72x decoding speedup over dense models on an RTX 5090 at 50% sparsity.
AI.conclusion: Fused lazy shifting and weight-aware rotation unlock practical, training-free activation sparsity and decoding speedups in SiLU-based LLMs.

title: One-Shot Calibration via Model Editing
summary: Model editing aims to correct errors in large, pretrained models by replacing model generations with user-provided responses. Existing editors assume a single target answer for each edit. However, many real tasks inherently entail uncertainty, resulting in multiple plausible answers with varying likelihoods in user feedback. Such feedback forms a target distribution to not only correct but also calibrate model generations. We therefore propose SoftEdit, the first model editor to leverage uncertainty in user responses and perform one-shot calibration during editing. To generalize calibration to unseen samples, SoftEdit uses co-plausibility relationships between answers while preserving real distributional shifts, balancing the new distributional generality-locality tradeoff. Across three language models, three vision-language models, and two large datasets, SoftEdit achieves state-of-the-art performance, ultimately showing that uncertainty in user responses enables generalizable calibration of pretrained models beyond single-answer corrections.

AI.tldr: SoftEdit is a model editor that uses uncertainty in user feedback to perform one-shot distributional calibration alongside error correction across language and vision-language models.
AI.motivation: Existing model editors assume a single target answer per edit, ignoring real-world tasks where user feedback reflects a distribution over multiple plausible answers.
AI.method: SoftEdit performs one-shot calibration during editing by leveraging co-plausibility relationships between answers while preserving real distributional shifts to balance distributional generality and locality.
AI.result: Across three language models, three vision-language models, and two large datasets, SoftEdit achieves state-of-the-art performance in both correction and calibration.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating user-response uncertainty into model editing enables generalizable calibration of pretrained models beyond single-answer fixes.

title: Memory-Efficient Speculative Decoding with Quantized Draft KV Cache
comment: Accepted at the AXIOM Foundations of Efficient Deep Learning Workshop at NeurIPS 2026
summary: Speculative decoding reduces generation cost, but it stores two KV caches: one for the target model and one for the draft model. We reduce this extra memory by quantizing the draft cache. The target cache and verifier remain in BF16, so that compression cannot change the target model's final correction rule. We first study how to divide precision between keys and values. A naive per-token quantizer makes keys appear much more sensitive: splitting a 12-bit budget, K8V4 beats K4V8 in acceptance by 10.87pp. However, with grouped per-channel keys, the gap becomes -0.25pp. A controlled Qwen test confirms that changing only the key quantizer can erase or reverse the preferred bit split. Hence, following KIVI, we propose K4V4 quantization with per-channel keys and per-token values. Across six model pairs, our method reduces draft cache memory by 66.20%, and combined memory across both caches by 23.95%. Mean acceptance drops from 57.93% to 57.14%, only 1.36% relative. Overall, quantized draft caches can make speculative decoding more memory efficient; as a predictive principle for efficient AI design, key and value precision must be co-designed with the quantizer layout.

AI.tldr: This paper reduces the memory overhead of speculative decoding by quantizing the draft model's KV cache to K4V4 while keeping the target cache and verifier in BF16.
AI.motivation: Speculative decoding lowers generation cost but requires storing separate KV caches for both the target and draft models, increasing memory usage.
AI.method: Following KIVI, the authors apply K4V4 quantization using grouped per-channel keys and per-token values on the draft KV cache, leaving the target cache and verifier in BF16 so the target model's correction rule is preserved.
AI.result: Across six model pairs, K4V4 draft cache quantization reduces draft cache memory by 66.20% and combined KV cache memory by 23.95%, while mean acceptance drops from 57.93% to 57.14% (a 1.36% relative decrease); controlled tests also show that switching from naive per-token to grouped per-channel key quantization erases the 10.87pp gap between K8V4 and K4V8.
AI.conclusion: Quantizing the draft KV cache makes speculative decoding more memory efficient without altering target verification, and key-value precision should be co-designed with the quantizer layout.

title: Quantum Computing-Based Wasserstein Generative Adversarial Networks for Airfoil Parameterization
summary: Airfoil geometry parameterization is essential in aerodynamic design optimization. Optimization search in the large space suffers from low efficiency and modest feasible region, which could further incur failures to convergence. Generative adversarial networks (GAN), aiming to learn the statistical distribution of existing data, pave a new avenue for shape generation and airfoil parameterization. GAN manages to implicitly reduce design space by generating only smooth, realistic airfoils. Meanwhile, quantum computing has been emergingly exhibiting great potential for achieving superior performance in specific types of engineering problems but has not been introduced to airfoil parameterization. To fill this gap, this work develops quantum computing-based Wasserstein GAN (Q-WGAN) and investigates the performance for airfoil parameterization. The Q-WGAN adopts parameterized quantum circuits as the generator to promote the generative performance, while the discriminator remains classical. The developed Q-WGAN is demonstrated on a dataset of optimal airfoils parameterized by free-form deformation (FFD) control points, resulting from 992 airfoil aerodynamic design optimizations. Results show that Q-WGAN achieves 92.1% mean fitting accuracy on the optimal FFD control points and 99.2% accuracy on airfoil coordinates, comparable with the classical WGAN performance of 92.28% on FFD control points and 99.26% on airfoil coordinates. Q-WGAN achieves lower Jensen-Shannon divergence, Fréchet distance, and Wasserstein distance than the classical WGAN, indicating an improved agreement with the reference airfoil distribution. Therefore, this work presents a convincing evidence that Q-WGAN makes a viable option for parameterizing airfoils and possesses a great potential for other relevant engineering applications.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a quantum computing-based Wasserstein GAN (Q-WGAN) for airfoil geometry parameterization and shows it matches classical WGAN accuracy while improving distributional agreement.
AI.motivation: Aerodynamic design optimization in large airfoil parameter spaces suffers from low efficiency and small feasible regions, and while classical GANs help reduce the design space, quantum computing has not yet been applied to airfoil parameterization.
AI.method: The authors develop Q-WGAN using parameterized quantum circuits as the generator paired with a classical discriminator, and evaluate it on a dataset of optimal airfoils parameterized by free-form deformation (FFD) control points from 992 aerodynamic design optimizations.
AI.result: Q-WGAN achieves 92.1% mean fitting accuracy on optimal FFD control points and 99.2% accuracy on airfoil coordinates, comparable to classical WGAN (92.28% and 99.26%), while achieving lower Jensen-Shannon divergence, Frechet distance, and Wasserstein distance.
AI.conclusion: Q-WGAN is a viable approach for airfoil parameterization that improves alignment with the reference airfoil distribution and shows potential for related engineering design tasks.

title: DNA: A Double-Helix Hierarchical Deep Interaction Network Architecture for Industrial Digital Twin
summary: High-fidelity modeling is fundamental to industrial digital twin, yet a trade-off persists between the physical transparency of mechanistic models and the superior predictive power of data-driven approaches. Existing hybrid methods often fail to bridge this gap, suffering from shallow integration and rigid one-shot modeling strategies that struggle with complex industrial systems. To address these issues, we propose a \textbf{Double-Helix Hierarchical Deep Interaction Network Architecture (DNA)}. Inspired by the double-helix structure of biological \textit{DNA}, our architecture intertwines mechanistic and data-driven modeling strands through two novel interaction strategies, forming a symbiotic architecture in which the two strands mutually enhance predictive capability. Furthermore, the hierarchical structure of DNA allows it to model complex systems in a multi-stage manner through two tailored deep learning frameworks. We evaluate the proposed approach on two distinct industrial systems, where DNA achieves reductions in MAE of 3.704\% and 3.175\%, respectively, compared to the strongest baseline. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of DNA and suggest its potential to provide new insights for the development of industrial digital twins.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes DNA, a Double-Helix Hierarchical Deep Interaction Network Architecture that intertwines mechanistic and data-driven modeling for industrial digital twins.
AI.motivation: Industrial digital twins face a trade-off between the physical transparency of mechanistic models and the predictive power of data-driven models, and existing hybrid approaches suffer from shallow integration and rigid one-shot modeling.
AI.method: Inspired by biological DNA, the architecture intertwines mechanistic and data-driven modeling strands through two interaction strategies and models complex systems in a multi-stage manner using two tailored deep learning frameworks.
AI.result: Evaluated on two distinct industrial systems, DNA reduces mean absolute error (MAE) by 3.704% and 3.175% compared to the strongest baseline.
AI.conclusion: DNA effectively bridges mechanistic and data-driven modeling, offering a promising architecture for high-fidelity industrial digital twins.

title: Newton-PINet: A fast physics-informed neural network with Newton linearization for meta-learning nonlinear PDEs
summary: Scientific machine learning has opened new avenues for solving parameterized partial differential equations (PDEs), enabling models to learn a family of PDEs and generalize to unseen instances. In this context, data-driven operator learning methods typically require large training datasets, while physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) suffer from difficult optimization and limited generalization, especially for nonlinear PDEs. We propose Newton-PINet, a physics-informed network enhanced by Newton linearization, offering an effective meta-learning framework for nonlinear PDEs. Newton-PINet (i) employs a physics-informed multilayer network with skip connections, where the output-layer weights are solved by least squares; (ii) adopts a two-stage learning strategy that first leverages gradient-based training to learn robust representations from the available training tasks, and then performs gradient-free fine-tuning on the output layer for fast task-specific generalization; and (iii) incorporates a Newton linearization method to speed up the least-squares iteration for nonlinear PDE problems. On a challenging nonlinear reaction-diffusion benchmark, Newton-PINet achieves up to three orders of magnitude lower relative error than recent neural solvers, while using 16x fewer training tasks and over an order of magnitude less training time (about 5 minutes versus several hours). This work advances the meta-learning of PINNs toward data-efficient, fast, and generalizable physics solvers. The code and datasets are publicly available at: this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Newton-PINet, a physics-informed neural network enhanced with Newton linearization for fast meta-learning of nonlinear partial differential equations.
AI.motivation: Data-driven operator learning requires large training datasets, whereas physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) face difficult optimization and poor generalization on nonlinear PDEs.
AI.method: Newton-PINet uses a physics-informed multilayer network with skip connections whose output-layer weights are solved by least squares, trains representations via a two-stage strategy (gradient-based pretraining followed by gradient-free output-layer fine-tuning), and applies Newton linearization to accelerate least-squares iterations.
AI.result: On a nonlinear reaction-diffusion benchmark, Newton-PINet achieves up to three orders of magnitude lower relative error than recent neural solvers while using 16x fewer training tasks and over an order of magnitude less training time (about 5 minutes versus several hours).
AI.conclusion: Newton-PINet advances meta-learning for PINNs toward faster, more data-efficient, and better-generalizing solvers for nonlinear PDEs.

title: GPromptShield: Elevating Resilience in Graph Prompt Tuning against Adversarial Attacks
summary: The paradigm of ``pre-training and prompt-tuning", with its effectiveness and lightweight characteristics, has rapidly spread from the language field to the graph field. Several pioneering studies have designed specialized prompt functions for diverse downstream graph tasks based on various graph pre-training strategies. These prompts concentrate on the compatibility between the pre-training pretext and downstream graph tasks, aiming to bridge the gap between them. However, designing prompts blindly to adapt to downstream tasks based on this concept neglects crucial security issues. By conducting covert attacks on downstream graph data, we find that even when the downstream task data closely matches that of the pre-training tasks, it is still feasible to generate highly misleading prompts using simple deceptive techniques. In this paper, we shift the primary focus of graph prompts from compatibility to vulnerability issues in adversarial attack scenarios. We design a highly extensible shield defense system for the prompts, which enhances their robustness from two perspectives: Direct Handling and Indirect Amplification. When downstream graph data contains unreliable biases, the former directly combats invalid information by incorporating hybrid multi-defense prompts to the input graph's feature space, while the latter adopts a training strategy to bypass the invalid components and amplifies valid part. We provide a theoretical derivation that proves their feasibility, indicating that unbiased prompts exist under certain conditions on unreliable data. Extensive experiments across various scenarios of adversarial attacks indicate that the prompts within our defense system exhibit enhanced resilience and superiority. This paper explores a new perspective in graph prompt learning, offering a novel option for robust prompt tuning in downstream tasks.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes GPromptShield, a defense framework that protects graph prompt tuning against adversarial attacks on downstream graph data.
AI.motivation: Existing graph prompt-tuning methods focus on bridging pre-training and downstream tasks but overlook security vulnerabilities, allowing simple covert attacks on downstream data to generate misleading prompts.
AI.method: GPromptShield defends prompts from two angles: Direct Handling, which adds hybrid multi-defense prompts to the input graph feature space to counter invalid biases, and Indirect Amplification, which uses a training strategy to bypass invalid components and amplify valid information, backed by theoretical feasibility analysis.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across various adversarial attack scenarios show that prompts protected by GPromptShield exhibit stronger resilience and superior performance compared to baselines.
AI.conclusion: Shifting focus from task compatibility to adversarial robustness provides a viable path for secure graph prompt tuning in downstream tasks.

title: Contrastive Activation-Guided Zeroth-Order Preference Optimisation for Memory-Efficient LLM Alignment
summary: Direct Preference Optimisation (DPO) simplifies reinforcement learning from human feedback, but still relies on traditional backpropagation and its associated activation-memory cost. Zeroth-order (ZO) optimisation avoids backpropagation, yet isotropic perturbations can produce noisy updates for preference objectives defined by differences between chosen and rejected responses. We introduce Contrastive Activation-guided Zeroth-Order Direct Preference Optimisation (CA-ZODPO), which constructs a low-rank search subspace from the activation discrepancy between the chosen and rejected responses in each preference pair. Perturbations are restricted to this subspace, while momentum is maintained in low-rank coordinates to preserve the memory advantages of ZO training. On Qwen2.5-1.5B with Anthropic HH-RLHF, CA-ZODPO outperforms common ZO baselines and remains competitive with first-order DPO in pairwise preference evaluation. It also reduces peak GPU memory by about 59\% at a sequence length of 2048 while retaining the sequence-length scaling behaviour of zeroth-order training.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Contrastive Activation-guided Zeroth-Order Direct Preference Optimisation (CA-ZODPO) to reduce GPU memory during LLM alignment without backpropagation.
AI.motivation: Direct Preference Optimisation (DPO) avoids full RLHF but still incurs high activation-memory costs from backpropagation, while standard zeroth-order (ZO) optimisation suffers from noisy updates under isotropic perturbations.
AI.method: CA-ZODPO constructs a low-rank search subspace from the activation discrepancy between chosen and rejected responses in each preference pair, restricts ZO perturbations to this subspace, and maintains momentum in low-rank coordinates.
AI.result: On Qwen2.5-1.5B with Anthropic HH-RLHF, CA-ZODPO outperforms common ZO baselines, remains competitive with first-order DPO in pairwise preference evaluation, and reduces peak GPU memory by about 59% at sequence length 2048.
AI.conclusion: Restricting zeroth-order updates to a contrastive activation subspace preserves the memory efficiency of ZO training while enabling effective preference alignment.

title: Instrumenting Failure: Scoring Language Model Agents at Every Decision Node in Imperfect-Information Games
comment: Accepted at the Interpreting Agent Behavior (IAB) Workshop, NeurIPS 2026. 26 pages, 6 figures. Code: this https URL
summary: Agent evaluations report task success and rarely say what an agent did at each decision. We score every decision node of three 12B to 14B instruct-tuned language models (LMs) playing five zero-sum imperfect-information games against four opponents on eight properties from decision and game theory, five of them against a CFR+ equilibrium reference. At each node, the LM also states a belief about the opponent's hidden state in a separate call. Without memory and at temperature 0, stated beliefs sit 0.250 to 0.288 in total variation distance from the equilibrium posterior, and where the action responds to the state its agreement with that belief exceeds chance by -0.04 to 0.19. The two calls frame the opponent differently, so the result is a behavioural inconsistency and makes no claim about internal beliefs. Under one prompt and greedy decoding, the LM's action never varies with the state in 10 of the 38 cells where the reference varies its own. Memory lowers the constant-action share in 9 of 13 testable ladders at temperature 0; at temperature 0.2 the cells at 1 fall from 16 to 5 of the 46 informative cells, while the belief results hold. A gate withholds, with a stated reason, any belief score the run cannot support, and seven of the eight non-zero defect rates are attributable to the instrument, a representation, or the LMs.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates language model agents at every decision node in imperfect-information games, revealing frequent behavioral inconsistencies between stated beliefs and actions.
AI.motivation: Standard agent evaluations only report overall task success and do not reveal what an agent does at individual decision points.
AI.method: The authors score three 12B to 14B instruct-tuned LMs across five zero-sum imperfect-information games against four opponents on eight decision- and game-theoretic properties (five compared against a CFR+ equilibrium reference), while querying stated beliefs about opponent hidden states in a separate call.
AI.result: Without memory at temperature 0, stated beliefs have 0.250 to 0.288 total variation distance from the equilibrium posterior, action-belief agreement exceeds chance by only -0.04 to 0.19, and actions never vary with state in 10 of 38 cells where the reference varies; adding memory lowers the constant-action share in 9 of 13 testable ladders, and a gating mechanism attributes seven of eight non-zero defect rates to the instrument, representation, or LMs.
AI.conclusion: Node-level instrumentation exposes systematic decision-making and belief-action inconsistencies in LM agents that aggregate task success metrics miss.

title: ParGLU: Partial Gating Improves Language Modeling in MoE Transformers
summary: Multiplicative gating improves Transformer feed-forward networks (FFNs), but it reduces intermediate representation width under a fixed parameter budget. This trade-off is particularly relevant to Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, where individual experts have limited capacity. We introduce ParGLU, a partially gated FFN that combines SwiGLU and ReLU$^2$ in two parallel branches. ParGLU matches the parameter count and principal matrix computation budget of conventional SwiGLU. We evaluate ParGLU in 30M, 75M, and 152M MoE language models using three random seeds per scale. ParGLU outperforms SwiGLU across all three seeds at 75M and 152M, reducing mean validation NLL by 0.0200 and 0.0249, respectively. Results at 30M are mixed. Controlled ablations show that increasing backbone width or expert width strengthens ParGLU's relative performance. Ablation studies further show that combining SwiGLU and ReLU$^2$ improves performance over either architecture alone. Token-frequency analysis reveals larger improvements on low-frequency tokens. These findings show that fully gated FFNs are not always the most effective use of an MoE expert's parameter budget. Partial gating can improve language modeling in MoE Transformers.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes ParGLU, a partially gated feed-forward network combining SwiGLU and ReLU^2 in parallel branches, which improves language modeling in MoE Transformers.
AI.motivation: Multiplicative gating in FFNs improves performance but reduces intermediate representation width under a fixed parameter budget, which constrains individual experts in Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models.
AI.method: ParGLU splits the FFN into two parallel branches using SwiGLU and ReLU^2 while matching the parameter count and principal matrix computation budget of conventional SwiGLU.
AI.result: Across 75M and 152M MoE language models (three seeds each), ParGLU outperforms SwiGLU on all seeds, reducing mean validation NLL by 0.0200 and 0.0249 respectively, while 30M results are mixed; ablations show larger gains with wider backbones or experts and stronger improvements on low-frequency tokens.
AI.conclusion: Fully gated FFNs are not always optimal for MoE expert parameter budgets, and partial gating offers a simple way to improve MoE language modeling.

title: Conditional Diffusion Models for Amortized Bayesian System Identification
summary: Generative diffusion models rapidly solve Bayesian inverse problems, such as image restoration and inpainting, with a single trained model and without retraining for each new observation or task. Bayesian system identification, which typically involves inferring the hidden states and parameters of a dynamical system from measurements, poses a closely related inverse problem. Yet it is often addressed with computationally heavy Monte Carlo methods that must be rerun for every new measurement record. Moreover, these methods are restricted to a single inference task, and their cost grows with the state dimension and the record length. To alleviate these restrictions, we interpret Bayesian system identification in hiddem Markov models (HMMs) as a general Bayesian inverse problem, taking advantage of conditional diffusion models. Specifically, a transformer-based diffusion model is trained once on short segments of simulated trajectories to approximate the joint posterior of states and parameters. Through an attention mask induced by the Markov property and a relative time encoding, it can then be deployed on any new measurement record of custom length. At inference time, the same model can flexibly and rapidly be conditioned for joint state and parameter inference, state smoothing, parameter inference, or reconstructing missing measurements, without retraining. We demonstrate these capabilities on four benchmark systems and examine how the length of the training segments affects state and parameter inference. On records five times longer than the training segments, the model maintains its state accuracy, whereas comparison methods either show a more than tenfold error increase or require ten times as much sampling time.

AI.tldr: This paper uses a transformer-based conditional diffusion model for amortized Bayesian system identification in hidden Markov models, generalizing to arbitrary trajectory lengths without retraining.
AI.motivation: Bayesian system identification typically relies on expensive Monte Carlo methods that must be rerun for every new measurement record and inference task, scaling poorly with state dimension and record length.
