For kernel value iteration with per-target variances that are assigned when a target is collected, we prove a high-probability bound on the error of the value estimate, uniform over the explored region. Pooled over five simulated benchmarks, which include a chemical reactor and a bioprocess, HGPQ approaches the best return found by any method in fewer episodes than GP, kernel and deep RL baselines.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Heteroscedastic Gaussian Process Q-learning (HGPQ), which uses a heteroscedastic GP to weight Bellman targets by state-dependent noise for sample-efficient control.
AI.motivation: Self-driving laboratories must learn control policies from tens to hundreds of expensive experiments, which is far too few for deep reinforcement learning.
AI.method: HGPQ models the Q-function directly with a Gaussian process where the Kalman gain acts as the MSE-optimal learning rate, and uses a heteroscedastic GP to assign per-target noise variances so noisy or high-gradient regions have less influence on value updates, backed by a high-probability uniform error bound.
AI.result: Across five simulated benchmarks including a chemical reactor and a bioprocess, HGPQ approaches the best return in fewer episodes than GP, kernel, and deep RL baselines.
AI.conclusion: Heteroscedastic GP value learning provides a sample-efficient, theoretically grounded RL approach for expensive physical experimentation.

title: Conformal Expert Pools: Training-Free Probabilistic Time-Series Forecasting Beyond Seasonality
comment: 21 pages, 3 figures, 11 tables. Successor to arXiv:2605.03789
summary: Conformal Seasonal Pools (CSP) showed that a forecaster with no training at all, built only from past values at the same point in the season and from past forecast errors, significantly outperformed DeepNPTS, Amazon's learned non-parametric forecaster. We propose Conformal Expert Pools (CEP), a training-free successor. CEP replaces the single seasonal-naive forecast by a pool of simple forecasters, builds its predictive distribution from their past forecast errors, and adapts both the pool and the errors to the series being forecast. No model is trained and no parameter is learned across series. On the CSP benchmark of 232 datasets and 24,502 forecast windows, CEP is better than CSP on 78% of datasets by CRPS, on 84% by MSIS and on 83% by Winkler score; on a typical dataset its CRPS is 14% lower and its MSIS 23% lower (both p < 1e-22, paired Wilcoxon test), and coverage of 95% intervals rises from 90.1% to 92.2%. CEP has a lower CRPS than DeepNPTS on 88% of datasets, than NPTS on 89% and than SeasonalNPTS on 83%. The improvement persists on dataset families outside the development set and on 36 additional fev-bench files. We also test the published claims that Laplace, an online ensemble forecaster, "beats (almost) everything" and "beats" CSP. On 228 datasets at multi-step horizons the claims do not hold: CSP outperforms Laplace on 60% of datasets by CRPS and on 64% by interval score, and Laplace ranks sixth of seven methods, with the widest intervals of all (69% wider than CEP's). Its point forecast is biased low and on 54% of datasets is less accurate than seasonal naive, and from a cold start it takes about 7,700 times longer than CSP. CEP is better than Laplace on 82% of datasets by CRPS and on 80% by MSIS, with intervals about 40% narrower, and runs 271 times faster.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Conformal Expert Pools (CEP), a training-free probabilistic time-series forecaster that outperforms Conformal Seasonal Pools (CSP), learned NPTS variants, and Laplace.
AI.motivation: Training-free Conformal Seasonal Pools (CSP) previously beat learned non-parametric forecasters, motivating a more flexible training-free approach beyond a single seasonal-naive baseline.
AI.method: CEP replaces the single seasonal-naive forecaster with an adaptive pool of simple forecasters and constructs predictive distributions from their past forecast errors, without training any model or learning parameters across series.
AI.result: On 232 datasets (24,502 windows), CEP beats CSP on 78% of datasets by CRPS (14% lower) and 84% by MSIS (23% lower, p < 1e-22), raises 95% interval coverage from 90.1% to 92.2%, beats DeepNPTS on 88%, NPTS on 89%, and SeasonalNPTS on 83%, and outperforms Laplace on 82% by CRPS with 40% narrower intervals and 271x faster runtime.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive pools of simple forecasters with conformal error distributions deliver strong, fast, training-free probabilistic forecasts that challenge complex online ensembles.

title: The Price of Not Planning: Parallel Sampling Depth Peaks at the Reconstruction Threshold
summary: Masked diffusion models sample the tokens of one round independently. Planned decoders first generate a coarse plan, then fill in the tokens in parallel. We ask when a plan saves rounds, how many it saves, and how fine it must be. We study this on broadcast trees: the leaves are the tokens, the internal nodes are the plan, and the edge correlation $\theta$ sets how strongly tokens depend on the plan. Errors are measured by the forward Kullback-Leibler divergence $\varepsilon$, and the lower bounds hold for every deterministic value-adaptive rule, also with learned conditionals. We show that a decoder without the plan needs of order $\min\{n,(n/\varepsilon)^{\alpha}\}$ rounds below the reconstruction threshold, where $\alpha=\log b/(4\log(1/\theta))$ rises to $1/2$ at the threshold, and that the exponent stays below $1/2$ above it (binary channel: $0.02\le\theta\le0.98$). With the plan, $\log_b n+1$ rounds suffice. In the binary model below the threshold, a plan with units of $m$ tokens needs of order $\log_b(n/m)+\min\{m,(n/\varepsilon)^{\alpha}\}$ rounds, so it gives logarithmic depth exactly when $m$ is logarithmic. A plan therefore helps most near the threshold, and only if its units are small. Exact divergence computations in the Gaussian model with up to $2^{20}$ leaves confirm these exponents below the threshold.

AI.tldr: This paper proves how much parallel sampling depth a coarse plan saves in masked diffusion models on broadcast trees, showing savings peak at the reconstruction threshold.
AI.motivation: Planned masked diffusion decoders generate a coarse plan before filling tokens in parallel, but it is unclear when planning reduces sampling rounds, by how much, and how fine the plan must be.
AI.method: The authors analyze broadcast trees where leaves are tokens, internal nodes are the plan, and edge correlation theta controls token-plan dependence, deriving lower bounds on rounds needed for forward KL error epsilon across deterministic value-adaptive rules and verifying exponents in a Gaussian model up to 2^20 leaves.
AI.result: Without a plan, decoding requires order min{n, (n/epsilon)^alpha} rounds below the reconstruction threshold (with alpha rising to 1/2 at the threshold and staying below 1/2 above it), whereas a plan reduces this to log_b(n) + 1 rounds; below the threshold, a plan with m-token units needs log_b(n/m) + min{m, (n/epsilon)^alpha} rounds, achieving logarithmic depth only when m is logarithmic.
AI.conclusion: Coarse planning yields its greatest parallel depth savings near the reconstruction threshold and only achieves logarithmic depth when plan units are logarithmically small.

title: Deep Learning for Physicists: From Linear Regression to Reasoning Models
comment: 115 pages, many figures. Based on lectures given at Queen Mary University of London
summary: These lecture notes are based on an introductory course on neural networks and deep learning that the author taught in the School of Mathematical Sciences at Queen Mary University of London in 2023/24 and 2024/25. The author, however, is a physicist, and it shows: wherever possible, ideas are explained with physical intuition rather than heavy formalism. Readers with a background in physics or mathematics who want a self-contained, introductory route into modern machine learning may therefore find these notes particularly friendly. The notes start from maximum likelihood, least squares, linear regression and (stochastic) gradient descent. They then cover neural networks, backpropagation, the vanishing gradient problem, batch and layer normalization, overfitting and regularization, adversarial examples, and the kernel method. The second half turns to natural language processing: word embeddings, recurrent networks and LSTMs, the attention mechanism and Transformers, and large language models, including scaling laws, the history of GPT, instruction tuning, reinforcement learning from human feedback, hallucination, alignment faking, chain-of-thought reasoning and test-time scaling. The emphasis on large language models reflects requests from the students. The notes are aimed at third- and fourth-year students in the UK system. Because the course was also taken by students from other departments, very little is assumed: even basic material such as matrix multiplication is explained from scratch, so readers familiar with it can safely skip such parts. No originality is claimed; the aim is a coherent, intuitive path through the material. Developments after spring 2025 are not covered, but the basic ideas emphasized here are unlikely to go out of date soon.

AI.tldr: These lecture notes provide a self-contained, physics-intuition-driven introduction to neural networks and deep learning, progressing from linear regression to modern large language models and reasoning models.
AI.motivation: Students with physics or mathematics backgrounds often encounter heavy formalism in standard machine learning texts, so a coherent, introductory path emphasizing physical intuition and minimal prerequisites is needed.
AI.method: Based on a 2023/24 and 2024/25 course at Queen Mary University of London for third- and fourth-year students, the notes explain core concepts from scratch, covering optimization, neural network architectures, NLP, Transformers, and LLM post-training and reasoning.
AI.result: The notes cover foundational topics (maximum likelihood, backpropagation, normalization, regularization, kernels) through modern LLMs (scaling laws, GPT history, instruction tuning, RLHF, hallucination, alignment faking, chain-of-thought, and test-time scaling) up to spring 2025.
AI.conclusion: While claiming no originality, the notes offer an accessible, intuition-first route into modern machine learning and language models for readers from quantitative backgrounds.

title: Programmable Semantic Interventions: Learning Causal Carriers from Behavioral Programs
summary: Causal abstraction explains a frozen network by aligning its activations with the variables of a simpler, interpretable model, and checking that interventions on the two agree. Finding such an alignment currently requires a counterfactual dataset: for every pair of prompts, the answer the network ought to give once the variable has been changed. In practice, those labels are produced by an executable algorithm for the behavior, written before studying the model supposed to implement it. However, the criterion these methods optimize only leverages the answer an intervention should produce. Here, we develop an approach that lets the investigator define that relationship directly: the answers the variable can produce, and which of them an intervention should yield. We call this interface a semantic program and introduce Programmable Semantic Interventions (PSI): a low-rank activation subspace learned so that interchanging it changes the model's answer as the program declares, with the expected answers read from the frozen model itself. On the MIB benchmark PSI performs on par with supervised alignment at matched data and training budget, without curated pairs, and it needs no ground-truth labels; while on natural science questions with gold labels withheld, it tracks the model's own answers better than a subspace trained on gold labels. The declaration also fixes a coordinate system with known semantics, enabling donor-free steering: jointly training PSI for both localization and control realizes 94.8% of held-out requests for answers the investigator chooses, without the need for donor prompts.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Programmable Semantic Interventions (PSI), a method that learns causal activation subspaces directly from a declared semantic program without requiring counterfactual prompt pairs or ground-truth labels.
AI.motivation: Existing causal abstraction methods require curated counterfactual datasets with labeled expected answers for every prompt pair, even though the optimization criterion only uses the answer an intervention should produce.
AI.method: PSI defines a semantic program specifying which answers a variable can produce and how interventions map between them, then learns a low-rank activation subspace whose interchange changes the frozen model's answer as declared, using expected answers read from the model itself.
AI.result: On the MIB benchmark, PSI matches supervised alignment at matched data and training budgets without curated pairs or ground-truth labels, outperforms gold-label subspaces on natural science questions with withheld labels, and achieves 94.8% of held-out donor-free steering requests.
AI.conclusion: PSI enables label-free causal localization and donor-free steering by fixing an interpretable coordinate system directly from behavioral declarations.

title: Can AI Mature a Model's Geometry? Training-Free Weight Baking in LLMs
summary: Can an AI make a trained language model more mature, in the sense of a better organized latent space, by looking only at the geometry of that space? An analyst model reads a fixed-size digest of topological descriptors of the layers of a frozen target and proposes a transformation, which closed-form ridge regression writes into the feed-forward weights without gradient training. Using lightweight models, 126 runs show that category purity rose on unseen words and sentences, benchmark accuracy stayed within sampling error, and the analyst matched a category-aware heuristic with gentler edits. In a five-model round robin approach, 16 pairs raised purity and four left the target unchanged. The results provide a baseline for future work on LLM-guided, training-free model editing without using raw weights.

AI.tldr: This paper tests whether an analyst LLM can improve the latent space geometry of a frozen target LLM without gradient training by proposing weight edits from topological descriptors.
AI.motivation: Editing a trained language model to better organize its latent space typically requires gradient-based training or raw weight inspection, raising the question of whether geometry-only, training-free editing is feasible.
AI.method: An analyst model reads a fixed-size digest of topological descriptors from a frozen target model's layers and proposes a transformation, which is written into the feed-forward weights via closed-form ridge regression.
AI.result: Across 126 runs on lightweight models, category purity increased on unseen words and sentences while benchmark accuracy stayed within sampling error, matching a category-aware heuristic with gentler edits; in a five-model round-robin, 16 pairs raised purity and four left the target unchanged.
AI.conclusion: The results establish a baseline for LLM-guided, training-free model editing using only latent-space geometry rather than raw weights.

title: Wavelet-Energy-Driven Dynamic Patching for Time Series Forecasting
summary: Patch-based transformers tokenise a time series into fixed-size, uniform windows, which commits the model to a single temporal resolution even though real signals are multi-scale. The discrete wavelet transform (DWT) is a natural alternative because it decomposes a signal across scales. A growing body of work makes the wavelet filter learnable, on the assumption that a more flexible wavelet forecasts better. That assumption has rarely been tested in isolation, because a single reported improvement usually credits three things at once. These are the use of any multi-resolution decomposition, the choice of wavelet and training the filter. We introduce a forecaster that turns a learnable-DWT per-scale energy map into variable-length patches by merging adjacent windows that share a dominant scale. Three findings follow. First, most of the improvement is there before any filter is learned. A frozen wavelet beats a fixed-patch baseline on eight of the nine datasets by 1.5% to 7.8%, and on four of them it recovers all of the gain. Traffic is the one exception, where it is 1.2% worse. Second, learning the filter gives a further improvement on only some datasets. It helps on three of the nine datasets and makes Traffic 2.7% worse. Third, having variable-length patches helps, but exactly where their boundaries fall does not. A fixed-size uniform grid, even with its patch size tuned per task, is worse than our variable-length patches on 27 of 36 settings. Recomputing the boundaries from the learned filter at every step, rather than caching them once, never helps. The improvement in wavelet-based forecasting comes from the multi-resolution structure and the variable-length patches it induces, not from making the wavelet learnable. In practice, start from any valid wavelet, cache the patch boundaries once and treat training the filter as a per-dataset decision rather than a default.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates learnable wavelet patching for time series forecasting and finds that performance gains come from multi-resolution decomposition and variable-length patching rather than learning the wavelet filter itself.
AI.motivation: Prior work on learnable discrete wavelet transforms (DWT) for time series forecasting conflates the benefits of multi-resolution decomposition, wavelet choice, and filter training, leaving the value of learning the filter untested in isolation.
AI.method: The authors build a forecaster that converts a learnable-DWT per-scale energy map into variable-length patches by merging adjacent windows sharing a dominant scale, and isolate the effects of frozen versus learned filters and fixed versus dynamic patch boundaries.
AI.result: A frozen wavelet beats a fixed-patch baseline on 8 of 9 datasets by 1.5% to 7.8% (recovering all gains on 4 datasets, with Traffic 1.2% worse), learning the filter helps on only 3 datasets (and worsens Traffic by 2.7%), and variable-length patches outperform tuned uniform grids in 27 of 36 settings while recomputing boundaries never helps.
AI.conclusion: Practitioners should start from any valid frozen wavelet, cache variable-length patch boundaries once, and treat wavelet filter training as a per-dataset choice rather than a default.

title: TEMPO: Regime-Aware Operator Learning with Locally Adapted POD Bases
summary: Operator learning approximates the solution map of a parametric partial differential equation from data, enabling fast prediction at new parameter values without repeated simulation. The dominant approach fits a single global low-rank basis, typically a proper orthogonal decomposition (POD), to all solution snapshots. This fails when the snapshots span qualitatively different solution shapes, from smooth diffusive profiles to near-discontinuous shocks. We propose TEMPO (Trajectory Expectation-Maximization Mixture of POD Operators), a two-phase framework for regime-aware operator learning. In the offline phase, TEMPO recovers latent regimes via expectation-maximization, fitting a dedicated linear or nonlinear basis to each discovered regime. In the online phase, a gating network and per-regime branch networks are trained jointly, routing new inputs to the regimes at inference. We test TEMPO on Burgers' flow, Sod shock tubes, Coanda flow, Darcy flow, Navier-Stokes flow and the heterogeneous Helmholtz equation. With 64 total POD modes, TEMPO gives 18.61% test error on Burgers', compared with 19.61% for global POD. It also gives lower errors on Coanda and Helmholtz.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes TEMPO, a two-phase regime-aware operator learning framework that discovers latent solution regimes and fits locally adapted POD bases instead of a single global basis.
AI.motivation: Standard operator learning fits a single global low-rank proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) basis to all PDE snapshots, which fails when solutions span qualitatively different regimes such as smooth profiles and shocks.
AI.method: TEMPO uses expectation-maximization offline to cluster snapshots into latent regimes with dedicated linear or nonlinear bases, and trains a gating network jointly with per-regime branch networks online to route new inputs at inference.
AI.result: Evaluated on Burgers' flow, Sod shock tubes, Coanda flow, Darcy flow, Navier-Stokes flow, and heterogeneous Helmholtz equations, TEMPO with 64 total POD modes achieves 18.61% test error on Burgers' compared to 19.61% for global POD, and also lowers errors on Coanda and Helmholtz.
AI.conclusion: Regime-aware decomposition with locally adapted POD bases and learned routing improves operator learning accuracy on multi-regime PDEs.

title: Representational Change Under Self-Consuming Training: A Sparse Autoencoder Analysis
summary: Large language models are increasingly exposed to model-generated text, raising the possibility that future models will be trained recursively on the outputs of their predecessors. Prior work on such self-consuming training loops has largely focused on output quality and downstream performance, leaving their effects on internal representations poorly understood. We study how representations evolve across five generations of self-consumption and whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) remain reliable under this shift. At each generation, we compare a lineage trained on synthetic data with a matched control trained on real data under the same training settings. We evaluate how well SAEs trained before self-consumption transfer to later generations, measuring reconstruction and sparsity across SAE widths, architectures, and model layers. We then fine-tune the original SAE on each generation and use sparse probing to test whether task-relevant information remains concentrated in a small number of latents or becomes more distributed across the representation. We find that zero-shot SAE performance degrades progressively under self-consumption, with growing reconstruction and sparsity gaps that vary substantially across layers. Fine-tuning largely restores reconstruction, but not feature-level usefulness: task-relevant information remains accessible in the full latent space while becoming less concentrated in individual features. These results show that self-consumption induces representational drift and that reconstruction fidelity alone is insufficient to establish that an adapted SAE remains equally useful for interpretation.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how internal representations change across five generations of self-consuming LLM training and evaluates whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) remain reliable interpretability tools under this shift.
AI.motivation: Prior work on recursive training on model-generated text has focused on output quality and downstream tasks, leaving its effects on internal representations and SAE interpretability poorly understood.
AI.method: Across five generations of synthetic-data training versus matched real-data controls, the authors evaluate zero-shot transfer of pre-existing SAEs across widths, architectures, and layers, then fine-tune SAEs per generation and use sparse probing to measure feature concentration.
AI.result: Zero-shot SAE reconstruction and sparsity degrade progressively across generations with layer-dependent gaps; fine-tuning restores reconstruction fidelity, but sparse probing shows task-relevant information becomes less concentrated in individual latents while remaining accessible in the full latent space.
AI.conclusion: Self-consuming training induces representational drift that degrades SAE interpretability, and reconstruction fidelity alone is insufficient to verify that an adapted SAE remains useful for interpretation.

title: Specificity-Guided Knowledge Diversion for Decomposable Generative Models
summary: Generative model pre-training typically optimizes a model as a whole without explicitly organizing its parameters for selective reuse. Decomposable pre-training instead learns reusable components for downstream adaptation while retaining strong generative performance. However, existing knowledge diversion methods incur substantial parameter overhead through weight factorization and rely on fixed component assignments to induce specialization, potentially compromising in-distribution generation quality. We therefore propose Specificity-Guided Knowledge Diversion (SGKDiv), which learns how generative knowledge is shared and specialized for effective generation and selective downstream reuse. SGKDiv constructs Knowledge Units from paired feed-forward channels, preserving native computational structure without SVD-based reparameterization. Calibrated condition-wise routing combines a shared usage prior with conditional adjustments, while complementary regularization shapes their allocation, diversity, and magnitude. Together, these designs replace predefined component assignments with adaptively learned and explicitly regulated knowledge specialization. Experiments across diverse model and training settings demonstrate better in-distribution generation than dense and MoE baselines, alongside stronger downstream adaptation than representative PEFT methods across eight datasets.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Specificity-Guided Knowledge Diversion (SGKDiv), a decomposable generative pre-training method that organizes paired feed-forward channels into Knowledge Units with calibrated conditional routing.
AI.motivation: Existing decomposable pre-training methods rely on weight factorization with high parameter overhead and fixed component assignments, which can degrade in-distribution generation quality.
AI.method: SGKDiv forms Knowledge Units from paired feed-forward channels without SVD reparameterization, and uses calibrated condition-wise routing combining a shared usage prior with conditional adjustments and regularization for allocation, diversity, and magnitude.
AI.result: Across diverse model and training settings, SGKDiv achieves better in-distribution generation than dense and MoE baselines and stronger downstream adaptation than representative PEFT methods across eight datasets.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive, explicitly regularized knowledge specialization in native feed-forward structures enables both high-quality generation and effective selective downstream reuse.

title: Agents Cannot Hand Over What They Have Not Yet Understood
summary: Agents that work beyond a single context window, or in teams, hand their work to a successor as a short written summary. Evaluation has focused on whether an agent can solve a task, and relatively little is known about how much of what an agent has learned survives being written down. We study this in 56 interactive worlds with hidden rules, where an agent that is told nothing fails and an agent given a 300-character statement of the rules succeeds. We compare one agent that plays eight lives and keeps its whole history with a chain of eight agents that each play one life and inherit a 300-character note. All six models we test learn less in the chain: after eight generations it stands where the single agent stood after about four lives. Controlled variants of the chain decompose this handoff loss into three components: none from changing the agent, a smaller loss from compressing to 300 characters, and a larger loss from compressing repeatedly. When each note is written from the full record of earlier lives instead of from the previous note, the same 300 characters recover 70% to 82% of the loss. The loss is robust across model sizes and is not alleviated by instructing the writer to record evidence, to revise the inherited note, or to keep a structured ledger. In simpler terms, an agent cannot hand over what it has not yet understood: a note holds what its writer has worked out, and a rule that takes several lives to see is lost with the lives that were not passed on.

AI.tldr: This paper measures how much knowledge is lost when AI agents hand off experience across generations via short written notes, finding that repeated compression loses multi-life rules.
AI.motivation: Agents operating beyond a single context window or in teams rely on short written summaries to pass knowledge to successors, yet little is known about how much learned understanding survives this handoff.
AI.method: Across 56 interactive worlds with hidden rules, the authors compare one agent playing eight lives with full history against an eight-agent chain passing 300-character notes, plus controlled variants isolating agent changes, single compression, and repeated compression.
AI.result: Across all six tested models, the eight-agent chain reaches only about the performance of a single agent after four lives; writing notes from full history recovers 70% to 82% of the loss, and instructing writers to record evidence, revise notes, or keep a ledger does not fix the loss.
AI.conclusion: Agents cannot hand over rules they have not yet understood, so multi-step patterns requiring several lives to discover are lost when only compressed notes are passed forward.

title: Just sort it! A note on the LP behind rank-one anti-loop edits
comment: 4 pages, 3 tables. Data, code and protocols: this https URL
summary: Weight-space programming removes the thinking loops of a small reasoning model by a rank-one edit W' = W + u v^T of an MLP output matrix, where u is a loop direction and v is the solution of a sparse Linear Program (LP) over the neuron activations. We investigate whether the LP is needed. We replace it by a sort: we take the 8 neurons whose activation has the smallest coefficient of variation, and give them equal shares of the push that the LP solution realizes. On Qwen3.5-0.8B the sorted edit scores 67.0% on 1000 problems (MATH-500 and GSM8K) against 67.4% for the LP edit and 9.5% for the unedited model; the paired difference is -0.4 points, with 95% confidence interval [-2.9, +2.1], inside a non-inferiority margin of 5 points declared before the runs. On three further sampling seeds the difference is -0.6 points, interval [-2.0, +0.8], and -0.8 points, interval [-2.3, +0.6], when the dose is set without the LP. The sort does not solve the LP, but the neurons it shares with the LP solution carry most of its mean push. The outcome is that, on this model, the edit acts as a nearly constant bias along u.

AI.tldr: This note shows that the sparse Linear Program (LP) used in rank-one anti-loop weight edits can be replaced by a simple sort over neuron activation variability with nearly identical performance.
AI.motivation: Weight-space programming removes thinking loops in small reasoning models via a rank-one MLP edit computed by solving a sparse LP, raising the question of whether solving the LP is actually necessary.
AI.method: Instead of solving the LP, the authors sort neurons by their activation coefficient of variation, select the 8 neurons with the smallest values, and assign them equal shares of the push.
AI.result: On Qwen3.5-0.8B across 1000 problems (MATH-500 and GSM8K), the sorted edit scores 67.0% versus 67.4% for the LP edit and 9.5% unedited (paired difference -0.4 points, 95% CI [-2.9, +2.1], within a 5-point non-inferiority margin), with similar results across three additional seeds even when the dose is set without the LP.
AI.conclusion: On this model, the anti-loop rank-one edit acts essentially as a constant bias along the loop direction, making the LP unnecessary.

title: Balanced Twin Weight Factorization for Efficient MLLMs
summary: Weight Factorization (WF) methods aim to reduce a model's latency, memory, or both. These typically decompose a pretrained model into two or more factors that approximate the original model weights with fewer parameters and floating point operations (FLOPs). However, translating fewer FLOPs into reduced latency is challenging for WF methods in practice due to overhead introduced by replacing a single large weight matrix with multiple smaller ones. To address this, we propose Balanced Twin Weight Factorization (BTWF), which uses the unique structure of factorized models to simultaneously lower latency and increase learning capacity. Specifically, BTWF operates in the shared basis WF setting, where two or more layers are decomposed into a shared basis matrix and a layer-specific mixing matrix. If these shared layers have the same input (i.e., are twins), then we need only perform this shared forward pass once, reducing inference time. However, twin layers are often of varying sizes, and methods from prior work tend to favor the larger layer. In contrast, our approach boosts performance by combining Factor Component Balancing (FCB), which ensures every shared member is well represented in the selected factors, with Block Contribution Balancing (BCB), which considers downstream model effects. Further, we also show that an overparameterized BTWF, where some layer's factors result in higher FLOPs than the original during training, can boost task performance without additional resources at test time. Experiments on six models over nine benchmarks show BTWF obtains a 2-6% gain over the state-of-the-art without expensive finetuning (1-3.5% gain with it) at comparable computational costs.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Balanced Twin Weight Factorization (BTWF), a shared-basis weight factorization method that balances factor representations and downstream block contributions to reduce latency and improve MLLM accuracy.
AI.motivation: Weight factorization reduces FLOPs and parameters, but replacing a large matrix with smaller ones often adds overhead that limits latency gains, and prior shared-basis methods favor larger layers when twin layers differ in size.
AI.method: BTWF shares a single forward pass across twin layers with the same input and combines Factor Component Balancing (FCB) to represent all shared members with Block Contribution Balancing (BCB) to account for downstream effects, alongside an overparameterized training option that adds no test-time cost.
AI.result: Experiments on six models across nine benchmarks show BTWF achieves 2-6% gains over state-of-the-art methods without finetuning and 1-3.5% gains with finetuning at comparable computational costs.
AI.conclusion: Balancing factor components and block contributions in shared-basis factorization simultaneously improves efficiency and task performance in MLLMs.

title: Detection-Efficient Watermarking for Vision--Language Agents via Risk-Constrained Strength Allocation
summary: Vision--language agents generate descriptions, decisions, and instructions that may be reused by users, downstream agents, and automated workflows, creating a need for provenance mechanisms that support content authenticity and post-deployment auditing without unnecessarily degrading response quality. We present a risk-aware semantic watermarking framework that combines predictive uncertainty with a zero-shot multimodal relevance-risk proxy to allocate watermark strength during decoding. A single risk penalty $\lambda$ exposes a continuous operating frontier, allowing deployment-time selection of a detection--quality trade-off without model retraining. At a selected operating point, mean watermark strength is reduced by approximately 59.4\% relative to fixed-strength watermarking, while perplexity change falls from 0.3634 to 0.1689 and clean/paraphrased ROC-AUC reaches 0.9552/0.9459. A matched-strength analysis shows that this advantage reflects the allocation policy rather than lower average intervention: at comparable mean strength, risk-constrained allocation achieves substantially higher ROC-AUC than fixed, entropy-only, and criticality-only policies, identifying it as detection-efficient rather than quality-dominant. We further show that threshold calibration on finite samples produces substantial false-positive-rate drift, motivating calibration variance reporting as standard practice for auditable provenance.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a risk-constrained semantic watermarking framework for vision-language agents that allocates watermark strength per token using predictive uncertainty and multimodal relevance-risk.
AI.motivation: Watermarking vision-language agent outputs for provenance and auditing often degrades response quality when applied uniformly at fixed strength.
AI.method: The framework combines predictive uncertainty with a zero-shot multimodal relevance-risk proxy during decoding, controlled by a single risk penalty parameter that exposes a continuous detection-quality operating frontier without retraining.
AI.result: At a selected operating point, mean watermark strength drops by ~59.4% versus fixed-strength watermarking while perplexity change falls from 0.3634 to 0.1689 and clean/paraphrased ROC-AUC reaches 0.9552/0.9459; at matched mean strength, it outperforms fixed, entropy-only, and criticality-only policies, while finite-sample calibration exhibits substantial FPR drift.
AI.conclusion: Risk-constrained strength allocation is detection-efficient rather than merely lower-strength, and calibration variance should be reported alongside provenance metrics.

title: Procedure without Judgment: What Small Language Models Learn under an Exact Verifier
summary: When an authorization policy blocks an agent's tool call, the audit log should name the facts that forced the decision and nothing more. For an executable policy over an enumerable context space this minimal sufficient reason can be computed exactly, so an explanation is scored against ground truth rather than a proxy for it. We use that exactness to ask what a model can learn from a verifier that has no error in it. The explainer sees one request and one decision, never the policy, and has thirty turns in which it may call the policy on altered requests and ask whether a candidate set of facts is sufficient. Frontier models find the exact reason about half the time with the tools alone, and one sentence telling them to shrink the answer lifts Haiku 4.5 from 58% to 75%. A 4B model fine-tuned on 2000 traces of the deletion algorithm reaches 92% on the policy it was trained on. Teacher kind is what moves this: at matched data size the algorithm-taught student leads the frontier-taught one in all three training seeds, and the two arms never overlap. What the student learns is a fixed schedule of sufficiency checks, and the schedule does not travel. On three public policies it never saw, its answers stay sufficient (94%) and stop being minimal (48%), while Haiku under the same sentence is exact on all 47 episodes. Reinforcement learning from the exact reward leaves held-out accuracy where it was and inverts the strategy, from probing the policy to spending the entire budget on sufficiency checks. The oracle made the effect of training legible, but it did not make training better.

AI.tldr: This paper uses an exact executable authorization policy verifier to study what a small language model learns from SFT and RL when explaining blocked tool calls.
AI.motivation: When an authorization policy blocks an agent's tool call, audit logs need the minimal sufficient reason, and an exact verifier over an enumerable context space lets researchers measure what models actually learn without proxy-reward noise.
AI.method: Models observe a request and decision without seeing the policy and have 30 turns to query the policy and test candidate sufficient sets; the authors compare frontier models, a 4B model fine-tuned on 2000 algorithmic deletion traces or frontier traces, and RL with exact reward.
AI.result: Frontier models succeed about half the time with tools alone (a shrink instruction lifts Haiku 4.5 from 58% to 75%); the algorithm-taught 4B student reaches 92% on the training policy and beats the frontier-taught student across all three seeds, but on three unseen public policies its answers remain sufficient (94%) while dropping to 48% minimal (versus 47/47 exact for Haiku), and RL fails to improve held-out accuracy while inverting the probing strategy.
AI.conclusion: An exact oracle made the effect of training legible—showing that SFT teaches a brittle, non-transferable schedule of sufficiency checks—but did not make training generalize better.

title: Optimistic Verifiers Get Hacked: Reward Hacking Under an Exact Process Oracle
comment: 30 pages. A shorter version, "The Verifier Gap", appears at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Meta-Agents (non-archival)
summary: Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards inherits whatever its verifier gets wrong. Outside mathematics and code the verifier is a proxy, a rubric, a learned judge or a hand-written checker, and its distance from the true objective is never measured, so a rising reward cannot be told apart from a hack. We build a setting where the true reward is exactly computable at the process level: executable authorization policies over 124,416 contexts admit an oracle that lists every minimal sufficient reason for every decision. We compile these policies into exact process rewards, degrade the verifier along seven realistic axes (outcome-only, sufficiency, recall-only, extraction noise, coarse taxonomy, stale policy, LLM judge), and train against each while the exact verifier scores every rollout. Four phenotypes appear. Optimistic verifiers are hacked by padding: the sufficiency proxy ends at 0.940 while true faithfulness falls from 0.731 to 0.667 on 96 held-out episodes. Outcome-only verifiers saturate and stop teaching, noise dilutes, and ranking-preserving gaps do no harm. A model-free audit of the verifier, its selection error and gap sign, together with a short saturation pilot, anticipates which phenotype a run will produce. Across nine configurations spanning two frameworks, two model vendors, two adapter sizes, three precisions, two initialisations and two seeds, the phenotypes recur, sufficiency damage is positive in all 10 replication cells and beyond two standard errors in 7, and optimistic gaps remain the steeper branch. The damage magnitude does not replicate, and five pre-registered attempts to explain it are reported as they fell. We release the testbed, the training instrumentation, and 14 real public policies (Cedar, OPA, Gatekeeper) ported to executable oracles.

AI.tldr: This paper builds an exact process-level oracle for authorization policies to measure reward hacking and training failure modes under seven realistic verifier degradations.
AI.motivation: Outside math and code, RL verifiers are imperfect proxies whose distance from the true objective is unknown, making it impossible to tell genuine progress from reward hacking.
AI.method: Using executable authorization policies over 124,416 contexts that admit an exact oracle for minimal sufficient reasons, the authors degrade the verifier along seven axes (outcome-only, sufficiency, recall-only, extraction noise, coarse taxonomy, stale policy, LLM judge) and score every rollout with the exact oracle.
AI.result: Four phenotypes emerge: optimistic verifiers are hacked by padding (sufficiency proxy reaches 0.940 while true faithfulness drops from 0.731 to 0.667 on 96 held-out episodes), outcome-only verifiers saturate, noise dilutes, and ranking-preserving gaps do no harm; these phenotypes recur across nine configurations, though damage magnitude does not replicate.
AI.conclusion: A model-free verifier audit (selection error and gap sign) plus a short saturation pilot can predict which training phenotype will occur before full RL runs.

title: Seen but Unsaid: Locating and Repairing Cross-Image Comparison in Vision-Language Models
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) often fail to match a point or an object across two images, even when the answer can be decoded from their own hidden states. We trace this failure from the visual tokens to the answer letter, in Qwen3-VL (2B-32B), InternVL3.5-8B, and Gemma-3-12B, on synthetic shape matching, same-instance point correspondence (HPatches), and semantic correspondence (SPair-71k), and find two distinct failure points, a small set of attention heads that carries the comparison, and a repair that touches 0.02% of the parameters. Two failure points: exact copies are compared but not read out. An answer-position probe exceeds the calibrated output by 15 to 25 points in every family, for nameable and unnameable shapes alike, and steering along the probe's direction moves no more answers than random directions. Semantic correspondences are present in the visual tokens but never reach the answer. One pathway: redistributing the cross-image attention of 16-32 heads, with its mass preserved, removes 17-22 points of synthetic and 15-32 points of HPatches accuracy, against at most 7 for random or attention-matched heads. A lever that training finds on its own: training only these heads' query and key projections raises SPair-71k accuracy by 28.3 points (Qwen3-VL-8B) and 25.1 points (InternVL3.5-8B), beats both layer-matched and attention-matched heads, and transfers to HPatches and BLINK. An unconstrained all-layer adapter routes 21-51% of its gain through the attention of the same heads, against at most 7% for random heads, and does so by changing what they read (83-86% of the effect) rather than their weights. Every decision rule was frozen before its run, and every reported number is recomputed by independent verification scripts.

AI.tldr: This paper locates a small set of attention heads responsible for cross-image comparison in VLMs and shows that training only their query and key projections repairs correspondence failures.
AI.motivation: Vision-language models frequently fail to match points or objects across two images even when the correct answer is decodable from their hidden states.
AI.method: Across Qwen3-VL (2B-32B), InternVL3.5-8B, and Gemma-3-12B on synthetic shape matching, HPatches, and SPair-71k, the authors trace visual-to-answer information flow, ablate 16-32 cross-image attention heads, and fine-tune only those heads' query and key projections (0.02% of parameters).
AI.result: Probes show exact-copy answers are present in hidden states (15-25 points above calibrated output) but not read out, while semantic correspondences fail to reach the answer; redistributing the 16-32 heads' attention removes 17-22 synthetic and 15-32 HPatches points, and QK-only tuning of these heads boosts SPair-71k accuracy by 28.3 points (Qwen3-VL-8B) and 25.1 points (InternVL3.5-8B) while transferring to HPatches and BLINK.
AI.conclusion: Cross-image comparison in VLMs is mediated by a compact attention-head pathway, and targeted QK adaptation repairs it more effectively than unconstrained adapters.

title: Right Reason, Wrong Advice: Evaluating Recourse in LLM Explanations of Denied Requests
summary: Language models increasingly write the explanations people receive when a rule system denies their request. If several rules deny the request independently, an explanation can name a true reason and still leave the person denied after they fix it. We call the missing property recourse validity: changing what the explanation cites, without changing what was asked for, can flip the decision. We compute it exactly, and a hitting-set argument predicts from the policy alone when a correct reason fails. In six of seven rule systems ported from access control and US benefit eligibility, a single correct reason almost never gives recourse when several reasons apply. Across 20 LLMs, checks of whether the cited reasons are correct, computed or asked of an LLM judge, are close to chance at spotting this failure, as the argument predicts. A strong judge asked whether acting on the explanation would work does spot it. Stronger and reasoning models do better but still fail on many denials with four or more independent reasons. Asking for every rule helps every open model with room to improve. Explanations of eligibility decisions should be built from the decision function and judged by whether acting on them works.

AI.tldr: This paper defines recourse validity for LLM explanations of denied requests and shows that citing a single true reason frequently fails to help users overturn multi-rule denials.
AI.motivation: When multiple rules independently deny a request, an LLM explanation can cite a factually true reason yet leave the user still denied even after they fix it.
AI.method: The authors formalize recourse validity—whether fixing what the explanation cites flips the decision—compute it exactly across seven rule systems from access control and US benefit eligibility, and evaluate 20 LLMs and LLM judges.
AI.result: In six of seven rule systems, a single true reason almost never provides recourse when multiple reasons apply; checks of reason correctness are near chance at catching this failure across 20 LLMs, whereas a strong judge asked if acting on the explanation works detects it, and even strong reasoning models struggle when four or more independent reasons apply.
AI.conclusion: Explanations for eligibility and access denials should be generated from the decision function itself and evaluated by whether acting on them actually changes the outcome.

title: Reading or Remembering? Measuring Temporal Contamination in Language Models
summary: Language models are now used to read central-bank text for economic forecasting, but most were trained on text written after the documents they read. A model reading a 2021 FOMC statement may already know that inflation rose in 2022, so part of its apparent skill can be memory of the outcome, a temporal form of test-set contamination. We measure this memory on FOMC statements and minutes from 2000 to 2026 by comparing modern open models with chronologically consistent models, which are trained only on text from before a fixed date. Asked about past GDP outcomes given only a date, models that cannot know the answer still reach an AUC of up to 0.64 from priors on dates and eras, so chance is the wrong baseline. Against these memory-free models on the same questions, most modern models recall which years had strong growth. Membership-inference scores sort documents by era and document type rather than by whether a model saw them, as exact counts in an open pretraining corpus show. In real-time nowcasts, every lookahead premium we estimate on US GDP is smaller than the forecast comparison can detect at macroeconomic sample sizes, and none on GDP or inflation survives correction for multiple testing. Lookahead audits should therefore measure memory directly against memory-free models on the same items.

AI.tldr: This paper measures temporal lookahead contamination in LLMs reading historical FOMC texts by comparing modern open models against chronologically consistent models trained only on pre-cutoff text.
AI.motivation: LLMs evaluated on historical central-bank documents for economic forecasting may rely on memorized future outcomes rather than reading the text, and chance baselines are misleading when date priors exist.
AI.method: Using FOMC statements and minutes from 2000 to 2026, the authors compare modern open models against chronologically consistent models on past GDP questions, membership-inference scores, and real-time nowcasts.
AI.result: Memory-free models already achieve up to 0.64 AUC from date and era priors alone; against these baselines, most modern models recall strong-growth years, membership-inference scores sort by era/document type rather than exact corpus presence, and estimated lookahead premia on US GDP and inflation nowcasts are too small to survive multiple-testing correction.
AI.conclusion: Lookahead audits should measure memory directly against chronologically consistent, memory-free models on the same items rather than relying on chance baselines or membership inference.

title: How VLMs Plan What's Next
summary: When a vision-language model describes an image, it names one object at a time and it rarely repeats itself, yet how the model plans this order is far from obvious. We characterize the mechanism a VLM uses to decide where to look before it looks. The mechanism has four main parts. First, binding heads match the relevant text tokens against the image and resolve them into pointers to the matched image region. Second, the same binding heads bind each written answer to the region it came from, and the model turns it into a progress signal: a cursor, the position in the image up to which the list has been written. Third, a select step chooses the nearest unwritten region after the cursor, or stops. Finally, gaze heads execute the chosen pointer and return a concept of what is drawn there, which language heads and the late MLPs turn into a word in the language of the question. We validate each part of this mechanism through causal patching in Qwen3-VL models on a synthetic visual retrieval task, and test our mechanisms against alternative hypotheses. We further show that the mechanism holds across input formats, natural photographs, and languages, and that its binding, relay, and gaze heads appear at every model size from 2B to 32B. This work allows us to investigate how a VLM turns a question and an image into a sequence of answers, layer by layer and token by token. More broadly, it opens a way to study how models plan over complex multi-step tasks with long rollouts. Our project is available at this https URL

AI.tldr: This paper uncovers a four-part attention-head mechanism by which vision-language models plan the sequential order of objects when describing an image.
AI.motivation: When describing an image, VLMs name objects sequentially without repetition, yet the internal mechanism that plans where to look next is unknown.
AI.method: Using causal patching on Qwen3-VL models (2B to 32B) in a synthetic visual retrieval task and natural images, the authors isolate binding heads, a cursor progress signal, a selection step, and gaze heads, testing them against alternative hypotheses.
AI.result: Binding heads match text tokens to image regions and track written answers via a cursor signal; a selection step picks the nearest unwritten region after the cursor (or stops); and gaze heads retrieve the object concept for language heads and late MLPs to verbalize, holding across input formats, natural photos, languages, and model sizes (2B-32B).
AI.conclusion: The findings reveal how VLMs convert an image and question into a planned sequence of answers layer by layer, offering a framework for studying multi-step planning in multimodal models.

title: Quantifying the added value of human forecaster discussions for tropical cyclone intensity prediction
summary: The National Hurricane Center routinely releases Tropical Cyclone Discussions that offer insights into its tropical cyclone forecasts. This study examines the added value of these discussions for intensity forecasting beyond a set of numerical predictors. For 637 Atlantic and eastern North Pacific tropical cyclones from the 2002-2023 hurricane seasons, we analyze the discussion text and its combination with 13 hurricane environmental predictors from SHIPS and ERA5 10-meter wind fields, for forecasting intensity changes at lead times of 24 to 120 hours using three modeling methods. In one approach, an end-to-end deep learning framework for the text shows that the discussions alone offer comparable value for 24-hour intensity forecasts to the SHIPS predictors. Adding discussion information to the SHIPS predictors in an ensemble of five such models reduces the mean absolute error of 24-hour maximum sustained wind forecasts for 2022-2023 cyclones from 9.89 to 8.90 kt, with a confidence interval that excludes zero when whole storms are resampled. The ERA5 wind fields have a minor effect on mean absolute error in wind predictions, and model rankings differ across predicted variables, lead times and model types. We provide prediction intervals for these forecasts, whose coverage falls below the 90% target during rapid intensification. Analysis of the text shows that words related to intensity and intensity change (such as intensify, weaken, eyewall and category) are important for the model predictions. This retrospective study shows the added value of the forecasters' discussions and suggests that multi-modal learning can help understand the predictive contribution of expert human judgment. The reanalysis data differ from real-time analyses, and the discussions are issued at least three hours after the valid time of the other inputs, so these results should not be interpreted operationally.

AI.tldr: This retrospective study quantifies the added predictive value of National Hurricane Center forecaster discussions for 24-to-120-hour tropical cyclone intensity forecasting alongside numerical predictors.
AI.motivation: While numerical predictors from SHIPS and ERA5 are standard for tropical cyclone intensity forecasting, the quantitative contribution of expert human forecaster discussions has not been systematically measured.
AI.method: Analyzing 637 Atlantic and eastern North Pacific tropical cyclones (2002-2023), the authors combine NHC Tropical Cyclone Discussions with 13 SHIPS predictors and ERA5 10-meter wind fields using three modeling approaches, including an end-to-end deep learning text framework.
AI.result: Discussion text alone matches SHIPS predictors for 24-hour intensity forecasts; ensembling five models combining discussions and SHIPS reduces 24-hour maximum sustained wind MAE for 2022-2023 cyclones from 9.89 to 8.90 kt (with a bootstrap CI excluding zero), while ERA5 winds have minor impact and prediction-interval coverage drops below 90% during rapid intensification.
AI.conclusion: Expert forecaster discussions contain genuine predictive signal beyond standard numerical features, though operational use is limited because discussions are issued at least three hours after the other inputs' valid time.

title: Latent Lattice Language Models
summary: Language models typically increase per-token computation through deeper or looped layers and latent reasoning steps, while richer residual connections improve information flow across layers. We instead increase computational capacity: the number of active computational states a model maintains. We introduce the Lattice of Latents, a set of per-layer horizontal latent streams that run recurrently along time, alongside the vertical residual stream that flows through depth. Like hyper-connections, mHC, and attention or value residuals, the Lattice enhances the residual stream, but rather than adding or rerouting residual pathways through depth, it provides companion computational states that persist across tokens. Unlike hybrid Transformer-SSM architectures, whose recurrent states primarily serve as internal memory for sequence mixing, these latents directly condition the vertical stream's attention, KV-cache writes, MLP computation, and decoding. On Transformers trained on 20B FineWeb-Edu tokens, a 406M-parameter Lattice model lowers validation perplexity from 15.41 to 14.40 over a parameter-matched Transformer. These gains extend across architectural variants. The Lattice composes with prior residual-stream enhancements: with hyper-connections and input residuals, it lowers validation perplexity from 15.41 (base Transformer) and 14.22 (Transformer with the same enhancements) to 13.61. On Gated DeltaNet, Mamba-2, Triadic GDN, and GDN-Mamba-2 hybrids, it improves perplexity at every tested native state size, with Lattice-GDN and Lattice-Triadic-GDN variants outperforming pure baselines with 4x larger native states. These results identify persistent per-layer state as a complementary axis for scaling language-model computation.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the Lattice of Latents, a set of persistent per-layer horizontal latent streams that run recurrently across tokens alongside the vertical residual stream.
AI.motivation: Language models typically scale per-token computation via depth or vertical residual enhancements, whereas maintaining persistent per-layer computational states across time offers an underexplored scaling axis.
AI.method: The Lattice adds horizontal latent streams at each layer that persist across tokens and directly condition the vertical stream's attention, KV-cache writes, MLP computation, and decoding.
AI.result: On 20B FineWeb-Edu tokens, a 406M-parameter Lattice Transformer lowers validation perplexity from 15.41 to 14.40 over a parameter-matched Transformer (and to 13.61 when combined with hyper-connections and input residuals, vs 14.22 without Lattice), and Lattice-GDN and Lattice-Triadic-GDN outperform pure baselines with 4x larger native states.
AI.conclusion: Persistent per-layer horizontal state provides a complementary, composable axis for scaling language-model computational capacity.

title: Efficient Multi-View Generation with Iterative Global-Local Proxy Attention
comment: 10 pages, 6 figures, 5 tables. Supplementary material is available as an ancillary file
summary: Generating consistent multi-view RGB images and normal maps from a single input image provides complementary appearance and geometric cues for 3D reconstruction. However, maintaining cross-view consistency requires information exchange across viewpoints, and dense cross-view attention becomes computationally expensive as the number of views and spatial resolution increase. In this paper, we propose Global-Local Proxy Attention (GLPA) to reduce cross-view communication costs while preserving fine-grained within-view processing. Specifically, GLPA retains full-resolution interactions within each view and uses compact global proxies for cross-view communication. To further leverage the exchanged information, GLPA incorporates iterative proxy refinement, which rebuilds the proxies from updated features and reuses the same attention parameters for subsequent interactions within a single denoising step. We evaluate GLPA on two structurally different diffusion backbones, FLUX and Stable Diffusion. Experiments on FLUX show that GLPA achieves a $2.65\times$ speedup in attention computation per denoising step over dense attention, while improving reconstruction IoU from 0.6849 to 0.7019 and reducing NVS LPIPS from 0.086 to 0.076. Results on Stable Diffusion further demonstrate the effectiveness of GLPA, with a $1.80\times$ attention speedup and improvements across all five quality metrics.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Global-Local Proxy Attention (GLPA) to accelerate multi-view RGB and normal-map generation while improving 3D reconstruction quality.
AI.motivation: Dense cross-view attention in multi-view diffusion models becomes computationally expensive as view count and spatial resolution grow.
AI.method: GLPA preserves full-resolution attention within each view and uses compact global proxies for cross-view communication, incorporating iterative proxy refinement that rebuilds proxies from updated features and reuses attention parameters within a single denoising step.
AI.result: On FLUX, GLPA achieves a 2.65x attention speedup per denoising step over dense attention while improving reconstruction IoU from 0.6849 to 0.7019 and reducing NVS LPIPS from 0.086 to 0.076; on Stable Diffusion, it achieves a 1.80x speedup and improves all five quality metrics.
AI.conclusion: Separating within-view full-resolution attention from iteratively refined cross-view proxies substantially reduces diffusion cost without sacrificing multi-view consistency.

title: QASK-Edit: Adaptive Sparse Attention Across Queries and Key Sources for Efficient Video Editing
summary: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) have achieved strong performance in generation based video editing, but suffer from high inference latency due to the long token sequences formed by conditioning inputs and generated videos. Although training-free sparse attention reduces this cost, existing methods typically apply a fixed retention ratio or a single threshold shared across all tokens. In this work, we view video editing as conditional generation and identify a key insight: attention demand varies significantly both across different key sources (e.g., source videos, reference images, audio, text, and generated videos) and across queries within each source. Motivated by this, we propose QASK-Edit (Query-Adaptive Sparsity over Key Sources for Video Editing), a training-free sparse attention framework that allocates computation independently for each query and key source. Specifically, for each query, QASK-Edit considers both the attention mass and approximation risk of each block. It then evaluates candidate routing thresholds against each key source's risk budget, choosing exact computation or approximations to dynamically adjust sparsity for each query. Extensive experiments on three video editing models demonstrate that QASK-Edit achieves up to $1.46\times$ end-to-end speedup over dense attention pipeline while preserving both editing quality and unedited region fidelity. Furthermore, QASK-Edit generalizes directly to Reference-to-Video generation, delivering up to $1.36\times$ speedup while maintaining generation quality.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes QASK-Edit, a training-free sparse attention framework for Diffusion Transformers that allocates computation independently per query and per conditioning key source in video editing.
AI.motivation: Video editing DiTs face high latency from long conditioning and generation token sequences, and existing sparse attention methods use a single fixed retention ratio or threshold across all tokens.
AI.method: QASK-Edit evaluates both attention mass and approximation risk for each block, then selects candidate routing thresholds against per-key-source risk budgets to choose exact or approximate computation dynamically for each query.
AI.result: Across three video editing models, QASK-Edit achieves up to 1.46x end-to-end speedup over dense attention while preserving editing quality and unedited-region fidelity, and transfers to Reference-to-Video generation with up to 1.36x speedup.
AI.conclusion: Query- and key-source-adaptive sparsity effectively accelerates conditional video generation without retraining.

title: CLIFT: Contrastive LiDAR Instance Features for 3D Pedestrian Tracking
summary: A social robot has to keep track of the people around it over time to plan its motion, a task handled by 3D multi-object tracking. For the LiDAR modality, trackers usually sit on top of a detector and link its detections across frames with a separate motion model or re-identification network. We instead show how a 3D LiDAR detector itself can be turned into a tracker by adding an instance-level contrastive objective on its intermediate voxel features. Each embedding is read from the voxels inside a detected box, and boxes are matched across frames by cosine similarity and the Hungarian algorithm, without a motion model. The detector backbone is fine-tuned together with this objective, which learns identity-aware features while leaving detection accuracy essen- tially intact. Because the method uses only the voxel features that Li- DAR detectors already produce, it is backbone-agnostic. On the JRDB 3D tracking leaderboard our LiDAR-only tracker ranks first on HOTA (38.58) and IDF1 (37.99), 13.04 and 9.30 points above the next pub- lished method, and second on MOTA and OSPA. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper turns a 3D LiDAR detector into a 3D pedestrian tracker by adding an instance-level contrastive objective to its intermediate voxel features, eliminating separate motion models or re-ID networks.
AI.motivation: LiDAR-based 3D multi-object trackers typically rely on separate motion models or re-identification networks on top of detector outputs.
AI.method: The detector backbone is fine-tuned with an instance-level contrastive loss on voxel features inside detected boxes, and boxes are linked across frames using cosine similarity and the Hungarian algorithm.
AI.result: On the JRDB 3D tracking leaderboard, the LiDAR-only tracker ranks first on HOTA (38.58) and IDF1 (37.99)—13.04 and 9.30 points above the next published method—and second on MOTA and OSPA, while leaving detection accuracy essentially intact.
AI.conclusion: Intermediate voxel features already produced by 3D LiDAR detectors can be made identity-aware with a simple contrastive objective, enabling accurate, backbone-agnostic tracking.

title: A Seismic Foundation Model for Dense Feature Extraction
summary: Deep-learning-based seismic interpretation is constrained by scarce high-quality annotations, and most existing models are trained separately for individual tasks. We present SeisDFE, a 7B-parameter seismic foundation model for dense feature extraction, pretrained on 5.34 million 2D images derived from more than 500 seismic volumes. A three-stage pretraining strategy, combining discriminative self-supervised learning, Gram feature anchoring, and multi-resolution adaptation, improves feature discriminability while preserving spatial coherence. With its encoder frozen, SeisDFE supports seismic facies classification, salt detection, fault detection, and relative geologic time estimation. It outperforms existing seismic foundation models on all four tasks and a natural-image-pretrained model on all but fault detection, with the largest gains under scarce supervision: using only two annotated sections of the F3 dataset, it improves whole-volume mIoU by 12-19 percentage points over the baselines. The learned features remain effective with task-specific decoders and extend to synthetic-to-field transfer and sparse 3D geobody interpretation. These results show that large-scale seismic pretraining organizes geological information into dense representations that are directly reusable across interpretation tasks.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces SeisDFE, a 7B-parameter seismic foundation model pretrained on 5.34 million 2D images from over 500 seismic volumes for dense feature extraction.
AI.motivation: Deep-learning seismic interpretation suffers from scarce annotations and task-specific models that do not share representations across geological tasks.
AI.method: SeisDFE uses a three-stage pretraining strategy—discriminative self-supervised learning, Gram feature anchoring, and multi-resolution adaptation—and is evaluated with a frozen encoder across four downstream tasks.
AI.result: With a frozen encoder, SeisDFE outperforms existing seismic foundation models on all four tasks (facies classification, salt detection, fault detection, relative geologic time estimation) and a natural-image model on all except fault detection, improving whole-volume mIoU by 12-19 percentage points using only two annotated F3 sections.
AI.conclusion: Large-scale seismic pretraining organizes geological structure into dense representations that transfer effectively across interpretation tasks under scarce supervision.

title: Deep Learning for Satellite-Based Mountain Hazard Screening: A Retrospective Failure Analysis on the 2021 Chamoli Rock-Ice Avalanche
summary: The approach utilizes 10 bands from Sentinel-2 imagery, along with terrain information, in a deep learning pipeline to classify potential hazard sources in any given mountainous region. The performance of our model has been evaluated against the data collected during the rock-ice avalanche event in the Chamoli region in the Indian Himalayas on 7th February 2021. U-Net performs segmentation of the detected land surface in the satellite image, detects changes in the identify candidate hazard zones, and then the following steps are performed to calculate the potential energy using the Monte Carlo sampling for steepest descent (D8) flow paths, finding the exposed structures in the downstream locations, and ranking the zones depending on the risk score. In comparison to the simple spectral rule, our approach achieved the higher macro F1 score of 0.648 (as compared to 0.519). But the F1 score in case of rock and soil was low, being in the range of 0.3s. In case of optical change detection in winter, it's only that northeast-facing slope which couldn't be detected, as it was under 73% of shade prior to the incident. The parameters have been set for this particular scene alone and not independently; hence, this is a retrospective test, and this test locates a failure which has occurred earlier. The primary contribution of this paper is locating the pipeline leak.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates a Sentinel-2 and terrain-based U-Net pipeline on the 2021 Chamoli rock-ice avalanche in a retrospective failure analysis, finding that winter slope shading prevented optical change detection.
AI.motivation: Satellite-based mountain hazard screening pipelines need to be audited against real failure cases to understand where optical change detection and risk scoring break down.
AI.method: Using 10 Sentinel-2 bands and terrain data, a U-Net segments land surfaces and detects changes, followed by Monte Carlo steepest-descent (D8) flow-path potential energy calculation and downstream exposure ranking, tested retrospectively on the February 7, 2021 Chamoli event.
AI.result: The pipeline achieves a macro F1 of 0.648 versus 0.519 for a simple spectral rule, but rock and soil F1 scores remain in the 0.3s, and the northeast-facing source slope went undetected because it was under 73% winter shade prior to the event.
AI.conclusion: The primary contribution is locating this pipeline leak, showing that scene-specific retrospective tuning and winter optical shading remain critical failure modes for satellite hazard screening.

title: ThermoSight: From Appearance to Internal Thermofluid Fields via Physics-Guided Neural Reconstruction
summary: Most neural reconstruction methods focus on reproducing scene appearance, yet inferring physical states from visual observations is essential for machine understanding of the physical world. Reconstructing the internal temperature and soot fields of radiating thermofluids such as flames is challenging yet essential for improving energy efficiency and assessing heat exposure and fire spread. In flames, temperature and soot concentration jointly govern visible emission, and soot self-absorption alters the light that reaches each camera. With limited views, changes in the two fields can offset one another in the recorded RGB images, making temperature and soot difficult to disentangle. ThermoSight, a physics-guided neural framework for scientific imaging, jointly reconstructs continuous three-dimensional temperature and soot volume fraction fields from limited calibrated flame images without field-level ground truth during optimization. A differentiable spectral model links these fields to measured RGB through thermal emission, self-absorption, and calibrated camera responses. Temperature-dependent emission spectra and wavelength-dependent attenuation constrain shared fields across RGB channels, reducing temperature-soot ambiguity. Chromaticity consistency, observation-derived spatial constraints, and soot regularization complement intensity fitting. In a synthetic ablation, wavelength-resolved attenuation reduces temperature RMSE in the hot, sooty region from 234 to 112 K relative to a three-channel approximation, with nearly identical RGB PSNR (65.23 vs. 65.24 dB). Measured data yield coherent fields and competitive RGB reconstructions. These results demonstrate that physics-guided neural fields recover interpretable internal physical quantities beyond visually consistent appearance.

AI.tldr: This paper presents ThermoSight, a physics-guided neural reconstruction framework that recovers continuous 3D temperature and soot volume fraction fields from limited calibrated RGB flame images.
AI.motivation: Inferring internal temperature and soot fields from limited-view RGB flame images is ill-posed because temperature and soot concentration jointly govern emission and self-absorption, allowing changes in one to offset the other.
AI.method: ThermoSight couples neural fields with a differentiable spectral model of thermal emission, wavelength-dependent soot self-absorption, and calibrated camera responses, regularized by chromaticity consistency and spatial constraints without field-level ground truth.
AI.result: In a synthetic ablation, wavelength-resolved attenuation reduces temperature RMSE in hot, sooty regions from 234 K to 112 K compared to a three-channel approximation at nearly identical RGB PSNR (65.23 vs 65.24 dB), and measured flame data yield coherent physical fields.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating wavelength-resolved physical transport into neural fields resolves temperature-soot ambiguity and recovers interpretable internal thermofluid states beyond appearance alone.

title: PhaseCLIP: Phase-Aware Frequency-Domain Adaptation of Vision-Language Models for Few-Shot Remote-Sensing Classification
comment: 23 pages, 7 figures, 5 tables. Code will be released at this https URL upon publication
summary: Remote-sensing (RS) image scene classification aims to assign a semantic category to an overhead image, and in practice must often do so from only a handful of labelled examples, since annotation requires expert interpretation and the resulting labels transfer poorly across sensors and regions. Recent progress has come from adapting vision-language models (VLMs) such as CLIP, through learned prompts or feature adapters. Although effective, these methods construct their representation entirely in the spatial domain. RS scenes are dominated by periodic texture and regular geometry, which the Fourier spectrum describes compactly through an amplitude component, carrying texture and contrast statistics, and a phase component, carrying spatial structure. Existing frequency-domain adaptation of VLMs either exploits amplitude alone or does not separate amplitude from phase, leaving the structural component unused. In this article, we propose PhaseCLIP, which inserts phase-capable spectral modules and a feature-gating module into a frozen CLIP visual encoder and trains only 1.30% of its parameters. Because the amplitude and phase pathways share an identical parameter layout, a single weight set is learned on phase and transferred exactly to amplitude, giving a two-stage scheme that adds no parameters. Experiments on five public RS datasets, EuroSAT, PatternNet, UC Merced, LSRS and RSSCN7, against eight baselines under a matched protocol, show that PhaseCLIP attains 84.28% mean accuracy and is the best method in 23 of 30 dataset-by-shot cells, with phase contributing 1.93 points overall and 4.36 points on the most difficult dataset. Because the modules act on the spectrum of image patches and transformer tokens and leave the text encoder untouched, the approach can be extended to other RS sensors and tasks, and to other domains in which class evidence lies in spatial structure.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes PhaseCLIP, which adapts a frozen CLIP visual encoder for few-shot remote-sensing scene classification by adding phase-aware spectral modules that share weights with the amplitude pathway.
AI.motivation: Spatial-domain CLIP adapters and amplitude-only frequency adapters ignore the Fourier phase component, which carries crucial spatial structure in periodic remote-sensing scenes.
