AI.method: PhaseCLIP inserts phase-capable spectral modules and a feature-gating module into a frozen CLIP visual encoder (training only 1.30% of parameters), learning weights on phase and transferring them identically to the amplitude pathway in a two-stage scheme.
AI.result: Across five public remote-sensing datasets (EuroSAT, PatternNet, UC Merced, LSRS, RSSCN7) and eight baselines, PhaseCLIP achieves 84.28% mean accuracy and ranks best in 23 of 30 dataset-by-shot settings, with phase contributing 1.93 points overall and 4.36 points on the hardest dataset.
AI.conclusion: Exploiting Fourier phase alongside amplitude in transformer token spectra provides a parameter-efficient, sensor-agnostic way to adapt VLMs for structured remote-sensing imagery.

title: VA-Assembly: View-Aligned Score Guidance for Training-Free 3D Part Assembly
summary: Image-to-3D foundation models have improved 3D reconstruction, but typically produce monolithic representations without explicit part-level structure. Part-aware generation and learning-based assembly methods often require part-level supervision, category-specific priors, or paired part-layout training data. We instead consider a practical but underexplored setting in which independently prepared or generated 3D parts have no predefined inter-part relationships, shared coordinate frames, or consistent scales, and must be assembled into a reference-consistent object from a single image. We present VA-Assembly, a training-free framework for 3D part assembly through part-level transformation estimation using view-aligned diffusion guidance. Given a reference image and fixed 3D part geometries, VA-Assembly optimizes each part's translation, rotation, and scale. We condition a frozen view-conditioned diffusion model on same-view renderings of a reference-derived monolithic 3D representation, producing score gradients geometrically aligned with the part configuration. This guidance provides multi-view structural cues under large initial misalignment. By repurposing pretrained visual-structural priors as transformation-level supervision, VA-Assembly requires no annotated part layouts, predefined part taxonomies, category-specific assembly training, or bounding-box-based layout initialization. Experiments compare VA-Assembly with geometric registration and compositional layout baselines using each baseline's supported transformation components, showing improved part-wise transformation estimation. Ablation studies show that view-aligned conditioning, rather than diffusion guidance alone, is critical for reliable transformation gradients. Updating only part transformations preserves explicit component separability and supports component-level editing, replacement, and reconfiguration.

AI.tldr: This paper presents VA-Assembly, a training-free 3D part assembly framework that optimizes part translations, rotations, and scales using view-aligned score gradients from a frozen diffusion model.
AI.motivation: Existing 3D part assembly methods require part-level supervision, category priors, or paired layout training data, whereas independently prepared 3D parts often lack shared coordinate frames, consistent scales, or predefined relationships.
AI.method: Given a single reference image and fixed 3D part geometries, VA-Assembly conditions a frozen view-conditioned diffusion model on same-view renderings of a reference-derived monolithic 3D model to produce geometrically aligned score gradients that optimize each part's 7-DoF transformation.
AI.result: VA-Assembly outperforms geometric registration and compositional layout baselines on part-wise transformation estimation without annotated layouts or category training, and ablations confirm that view-aligned conditioning is critical for reliable transformation gradients.
AI.conclusion: Repurposing pretrained view-conditioned diffusion priors as transformation-level supervision enables training-free 3D part assembly while preserving explicit component separability for editing.

title: TRR: A Thermal Interaction Engine for Robot Simulation and RGBT Data Generation
summary: A robot's actions change the thermal conditions of its next interaction: heat retained after release, carried with objects or stored beneath the surface can change a later contact's outcome despite similar current temperatures. Training trajectories must capture how these effects connect earlier actions to later observations and task outcomes. We present TRR, a \emph{Thermal Robot Renderer} that attaches spatial and depth-resolved thermal state to both contact partners, updates local heat exchange through contact, transport and separation, and generates synchronized RGB--thermal (RGBT) observations and event-local task checks on one execution clock. Controlled interventions show why retained heat, spatial transport and internal storage matter for subsequent contact outcomes. From the same state, TRR produces a paired six-task benchmark of 2,224 static--dynamic pairs, that is, 4,448 trajectories with synchronized dual-view observations, states and actions. Visible thermal history raises safe contact-site selection from 75.0\% to 91.7\% on a dedicated learning corpus, and training on dynamic histories raises simulated transfer completion by 50 percentage points under a new heating procedure with shared feedback execution. We demonstrate RGBT observation adapters on MuJoCo and Isaac Sim, report an engineering inventory of ten prepared robot configurations and six demonstrated camera viewpoints, and describe a developer workflow that carries an existing robot scene to exported RGBT records. The benchmark, the workflow and the platform resources described in Section 6 form the first items of a planned public release. Demonstrations and resource updates are available on the project page.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces TRR, a Thermal Robot Renderer that simulates spatial and depth-resolved contact heat exchange and generates synchronized RGB-thermal (RGBT) observations and benchmarks for robotic manipulation.
AI.motivation: Robot actions alter object temperatures through contact, transport, and subsurface heat storage, yet standard simulators lack coupled thermal state and synchronized RGBT data to train and evaluate thermal-aware policies.
AI.method: TRR attaches spatial and depth-resolved thermal state to contact partners, updates local heat exchange on a unified execution clock, and provides RGBT observation adapters for MuJoCo and Isaac Sim across ten robot configurations and six viewpoints.
AI.result: TRR produces a six-task benchmark of 2,224 static-dynamic pairs (4,448 trajectories); visible thermal history raises safe contact-site selection from 75.0% to 91.7%, and training on dynamic histories improves simulated transfer completion by 50 percentage points under a new heating procedure.
AI.conclusion: Modeling coupled contact heat exchange and synchronized RGBT histories enables robots to reason about retained and transported heat in physical interactions.

title: Correspondence-Free Camera Pose Estimation by Matching Moments
comment: 65 pages, including references and appendices; under review
summary: The blind perspective-$n$-point (PnP) problem is to estimate the pose of a calibrated camera from 2D and 3D point sets with unknown correspondences. We show that, for complete, noiseless observations, fourteen permutation-invariant image moments up to order four identify a fixed camera pose for almost every 3D point set containing at least twenty points. Our learning-free method, MomentPnP, matches these moments between the observed 2D points and the projected 3D points to initialize a camera pose without correspondences and refines the pose and correspondence weights using expectation--maximization. Across the test sets of three benchmarks, our method reduces median rotation error by $5$--$170\times$ relative to the best learned baseline, both with and without outliers. We recover accurate poses even with as many outliers as inliers. On dense ETH3D scans, pose accuracy improves as the point sets grow, even as individual correspondences become harder to resolve.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes MomentPnP, a learning-free blind PnP method that estimates calibrated camera pose without 2D-3D correspondences by matching fourteen permutation-invariant image moments up to order four.
AI.motivation: Blind perspective-n-point (PnP) must recover camera pose from 2D and 3D point sets with unknown correspondences, which is challenging under outliers and dense point clouds.
AI.method: MomentPnP matches fourteen permutation-invariant image moments up to order four between observed 2D points and projected 3D points to initialize pose without correspondences, then refines pose and correspondence weights via expectation-maximization.
AI.result: Across three benchmark test sets, MomentPnP reduces median rotation error by 5-170x compared to the best learned baseline with and without outliers, recovers accurate poses even with 50% outliers, and improves accuracy as point sets grow on dense ETH3D scans.
AI.conclusion: Permutation-invariant image moments uniquely identify camera pose for almost every 3D set of at least twenty points, providing a fast, outlier-robust initialization for correspondence-free pose estimation.

title: An Efficient Training Paradigm for Image Restoration via Improved Fréchet Loss
summary: Diffusion-based image restoration achieves strong perceptual quality but typically relies on iterative sampling, leading to slow inference. Existing single-step methods often use diffusion distillation or adversarial training, complicating optimization. To simplify training, we propose FDIR, a framework for training single-pass generative restoration models through regression-style supervised optimization using directly computable objectives. To realize this paradigm, FDIR employs the Fréchet distance to match the feature distributions of restored and real images in frozen representation spaces, providing explicit distribution-level supervision. To better accommodate image restoration, we incorporate local patch features to capture fine-grained restoration discrepancies. Moreover, we introduce instance-adaptive statistics by combining the feature moments of each SR-HQ pair with synchronized historical statistics, allowing distribution matching to incorporate input-specific correspondence while retaining distribution-level context. FDIR optimizes only the LoRA parameters of the restoration backbone. Experiments demonstrate strong perceptual restoration quality and efficient training, suggesting a simpler paradigm for generative image restoration.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes FDIR, a single-step generative image restoration framework trained with regression-style supervision using an improved Fréchet loss over local patches and instance-adaptive statistics.
AI.motivation: Diffusion-based image restoration requires slow iterative sampling, while existing single-step methods rely on complex diffusion distillation or adversarial training.
AI.method: FDIR optimizes only LoRA parameters of a restoration backbone using a directly computable Fréchet distance in frozen representation spaces, incorporating local patch features and instance-adaptive statistics that combine per-pair moments with synchronized historical statistics.
AI.result: Experiments show that FDIR achieves strong perceptual restoration quality with efficient, simplified training.
AI.conclusion: Distribution matching via local and instance-adaptive Fréchet loss offers a simpler, single-pass alternative to distillation and adversarial training for generative image restoration.

title: Interpretable deep concepts of organoid morphology
summary: Image-based classification of organoid morphologies can indicate drug response, viability, or successful differentiation. In recent work, learned representations outperform handcrafted features as the basis for downstream classifiers. However, their black-box nature hides the morphological cues a classifier relies on. Based on the foundation models DINOv3 (general-purpose) and ViTAMIn-O (organoid-specific), we train sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to learn interpretable concepts related to distinct organoid morphologies. We annotate concepts with spatial labels (organoid, organoid wall, background) and compute their dataset specificity and task relevance across five tasks. The spatial labels of DINOv3 concepts yield coarse organoid segmentations on out-of-domain datasets. Filtering concepts by spatial label in the DINOv3-SAE improves downstream AUROC for three of the five tasks. Qualitative analysis of the most relevant concepts further reveals a confounding factor introduced by our preprocessing in one task. Through such insights, interpretable concepts could help improve the reliability of classifiers and guide the future development of organoid representation models. The trained SAEs will be made available upon publication.

AI.tldr: This paper trains sparse autoencoders (SAEs) on DINOv3 and ViTAMIn-O representations of organoid images to extract spatially grounded, interpretable morphological concepts.
AI.motivation: Foundation model representations outperform handcrafted features for organoid classification, but their black-box nature obscures which morphological cues drive predictions.
AI.method: The authors train SAEs on DINOv3 (general-purpose) and ViTAMIn-O (organoid-specific), annotate learned concepts with spatial labels (organoid, organoid wall, background), and measure dataset specificity and task relevance across five tasks.
AI.result: Spatial labels of DINOv3 concepts yield coarse out-of-domain organoid segmentations, filtering concepts by spatial label in DINOv3-SAE improves downstream AUROC on three of five tasks, and qualitative inspection uncovers a preprocessing confounding factor in one task.
AI.conclusion: SAE-based concept decomposition makes organoid representation models interpretable, enabling both confound detection and targeted feature filtering.

title: Vision-Language Model-Based Phase-OTDR Event Classification
summary: Phase-sensitive optical time-domain reflectometry (Phase-OTDR) enables distributed vibration sensing, but reliable event classification has traditionally relied on fully supervised models that require extensive annotated data. This study examines the adaptability of a Vision-Language Model (VLM) for Phase-OTDR event recognition through few-shot learning. Raw samples are converted into Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT) dB-magnitude spectrogram mosaics, color-mapped and resized to RGB images, and processed by a Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP) image encoder; few-shot adaptation optimizes only the Tip-Adapter-F cache keys, leaving both encoders unchanged. Under a leakage-controlled protocol (train-side support/validation pool of 512 images per class, fixed held-out test of 120 per class, no test-set access during selection, 20 distinct support-sampling trials), the selected configuration (the ViT-L-14 Vision Transformer encoder with OpenAI weights, 128 shots per class) reaches 96.81 +/- 0.42% accuracy and a macro-averaged F1 score of 96.79 +/- 0.42% on the held-out test set; a label-efficient 16-shot setting, that is, 96 labeled support images at adaptation time across the six classes, already attains 90.17 +/- 0.81%. Tip-Adapter-F clearly outperforms both zero-shot CLIP and the standard training-free Tip-Adapter, and prompt and backbone analyses show that performance is stable across Vision Transformer encoders and insensitive to prompt wording at the selected operating point. Overall, CLIP visual features carry a transferable structure that a lightweight support cache turns into a label-efficient Phase-OTDR event classifier. The code and the corresponding image dataset are made publicly available on GitHub to support further research: this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper adapts a frozen CLIP image encoder with Tip-Adapter-F on STFT spectrogram mosaics for few-shot Phase-OTDR distributed vibration event classification.
AI.motivation: Reliable Phase-OTDR event classification typically requires fully supervised models trained on large annotated datasets.
AI.method: Raw vibration signals are converted into STFT dB-magnitude spectrogram mosaics, color-mapped to RGB, and passed through a frozen CLIP ViT-L-14 encoder, adapting only Tip-Adapter-F cache keys under a leakage-controlled protocol (512 support/val pool per class, 120 held-out test per class, 20 trials).
AI.result: At 128 shots per class, Tip-Adapter-F reaches 96.81 +/- 0.42% accuracy and 96.79 +/- 0.42% macro-F1 on the held-out test set, while 16 shots per class (96 total labeled images across six classes) already achieves 90.17 +/- 0.81%, outperforming zero-shot CLIP and training-free Tip-Adapter.
AI.conclusion: Frozen CLIP visual features paired with lightweight cache-key adaptation provide a label-efficient, prompt-insensitive classifier for Phase-OTDR sensing.

title: When Is the Expensive Method Worth It? A Content-Driven Analysis of Classical Bayer Demosaicing
summary: Demosaicing reconstructs a full-colour image from a single-sensor colour-filter-array (CFA) mosaic, where only one colour is measured per pixel. Classical methods make different assumptions about images, from simple averaging to directional edge-aware interpolation, and the directional methods cost markedly more compute. We ask a practical question that a per-image quality ranking does not answer: for a given image, is the expensive directional method worth its cost? Using a controlled simulate-reconstruct pipeline on 80 benchmark images from four public datasets (Kodak, McMaster, BSD100, Urban100), six classical methods, and image-content descriptors fixed before any results were seen, we show that the quality gain of the edge-aware method (Menon 2007) over the best cheap linear method is not constant. It ranges from $-6.6$ to $+6.8$ dB, and on 31% of images it is zero or negative, meaning a cheap method matches or beats the expensive one. The gain is also predictable from content: it correlates with mean image saturation at $r=-0.86$ ($p<10^{-6}$). We then build an interpretable depth-2 decision tree that recommends the best cheap method from image descriptors, beating an always-pick-the-most-common baseline by 20.0 percentage points under leave-one-image-out validation. The analysis uses no deep learning, and every step can be inspected.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes classical Bayer demosaicing across 80 benchmark images and builds an interpretable depth-2 decision tree to predict when an expensive edge-aware method is worth its compute over cheap linear methods.
AI.motivation: Directional edge-aware demosaicing costs substantially more compute than linear interpolation, yet per-image quality rankings do not tell practitioners whether the extra cost is actually worthwhile on a given image.
AI.method: Using a controlled simulate-reconstruct pipeline on 80 images from Kodak, McMaster, BSD100, and Urban100 with six classical methods and pre-fixed content descriptors, the authors measure the quality gain of Menon (2007) over the best cheap linear method and train a depth-2 decision tree.
AI.result: Menon's gain ranges from -6.6 to +6.8 dB and is zero or negative on 31% of images; the gain correlates strongly with mean image saturation (r = -0.86, p < 10^-6), and the depth-2 tree beats an always-pick-most-common baseline by 20.0 percentage points under leave-one-image-out validation.
AI.conclusion: Simple content descriptors such as saturation accurately predict when cheap linear demosaicing matches or beats expensive directional methods.

title: LiDSeg: Linear DehazeFormer Guidance for Efficient Semantic Segmentation in Adverse Weather Conditions
summary: Robust semantic segmentation in adverse weather is essential for safety-critical autonomous systems. Existing restore-then-segment pipelines introduce latency and prioritize pixel-level restoration over semantic discriminability, while domain adaptation methods often face representation bottlenecks and computational complexity. We introduce LiDSeg, a framework that uses reconstruction-informed guidance to improve segmentation under adverse weather. During training, a lightweight guidance encoder is jointly optimized with the segmentation branch using segmentation and auxiliary reconstruction objectives. At inference, the reconstruction decoder is discarded, while the guidance encoder is retained to extract weather-robust features. A lightweight gated fusion module integrates these features into the segmentation branch, preserving clear-weather accuracy while improving adverse-weather robustness. On Foggy Cityscapes, LiDSeg limits the clear-to-dense-fog mIoU degradation to 2.5-2.8 percentage points, reducing the baseline performance drop by more than fivefold. On the official ACDC test server, LiDSeg-PIDNet achieves 75.07% pooled all-condition mIoU, comparable to supervised HRNet-W48 at 75.0%, while remaining substantially smaller. The gains generalize zero-shot to Foggy Driving and Foggy Zurich without training on real-fog images. LiDSeg adds only 1.9-3.1M parameters across several models, with total model sizes of 5.2-39.5M parameters and no inference-time reconstruction overhead. It delivers real-time inference on the NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin. Code: this https URL

AI.tldr: This paper proposes LiDSeg, a semantic segmentation framework for adverse weather that uses an auxiliary reconstruction branch during training to guide a lightweight encoder without adding inference-time reconstruction overhead.
AI.motivation: Restore-then-segment pipelines add inference latency and prioritize pixel fidelity over semantics, while domain adaptation methods suffer from representation bottlenecks and high compute.
AI.method: A lightweight guidance encoder is jointly trained with the segmentation branch using segmentation and auxiliary reconstruction losses; at inference, the reconstruction decoder is discarded and a gated fusion module integrates the guidance features into the segmentation branch.
AI.result: On Foggy Cityscapes, LiDSeg limits clear-to-dense-fog mIoU drop to 2.5-2.8 percentage points (over 5x smaller drop than baseline); on the ACDC test server, LiDSeg-PIDNet reaches 75.07% pooled mIoU (comparable to HRNet-W48 at 75.0%) while remaining much smaller, generalizes zero-shot to Foggy Driving and Foggy Zurich, adds 1.9-3.1M parameters (5.2-39.5M total), and runs in real time on Jetson AGX Orin.
AI.conclusion: Training-time reconstruction guidance with inference-time decoder removal delivers weather-robust, real-time semantic segmentation.

title: MVSTF: Multi-View Spatio-Temporal Fusion for LiDAR-Based Moving Object Segmentation
summary: Autonomous mobile robots confront significant chal lenges in recognizing the motion properties of objects in dy namic environments. However, existing methods are hindered by limitations such as boundary ambiguity, occlusion, viewpoint constraints, and training complexity. In this paper, we propose an innovative end-to-end Multi-View Spatio-Temporal Fusion network, named MVSTF, which utilizes sequential point clouds to generate multi-view images and feature differences, and designs a multi-branch network to extract spatio-temporal and dimen sional features in parallel, and realizes high-precision moving object segmentation. First, sequential point clouds are utilized to generate multi-view images and feature differences. Then, an end-to-end multi-branch network including Dual Down-sampling Blocks (DDB), Spatial Attention Blocks (SAB), Multi-Kernel Convolutional Neural Network blocks (MKCNN), Dual Feature Fusion Blocks (DFFB), and the Point Fusion (PF) module, is designed to extract motion features from feature differences and geometric and semantic features from multi-view images. Finally, an auxiliary semantic head is introduced to further improve the algorithm's robustness and the model's interpretability. This work is validated on the SemanticKITTI and KITTI-Road bench marks, achieving state-of-the-art results on the SemanticKITTI MOS validation set and the KITTI-Road validation set, and competitive results on the hidden SemanticKITTI-MOS test set. The code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes MVSTF, an end-to-end Multi-View Spatio-Temporal Fusion network that projects sequential LiDAR point clouds into multi-view images and feature differences for moving object segmentation.
AI.motivation: Existing LiDAR moving object segmentation methods struggle with boundary ambiguity, occlusion, viewpoint constraints, and training complexity.
AI.method: MVSTF generates multi-view images and feature differences from sequential point clouds, processes them with a multi-branch network (DDB, SAB, MKCNN, DFFB, and Point Fusion modules) to extract motion, geometric, and semantic features in parallel, and adds an auxiliary semantic head.
AI.result: MVSTF achieves state-of-the-art results on the SemanticKITTI MOS validation set and KITTI-Road validation set, and competitive performance on the hidden SemanticKITTI-MOS test set.
AI.conclusion: Parallel multi-view spatio-temporal fusion with an auxiliary semantic head improves LiDAR moving object segmentation robustness and accuracy.

title: Multi-Rate Flow Matching for Point Cloud Upsampling
summary: Flow-matching point-cloud upsamplers refine sparse inputs into dense point clouds by integrating a learned velocity field with a fixed temporal discretization. However, local reconstruction requirements vary substantially across a shape, while a shared solver budget applies the same temporal resolution everywhere. We propose Multi-Rate Flow Matching (MRFM), a patch-adaptive framework that selects an integration budget for each local patch at inference time while keeping the learned velocity field frozen. MRFM relaxes the discrete budget into a continuous variable, optimizes it online through differentiable soft rollouts using an input-derived geometric fidelity objective, and projects the result back to a discrete budget for the final solver rollout. Experiments on PU1K and PUGAN show strong reconstruction quality, while matched-budget permutation and multi-factor analyses demonstrate that the benefit depends on patch-specific allocation rather than on the step distribution alone. MRFM is accuracy-oriented and intentionally uses additional test-time optimization to obtain more suitable local temporal resolutions.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Multi-Rate Flow Matching (MRFM), a test-time optimization framework that selects per-patch ODE integration budgets for a frozen flow-matching point cloud upsampler.
AI.motivation: Flow-matching point cloud upsamplers apply a uniform temporal discretization across the entire shape, even though local reconstruction difficulty varies substantially across patches.
AI.method: Keeping the learned velocity field frozen, MRFM relaxes discrete per-patch integration budgets into continuous variables, optimizes them online via differentiable soft rollouts against an input-derived geometric fidelity objective, and projects back to discrete budgets for final rollout.
AI.result: Experiments on PU1K and PUGAN demonstrate strong reconstruction quality, and matched-budget permutation and multi-factor analyses confirm that gains stem from patch-specific budget allocation rather than the step distribution alone.
AI.conclusion: Trading additional test-time optimization for patch-adaptive temporal resolution improves flow-matching point cloud upsampling accuracy without retraining.

title: ProSE: Probing Reconstruction Error for Semantic-guided Expert Skipping in MoE-MLLMs
summary: Mixture-of-Experts Multimodal Large Language Models (MoE-MLLMs) offer scalable inference through sparse expert activation, yet substantial computational redundancy remains among the activated experts. Existing expert skipping methods typically calibrate thresholds based on target skipping ratios or final-output divergence, overlooking the accumulation of skipping-induced error across layers and the varying semantic importance of individual tokens. To address that, we propose ProSE, a training-free, semantic-guided expert skipping framework that probes layer-wise reconstruction error to promote representation consistency compared with default activation. Specifically, we construct query-aware semantic masks to identify salient visual tokens and progressively calibrate modality-specific skipping thresholds for each MoE layer. By minimizing masked reconstruction error under a given budget, ProSE maintains semantic consistency after skipping and allows adaptive expert allocation under limited activation budgets. Extensive experiments on 9 benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements on average over existing expert skipping methods, particularly under aggressive skipping settings. ProSE maintains over 96\% performance on KimiVL-A3B-Inst with 83\% expert skipping and accelerates prefilling by $1.7\times$.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes ProSE, a training-free semantic-guided expert skipping framework for MoE-MLLMs that minimizes layer-wise masked reconstruction error to allocate experts under activation budgets.
AI.motivation: Existing expert skipping methods in MoE-MLLMs calibrate thresholds using target ratios or final-output divergence, ignoring layer-wise error accumulation and differences in token semantic importance.
AI.method: ProSE constructs query-aware semantic masks to identify salient visual tokens and progressively calibrates modality-specific skipping thresholds per MoE layer to minimize masked reconstruction error.
AI.result: Across 9 benchmarks, ProSE consistently outperforms existing expert skipping methods, retaining over 96% performance on KimiVL-A3B-Inst with 83% expert skipping and achieving a 1.7x prefilling speedup.
AI.conclusion: Probing layer-wise masked reconstruction error enables aggressive, training-free expert skipping in MoE-MLLMs while preserving semantic consistency.

title: Certified, Not Explained: Exact Token Erasure in Gated Vision State Space Models
summary: Vision models built on Mamba are often explained through their selective step size Delta, on the assumption that a token the scan does not admit cannot influence the prediction. We test that in a concept bottleneck model for lung-nodule malignancy built on a single gated, bidirectional selective state-space block. The answer becomes an interpretability framework: a guarantee, a procedure that checks it, and a pre-registered audit of what it explains. For a fixed gate pattern, masking the input of the causal convolution of the block and giving closed tokens zero weight at readout makes the concept and task logits exactly invariant to the closed tokens. Gating Delta is neither necessary nor sufficient. On LIDC-IDRI, a path-by-path knockout over 15 cross-validated models agrees with this in every run: the largest logit change is exactly 0 whenever the conditions hold and between 4.1 and 6.7 when they do not. The gated model reaches a pooled out-of-fold AUROC of 0.8425 +/- 0.0085, level with an ungated Mamba bottleneck (0.8428). The guarantee belongs to the masked model, not to the gate as an explanation. Post-hoc rankers, which inherit the guarantee on this model, order tokens better than the gate. Gate maps from a model trained on permuted labels are as close to the real maps as two real-label seeds are to each other. Under retraining, the tokens of the gate carry more task information than random tokens and, on shifted crops, more than central ones, but no more than the tokens chosen by hidden attention. We therefore read the gate as a certified support set produced by mask supervision. Splitting the Oracle Impurity Score into own-concept and cross-concept parts reveals differences the aggregate score misses. Partitioning the readout reduced leakage slightly under an earlier recipe, and the final model sits at, rather than below, the level implied by correlations among the true concepts.

AI.tldr: This paper proves exact conditions for token erasure in a gated bidirectional Mamba vision model and shows that the learned gate acts as a certified support set rather than a reliable explanation.
AI.motivation: Selective state-space (Mamba) vision models are often explained via their selective step size Delta under the assumption that closed tokens cannot affect predictions, but this assumption had not been rigorously tested.
AI.method: In a lung-nodule malignancy concept bottleneck model built on a gated bidirectional Mamba block, the authors derive exact invariance conditions (masking the causal convolution input and zeroing readout weights for closed tokens) and audit them via path-by-path knockout across 15 cross-validated LIDC-IDRI models.
AI.result: When the conditions hold, the largest logit change is exactly 0 across all 15 runs (versus 4.1-6.7 when violated), and the gated model matches an ungated Mamba bottleneck (0.8425 +/- 0.0085 vs 0.8428 AUROC); however, post-hoc rankers order tokens better than the gate, and gate maps from permuted-label models resemble real-label maps as closely as two real seeds.
AI.conclusion: Gating Delta alone is neither necessary nor sufficient for token erasure; the guarantee belongs to the masked readout mechanism, making the gate a certified support set rather than an intrinsic explanation.

title: SciWorldBench: Do Video World Models Really Understand Scientific Experiments?
comment: Preprint. Benchmark paper with paired scientific experiments for evaluating video world models. 8 pages of main text, 16 pages including figures and references
summary: While the ability of video generation models to accurately depict scientific phenomena has received growing attention, determining whether these models genuinely understand the underlying principles remains a critical challenge. Existing benchmarks typically evaluate video samples in isolation, making it difficult to expose models that simply fit superficial visual priors. In scientific experiments, a small change in one condition produces a markedly different outcome even when the rest of the setup remains fixed. Capitalizing on this sensitivity, we introduce SciWorldBench, a benchmark comprising paired scientific experiments. Each pair varies a single condition in an otherwise fixed setup, yielding two mutually exclusive expected outcomes. Each generation prompt specifies the condition but omits the expected outcome. We evaluate ten text-and-image-to-video (TI2V) models using an independent vision-language model (VLM) that assesses each video without access to the condition text or the label identifying the correct outcome. A pair is scored as correct only when both videos depict their respective scientifically correct outcomes. Across all ten models, we find that the two videos in an experimental pair frequently depict the same outcome even though the conditions require different results. This recurring failure suggests that current video world models struggle to apply the underlying scientific principles reliably during generation. We will publicly release the benchmark dataset and open-source the evaluation code.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces SciWorldBench, a benchmark of paired scientific experiments that vary a single condition to test whether video world models understand underlying scientific principles.
AI.motivation: Evaluating generated scientific videos in isolation makes it hard to tell whether video models genuinely understand physical or scientific principles or merely fit superficial visual priors.
AI.method: SciWorldBench pairs experiments with identical setups except for one condition that yields two mutually exclusive outcomes; ten text-and-image-to-video (TI2V) models are prompted without stating the expected outcome and scored by an independent VLM, requiring both videos in a pair to be scientifically correct.
AI.result: Across all ten evaluated TI2V models, the two videos in a pair frequently depict the same outcome despite differing conditions that require opposite results.
AI.conclusion: Current video world models struggle to apply underlying scientific principles reliably during generation, often defaulting to superficial visual priors.

title: Can Image Generators Hold a Scene Together When Space Is Broken Apart?
summary: Image generators are good at drawing scenes in which things that belong together appear next to each other. In almost every image they generate, and in almost every benchmark used to evaluate these images, "belonging to the same whole" and "adjacent to each other" go together. Therefore, we cannot know whether the model truly grasps the scene as a whole, or simply makes each part connect with its adjacent parts. We propose GJBench to disentangle the two. It requires the model to draw a scene as a scattered jigsaw puzzle: an image is cut into interlocking pieces, then moved apart and rotated. Thus, the spatial plausibility of the scene exists only in how these pieces collectively point to a whole. The model may have a reference image, a target layout, both, or neither. We separately evaluate three requirements: whether the scene is broken down into a specified number of separate pieces, whether the pieces interlock, and whether the pieces can reconstruct the reference scene. While every open and closed model we evaluated could draw these scenes well as a whole, none could keep them together as scattered puzzle pieces, and the three requirements categorized failures into different patterns. The models draw separate pieces but miscount them in different ways, and unless their outlines are provided, the pieces rarely interlock, and their content does not reconstruct the reference image. We also found that the target layout helps the puzzle pieces fit together, while the reference image improves neither their count nor their fit. These findings show that keeping a scene continuous across space that the canvas no longer shows remains an open problem for image generators.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces GJBench, a scattered jigsaw puzzle benchmark that tests whether image generators understand global scene structure when adjacent parts are spatially separated.
AI.motivation: Standard image generation benchmarks conflate global scene understanding with local adjacency, because objects that belong together always appear next to each other.
AI.method: GJBench asks models to draw a scene as a scattered jigsaw puzzle—cut into interlocking pieces, separated, and rotated—under four conditioning modes (reference image, target layout, both, or neither), evaluating piece count, interlocking fit, and reference reconstruction.
AI.result: While all evaluated open and closed models draw whole scenes well, none can hold a scene together as scattered pieces: they miscount pieces, rarely interlock pieces without outlines, and fail to reconstruct the reference; target layouts help pieces fit, whereas reference images improve neither count nor fit.
AI.conclusion: Maintaining global scene continuity across broken, non-adjacent space remains an open problem for current image generators.

title: Palmprint Decomposer: Interpretable and Editable Factorization via Synthetic Learning and Instance-Wise Refinement
summary: Palmprint recognition and synthesis methods focus on extracting discriminative textures or generating images with varied textures and appearances. However, they do not generally provide an explicit image-level representation that separates palmprint texture from its underlying base appearance for independent analysis or controlled editing. We introduce Palmprint Decomposer, an interpretable framework that represents a palmprint through independently editable factors and reconstructs the image through a multiplicative composition model. A color map and a light map characterize the base appearance, while a structure map and a global texture strength parameter describe texture modulation. However, accurate reconstruction alone does not guarantee separation of palmprint texture from base appearance, as fine palmprint textures may leak into the estimated base appearance. To mitigate this ambiguity, we train the decomposer exclusively on synthetic data with direct factor supervision, using asymmetric decoding paths and decomposition constraints to suppress texture leakage. Instance-Wise Refinement further improves real-image reconstruction by directly optimizing the predicted factors for each input without relying on the trained network. Experiments across seven datasets demonstrate high reconstruction fidelity, with the extracted structure maps generally achieving verification performance comparable to the original images. Compared with existing methods, our approach achieves better factor separation while preserving more discriminative palmprint texture information.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Palmprint Decomposer, an interpretable framework that factorizes palmprint images into independently editable base appearance and texture components via synthetic learning and instance-wise refinement.
AI.motivation: Existing palmprint recognition and synthesis methods focus on discriminative feature extraction or image generation, lacking an explicit image-level representation that separates palmprint texture from underlying base appearance for independent analysis and controlled editing.
AI.method: The framework represents a palmprint using a color map, a light map, a structure map, and a global texture strength parameter combined via a multiplicative composition model, trained on synthetic data with asymmetric decoding paths and decomposition constraints to prevent texture leakage, followed by instance-wise refinement on real images.
AI.result: Experiments across seven datasets show high reconstruction fidelity, with extracted structure maps achieving verification performance comparable to original images and outperforming existing methods in factor separation and discriminative texture preservation.
AI.conclusion: Palmprint Decomposer enables interpretable, editable palmprint factorization while maintaining strong biometric verification utility.

title: EviBridge: Encoding Predictive Visual Evidence for Proactive Interaction
summary: Tool-handover interaction calls for preparation before a response is warranted. The model waits until interaction cues appear, then prepares while assessing whether the accumulating evidence supports a response or calls for cancellation. We introduce EviBridge, a framework that integrates predictive visual representations into a vision-language interaction model for joint state and tool prediction. A trainable evidence interface maps features from a frozen V-JEPA 2 encoder into the language decoder alongside native visual inputs, preserving their temporal context and using only observations available at each decision time. The framework has two instantiations. EviBridge-E distinguishes recent from historical evidence and encodes the timing and spatial location of each observation. EviBridge-I preserves the temporal order of pooled V-JEPA 2 features and interaction turns and generates dedicated interaction tokens. We evaluate on FuGIBench, a streaming-video benchmark for preparation, response, and cancellation in tool-handover assistance. The best-performing variants of EviBridge-E and EviBridge-I achieve Overall scores of 0.6448 and 0.5892, compared with 0.2178 and 0.5327 for their respective task-adapted native baselines. These gains span target handovers, long waits, and cancelled requests, demonstrating the value of predictive visual evidence for interaction decisions.

AI.tldr: This paper presents EviBridge, a framework that integrates predictive visual representations from a frozen V-JEPA 2 encoder into a vision-language interaction model for proactive tool-handover assistance.
AI.motivation: Proactive tool-handover interaction requires preparing before a response is warranted and deciding whether accumulating evidence supports responding or cancelling, which standard reactive vision-language models struggle to handle.
AI.method: A trainable evidence interface maps features from a frozen V-JEPA 2 encoder into a language decoder alongside native visual inputs, with two variants: EviBridge-E (encoding timing and spatial location of recent vs. historical evidence) and EviBridge-I (preserving temporal order of pooled features and interaction turns with dedicated interaction tokens).
AI.result: On the FuGIBench streaming-video benchmark, the best EviBridge-E and EviBridge-I variants achieve Overall scores of 0.6448 and 0.5892, outperforming task-adapted native baselines at 0.2178 and 0.5327 across target handovers, long waits, and cancelled requests.
AI.conclusion: Integrating predictive visual evidence into vision-language models substantially improves proactive interaction decisions in streaming scenarios.

title: ReAccess: Look Once, Stay Focused with Efficient Test Time Memory
summary: Despite recent advances, vision-language models (VLMs) still struggle with fine-grained visual understanding, often failing to effectively utilize critical evidence already encoded in their visual representations. Existing approaches address this limitation through repeated visual processing or explicit reasoning, introducing substantial computational overhead. In this paper, we propose ReAccess, a lightweight framework that preserves and reuses question-relevant visual evidence through compact associative memory. Constructed during a single visual prefill, the memory supports progressive evidence retrieval that steers both attention queries and hidden representations, enabling effective visual grounding without repeated image encoding or explicit reasoning traces. Extensive experiments demonstrate consistent improvements in both general visual understanding and fine-grained perception, while achieving substantially faster inference than existing reasoning-intensive approaches, demonstrating a promising path to efficient multimodal reasoning.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes ReAccess, a lightweight framework that stores and reuses question-relevant visual evidence in a compact associative memory during a single visual prefill to improve fine-grained VLM understanding.
AI.motivation: Vision-language models often fail to use fine-grained visual evidence already encoded in their representations, and existing remedies rely on repeated visual processing or explicit reasoning traces that add heavy computational overhead.
AI.method: Constructed during a single visual prefill, ReAccess builds a compact associative memory that supports progressive evidence retrieval to steer attention queries and hidden representations without re-encoding images or generating explicit reasoning traces.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show consistent improvements in both general visual understanding and fine-grained perception while achieving substantially faster inference than reasoning-intensive approaches.
AI.conclusion: ReAccess offers an efficient path to multimodal reasoning by reusing visual evidence via test-time associative memory.

title: vividRGB: Various visual cue detection in RGB photographs with forced focused attention
comment: 32 pages including supplementary material; 6 numbered figures and a graphical summary
summary: Natural photographs contain dense, overlapping structures that can be weakly expressed in feature maps from whole-image vision encoders. We introduce forced focused attention (FFA) and its Python implementation, vividRGB. FFA is an encoder-agnostic inference-time procedure that applies a frozen encoder to enlarged, overlapping local crops, averages inverse-aligned reflections, and reconstructs a feature field in source coordinates. We evaluate 50 high-resolution photographs from grassland vegetation, fungal networks, airborne forests, coral reefs, and phytoplankton microscopy, using DINOv3 ViT-B/16. Across the five domains, FFA at 5% or 10% focus produces higher mean RGB-edge boundary F1 than direct DINOv3 encoding and automatic SAM3 masks. Domain means range from 0.244 to 0.596 for FFA, versus 0.028-0.076 for direct DINOv3 and 0.020-0.090 for SAM3. Qualitative feature maps also show finer appearance structure. These results concern RGB-edge preservation rather than verified species, traits, or biological segmentation. Narrower focus generally improves boundary preservation, while extraction time and GPU energy use increase sharply and gains diminish at finer settings. FFA may be useful for relatively small, high-resolution ecological image collections where dense visual cues matter. The alpha release vividRGB 0.1.0 and versioned research resources support reproducible cue inspection.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces forced focused attention (FFA) and its Python implementation vividRGB, an encoder-agnostic inference-time procedure that reconstructs high-resolution feature fields from overlapping local crops.
AI.motivation: Whole-image vision encoders weakly express dense, overlapping structures in natural photographs, limiting fine-grained visual cue detection in complex scenes.
AI.method: FFA applies a frozen encoder to enlarged, overlapping local crops, averages inverse-aligned reflections, and reconstructs a feature field in source coordinates, evaluated using DINOv3 ViT-B/16 on 50 high-resolution ecological photographs.
AI.result: Across five domains (grassland vegetation, fungal networks, airborne forests, coral reefs, and phytoplankton microscopy), FFA at 5% or 10% focus achieves mean RGB-edge boundary F1 scores of 0.244 to 0.596, compared to 0.028-0.076 for direct DINOv3 and 0.020-0.090 for automatic SAM3 masks, though narrower focus increases extraction time and GPU energy use.
AI.conclusion: FFA and vividRGB provide a reproducible, training-free way to preserve fine RGB-edge cues in small, high-resolution ecological image collections.

title: FAVR: Flow-Aware Visual Residual Alignment for Vision-Language-Action Policies
comment: 10 pages, 5 figures. Equal contribution: Qixuan Wu and Xiaole Yang. Corresponding authors: Yuguang Yang and Baochang Zhang
summary: Pretrained video representations provide rich temporal information for robotic manipulation, yet effectively integrating them into existing vision-language-action (VLA) policies remains challenging. We present Flow-Aware Visual Residual Alignment (FAVR), a lightweight framework for flow-aware visual conditioning of frozen VLA policies. FAVR maintains a compact temporal visual state through linear Test-Time Training (TTT) and retrieves action-conditioned visual features throughout flow-based action generation. By exploiting the affine structure of the frozen action head, we explicitly characterize how injected visual features influence predicted action velocities and formulate flow-aware channel selection as a box-constrained optimization problem. We develop a FISTA-based solver for joint gate optimization and derive an efficient closed-form approximation through diagonalization and rescaling. With only 1.74-2.19M trainable parameters and 5,000 adaptation steps, FAVR improves pretrained VLA policies across benchmarks. On RoboTwin 2.0, FAVR improves LingBot-VLA from 87.12% to 90.04% under clean conditions and from 86.88% to 89.38% under randomized conditions. A controlled ablation on five RoboTwin tasks further shows that flow-aware gating increases average success from 72.0% with a gate shared across flow steps to 82.0%, demonstrating the benefit of adapting visual conditioning throughout action generation.

AI.tldr: This paper presents FAVR, a lightweight framework that conditions frozen vision-language-action (VLA) policies on temporal video representations through flow-aware visual residual alignment.
AI.motivation: Integrating pretrained video representations into existing VLA policies is challenging because injected visual features must adapt dynamically throughout flow-based action generation.
AI.method: FAVR maintains a compact temporal visual state via linear Test-Time Training and formulates flow-aware channel selection as a box-constrained optimization problem solved with a FISTA-based solver and a closed-form diagonalized approximation, using 1.74-2.19M trainable parameters.
AI.result: On RoboTwin 2.0, FAVR improves LingBot-VLA from 87.12% to 90.04% under clean conditions and from 86.88% to 89.38% under randomized conditions, while flow-aware gating increases average success on five RoboTwin tasks from 72.0% to 82.0% compared to a shared gate.
AI.conclusion: Flow-aware visual conditioning effectively enhances frozen VLA policies with minimal parameter overhead.

title: MedJev: A System One Vision-Language Decision Model for Fast and Effective Medical Image Understanding
summary: Medical image understanding with vision-language models (VLMs) typically relies on autoregressively generating reasoning and answer tokens. These unnecessary tokens make the inference cost scale with the response length and force the answer to be parsed from free-form text, incurring avoidable latency and decision errors. To this end, we introduce \textsc{MedJev}, a \emph{system one} vision-language decision model that maps medical images, questions, and candidate answers directly to decisions in a single multimodal forward pass, without any autoregressive generation process. For fast inference, \textsc{MedJev} removes the upper language layers and the generative output pathway, while keeping the full vision pathway and all visual tokens. On this shortened backbone, a decision head scores each candidate by pretrained query--key matching and refines the scores with a lightweight multilayer perceptron (MLP) residual, coupling the pretrained matching structure with task-specific nonlinear discrimination. Built on Qwen3.5-4B, \textsc{MedJev}-4B improves both accuracy and speed over the original model on each of four medical image classification and visual question answering benchmarks, with an absolute accuracy gain of \textbf{7.93\%} and a \textbf{6.04$\times$} end-to-end speedup. Further comparison with 20 cutting-edge models shows that \textsc{MedJev}-4B achieves state-of-the-art performance and inference speed among 4B--9B general and medical VLMs, indicating that direct multimodal decision making is an effective route to fast and effective medical image understanding.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces MedJev, a system-one vision-language decision model that maps medical images, questions, and candidate answers directly to decisions in a single multimodal forward pass.
AI.motivation: Autoregressive generation of reasoning and answer tokens in medical VLMs scales inference cost with response length and requires parsing free-form text, causing avoidable latency and decision errors.
AI.method: Built on Qwen3.5-4B, MedJev removes upper language layers and the generative output pathway while retaining the full vision pathway, using a decision head that scores candidates via pretrained query-key matching refined by a lightweight MLP residual.
AI.result: On four medical image classification and VQA benchmarks, MedJev-4B achieves a 7.93% absolute accuracy gain and a 6.04x end-to-end speedup over Qwen3.5-4B, and achieves state-of-the-art performance and speed among 20 compared 4B-9B general and medical VLMs.
AI.conclusion: Direct single-pass multimodal decision making is an effective alternative to autoregressive generation for fast and accurate medical image understanding.

title: Digits in Notation Are Not Numbers: A Scoring Pitfall in PDF-to-Markdown Conversion of Japanese Technical Documents (Preliminary Evaluation)
summary: Converting PDFs to Markdown is now routine preprocessing for search and language models, yet scoring the numbers in the output is easy to get wrong. We evaluate MinerU, a plain-text OCR baseline (NDLOCR-Lite), and a deterministic post-processing pipeline (anchor insertion, footnote reordering, fixes of look-alike characters in fixed contexts, gated formula repair using two independent OCR partners, and heading reconstruction) on 48 public Japanese pages (three documents), text-layer and rasterized. Our pre-specified number-and-unit F1 favored the OCR baseline (0.575 vs 0.397), and a disagreement check between the two engines seemed to flag about half of the converter's number errors (54.6%). Both were artifacts. The scorer counted digits in the converter's notation (image-link paths, HTML attributes), which plain text lacks. With the notation removed (a post-hoc check), the F1 scores tie (0.575 vs 0.594), and the check flags only 13% of number errors, because most errors are misses that both engines share. What remains: the OCR baseline has a lower body character error rate (0.012 vs 0.053 rasterized). The pipeline raises extra-number recall at page level (+0.145; the document-level interval touches 0), mostly by restoring page numbers, but lowers heading-level agreement (0.133 to 0.061) and leaves spurious formulas unchanged; its formula repair never fires. A pre-specified precision gate for its flags (0.80, human-judged) is met at 0.929, yet the post-processing hypothesis fails on its improvement items. We recommend scoring numbers after removing notation and checking critical figures against the source. By the pre-specified criteria, the study stays a technical report.

AI.tldr: This preliminary evaluation shows that a number-and-unit F1 artifact in PDF-to-Markdown conversion of Japanese technical documents stemmed from counting digits in Markdown notation rather than text.
AI.motivation: Scoring numerical accuracy in PDF-to-Markdown conversion is prone to methodological pitfalls, and deterministic post-processing pipelines need rigorous validation against plain-text OCR baselines.
AI.method: The authors evaluate MinerU, NDLOCR-Lite, and a deterministic post-processing pipeline (anchor insertion, footnote reordering, look-alike character fixes, gated formula repair, and heading reconstruction) on 48 public Japanese pages in both text-layer and rasterized forms.
AI.result: Removing Markdown notation digits eliminates the apparent F1 gap between NDLOCR-Lite and MinerU (0.575 vs. 0.594) and drops the engine-disagreement error flag rate from 54.6% to 13%; NDLOCR-Lite has a lower rasterized body character error rate (0.012 vs. 0.053), while the post-processing pipeline improves page-level extra-number recall (+0.145) but lowers heading-level agreement (0.133 to 0.061).
AI.conclusion: Numerical evaluation of PDF-to-Markdown converters should strip notation digits first and verify critical figures against the source document.

title: Sparse Attention for Visual Generation: Toward Algorithm-System Co-Design
summary: Rapid advances in image and video generation have enabled high-fidelity synthesis at higher resolutions and longer durations, making the quadratic cost of dense self-attention a major bottleneck as visual token sequences grow. Sparse attention seeks to preserve generation quality at lower computational cost by retaining informative query-key interactions and omitting less consequential ones, with end-to-end gains depending on the cost of constructing sparse support and the efficiency with which the system maps the resulting workload to hardware. We survey sparse attention for visual generation through a 4+1+3 analytical framework that links algorithmic design to system implementation. The framework examines how static and dynamic methods use source information and the evidence derived from it to decide which interactions to retain and at what granularity, while accounting for the roles of reuse in reducing repeated computation and correction in compensating for omitted contributions. We relate these algorithmic choices to their implementation on hardware through the framework's three system dimensions of data organization, execution, and dataflow. We summarize common evaluation metrics and discuss open challenges and research directions, providing researchers and practitioners with a reference for the joint design of sparse attention algorithms and systems.

AI.tldr: This survey reviews sparse attention for visual generation through a 4+1+3 analytical framework that connects algorithmic design choices to hardware-level system implementations.
AI.motivation: High-resolution and long-duration image and video generation suffer from the quadratic cost of dense self-attention, and end-to-end speedups depend on jointly optimizing sparse support construction and hardware mapping.
AI.method: The authors categorize static and dynamic sparse attention methods across four algorithmic dimensions plus reuse and correction, and map them to three system dimensions: data organization, execution, and dataflow.
AI.result: The survey synthesizes existing methods, summarizes common evaluation metrics, and outlines open challenges and research directions for algorithm-system co-design.
AI.conclusion: The 4+1+3 framework provides researchers and practitioners with a structured reference for co-designing sparse attention algorithms and systems in visual generation.

title: POKE: Probe Offline, Keep Efficiently for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Visual token pruning reduces the inference cost of Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, but attention-based scores do not directly measure a token's effect on the predicted action. We define action sensitivity as the magnitude of the first-order action change when a token is replaced by its camera's mean token and estimate it for all tokens with a single backward pass. Computing it online is costly: scoring on the full (unpruned) graph needs an extra forward pass at every control step. Scoring on the pruned forward pass is cheaper but causes scoring-graph lock-in: removed tokens lose their direct paths through later layers and tend to receive lower scores, making those locations less likely to return. On replayed observations, even with a random conditioning mask, pruned-graph scoring re-selects 59% of the mask's tokens, versus 6% expected by chance; attention histories show a similar bias. POKE (Probe Offline, Keep Efficiently) computes full-graph action sensitivities offline and distills them into a student with under 0.3M parameters. At inference, the student scores the current observation without backpropagation or previous masks, and score-guided diversity selection retains the tokens. Keeping 32 of 512 visual tokens on LIBERO, POKE achieves 95.2% success on OpenVLA-OFT and 90.8% on $\pi_{0.5}$ at $1.85\times$ and $1.26\times$ speedups, outperforming attention-, diversity-, and distillation-based pruners, with larger margins on LIBERO-Plus.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes POKE, a visual token pruning method for VLA models that computes full-graph action sensitivities offline and distills them into a lightweight student for inference-time token selection.
AI.motivation: Attention-based pruning scores do not directly measure a token's impact on predicted actions, while online sensitivity scoring is either too expensive on the full graph or suffers from scoring-graph lock-in on the pruned graph.
AI.method: POKE defines action sensitivity as the first-order action change when replacing a token with its camera mean, computes full-graph sensitivities offline, distills them into a student with under 0.3M parameters, and uses score-guided diversity selection at inference.
AI.result: Keeping 32 of 512 visual tokens on LIBERO, POKE achieves 95.2% success on OpenVLA-OFT (1.85x speedup) and 90.8% on pi_0.5 (1.26x speedup), outperforming attention-, diversity-, and distillation-based pruners with larger margins on LIBERO-Plus.
AI.conclusion: Offline action-sensitivity distillation avoids scoring-graph lock-in and enables fast, accurate visual token pruning for VLA models.

title: ScoutCache: Efficient Few-Step Autoregressive Video Diffusion via Conditional Readout and Selective Caching
summary: Few-step autoregressive video diffusion enables efficient long video generation, but inference still incurs substantial computational costs from repeated denoising and KV cache operations. Existing acceleration methods reduce parts of this overhead, while historical KV reading and cache construction remain costly across video chunks. To address these challenges, we propose ScoutCache, a training-free framework that jointly optimizes denoising, historical KV reading, and cache construction. We observe that shallow feature changes provide useful information for estimating clean latent updates, while historical KV dependence varies across Transformer layers and attention heads but remains relatively stable across video chunks. Based on these observations, we develop Conditional Denoising Readout (CDR) to estimate intermediate denoising updates from shallow feature changes and known noise variations. We further introduce Output Risk Guided Historical KV Reading (ORHR) to allocate historical reading budgets based on attention output perturbations, and Content and Coverage Guided Sparse Cache Construction (CCSC) to reduce cache construction costs by selecting informative spatial tokens while maintaining spatial coverage. Extensive experiments on Self-Forcing and LongLive using VBench and MovieGen demonstrate that ScoutCache achieves up to 2.28$\times$ and 1.86$\times$ speedups, respectively, while consistently improving generation quality without modifying pretrained model parameters.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces ScoutCache, a training-free framework that accelerates few-step autoregressive video diffusion by jointly optimizing denoising, historical KV reading, and cache construction.
AI.motivation: Despite using few denoising steps, autoregressive video diffusion still incurs high inference overhead from repeated denoising and costly historical KV reading and cache construction across video chunks.
AI.method: ScoutCache combines Conditional Denoising Readout (estimating clean latent updates from shallow feature changes), Output Risk Guided Historical KV Reading (allocating reading budgets by attention output perturbations), and Content and Coverage Guided Sparse Cache Construction.
AI.result: On Self-Forcing and LongLive using VBench and MovieGen, ScoutCache achieves up to 2.28x and 1.86x speedups while consistently improving generation quality without modifying pretrained weights.
AI.conclusion: Jointly optimizing denoising readout and KV cache management enables training-free acceleration of autoregressive video diffusion.

title: Body of Evidence: Triangulating 3D Human Pose with Geometry-Conditioned Depth
summary: Even in multi-camera setups, occlusions can leave individual body joints with only a single usable 2D observation. Such an observation defines a viewing ray but leaves the joint's depth undetermined. We introduce Body of Evidence (BoE), a multi-view 3D human pose estimator that predicts per-camera joint depths alongside 2D joint locations. To reduce monocular depth ambiguity, we propose geometry-conditioned depth prediction, which combines image features with previously reconstructed 3D body geometry as contextual depth cues. We further introduce learnable depth-aware triangulation (LDAT), which augments differentiable algebraic triangulation with predicted depth constraints, enabling reconstruction even from a single contributing camera while preserving the benefits of geometric triangulation when multiple views are available. The reconstructed 3D poses subsequently guide depth prediction in the next iteration, allowing depth estimates and 3D geometry to progressively refine each other. Experiments on CMU Panoptic demonstrate state-of-the-art in-domain performance and superior average performance across evaluated camera subsets and unseen camera arrangements. BoE is particularly effective under sparse camera coverage, outperforming the previous state of the art by 10.6 AP25 points in the challenging three-camera setting.

AI.tldr: This paper presents Body of Evidence (BoE), a multi-view 3D human pose estimator that combines geometry-conditioned depth prediction with learnable depth-aware triangulation to handle single-view occlusions.
AI.motivation: Occlusions in multi-camera setups often leave body joints visible in only one camera, leaving their depth undetermined under standard geometric triangulation.
AI.method: BoE predicts per-camera joint depths alongside 2D locations by conditioning on image features and previously reconstructed 3D body geometry, and integrates these depth constraints into differentiable algebraic triangulation for iterative refinement.
AI.result: On CMU Panoptic, BoE achieves state-of-the-art in-domain performance and superior average accuracy across evaluated camera subsets and unseen arrangements, outperforming the previous state of the art by 10.6 AP25 points in the three-camera setting.
AI.conclusion: Geometry-conditioned depth prediction and depth-aware triangulation substantially improve 3D human pose estimation under sparse camera coverage and occlusion.

title: Dataset Distillation for Handwritten Text Recognition: An Empirical Study
summary: Dataset distillation (DD) replaces large training datasets with smaller synthetic ones to reduce computational costs. While traditionally used for classification, we present, to our knowledge, the first DD study for line-level handwritten text recognition (HTR). Unlike classification tasks, which use discrete labels, HTR employs unaligned sequences from a virtually infinite output space as labels. To adapt classification-based DD methods to this scenario, we define text pseudo-classes by clustering transcriptions based on character n-grams. We adapt gradient matching (GM), distribution matching (DM) and trajectory matching (MTT) to a Convolutional Recurrent Neural Network (CRNN) trained with Connectionist Temporal Classification (CTC). In this process, synthetic line images are generated by optimising only the pixels of real starting lines (either randomly chosen or selected as text medoids), while keeping their original transcriptions fixed. Across four datasets (IAM, George Washington, READ\,2016, LAM) and three budgets (1--10\,\% of the training lines), no distilled set outperforms its real initialisation lines. Random lines prove better than medoids, and further optimisation only degrades recognition. Methodologically, DM lowers its objective without benefit, while GM and MTT barely move theirs. We turn these findings into guidelines for evaluating data compression in HTR.

AI.tldr: This empirical study adapts classification-based dataset distillation methods to line-level handwritten text recognition (HTR) and finds that no distilled dataset outperforms its real initialization lines.
AI.motivation: Dataset distillation has been studied primarily for discrete-label classification, leaving its applicability to sequence-based HTR with unaligned, virtually infinite output spaces unexplored.
AI.method: The authors cluster transcriptions by character n-grams into pseudo-classes and adapt gradient matching (GM), distribution matching (DM), and trajectory matching (MTT) to a CRNN trained with CTC loss by optimizing pixels of real starting lines.
AI.result: Across IAM, George Washington, READ 2016, and LAM at 1-10% budgets, no distilled set beats its real initialization lines, random initialization outperforms medoids, and further pixel optimization degrades recognition.
AI.conclusion: Current classification-oriented dataset distillation objectives do not transfer effectively to CTC-based HTR, motivating new evaluation guidelines for HTR data compression.

title: MetricHand: Geometry-Aware Flow Matching for 4D Hand Reconstruction in Metric World Space
summary: Egocentric hand motion provides physical motion supervision for dexterous manipulation and vision-language-action pretraining. Reliable use of this supervision requires accurate and temporally coherent 4D hand reconstruction in metric world space. Existing methods typically lift framewise estimates produced under weak perspective into world coordinates. By ignoring joint-dependent depth variation at close range, this approximation couples errors in translation, orientation, and articulation that persist after world lifting and worsen under occlusion. We present MetricHand, a geometry-aware flow matching framework for 4D hand reconstruction in metric world space. MetricHand encodes depth priors from hand-object interaction regions into joint-associated representations that preserve local spatial structure and metric scale. Fused with visual features, this geometry guides coarse metric estimation and conditions every step of temporal generation. The model jointly recovers world-space translation, global orientation, MANO articulation, and shape, while structural priors and temporal context support estimation under partial occlusion. MetricHand reduces camera-space MPJPE by 49.3% and 52.9%, absolute world-space MPJPE by 28.7% and 21.7%, and wrist localization error by 48.5% and 37.9% relative to HaWoR, respectively. World-space acceleration error decreases by 44.2% and 64.3%, demonstrating improved temporal fidelity alongside more accurate absolute localization.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces MetricHand, a geometry-aware flow matching framework for temporally coherent 4D hand reconstruction in metric world space.
AI.motivation: Existing methods lift framewise weak-perspective estimates into world coordinates, which ignores close-range joint-dependent depth variation and couples translation, orientation, and articulation errors under occlusion.
AI.method: MetricHand encodes depth priors from hand-object interaction regions into joint-associated representations, fuses them with visual features to guide coarse metric estimation, and conditions every step of temporal flow matching to jointly recover translation, orientation, MANO articulation, and shape.
AI.result: Relative to HaWoR, MetricHand reduces camera-space MPJPE by 49.3% and 52.9%, absolute world-space MPJPE by 28.7% and 21.7%, wrist localization error by 48.5% and 37.9%, and world-space acceleration error by 44.2% and 64.3%.
AI.conclusion: Conditioning temporal flow matching on interaction depth priors yields more accurate and temporally coherent 4D hand reconstruction in metric world space.

title: What Makes a Good Move? Learning to Act from Experience in Visual Worlds
summary: Learning visual policies requires turning interaction experience into guidance for individual decisions. Trajectory outcomes obscure action quality, while unguided exploration can revisit familiar situations. We present \textsc{LightAct}, an experience-learning framework that connects skill-guided exploration with policy internalization. Interaction segments are summarized into experience entries and consolidated into a game-specific skill that guides root collection toward broader state coverage. At each root, candidate actions are compared through short rollouts under a shared frozen policy. Environment-reported score gains are averaged across continuations and normalized into relative action rewards, producing reusable supervision for reinforcement learning. Policy training uses a compact dataset of just 1,024 decision roots collected in a single source game and paired with their action rewards. Across 170 GameWorld tasks spanning 34 games, \textsc{LightAct} improves overall progress by 23.6, 29.2, and 13.0 percentage points at the 2B, 4B, and 9B scales, respectively, with our strongest model competitive with reported proprietary-model results. Ablations show broader root-state coverage with skill guidance and consistent gains across three policy optimizers. Case studies show how rollouts distinguish actions with identical immediate gains.

AI.tldr: This paper presents LightAct, an experience-learning framework that uses skill-guided exploration and short rollout comparisons to train visual policies from a compact set of decision roots.
AI.motivation: Learning visual policies from trajectory outcomes obscures individual action quality, while unguided exploration repeatedly revisits familiar states.
AI.method: LightAct summarizes interaction segments into game-specific skills to guide root collection toward broader state coverage, compares candidate actions at each root via short rollouts under a frozen policy, and normalizes score gains into relative action rewards for reinforcement learning on 1,024 roots from a single source game.
AI.result: Across 170 GameWorld tasks spanning 34 games, LightAct improves overall progress by 23.6, 29.2, and 13.0 percentage points at 2B, 4B, and 9B model scales, with the strongest model competitive with proprietary models.
AI.conclusion: Skill-guided exploration paired with rollout-based relative action rewards enables sample-efficient visual policy learning that generalizes across games.

title: MORE: Merge Once, Route Early for Training-Free Multi-Subject Composition from Large LoRA Pools
summary: Public hubs offer many personalized LoRAs per text-to-image backbone, yet composing two of them in one image remains fragile. In FLUX, keeping a pool of $K=10$ or $20$ subject LoRAs loaded makes their deltas interfere, and even loading only the two requested LoRAs keeps both subjects in fewer than 4% of images: one subject vanishes, the two fuse, or the image splits into a collage. We present MORE (Merge Once, Route Early), a training-free two-stage pipeline for FLUX. Merge once: the whole pool is folded into a single fixed-rank adapter by the subspace-regression router of SSR-Merge, made reliable by ridge, rank and calibration choices, and factored exactly into a shared part and per-subject parts. Route early: during the first 30% of the denoising steps each subject's part is gated to its layout region; a decaying soft attention bias ties every region to its own subject tokens, and a cyclic swap guidance extrapolates away from the prediction with the subjects' regions permuted, which counteracts region homogenization. On held-out seeds, MORE keeps both subjects in 94.2% ($K=10$) and 78.3% ($K=20$) of images, against 50.8% / 35.8% for FreeFuse and 25.0% / 24.2% for LoRAShop, and reaches an ImageReward of 1.32 (best baseline 0.07), while all $K$ subjects stay in one adapter. With layouts inferred automatically it still keeps both subjects in 70.0% / 55.0% of images.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes MORE, a training-free two-stage pipeline for FLUX that merges a large pool of subject LoRAs into one adapter and routes them spatially during early denoising steps.
AI.motivation: Composing multiple personalized LoRAs in FLUX fails due to delta interference when pools are loaded and subject vanishing, fusion, or collage artifacts even when only two LoRAs are loaded.
AI.method: MORE folds a pool of K subject LoRAs into a single fixed-rank adapter via SSR-Merge factored into shared and per-subject parts, then gates each subject's part to its layout region during the first 30% of denoising steps using decaying soft attention bias and cyclic swap guidance.
AI.result: On held-out seeds, MORE preserves both subjects in 94.2% (K=10) and 78.3% (K=20) of images compared to 50.8%/35.8% for FreeFuse and 25.0%/24.2% for LoRAShop, achieves an ImageReward of 1.32 (vs. 0.07 best baseline), and retains 70.0%/55.0% accuracy with automatically inferred layouts.
AI.conclusion: Merging LoRA pools once and routing them early enables reliable training-free multi-subject composition from large LoRA libraries.

title: State-Message Interaction Adapter for Cross-Domain Few-Shot Segmentation
comment: 17 pages, 9 figures, 7 tables, including the appendix
summary: Cross-domain few-shot segmentation adapts natural-image pretrained encoders to medical or industrial domains from a few pixel-annotated support masks.
