Within frozen DINOv3, intermediate per-head attention messages already carry target-background distinctions that baseline final-layer similarities and predictions do not consistently reflect. We propose the State-Message Interaction Adapter (SMIA) to learn how per-head messages should update each receiving token representation while keeping pretrained attention and FFN parameters frozen. Inserted right after per-head aggregation, SMIA conditions the transformation of each head's aggregated output (message) on each patch's pre-attention feature (state), allowing similar contextual messages to produce distinct or opposing updates depending on the receiving position. Because scarce support masks cover only limited state-message combinations, a shared low-rank bilinear map confines the learned interactions to low-dimensional state, message, and output subspaces. Added before each adapted block's frozen FFN, these updates yield adapted features that are refined by frozen FFNs and deeper blocks for linear readout. With only 0.51M trainable parameters and single-pass, support-free inference, SMIA achieves six-dataset mean mIoUs of 77.40% at 5 shots and 80.99% at 10 shots across 20 medical and industrial tasks, surpassing the strongest prior methods by +3.61 and +3.93 percentage points. In controlled 10-shot comparisons across three benchmarks on the same DINOv3 backbone, SMIA also outperforms parameter-matched AdaptFormer, LoRA, and ParaX with a better precision-recall balance.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the State-Message Interaction Adapter (SMIA) for cross-domain few-shot segmentation, adapting frozen DINOv3 encoders with 0.51M trainable parameters.
AI.motivation: Frozen DINOv3 intermediate per-head attention messages already contain target-background distinctions that final-layer features miss, but scarce support masks limit how much adaptation can be learned without overfitting.
AI.method: Inserted after per-head aggregation before each frozen FFN, SMIA uses a shared low-rank bilinear map to condition each head's message transformation on each patch's pre-attention state.
AI.result: Across 20 medical and industrial tasks on six datasets, SMIA achieves 77.40% mIoU at 5 shots and 80.99% at 10 shots, surpassing prior methods by +3.61 and +3.93 percentage points, and outperforms parameter-matched AdaptFormer, LoRA, and ParaX in 10-shot comparisons.
AI.conclusion: Low-rank state-message interaction adaptation effectively unlocks frozen foundation model features for cross-domain few-shot segmentation.

title: MedicalDPO: Multi-Objective Direct Preference Optimization for CT to PET Translation
summary: CT-to-PET synthesis estimates functional PET images from anatomical CT scans for auxiliary analysis, representation pretraining, and missing-modality completion. Brownian Bridge diffusion models can produce multiple PET candidates of different quality under the same CT condition, exposing an intra-condition quality hierarchy. Candidate quality spans complementary spatial, structural, and intensity dimensions, while DPO-only fine-tuning may compromise absolute synthesis fidelity. We propose MedicalDPO which converts this hierarchy into preference supervision automatically constructed from paired CT-PET training data. Multiple candidates are ranked across the three fidelity dimensions, and strict cross-metric verification retains preferred-rejected pairs with consistent quality separation. Relative denoising-error preference optimization is jointly trained with the original Brownian Bridge objective to anchor the pretrained CT-to-PET mapping, while condition-balanced multi-pair rotation distributes preference supervision across CT conditions. Experiments on BBDM and CPDM show improvements across LPIPS, MAE, SSIM, and PSNR. Further analyses demonstrate metric complementarity and clear pair separation, while ablations show that the original training objective prevents the substantial degradation caused by DPO-only fine-tuning.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes MedicalDPO, a multi-objective direct preference optimization framework for CT-to-PET image translation using Brownian Bridge diffusion models.
AI.motivation: Brownian Bridge diffusion models generate CT-to-PET candidates with varying spatial, structural, and intensity quality, while DPO-only fine-tuning can degrade absolute synthesis fidelity.
AI.method: MedicalDPO ranks multiple candidates from paired CT-PET data across three fidelity dimensions with cross-metric verification, jointly trains relative denoising-error preference optimization with the original Brownian Bridge objective, and applies condition-balanced multi-pair rotation.
AI.result: Experiments on BBDM and CPDM show consistent improvements across LPIPS, MAE, SSIM, and PSNR, with ablations confirming that retaining the original objective prevents DPO-only degradation.
AI.conclusion: Anchoring multi-objective preference optimization to the original diffusion objective improves CT-to-PET translation fidelity.

title: Beyond Family Labels: A Taxonomic Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Prior for Avian 3D Shape Recovery
summary: Recovering 3D pose and shape of birds from single images is bottlenecked by the long tail of avian diversity: out of ~10,000 species, only a few dozen have 3D-labeled training data, and in-the-wild test sets routinely contain species never seen at training. Generalizing across clades is therefore a central problem. The current state of the art, AniMer+, mitigates it with a family-level contrastive loss that conveys only a binary same-family indicator per pair and discards the continuous structure of the species tree. We propose a taxonomic Ornstein-Uhlenbeck prior on the shape code of the AVES parametric bird mesh model: a multivariate Gaussian whose covariance decays exponentially with Linnaean rank distance, with a learnable selection strength and noise scale. The prior generalizes family contrastive into a continuous, generative form, exposing the graded cross- and within-family similarity that a binary indicator cannot, and brings continuous comparative phylogenetics in as a biology-grounded inductive bias for the long tail. Our method improves over AniMer+ on both metrics of the unseen-species CowBird benchmark and on CtrlAVES3D, while remaining comparable on seen-species CUB. A permutation ablation isolates taxonomic structure from generic Gaussian smoothing, and a rank-granularity ablation identifies cross-order distinctions (the structure beyond a family-vs-not indicator) as the dominant source of the unseen-species gain.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a taxonomic Ornstein-Uhlenbeck prior on the AVES shape code to improve 3D bird shape recovery for unseen species in the long tail of avian diversity.
AI.motivation: Few avian species have 3D-labeled training data, and existing family-level contrastive losses discard continuous phylogenetic relationships by using only binary same-family indicators.
AI.method: The authors place a multivariate Gaussian prior on the AVES shape code whose covariance decays exponentially with Linnaean rank distance, with learnable selection strength and noise scale.
AI.result: The method improves over AniMer+ on both metrics of the unseen-species CowBird benchmark and on CtrlAVES3D while remaining comparable on seen-species CUB, with ablations showing cross-order distinctions drive the unseen-species gain.
AI.conclusion: Continuous comparative phylogenetics provides an effective biological inductive bias for generalizing 3D shape recovery across unseen species.

title: GRAZE: Text-Free Grasp Synthesis for Unseen Objects from Human Gaze
summary: Text-conditioned hand-object interaction (HOI) generation provides intuitive semantic control, but language is an indirect way to specify where an interaction should occur on an object. Naming the part to grasp requires object-specific words, and naming the approach side requires a reference frame that a prompt lacks. We propose GRAZE (GRAsp from gaZE), which generates hand-object grasp motion from recorded gaze instead of object and part names. Its Geometry-Aware Gaze Encoding (GeoGaze) maps gaze rays to cues on object geometry, and cross-attention conditions a diffusion Transformer on these cues. We also introduce HOT3D-Grasp, a grasp-centered benchmark with object-disjoint folds built on HOT3D recordings. On unseen objects, GRAZE grasps the target part more often than the strongest text-conditioned baseline (49.3% vs. 43.6%), achieves the highest grasp success (66.3% vs. 46.6%), and transfers without fine-tuning to GazeHOI (45.3% vs. 33.8%). Gaze conveys the approach side: when gaze is rotated around the object, the approach turns with it in 59.1% of cases, against 20.5% for a text model retrained with clock words. On the same backbone, a text prompt names parts better, but gaze adds the approach side. Given both, GRAZE keeps the prompt's part accuracy and follows gaze.

AI.tldr: This paper presents GRAZE, a diffusion Transformer that synthesizes hand-object grasps for unseen objects from human gaze instead of text prompts, alongside the HOT3D-Grasp benchmark.
AI.motivation: Text prompts are an indirect way to specify grasp location and approach side on unseen objects because they require object-specific part names and lack a spatial reference frame.
AI.method: GRAZE uses Geometry-Aware Gaze Encoding (GeoGaze) to map gaze rays onto object geometry and conditions a diffusion Transformer via cross-attention, evaluated on the newly introduced object-disjoint HOT3D-Grasp benchmark.
AI.result: On unseen objects, GRAZE grasps the target part more often than the strongest text baseline (49.3% vs. 43.6%), achieves higher grasp success (66.3% vs. 46.6%), transfers zero-shot to GazeHOI (45.3% vs. 33.8%), and follows rotated gaze approach sides in 59.1% of cases (vs. 20.5% for text).
AI.conclusion: Human gaze provides a direct geometric signal for specifying grasp target and approach direction on unseen objects.

title: Source-Free Domain Adaptation for Multi-Label Image Classification: A Framework, Baselines, and Benchmark
summary: Source-free domain adaptation (SFDA) adapts a model trained on a labelled source domain to an unlabelled target domain without access to the source data. Almost the entire SFDA literature assumes mutually exclusive classes, yet many deployed settings are multi-label. This paper formulates SFDA for multi-label classification and establishes the first benchmark for it: five adaptation tasks over six datasets spanning remote sensing, natural, clipart-style and driving imagery, with four single-label SFDA methods extended to provide the first baselines and a published multi-label method run alongside them, over three seeds. The benchmark shows that extending a single-label method is unreliable rather than merely suboptimal: half of the extended baselines fail to improve on the unadapted source model at all, and on two of the five tasks none of them does. The failures are not incidental. Nearest-centroid pseudo-labelling, softmax-based confidence, the diversity term of information maximization and confidence-weighted prototype construction each rely on mutual exclusivity, and each fails differently without it, so replacing the softmax with per-class sigmoids is a valid but insufficient extension. Multi-label Prototype Alignment with Contrastive Teaching (MPACT) is proposed in response, a mean-teacher framework whose objective, prototype construction and alignment term are each reconsidered for overlapping label sets. It attains the best average on every reported metric and is the only method that improves on the unadapted source model on all five tasks. The analysis further introduces a prototype-agreement diagnostic separating feature-space alignment from self-reinforcing agreement with the classifier, and reports a negative result for confidence-based pseudo-label filtering.

AI.tldr: This paper formulates source-free domain adaptation (SFDA) for multi-label image classification, establishes a five-task benchmark, and proposes Multi-label Prototype Alignment with Contrastive Teaching (MPACT).
AI.motivation: Existing SFDA methods assume mutually exclusive classes and fail when extended naively to multi-label settings, where half of the extended single-label baselines fail to improve over the unadapted source model.
AI.method: MPACT is a mean-teacher framework that redesigns the adaptation objective, prototype construction, and alignment term for overlapping label sets, evaluated across five adaptation tasks over six datasets.
AI.result: MPACT achieves the best average score on every reported metric and is the only method to improve over the unadapted source model on all five tasks, while diagnostic analysis reveals negative results for confidence-based pseudo-label filtering.
AI.conclusion: Multi-label SFDA requires dedicated prototype alignment and contrastive teaching rather than simple sigmoid-based extensions of single-label methods.

title: VAE Rhythm: Temporal Decoding Traces for AI-Generated Video Detection
comment: 24 pages, 7 figures. Project page: this https URL
summary: Visible artifacts are an unreliable cue for detecting generated videos, because newer generators learn to remove them. We instead detect a trace left by the generation pipeline itself. Most video generators decode latents with a 3D causal VAE that groups consecutive frames in time, so the fidelity of generated frames rises and falls periodically with their position in a group. We call this periodic trace VAE Rhythm. Real videos are captured frame by frame and do not have it. To reveal it without training, we propose a phase scan. The scan reconstructs a clip with an off-the-shelf VAE from successive start offsets and measures the periodicity of the reconstruction error across these offsets. We find VAE Rhythm in most of the 39 variants of 31 generators we test, including the closed-source Sora, Kling 3.0 and Seedance 2.0. We use the rhythm as a zero-shot score, as a plug-in for existing detectors and as a data engine that pairs real videos with their VAE reconstructions to train our detector CaDet. On DF26, the training-free rhythm score outperforms all 15 retrained baselines, and as a plug-in it improves all 19 tested detectors by 6.7% to 23.7% AUROC. CaDet achieves the best AUROC on AIGVDBench, DF26 and three 2026 closed-source models, and its variant trained without any generated video still exceeds 90% on AIGVDBench.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces VAE Rhythm, a periodic temporal decoding trace left by 3D causal VAEs in AI-generated videos, and uses it for zero-shot detection, detector augmentation, and training the CaDet detector.
AI.motivation: Visible artifacts are becoming unreliable for detecting AI-generated videos as newer generators eliminate them, requiring detection cues rooted in the generation pipeline itself.
AI.method: A training-free phase scan reconstructs a clip with an off-the-shelf VAE from successive start offsets to measure reconstruction-error periodicity, which is used as a zero-shot score, a plug-in feature, and a data engine pairing real videos with VAE reconstructions to train CaDet.
AI.result: VAE Rhythm appears in most of 39 variants across 31 generators (including Sora, Kling 3.0, and Seedance 2.0); on DF26, the zero-shot score beats all 15 retrained baselines, the plug-in boosts all 19 tested detectors by 6.7% to 23.7% AUROC, and CaDet achieves the best AUROC on AIGVDBench, DF26, and three 2026 closed-source models.
AI.conclusion: Periodic temporal decoding traces from 3D causal VAEs provide a robust, generalizable signal for detecting AI-generated videos.

title: IGRecon4D: Dynamic-Object-Aware Feed-Forward Reconstruction of Driving Scenes
summary: Feed-forward 4D driving-scene reconstruction enables efficient modeling of dynamic autonomous-driving scenes, but current methods suffer from two complementary failure modes: semantic leakage of traffic participants into the static representation and geometric drift of Gaussian locations across viewpoints. We propose \textbf{IGRecon4D}, a feed-forward dynamic scene reconstruction framework that addresses these failures with training-time instance-prior distillation and LiDAR-anchored Gaussian positioning. Specifically, an instance-level semantic branch provides a potentially dynamic participant prior, which is distilled into dynamic-mask learning through the Instance-Dynamic Consistency Constraint to encourage high-recall localization of traffic-participant regions prone to dynamic-static leakage. In parallel, sparse LiDAR measurements guide dense depth estimation, and the resulting depths are back-projected to anchor Gaussian positions for improved multi-view geometric consistency. Experiments on the Waymo Open Dataset and zero-shot evaluation on nuScenes demonstrate improved full-image reconstruction on the main benchmark and stronger traffic-participant-region reconstruction under cross-dataset evaluation.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes IGRecon4D, a feed-forward 4D driving-scene reconstruction framework that combines instance-prior distillation and LiDAR-anchored Gaussian positioning.
AI.motivation: Existing feed-forward 4D driving-scene reconstruction methods suffer from semantic leakage of traffic participants into static backgrounds and geometric drift of Gaussians across viewpoints.
AI.method: IGRecon4D distills an instance-level semantic branch into dynamic-mask learning via an Instance-Dynamic Consistency Constraint and back-projects sparse LiDAR-guided dense depth to anchor Gaussian positions.
AI.result: Experiments on the Waymo Open Dataset and zero-shot evaluation on nuScenes show improved full-image reconstruction on the main benchmark and stronger traffic-participant reconstruction under cross-dataset evaluation.
AI.conclusion: Combining instance-prior distillation with LiDAR-anchored positioning mitigates dynamic-static leakage and multi-view geometric drift in feed-forward 4D driving reconstruction.

title: How to Explain your Unexplainable Video Anomaly Detector
comment: This paper has been accepted at the RWS workshop WACV 2027
summary: Weakly-supervised Video Anomaly Detection (VAD) models assign anomaly scores from high-dimensional features, and their predictions remain unexplained. Saliency maps show where a model looks but not what it relies on, and the descriptions produced by Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are generated by branches that the anomaly score never reads. To address this faithfulness gap, we propose \textbf{Explain The Unexplainable (ETU)}, a classifier-agnostic framework that audits frozen VAD models through counterfactual interventions in their feature space. ETU maps video features to a discrete dependency graph of agents, actions and outcomes ($A_r \to A_a \to A_o$), regenerates the features by graph-conditioned diffusion with selected nodes of the graph masked, and measures the change in the score of a frozen detector; one set of interventions is applied unchanged to every detector. The generator is trained only to reconstruct the input features, so it cannot learn the contrast it is asked to measure, and we validate the audit with experiments that test every alternative explanation of its results, from the cost of regeneration to random deletions of matched size. On UCF-Crime features obtained from a CLIP encoder, we show that substituting the scene semantics results in the largest drop for most detectors, and that removing the outcome chain of the graph ($\Delta_{rel}$) changes the anomaly score of all six audited detectors far more than removing the same number of random nodes, even though the random deletion perturbs the features about as much. We show that this targeted behavior comes from the divergence objective of the graph embedding. Without it, the two interventions become indistinguishable, and with a divergence objective in the generator as well, the score change of the detector follows the displacement of the reconstruction rather than the semantics that were removed.

AI.tldr: This paper presents Explain The Unexplainable (ETU), a classifier-agnostic framework that audits frozen weakly-supervised video anomaly detectors via counterfactual feature-space interventions.
AI.motivation: Saliency maps and VLM-generated descriptions do not faithfully explain what frozen video anomaly detectors rely on because they do not intervene on the features the anomaly score actually reads.
AI.method: ETU maps video features to a discrete dependency graph of agents, actions, and outcomes, regenerates features via graph-conditioned diffusion with selected nodes masked, and measures the resulting score change in the frozen detector.
AI.result: On UCF-Crime CLIP features across six audited detectors, substituting scene semantics causes the largest score drop for most detectors, and removing the outcome chain changes scores far more than removing the same number of random nodes, driven by the graph embedding's divergence objective.
AI.conclusion: Counterfactual graph-conditioned feature interventions provide a faithful way to audit what frozen video anomaly detectors depend on.

title: Region-VAD: Video Anomaly Localization and Detection via Region Selection
comment: This paper has been accepted in the RWS workshop at WACV 2027
summary: Anomalies are local events, yet weakly supervised video anomaly detection scores them globally. Most methods pool an entire frame into a single vector, rank frames by that vector, and derive a location afterwards as a saliency map of the score. Full-frame pooling mixes the anomaly with its background, so a detector can reach competitive benchmark scores from scene context without being able to show where in the scene the anomaly occurs. We introduce Region-VAD, which first selects a region and then detects the anomaly from that region alone. Region-VAD selects an explicit rectangle over the tokens of a frozen foundation model and scores anomalousness only from the tokens inside the box, through attention pooling followed by a standard temporal head. The rectangle is not learned, it is the box in which the frozen tokens change most between consecutive segments, in all four feature projections of the encoder, and it is found by exhaustive search over the rectangles of the token grid. Only the pooling and the temporal head are trained, from video-level labels without boxes, masks or frame-level annotations, and no trained component reads a token outside the selected region. Experiments on five datasets, with one localizer configuration shared by all datasets and backbones, show that Region-VAD achieves state-of-the-art anomaly localization on UCF-Crime and MSAD at competitive detection performance.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Region-VAD, a weakly-supervised video anomaly detection and localization method that selects a high-change token rectangle before scoring anomalies solely from tokens inside that box.
AI.motivation: Standard weakly-supervised VAD pools entire frames into a single vector, mixing anomalies with background context and hurting spatial localization.
AI.method: Region-VAD exhaustively searches the frozen foundation-model token grid for the rectangle with the largest inter-segment change across all four encoder feature projections, then trains only attention pooling and a temporal head on tokens inside the box using video-level labels.
AI.result: Evaluated across five datasets with a single shared localizer configuration, Region-VAD achieves state-of-the-art anomaly localization on UCF-Crime and MSAD with competitive detection performance.
AI.conclusion: Isolating the highest-change token region prior to scoring improves weakly-supervised anomaly localization without box or frame-level annotations.

title: Model-based neural network for global floodplains analysis
summary: We address the super-resolution of multispectral remote sensing imagery for long-term floodplain monitoring, enhancing Landsat acquisitions towards Sentinel-2 resolution. Exploiting the period during which both missions observed the same areas, we build DLhasa-L2S , to our knowledge the first paired dataset dedicated to multispectral super-resolution for river analysis. It covers the Lhasa River (Tibet), whose strong anthropogenic changes and diverse hydromorphological profiles make it an ideal study area. We developed two model-based neural networks: a forward-backward (FB) plug-and-play scheme and an unfolded FB scheme. We compared them against learned neural networks baselines (SwinIR, RDN) on synthetic data, on real scenes, and through a statistical test over the whole real paired Landsat-Sentinel dataset. The unfolded network achieves the highest PSNR and SSIM on the real RGB components with fast inference, offering the best trade-off between accuracy and computational cost. For NDWI-based water segmentation, its performance shows no statistically significant difference from that of the best methods.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the DLhasa-L2S paired Landsat-Sentinel dataset and evaluates two model-based neural networks for multispectral floodplain super-resolution.
AI.motivation: Long-term floodplain monitoring requires enhancing coarser Landsat imagery toward Sentinel-2 resolution, but dedicated paired multispectral datasets and physically grounded super-resolution models for river analysis are lacking.
AI.method: The authors build DLhasa-L2S over the Lhasa River in Tibet and develop a forward-backward (FB) plug-and-play scheme and an unfolded FB neural network, comparing them against SwinIR and RDN on synthetic and real paired scenes.
AI.result: The unfolded FB network achieves the highest PSNR and SSIM on real RGB components with fast inference, while showing no statistically significant difference from the best methods on NDWI-based water segmentation.
AI.conclusion: Unfolded forward-backward networks offer an effective accuracy-speed trade-off for multispectral floodplain super-resolution.

title: DRaGAN: Dynamic Graph Attention Network for Multi-Radar Point Cloud Encoding in Automotive Radar Perception
comment: Accepted to 2027 IEEE/SICE International Symposium on System Integration (SII)
summary: Radar represents a key modality for weather-robust perception. Unlike optical sensors such as camera and LiDAR, radar can penetrate fog, rain and snow due to its longer wavelength, and recent hardware advances have steadily improved its spatial resolution, thus making it increasingly relevant for autonomous systems. While processing raw radar data requires substantial memory computation, most existing work has focused on preprocessed point-cloud data similar to LiDAR. However, the sparse radar points and sensor-relative anisotropy make LiDAR-oriented encoders suboptimal. To address this problem, we present DRaGAN, a dynamic graph attention network for multi-radar point clouds. DRaGAN introduces a sensor-relative Fourier encoding of angle and range to capture fixed-aperture radar characteristics, gated short- and long-range hub nodes along each sensor's line of sight for efficient local-global message passing, and attention-guided dynamic rewiring that prunes weak edges and adds a bounded number of latent connections restricted to two-hop neighborhoods. This reduces the number of processed edges in deeper layers while preserving representation quality. On TruckScenes, DRaGAN improves test NDS by 10.10 points over the evaluated RadarGNN baseline and reduces the reported model FLOP count by 63.7%. This trade-off includes an increase in model latency from 40 to 53.16 ms and in trainable parameters from 1.2M to 1.7M on the evaluated implementations. Code and pretrained models are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper presents DRaGAN, a dynamic graph attention network tailored for multi-radar point cloud encoding in automotive perception.
AI.motivation: Sparse radar points and sensor-relative anisotropy make LiDAR-oriented point-cloud encoders suboptimal for automotive radar perception.
AI.method: DRaGAN combines sensor-relative Fourier encoding of angle and range, gated short- and long-range hub nodes along each sensor's line of sight, and attention-guided dynamic rewiring that prunes weak edges and adds bounded two-hop connections.
AI.result: On TruckScenes, DRaGAN improves test NDS by 10.10 points over RadarGNN and reduces model FLOPs by 63.7%, while increasing latency from 40 ms to 53.16 ms and parameters from 1.2M to 1.7M.
AI.conclusion: Sensor-relative encoding and dynamic graph rewiring substantially improve multi-radar point cloud perception accuracy and FLOP efficiency.

title: Beyond Token Stacking: Multi-scale Visual Modulation and Adaptive Fused-feature Calibration for MLLMs
summary: Current Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have advanced rapidly and follow two main paradigms: one involves concatenating visual and textual tokens for input into Large Language Model (LLM), while the other injects visual knowledge into Feed-Forward Networks (FFNs) of the LLM. However, the former introduces a large number of redundant visual tokens, substantially increasing computational overhead. The latter reduces sequence length but removes images from the input stage entirely, which may hinder the activation of image-related knowledge. Moreover, naively injecting visual knowledge into the FFNs could induce activation distribution shifts due to cross-modal semantic discrepancies. To address these challenges, we develop Beyond Token Stacking (BTS), a novel visual enhancement framework for MLLMs. Specifically, we propose a Multi-scale Visual Modulation (MVM) mechanism that injects multi-scale visual information at the input stage via modulation without increasing the token sequence length. Furthermore, we develop an Adaptive Fused-feature Calibration (AFC) module that performs per-channel affine calibration to decouple visual injection from distribution alignment in the FFN layers, improving multimodal fusion stability while preserving language priors. Experiments show that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Beyond Token Stacking (BTS), a visual enhancement framework for MLLMs that injects multi-scale visual features via input modulation and per-channel FFN calibration.
AI.motivation: Concatenating visual and textual tokens incurs high computational overhead from redundant tokens, while injecting visual knowledge only into FFNs omits input-stage visual cues and causes activation distribution shifts.
AI.method: BTS introduces Multi-scale Visual Modulation (MVM) to modulate input representations without increasing sequence length, and Adaptive Fused-feature Calibration (AFC) to apply per-channel affine calibration in FFN layers.
AI.result: Experiments demonstrate that BTS achieves state-of-the-art performance while avoiding token-length expansion and stabilizing multimodal fusion.
AI.conclusion: Combining input-stage visual modulation with calibrated FFN injection improves MLLM efficiency and multimodal fusion stability.

title: RAGE: Residual-Adaptive Gating for Flow-Based Image Editing
summary: Recent inversion-free, flow-based image editing methods evolve the source image toward the target via a differential velocity field. We observe that this velocity field does not explicitly account for which regions should be preserved, leading to unintended drift in non-editing regions. To address this, we formulate source fidelity control as a stochastic optimal control problem in which a selective fidelity term on the editing residual is enforced along the editing trajectory. Solving this problem and approximating its solution yields the Residual Gating Principle: each latent component is pulled back toward the source with a gain that decays exponentially with the local residual magnitude, so that small deviations are suppressed while large, semantically meaningful edits pass through unimpeded. The proposed method, RAGE, requires only one lightweight gated interpolation per sampling step, involves no mask estimation, attention maps, retraining, or architecture-specific modifications, and is applied on top of FlowEdit-based editors. On PIE-Bench, RAGE achieves the best overall rank among 17 methods and substantially improves background preservation on both Stable Diffusion 3 and FLUX backbones while maintaining competitive editing quality.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces RAGE, a training-free residual-adaptive gating method for flow-based image editing that preserves non-editing regions without masks or attention maps.
AI.motivation: Inversion-free flow-based image editors evolve the source image via a differential velocity field that does not explicitly protect unedited regions, causing unintended background drift.
AI.method: Formulating source fidelity as a stochastic optimal control problem, RAGE derives a Residual Gating Principle that pulls each latent component back toward the source with a gain decaying exponentially with local residual magnitude, applied on top of FlowEdit-based editors.
AI.result: On PIE-Bench, RAGE ranks first overall among 17 methods and substantially improves background preservation on both Stable Diffusion 3 and FLUX backbones while maintaining competitive editing quality.
AI.conclusion: Lightweight residual-adaptive gating provides an effective, architecture-agnostic way to preserve source fidelity in flow-based image editing.

title: Oriented Semi-DETR for Semi-Supervised Aerial Object Detection
summary: Semi-supervised object detection has recently been extended to DETR, where oriented boxes introduce an ambiguity that does not arise for axis-aligned boxes: the map from parameters to rectangles is two-to-one, since $(c_x,c_y,w,h,\theta)$ and $(c_x,c_y,h,w,\theta+\pi/2)$ denote the same rotated rectangle. Losses and matching costs are computed from the parameters, so two boxes that coincide in space can be far apart in the metric that drives training. A correctly localized student box is then penalized by the regression loss, and the inflated matching cost leads the Gaussian mixture model (GMM) filter to discard it. We propose Oriented Semi-DETR, which removes this ambiguity wherever a pseudo box enters training. Swap-aligned Target Selection regresses towards the encoding closer to the student prediction. A Swap-invariant Reliability Cost minimizes over the two encodings inside the matching cost, so the filter decides on geometry alone. Swap-aware Pseudo-label Denoising starts denoising earlier, ramps its loss weight linearly, and weights each query by the teacher score and encoding margin. All three are parameter-free and require no additional forward pass. Across all label ratios of DOTA-v2.0, Oriented Semi-DETR outperforms DETR-based supervised and semi-supervised baselines, with the largest gains at the strict IoU threshold.

AI.tldr: This paper presents Oriented Semi-DETR, which resolves the two-to-one angle-size parameterization ambiguity in semi-supervised oriented aerial object detection.
AI.motivation: In DETR-based oriented object detection, identical rotated rectangles can have two distinct parameterizations, causing false regression penalties and inflated matching costs that lead GMM filters to discard accurate student predictions.
AI.method: Oriented Semi-DETR introduces parameter-free Swap-aligned Target Selection, Swap-invariant Reliability Cost, and Swap-aware Pseudo-label Denoising without adding forward passes.
AI.result: Across all label ratios on DOTA-v2.0, Oriented Semi-DETR outperforms DETR-based supervised and semi-supervised baselines, with the largest gains at strict IoU thresholds.
AI.conclusion: Resolving parameterization ambiguity in target selection, reliability scoring, and denoising significantly improves semi-supervised oriented aerial object detection.

title: A Study on Performance Enhancement of a Webcam-Based Real-Time Eye-Tracking System
summary: This study proposes a real-time gaze-tracking system that uses a standard RGB webcam to estimate screen coordinates. The system combines ETH-XGaze-based gaze estimation with nine-point calibration and polynomial ridge regression. To reduce errors caused by changes in head position, it also applies a conditional residual correction derived from head and pose features extracted with RTMPose. Whether this correction is used depends on the reliability of the detected features and the characteristics of the calibration data. In a preliminary experiment, one participant completed trials at 12 screen targets. The resulting mean screen-coordinate error was 204.24 pixels, which was 35.83% lower than that of xgaze-js and 57.69% lower than that of gaze_tracker. The system produced valid gaze estimates for all 12 targets. These preliminary findings demonstrate the feasibility of combining user-specific calibration with conditional pose-based correction for webcam gaze tracking. Because the evaluation involved only one participant, further experiments with more participants and a wider range of postures are required.

AI.tldr: This study proposes a real-time webcam-based eye-tracking system combining ETH-XGaze, nine-point polynomial ridge regression calibration, and conditional head-pose residual correction via RTMPose.
AI.motivation: Standard RGB webcam gaze trackers suffer from accuracy degradation when users change head position or posture.
AI.method: The system pairs ETH-XGaze estimation with nine-point calibration and polynomial ridge regression, and conditionally applies a residual correction derived from RTMPose head and pose features based on feature reliability and calibration data.
AI.result: In a preliminary experiment with one participant across 12 screen targets, the system achieved a mean error of 204.24 pixels, 35.83% lower than xgaze-js and 57.69% lower than gaze_tracker, with valid estimates on all targets.
AI.conclusion: Combining user-specific calibration with conditional pose-based correction is feasible for webcam gaze tracking, though multi-participant evaluation is still needed.

title: QuantileGS: Quantile-Based Conformal Bounds on RGB Rendering Errors for Novel View Synthesis with 3D Gaussian Splatting
summary: Uncertainty quantification for novel view synthesis with 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) assesses rendering reliability at unseen viewpoints. This reliability depends on the discrepancy between rendered and true colors, which cannot be measured without ground-truth images. We therefore quantify uncertainty in this unknown discrepancy through upper bounds on per-pixel RGB mean absolute error. However, learned bounds may underestimate these errors and overstate rendering reliability, motivating calibration to a prescribed coverage level. In this paper, we propose QuantileGS, a post-hoc framework that combines learned rendering-error quantiles with scale-normalized conformal calibration to produce spatially adaptive error bounds. The framework comprises three phases. Phase 1, Rendering-Error Computation, measures RGB mean absolute error between observed images and predictions from a frozen 3DGS model. Phase 2, Ordered Gaussian Quantile Fields, learns two scalar attributes per Gaussian to predict lower and upper rendering-error quantiles. Phase 3, Scale-Normalized Conformal Calibration, calibrates the upper prediction on held-out images, using the quantile gap to scale the correction. Under the stated assumptions, the resulting bounds provide finite-sample marginal coverage. At a nominal coverage level of 90%, calibration raises mean empirical test coverage from 69.6% to 89.6% on LLFF and from 80.1% to 92.1% on Mip-NeRF 360. On LF, coverage remains conservative at 96.3% before and 96.4% after calibration. Applications to active view selection, Gaussian pruning, and RGB-D simultaneous localization and mapping illustrate how these bounds inform downstream decisions.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces QuantileGS, a post-hoc conformal calibration framework that produces spatially adaptive upper bounds on per-pixel RGB rendering errors for 3D Gaussian Splatting.
AI.motivation: Learned uncertainty bounds for novel view synthesis with 3DGS can underestimate true rendering errors and overstate reliability at unseen viewpoints.
AI.method: QuantileGS computes RGB MAE on observed images from a frozen 3DGS model, learns lower and upper quantile attributes per Gaussian, and applies scale-normalized conformal calibration on held-out images to guarantee finite-sample marginal coverage.
AI.result: At a 90% nominal coverage level, calibration raises empirical test coverage from 69.6% to 89.6% on LLFF and from 80.1% to 92.1% on Mip-NeRF 360, while remaining conservative on LF (96.3% to 96.4%), with demonstrated utility in active view selection, pruning, and RGB-D SLAM.
AI.conclusion: Scale-normalized conformal calibration turns learned 3DGS quantile fields into reliable, finite-sample error bounds for downstream tasks.

title: PLECTA: Overlap-aware instance segmentation of dense strand networks from binary masks
summary: Many materials and tissues, including carbon-nanotube sheets, collagen and paper, comprise overlapping strands whose arrangement influences their effective properties. Measuring this geometry from micrographs requires individual strands to be traced through crossings and signal gaps, which merge distinct strands or split one strand into disconnected fragments. We present PLECTA (from Latin plecta, a braid), a deterministic method that segments individual strands using only a binary image whose foreground pixels mark strand centrelines. At each junction, PLECTA selects which strand segments continue into one another while allowing segments to terminate. It formulates this decision as an exact maximum-weight partial-matching problem, with an explicit penalty for unpaired segments and no restriction on the number of segments entering a junction. The output permits crossing pixels to belong to multiple strands. On synthetic scenes, PLECTA resolved strand identities more accurately than three released alternatives at every density tested. The same ranking held on an independently published generator run at its own settings. A separate stage uses the corresponding greyscale micrograph to estimate which strand lies on top at each crossing. The complete workflow is demonstrated on scanning electron micrographs of carbon nanotube sheets, from raw images to individual strand instances with estimated crossing order, without manual annotations for training or as pipeline inputs.

AI.tldr: This paper presents PLECTA, a deterministic method for overlap-aware instance segmentation of dense strand networks from binary centreline masks, plus crossing-order estimation from greyscale micrographs.
AI.motivation: Tracing individual strands in dense networks such as carbon-nanotube sheets or collagen is difficult because crossings and signal gaps merge distinct strands or split single strands.
AI.method: PLECTA formulates junction continuation as an exact maximum-weight partial-matching problem with an unpaired-segment penalty and no degree limit, allowing crossing pixels to belong to multiple strands, followed by greyscale-based crossing-order estimation.
AI.result: PLECTA resolves strand identities more accurately than three released alternatives across all tested densities on synthetic scenes and an independent generator, and runs end-to-end on carbon-nanotube SEMs without manual training annotations.
AI.conclusion: Exact maximum-weight partial matching enables accurate, training-free instance segmentation of dense overlapping strand networks.

title: FM-Recon: Exploring Foundation Model Features for Accelerated Cardiac Cine MRI Reconstruction
summary: Foundation models have demonstrated strong feature extraction capabilities across various medical imaging tasks, yet their potential for MRI reconstruction remains largely unexplored, particularly within unrolled reconstruction networks and under artifact-corrupted inputs. In this work, we explore whether and how features from pretrained foundation models can benefit accelerated cardiac cine MRI reconstruction. To this end, we propose FM-Recon, a framework that refines and integrates extracted features from frozen image encoder of foundation models into an unrolled reconstruction network. Through extensive experiments on the CMRxRecon2023 dataset, we systematically evaluate foundation model features across different reconstruction settings. Our results show that foundation models can extract informative representations from artifact-corrupted inputs and improve reconstruction performance, particularly at moderate acceleration factors. These findings demonstrate the potential of foundation model features for accelerated MRI reconstruction and provide insights into their effective integration into unrolled reconstruction networks.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes FM-Recon, a framework that refines and integrates frozen foundation-model image features into unrolled reconstruction networks for accelerated cardiac cine MRI.
AI.motivation: The potential of pretrained foundation model features for MRI reconstruction, especially within unrolled networks and under artifact-corrupted inputs, remains largely unexplored.
AI.method: FM-Recon extracts features from frozen foundation model image encoders, refines them, and integrates them into an unrolled MRI reconstruction network evaluated on CMRxRecon2023.
AI.result: Systematic experiments on CMRxRecon2023 show that foundation models extract informative representations from artifact-corrupted inputs and improve reconstruction quality, particularly at moderate acceleration factors.
AI.conclusion: Pretrained foundation model features can be effectively integrated into unrolled networks to enhance accelerated cardiac cine MRI reconstruction.

title: Déjà-Events: Multi-view 3D Geometry with Event Cameras via Sparsity-Aware Adaptive Gating
summary: Event cameras keep capturing structure where conventional cameras blur or saturate, which makes them attractive for 3D perception in fast or poorly lit scenes. Event datasets with dense 3D ground truth, however, are far smaller and less diverse than the image collections behind feed-forward 3D reconstruction models. We present Déjà-Events, an event-only model that predicts depth, camera pose and pointmaps from multiple views in a single forward pass. Rather than relying on scarce 3D labels, we distil it from Déjà View, a feed-forward RGB model that refines its tokens by repeatedly applying one shared transformer block. On paired RGB and event recordings, the event student learns to reproduce the frozen teacher's final tokens, which requires no depth or pose ground truth and trains only about 1% of its parameters. Because events are dense at edges and moving texture but nearly absent in textureless regions, we further introduce sparsity-aware adaptive gating, which adapts the shared block's gates to events and adjusts them per patch by event density, so that accuracy holds as refinement steps are added. Trained only on simulated data, Déjà-Events achieves the lowest pointmap error among the event-based methods we evaluate, on EventScape and zero-shot on the real MVSEC and DSEC datasets. On DSEC it halves the error of the strongest baseline (0.15 vs. 0.30 AbsRel) with about a tenth of its parameters. It also has the lowest depth error on EventScape and DSEC and the lowest trajectory error on EventScape.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Déjà-Events, an event-only multi-view 3D reconstruction model distilled from an RGB teacher using sparsity-aware adaptive gating.
AI.motivation: Event cameras excel in fast or poorly lit scenes where RGB cameras blur, but event datasets with dense 3D ground truth are too small to train feed-forward 3D models directly.
AI.method: Déjà-Events distills final tokens from a frozen Déjà View RGB teacher on paired RGB-event data without 3D labels (training ~1% of parameters) and uses sparsity-aware adaptive gating per patch based on event density.
AI.result: Trained only on simulated data, Déjà-Events achieves the lowest pointmap error on EventScape and zero-shot MVSEC and DSEC, halving the error of the strongest baseline on DSEC (0.15 vs. 0.30 AbsRel) with roughly one-tenth the parameters, while also achieving the lowest depth and trajectory errors on EventScape.
AI.conclusion: Distilling RGB 3D teachers with sparsity-aware gating enables accurate, parameter-efficient event-only 3D geometry reconstruction.

title: Fix, Don't Retake: Physics-Simulated Training for Correcting Patient Positioning Errors in Dental Panoramic Radiographs
summary: Patient-positioning errors can distort panoramic radiographs and lead to repeat examinations. This study investigated artificial intelligence for correcting these errors in existing images. A physics-based simulator generated paired correctly positioned and mispositioned panoramics from cone-beam computed tomography volumes, with controlled individual and combined positioning errors. Five approaches were compared: U-Net, pix2pix, conditional diffusion, an error-conditioned model, and a mixture of error-specific specialists. Evaluation used image similarity and geometric metrics across three test sets. All approaches improved mean image similarity and reduced geometric errors, with U-Net and the two error-aware approaches outperforming pix2pix and conditional diffusion.

AI.tldr: This study uses a physics-based CBCT simulator to generate paired panoramic radiographs for training and comparing five AI models to correct patient-positioning errors.
AI.motivation: Patient-positioning errors distort dental panoramic radiographs and often force repeat examinations.
AI.method: A physics-based simulator generates paired correctly positioned and mispositioned panoramics from CBCT volumes, used to train and evaluate U-Net, pix2pix, conditional diffusion, an error-conditioned model, and a mixture of error-specific specialists across three test sets.
AI.result: All five approaches improve mean image similarity and reduce geometric errors, with U-Net and the two error-aware models outperforming pix2pix and conditional diffusion.
AI.conclusion: Physics-simulated paired training data enables effective post-hoc correction of positioning errors in dental panoramic radiographs.

title: A2A-UAV: A Multimodal Air-to-Air Dataset for UAV Detection and Identification
summary: The rapid growth of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) in low-altitude airspace increases the risk of unauthorized intrusions, making reliable detection and identification of non-cooperative UAVs essential for low-altitude airspace safety. However, the existing public UAV datasets are mostly acquired from fixed ground-based viewpoints and are limited to imaging or radio-frequency (RF) observations, which restricts the sensing coverage and deployment flexibility. To address this gap, we present A2A-UAV, a multimodal air-to-air dataset for UAV detection and identification. Specifically, 15 target UAVs of 13 commercial models were recorded at three outdoor sites under daytime and nighttime conditions by using a UAV-mounted platform equipped with an RGB-thermal gimbal camera, a panoramic camera, an RF spectrum analyzer, and a millimeter-wave radar. The dataset contains 105,294 time-aligned samples of RGB, panoramic, thermal, and RF time-frequency images and radar point clouds. Moreover, all 209,539 bounding boxes of the predominantly small UAV targets were manually annotated and cross-checked. Therefore, A2A-UAV provides a valuable resource for air-to-air UAV detection, identification, and multimodal fusion in low-altitude airspace.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces A2A-UAV, a multimodal air-to-air dataset for UAV detection and identification captured from a UAV-mounted sensing platform.
AI.motivation: Existing public UAV datasets rely mostly on fixed ground-based viewpoints and single modalities, limiting sensing coverage and deployment flexibility in low-altitude airspace.
AI.method: The authors recorded 15 target UAVs across 13 commercial models at three outdoor sites in daytime and nighttime using a UAV-mounted RGB-thermal gimbal camera, panoramic camera, RF spectrum analyzer, and millimeter-wave radar.
AI.result: A2A-UAV provides 105,294 time-aligned multimodal samples and 209,539 manually annotated, cross-checked bounding boxes of predominantly small UAV targets.
AI.conclusion: A2A-UAV offers a comprehensive benchmark for air-to-air multimodal UAV detection, identification, and sensor fusion.

title: MovieRoll: A Systematic Framework for Rolling Out Long-Form Videos
summary: Streaming video generation must sustain quality beyond the training horizon while handling self-generated history and growing cache costs. To address these challenges, we present MovieRoll, a base-to-distilled framework that connects streaming fine-tuning, long-rollout distillation, and long-horizon inference. We first establish a robust multi-step base through Window-wise Teacher Forcing (WinTF), which jointly denoises chunks at progressive noise levels with bidirectional attention within each window and causal access to preceding history. To retain historical context efficiently, hierarchical KV-cache compression (HieraKV) exploits layer-wise attention patterns, retaining full history in shallow layers and sink--recent history in deeper layers. This reduces cache memory by up to 78% while improving generation quality. Building on this base, cumulative long tuning with distribution matching distillation (CuLT-DMD) holds parameters fixed throughout each long self-rollout and averages local gradients before updating. Each update therefore combines supervision across temporal positions while retaining only one local computation graph, enabling efficient long-rollout training of a few-step generator. To extend generation beyond the training horizon, KV recomputation bounds context for both models, while guidance annealing (AnnealCFG) reduces guidance toward the clean endpoint to stabilize MovieRoll-Base. Complementing these modeling advances, FBCA attention and PS-VAE decoding support efficient training and streaming output. On HeliosBench, MovieRoll-Base remains competitive at 30s after training on videos of up to 15s, and MovieRoll-Distilled achieves the highest total scores among the compared methods across single- and multi-event evaluations up to 60s, combining sustained naturalness with active motion.

AI.tldr: This paper presents MovieRoll, a base-to-distilled streaming video generation framework that sustains quality up to 60s through window-wise teacher forcing, hierarchical KV compression, and cumulative long-rollout distillation.
AI.motivation: Streaming video generators struggle to maintain quality beyond their training horizon due to self-generated history drift and growing KV-cache memory costs.
AI.method: MovieRoll combines Window-wise Teacher Forcing (WinTF), hierarchical KV-cache compression (HieraKV, cutting cache memory up to 78%), cumulative long tuning with distribution matching distillation (CuLT-DMD), KV recomputation, and guidance annealing (AnnealCFG).
AI.result: On HeliosBench, MovieRoll-Base remains competitive at 30s after training on up to 15s videos, and MovieRoll-Distilled achieves the highest total scores among compared methods across single- and multi-event evaluations up to 60s.
AI.conclusion: Connecting streaming fine-tuning, hierarchical cache compression, and cumulative long-rollout distillation enables stable long-form video generation.

title: Symmetry Detection with Patch Embedding Models by Means of a Scalar Product Transform
summary: We present a transformation of vector embeddings representing image patches into scores for point reflection symmetry at the crossing points of patches. The transformation is heavily inspired by the Gradient Product Transform, but it uses the vector embeddings instead of the grayscale gradients. We therefore call it the "Scalar Product Transform" (SPT). Unlike deep learning models for symmetry detection, the method does not require a specific training step tailored for symmetry detection, but it works with arbitrary pre-trained patch embedding models. We have tested the method with DINOv3 and Franca. In our tests, the method outperformed the Gradient Product Transform and was even better than EquiSym, a convolutional neural network specifically designed and trained for symmetry detection. Although the runtime of the SPT is greater than that of EquiSym, the SPT has the advantage that it directly yields a bounding box for the symmetric region.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the Scalar Product Transform (SPT), a training-free method that detects point reflection symmetry using pre-trained patch embeddings such as DINOv3 and Franca.
AI.motivation: Deep learning symmetry detectors require task-specific training, whereas classical gradient-based transforms rely on low-level grayscale gradients.
AI.method: Inspired by the Gradient Product Transform, SPT computes scalar products of vector patch embeddings from arbitrary pre-trained models at patch crossing points to score point reflection symmetry and output bounding boxes.
AI.result: Tested with DINOv3 and Franca, SPT outperforms the Gradient Product Transform and the trained CNN EquiSym in accuracy while directly yielding symmetric-region bounding boxes, though with higher runtime than EquiSym.
AI.conclusion: Pre-trained patch embeddings enable accurate, training-free point reflection symmetry detection.

title: Exploring the link between predictive uncertainty and the sim-to-real gap in deep learning models utilizing synthetic data
summary: Today, state-of-the-art methods for quality control (QC) are based on Machine Vision, combining deep learning (DL) models with camera-based inspection. Yet, the integration of such solutions in industrial applications is often impeded by data sparsity and trust in model reliability. While synthetic data offers a promising approach to generate the necessary data with perfect annotations, it poses risks related to performance degradation due to the possible occurrence of the sim-to-real gap. This study conducts experiments using the ensemble method to estimate the predictive uncertainty of DL models trained on synthetic data. The results show that predictive uncertainty increases under the sim-to-real domain shift. However, the observed performance drop is dominated by a systematic sim-to-real bias rather than by ensemble this http URL findings contribute to the effective utilization of synthetic data in industrial settings while highlighting the importance of risk assessment for the deployment of DL solutions for QC tasks.

AI.tldr: This study investigates ensemble-based predictive uncertainty under sim-to-real domain shift in industrial quality control, finding that performance drops are driven by systematic sim-to-real bias rather than ensemble uncertainty.
AI.motivation: Synthetic data helps overcome data sparsity in machine-vision quality control, but practitioners need reliable ways to assess model trust and performance degradation under sim-to-real shifts.
AI.method: The authors conduct experiments using deep ensembles to estimate predictive uncertainty of models trained on synthetic data when evaluated across sim-to-real domain shifts.
AI.result: Predictive uncertainty increases under sim-to-real shift, but the observed performance drop is dominated by systematic sim-to-real bias rather than ensemble variance.
AI.conclusion: Deploying synthetic-data models in industrial quality control requires addressing systematic sim-to-real bias alongside monitoring predictive uncertainty.

title: ALIVE: Making Streaming Video Models Interactive
summary: Streaming video LLMs can continuously observe the world, yet often handle user requests in isolation. We introduce ALIVE, an interactive streaming video model supporting proactive monitoring, streaming task coordination, and feedback-seeking interaction. We construct ALIVE-SFT-288K and ALIVE-RL-3K for two-stage training. Contrastive supervised fine-tuning teaches when and how to respond, while reinforcement learning with Behavior-Aligned Credit Assignment (BACA) combines trajectory-level and local advantages to refine decisions, responses, and silence across multi-turn interactions. We also introduce FSI-Bench to evaluate feedback seeking and subsequent task completion. ALIVE achieves the highest overall scores among the compared models on four public benchmarks and FSI-Bench, demonstrating strong streaming understanding and interactive capabilities.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces ALIVE, an interactive streaming video LLM trained with contrastive SFT and behavior-aligned reinforcement learning, alongside the FSI-Bench benchmark.
AI.motivation: Existing streaming video LLMs handle user requests in isolation and lack proactive monitoring, task coordination, and feedback-seeking capabilities.
AI.method: The authors construct ALIVE-SFT-288K and ALIVE-RL-3K for two-stage training, using contrastive SFT to teach when and how to respond and Behavior-Aligned Credit Assignment (BACA) RL to refine multi-turn decisions, responses, and silence.
AI.result: ALIVE achieves the highest overall scores among compared models on four public benchmarks and the newly introduced FSI-Bench.
AI.conclusion: Combining contrastive SFT with behavior-aligned credit assignment enables proactive, feedback-seeking interactive streaming video models.

title: WeVisForensics: Self-Evolving Agent for Omni AI-Generated Video Detection
summary: Recent advances in video generation call for reliable detection grounded in explicit forensic evidence. However, current methods primarily depend on single-pass chain-of-thought reasoning that overlooks brief or localized artifacts, or on predefined multi-agent workflows that offer limited flexibility in selecting relevant inspections. Even with adaptive investigation, optimizing the investigation policy alone does not directly improve the forensic capabilities of fixed experts. We introduce WeVisForensics, an agentic framework in which a main investigator agent coordinates a self-evolving library of forensic inspector sub-agents spanning visual and audio cues. The investigator learns which artifact type to examine, over which window, and when to conclude, and these interactions provide shared feedback for both levels of agents. Our dual-timescale policy optimization strategy, DTPO, closes this loop through fast reinforcement learning of the investigator and slower refinement of the inspectors, guided by annotated artifact intervals, to report subtle artifacts they once dismissed. Furthermore, we curate ForenCue-30K, combining role-specific forensic annotations and interaction trajectories to supervise individual inspections and their coordination, with an accompanying reinforcement-learning pool. Experiments show that WeVisForensics averages 95.2% detection accuracy across in-domain, out-of-domain and agentic benchmarks, 9.0% above the strongest prior detector, while grounding its verdicts in localized evidence.

AI.tldr: WeVisForensics is a self-evolving agentic framework for omni AI-generated video detection that coordinates a main investigator and forensic inspector sub-agents, achieving 95.2% average accuracy across benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Current AI-generated video detectors rely on single-pass chain-of-thought reasoning that misses brief or localized artifacts, or on predefined multi-agent workflows with rigid inspection selection and fixed expert capabilities.
AI.method: A main investigator agent coordinates a self-evolving library of visual and audio forensic inspector sub-agents, trained via dual-timescale policy optimization (DTPO) with fast RL for the investigator and slower artifact-interval-guided refinement for the inspectors, supported by the curated ForenCue-30K dataset.
AI.result: WeVisForensics averages 95.2% detection accuracy across in-domain, out-of-domain, and agentic benchmarks, outperforming the strongest prior detector by 9.0% while grounding verdicts in localized evidence.
AI.conclusion: Jointly evolving both the investigator policy and forensic inspector sub-agents enables accurate, evidence-grounded AI-generated video detection.

title: The Mask Is Not the Object: Volumetric Supervision for 3D Gaussian Segmentation
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. Project page: this https URL
summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting enables object-level operations on Gaussian primitives, yet existing segmentation methods are largely trained and evaluated through rendered views. This mismatch can produce accurate rendered masks from incomplete 3D selections since alpha-blended feature supervision concentrates learning on dominant contributors while leaving occluded or low-contribution Gaussians weakly supervised. We propose VODA, a plug-and-play supervision objective that exploits local depth structure to group per-pixel contributors and directly supervises all Gaussians in selected depth clusters, bypassing contribution-weighted gradient delivery. To evaluate volumetric completeness, we introduce Removal-3D, a synthetic object-removal benchmark, and the Removal Depth Error (RDE), a metric comparing predicted and ground-truth depth changes. Across four rendering-based baselines, VODA consistently improves volumetric segmentation on Removal-3D while maintaining or improving performance on LERF and ScanNet. Further analysis shows that VODA recovers lower-contribution Gaussians, while simple gradient reweighting and spatial propagation fail to reproduce comparable gains.

AI.tldr: VODA is a plug-and-play volumetric supervision objective for 3D Gaussian Splatting segmentation that groups per-pixel contributors by local depth structure to directly supervise occluded or low-contribution Gaussians.
AI.motivation: Existing 3D Gaussian Splatting segmentation methods train through rendered views, where alpha-blended feature supervision concentrates on dominant contributors and leaves occluded or low-contribution Gaussians weakly supervised.
AI.method: VODA exploits local depth structure to group per-pixel contributors and directly supervises all Gaussians in selected depth clusters, bypassing contribution-weighted gradient delivery, and is evaluated on a new synthetic benchmark Removal-3D using the Removal Depth Error (RDE) metric.
AI.result: Across four rendering-based baselines, VODA consistently improves volumetric segmentation on Removal-3D and maintains or improves performance on LERF and ScanNet, recovering lower-contribution Gaussians where gradient reweighting and spatial propagation fail.
AI.conclusion: Depth-clustered direct supervision resolves the rendering-versus-volume mismatch in 3D Gaussian segmentation, enabling more complete 3D object selection.

title: VideoNexus: Video Perception Beyond the Reasoning Context
summary: Understanding long videos requires locating evidence, resolving visual details, and integrating observations into an answer. Even when relevant evidence is present, performing these operations within long, dense visual sequences burdens both perception and reasoning. Video agents enable selective inspection, but returning frames to the planner still accumulates visual information in its reasoning context. Delegating perception reduces this burden, yet sparse sampling can miss decisive details, and per-frame descriptions can preserve context growth. We introduce VideoNexus, a training-free framework that separates detailed video perception from evidence-driven planning and reasoning. The planner controls where to inspect, what to resolve, and how densely to sample. Perception sub-agents process native audio-video in independent contexts and return compact, temporally grounded evidence for iterative search and verification. Using Gemini 3.8 Flash for both planning and perception, VideoNexus achieves 88.6% accuracy on full LVBench, exceeding same-backbone static ingestion and built-in agentic processing by 3.6 and 1.1 points, respectively, at 44% of the latter's measured API cost. A paired LVBench subset ablation shows lower planner input and higher accuracy. With Kimi K3 as the shared backbone, VideoNexus improves over the official Video-GAIA ReAct harness by 8.5 points in our evaluation. These results support compact evidence exchange for combining detailed observation with efficient planning and reasoning.

AI.tldr: VideoNexus is a training-free framework that separates detailed audio-video perception from evidence-driven planning, achieving 88.6% accuracy on full LVBench at 44% of the API cost of built-in agentic processing.
AI.motivation: Long-video understanding burdens reasoning when visual frames or per-frame descriptions accumulate in the planner's context, while sparse sampling risks missing decisive details.
AI.method: A planner controls where to inspect, what to resolve, and how densely to sample, while perception sub-agents process native audio-video in independent contexts and return compact, temporally grounded evidence for iterative search and verification.
AI.result: Using Gemini 3.8 Flash, VideoNexus reaches 88.6% accuracy on full LVBench, beating same-backbone static ingestion by 3.6 points and built-in agentic processing by 1.1 points at 44% of the latter's API cost; with Kimi K3, it improves over the Video-GAIA ReAct harness by 8.5 points.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling perception into independent sub-agents with compact evidence exchange enables accurate long-video reasoning without bloating the planner's context.

title: Portrait Fitness as a Pretext: Probing Implicit Demographic Bias in VLMs
summary: We audit face-related bias in VLMs using BALPORTRAITS, a new balanced dataset of 9,000 fictional portraits across ethnicity, gender, and age segments. Sixteen VLMs estimate portrait fitness scores for occupations, brands, activities, and banking or insurance products within an advertising-casting framework designed to avoid direct inference of protected attributes. Item-level estimations are aggregated with scenario-specific prestige scores to compare rankings across demographic groups. While the magnitude and direction of these biases vary across scenarios, model families, and demographic dimensions, with age, ethnicity, and gender contributing differently depending on the task, we find demographic dispersion across all evaluated models, with a majority of pairwise segment differences reaching statistical significance. This study introduces a controlled protocol to assess implicit face-related associations and demonstrates that single-scenario or single-attribute audits are insufficient.

AI.tldr: This study audits implicit face-related demographic bias across 16 VLMs using BALPORTRAITS, a balanced dataset of 9,000 fictional portraits, finding statistically significant demographic dispersion across all evaluated models.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of VLM demographic bias often rely on single-scenario or single-attribute audits and direct inference of protected attributes rather than controlled, multi-dimensional implicit association testing.
AI.method: Sixteen VLMs estimate portrait fitness scores for occupations, brands, activities, and banking or insurance products on BALPORTRAITS (9,000 fictional portraits balanced across ethnicity, gender, and age), aggregated with scenario-specific prestige scores to compare group rankings.
AI.result: Bias magnitude and direction vary across scenarios, model families, and demographic dimensions, but demographic dispersion appears in all 16 evaluated models with a majority of pairwise segment differences reaching statistical significance.
AI.conclusion: Implicit face-related demographic biases are pervasive in VLMs, and controlled multi-scenario, multi-attribute protocols are necessary to characterize them.

title: Flexible Multi-Stack Super-Resolution of Clinical Brain MRI Using Hetero-Orientation Variational Encoding: Expert Reader Evaluation in a Nigerian Cohort
summary: High-resolution brain MRI is important for neuroradiological assessment, yet routine clinical protocols often rely on fast, anisotropic 2D acquisitions, particularly in resource-constrained settings. These acquisitions may differ in orientation, alignment and anatomical coverage, resulting in partially overlapping image stacks. Existing learning-based super-resolution methods typically rely on single, under-constrained inputs or fixed multi-stack configurations with idealised acquisition geometry. We introduce MS-HVED, a sequence-agnostic framework for flexible multi-stack brain MRI super-resolution. Available axial, coronal and sagittal stacks are independently encoded into multi-scale Gaussian posteriors and fused using a field-of-view-aware Product-of-Gaussians formulation that limits contributions from unsupported regions. Physics-informed domain randomisation simulates heterogeneous clinical acquisition conditions, including obliqueness, partial coverage and imaging artefacts. MS-HVED achieved competitive or superior reconstruction fidelity across synthetic benchmarks and improved downstream tissue segmentation relative to low-resolution inputs. To assess generalisation beyond the training cohorts, we performed external clinical validation on 30 routine brain MRI examinations from a Nigerian cohort, representing an under-represented population in medical imaging research. These examinations formed the largest component of a blinded reader study involving 44 real cases and seven expert neuroradiologists. In the Nigerian cohort, MS-HVED was preferred over the supervised baseline for overall image quality in 187 of 210 paired assessments. Across all clinical cohorts, MS-HVED achieved higher overall-quality scores with all available inputs (5.93 vs. 4.49, p<.001), with the preference persisting when axial or coronal inputs were omitted (p<.001). Code at this http URL

AI.tldr: MS-HVED is a sequence-agnostic multi-stack brain MRI super-resolution framework using hetero-orientation variational encoding and Product-of-Gaussians fusion, preferred over the supervised baseline in 187 of 210 expert assessments on a Nigerian clinical cohort.
AI.motivation: Routine clinical brain MRI often relies on fast, anisotropic 2D acquisitions with varying orientations and partial coverage, whereas existing super-resolution methods assume single under-constrained inputs or fixed multi-stack geometries.
AI.method: Available axial, coronal, and sagittal stacks are independently encoded into multi-scale Gaussian posteriors and fused via a field-of-view-aware Product-of-Gaussians formulation, trained with physics-informed domain randomisation for obliqueness, partial coverage, and artefacts.
AI.result: MS-HVED achieves competitive or superior reconstruction fidelity on synthetic benchmarks, improves downstream tissue segmentation, and in a blinded study of 44 clinical cases with seven neuroradiologists was preferred in 187 of 210 paired assessments on 30 Nigerian routine cases, scoring 5.93 vs. 4.49 overall quality (p<.001).
AI.conclusion: Flexible, orientation-agnostic variational fusion enables robust clinical brain MRI super-resolution that generalizes to resource-constrained, under-represented cohorts.

title: Quality and Similarity Indicators for Video-Based Heart Rate and Respiratory Rate Fusion: A Controlled Evaluation
comment: 15 pages, 7 figures, 4 tables; with 14 pages supplementary material included
summary: Camera-based heart rate (HR) and respiratory rate (RR) estimates vary in reliability from window to window, and a common remedy is to fuse several extraction methods with weights from reference-free signal quality indicators. However, few studies test whether these indicators identify the most accurate method in each window or outperform simpler fusion. We evaluate 11 quality indicators and 8 inter-method similarity measures for fusing 7 HR and 10 RR extractors on four public datasets (75 test subjects). Filters, indicator directions, weighting parameters and a learned ridge baseline are selected on a separate five-subject set before testing. Fusion is compared with equal averaging, a constant typical-rate predictor, the best single method selected in advance and in hindsight, and a per-window oracle with a permutation-based null, using subject-level bootstrap confidence intervals. For HR, quality-weighted fusion reduced mean absolute error by 10.9% [5.2, 18.4] relative to averaging and by 15.6% [8.1, 23.1] relative to the method selected in advance, and was statistically indistinguishable from the best method selected in hindsight. Weighting methods by their agreement did not improve on averaging. For RR, the indicators could not identify the more accurate estimates: sharpened quality weighting increased error (-2.6% [-4.8, -0.8]), fused estimates were uncorrelated with the reference (r <= 0.22), and averaging was less accurate than the typical-rate predictor (-3.1% [-6.1, -0.4]). With a second respiratory reference, apparent RR gains reflected estimates moving toward its typical rate. Quality-guided fusion is worthwhile for video HR; for RR, 30-s windows improved estimates but not fusion.

AI.tldr: A controlled evaluation of 11 quality indicators and 8 similarity measures across four datasets shows that quality-guided fusion improves video-based heart rate estimation by 10.9% MAE over averaging, but fails for respiratory rate.
AI.motivation: Reference-free signal quality indicators are widely used to fuse camera-based heart rate (HR) and respiratory rate (RR) extractors, yet few studies test whether they identify the most accurate window-level method or beat simple baselines.
AI.method: The authors evaluate 11 quality indicators and 8 inter-method similarity measures for fusing 7 HR and 10 RR extractors across four public datasets (75 test subjects, 5-subject selection set), comparing against equal averaging, a constant typical-rate predictor, best single methods, and a per-window oracle using subject-level bootstrap confidence intervals.
AI.result: For HR, quality-weighted fusion reduces MAE by 10.9% [5.2, 18.4] over averaging and 15.6% [8.1, 23.1] over the pre-selected best method, matching the hindsight best method; for RR, sharpened quality weighting increases error (-2.6% [-4.8, -0.8]), fused estimates do not correlate with the reference (r <= 0.22), and averaging trails the typical-rate predictor (-3.1% [-6.1, -0.4]).
AI.conclusion: Quality-guided fusion is effective for video-based HR estimation, whereas for RR, current quality indicators cannot identify accurate estimates and longer 30-s windows are needed instead.

title: Power Line Detection in Point Clouds with Point-SAM and RANSAC
summary: This article deals with the problem of detecting the position of power lines in airborne laser scanning point clouds. We address both the problem of segmenting power lines from background like ground and vegetation and of identifying individual lines. For segmentation we compare a rule-based approach with one based on transfer learning (Point-SAM). For individual line detection, we derive the mathematical formulas for RANSAC applied to 3D catenaries and compare it with a non-parametric method (TriplClust). All methods are evaluated on a newly created dataset "PowLiDFR", which we make publicly available. The samples have been taken from the French project LiDAR HD and cover a variety of terrain layouts and point cloud resolutions. On this dataset, an unsupervised transfer learning outperformed a mere rule-based segmentation, and for individual power line detection, RANSAC was better in following the shape of catenaries than the non-parametric algorithm.
