AI.tldr: This paper compares rule-based and transfer-learning (Point-SAM) segmentation and evaluates RANSAC against TriplClust for 3D catenary power line detection on a new public airborne LiDAR dataset, PowLiDFR.
AI.motivation: Detecting individual power lines and separating them from ground and vegetation in airborne laser scanning point clouds remains challenging across diverse terrain layouts and point cloud resolutions.
AI.method: The authors compare rule-based segmentation against unsupervised transfer learning with Point-SAM, derive mathematical formulas for RANSAC applied to 3D catenaries, and compare RANSAC with the non-parametric TriplClust algorithm on PowLiDFR, a new dataset sampled from France's LiDAR HD project.
AI.result: On PowLiDFR, unsupervised transfer learning with Point-SAM outperforms rule-based segmentation, and RANSAC follows 3D catenary shapes better than TriplClust for individual power line detection.
AI.conclusion: Combining transfer-learning point cloud segmentation with catenary-based RANSAC provides an effective pipeline for airborne LiDAR power line detection, supported by the public PowLiDFR benchmark.

title: [CLS] and [EOS] Tokens are not Enough for CLIP-based Class-Incremental Learning
comment: Accepted to TMM. Code is available at: this https URL
summary: Class-Incremental Learning (CIL) aims to empower models to continuously acquire new knowledge while mitigating catastrophic forgetting. With the advent of vision-language models like CLIP, leveraging their cross-modal alignment capabilities to address CIL challenges has emerged as a dominant paradigm. Existing methods leverage CLIP's global representations (i.e., the visual [CLS] token and the textual [EOS] token) for cross-modal alignment. While achieving effective classification, they overlook the rich patch-level visual features and token-level textual semantics inherent in CLIP. For example, the [CLS] token aggregates local information to capture the general concept of "cat", while the patch-level details retain specific localized features essential for recognition, such as the tail, fur, and face. We propose PACE (PAtch-token Cross-modal Enhancement) to uncover the long-neglected local representations within CLIP. First, based on the global representations like [CLS] token and [EOS] token, we identify the top-k most crucial visual patches and textual tokens. Subsequently, to better utilize the extracted key local features, we design a cross-modal fusion module. This module leverages local textual semantics to refine visual representations, while augmenting textual semantics with local visual features. As the fusion module is shared across all tasks, directly fine-tuning it on new tasks would interfere with the knowledge learned from previous tasks, leading to catastrophic forgetting. To alleviate this, we employ a projection-based update strategy to effectively preserve the critical parameter space of previous tasks during the adaptation to new tasks. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PACE significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods across multiple CIL benchmarks.

AI.tldr: PACE (PAtch-token Cross-modal Enhancement) exploits CLIP's local visual patches and textual tokens with a projection-protected cross-modal fusion module to outperform state-of-the-art Class-Incremental Learning methods.
AI.motivation: Existing CLIP-based Class-Incremental Learning (CIL) methods rely solely on global [CLS] and [EOS] tokens, overlooking fine-grained patch-level visual features and token-level textual semantics.
AI.method: PACE selects the top-k most crucial visual patches and textual tokens using global representations, refines both modalities through a shared cross-modal fusion module, and applies a projection-based update strategy to preserve critical parameter spaces from previous tasks.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across multiple CIL benchmarks show that PACE significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating local patch-token cross-modal enhancement alongside parameter-space projection mitigates catastrophic forgetting and advances CLIP-based Class-Incremental Learning.

title: Out of Sight, Into Memory: Compact Visual Latents Retain Local Evidence in Ultra-High-Resolution Remote Sensing
summary: Question answering over ultra-high-resolution (UHR) remote sensing scenes poses a tension for multimodal large language models: global overviews obscure small objects and local attributes, whereas detailed crops consume substantial context. Compressing inspected crops into short sequences of continuous visual latents offers a compact memory once crop tokens are discarded, yet diagnostic studies on natural images find that models often ignore latent content, leaving unclear whether compact latents can retain fine-grained targets lost in downsampled UHR remote sensing scenes. To isolate evidence retention from region selection, we encode high-resolution crops into latent memory tokens for frozen backbones and evaluate both their predictive utility and content dependence. Across two generations of Qwen-VL on LRS-GRO, a 64-token memory achieves 7.6- to 9.9-fold compression of retained crop tokens and improves accuracy by 2.5 to 4.8 percentage points over the downsampled global image alone, recovering most of the high-resolution crop gain with consistent behavior on XLRS-Bench. Substituting memory from another image or another region of the same scene reduces accuracy by 5.8 to 7.4 percentage points and yields lower accuracy than removing memory altogether, demonstrating that predictions depend on the encoded regional evidence. Restoring the source crop within the same model reduces the accuracy loss caused by zeroing or removing memory. These findings establish that compact visual latents retain useful local evidence in UHR remote sensing and identify evidence availability as a key factor governing their contribution.

AI.tldr: Encoding high-resolution crops into 64-token continuous visual latents achieves 7.6- to 9.9-fold compression and improves ultra-high-resolution remote sensing VQA accuracy by 2.5 to 4.8 percentage points over downsampled global images.
AI.motivation: Multimodal LLMs face a trade-off on ultra-high-resolution (UHR) remote sensing scenes between losing small targets in global overviews and incurring high context costs from raw crops, and it was unclear whether compact latents retain fine-grained evidence.
AI.method: The authors encode high-resolution crops into 64-token latent memory for frozen Qwen-VL backbones across two generations, evaluating predictive utility and content dependence on LRS-GRO and XLRS-Bench via memory substitution, zeroing, and source-crop restoration.
AI.result: A 64-token memory achieves 7.6- to 9.9-fold compression and improves accuracy by 2.5 to 4.8 percentage points over the downsampled global image alone on LRS-GRO, with consistent behavior on XLRS-Bench; substituting memory from another image or region drops accuracy by 5.8 to 7.4 percentage points below removing memory.
AI.conclusion: Compact visual latents genuinely retain fine-grained regional evidence in UHR remote sensing, with evidence availability governing their effectiveness.

title: Event-Triggered Visual Perception for Real-Time Harvest Outcome Estimation in Mechanical Blueberry Harvesting
summary: Mechanical blueberry harvesting requires a balance between removing ripe fruit and avoiding premature removal of unripe berries that could remain on the bush for a later harvest. However, operators generally lack real-time information about the maturity composition of the fruit being collected. This study develops an event-triggered machine-vision system that measures the maturity of harvested blueberries directly on the harvester. When a filled crate is moved by the machine, an RGB image is automatically captured and analysed using a three-class detector that identifies ripe, semi-ripe, and unripe berries. The system operates locally on the existing CPU-only industrial computer and therefore requires neither continuous image processing nor dedicated GPU hardware. During field testing, 79 crate images containing 48,634 visible blueberries in manually verified reference annotations were evaluated. The vision system estimated an overall ripe-fruit fraction of 90.22%, compared with 90.97% determined manually. Per-image ripe-fruit estimates showed a mean absolute error of 0.935 percentage points and a Pearson correlation of r=0.967. Maturity estimates remained similar between the two sides of the harvester for which the light conditions varied despite poorer absolute counting performance under direct sunlight. All field events were processed within the available 14 s per-side crate interval. The proposed approach provides a practical means of quantifying one component of harvest selectivity while the machine is operating. Such information could support operator decision-making and, when combined with measurements of fruit recovery and losses, contribute to future feedback-based control of mechanical harvesting.

AI.tldr: An event-triggered CPU-only machine-vision system estimates harvested blueberry maturity in real time on a mechanical harvester, achieving 0.935 percentage points MAE and r=0.967 correlation against manual annotations.
AI.motivation: Mechanical blueberry harvesters lack real-time feedback on the maturity composition of collected fruit, which operators need to balance ripe fruit removal against premature harvesting of unripe berries.
AI.method: When a filled crate moves, an RGB image is captured and processed on the harvester's existing CPU-only industrial computer by a three-class detector (ripe, semi-ripe, unripe) within the 14 s per-side crate interval.
AI.result: Across 79 field crate images (48,634 annotated berries), the system estimates 90.22% overall ripe-fruit fraction versus 90.97% manual ground truth, with 0.935 percentage points per-image MAE, r=0.967 Pearson correlation, consistent maturity estimates across varying lighting, and <14 s processing time.
AI.conclusion: Event-triggered CPU-based vision provides a practical, hardware-free way to monitor harvest selectivity in real time and support future feedback-based harvester control.

title: Federated TD Learning in Heterogeneous Environments with Average Rewards: A Two-timescale Approach with Polyak-Ruppert Averaging
summary: Federated Reinforcement Learning (FRL) provides a promising way to speedup training in reinforcement learning when one has access to multiple edge devices that can operate in parallel. Recently, it has been shown that even when these edge devices have access to different dynamic models---such as cars or robots with differing system configurations---an optimal convergence rate that has a linear speedup proportional to the number of devices is achievable. However, this result requires that the algorithm's stepsize be chosen in a manner that depends on the unknown model parameters. Also, it applies only to a discounted setting, which has been argued to fit episodic tasks better than continuing control tasks. In this paper, we obtain finite-time bounds for heterogeneous FRL with average rewards. We show that optimal convergence rate and linear speedup are achievable even with a universal stepsize choice, independent of the underlying dynamics. To achieve our result, we modify the existing one-timescale FRL method to a novel two-timescale variant that additionally incorporates iterate averaging. We remark that this idea also extends to other settings already studied in the literature, such as the homogeneous FRL or the heterogeneous case with a discounted cost function.

AI.tldr: A two-timescale federated TD learning algorithm with Polyak-Ruppert averaging achieves optimal convergence rate and linear speedup in heterogeneous average-reward environments using a universal stepsize.
AI.motivation: Existing finite-time bounds for heterogeneous Federated Reinforcement Learning (FRL) are limited to discounted settings and require stepsizes tuned to unknown model parameters, making them unsuitable for continuing average-reward control tasks.
AI.method: The authors modify one-timescale FRL into a two-timescale variant incorporating Polyak-Ruppert iterate averaging and derive finite-time bounds under heterogeneous dynamics with average rewards.
AI.result: The proposed algorithm achieves the optimal convergence rate and linear speedup proportional to the number of devices using a universal stepsize independent of underlying dynamics, and the approach extends to homogeneous and discounted FRL settings.
AI.conclusion: Two-timescale updates with iterate averaging eliminate model-dependent stepsize requirements while preserving linear speedup in heterogeneous average-reward FRL.

title: Learning What Pairs Miss for Higher-Order Multimodal Alignment
summary: Contrastive learning beyond two modalities now scores the whole tuple with multilinear products, volumes, and fusion heads, critics that can represent the joint distribution. In practice these critics still behave like bags of pairs. Their negatives break at least two of the three pairs, a single pairwise check rejects them, and when most samples can be solved by pairs the higher-order term receives almost no gradient. To solve this problem, we propose CHORD (Contrastive Higher-Order Residuals with Decoys), which trains a residual against decoys drawn from a calibrated pairwise model, negatives that the pairwise model finds plausible, so that rejecting them often needs all three modalities. Drawing decoys costs one inner-product query over a memory bank, and the optimal residual is the log-ratio between the data and the pairwise model, so the decoy loss also bounds what that model misses. On M3-Mix, where one in ten training samples needs all three modalities, our CHORD improves accuracy on those samples by 21.2 percentage points over the strongest of eight baselines. CHORD also gives the best two-to-one results on every real dataset, and its residual improves other retrievers without retraining.

AI.tldr: CHORD trains a higher-order multimodal residual against decoys sampled from a calibrated pairwise model, improving three-modality accuracy on M3-Mix by 21.2 percentage points over eight baselines.
AI.motivation: Higher-order multimodal critics often behave like bags of pairs because standard negatives break multiple pairs, leaving the higher-order term with almost no gradient when most samples are solvable pairwise.
AI.method: CHORD (Contrastive Higher-Order Residuals with Decoys) draws plausible negatives via a single inner-product query over a memory bank from a calibrated pairwise model and trains a residual whose optimum is the log-ratio between the data and pairwise distributions.
AI.result: On M3-Mix, where 10% of samples require all three modalities, CHORD improves accuracy on those samples by 21.2 percentage points over the strongest of eight baselines, achieves the best two-to-one results on every real dataset, and boosts other retrievers without retraining.
AI.conclusion: Training residuals against pairwise-plausible decoys forces multimodal models to learn genuine higher-order interactions missed by pairwise alignment.

title: MegNIST, A Benchmark for Non-Invasive Inner Speech Decoding
summary: MegNIST is a benchmark dataset for developing and evaluating machine learning methods for inner speech decoding from magnetoencephalography (MEG). The dataset comprises 12,000 trials of a single participant imagining speaking the digits zero through nine, recorded across four sessions. Each trial contains 306-channel MEG recordings sampled at 250 Hz, preprocessed using signal space separation, filtering, and downsampling. Data are provided as pre-defined training (10,000 trials), validation (1,000 trials), and test (1,000 trials) splits, with entire experimental runs assigned to each split to preserve temporal independence. The dataset is available in both BIDS format for neuroimaging analysis and as serialised tensors for machine learning workflows. Baseline classification results demonstrate that imagined digits can be decoded significantly above chance. Standardised splits, validated baselines, example code, and a PyTorch-compatible loader in the pnpl Python library enable straightforward integration with machine learning frameworks, lowering barriers for researchers to rapidly develop and benchmark inner speech decoding methods for non-invasive brain-computer interfaces.

AI.tldr: MegNIST is a 12,000-trial magnetoencephalography (MEG) benchmark dataset for non-invasive inner speech decoding of digits zero through nine, complete with standardized splits, baselines, and a PyTorch loader.
AI.motivation: Developing and benchmarking machine learning methods for non-invasive inner speech decoding from MEG lacks standardized, easily accessible datasets with run-level splits and ready-to-use ML tooling.
AI.method: MegNIST provides 306-channel, 250 Hz preprocessed MEG recordings from a single participant imagining digits 0-9 across four sessions, split by experimental run into 10,000 training, 1,000 validation, and 1,000 test trials in BIDS and tensor formats with a pnpl PyTorch loader.
AI.result: Baseline classification experiments confirm that imagined digits can be decoded significantly above chance on the standardized splits.
AI.conclusion: MegNIST lowers the barrier to reproducible benchmarking and method development for non-invasive MEG-based inner speech brain-computer interfaces.

title: Efficient Modeling of Multi-Agent Systems via Structure-Aware Physics-Informed Learning
summary: Modeling large multi-agent systems poses challenges for trajectory inference and parameter identification, as network size and coupling increase computational demands and partial observations require reconstructing unobserved states. We propose MAS-PINN, a neural-network architecture with a tailored training algorithm for a physics-informed learning framework that leverages the network topology and the agents' similarity to reduce computational and memory costs of simulating and identifying multi-agent systems. Its architecture represents agent trajectories through shared temporal features and agent-specific coefficients. Training alternates between learning features, fitting coupled trajectories, and estimating physical parameters. A matrix-free update exploits local interactions to fit trajectories without forming large global matrices. Experiments on Lorenz rings, Lotka--Volterra networks, and Rössler oscillators show improved trajectory and parameter accuracy over baselines, including inference in large systems and identification under partial observations or unknown topology, alongside substantial computational savings in coefficient fitting.

AI.tldr: MAS-PINN is a structure-aware physics-informed learning framework that models large multi-agent systems using shared temporal features and matrix-free local updates, improving trajectory and parameter accuracy while reducing computational cost.
AI.motivation: Trajectory inference and parameter identification in large coupled multi-agent systems face growing computational and memory demands as network size increases, alongside partial observations.
AI.method: MAS-PINN represents agent trajectories via shared temporal features and agent-specific coefficients, alternating between feature learning, matrix-free local trajectory fitting, and physical parameter estimation.
AI.result: On Lorenz rings, Lotka-Volterra networks, and Rössler oscillators, MAS-PINN outperforms baselines in trajectory and parameter accuracy, including under partial observations or unknown topology, with substantial computational savings in coefficient fitting.
AI.conclusion: Exploiting network topology and agent similarity through shared features and matrix-free updates makes physics-informed modeling scalable for large multi-agent systems.

title: Emergent Steering Beyond Endpoint Alignment in Chemical Reaction Models
summary: Machine learning models for chemical reaction prediction are usually evaluated by endpoint accuracy, but endpoint correctness alone does not reveal how a model represents chemical transformation or why it fails. We introduce UniRxnAxis, a unified forward-retrosynthesis framework that models both tasks as direction-conditioned endpoint redistribution in a shared latent space. By aligning source states, transformed states, and encoded target endpoints, UniRxnAxis enables directional auditing of learned latent updates. This shared latent geometry allows the learned displacement (from the encoder source state $S_0$ to the decoder-facing transformed state $S_1$) to be decomposed into an endpoint-parallel component and an endpoint-orthogonal residual, which we call emergent steering. Our evaluation shows that emergent steering is functionally important: in retrosynthesis, it recovers most of the model's utility, remains effective under random, shuffled, and prototype controls, and directly affects which bond edits are promoted or suppressed. The residual-over-parallel ordering persists across alignment strengths, after decoder-interface calibration, against angle-matched random axes, and in a second graph-edit architecture, although its magnitude depends on the reference axis and optimization. The decomposition also supports a proxy taxonomy of model-side failures, showing how reaction models can be audited beyond endpoint accuracy.

AI.tldr: UniRxnAxis models forward and retrosynthesis prediction as direction-conditioned endpoint redistribution in a shared latent space, revealing that an endpoint-orthogonal residual ("emergent steering") drives most retrosynthesis utility.
AI.motivation: Evaluating chemical reaction models solely by endpoint accuracy fails to explain how models represent chemical transformations or why they fail.
AI.method: UniRxnAxis aligns source states, transformed states, and target endpoints in a shared latent space, decomposing the learned latent displacement into an endpoint-parallel component and an endpoint-orthogonal residual (emergent steering), audited across alignment strengths, controls, and a second graph-edit architecture.
AI.result: Emergent steering recovers most of the model's retrosynthesis utility, persists under random, shuffled, and prototype controls as well as decoder calibration, directly governs which bond edits are promoted or suppressed, and enables a proxy taxonomy of model-side failures.
AI.conclusion: Decomposing latent reaction displacements exposes functional steering mechanisms beyond endpoint alignment, offering a principled way to audit chemical reaction models.

title: Variational Monte Carlo for Quantum Excited States via Nested Low-Rank Approximation
comment: Accepted for NeurIPS 2026. The first two authors contributed equally. 41 pages, 6 figures, 9 tables. Code is available at this https URL
summary: The electronic Schrödinger equation encodes a molecule's electronic structure and quantum properties, but solving it scales exponentially with the number of electrons. Solving this equation with neural-network variational Monte Carlo (VMC) has reached chemical accuracy on the ground state of small molecules; extending this success to excited states is constrained by two existing paradigms. Penalty-based methods need $K$ Laplacians per step but require tuning the overlap-penalty weights against the energy gaps they aim to compute. Natural excited states VMC (NES-VMC) is penalty-free, but it combines the $K$ ansatzes into one determinant, whose local energy requires $K^2$ Laplacians per step. We resolve this trade-off via low-rank approximation (LoRA) reparameterization of the rank-$K$ variational objective. The reparameterized objective admits a VMC-compatible stochastic gradient estimator via MCMC sampling from the per-state Born densities, and a sequential nesting scheme recovers the lowest $K$ eigenstates in eigenvalue order. The resulting algorithm, NestedLoRA-VMC, inherits a global optimality guarantee from the LoRA principle. On the first-row atoms Li through Ne at $K=10$, its accuracy is comparable to that of NES-VMC and of a state-of-the-art penalty-based method.

AI.tldr: NestedLoRA-VMC applies sequential low-rank approximation (LoRA) reparameterization to neural-network variational Monte Carlo for quantum excited states, matching state-of-the-art accuracy on first-row atoms without K^2 Laplacian scaling or overlap-penalty tuning.
AI.motivation: Extending neural-network VMC to excited states forces a trade-off between penalty-based methods that require tuning overlap weights and penalty-free NES-VMC, which requires K^2 Laplacians per step.
AI.method: NestedLoRA-VMC reparameterizes the rank-K variational objective via LoRA, yielding an unbiased MCMC stochastic gradient estimator from per-state Born densities and a sequential nesting scheme that recovers the lowest K eigenstates in eigenvalue order.
AI.result: On first-row atoms Li through Ne at K=10, NestedLoRA-VMC achieves accuracy comparable to NES-VMC and a state-of-the-art penalty-based method while inheriting a global optimality guarantee.
AI.conclusion: Nested low-rank reparameterization eliminates both penalty hyperparameter tuning and quadratic Laplacian scaling in excited-state VMC.

title: A Reinforcement Learning Method to Navigate SMEFT Operator Space
comment: 15 pages, 3 figures, GitHub Link: this https URL
summary: In particle physics, discrepancies between experimental measurements and Standard Model (SM) predictions are commonly interpreted within new theoretical models. In this context, the Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT) provides a general framework encompassing a broad class of models. However, exploring the enormous space of possible SMEFT operators rapidly becomes a challenging combinatorial problem: many operators can contribute simultaneously to different observables, their effects are correlated, and distinct operator combinations can provide comparably good descriptions of the data. In this work, we formulate the exploration of the SMEFT operator space as a sequential decision-making problem using reinforcement learning (RL). Our RL agent employs a lightweight actor-critic architecture with approximately 40K trainable parameters in total. Rather than searching for a single best-fit theory, our method is designed to discover a diverse set of high-quality theory hypotheses. We test the method in a complex phenomenological environment comprising 132 observables across several sectors of particle physics, including 24 measurements that deviate from their SM predictions by more than $1.5\sigma$. We show that the learned RL policy efficiently constructs multi-operator theories that substantially improve the global fit. Comparisons with independent random-subset and random-sequential searches demonstrate the ability of the RL policy to navigate this large combinatorial space. Our results establish RL as a systematic framework for exploring diverse patterns of new physics (NP) interactions within SMEFT.

AI.tldr: A lightweight 40K-parameter actor-critic reinforcement learning agent navigates the combinatorial SMEFT operator space to discover diverse multi-operator new-physics hypotheses across 132 particle physics observables.
AI.motivation: Exploring the Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT) operator space is a difficult combinatorial problem because many correlated operators contribute simultaneously and distinct combinations can fit the data comparably well.
AI.method: The authors formulate SMEFT operator selection as sequential decision-making with a 40K-parameter actor-critic RL agent designed to discover diverse high-quality theory hypotheses rather than a single best fit, tested on 132 observables (including 24 deviating >1.5 sigma from the SM).
AI.result: The RL policy efficiently constructs multi-operator theories that substantially improve the global fit, outperforming independent random-subset and random-sequential searches.
AI.conclusion: Reinforcement learning provides a systematic, scalable framework for discovering diverse new-physics interaction patterns in SMEFT.

title: Warm Starting Neural Dynamics Models From Few Jacobian Samples
summary: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) leverages a model of the environment, used for planning and generating samples without interacting with the real world. Motivated by evidence that informed initialization significantly improves the efficiency of MBRL, we propose TDec-Init, an algorithm to warm-start neural dynamics models using transition Jacobians. Using a decoupling algorithm based on the decomposition of a tensor of stacked Jacobian samples, we recover weights and flexible nonlinearities, and use them to initialize a feedforward neural network. In the low-data regime, we show on several benchmark environments that our approach outperforms random initialization and value training, and either matches or outperforms Sobolev training, while requiring fewer training steps between episodes.

AI.tldr: TDec-Init warm-starts neural dynamics models in model-based reinforcement learning by decomposing a tensor of few transition Jacobian samples, outperforming random initialization and value training in low-data regimes.
AI.motivation: Informed initialization can substantially improve sample efficiency in model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL), yet standard neural dynamics models typically start from random weights.
AI.method: TDec-Init stacks transition Jacobian samples into a tensor and applies a decoupling decomposition to recover weights and flexible nonlinearities for initializing a feedforward neural network.
AI.result: Across several low-data benchmark environments, TDec-Init outperforms random initialization and value training, and matches or outperforms Sobolev training while requiring fewer training steps between episodes.
AI.conclusion: Tensor decomposition of few Jacobian samples offers a fast, data-efficient initialization strategy for neural dynamics models in MBRL.

title: Algorithm Distillation for Safe In-Context Reinforcement Learning
summary: Safe in-context reinforcement learning (Safe ICRL) asks a policy with fixed parameters to improve on an unseen constrained task from its interaction history while aiming to keep its cost within a budget. Prior work studied Safe ICRL on five benchmarks in three families: a grid world with a hidden goal and obstacles (DarkRoom), continuous navigation where goals and hazards stay invisible until reached (PointGoal, CarGoal), and locomotion with a hidden velocity limit (HalfCheetah, Ant). Safe Algorithm Distillation (Safe AD), trained on the learning histories of a safe RL algorithm, has shown adaptation failures in prior evaluations. For example, in the locomotion tasks its return stays below zero, and it rarely reaches the goal in CarGoal. We revisit two parts of Safe AD. First, we distill a budget-aware teacher with two phases. It searches for the hidden task, exploring more when more budget remains. After its first reward or cost, an expert policy exploits the task within the remaining budget. We collect the teacher's histories under fixed or dynamic budgets. Dynamic budgets increase the occupancy entropy of the return and budget inputs in every environment, and at test time they improve return and lower cost in DarkRoom and HalfCheetah. Second, we propose A-Lag, a test-time adjustment that reweights the distilled policy's actions by their predicted cost, with an adaptive Lagrange multiplier that is updated from the costs observed. In our experiments, A-Lag had lower mean episode cost than Safe AD in all five environments, with lower mean final return in four.

AI.tldr: Distilling a budget-aware two-phase teacher with dynamic budgets and applying A-Lag test-time cost reweighting reduces mean episode cost across all five Safe ICRL benchmarks compared to Safe Algorithm Distillation.
AI.motivation: Safe Algorithm Distillation (Safe AD) struggles to adapt on unseen constrained tasks in Safe In-Context Reinforcement Learning (Safe ICRL), yielding negative returns in locomotion and low goal-reaching rates in CarGoal.
AI.method: The authors distill a two-phase budget-aware teacher (exploring proportional to remaining budget, then exploiting) with dynamic budgets, and introduce A-Lag, a test-time adjustment that reweights distilled actions by predicted cost using an adaptive Lagrange multiplier.
AI.result: Dynamic budgets increase return-budget occupancy entropy in all five environments (DarkRoom, PointGoal, CarGoal, HalfCheetah, Ant) and improve DarkRoom and HalfCheetah test performance; A-Lag achieves lower mean episode cost than Safe AD in all five environments, with lower mean final return in four.
AI.conclusion: Budget-aware teacher distillation and adaptive test-time Lagrange reweighting substantially improve constraint satisfaction in Safe ICRL, though trading off return on most tasks.

title: Severe but Harmless: Stress-Testing Shift Severity for Frozen Time-Series Forecasters
comment: 10 pages, 6 figures, 5 tables. Accepted at IEEE BigData 2026
summary: Zero-shot time-series foundation models (TSFMs) have become attractive alternatives to task-specific models because they handle diverse downstream tasks, including anomaly detection and forecasting, without per-series training. However, time-series data undergo distribution shifts, and the dissimilarity between two regimes is commonly scored with statistical measures such as Wasserstein-1, where a higher score is read as a more severe shift. In systematic experiments using three established severity measures on nine regime shifts from three standard traffic datasets, we show that these measures do not reliably predict degradation for instance-normalized TSFMs. The regimes rated most severe are not the regimes that degrade the models most, and degradation reaches 29% in the lowest-scoring regime. In most cases, the audit shows no positive relationship between measured severity and model degradation. We provide an equivariance-based stress-testing analysis that explains why severity readings can become decoupled from model degradation.

AI.tldr: Systematic experiments on nine traffic regime shifts show that standard shift-severity metrics like Wasserstein-1 do not reliably predict performance degradation in frozen, instance-normalized time-series foundation models.
AI.motivation: Distribution shifts in time-series data are commonly scored with statistical severity metrics like Wasserstein-1, assuming higher severity implies greater model degradation for zero-shot time-series foundation models (TSFMs).
AI.method: The authors evaluate three established severity measures across nine regime shifts from three traffic datasets on instance-normalized TSFMs, accompanied by an equivariance-based stress-testing analysis.
AI.result: Most cases show no positive correlation between measured shift severity and model degradation; the highest-scoring regimes do not cause the worst degradation, whereas degradation reaches 29% in the lowest-scoring regime.
AI.conclusion: Equivariance properties of instance-normalized TSFMs decouple statistical shift severity from actual forecasting degradation, rendering standard severity scores unreliable for auditing.

title: DynSurvX: Time-Resolved Explanations for Dynamic Survival Predictions
summary: Recent survival models integrating longitudinal data achieve strong predictive performance, but their predictions are often difficult to interpret, limiting their clinical use. We propose DynSurvX, a model-agnostic explainability framework for dynamic survival prediction with mixed static and longitudinal covariates. Based on Shapley values, DynSurvX introduces a hierarchical two-phase strategy that first identifies influential longitudinal features and then adaptively refines their temporal importance, enabling fine-grained explanations while reducing computational cost. The framework provides time-resolved explanations that evolve as new patient data become available. Experiments on simulated and two clinical datasets show varying agreement with theoretical importance across prediction models, with closer agreement for better-performing models, alongside clinically interpretable insights in real-world settings. It remains robust across prediction settings and reduces computation time by 41--80\% relative to the temporal explanation baseline, making dynamic explanations practical.

AI.tldr: DynSurvX is a model-agnostic Shapley-based framework for time-resolved explanations of dynamic survival predictions, cutting computation time by 41-80% relative to temporal explanation baselines.
AI.motivation: Dynamic survival models using longitudinal data achieve strong predictive accuracy, but their lack of interpretability and the high cost of temporal explanations hinder clinical adoption.
AI.method: DynSurvX uses a hierarchical two-phase Shapley value strategy that first identifies influential longitudinal features and then adaptively refines their temporal importance as new patient data arrive.
AI.result: On simulated and two clinical datasets, DynSurvX shows closer agreement with theoretical importance for better-performing models, provides clinically interpretable insights, remains robust across settings, and reduces computation time by 41-80% compared to the temporal baseline.
AI.conclusion: Hierarchical two-phase Shapley refinement makes time-resolved, model-agnostic explanations practical for clinical dynamic survival prediction.

title: CertiSum: Bitwise-Identical MXFP4 Training Across Platforms and Parallelism Layouts
summary: Training with MXFP4, a 4-bit microscaling format, is non-deterministic: identical inputs can produce different results across parallelism layouts and GPU vendors. These differences complicate debugging and training audits and can cause training and inference engines to disagree. We present CertiSum to make MXFP4 training bitwise invariant across runs, parallelism layouts, and GPU vendors. Its key insight is that native FP32 accumulation of MXFP4 products is often already exact for every summation order. CertiSum collects statistics during quantization to certify native matrix multiplication results, recomputes uncertified outputs exactly, and uses exact kernels directly where certification rarely succeeds. CertiSum keeps quantization blocks unchanged across layouts and merges partial sums without rounding, including in attention and weight-gradient computation. In 200-step Qwen3-8B-Base experiments, CertiSum preserves training states bit for bit across AMD MI350X and NVIDIA GB200 and across changes in data, tensor, and context parallelism on MI350X. Across three 8B--14B models on FineWeb-Edu using MI350X, it adds 11.8--60.5% to training-step latency relative to its non-exact MXFP4 counterpart at the larger evaluated input shapes, with speedups of up to $1.24\times$ over BF16 and $1.70\times$ over deterministic BF16.

AI.tldr: CertiSum achieves bitwise-identical MXFP4 training across AMD MI350X and NVIDIA GB200 GPUs and varying parallelism layouts by certifying exact FP32 accumulations and recomputing uncertified outputs, with up to 1.70x speedup over deterministic BF16.
AI.motivation: 4-bit microscaling (MXFP4) training is non-deterministic across parallelism layouts and GPU vendors, complicating debugging, audits, and training-inference consistency.
AI.method: CertiSum collects quantization statistics to certify when native FP32 accumulation of MXFP4 products is exact for any summation order, recomputes uncertified outputs exactly, uses exact kernels where certification rarely succeeds, and merges partial sums without rounding while keeping quantization blocks invariant.
AI.result: In 200-step Qwen3-8B-Base runs, CertiSum preserves bitwise-identical states across MI350X and GB200 and across data, tensor, and context parallelism; on 8B-14B models, it adds 11.8-60.5% latency over non-exact MXFP4 at larger shapes while achieving up to 1.24x speedup over BF16 and 1.70x over deterministic BF16.
AI.conclusion: Certifying native accumulations and selectively recomputing uncertified sums enables reproducible, cross-platform MXFP4 training faster than BF16.

title: Mitigating Catastrophic Forgetting with Physics-Indexed Specialist Memory: the Evolutionary Neuroplastic Agent
comment: 25 pages, 7 figures, 23 tables. Code and data: this https URL
summary: Continual reinforcement learning requires adaptation to changing conditions while preserving performance under previously encountered dynamics. It was investigated whether specialists generated by evolutionary search can provide a reusable memory when combined with environment detection and failure-driven search. The Evolutionary Neuroplastic Agent (ENA) evolves small neural networks without gradients, archives selected policies by detected dynamic regime, and retrieves them through Bayesian policy reuse. The architecture was evaluated in non-stationary CartPole and HalfCheetah environments. In the 30-replicate CartPole ablation, the complete architecture achieved a mean success rate of 83.2% across the five test environments. Among variants that learned the harder CartPole environments, the complete architecture showed the most consistent retention. A selection ablation also showed that the retrieval rule affected performance. In the evaluated sequences, ENA adapted more slowly than PPO on CartPole and achieved lower returns than SAC on HalfCheetah. The evidence concerns the complete architecture and does not isolate gradient-free optimization as the cause of retention or establish superiority over other continual-learning methods.

AI.tldr: The Evolutionary Neuroplastic Agent (ENA) combines gradient-free evolutionary search, physics-indexed policy archiving, and Bayesian policy reuse to achieve an 83.2% mean success rate in non-stationary CartPole continual RL.
AI.motivation: Continual reinforcement learning requires adapting to changing dynamics without forgetting previously learned behaviors, and it was unclear whether evolutionary specialists with retrieval could provide a reusable memory.
AI.method: ENA evolves small neural networks without gradients, archives selected policies indexed by detected dynamic regime, and retrieves them via Bayesian policy reuse, evaluated on non-stationary CartPole and HalfCheetah.
AI.result: In a 30-replicate CartPole ablation, the full ENA achieved an 83.2% mean success rate across five test environments with the most consistent retention among variants, though it adapted slower than PPO on CartPole and scored lower returns than SAC on HalfCheetah.
AI.conclusion: Physics-indexed evolutionary memory with Bayesian reuse supports retention in non-stationary RL, though the evidence does not isolate gradient-free search as the cause or establish superiority over other continual-learning methods.

title: No Convergence in Learned Eavesdropping-Detection Dynamics for BB84 Quantum Key Distribution
summary: In prior work we showed that a reinforcement-learning eavesdropper can intercept BB84 quantum key distribution while holding the quantum bit error rate below the abort threshold and keeping a usable distillable key. In this paper we ask whether an equally adaptive learning detector can close this stealth window. We cast the interaction as an alternating best-response game between a tabular eavesdropper and a tabular threshold-adapting detector. We measure exploitability, which is the detection rate and distillable key fraction achieved by a fresh attacker best-responding to the final detector. Across three learning rules (Q-Learning, SARSA, Double Q-Learning), three channel-noise levels, and a uniform false-alarm discipline, the dynamics do not settle out to twenty rounds. The exploitability does not approach a fixed point, and its round-to-round swings do not decay. Two controls, one retraining the attacker against a frozen defender and one retraining the defender against a frozen attacker, show that the swings on each side match the variance of the best-response procedure itself. The dynamics fluctuate at the scale of best-response variance rather than converging, with neither player settling to a fixed response. The behavior is noise-dependent, and the stealth window stays open at the low noise where practical QKD operates. The defender contains the attacker on average at intermediate noise without the contest settling, and at high noise the channel rather than the learned policy suppresses the attack. As a candidate mechanism we examine a last-mover information asymmetry, supported by significant anti-persistence at intermediate noise and consistent with best-response noise at low noise. The results suggest that a learned detector cannot be certified from any single round, and that closing the window calls for breaking the information structure rather than out-adapting the attacker.

AI.tldr: In BB84 quantum key distribution, an alternating best-response game between a tabular RL eavesdropper and a threshold-adapting detector fails to converge over 20 rounds, leaving the stealth window open at low practical channel noise.
AI.motivation: Prior work showed an RL eavesdropper can intercept BB84 QKD while keeping quantum bit error rate below abort thresholds, raising the question of whether an adaptive learning detector can close this stealth window.
AI.method: The authors model the interaction as an alternating best-response game between a tabular eavesdropper and a tabular threshold-adapting detector across Q-Learning, SARSA, and Double Q-Learning, three noise levels, and a uniform false-alarm discipline, measuring exploitability and running frozen-opponent controls.
AI.result: Dynamics do not converge within 20 rounds, with exploitability swings matching the variance of the best-response procedure itself; the stealth window stays open at low noise, while intermediate noise shows average containment with anti-persistence and high noise suppresses attacks via the channel.
AI.conclusion: Learned detectors cannot be certified from any single round due to last-mover information asymmetry, meaning closing the QKD stealth window requires breaking the information structure rather than out-adapting the attacker.

title: Physics-informed and event-aware forecasting of ammonia emissions in aerobic chicken manure composting bioreactors: A PINN-PatchTST-GPR framework with symbolic dynamic extraction
summary: Predicting ammonia (NH3) concentrations during aerobic chicken manure composting provides critical feedforward signals for intelligent aeration. However, the concurrence of long-term biochemical evolution and intermittent forced-aeration pulses poses significant modeling hurdles across steady baselines, transient surges, and risk quantification. Existing data-driven models lack physical consistency, while mechanistic kinetic models struggle with environmental disturbances. To bridge this gap, we propose PINN-PatchTST-GPR, a physics-informed neuro-symbolic forecasting framework. Validated on a 28-day composting campaign across six vertical bioreactors, the framework couples a channel-independent PatchTST backbone with macroscopic kinetic constraints, dynamic physical bounds, and a Gaussian process regression (GPR) event specialist. Multi-channel sensor streams drive discrete differential equation residuals and non-negativity bounds, strictly ensuring physical plausibility. A block-split conformal prediction module yields nominal 90% distribution-free prediction intervals, while PySINDy and PySR extract low-complexity symbolic equations for quiescent and surge regimes. The model achieves an overall RMSE of 0.8256 +/- 0.0132 ppm, R2 of 0.9817 +/- 0.0006, Epeak of 1.6793 +/- 0.0725 ppm, and Etime of 0.7 +/- 0.2 min. For uncertainty quantification, it attains PICP90 of 99.792 +/- 0.047%, MPIW of 6.951 +/- 0.128 ppm, and IS0.1 of 6.968 +/- 0.128 ppm. Symbolically, PySINDy yields an RMSE of 0.4624 +/- 0.0758 ppm (R2 = 0.9896), while PySR yields 2.4084 +/- 0.0864 ppm (R2 = 0.9523). Biologically, the 20-min aeration strategy minimizes cumulative NH3 emissions. Overall, PINN-PatchTST-GPR harmonizes global forecasting, localized transient responsiveness, and risk quantification for precision composting.

AI.tldr: PINN-PatchTST-GPR couples a PatchTST backbone with kinetic constraints, a GPR event specialist, conformal prediction, and symbolic extraction to forecast NH3 emissions in chicken manure composting with 0.8256 ppm RMSE and R2 of 0.9817.
AI.motivation: Forecasting ammonia (NH3) during aerobic composting is challenging because intermittent forced-aeration pulses create transient surges alongside slow biochemical evolution, which purely data-driven or mechanistic models struggle to capture jointly.
AI.method: Validated on a 28-day campaign across six vertical bioreactors, PINN-PatchTST-GPR combines channel-independent PatchTST, discrete differential equation residuals, non-negativity bounds, a Gaussian process regression (GPR) event specialist, block-split conformal prediction, and PySINDy/PySR symbolic extraction.
AI.result: The framework achieves 0.8256 +/- 0.0132 ppm RMSE, R2 of 0.9817 +/- 0.0006, Epeak of 1.6793 +/- 0.0725 ppm, and PICP90 of 99.792 +/- 0.047%; PySINDy yields 0.4624 ppm RMSE (R2 = 0.9896), and a 20-min aeration strategy minimizes cumulative NH3 emissions.
AI.conclusion: Combining physics-informed neural forecasting, event-aware GPR, conformal intervals, and symbolic dynamics provides accurate, interpretable, and risk-quantified NH3 control for precision composting.

title: Random matrix discrepancy -- CLuP algorithm and parametric RDT approach
summary: We study information-theoretic and algorithmic aspects of random matrix discrepancy in proportional regime. The problem amounts to finding $\kappa=\min_{\x\in\mB^n}\|\sum_{i=1}^{n}\bar{A}_i\x_i\|_2$, where $\bar{A}_i\in\mR^{d\times d}$ is a collection of $n$ iid GOE matrices, $\mB^n$ are vertices of the unit cube in $\mR^n$, and $\alpha=\lim_{n\rightarrow \infty}\frac{n}{d^2}$ is a proportionality constant. Strong progress is made in several directions: (i) We develop a Random duality theory (RDT) framework and utilize its a lifted variant to establish lower bounds on $\kappa$, which precisely match the bounds obtained via the first moment in [81]. (ii) To address analytical challenges, we propose a negative Hopfield model as a proxy for implementation of a fully lifted RDT. On the 2nd lifting level, this model fits remarkably well between the information-theoretic lower bounds from [81] and the algorithmic upper bounds from [38]. (iii) On the 3rd and 4th lifting levels, parametric RDT concepts predict a sizeable computational gap for lower $\kappa$ values in the proxy model. Extending proxy information-theoretic fitting to algorithmic suggests a similar computational gap for matrix discrepancy in low $\kappa$ regime, aligning with [73]. (iv) We design a Controlled Loosening Up (CLuP) algorithm for matrix discrepancy. Its performance strongly matches our analytical results -- closely approaching information-theoretic predictions in lower $\alpha$ ranges (indicating a small or nonexistent computational gap) and following the proxy model's algorithmic predictions in higher $\alpha$ ranges (indicating a sizeable computational gap). Both the information-theoretic and algorithmic predictions match the corresponding phenomenologies of the symmetric binary perceptron (SBP) vector analogue in the entire $\alpha\in(0,\infty)$ range [1,2,14,31,51,92,111].

AI.tldr: This paper develops a lifted Random Duality Theory (RDT) framework and a Controlled Loosening Up (CLuP) algorithm for random matrix discrepancy, predicting and matching a sizeable computational gap at higher aspect ratios.
AI.motivation: Understanding the information-theoretic limits and algorithmic hardness of random matrix discrepancy in the proportional regime requires bridging analytical bounds with tractable algorithms.
AI.method: The authors develop a lifted RDT framework with a negative Hopfield proxy model up to the 4th lifting level to predict information-theoretic and algorithmic thresholds, and design the Controlled Loosening Up (CLuP) algorithm.
AI.result: Lifted RDT bounds match first-moment bounds, predict a sizeable computational gap for lower discrepancy values at higher lifting levels, and CLuP closely tracks the information-theoretic predictions at low aspect ratios and the proxy algorithmic predictions at high aspect ratios, paralleling the symmetric binary perceptron.
AI.conclusion: Parametric RDT and CLuP tightly characterize both the achievable discrepancy and the onset of computational hardness in random matrix discrepancy.

title: Selection-Aware Certification of Client-Constrained Fraud Rule Portfolios Under Synthetic Distribution Shift
summary: Selecting fraud-rule portfolios to satisfy a precision or recall floor can overfit the data used for selection. We study finite-family certification for bounded OR portfolios, comparing point-estimate selection, a fixed safety margin, and one-sided Clopper-Pearson lower bounds with Bonferroni adjustment. In a factorial follow-up with 6,400 datasets from two author-designed synthetic generators, full-validation certification reduced the held-out floor-violation rate by 29.1 percentage points on average versus full-validation point selection, while reducing deployment by 31.7 points. Compared with a fixed 0.05 margin, certification reduced violations by 22.2 points and deployment by 29.4 points; results varied across conditions. Using the full rather than half validation sample increased deployment by 17.1 points on average, without a uniform reduction in shifted-test violations. In a separate 400-dataset no-shift sweep, certification deployment rose from 61.3% to 90.2% as validation size increased from 1,500 to 15,000; no violations occurred among 2,887 deployed portfolios tested on 100,000-row holdouts. A temporal case study on the public synthetic Bank Account Fraud Base dataset used recall at a 5% false-positive-rate cap; the selected candidate pool captured less than 1% of test fraud, showing limited coverage in this setup. Together, these experiments characterize how finite-family certification changes the reliability-deployment tradeoff for bounded OR portfolios under specified synthetic conditions. The evidence covers the evaluated generators and one public synthetic BAF case study; it does not estimate performance on real transaction populations or robustness to arbitrary distribution shift. The authors revised and rewrote this abstract after receiving a draft from OpenAI Codex.

AI.tldr: Finite-family certification using Clopper-Pearson lower bounds with Bonferroni adjustment reduces held-out floor-violation rates by 29.1 percentage points on average compared to point selection across 6,400 synthetic datasets, while reducing deployment by 31.7 points.
AI.motivation: Selecting fraud-rule portfolios to meet precision or recall floors can overfit the selection data, leading to floor violations on held-out or shifted populations.
AI.method: The authors compare point-estimate selection, a fixed 0.05 safety margin, and one-sided Clopper-Pearson lower bounds with Bonferroni adjustment for bounded OR portfolios across 6,400 synthetic datasets, a 400-dataset no-shift sweep, and a temporal case study on the synthetic Bank Account Fraud (BAF) Base dataset.
AI.result: Full-validation certification cuts held-out floor violations by 29.1 percentage points versus point selection (and 22.2 points versus a 0.05 margin) while reducing deployment by 31.7 (and 29.4) points; in the no-shift sweep, deployment rises from 61.3% to 90.2% with larger validation sets with zero violations, while the BAF candidate pool captures <1% of test fraud at a 5% FPR cap.
AI.conclusion: Finite-family certification sharply reduces floor violations under the evaluated synthetic conditions at the cost of lower deployment, though real-world population behavior remains unestimated.

title: Hybrid quantum learning for imbalanced blood-cell classification: domain adaptation and classifier design
summary: Limited annotated data, class imbalance, and morphological similarity make white blood cell classification challenging. We benchmark hybrid variational quantum classifier heads against an affine baseline on 821 microscopy images across seven morphological classes. Using ImageNet-initialised ResNet34 backbones and repeated stratified five-fold cross-validation, we first compare direct transfer with intermediate adaptation on MLL23, a larger peripheral blood cell microscopy dataset. To guide the head comparison, we explore different encoding strategies, variational depth, and the number of independent circuit blocks. We then compare the classifier performance using the affine head and two hybrid heads across multiple random seeds, under a shared training and evaluation protocol. For this comparison, all backbones share the same MLL23-adapted initialisation. Intermediate adaptation increases mean macro-F1 across all four affine-head fine-tuning configurations. The largest gain occurs with a frozen backbone, where macro-F1 rises from $0.685$ to $0.786$, a relative improvement of approximately $14.7\%$. The shallow two-block hybrid head achieves a mean pooled out-of-fold macro-F1 of $0.865 \pm 0.010$, compared with $0.879 \pm 0.008$ for the affine head. The corresponding balanced accuracies are $0.886 \pm 0.008$ and $0.889 \pm 0.010$, respectively. In the architectural exploration, the two-block hybrid head achieves the highest macro-F1 and balanced accuracy among the evaluated hybrid configurations, while the effect of encoding varies across the considered metrics. Our results help guide the design and evaluation of hybrid classifier heads for imbalanced microscopy by linking architectural choices to overall performance and class-specific precision-recall trade-offs.

AI.tldr: Intermediate domain adaptation on MLL23 boosts frozen ResNet34 macro-F1 by 14.7% for imbalanced blood-cell classification, while a shallow two-block hybrid quantum head reaches 0.865 macro-F1 compared to 0.879 for an affine baseline.
AI.motivation: White blood cell classification suffers from limited annotated data, class imbalance, and morphological similarity, motivating evaluation of domain adaptation and hybrid variational quantum classifier heads.
AI.method: Using ImageNet-initialized ResNet34 backbones and repeated stratified five-fold cross-validation on 821 seven-class microscopy images, the authors compare direct transfer against intermediate MLL23 adaptation and benchmark two hybrid quantum heads (varying encodings, depth, and blocks) against an affine head.
AI.result: Intermediate MLL23 adaptation improves mean macro-F1 across all four affine fine-tuning setups (rising from 0.685 to 0.786, +14.7% relative, when frozen); the two-block hybrid head achieves 0.865 +/- 0.010 macro-F1 (0.886 balanced accuracy) versus 0.879 +/- 0.008 (0.889 balanced accuracy) for the affine head.
AI.conclusion: Intermediate domain adaptation substantially aids imbalanced microscopy transfer, and shallow multi-block hybrid quantum heads approach affine baseline performance.

title: Multi-Assay Antibody Developability Prediction with Shared Structure-Language Representations
summary: Early assessment of antibody developability is critical in drug discovery, but computational approaches remain limited by the scarcity of experimental data. We explore two strategies for working within that limit. First, we designed per-residue physicochemical descriptors encoding the local structural environment, including new terms such as directional charge asymmetry and screened electrostatic potential. These feed a convolutional network, combined with protein language model (PLM) embeddings in a two-stream architecture: the two are encoded and predicted independently and merged only at the prediction stage. Second, a shared trunk with per-assay heads passes information between related assays. Both are implemented in the Multi-Assay Developability Model (MADM) and evaluated on eight assays: HIC, heparin affinity (HAC), AC-SINS, and polyspecificity ELISA against BVP, dsDNA, insulin, ovalbumin and soluble membrane proteins (SMP), with labels from 29 open sources. Structural descriptors match or exceed PLM embeddings (AbLang2, ESM2) on several assays; combining the streams gives a small but consistent gain in accuracy and reduces seed-to-seed variance. Multi-assay training raises Spearman rho for ovalbumin and SMP by about 0.1, where assays correlate and share sequence space. Under cluster-split cross-validation the strongest results are for HAC, ovalbumin, insulin, SMP and HIC (rho = 0.70-0.82); AC-SINS, BVP and dsDNA are weaker (0.50-0.55). In these three, sequence clusters largely coincide with data source, so a held-out fold measures transfer to differently calibrated measurements as well as to new sequences. On the 80-antibody GDPa3 hold-out, performance falls by rho around 0.1 for all but SMP (0.22). Transfer to the VHH panel of Ginkgo GDPa5 gives comparable results, and scFv validation against binary SMP labels yields F1 = 0.89, AUC = 0.95.

AI.tldr: MADM combines per-residue structural descriptors with protein language model embeddings in a two-stream, multi-assay architecture across eight developability assays, improving Spearman rho by ~0.1 on correlated assays and reaching F1=0.89 on scFv SMP validation.
AI.motivation: Computational antibody developability prediction is constrained by scarce experimental data and calibration differences across open-source datasets.
AI.method: The Multi-Assay Developability Model (MADM) pairs a convolutional network over novel per-residue physicochemical descriptors (e.g., directional charge asymmetry, screened electrostatic potential) with protein language model embeddings (AbLang2, ESM2) merged at prediction, plus a shared trunk with per-assay heads trained across eight assays from 29 open sources.
AI.result: Structural descriptors match or exceed PLM embeddings on several assays, two-stream fusion lowers seed variance, and multi-assay training raises Spearman rho by ~0.1 on ovalbumin and SMP; cluster-split CV reaches rho=0.70-0.82 on five assays (0.50-0.55 on three), GDPa3 hold-out drops by ~0.1 (0.22 on SMP), and scFv SMP validation yields F1=0.89 and AUC=0.95.
AI.conclusion: Combining local structural descriptors with PLM embeddings and multi-assay sharing improves data-scarce antibody developability prediction and generalizes across antibody formats.

title: Exstill: The Most Efficient Single-Chip Processor for the Next Token
comment: 62 pages plus references (72 total), 16 figures, 22 tables. Technical report
summary: Generating a token with a language model requires a fixed amount of arithmetic, whose energy sets a floor beneath any hardware. For Qwen3-1.7B at a 16K-token context, gate-level measurements at 5 nm place this floor at 0.89 mJ per token, yet an NVIDIA B300 spends 391-1,120x that. The excess is the price of generality, software layers, programmable hardware and moving weights and key-value (KV) caches from external memory, and it widens with each process generation. We present a co-design approach that brings token generation close to this floor and then lowers the floor itself, optimizing silicon and model together in a gate-level search loop. Fixing one model architecture in the datapath, with weights still loadable, and holding weights and every conversation's KV cache on-die, a pre-silicon 5 nm design brings an unchanged Qwen3-1.7B token to 3.4x its floor. Co-designing the model with the circuits at fixed quality lowers the floor to 0.29 mJ and the token to 0.52 mJ, 1.8x the new floor and less than the baseline model's arithmetic alone, while on-die capacity grows from one user to twelve. Against a measured B300 serving the same twelve users, the design decodes each user's tokens 110x faster at 690x lower energy. To show that one fixed architecture can serve, as a co-processor, the latency-critical workloads around a frontier model, we introduce Polyglot-DC (1.7B and 4B, each with its own design), specialized for each job by distillation and task-specific training into its own weights. As a drafter it speeds single-user speculative decoding of large open models by up to 6.6x at the maximum reasoning effort. Its guard returns multilingual verdicts in a millisecond or less, within a point of the strongest open guard. Its agent and financial-reasoning models lead comparable open models on established benchmarks, with a reasoning turn falling from seconds to tens of milliseconds.

AI.tldr: Exstill co-designs silicon and language models in a gate-level search loop to lower 5 nm token generation energy to 0.52 mJ, decoding 110x faster at 690x lower energy than an NVIDIA B300 serving twelve users.
AI.motivation: General-purpose GPUs like the NVIDIA B300 spend 391-1,120x more energy per token than the 5 nm arithmetic floor (0.89 mJ for Qwen3-1.7B at 16K context) due to generality, software overhead, and external memory movement.
AI.method: Exstill fixes one model architecture in the datapath while keeping weights loadable and storing weights and KV caches on-die, co-designing model and circuits in a gate-level search loop; it also introduces specialized 1.7B and 4B Polyglot-DC co-processors via distillation and task-specific training.
AI.result: A pre-silicon 5 nm design brings unchanged Qwen3-1.7B to 3.4x its floor, and co-design lowers the floor to 0.29 mJ and token energy to 0.52 mJ for 12 users (110x faster, 690x lower energy than B300); Polyglot-DC speeds speculative decoding up to 6.6x, runs guardrails in <=1 ms, and cuts agent/financial reasoning turns from seconds to tens of milliseconds.
AI.conclusion: Model-circuit co-design with on-die weight and KV-cache storage dramatically closes and lowers the energy floor for latency-critical LLM inference.

title: Quantifying Membership Inference Risks in Genomic Data Sharing: The Role of Attacker's Auxiliary Information
summary: Genomic data sharing is essential for biomedical research but introduces significant privacy risks, including membership inference attacks, in which an adversary determines whether a specific individual's data was used in a study. Existing privacy protections are typically applied after a release format has already been chosen, leaving researchers without a principled method to assess dataset-specific risk beforehand. We propose a server-assisted, principal component analysis-based pre-release auditing framework that maps genomic data into a shared low-dimensional space, applies epsilon-local differential privacy via the Laplace mechanism with a formally derived sensitivity for principal component analysis scores, and estimates membership inference attack power at a controlled 5% false-positive rate using a distance-threshold attack. A membership-neutrality diagnostic based on Unbiased Reconstruction Robustness is reported alongside attack power, precision, and recall. Experiments using the openSNP and 1000 Genomes Project datasets across multiple dimensionalities and privacy budgets show that separation between the researcher's dataset and public auxiliary data in principal component analysis space is a dominant determinant of attack success, exceeding the effect of perturbation level alone. Comparison against a genome-wide association study-style likelihood ratio test baseline further contextualizes the measured risk. This framework enables researchers, data repositories, and institutional review bodies to quantify dataset-specific membership inference risk before genomic data publication, supporting more informed and privacy-aware biomedical data-sharing decisions.

AI.tldr: A PCA-based pre-release auditing framework with epsilon-local differential privacy quantifies membership inference risks in genomic data sharing on openSNP and 1000 Genomes, showing dataset-to-auxiliary separation dominates attack success.
AI.motivation: Privacy protections for genomic data sharing are typically applied after choosing a release format, leaving researchers without a principled pre-release method to assess dataset-specific membership inference risk.
AI.method: The server-assisted framework maps genomic data into a shared PCA space, applies epsilon-local differential privacy via the Laplace mechanism with formally derived PCA-score sensitivity, and estimates distance-threshold attack power at 5% FPR alongside an Unbiased Reconstruction Robustness diagnostic and a GWAS likelihood-ratio baseline.
AI.result: Experiments on openSNP and 1000 Genomes across multiple dimensionalities and privacy budgets show that separation between the target dataset and public auxiliary data in PCA space dominates attack success, exceeding the effect of perturbation level alone.
AI.conclusion: Pre-release PCA-based auditing enables researchers and repositories to quantify dataset-specific membership inference risks before publishing genomic data.

title: Privacy-Preserving Clustering Algorithm and Parameter Selection for Collaborative Population Stratification Using Distributed PCA
summary: We propose a privacy-preserving selection layer for collaborative population stratification workflows, enabling an honest-but-curious server to recommend a strong clustering algorithm-hyperparameter configuration from privacy protected shares. Instead of using a fixed workflow such as PCA followed by K-Means with a preset number of clusters, the framework compares multiple clustering methods and parameter settings under privacy constraints. To avoid relying on a public reference basis, we construct a shared low-dimensional representation through a distributed-PCA (DPCA) procedure in which each party computes local top-$r$ principal-component information and the server aggregates only low-rank summaries to recover a global basis. Building on this representation, the framework supports three LDP-protected pipelines: PCA then Noise, Noise then PCA, and Noise-Only. The server evaluates clustering methods and parameter settings using internal validation metrics and recommends a top-performing configuration from the perturbed data; this step is pure post-processing. Experiments on openSNP and 1000 Genomes show that the server-side selection layer reliably identifies strong settings from LDP-protected data. Across both datasets, the PCA-based pipelines outperform Noise-Only in clustering utility, communication cost, and runtime, and show lower membership-inference attack (MIA) power at small privacy budgets. Overall, they provide the best utility--scalability trade-off in our setting.

AI.tldr: A distributed-PCA privacy-preserving selection layer enables an honest-but-curious server to recommend clustering algorithms and hyperparameters on openSNP and 1000 Genomes, with PCA-based LDP pipelines outperforming Noise-Only in utility, cost, and MIA resistance.
AI.motivation: Collaborative population stratification workflows typically hardcode PCA followed by K-Means with a preset cluster count, lacking a privacy-preserving way to compare clustering methods and hyperparameters without a public reference basis.
AI.method: Parties compute local top-r principal-component summaries aggregated by a server via distributed PCA (DPCA) to form a global basis, supporting three LDP pipelines (PCA then Noise, Noise then PCA, Noise-Only) from which the server selects top configurations using internal validation metrics as pure post-processing.
AI.result: On openSNP and 1000 Genomes, the server-side selection layer reliably identifies strong configurations from LDP-protected data, and PCA-based pipelines outperform Noise-Only in clustering utility, communication cost, runtime, and membership-inference attack (MIA) power at small privacy budgets.
AI.conclusion: Distributed-PCA post-processing selection provides an effective utility-scalability-privacy trade-off for collaborative population stratification.

title: Supercharging Olmo-core for Efficient and Scalable MoE Training
comment: 169 pages. Web version and video: this https URL
summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models add parameters without proportionally increasing per-token compute. However, training cost also depends on bytes moved, memory held, and kernels launched, and many of those costs follow total parameter size rather than active compute. On infrastructure built for dense models, this mismatch is costly: in early baselines, throughput fell as stored expert parameter size grew, even though the useful work per token stayed nearly fixed. To close this gap, we present a redesigned training stack in Olmo-core, built for efficient, scalable MoE training. We replace the Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP) of earlier Olmo-core versions with an architecture built on Distributed Data Parallel (DDP), and add Expert Parallelism (EP), Pipeline Parallelism (PP), a distributed optimizer, and activation recompute. We propose NVSHMEM-based rowwise EP, which writes each token directly into its expert's buffer, avoiding dispatch and combine permutation overhead. We make EP fully synchronization-free by keeping routing metadata on the GPU and using device-scheduled grouped GEMMs. Closely integrated MXFP8 cuts compute, activation-memory, and transport costs, and topology-agnostic checkpoints let the parallel layout change between runs. On NVL8 B300 nodes, the stack supports training configurations from 12.9 billion to 1.2 trillion total parameters on up to 512 GPUs, reaching 858 useful-model TFLOP/s/GPU at 1.2 trillion with MXFP8 and per-layer recompute; an experimental capacity test with the optional DeepEP v2 backend reaches 2.38 trillion. We also explain each design choice and share findings for other training systems; for example, we identify a failure pattern we call Token Gerrymandering, in which the MoE router can learn to hack the load-balancing loss, and find that overlapping communication with computation can slow the overlapped kernels by more than it hides.

AI.tldr: Olmo-core's redesigned MoE training stack replaces FSDP with DDP, synchronization-free NVSHMEM rowwise EP, PP, and MXFP8, scaling up to 1.2T parameters on 512 B300 GPUs at 858 TFLOP/s/GPU.
AI.motivation: Training infrastructure built for dense models suffers throughput drops on Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models because memory movement, kernel launches, and storage scale with total parameters rather than active compute.
AI.method: The authors replace FSDP with DDP, Expert Parallelism (EP), Pipeline Parallelism (PP), a distributed optimizer, and activation recompute, introducing synchronization-free NVSHMEM rowwise EP with device-scheduled grouped GEMMs, integrated MXFP8, and topology-agnostic checkpoints.
AI.result: On NVL8 B300 nodes, the stack scales from 12.9B to 1.2T parameters on up to 512 GPUs, achieving 858 useful-model TFLOP/s/GPU at 1.2T with MXFP8 (and reaching 2.38T in a DeepEP v2 capacity test), while also uncovering Token Gerrymandering and communication-computation overlap slowdowns.
AI.conclusion: Synchronization-free rowwise EP and MXFP8 integration eliminate dense-centric bottlenecks for trillion-parameter MoE training.

title: Accelerating Atomistic-Continuum Simulations of Multilayer 2D Materials with Functional Principal Component Analysis-Based Machine Learning
summary: Atomistic-continuum simulations of complex wrinkling deformations in large-area multilayer two-dimensional (2D) materials are computationally expensive. To accelerate these simulations, this work presents a machine-learning (ML) framework that first constructs a low-dimensional representation of the deformation field, then learns the deformation in this reduced space. Dimensionality reduction of deformed 2D membranes is challenging because of the extremely high dimensionality of discretized deformation fields, the need to preserve surface continuity and prescribed geometric constraints, the stochastic nature of wrinkling patterns, and the limited availability of training data. We address these challenges using two-dimensional functional principal component analysis (FPCA). The proposed FPCA representation reduces deformation fields containing millions of degrees of freedom to latent spaces with only tens of dimensions while preserving the continuity of the deformed surface. In addition, prescribed homogeneous boundary constraints are satisfied exactly through an appropriate choice of basis functions in the FPCA representation. A neural network is then trained to predict the principal components from the system and loading parameters. The resulting ML-predicted deformation fields are used as high-quality initial configurations for the atomistic-continuum solver, which subsequently performs energy minimization to obtain equilibrium solutions. The framework is demonstrated for multilayer graphene subjected to uniaxial compression, biaxial compression, and combined biaxial compression and simple shear. For the most computationally intensive large-strain cases, the proposed approach achieves speedups of at least 6.8 times while converging to final energies comparable to, and in some cases lower than, those obtained using conventional atomistic-continuum initialization.

AI.tldr: A 2D functional principal component analysis (FPCA) and neural network framework accelerates atomistic-continuum wrinkling simulations of multilayer graphene by at least 6.8x while matching or improving final equilibrium energies.
AI.motivation: Atomistic-continuum simulations of wrinkling in large-area multilayer 2D materials are computationally expensive due to high-dimensional deformation fields, continuity and boundary constraints, stochasticity, and scarce training data.
AI.method: Two-dimensional FPCA reduces million-DOF deformation fields to tens of latent dimensions while preserving surface continuity and exact homogeneous boundary constraints via basis choice, and a neural network predicts principal components from loading parameters to initialize the atomistic-continuum energy minimizer.
AI.result: On multilayer graphene under uniaxial compression, biaxial compression, and combined compression-shear, the framework achieves speedups of at least 6.8x in large-strain cases while converging to equilibrium energies comparable to or lower than conventional initialization.
AI.conclusion: Coupling FPCA dimensionality reduction with ML-predicted initializations substantially accelerates large-strain atomistic-continuum simulations of 2D materials.

title: SpecRelay: Amortize or Avoid the Round Trip in Edge-Cloud Speculative Decoding
summary: Edge-cloud speculative decoding moves autoregressive drafting to an edge device while a larger cloud model verifies draft tokens in parallel, so that edge drafting and cloud verification overlap under a synchronous draft-verify schedule. Beyond low-latency local networks, however, the next verification request of that schedule can be sent only after the previous reply arrives, so every round still waits out a full round trip, and throughput falls as the network RTT grows. To recover this loss, we present SpecRelay, an edge-cloud LLM inference system that addresses this cost at two levels: it amortizes round trips when cloud verification is necessary and avoids them when local reasoning suffices. For cloud-bound queries, an asynchronous verification pipeline keeps fixed-budget draft trees in flight while earlier replies are still outstanding, and the cloud rejects stale requests before the target-model forward pass (the asynchronous schedule).
