At the query level, an RTT-conditioned router (the Latency-Aware Router) estimates quality and completion latency for three on-device modes (direct generation, Chain-of-Draft, and full reasoning) and cloud speculative decoding, selecting among them under a configurable accuracy-latency objective without adding latency during inference, since the router runs concurrently with the draft-model prefill. The asynchronous schedule alone improves decoding throughput by up to 50% over a reproduced synchronous baseline across multiple benchmarks. At matched target-model accuracy and 250 ms of added round-trip latency, the full system with the router delivers 1.95x and 1.55x the throughput of the same baseline on SPROUT and OlympiadBench, respectively, while sending only 47% and 39% of the queries to the cloud.

AI.tldr: SpecRelay combines asynchronous cloud verification with an RTT-conditioned Latency-Aware Router to deliver 1.95x and 1.55x throughput over synchronous edge-cloud speculative decoding on SPROUT and OlympiadBench at 250 ms RTT.
AI.motivation: Synchronous edge-cloud speculative decoding stalls for a full network round trip on every verification round, causing throughput to degrade as round-trip time (RTT) increases.
AI.method: SpecRelay introduces an asynchronous verification pipeline that keeps fixed-budget draft trees in flight while rejecting stale requests before target-model forward passes, paired with an RTT-conditioned Latency-Aware Router running concurrently with prefill to choose among three on-device modes and cloud speculative decoding.
AI.result: The asynchronous schedule alone boosts throughput by up to 50% over a synchronous baseline; at matched accuracy and 250 ms added RTT, the full system achieves 1.95x throughput on SPROUT and 1.55x on OlympiadBench while offloading only 47% and 39% of queries to the cloud.
AI.conclusion: Amortizing round trips via asynchronous verification and avoiding unnecessary offloading via RTT-aware routing restores edge-cloud speculative decoding throughput over high-latency networks.

title: Context Matters: Improving LLM-Based Code Summarization with Hierarchical Information
comment: 11 pages, 4 figures, 10 tables. Accepted and presented at the Brazilian Symposium on Software Quality (SBQS 2026), Technical Track. Replication package: this https URL
summary: Source code documentation plays an important role in software quality activities, such as code review, program comprehension, maintenance, and bug fixing. However, it is often fragmented across individual code elements and focuses on local implementation details, providing little information about their surrounding context. This limits both developers' understanding of software systems and the effectiveness of Large Language Models (LLMs), whose reasoning is constrained by finite context windows. Enriching documentation with hierarchical context has the potential to improve software comprehension and support downstream, quality-related tasks for both developers and LLM-based tools. In this paper, we present an in silico study that showcases the impact of augmenting context on the generation of code-level documentation, using a variety of LLMs. By varying the function, class, and module hierarchy visible to the LLMs, we assess whether this variation produces a significant difference in the resulting code documentation compared with the existing documentation, which serves as a proxy for developer intent. Our results show that Documentation-Aware prompts with class or module-level context consistently yield summaries that are closest to the original documentation. Adding surrounding documentation yields statistically significant improvements over the baseline across models, with effect sizes ranging from negligible (DeepSeek) through weak (GPT-4o-mini) to medium (Gemini). We restrict the study to this immediate hierarchical context; call-graph traversal and cross-module dependency context fall outside our scope and are left to future work. These findings provide a clear path to improve automated documentation tools and enhance LLMs' ability to reason about codebases for downstream tasks, such as code retrieval.

AI.tldr: An in silico study across multiple LLMs shows that augmenting prompts with hierarchical class- or module-level documentation significantly improves code summarization alignment with developer intent.
AI.motivation: Source code documentation is often fragmented around local implementation details, limiting both developer comprehension and LLM reasoning within finite context windows.
AI.method: The authors vary function-, class-, and module-level hierarchical context in Documentation-Aware prompts across several LLMs (including DeepSeek, GPT-4o-mini, and Gemini) and measure alignment against existing code documentation as a proxy for developer intent.
AI.result: Documentation-Aware prompts with class- or module-level context consistently produce summaries closest to original documentation, yielding statistically significant improvements over baselines with effect sizes from negligible (DeepSeek) to weak (GPT-4o-mini) to medium (Gemini).
AI.conclusion: Incorporating immediate hierarchical context provides a clear, effective path to improve automated LLM code documentation and downstream codebase reasoning.

title: Video-as-Experience: Learning Computer Use via Audio-Visual Understanding
summary: Multimodal large language models (LLMs) have enabled capable computer-use agents that perceive graphical user interfaces, reason over instructions, and execute actions. However, existing approaches to learning from video demonstrations typically convert videos into screenshot-based action trajectories, rather than directly leveraging their rich audio-visual information. We introduce VEX (Video as EXperience), a framework that uses audio-visual understanding to unify learning from external demonstrations and reflecting on an agent's own behavior. Following a watch-act-rewatch paradigm, the agent extracts procedural guidance from tutorial videos containing visual demonstrations and spoken explanations, executes tasks, and verifies its progress by rewatching its execution as video. We instantiate VEX with video-SALMONN-VEX, a 9B-scale audio-visual computer-use agent built on the video-SALMONN 2 architecture with a Qwen3.5-9B backbone. We further introduce Action-Grounded Guide Optimization (AGGO), a reinforcement learning method that optimizes video-derived guidance for downstream action prediction, and augment AgentNet, OSWorld, and CUA-Gym with over 24K real-world tutorial videos. Experiments on OSWorld and a complementary subset of CUA-Gym demonstrate consistent improvements, with video-SALMONN-VEX achieving a 22% relative increase in task success over its Qwen3.5 backbone on OSWorld. Moreover, its generated guidance improves Gemini-3.5-flash by 10% relatively on OSWorld. These results highlight the potential of audio-visual understanding as a unified interface for procedural learning and self-verification in computer-use agents.

AI.tldr: VEX is an audio-visual computer-use agent framework using a watch-act-rewatch paradigm and Action-Grounded Guide Optimization, achieving a 22% relative task success gain over Qwen3.5-9B on OSWorld.
AI.motivation: Existing computer-use agents learn from video demonstrations by converting them into screenshot-based action trajectories, discarding rich spoken explanations and audio-visual cues.
AI.method: Instantiated as video-SALMONN-VEX (9B, Qwen3.5-9B backbone), VEX extracts procedural guidance from tutorial videos, executes tasks, and rewatches its own execution video to verify progress, trained with Action-Grounded Guide Optimization (AGGO) RL on AgentNet, OSWorld, and CUA-Gym augmented with >24K tutorial videos.
AI.result: On OSWorld and CUA-Gym, video-SALMONN-VEX achieves a 22% relative increase in task success over its Qwen3.5 backbone on OSWorld, and its generated guidance improves Gemini-3.5-flash by 10% relatively on OSWorld.
AI.conclusion: Audio-visual understanding provides a unified interface for procedural learning and self-verification in computer-use agents.

title: Multimodal Fusion: A Review of Breast Cancer Advanced and Traditional Modalities
summary: Purpose: Multimodal medical imaging fusion (MMIF) is an increasingly important approach to breast cancer detection (BCD), as different imaging modalities rely on different physical principles and provide complementary information. No single modality can capture all the structural, functional, and biological information needed for accurate diagnosis and characterization. Methods: This review examines more than 15 imaging modalities used in breast cancer detection, including conventional techniques such as mammography, ultrasound, and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), as well as emerging approaches such as thermal imaging, photoacoustic imaging, microwave imaging, and multimodal microscopy. Results: Mammography, ultrasound, and MRI remain among the most widely used modalities, providing complementary structural and functional information. Recent AI advances have enabled fusion at the data, feature, and decision levels, with applications in detection, classification, segmentation, prognosis, and personalized cancer management. Multimodal approaches increasingly combine imaging data with clinical, histopathological, and genomic information. However, important challenges remain, including limited availability of large and diverse multimodal datasets, variations in imaging protocols, missing modalities, limited external validation, and the need for interpretable and clinically reliable AI models. Conclusion: MMIF offers promising opportunities to improve breast cancer detection and characterization by combining complementary imaging and non-imaging information. Future research should prioritize robust fusion strategies, standardized and diverse datasets, multicenter validation, explainable and privacy-preserving AI, and the integration of imaging with clinical and molecular data to facilitate reliable translation into clinical practice.

AI.tldr: This review examines over 15 breast cancer imaging modalities and AI-driven multimodal fusion strategies, highlighting clinical potential alongside key barriers such as dataset scarcity and lack of external validation.
AI.motivation: No single imaging modality captures all structural, functional, and biological information needed for accurate breast cancer detection and characterization, necessitating multimodal medical imaging fusion (MMIF).
AI.method: The authors review more than 15 conventional (mammography, ultrasound, MRI) and emerging (thermal, photoacoustic, microwave, multimodal microscopy) modalities, along with data-, feature-, and decision-level AI fusion with clinical, histopathological, and genomic data.
AI.result: Mammography, ultrasound, and MRI remain the primary complementary modalities, while AI fusion advances detection, classification, segmentation, prognosis, and personalized management, though limited by small/non-diverse datasets, protocol variations, missing modalities, scarce external validation, and interpretability gaps.
AI.conclusion: Advancing clinical translation of MMIF in breast cancer requires robust fusion strategies, standardized multicenter datasets, and explainable, privacy-preserving AI.

title: Découpage: Directorial Audio-Visual Control for Long Multi-Shot Video Generation
summary: In cinematic storytelling, sound and visual transitions do not always coincide in lockstep: dialogue frequently bridges across cuts to reveal reactions or introduces new scenes via J- and L-cuts, while deliberate silences pace the scene. Existing audio-visual generative frameworks, however, lack explicit mechanisms to coordinate independent visual and acoustic timing over extended horizons. As narrative duration and shot complexity scale, these systems struggle to maintain long-range dialogue pacing, often hallucinating speech during intended silences or erroneously driving mouth movements on silent listeners. To enable fine-grained cinematic control, we present DECOUPAGE, a screenplay-driven framework for long-form, multi-shot, and multi-character joint audio-video generation. Rather than coupling modality boundaries by default, DECOUPAGE uncouples generation into independently bounded visual and acoustic tracks governed by persistent character identities. DECOUPAGE builds on a joint audio-video diffusion model with dual-schedule temporal cross-attention, incorporating a directorial Lip-sync mechanism that selectively decouples speech conditioning from visual facial dynamics during off-screen dialogue. On multi-shot conversational benchmarks, DECOUPAGE achieves precise control over shot transitions, audio timing, and visibility-aware lip synchronization, directing 15- to 60-second screenplay-driven audio-video generation with multimodal coherence.

AI.tldr: DECOUPAGE is a screenplay-driven joint audio-video diffusion framework that decouples visual and acoustic tracks to direct 15- to 60-second multi-shot, multi-character videos with J/L-cuts and visibility-aware lip sync.
AI.motivation: Existing audio-visual generative models lockstep sound and visual transitions, failing to handle cinematic J- and L-cuts, deliberate silences, or off-screen dialogue without hallucinating speech or driving silent listeners' lips.
AI.method: DECOUPAGE uncouples generation into independently bounded visual and acoustic tracks governed by persistent character identities, using a joint audio-video diffusion model with dual-schedule temporal cross-attention and a directorial lip-sync mechanism for off-screen dialogue.
AI.result: On multi-shot conversational benchmarks, DECOUPAGE achieves precise control over shot transitions, audio timing, and visibility-aware lip synchronization across 15- to 60-second screenplay-driven generations.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling visual and acoustic track boundaries enables fine-grained directorial control and multimodal coherence in long-form multi-shot video generation.

title: SPLICE: Structured Prompt Local Iterative Combinatorial Evolution
summary: Natural language optimization (NLO) improves an agent by having a model critique and rewrite its natural language policy parameters: system prompts, tool instructions, reasoning directives, few-shot demonstrations. These artifacts are multi-section documents in which some sections encode contracts (safety clauses, tool schemas, output formats) that must not drift, while others are legitimate optimization targets. Most iterative NLO methods treat the artifact as a single editable string, producing three recurrent failure modes: unsafe global rewrites, beam collapse onto a single lineage, and unchecked bloat, none addressed by formal guarantees. We introduce SPLICE, a unified NLO framework that poses optimization as constrained combinatorial search over an edit graph of block-structured, selectively-mutable states. We map each failure mode to a matched guarantee: (i) per-block mutability preserves contract text verbatim, with a price-of-freezing bound; (ii) elitist beam search with diversity slots never lets the leader regress on validation, bounds regression under noisy re-evaluation by an exponential tail, and keeps a competitive candidate from a different parent whenever one exists; (iii) a ratio length regularizer comes with an explicit accuracy-length bias bound. Candidates are proposed from dual section-local textual gradients; under a proposer-competence condition whose proxy we measure, edit-graph reachability and a convergence rate bound how quickly improving children arrive. Across seven public benchmarks under five reproduced protocols, SPLICE wins on four and matches the strongest prior method on three. On a production-style contract stress test it keeps the contract clauses that unconstrained optimizers trade away to raise the proxy metric, and ablations attribute gains to critique and elitist search.

AI.tldr: SPLICE poses natural language prompt optimization as constrained combinatorial search over block-structured states with formal guarantees on contract preservation, diversity, and length, winning on four and matching on three of seven benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Iterative natural language optimization (NLO) treats multi-section prompts as single editable strings, causing unsafe global rewrites of contract clauses, beam collapse, and unchecked prompt bloat without formal guarantees.
AI.method: SPLICE optimizes over an edit graph of block-structured, selectively mutable states using dual section-local textual gradients, per-block mutability (preserving contracts verbatim), elitist beam search with diversity slots, and a ratio length regularizer with explicit theoretical bounds.
AI.result: Across seven public benchmarks under five reproduced protocols, SPLICE wins on four and matches the strongest prior method on three, while preserving contract clauses on a production-style stress test where unconstrained optimizers trade them away.
AI.conclusion: Block-structured constrained search with matched theoretical guarantees prevents contract drift, beam collapse, and bloat in natural language optimization.

title: Bring Back Language to Actions: Restoring VLM capabilities in VLA Models via Parameter Merging
summary: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) are obtained by fine-tuning pre-trained Vision-Language Models (VLMs) on robot demonstration data, enabling action prediction from visual observations and language instructions. However, this fine-tuning induces catastrophic forgetting, substantially degrading the semantic and visual grounding capabilities of the original VLM. We address this by merging the parameters of a VLM and its VLA derivative without retraining either model. Concretely, we extract the task vector (the difference between VLA and VLM weights) and decompose it via Singular Value Decomposition. For each component, we learn a scalar mixing coefficient controlling how much of the VLA adaptation is retained, optimised to jointly preserve action prediction and vision-language capabilities. Experiments show that our merged model performs well on both axes simultaneously, consistently outperforming established merging baselines.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a parameter-merging method using Singular Value Decomposition of task vectors to restore vision-language capabilities in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models without retraining.
AI.motivation: Fine-tuning pre-trained Vision-Language Models (VLMs) on robot demonstration data to create VLA models causes catastrophic forgetting, degrading the original VLM's semantic and visual grounding capabilities.
AI.method: The authors extract the task vector (weight difference between VLA and VLM), decompose it via Singular Value Decomposition, and learn a scalar mixing coefficient for each component to jointly preserve action prediction and vision-language capabilities.
AI.result: Experiments show the merged model performs well on both action prediction and vision-language axes simultaneously, consistently outperforming established merging baselines.
AI.conclusion: Component-wise SVD task-vector merging effectively mitigates catastrophic forgetting in VLA models without retraining either the VLM or VLA.

title: Ask Precisely, Assume Wisely: Interactive Evaluation of Ambiguity Resolution in Large Language Models
comment: 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). Workshop: Evaluation of Interactive Agents
summary: Ambiguity is a core challenge in human--AI interaction, where models must decide when to make assumptions and when to seek clarification. Existing approaches to ambiguity evaluation largely focus on coverage over multiple interpretations using static metrics, offering limited insight into how efficiently a model converges toward a single user-intended interpretation through interaction. We introduce a preference-grounded simulated user framework for controlled, multi-turn evaluation of ambiguity resolution, grounding simulator responses strictly in user disambiguation preferences to avoid hallucination and over-disclosure. Alongside this, we define three observable dissatisfaction signals --- incorrect assumptions, repeating clarifications, and irrelevant clarifications --- that characterize interaction quality beyond task accuracy. Our analysis reveals a clear trade-off: models that frequently seek clarification tend to over-clarify and prolong interactions, while assumption-driven models are more prone to misaligning with user intent. We demonstrate that system prompts optimized on these dissatisfaction signals achieve a Pareto-optimal balance across all three metrics, reducing overall error rates by up to 7.65%, underscoring the value of our framework in designing agents that ask precisely and assume wisely.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a preference-grounded simulated user framework and three dissatisfaction signals to evaluate and optimize multi-turn ambiguity resolution in LLMs.
AI.motivation: Existing ambiguity evaluations rely on static coverage metrics over multiple interpretations, offering limited insight into how efficiently a model converges to a single user-intended interpretation through interaction.
AI.method: The authors build a simulated user grounded strictly in user disambiguation preferences to prevent hallucination and over-disclosure, define three dissatisfaction signals (incorrect assumptions, repeating clarifications, irrelevant clarifications), and optimize system prompts on these signals.
AI.result: Analysis reveals a trade-off between over-clarifying models and assumption-driven models prone to misalignment; system prompts optimized on the dissatisfaction signals achieve a Pareto-optimal balance across all three metrics and reduce overall error rates by up to 7.65%.
AI.conclusion: Preference-grounded multi-turn evaluation and dissatisfaction-signal optimization enable LLM agents to balance asking precisely and assuming wisely.

title: Between Rigor and Reality: How AI Safety Benchmark Developers Understand Benchmark Use and Maintenance
comment: Poster at the Eval Eval Workshop at ACL 2026. 11 pages. this https URL
summary: Safety benchmarks are cited as the primary tool to understand the risks posed by generative AI (GenAI) systems, yet growing evidence suggests they often fail to meet the needs of real-world safety evaluation. We present findings from five interviews with AI safety benchmark developers in academia and industry. We find a disconnect between perceptions of the intended usefulness of safety benchmarks and their practical usefulness in safety evaluations of deployed systems. Our participants offered perspectives on two challenges contributing to this disconnect: (1) the difficulty of achieving inter-rater reliability on safety constructs, and (2) a lack of clarity regarding how to address persistent threats to external validity. Based on our analysis, we argue that safety benchmarks must not only be grounded in deployment contexts, but actively integrated with them. To facilitate this, we outline pathways for more transparent communication between academic and industry AI safety stakeholders.

AI.tldr: Through five interviews with AI safety benchmark developers, this paper identifies a disconnect between intended and practical usefulness of safety benchmarks in deployed GenAI systems.
AI.motivation: Although safety benchmarks are primary tools for assessing generative AI risks, growing evidence indicates they often fail to meet real-world safety evaluation needs.
AI.method: The authors conduct and analyze five interviews with AI safety benchmark developers across academia and industry.
AI.result: Participants highlight two core challenges driving the disconnect: difficulty achieving inter-rater reliability on safety constructs and lack of clarity on addressing persistent threats to external validity.
AI.conclusion: Safety benchmarks must be actively integrated with, rather than merely grounded in, deployment contexts, supported by more transparent communication between academic and industry stakeholders.

title: Dual-Stage Channel-Posterior Integration for MLM-Aided Token Communications
comment: 6 pages, 5 figures, This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible
summary: Token transmission over conventional digital modulation is vulnerable to channel impairments, leading to bit errors that cause received tokens to become contextually inconsistent. This paper proposes a receiver-side dual-stage channel-posterior integration framework for masked language model (MLM)-aided token reconstruction. In the proposed framework, the receiver detects unreliable token positions from channel reliability and constructs a vocabulary-level channel-posterior. In particular, within the receiver, Posterior-Weighted Input Embedding (PWE) injects this posterior into the MLM input, while Adaptive Output Logit Fusion (AOF) reuses it at the output with a channel-adaptive weight. Consequently, multiple unreliable tokens can be reconstructed in a single bidirectional MLM inference without retransmission, transmitter-side encoding, or additional MLM training. Experiments over noisy channels show up to a $67.2$\% improvement in cosine similarity over context-only MLM reconstruction, with consistent gains across different MLM architectures and existing language-model-aided methods.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a receiver-side dual-stage channel-posterior integration framework for masked language model (MLM)-aided token reconstruction over noisy channels.
AI.motivation: Bit errors from digital modulation over impaired channels cause received tokens to become contextually inconsistent, and existing context-only MLM reconstruction does not exploit channel reliability.
AI.method: The receiver detects unreliable token positions from channel reliability, constructs a vocabulary-level channel-posterior, injects it into the MLM input via Posterior-Weighted Input Embedding (PWE), and reuses it at the output via Adaptive Output Logit Fusion (AOF) in a single bidirectional MLM inference without retransmission, transmitter encoding, or additional MLM training.
AI.result: Experiments over noisy channels show up to a 67.2% improvement in cosine similarity over context-only MLM reconstruction, with consistent gains across different MLM architectures and existing language-model-aided methods.
AI.conclusion: Integrating channel-posterior information at both input and output stages of an MLM enables accurate, training-free multi-token reconstruction in a single inference pass.

title: Match and Correct: A Repeated Computational Motif in Evoformer Layers
comment: 27 pages, 4 figures (main text), 16 supplementary figures. NeurIPS 2026 Workshop: Interpretability for Discovery. Code: this https URL
summary: Triangle attention and triangle multiplicative updates form key components of the Evoformer, and were introduced specifically to encourage consistency with the triangle inequality. Yet whether representational changes over layers reduce triangle inequality violations has not been tested. We probe the pair representation at each of OpenFold's 48 Evoformer layers, decoding final C$_\alpha$-C$_\alpha$ distances with four probe families (a shared linear probe, per-protein linear probes, a sequence-separation-gated linear probe, and XGBoost) and reconstructing intermediate 3D structures from the decoded distances via multidimensional scaling. Across a cohort of 552 CAMEO and ECOD proteins, distance decodability ($R^2$) and reconstruction quality (TM-score) rise in early layers, plateau in the middle of the network, and rise again in late layers. Directly measuring triangle-inequality violations in the decoded distances reveals a similar, more exaggerated pattern: violations rise to a peak, fall to a trough, rise to a second peak, and only then decline, revealing two distinct episodes of decreasing normalized triangle violations rather than one continuous improvement. Cumulative forward and reverse layer-wise ablations of the Pair Transition, MSA Transition, and triangle mechanisms localize the regions in which specific Evoformer components become essential. The two stages of geometric refinement coincide with the use of the Pair Transition MLP and the triangle mechanisms. These results characterize how distance information and decoded geometric consistency evolve across layers, and motivate hypotheses about the computations behind their trajectories.

AI.tldr: This paper probes OpenFold's 48 Evoformer layers and reveals that distance decodability, 3D reconstruction quality, and triangle-inequality violations evolve in two distinct stages rather than one continuous improvement.
AI.motivation: Triangle attention and triangle multiplicative updates were designed to encourage triangle-inequality consistency in Evoformer, but whether representational changes across layers actually reduce triangle-inequality violations has not been tested.
AI.method: Across 552 CAMEO and ECOD proteins, the authors decode C_alpha-C_alpha distances from each layer's pair representation using four probe families, reconstruct 3D structures via multidimensional scaling, measure triangle-inequality violations, and perform cumulative forward and reverse layer-wise ablations of Pair Transition, MSA Transition, and triangle mechanisms.
AI.result: Distance decodability (R^2) and TM-score rise in early layers, plateau in the middle, and rise again in late layers, while normalized triangle violations rise to a peak, fall to a trough, rise to a second peak, and then decline; ablations show these two geometric refinement stages coincide with Pair Transition MLP and triangle mechanism usage.
AI.conclusion: Evoformer performs geometric refinement in two distinct episodes rather than monotonically, linking specific architectural components to each stage.

title: Policy Optimization With Multiple Verifiers via Pareto Rankings
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become an important approach to improving the reasoning capabilities of large language models. In tasks such as code generation and instruction following, multiple verifiers evaluate whether a response satisfies different requirements. Their outcomes provide detailed feedback about partial success, yet this feedback is commonly aggregated into a scalar reward for policy optimization. Rewarding only complete success discards distinctions among partial solutions, while counts and weighted sums impose comparisons between responses that satisfy different subsets of requirements. We introduce Partial-Order Likelihood Policy Optimization (POLPO), which learns from the comparisons established by verification without first constructing an aggregate reward. Pareto dominance identifies responses that satisfy additional requirements without losing any already satisfied, while leaving responses with conflicting outcomes incomparable. POLPO extends the listwise likelihood underlying Direct Preference Optimization by maximizing the total probability of all complete rankings consistent with these partial orders. This objective provides supervision from verified improvements even before complete solutions are available, without requiring a prescribed ordering of incomparable responses. Experiments on code generation and instruction following demonstrate improved learning efficiency and higher rates of complete requirement satisfaction compared with scalar-reward training. These results support partial-order likelihood as an effective approach to learning from multiple verifiers.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Partial-Order Likelihood Policy Optimization (POLPO) to train LLMs from multiple verifiers using Pareto dominance instead of scalar reward aggregation.
AI.motivation: In RLVR with multiple verifiers, rewarding only complete success discards partial-solution distinctions, while counts and weighted sums impose arbitrary comparisons between responses that satisfy different requirement subsets.
AI.method: POLPO uses Pareto dominance to identify responses that satisfy additional requirements without losing previously satisfied ones while leaving conflicting outcomes incomparable, and extends Direct Preference Optimization's listwise likelihood to maximize the total probability of all complete rankings consistent with these partial orders.
AI.result: Experiments on code generation and instruction following show improved learning efficiency and higher rates of complete requirement satisfaction compared with scalar-reward training.
AI.conclusion: Partial-order likelihood provides effective supervision from multiple verifiers before complete solutions are available without requiring a prescribed ordering of incomparable responses.

title: Assume/Guarantee Contracts for the Compositional Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning of Heterogeneous Teams
summary: Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) problems for heterogeneous teams require agents to collaborate to complete team tasks while making the best use of diverse agent capabilities. We introduce assume/guarantee contracts for heterogeneous multi-agent systems (AGC-MAS) and Iterative Heterogeneous Assignment for MARL (IHA-MARL). AGC-MAS contracts are compositional objects that encode the assumptions provided to, and the guarantees required of, each subtask contributing to the overall team task. We formulate contracts as tuples that specify a subtask, an automaton, timeout and success-probability requirements, and dispatch behavior. The automaton tracks an agent's high-level progress through the subtask associated with its contract and provides a natural mechanism for synchronization across contracts. Our abstraction enables robust interaction across heterogeneous low-level subtask implementations, allows heterogeneous agents to substitute for one another in satisfying contracts, and supports reuse of previously satisfied contracts in new team contexts. Having defined our theoretical framework, we develop a decomposition algorithm that breaks down a team task into a set of contracts. We then propose an iterative algorithm for task assignment and MARL that alternates between assigning contracts representing subtasks to individual agents, training the assigned agents to satisfy their contracts, and assessing their resulting capabilities to inform the next round of task assignments until the team's success probability meets the desired threshold. Our experimental results demonstrate the versatility of contracts in enabling agent substitution and contract reuse. Across three benchmarks with five seeds each, IHA-MARL achieves observed $100\%$ final evaluation success. In CPU timing pilots, comparable baselines required approximately $7$--$11\times$ more training-loop time.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces assume/guarantee contracts (AGC-MAS) and Iterative Heterogeneous Assignment for MARL (IHA-MARL) to compositionally decompose, assign, and train heterogeneous multi-agent teams.
AI.motivation: Heterogeneous multi-agent reinforcement learning requires coordinating diverse agent capabilities on team tasks, where flat or monolithic approaches lack compositional abstraction, agent substitutability, and subtask reuse.
AI.method: The authors formulate AGC-MAS contracts as tuples specifying a subtask, an automaton for high-level progress and synchronization, timeout and success-probability requirements, and dispatch behavior, alongside a task-decomposition algorithm and IHA-MARL, which alternates between assigning contracts, training agents, and reassessing capabilities.
AI.result: Across three benchmarks with five seeds each, IHA-MARL achieves 100% observed final evaluation success, while comparable baselines in CPU timing pilots required approximately 7 to 11 times more training-loop time; experiments also demonstrate agent substitution and contract reuse.
AI.conclusion: Assume/guarantee contracts provide a compositional, reusable abstraction that accelerates training and improves reliability in heterogeneous MARL.

title: CONTEXT-PCa: Evaluating the role of clinical context in MRI-based AI for detecting clinically significant prostate cancer (study protocol)
summary: The objective of this study is to investigate the role of clinical variables - their breadth, source, and quality - in the development, utility, and generalisability of an AI system for bi-parametric MRI (bpMRI)-based diagnosis of clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa). Clinical context is added to the published PI-CAI-2B image-only model, whose weights are fixed. The study cohort comprises 6,022 biparametric MRI cases from 4,540 patients at University College London Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust (2019-2024), of which 4,834 cases (3,632 patients) are held out for internal testing. Forty-three clinical variables are drawn from structured health records, clinical letters, MRI reports, and automated image measurements. The primary endpoint is the difference in the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) between the image-context and image-only models on the internal test set. Secondary analyses compare combining strategies, the contribution of individual variables, and performance across subgroups. All models are further tested on five external cohorts from primary diagnosis and population-based screening.

AI.tldr: This study protocol outlines CONTEXT-PCa, an evaluation of how adding 43 clinical variables to a fixed image-only bpMRI AI model (PI-CAI-2B) affects clinically significant prostate cancer diagnosis.
AI.motivation: The role of clinical variables—their breadth, source, and quality—in the development, utility, and generalisability of MRI-based AI for diagnosing clinically significant prostate cancer remains to be systematically established.
AI.method: Using 6,022 biparametric MRI cases from 4,540 patients at University College London Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust (4,834 cases held out for internal testing) plus five external cohorts, the study adds 43 clinical variables from structured health records, clinical letters, MRI reports, and automated image measurements to the fixed PI-CAI-2B model, with AUROC difference on the internal test set as the primary endpoint.
AI.result: As a study protocol, no empirical results are reported yet; secondary analyses will compare combining strategies, individual variable contributions, subgroup performance, and external generalisability.
AI.conclusion: CONTEXT-PCa will systematically quantify whether and how clinical context improves the diagnostic utility and generalisability of bpMRI-based prostate cancer AI.

title: Instructor-designed AI improves learning in a randomized trial across 19 universities
summary: Universities are alarmed by recent evidence that artificial intelligence (AI) can undermine learning, with students prescribed generic chatbots or centrally designed AI tools performing worse. In a pre-registered randomized controlled trial across 7,200 students at 19 universities over three semesters, we tested whether AI designed by frontline instructors can improve learning. We encouraged instructors to design AI solutions they believed would best help their students. Drawing on their unique knowledge of their classes and students, the instructors created a wide array of innovations. We show that these instructor-designed AI innovations improved student learning, measured by AI-proof assessments (proctored, in-person examinations). We found no change in student engagement, measured by course activity records, or satisfaction, measured by course evaluations. Our findings demonstrate that AI can improve student learning when its adoption is frontline-driven, with instructors empowered to design and refine AI solutions for their own classrooms.

AI.tldr: In a pre-registered randomized controlled trial across 7,200 students at 19 universities, instructor-designed AI innovations improved student learning on proctored in-person exams.
AI.motivation: Recent evidence suggests generic chatbots or centrally designed AI tools can undermine learning, raising the question of whether AI designed by frontline instructors for their own classes can instead improve outcomes.
AI.method: Over three semesters, instructors at 19 universities were encouraged to design AI solutions tailored to their own classrooms and students, evaluated in a pre-registered randomized controlled trial using proctored, in-person examinations, course activity records, and course evaluations.
AI.result: Instructor-designed AI innovations improved student learning on AI-proof proctored exams, with no observed change in student engagement (course activity records) or satisfaction (course evaluations).
AI.conclusion: Frontline-driven AI adoption, where instructors design and refine solutions for their own classrooms, can improve student learning.

title: Guiding AI Agents to Generate Conjectures by Encoding How Theorems Build on One Another
summary: Recently, LLMs have been making headlines, and headway, in mathematical research. Much of this work focuses on proving existing open conjectures. Deciding what to prove is harder and less studied, because of the lack of a clear criterion for what makes a conjecture worth pursuing. We present a method for conjecture generation that builds on the observation that mathematical theorems build on one another: new theorems can modify the setting or hypotheses of earlier theorems, strengthen their conclusions, or extend their scope. We encode these relationships in a new kind of graph, the Theorem Evolution Graph (TEG), which we instantiate as an online search method for LLM agents. An agent builds a TEG in two steps: (1) identifying relevant theorems from papers found by following citations backward and forward from a seed paper; and (2) comparing those theorems to record how one builds on another. LLM judges and an expert mathematician preferred TEG-generated conjectures over those from an unconstrained baseline. LLM judges favored TEG conjectures for significance, ambition, and insight, and favored baseline conjectures for plausibility. Ablations suggest a benefit from constructing and using a TEG even when the available papers are fixed.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the Theorem Evolution Graph (TEG) to guide LLM agents in generating mathematical conjectures by encoding how theorems build on one another.
AI.motivation: Most LLM math research focuses on proving existing open conjectures, whereas deciding what to conjecture is understudied due to the lack of clear criteria for what makes a conjecture worth pursuing.
AI.method: An LLM agent constructs a TEG in two steps: following citations backward and forward from a seed paper to identify relevant theorems, and comparing those theorems to record how new theorems modify hypotheses, strengthen conclusions, or extend scope.
AI.result: Both LLM judges and an expert mathematician preferred TEG-generated conjectures over an unconstrained baseline; LLM judges favored TEG conjectures for significance, ambition, and insight (and baseline for plausibility), and ablations indicate TEG helps even with fixed papers.
AI.conclusion: Encoding theorem-building relationships in a Theorem Evolution Graph provides effective structure for LLM agents to generate insightful mathematical conjectures.

title: CLEAR: Legible and Steerable Recommendation via Grounded Natural-Language Interests
summary: Modern recommenders keep learned preferences in representations people cannot inspect or change. We present CLEAR (Controllable and Legible End-to-end Architecture for Recommendation), an end-to-end system deployed at Meta and built around an editable natural-language interest layer. CLEAR makes a ranked subset of inferred interests readable and stores accepted additions and suppressions as authoritative preference state. Behavioral grounding maps each inferred interest back to supporting events in the user's own history. The resulting interest object is also a serving address: its label and profile-conditioned rewrites drive lexical retrieval, its supporting events seed behavioral retrieval, its projection queries an embedding index, and its stable identity supports ranking, attribution, and exposure control. A fresh user declaration may precede behavioral support, so it enters through the same serving identity and initially draws candidates from topical retrieval. Ranking makes those candidates competitive, while a delivery controller observes attributable exposure and replenishes underexposed interests. Direct user review found that users rated about 88.5% of displayed interests accurate. In an offline benchmark using a shared evaluation protocol, the Specialized 3B generator reached 0.3967 mean-user F1@10, compared with 0.3633 for Gemini 2.5 Pro and 0.1911 for the prior generator. For a newly declared interest, a user-randomized cumulative ablation measured same-day delivery losses of 8.7 percentage points for added-interest ranking terms, 11.1 for reserved top-slot insertion, and 13.7 for interest-conditioned candidate sourcing, conditional on the tested removal sequence. CLEAR components have operated in production for over one year; the system spans four surfaces on Instagram and Facebook, with an interest layer people can inspect, correct, and use to direct recommendations.

AI.tldr: This paper presents CLEAR, an end-to-end recommendation architecture deployed at Meta that exposes an editable, behaviorally grounded natural-language interest layer for user inspection and control.
AI.motivation: Modern recommenders store learned preferences in opaque representations that users cannot inspect or directly modify.
AI.method: CLEAR surfaces a ranked subset of inferred interests grounded to supporting user events, stores user additions and suppressions as authoritative state, and uses each interest object as a serving address for lexical retrieval, behavioral retrieval, embedding queries, ranking, attribution, and delivery control.
AI.result: Users rated about 88.5% of displayed interests accurate; offline, a Specialized 3B generator reached 0.3967 mean-user F1@10 versus 0.3633 for Gemini 2.5 Pro and 0.1911 for the prior generator; user-randomized ablations for newly declared interests measured same-day delivery losses of 8.7, 11.1, and 13.7 percentage points for removing ranking terms, reserved top-slot insertion, and interest-conditioned sourcing, respectively.
AI.conclusion: CLEAR has operated in production for over a year across four surfaces on Instagram and Facebook, demonstrating that legible, user-steerable natural-language interest layers are practical at scale.

title: Conditional Endorsement: Simulating How Adults with Different Skills Evaluate Canada's National AI Strategy
comment: This research was funded by the Future Skills Centre, and an earlier version of this pre-print was submitted as a report to them
summary: Canada's 2026 national AI strategy, AI for All, commits to free AI training for everyone and to expanding business AI adoption, yet it is difficult to anticipate whether these policies will reach adults with uneven skills and circumstances. We ask how adults with diverse skills might rate these policies on support, effectiveness, and personal benefit, how their skills and circumstances shape these evaluations, and what implementation conditions they raise. We built 3,200 generative agents from a weighted sample of the Programme for the International Assessment of Adult Competencies (PIAAC) Cycle 2 respondents, collected their ratings and explanations for 20 policies, and analyzed dialogues between agents with contrasting ratings. The agents supported nearly every policy but were far less confident that they would improve adult AI literacy or benefit them personally. This gap widened as digital technology use declined: agents modeled on adults who had never used a digital device still endorsed the policies but rarely expected to benefit. Agents traced the gap to participation costs, hard-to-exercise rights, and limited community control, and their dialogues specified these conditions rather than resolving disagreement. We describe this pattern as conditional endorsement and argue that AI literacy policy should be designed and evaluated for adults with the fewest digital skills.

AI.tldr: Using 3,200 generative agents modeled on PIAAC Cycle 2 respondents, this study finds that adults broadly endorse Canada's 2026 national AI strategy but doubt it will benefit those with fewer digital skills.
AI.motivation: Canada's AI for All strategy commits to free AI training and business AI adoption, but it is difficult to anticipate how adults with uneven skills and circumstances will evaluate or benefit from these policies.
AI.method: The authors construct 3,200 generative agents from a weighted sample of PIAAC Cycle 2 respondents, collect their ratings and explanations across 20 policies on support, effectiveness, and personal benefit, and analyze dialogues between agents with contrasting ratings.
AI.result: Agents supported nearly every policy but were much less confident about personal benefit or improved adult AI literacy, with this gap widening as digital technology use declined; dialogues traced the gap to participation costs, hard-to-exercise rights, and limited community control.
AI.conclusion: The authors term this pattern conditional endorsement and argue that AI literacy policies should be designed and evaluated for adults with the fewest digital skills.

title: Learning inadequacy of Bayesian neural operators for PDE-constrained inference and design
summary: Partial differential equations (PDEs) underpin predictive modeling across science, engineering and medicine. Their use in digital twins, parameter inference and optimal design requires repeated solutions across parameters and scenarios. For nonlinear, transient and multiphysics systems, these calculations can make numerical simulation prohibitively expensive. Here we introduce the residual-informed Bayesian neural operator (RI-BNO), which learns operator inadequacy using a posteriori error estimates from the governing PDEs and incorporates its correction and uncertainty into Bayesian training and prediction. We establish local error bounds for the residual-informed estimates under stability and smoothness assumptions. We demonstrate RI-BNO on a non-linear reaction-diffusion benchmark with DeepONet and latent-subspace architectures, Markov chain Monte Carlo inference of glioma parameter fields from magnetic resonance imaging, and Monte Carlo risk-averse optimization of three-dimensional thermal breaks in building envelopes under manufacturing uncertainty. Across the evaluated examples, RI-BNO improves agreement with finite element (FE) reference predictions, parameter posteriors and optimized designs while using half as many full nonlinear or transient training simulations as the vanilla Bayesian neural operator (vBNO). For thermal break design, online optimization time decreases from 178 hours with the FE model to 18 minutes with RI-BNO. These results demonstrate the value of explicit inadequacy modeling in neural operators for reliable PDE-based inference and design.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the residual-informed Bayesian neural operator (RI-BNO), which learns operator inadequacy from PDE a posteriori error estimates to improve PDE-constrained inference and design.
AI.motivation: Repeatedly solving nonlinear, transient, and multiphysics PDEs for digital twins, parameter inference, and optimal design is computationally prohibitive, while standard neural operators lack explicit inadequacy modeling.
AI.method: RI-BNO uses a posteriori error estimates from the governing PDEs to learn operator inadequacy, incorporates the correction and its uncertainty into Bayesian training and prediction, and establishes local error bounds under stability and smoothness assumptions.
AI.result: Across a nonlinear reaction-diffusion benchmark (with DeepONet and latent-subspace architectures), MRI glioma parameter inference, and 3D thermal break optimization, RI-BNO improves agreement with finite element references using half as many full simulations as vanilla BNO, and cuts online thermal break optimization time from 178 hours (FE) to 18 minutes.
AI.conclusion: Explicit PDE-residual inadequacy modeling makes Bayesian neural operators more accurate and sample-efficient for reliable scientific inference and design.

title: A Hybrid State Space-Attention Architecture for Forecasting the Trajectories of Battery Degradation
summary: Early-life battery degradation trajectory forecasting aims to predict a battery cell's full state-of-health (SOH) trajectory from its initial charge-discharge cycles, potentially reducing cell qualification and evaluation time from months to days. Despite recent advances, accurate forecasting remains challenging for emerging battery chemistries, data-scarce domains, and cells exhibiting degradation behaviors beyond those observed during training. Existing state-of-the-art approaches increasingly rely on model scaling, large language model-derived aging-condition embeddings, and extensive fold-specific hyperparameter tuning, raising concerns about computational efficiency, reproducibility, and generalization. This work introduces DecayFormer, a compact hybrid state-space and attention architecture designed for early-life degradation trajectory forecasting. DecayFormer combines cycle-level selective recurrence, using a single scalar state per channel, with an attention mechanism queried by the recurrent state. It further incorporates state-of-charge (SOC) interval statistics and a master curve head that jointly estimates a scalar lifetime and a monotonically non-increasing SOH profile parameterized by normalized lifetime. We evaluate DecayFormer on the BatteryLife benchmark using all 22 aging-condition-exclusive folds, with a single run per fold and one fixed configuration across all folds, without fold-specific tuning. DecayFormer achieves mean test MAPE values of 2.25% on Li-ion, 2.76% on CALB, 0.95% on Na-ion, and 7.19% on Zn-ion. These results demonstrate the potential of compact sequence models to deliver accurate early-life degradation forecasts across diverse battery chemistries and aging conditions, without relying on extensive model scaling or per-fold optimization.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces DecayFormer, a compact hybrid state-space and attention architecture for early-life battery degradation trajectory forecasting across diverse chemistries without fold-specific tuning.
AI.motivation: Existing early-life battery SOH forecasting methods increasingly rely on model scaling, LLM-derived aging embeddings, and extensive fold-specific hyperparameter tuning, harming efficiency, reproducibility, and generalization to emerging chemistries.
AI.method: DecayFormer combines cycle-level selective recurrence (one scalar state per channel) with attention queried by the recurrent state, incorporates SOC interval statistics, and uses a master curve head that jointly predicts a scalar lifetime and a monotonically non-increasing SOH profile.
AI.result: Evaluated on all 22 aging-condition-exclusive folds of BatteryLife with a single fixed configuration and one run per fold, DecayFormer achieves mean test MAPE of 2.25% on Li-ion, 2.76% on CALB, 0.95% on Na-ion, and 7.19% on Zn-ion.
AI.conclusion: Compact hybrid sequence models can deliver accurate, reproducible early-life battery degradation forecasts across chemistries without heavy scaling or per-fold tuning.

title: Agent-Guided Process Verification for Mathematical Self-Correction
summary: Large language models have made substantial progress in mathematical reasoning, yet in complex multi-step reasoning, an error at any step may propagate along an incorrect path, and the resulting solution may omit necessary branches. Existing natural-language reflection methods often struggle to locate critical errors precisely, while outcome verification typically checks only whether the available candidate answers satisfy the problem conditions and can therefore overlook necessary branches. To address these limitations, we propose Agent-Guided Process Verification (AGPV) for mathematical self-correction. AGPV decomposes the current solution into an ordered sequence of key claims, verifies them individually while invoking a shared mathematical toolbox when needed, and stops upon detecting the first error. A summarization agent converts the failure evidence into a diagnosis that guides a correction agent to re-derive the subsequent solution from that point; AGPV then adapts the next verification iteration to the revised solution. AGPV also verifies solution completeness. We further prove that AGPV guarantees solution correctness and completeness when key claims provide sufficient coverage and local verification is reliable, provided that all key claims pass verification. The implementation compresses long working contexts and reuses successful tool results within each problem. We evaluate AGPV on five challenging mathematical reasoning datasets with four models from DeepSeek, Qwen, and GPT. AGPV achieves an average accuracy of 63.8%, outperforming the strongest among the representative baselines evaluated (50.3%) by 13.5 percentage points, with higher repair coverage than the programmatic-verification baselines.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Agent-Guided Process Verification (AGPV) to improve mathematical self-correction in LLMs by decomposing solutions into ordered claims, verifying them with tools, and repairing from the first error.
AI.motivation: In multi-step math reasoning, natural-language reflection struggles to pinpoint critical errors, while outcome verification only checks candidate answers and can miss necessary solution branches.
AI.method: AGPV decomposes a solution into an ordered sequence of key claims, verifies each claim with a shared mathematical toolbox, stops at the first error, uses a summarization agent to diagnose the failure for a correction agent that re-derives from that point, and checks solution completeness while compressing context and reusing tool results.
AI.result: Across five mathematical reasoning datasets and four models from DeepSeek, Qwen, and GPT, AGPV achieves 63.8% average accuracy, outperforming the strongest evaluated baseline (50.3%) by 13.5 percentage points with higher repair coverage than programmatic-verification baselines.
AI.conclusion: Step-level claim decomposition, tool-assisted diagnosis, and completeness checking substantially improve LLM mathematical self-correction.

title: FundingClaw: Automated Grant Proposal Writing Agents System
summary: Grant proposal writing remains a manual, labor-intensive bottleneck: proposals must satisfy rigid, agency-specific templates, and the same intellectual content must be repeatedly re-encoded into incompatible formats across funding organizations. We introduce FundingClaw, a multi-agent framework built on template-driven skill selection, where a Template Parser ingests any agency's specification and selects the appropriate writing skills for each stage, so that one research brief can produce compliant proposals for NSFC, NSF, KAKENHI, or ERC without modifying generation logic. A blueprint-skeleton strategy drafts a structured outline before any prose is written, mitigating the semantic drift that plagues long-form generation. Three sequential stages produce the rationale, research content, and research foundation sections, with multi-source verification of the PI's record and optional PDF-grounded extraction of representative works. Optional human feedback checkpoints and a closed-loop self-review complete the pipeline. Evaluated on ten research topics with an eight-dimension rubric, FundingClaw outperforms the baseline, narrowing the gap with human level for laborious funding proposal. The code will be released upon acceptance.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces FundingClaw, a multi-agent framework that generates agency-compliant grant proposals from a single research brief using template-driven skill selection and blueprint-skeleton outlining.
AI.motivation: Grant proposal writing is a manual bottleneck requiring repeated re-encoding of the same research ideas into rigid, incompatible templates across funding agencies.
AI.method: FundingClaw uses a Template Parser to ingest agency specifications (NSFC, NSF, KAKENHI, ERC) and select writing skills, drafts a blueprint-skeleton outline to prevent semantic drift, sequentially generates rationale, research content, and research foundation sections with multi-source PI record verification and optional PDF extraction, and includes human feedback checkpoints and closed-loop self-review.
AI.result: Evaluated on ten research topics with an eight-dimension rubric, FundingClaw outperforms the baseline and narrows the gap with human-level grant proposals.
AI.conclusion: Template-driven skill selection and structured outlining enable automated multi-agent systems to adapt one research brief across diverse funding agency formats.

title: From Sensors to Silicon: Causal Cross-Layer Self-Healing Edge AI for Secure and Energy-Adaptive IoT Systems
summary: The migration of artificial intelligence from centralized cloud infrastructure to resource-constrained Internet-of-Things (IoT) devices reduces communication latency and improves data locality, but it also tightly couples sensing quality, inference behavior, microarchitectural activity, hardware reliability, security, and energy management within the same physical node. Existing edge-intelligence solutions predominantly address these dimensions in isolation, making it difficult to determine whether an observed degradation originates from sensor malfunction, data-distribution shift, malicious execution, hardware faults, or resource and thermal stress. This paper presents a causal cross-layer self-healing Edge-AI framework that continuously observes synchronized telemetry spanning sensor health, inference uncertainty, processor hardware-performance counters, accelerator and memory activity, power and thermal state, and communication conditions. A temporally informed causal reasoning engine estimates the most probable origin of abnormal behavior and quantifies diagnostic uncertainty, including under concurrent perturbations.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a causal cross-layer self-healing Edge-AI framework that fuses synchronized hardware, sensor, inference, and communication telemetry to diagnose faults on IoT devices.
AI.motivation: Deploying AI on resource-constrained IoT devices couples sensing, inference, microarchitecture, reliability, security, and energy on one node, while existing solutions handle these dimensions in isolation and cannot pinpoint the origin of observed degradations.
AI.method: The framework continuously collects synchronized telemetry across sensor health, inference uncertainty, processor hardware-performance counters, accelerator/memory activity, power/thermal state, and communication conditions, and applies a temporally informed causal reasoning engine to estimate the most probable fault origin and diagnostic uncertainty, even under concurrent perturbations.
AI.result: The abstract describes the framework's architecture and capabilities without reporting quantitative experimental benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Temporally informed causal reasoning over cross-layer telemetry offers a unified path toward self-healing, secure, and energy-adaptive Edge-AI IoT systems.

title: LABEL: Literature Asymmetry between Efficacy and Limits in Drug Knowledge and Language Models
comment: 27 pages (9 main + supplementary material), 8 figures, 7 tables
summary: Every medication comes with two types of medical facts: indications, which describe what conditions the drug treats (benefits), and contraindications, which describe who must avoid it to prevent serious harm (safety limits). Although contraindications are critical for patient safety and FDA regulations require listing them as rigorously as indications, we find that contraindications are far less documented than indications in general prose. In this paper, we measure how often these texts contain both facts across 574 drugs from PrimeKG by comparing a drug's indications against its own contraindications. Across Wikipedia articles and PubMed abstracts, we find that reference prose names a drug's benefits about twice as often as its safety limits (within-drug odds ratio 2.19). We call this documentation gap LABEL (Literature Asymmetry between Efficacy and Limits). Language models mirror this gap. As we scale Qwen2.5 from 0.5B to 14B, accuracy on indications rises by 18.3 points, whereas accuracy on contraindications remains flat near random guessing. However, when we provide models with a retrieved passage that states the answer, they use safety facts just as effectively as benefits. Furthermore, routing safety questions to official FDA labels boosts accuracy by 15.8 points whenever the label states the fact. Overall, our findings show that models fail on medication safety not because they cannot reason about risk, but because free-text corpora lack safety facts. Clinical AI systems should therefore route medication-safety questions to official regulatory labels and structured databases rather than relying on general public records. Code and data are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies LABEL, a documentation asymmetry where medical prose mentions drug indications roughly twice as often as contraindications, causing LLMs to fail on medication safety unless routed to official FDA labels.
AI.motivation: Contraindications are critical for patient safety, yet it is unclear why language models perform poorly on medication safety limits compared to drug benefits.
AI.method: The authors measure indication versus contraindication coverage across 574 drugs from PrimeKG in Wikipedia and PubMed, evaluate Qwen2.5 (0.5B to 14B) on both fact types, and test retrieval-augmented generation and routing to official FDA labels.
AI.result: Reference prose names benefits about twice as often as safety limits (within-drug odds ratio 2.19); scaling Qwen2.5 from 0.5B to 14B improves indication accuracy by 18.3 points while contraindication accuracy stays near random guessing, whereas providing a retrieved passage equalizes performance and routing to FDA labels boosts accuracy by 15.8 points when the label states the fact.
AI.conclusion: LLMs fail on medication safety due to missing safety facts in free-text corpora rather than reasoning inability, so clinical AI systems should route safety queries to official regulatory labels and structured databases.

title: Executable Archaeology: Reanimating the Logic Theorist
comment: This paper builds upon a previous ArXiv paper of a similar name: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.13514. This paper is NOT a mere rehash of the previous paper; appropriate citations and comparison are provided in the discussion. This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible
summary: The Logic Theorist (LT), created by Allen Newell, J. C. Shaw, and Herbert Simon in 1955--1956, is regarded by some as the first artificial intelligence program. It was originally simulated by hand and written in a pseudocode called the Logic Language (LL), which was later called Information Processing Language One (IPL-I). LT was revised many times. The first machine-executed version was written in IPL-II and ran on the JOHNNIAC, and a late version was published in 1963 by Einar Stefferud as a pedagogical document and written in IPL-V, the only version of IPL that was formally released to the public. We describe a reanimation of both the IPL-I (LL) version of LT and the 1963 IPL-V version. Comparing the two reanimations illuminates the process of the invention of early AI algorithms and computer languages.

AI.tldr: This paper describes the executable reanimation of both the 1955-1956 IPL-I (Logic Language) and 1963 IPL-V versions of the Logic Theorist, one of the earliest AI programs.
AI.motivation: Studying early AI programs like the Logic Theorist only through static historical texts obscures how early AI algorithms and programming languages were actually invented and evolved.
AI.method: The authors create executable reanimations of the original hand-simulated IPL-I (LL) version and Einar Stefferud's 1963 pedagogical IPL-V version of the Logic Theorist and compare them.
AI.result: Comparing the two reanimated versions illuminates the invention and evolution of early AI algorithms and computer languages.
AI.conclusion: Executable archaeology provides concrete insight into the foundational design of early AI systems and programming languages.

title: When Does Confidence Reveal Problem Difficulty?
summary: While confidence signals are commonly evaluated for their ability to predict a model's own correctness, their relationship with problem difficulty remains less understood. In this work, we investigate a wide range of confidence-related signals and whether they can serve as indicators of problem difficulty across various task domains. We find that perturbation inconsistency, semantic entropy, and solution length exhibit strong associations with population difficulty than token-level uncertainty. Notably, these relationships persist even when restricting the analysis to problems correctly answered by the focal model, suggesting that such signals capture information about difficulty beyond their ability to predict the model's own correctness. We further explore applications of these signals, illustrating the potential and limitations of using confidence-related signals to guide inference-time decisions. Our findings highlight the utility of model-specific signals as imperfect but informative proxies for population-level problem difficulty.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates confidence-related signals across task domains and finds that perturbation inconsistency, semantic entropy, and solution length track population-level problem difficulty better than token-level uncertainty.
AI.motivation: Confidence signals are widely used to predict a model's own correctness, but their relationship to broader problem difficulty—even on problems the model answers correctly—is poorly understood.
AI.method: The authors evaluate a range of confidence-related signals across multiple task domains, analyzing their association with population difficulty (including when restricted to correctly answered problems) and exploring their use for inference-time decisions.
AI.result: Perturbation inconsistency, semantic entropy, and solution length show stronger associations with population difficulty than token-level uncertainty, and these relationships persist even on problems the focal model answers correctly.
AI.conclusion: Model-specific confidence signals serve as imperfect but informative proxies for population-level problem difficulty, offering utility for inference-time decision making.

title: What Moves a LoCoMo Score? Memory Context, Answer Prompts and Judges
comment: 13 pages, 2 figures. Answers, judge verdicts, human-check grades and scoring script: this https URL
summary: LoCoMo is a widely reported benchmark for long-term conversational memory, but published scores mix memory quality with choices of answer prompt, judge and baseline layout that are rarely reported together. We measure how much these choices move a score, and evaluate Becos, a team memory system for coding agents, as a black box under all of them: ten conversations (1,540 questions), two answer models (gpt-4o-mini, gpt-4.1-mini), two answer prompts and three LLM judges, against a whole-conversation baseline rerun under identical conditions. Changing only the judge moves a score by up to 7.2 points and changing only the answer prompt by up to 9.3. A blind human check of 150 answers finds the judges reliable when they agree, and the primary judge's errors on disputed answers working against Becos rather than for it. Becos answers from a context with 90% fewer characters than the whole conversation. Its configuration was developed on LoCoMo itself, so there is no held-out set. With gpt-4o-mini answers it scores clearly higher than the whole conversation (79.7 vs 73.0 with the short prompt, paired 95% interval for the difference +3.8 to +9.5; 88.8 vs 77.5 with a step-by-step prompt). With gpt-4.1-mini answers the two score about the same (83.2 vs 83.1; 92.5 vs 92.1). We release every answer and verdict and the scoring script.

AI.tldr: This paper measures how answer prompts, LLM judges, and memory context affect LoCoMo benchmark scores and evaluates the Becos team memory system under controlled conditions.
AI.motivation: Published LoCoMo scores conflate memory quality with unreported choices of answer prompt, judge, and baseline layout.
AI.method: The authors evaluate Becos as a black box against a whole-conversation baseline across 10 conversations (1,540 questions), two answer models (gpt-4o-mini, gpt-4.1-mini), two answer prompts, and three LLM judges, supplemented by a blind human check of 150 answers.
AI.result: Changing only the judge shifts scores by up to 7.2 points and changing only the prompt shifts scores by up to 9.3 points; using 90% fewer characters than the full conversation, Becos outperforms the baseline with gpt-4o-mini (79.7 vs 73.0 short prompt; 88.8 vs 77.5 step-by-step prompt) and matches it with gpt-4.1-mini (83.2 vs 83.1; 92.5 vs 92.1), though Becos was developed on LoCoMo without a held-out set.
AI.conclusion: LoCoMo evaluations are highly sensitive to prompt and judge choices, requiring identical controlled conditions and full release of scripts and verdicts for fair comparison.

title: STaSBO: LLM-Guided Strategy Planning and Configuration Selection for Bayesian Optimization
summary: Bayesian optimization (BO) enables sample-efficient search for expensive black-box problems, but its performance depends strongly on surrogate-acquisition configurations whose suitability varies across problems and optimization states. We take a significant step toward LLM-driven strategic management of BO with STaSBO, a task-agnostic meta-controller that plans search behavior and jointly selects surrogate-acquisition configurations, while numerical BO retains responsibility for probabilistic modeling and candidate generation. STaSBO comprises two coordinated stages: strategy planning and strategy-guided configuration selection. A structured memory system connects prior plans, configuration selections, and candidate behaviors to optimization states, allowing the controller to revise its trajectory summary and behavioral plans during planning. To navigate the large joint configuration space, the selection stage shortlists configurations using surrogate fit evidence. Prospective BO-action diagnostics then expose the candidate behaviors, supporting final joint selection against the behavioral plans. Across 12 synthetic mathematical and 10 scientific and engineering application tasks, STaSBO achieves the best average rank against 11 baselines: 2.17 and 2.60, compared with 4.08 and 4.10 for the strongest baseline in each suite, respectively.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces STaSBO, an LLM-guided meta-controller that plans search strategy and jointly selects surrogate-acquisition configurations for Bayesian optimization.
AI.motivation: Bayesian optimization performance depends heavily on surrogate-acquisition configurations whose suitability varies across problems and optimization states.
AI.method: STaSBO pairs strategy planning (using a structured memory linking prior plans, configurations, and candidate behaviors to optimization states) with strategy-guided configuration selection (shortlisting via surrogate fit evidence and using prospective BO-action diagnostics for final selection), while numerical BO handles probabilistic modeling and candidate generation.
AI.result: Across 12 synthetic mathematical tasks and 10 scientific and engineering tasks, STaSBO achieves the best average rank against 11 baselines (2.17 and 2.60, versus 4.08 and 4.10 for the strongest baseline in each suite).
AI.conclusion: Separating strategic LLM planning and configuration selection from numerical BO modeling yields strong, task-agnostic optimization performance.

title: Mem2Fair: Online Fairness Control for Text-to-Video Generation via Fair Memory
summary: Text-to-video (T2V) generation models can produce systematically unfair demographic outcomes when prompts leave protected attributes unspecified. For example, prompts describing nurses without specifying gender may disproportionately generate videos depicting female nurses. Mitigating unfairness in T2V generation is particularly challenging: training-based methods that modify model internals require architecture-specific access and risk disrupting temporal consistency, while sampling-based methods often incur costly pre-deployment video generation. We present the first conditional online approachability formulation of attribute-level fairness for T2V generation. Building on this formulation, we introduce Mem2Fair, a plug-and-play framework that maintains concept-conditioned Fair Memory. Using generated videos at inference time as feedback, Mem2Fair selects prompt-level attribute interventions based on the deviation from each concept's prescribed fairness target, without training or separate pre-deployment sampling. Experiments demonstrate that Mem2Fair consistently improves fairness over the unmodified generator and existing baselines across multiple demographic attributes, prompt settings, and target distributions, while maintaining comparable prompt-video alignment and video quality. We further demonstrate its effectiveness on commercial black-box T2V models.

AI.tldr: This paper presents Mem2Fair, a plug-and-play inference-time framework that improves demographic fairness in text-to-video (T2V) generation using concept-conditioned Fair Memory.
AI.motivation: T2V models can produce demographically skewed outputs when prompts omit protected attributes, while training-based fixes risk temporal consistency and sampling-based fixes require costly pre-deployment video generation.
AI.method: Formulating attribute-level fairness as conditional online approachability, Mem2Fair maintains concept-conditioned Fair Memory and uses generated videos at inference time as feedback to select prompt-level attribute interventions based on deviations from target distributions, without training or pre-deployment sampling.
AI.result: Experiments show Mem2Fair consistently improves fairness over unmodified generators and existing baselines across multiple demographic attributes, prompt settings, and target distributions—including commercial black-box T2V models—while preserving prompt-video alignment and video quality.
AI.conclusion: Inference-time feedback with concept-conditioned Fair Memory enables practical, model-agnostic fairness control for T2V generation.

title: Can an Agent Rethink What It Knows? Selective Scene Memory Updates in a Changing World
summary: Task configurations in factories, warehouses, and everyday physical environments change over time. Physical AI systems therefore need to incorporate new facts into scene memory while preserving valid information about equipment, objects, and operating constraints.
