We study updates to this parametric semantic-memory layer and present a joint evaluation of correction and preservation under finite update budgets. At fixed current fact count and memory parameter count, the protocol combines independent single-fact updates, budget trajectories, old-to-new answer diagnostics, and first stable success. Using a frozen 4B language model with late-layer LoRA, we evaluate seven preparation conditions and six update budgets on four-field synthetic semantic configurations. In two exposure-matched history conditions, increasing the budget from eight to 32 updates raises joint success from 6.25% to 94.79% and 91.15%, respectively, while exact obsolete-value outputs fall from 174/192 and 166/192 to zero. Constant32, which matches preparation steps but repeatedly trains on unchanged content during the first 32 events, achieves higher early joint success at eight steps (53.65%); at 32 steps, it reaches 85.42%, below both changing-history conditions. These results distinguish rapid correction under a small budget from simultaneous correctness of the new fact and the other three facts after further training. For both changing histories, most cases remain jointly correct at all subsequent measured points from step 16 onward. Output analysis shows that short-budget failures primarily retain the old value; repeated training on the new fact together with the other current facts progressively replaces these obsolete answers.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates how a frozen 4B language model with late-layer LoRA updates parametric semantic scene memory, distinguishing rapid single-fact correction from preserving all current facts.
AI.motivation: Physical AI systems must update parametric scene memory with new facts as environments change while preserving still-valid information about equipment, objects, and constraints.
AI.method: Using a frozen 4B LM with late-layer LoRA on four-field synthetic semantic configurations, the authors evaluate seven preparation conditions and six update budgets with independent single-fact updates, budget trajectories, old-to-new answer diagnostics, and first stable success.
AI.result: Increasing the budget from 8 to 32 updates raises joint success in two exposure-matched changing-history conditions from 6.25% to 94.79% and 91.15% (cutting obsolete-value outputs from 174/192 and 166/192 to zero), whereas Constant32 achieves higher early success at 8 steps (53.65%) but lower final success at 32 steps (85.42%).
AI.conclusion: Short-budget failures mainly retain obsolete values, and repeated training on the new fact alongside other current facts is needed to achieve joint correctness and stability.

title: CompoundingKernel: Self-Improving from Zero to First
comment: 47 pages, 23 figures, 6 tables. URL: this https URL
summary: We present CompoundingKernel, a self-improving agent system that writes GPU kernels by search. As of 2026-11-11, its generated kernels rank #1 on the public L1, L2 and Quantization boards of SOL-ExecBench (NVIDIA B200). They have held #1 on L1 since 2026-10-27, albeit a short loss on 2026-11-07. All 235 problems have a site-verified correct kernel; on the 209 public-board problems they are 4.40x faster than the benchmark's reference baseline. The search starts from zero: agents get each problem's PyTorch definition but no reference kernels or official scores. A per-problem archive outside the model holds every correct kernel and its lineage. An LLM controller reads it, picks a parent or a new design, and gives each parallel child agent one direction. Checks outside the model decide correctness. At equal wall time, it beat a coded UCB style tree on 35 of 38 problems by making 2.4x as many correct attempts. Over a thousand agents ran at once, and one warm restart fix raised their evaluation rate 3.6x. We find that the rate of reliable measurements, not the number of agents, limits how far such a search scales. Our code and kernels are available on URL.

AI.tldr: This paper presents CompoundingKernel, a self-improving LLM agent system that searches for GPU kernels from scratch and ranks #1 on SOL-ExecBench's public L1, L2, and Quantization boards.
AI.motivation: Writing high-performance GPU kernels is challenging, and it is unclear how far automated LLM search can scale without reference kernels or official scores.
AI.method: Starting from PyTorch definitions alone, an LLM controller reads an external per-problem archive of verified correct kernels and their lineage, selects a parent or new design, and dispatches parallel child agents with external correctness checks.
AI.result: CompoundingKernel produced site-verified correct kernels for all 235 problems, achieving 4.40x speedup over the reference baseline on the 209 public-board problems (NVIDIA B200), beating a coded UCB-style tree on 35 of 38 problems at equal wall time with 2.4x more correct attempts, and scaling to over 1,000 concurrent agents where a warm restart fix raised evaluation rate 3.6x.
AI.conclusion: The rate of reliable external measurements, rather than agent count, is the primary bottleneck limiting how far self-improving GPU kernel search scales.

title: Auditable Authorization for LLM Agents: Empirical Evidence Across Model, Harness, and Workflow Layers
summary: Human approval provides effective control only if rejected work stops and authorized work completes. We formalize refusal safety and bounded authorization completeness, and audit three execution boundaries: the model selects a call, the harness schedules and resumes it, and the workflow routes the decision to a protected effect. Paired decisions, exact traces, and native business-state witnesses support experiments with three models, five prompt arms, four runtime approval designs, two additional framework replays, and 100 public workflow sources. The paired model panel leaves seven of 300 approvals unfinished despite zero denied effects; parallel confirmation loses an approved branch in three tasks per model, restoration omits 336/672 CrewAI approvals, and four of 59 comparable n8n workflows execute after Reject. Comparing intent, generated calls, dispatch, and native effects identifies the first observable divergence and its repair target. This yields a practical audit contract that makes both refusal safety and authorization completeness independently verifiable, converting human approval from a procedural formality into an enforceable control boundary between intent and real-world effect.

AI.tldr: This paper formalizes refusal safety and bounded authorization completeness for human-in-the-loop LLM agents and audits where approval guarantees break across model, harness, and workflow layers.
AI.motivation: Human approval only provides effective control if rejected actions stop and authorized actions complete, yet failures across execution layers can violate both guarantees.
AI.method: The authors audit three execution boundaries (model call selection, harness scheduling/resumption, workflow routing) using paired decisions, exact traces, and native business-state witnesses across three models, five prompt arms, four runtime approval designs, two framework replays, and 100 public workflow sources.
AI.result: Audits reveal concrete breakdowns: the paired model panel leaves 7/300 approvals unfinished, parallel confirmation loses an approved branch in 3 tasks per model, restoration omits 336/672 CrewAI approvals, and 4/59 comparable n8n workflows execute after Reject.
AI.conclusion: Comparing intent, generated calls, dispatch, and native effects pinpoints the first divergence and repair target, turning human approval into a verifiable control boundary.

title: Agentic On-Policy Distillation Implicitly Reshapes LLMs' ReAct Patterns
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) transfers specialized capabilities to language-model agents, but its cross-domain effects on interaction remain unclear. We investigate how OPD reshapes ReAct interaction patterns across mathematics, ALFWorld, and $\tau^2$-bench, focusing on reasoning, actions, and observation acquisition. General-reasoning supervision reduces mathematical tool attempts from 70.4% to 14.4% while increasing accuracy from 16.7% to 38.0%; code-interpreter supervision improves household actions and retail queries. In contrast, ALFWorld supervision reduces $\tau^2$-bench accuracy from 41.5% to 6.6%, accompanied by frequent tool calls that violate user-information dependencies. To address negative transfer using only source-domain training trajectories, we explore selective OPD guided by teacher preference changes before and after domain-specific RL. Retaining the top 95% of positions raises $\tau^2$ accuracy from 11.5% to 29.9% with a source-learning trade-off.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how on-policy distillation (OPD) reshapes ReAct interaction patterns across domains and proposes selective OPD to mitigate negative cross-domain transfer.
AI.motivation: While OPD transfers specialized capabilities to LLM agents, its cross-domain effects on reasoning, action, and observation-acquisition patterns remain poorly understood.
AI.method: The authors analyze OPD across mathematics, ALFWorld, and tau^2-bench, and test selective OPD guided by teacher preference changes before and after domain-specific RL using only source-domain trajectories.
AI.result: General-reasoning supervision cuts math tool attempts from 70.4% to 14.4% while raising accuracy from 16.7% to 38.0%, whereas ALFWorld supervision drops tau^2-bench accuracy from 41.5% to 6.6% due to dependency-violating tool calls; retaining the top 95% of positions in selective OPD raises tau^2 accuracy from 11.5% to 29.9% with a source-learning trade-off.
AI.conclusion: OPD implicitly alters agentic ReAct behaviors across domains, and filtering distillation positions by teacher preference shifts can substantially reduce negative transfer.

title: Beyond Clumsy Agentic Tool Calling: How Cueing and Spotting Make the Difference
comment: The code of reference implementation and instructions for reproducing the experiments are available in the following repositories: this https URL and this https URL
summary: LLM-based task-oriented agents depend on tools to interact with their environments, but may overlook execution feedback, repeat ineffective calls, or persist with unproductive strategies. These behaviors can hinder agents' ability to use tools autonomously and sustain task progress. We characterize tool-use symptoms at two temporal granularities: local clumsy tool-use behaviors and tool-use detours spanning multiple interactions. Towards greater autonomy in tool use, we present ToolPulse, an online middleware supporting autonomous tool use through cueing and spotting. ToolPulse tracks execution state and temporal interaction patterns, monitoring proposed calls before dispatch and inspecting execution feedback prior to the agent resumes reasoning. It combines state-based rules, semantic sequence analysis, and interaction-feature similarity to identify intervention opportunities and provide verbal reminders, structured feedback, or context-specific advice from auxiliary models. Our process-oriented evaluation distinguishes trigger validity, behavioral cessation, and substantive correction alongside task outcomes and resource costs. Using SWE-agent with three backbone models, we evaluate 1,350 trajectories on 90 Python, C++, and Java bug-fix tasks, comparing unassisted execution with four assistance strategies. Substantive responses follow 61.6-90.9% of valid triggers for tool-use detours. Concise reminders achieve the highest observed aggregate substantive-response rate; more elaborate assistance offers symptom-dependent benefits and can be less effective. Aggregate repair outcomes remain close to baseline, with token savings in selected settings. These findings support proactive runtime assistance for autonomous tool use. The gap between behavioral adjustment and aggregate repair gains calls for careful decisions on intervention timing and assistance strategy in autonomous agents.

AI.tldr: This paper characterizes two granularities of agentic tool-use failures and introduces ToolPulse, an online middleware that provides runtime cues and feedback to improve autonomous tool use.
AI.motivation: LLM agents often overlook execution feedback, repeat ineffective calls, or persist in unproductive strategies, hindering autonomous task progress.
AI.method: ToolPulse monitors proposed calls and execution feedback using state-based rules, semantic sequence analysis, and interaction-feature similarity to deliver verbal reminders, structured feedback, or auxiliary-model advice, evaluated across 1,350 SWE-agent trajectories on 90 Python, C++, and Java bug-fix tasks with three backbones.
AI.result: Substantive responses follow 61.6-90.9% of valid triggers for multi-step tool-use detours, with concise reminders achieving the highest aggregate substantive-response rate; however, aggregate repair outcomes remain close to baseline, with token savings in selected settings.
AI.conclusion: Proactive runtime assistance effectively corrects local tool-use behaviors, but translating behavioral adjustments into aggregate task-repair gains requires careful intervention timing and strategy design.

title: Zero-Shot Weight-Space Programming for Prediction and Classification of Target Variables in Structured Datasets
summary: Weight-space programming fixes every parameter of a feed-forward network by hand, with no gradient descent anywhere in the construction. Every demonstration so far starts from a target function handed to the model as a rule system, making it a compilation problem. A supervised dataset withholds that specification, so the procedure must do the statistical inference itself and then express the result in the parameterisation it was given. We ask whether a large language model can do both. It is shown a small dataset in full, with the architecture of a feed-forward network, and writes out every weight and bias as a literal number, with no optimizer, no gradient, no code execution, and no chance to evaluate it first. Each construction is sealed and pre-registers its expected score. The graded suite runs from two toy problems, through nine synthetic problems disguised by a hidden rotation, to the classical benchmarks and one real engineering regression. The frozen network matches the closed-form optimum wherever that optimum is linear, reaches the irreducible error of the generating process on three rungs where it is not, and beats every fitted baseline on two of those, including the same architecture trained by gradient descent. It fails on two rungs, both times because the structure to be found is oblique to the coordinates it analysed. Three further constructors separate two failure modes a single score conflates: one returns no parameter vector at all on the hardest rungs, another delivers everywhere while writing networks worse than predicting the mean. One of those failures proves avoidable: another constructor solves the oblique-hinge rung by a margin that survives multiple-comparison correction. What predicts whether the hidden layer earns its keep is the training error of a linear separator, which the composite complexity index misses.

AI.tldr: This paper tests whether LLMs can perform zero-shot weight-space programming on supervised datasets by directly writing literal feed-forward network weights and biases without gradient descent or code execution.
AI.motivation: Prior weight-space programming compiled explicit rule systems into network weights, whereas supervised datasets withhold the target rule and require the LLM to perform statistical inference and parameterization simultaneously.
AI.method: Shown a small dataset and network architecture, the LLM outputs every weight and bias as a literal number with no optimizer, gradient, code execution, or prior evaluation, tested across toy problems, rotated synthetic problems, classical benchmarks, and an engineering regression.
AI.result: The frozen network matches the closed-form optimum on linear problems, reaches the irreducible error on three nonlinear rungs, and beats all fitted baselines (including gradient-descent-trained networks) on two of them, while failing on two oblique-structure rungs; a separate constructor solves the oblique-hinge rung.
AI.conclusion: LLMs can perform zero-shot statistical inference directly into literal neural network parameters on several problem classes, with linear-separator training error predicting when the hidden layer is needed.

title: Hardening Agentic Web Populations Through Multi-Criterion Competitive Co-Evolution: Lessons from Wargame Strategy Optimization
comment: Accepted at the 1st NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Agentic Web: Decentralized, Continually-Adapting Agent Ecosystems (this https URL)
summary: Agents on the open web will face adversaries that keep adapting, so a defense that is only tested once will eventually be found and broken. We propose treating jailbreak attacks and safety guardrails as two populations that evolve against each other, rather than as a fixed attacker probing a fixed defense. This idea comes directly from wargame strategy optimization, where two-population competitive co-evolution with alternating evolution cycles and cross-play evaluation has already been shown to produce strategies that are robust to a moving opponent, and where a companion line of work has shown that the same machinery can measure how much competitive pressure a population must absorb. However, real-world applications can never rely on a single criterion as a key performance indicator, rather must use multiple conflicting criteria, such as, cost and efficiency. We describe how this mechanism transfers to language model safety, argue why the resulting multi-criteria, competitive and coevolutionary arms race is a genuinely networked, population-level problem rather than a two-agent toy setting, and lay out the open problems that stand between the wargame version of this idea and an agentic web version of it.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes modeling LLM jailbreak attacks and safety guardrails as two populations undergoing multi-criterion competitive co-evolution, drawing on lessons from wargame strategy optimization.
AI.motivation: Fixed safety defenses tested against static attackers are eventually bypassed by adaptive adversaries on the open web, and real-world deployments must balance multiple conflicting criteria such as cost and efficiency.
AI.method: Transferring two-population competitive co-evolution with alternating evolution cycles and cross-play evaluation from wargame strategy optimization, the authors frame LLM safety as a networked, population-level, multi-criteria arms race and outline the open problems for an agentic web implementation.
AI.result: As a conceptual and position paper, it presents no empirical experiments, instead mapping the wargame co-evolutionary machinery and identifying the open challenges for agentic web safety.
AI.conclusion: Multi-criterion competitive co-evolution offers a principled framework for hardening agentic web populations against continuously adapting adversaries.

title: The Data Debt of Stockouts: Partial Identification and Minimax-Regret Inventory Control
summary: Problem definition: Inventory decisions select which demand enters sales logs. Unrecorded forecasts can leave demand frequencies unidentified even when stocking levels are recorded. We study which multistage ordering decisions these logs can justify and what finite samples can guarantee. Methodology/results: Nested stockout thresholds yield exact sets of compatible demand laws and finite representations for policy evaluation. We choose one deterministic inventory rule to minimize its largest expected cost gap from the informed optimum under the same law. This population value is data debt for the specified information and policy class. Under independent demand, carryover can create positive debt despite common optimal actions in every isolated period. Finite samples add learning error above debt. The required sample count grows linearly with the selection bound, with upper and lower orders matching up to logarithmic factors. This rate requires fixed demand and cost bounds, sufficient revelation, and a uniformly positive probability of clearing all feasible stock across the confidence sets. Controlled and semi-synthetic studies separate policy improvements from tighter guarantees. Managerial implications: More records can tighten guarantees while debt persists. Deeper revelation can establish common optimality without fully identifying demand. Using these guarantees requires validated logging, a credible selection range, and a regret tolerance in cost units. Information acquisition must distinguish tighter assurance from operating savings.

AI.tldr: This paper characterizes "data debt" in multistage inventory control when stockouts censor demand logs and unrecorded forecasts leave demand frequencies partially identified.
AI.motivation: Inventory decisions determine which demand is observed in sales logs, so stockouts and unrecorded forecasts can prevent full demand identification even when stocking levels are recorded.
AI.method: The authors use nested stockout thresholds to construct exact sets of compatible demand laws and finite representations for policy evaluation, choosing a deterministic inventory rule to minimize worst-case expected cost gap (data debt) against the informed optimum, and analyze finite-sample learning rates.
AI.result: Under independent demand, carryover can create positive data debt even when every isolated period shares a common optimal action; finite-sample requirements scale linearly with the selection bound (matching upper and lower orders up to log factors) under bounded demand/cost, sufficient revelation, and uniformly positive stock-clearing probability, while controlled and semi-synthetic studies separate policy gains from tighter guarantees.
AI.conclusion: More data can tighten guarantees while structural data debt persists, so inventory information acquisition must distinguish tighter assurance from operating savings.

title: NI-ACT: A Neural Intent Interface for Brain-Embodied Manipulation
summary: Intracortical brain-computer interfaces can drive robotic arms, but they keep the user inside the fast sensorimotor loop: every approach, correction, and grasp must be neurally specified. Whether intracortical population activity can instead serve as a task-level condition for a learned embodied policy, without symbolic commands or hand-designed skill libraries, remains unknown. NI-ACT addresses this question with a hierarchical brain-embodied framework: a brief motor-cortical signal is read once as a persistent intent, and a visuomotor policy then closes the perception-action loop from vision and proprioception. In a counterfactual grasping task where the scene cannot specify the target, the neural intent alone determined which object the robot grasped; replacing the intent changed the behavior accordingly. Passing the full population latent as a dedicated intent token, rather than a one-hot decoded direction, raised grasp completion from 69% to 81% over 132 held-out scenes, whereas a continuous direction alone did not improve on a one-hot label. Where the signal was read also mattered: in one dual-array session, with the readout window matched, premotor (PMd) intent completed more grasps than primary motor (M1) intent (77% vs. 53%), and the conventional post-cue M1 readout reached 42%. Preparatory activity was itself sufficient: in a center-out task, intent read only from PMd before the go cue (that is, before any movement) drove complete grasps, and in one recording it completed more grasps than the same animal's post-cue readout. These results show that how a neural signal is represented, and where and when it is read, jointly determine how effectively it conveys movement goals to an embodied agent.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces NI-ACT, a hierarchical brain-embodied framework where a single-shot motor-cortical neural intent conditions a visuomotor robotic policy.
AI.motivation: Traditional intracortical brain-computer interfaces keep the user inside the fast sensorimotor loop, requiring continuous neural specification of every approach, correction, and grasp.
AI.method: NI-ACT reads a brief motor-cortical signal once as a persistent intent token and lets a visuomotor policy close the perception-action loop from vision and proprioception, tested on counterfactual grasping and center-out tasks.
AI.result: Passing the full population latent as an intent token raised grasp completion from 69% to 81% over 132 held-out scenes compared to a one-hot decoded direction; in a dual-array session, premotor (PMd) intent outperformed primary motor (M1) intent (77% vs. 53%, post-cue M1 42%), and preparatory PMd activity before the go cue was sufficient to drive complete grasps.
AI.conclusion: Neural signal representation, brain region, and readout timing jointly determine how effectively intracortical intent conveys movement goals to an embodied agent.

title: From Mutation to Medication: Characterizing Failures of Clinical LLMs to Respect Genomic Resistance
comment: Accepted for publication in the Proceedings of the Machine Learning for Health (ML4H) 2026 Symposium
summary: Language models are increasingly proposed to support molecular tumour boards, but may recommend cancer therapies despite genomic evidence of resistance. We evaluated ten models on 1,464 resistance cases from five curated oncology knowledge bases, collecting 58,910 judgments. Models endorsed resisted therapies in 21.8-81.4% of cases. However, raw rates can reflect a tendency to agree rather than an ability to distinguish resistance from drug sensitivity: one open-weight model endorsed 81.4% of resistance cases and 82.3% of sensitivity controls. We therefore compared endorsement within matched gene and evidence-level groups. This analysis is exploratory because it was specified after the pre-registered analysis, which yielded null-to-weak results. Measured failures depended strongly on the reference knowledge base and evidence strength. When a second source independently confirmed resistance, four models across three vendors endorsed at most 2.4% of cases; at weaker evidence tiers, discrimination was not measurable. Models sometimes acknowledged resistance yet recommended the therapy. Repeating a model's own resistance conclusion reduced endorsement to 0.0-3.5% on cases where it had stated resistance. Falsely attributing the opposite conclusion increased endorsement above baseline for all seven hosted models, reaching 95.2% for GPT-4o; an instruction without an attributed conclusion changed endorsement by only 0.9 percentage points. Providing the correct curated evidence reduced unqualified strong recommendations to 0.3-3.5%, testing evidence use under an oracle condition rather than retrieval.

AI.tldr: Evaluating ten clinical LLMs on 1,464 genomic resistance cases, this paper finds they frequently endorse resisted cancer therapies unless backed by strong multi-source evidence or explicit oracle evidence.
AI.motivation: Language models are increasingly proposed for molecular tumor boards, but recommending therapies despite genomic resistance poses serious patient safety risks.
AI.method: The authors collect 58,910 judgments across ten models on 1,464 resistance cases from five oncology knowledge bases, comparing matched gene and evidence-level groups, testing self-repetition, false conclusion attribution, and oracle curated evidence.
AI.result: Models endorsed resisted therapies in 21.8-81.4% of cases (with one open-weight model endorsing 81.4% of resistance cases and 82.3% of sensitivity controls); when a second source confirmed resistance, four models endorsed at most 2.4%, repeating a model's own resistance conclusion cut endorsement to 0.0-3.5%, falsely attributing the opposite conclusion pushed endorsement up to 95.2% for GPT-4o, and oracle curated evidence cut strong recommendations to 0.3-3.5%.
AI.conclusion: Clinical LLMs struggle to respect genomic resistance under weak evidence or sycophantic/misleading framing, underscoring the need for verified curated evidence integration.

title: Information Limits of Replay-Free Recurrent State Migration
summary: When a recurrent model is replaced, its old state may not determine what the new model would compute from the same history. We characterize the information that must be retained before the replacement is known. For a time-invariant affine linear family, the minimum continuous causal memory for order-$k$ local migration equals the reachable dimension of a lifted coefficient system minus the information in the anchor state. A controllable $d$-state model with scalar input needs at most $kd$ additional real coordinates, even when arbitrary matrix replacement directions are revealed only after streaming. A single rank-one direction can already require all $kd$. Conditional singular values and auxiliary-bit bounds distinguish this local information law from recovery at a fixed tolerance. We also give invariant-subspace and future-output constructions. Controlled experiments compare the resulting representations. In a small language model, equal-memory cubic interpolation improves mean state fidelity over third-order coefficients but provides no meaningful predictive gain. An analytic history basis preserves useful adaptation more economically in a coupled identification task. With repeated slow poles, eight history coordinates meet normalized output error $10^{-4}$ across five fitted seeds despite substantial full-state error. Splitting the poles raises the smallest tested successful width to 64.

AI.tldr: This paper characterizes the fundamental information limits of replay-free recurrent state migration when a recurrent model is replaced by a new one.
AI.motivation: When replacing a recurrent model without replaying history, the old state may not determine what the new model would compute from the same history, and the minimal memory needed before knowing the replacement is unknown.
AI.method: For time-invariant affine linear families, the authors derive the minimum continuous causal memory for order-k local migration as the reachable dimension of a lifted coefficient system minus anchor-state information, provide invariant-subspace and future-output constructions, and test representations on a small language model and a coupled identification task.
AI.result: A controllable d-state scalar-input model needs at most kd additional real coordinates (and a single rank-one direction can require all kd); in a small LM, equal-memory cubic interpolation improves state fidelity over third-order coefficients without predictive gain, while in coupled identification with repeated slow poles, 8 history coordinates reach 10^-4 normalized output error (rising to width 64 when poles are split).
AI.conclusion: Local migration imposes sharp dimension bounds on replay-free state retention, and analytic history bases preserve adaptation more economically than polynomial state interpolation.

title: Attention U-Net Cellular Automata for Multi-Class Land Use and Land Cover Change Simulation in Lucknow, India: Evaluation Against Null and Classical Baselines
summary: Convolutional networks are often used to learn the transition rules of land-use cellular automata (CA), yet their predictions are seldom compared with a null model that predicts no change. We built AttentionUNet-CA, which reads a 32 x 32 neighbourhood of land-cover states with four drivers (elevation, distance to major roads, distance to the central business district (CBD) and population density) and predicts the state of each cell ten years later. We tested it on Lucknow, India, with GLC_FCS30D land cover for 1990, 2000, 2010 and 2020, a 30 m series mapped consistently over time, and compared its built-up class with GHSL and ESA WorldCover. AttentionUNet-CA was trained on 1990-2010, selected on held-out spatial blocks and evaluated once on 2010-2020, with three seeds. Baselines were the null model, a random-forest CA (RF-CA) and a U-Net CA without attention; each network was trained with and without class weights. Only 8.1% of the study area changed in the test decade, so no model matched the overall agreement of the null model (91.9%). On change, measured by the figure of merit, the class-weighted networks scored highest (U-Net CA 22.0 +/- 1.2%, AttentionUNet-CA 21.0 +/- 1.4%), ahead of RF-CA (20.3%), but by margins comparable to seed-to-seed variation; the networks estimated the amount of change better than RF-CA. The attention gates did not improve accuracy. Population density and distance to the CBD were the most useful drivers. Projected to 2030, built-up land grows by 22-35%, mostly at the city edge.

AI.tldr: Evaluating AttentionUNet-CA on 30 m land-cover change in Lucknow, India (1990-2020), this paper finds class-weighted CNNs slightly edge out random forests on change but attention gates add no accuracy gain.
AI.motivation: Convolutional networks are widely used to learn land-use cellular automata transition rules, yet they are rarely benchmarked against a no-change null model or classical baselines.
AI.method: AttentionUNet-CA reads a 32x32 land-cover neighborhood and four spatial drivers (elevation, distance to roads, distance to CBD, population density) trained on 1990-2010 GLC_FCS30D data and tested on 2010-2020 against a null model, RF-CA, and U-Net CA without attention across three seeds.
AI.result: Because only 8.1% of the area changed, no model beat the null model's 91.9% overall agreement; on change (figure of merit), class-weighted U-Net CA (22.0 +/- 1.2%) and AttentionUNet-CA (21.0 +/- 1.4%) slightly outperformed RF-CA (20.3%) within seed-to-seed variation, attention gates did not improve accuracy, and 2030 projections show 22-35% built-up growth.
AI.conclusion: Benchmarking against null and classical baselines shows that class weighting and key spatial drivers (population density, CBD distance) matter more than attention gates for land-cover CA.

title: One Run Is Not Enough: Reminding a small Gemma 4 coding agent of its last finding made no measurable difference in a paired test
comment: 10 pages, 2 figures. Code, data and the commit history of the pre-registration: this https URL
summary: When a coding agent runs out of room, its earlier findings are cut and it forgets them. We tested a simple fix: automatically putting the agent's last finding back in front of it. We fixed the rules in advance and ran 98 paired coding tasks with and without this reminder, using Gemma 4 31B (QAT, 4-bit) in the Gemma 4 Developer Agent harness. The reminder made no measurable difference: across all 98 tasks, 47 were solved with it and 48 without (-1.0 points, 95% interval [-8.3, +6.3], exact McNemar p=1.0). The primary outcome (a documented deviation from our preregistration), the first 48 pairs, was 29/48 with memory against 25/48 without (+8.3 points, [-2.1, +18.3], p=0.22); the extension of 50 tasks, decided after that result, pointed the other way (18/50 against 23/50, -10.0 points, p=0.125), so the sign did not replicate. With 19% of tasks flipping between two identical no-memory runs, the combined interval excludes harms larger than about 8 points and gains larger than about 6, and the design had 80% power only for effects of about +-12 points or more. The model almost never wrote notes (2 of 16 and 4 of 32 runs), and memory cost context: the first request is larger and something was injected at only 47% to 65% of compactions. The registered secondary, repeated actions per compaction, was also null. Two directional hypotheses found on Modal did not replicate on Kaggle. We also report an A/A calibration and a validity funnel (129 tasks, 105 valid). Together these results show that single-run memory claims on task sets of this size sit inside run-to-run noise. The treatment is a harness mechanism and does not test agent-written memory.

AI.tldr: In a 98-task paired evaluation of a Gemma 4 31B coding agent, automatically reminding the agent of its last finding after context compaction made no measurable difference.
AI.motivation: Coding agents forget earlier findings when context is truncated, and it is unclear whether automatically re-injecting the agent's last finding improves task resolution.
AI.method: The authors ran 98 paired coding tasks with and without the automatic reminder using Gemma 4 31B (QAT, 4-bit) in the Gemma 4 Developer Agent harness, alongside an A/A calibration and a 129-task validity funnel (105 valid).
AI.result: Across all 98 tasks, 47 were solved with the reminder and 48 without (-1.0 points, 95% CI [-8.3, +6.3], McNemar p=1.0); an initial +8.3 point gain on the first 48 pairs reversed to -10.0 points on the 50-task extension, 19% of tasks flipped between identical no-memory runs, and the secondary outcome (repeated actions per compaction) was also null.
AI.conclusion: Harness-level last-finding reminders had no measurable effect at this sample size, demonstrating that single-run memory claims on ~50-100 tasks sit inside run-to-run noise.

title: Does a completed simulation run mean a usable urban wind result for AI agents?
summary: AI agents based on large language models (LLMs) can now configure and run computational fluid dynamics (CFD) solvers, but a completed run does not ensure that delivered metrics can be recomputed from raw outputs. This gap was examined for urban wind simulation, where multi-case comparisons must hold non-target conditions fixed and reported values must be traceable to raw samples. UrbanWind-AgentBench, comprising 200 tasks and 367 cases in 10 engineering task families, was constructed. Public task contracts specify variable factors, fixed conditions, numerical thresholds and deliverable requirements, and two-layer scoring separates a structural score for deliverables, run provenance and raw evidence from a numerical score obtained by independent recomputation against references. WindPilot was then proposed as an execution framework that incorporates contract parsing, execution provenance, deterministic verification and bounded acceptance review into the LLM execution loop. On 30 OpenFOAM tasks with independent references, at least the structural maximum of 60 points was reached by a base agent on 28 tasks, but numerical credit was obtained on only 6. With the same model name and budget, WindPilot increased the number of tasks with numerical credit to 17, full-score tasks from 0 to 3 and the mean task score from 62.5 to 72.5. Mean action steps fell from 130.4 to 104.9, and mean token consumption decreased by 12.9%. The mean gain for atmospheric boundary layer (ABL) tasks was 18.5 points. A completed simulation run is therefore not sufficient for a usable urban wind result; usability depends on checks that tie reported metrics to raw evidence during execution.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces UrbanWind-AgentBench and the WindPilot framework, showing that completed CFD runs by LLM agents often fail numerical recomputation from raw outputs.
AI.motivation: LLM agents can now run CFD solvers, but a completed simulation does not guarantee that reported metrics are traceable to raw outputs or that non-target conditions were held fixed.
AI.method: The authors build UrbanWind-AgentBench (200 tasks, 367 cases across 10 engineering families) with two-layer scoring (structural vs. independent numerical recomputation) and propose WindPilot, which integrates contract parsing, execution provenance, deterministic verification, and bounded acceptance review into the LLM loop.
AI.result: On 30 OpenFOAM tasks, a base agent reached the 60-point structural maximum on 28 tasks but earned numerical credit on only 6; WindPilot raised numerical-credit tasks to 17, full-score tasks from 0 to 3, and mean score from 62.5 to 72.5 (+18.5 on ABL tasks) while cutting mean action steps from 130.4 to 104.9 and tokens by 12.9%.
AI.conclusion: Usable agentic CFD results require in-loop provenance and deterministic verification tying reported metrics to raw simulation evidence.

title: SARGO: Agreement-Gated Reinforcement and Suppression via On-Policy Self-Guidance for Visual Hallucination Mitigation
summary: Vision-language models remain susceptible to visual hallucinations, often mixing grounded information with unsupported claims in the same response. Response-level reinforcement learning assigns a shared advantage to all tokens in a response, causing negative updates to suppress correct information alongside unsupported claims. To reduce hallucination while preserving useful visual information, we introduce SARGO (Self-guided Advantage-Routed Grounding Optimization), a post-training framework for selective reinforcement and suppression through on-policy self-guidance. Direct and reciprocal weighting gives better-supported tokens stronger reinforcement on positive updates and weaker penalties on negative updates. Agreement between overall and hallucination-specific advantages selects when to apply this guidance. At the response level, a reference-calibrated reward couples factuality with the retention and expansion of grounded information, discouraging lower hallucination scores obtained through omission. Experiments on Qwen3-VL-4B, Qwen3-VL-8B, and Gemma3-4B demonstrate that SARGO outperforms the evaluated mitigation baselines across Obj-Hal, AMBER, THRONE, and SHR evaluations. SARGO achieves these gains while preserving useful visual information and general multimodal capabilities.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces SARGO, an on-policy self-guidance post-training framework that mitigates visual hallucinations in VLMs without suppressing grounded visual information.
AI.motivation: Response-level RL assigns a shared advantage to all tokens, causing negative updates to penalize grounded details alongside unsupported claims and encouraging omission.
AI.method: SARGO applies direct and reciprocal token weighting so better-supported tokens receive stronger reinforcement on positive updates and weaker penalties on negative updates, gated by agreement between overall and hallucination-specific advantages, paired with a reference-calibrated response reward.
AI.result: Across Qwen3-VL-4B, Qwen3-VL-8B, and Gemma3-4B, SARGO outperforms evaluated mitigation baselines on Obj-Hal, AMBER, THRONE, and SHR while preserving useful visual information and general multimodal capabilities.
AI.conclusion: Agreement-gated, token-level advantage routing effectively reduces VLM hallucinations without sacrificing grounded visual detail.

title: Confidence Without Cause: Predicting and Localizing Physics-Shortcut Sensitivity in Language Model Hidden States
summary: A language model's confidence on a physics problem deserves trust only if it ignores details irrelevant to the answer. We introduce DECOY (Distractor-Embedded Certified cOunterfactuals for phYsics): 155 families of four prompts differing in one irrelevant detail. A symbolic solver certifies that each edit preserves the answer. Families are labelled by the largest drop in the model's log-probability of the certified answer, using a threshold fixed before probe training. Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct is sensitive on 50.0% of the 140 families yielding labels, and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on 22.9%. Effects are largest when distractor values lie numerically close to the answer. A linear probe on Qwen's layer-18 hidden state, averaged over four renderings, predicts sensitivity before generation at AUROC 0.760 with whole families held out. A separately tuned single-rendering probe reaches 0.747. A frozen layer-16 probe reaches 0.820 pooled AUROC on 15 families built after training, though within-cue-type AUROC is lower (0.667-0.6875). Under a paired family bootstrap, the probe performs on par with a fitted token-entropy baseline (AUROC 0.727) and achieves the lowest Brier score among tested predictors (0.204 versus 0.214). Knocking out four attention heads at layer 16 cancels sensitivity on a 20-family panel, localising it to a narrow mechanism. These results show that Qwen's confidence can track irrelevant details, that this failure is detectable before generation, and that targeted intervention can suppress it. DECOY provides certified ground truth and paired-tested baselines for evaluating hidden-state monitors.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the DECOY benchmark and shows that LLM confidence can track irrelevant physics-problem distractors, a failure predictable before generation and suppressible via four attention heads.
AI.motivation: A model's confidence on physics problems should not depend on irrelevant details, yet whether hidden states encode such shortcut sensitivity before generation is unknown.
AI.method: The authors construct DECOY (155 families of four prompts differing in one symbolically certified irrelevant detail), train linear probes on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct hidden states to predict log-probability drops, and ablate attention heads.
AI.result: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct is sensitive on 50.0% of 140 labeled families and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on 22.9%; a layer-18 linear probe predicts sensitivity before generation at 0.760 AUROC (0.820 pooled AUROC on 15 post-training families for a frozen layer-16 probe, Brier score 0.204 vs. 0.214 for token entropy), and knocking out four layer-16 attention heads cancels sensitivity on a 20-family panel.
AI.conclusion: Physics-shortcut sensitivity in LLM confidence is detectable in hidden states prior to generation and localized to a narrow attention-head mechanism.

title: PMR: MoE Routing with Shared Prototypes and Congestion Pricing
summary: Conventional linear routers in sparse mixture-of-experts models select experts directly from token-expert matching scores, coupling input matching with expert allocation. We propose Prototype-Mediated Routing (PMR), a two-stage router with shared prototypes. PMR first computes each token's distribution over prototypes, then uses it to mix prototype-conditioned expert distributions according to the law of total probability. This formulation models input matching and expert allocation separately, explicitly represents many-to-many associations between prototypes and experts, and provides separate interfaces for context adaptation and load regulation. Within this framework, short-term states summarize preceding tokens to adapt the prototypes, while congestion prices updated from dispatch feedback achieve loss-free load balancing by adjusting the conditional expert distributions. We use a two-pass blockwise approximation to accelerate short-term state processing, achieving over 20 times the training throughput of the eager tokenwise PMR implementation while maintaining high agreement in routing decisions. Across three pretraining configurations with 0.43B, 1.18B, and 0.48B total parameters, PMR improves mean zero-shot accuracy on seven benchmarks over linear routing baselines with matched expert architectures by 1.54, 2.65, and 1.45 percentage points (pp), respectively. The corresponding gains on ARC-Easy are 6.71, 5.80, and 3.92 pp. In parameter-efficient fine-tuning of 7B-8B backbones, PMR's improvements over MixLoRA vary across backbones, with gains of up to 1.76 pp in mean accuracy across four tasks.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Prototype-Mediated Routing (PMR), a two-stage MoE router using shared prototypes and congestion pricing that improves pretraining and PEFT accuracy over linear routing.
AI.motivation: Conventional linear MoE routers select experts directly from token-expert scores, coupling input matching with expert allocation and lacking separate interfaces for context adaptation and load balancing.
AI.method: PMR computes each token's distribution over shared prototypes and mixes prototype-conditioned expert distributions via the law of total probability, using short-term states to adapt prototypes, congestion prices for loss-free load balancing, and a two-pass blockwise approximation for throughput.
AI.result: The blockwise approximation achieves over 20x the training throughput of eager tokenwise PMR; across 0.43B, 1.18B, and 0.48B pretraining setups, PMR improves mean zero-shot accuracy on seven benchmarks by 1.54, 2.65, and 1.45 percentage points (up to 6.71 pp on ARC-Easy), and improves PEFT on 7B-8B backbones by up to 1.76 pp over MixLoRA.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling input matching from expert allocation via shared prototypes and congestion pricing yields more accurate, load-balanced sparse MoE routing.

title: Program Distillation: Transferring LLM Capability from System 2 to System 0
summary: Recent studies leverage large language models (LLMs) to construct executable programs through environment interaction, feedback analysis, and code revision. However, prior work has mainly treated LLMs as optimizers, overlooking their ability to transfer knowledge across system levels. We propose Program Distillation (PD), a framework that formalizes the transfer of abilities from System 2 to System 0. During learning, the LLM provides task knowledge and draft strategies; at deployment, a student program executes the resulting policy. We show that this approach can improve performance while reducing inference time. We introduce PDBench, a benchmark comprising 27 discrete- and continuous-control tasks with fixed initial policies, and PDMetaHarness, a model-harness-independent meta-system for monitoring and guiding the learning process. The strongest model achieves a normalized mean score of 0.728, surpassing PPO (0.656) and Jev-like decision models (0.239), while running exclusively on CPUs and reducing inference costs. Our analysis shows that performance is largely driven by the first breakthrough during learning, and structural modifications have a slightly lower success rate than parameter modifications but typically yield larger gains. We further introduce style distillation, which enables interpretable stylistic control over the learning process. Overall, we present an analytical framework for PD and demonstrate its practical viability.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Program Distillation (PD), a framework that transfers LLM capabilities from System 2 to System 0 by having an LLM synthesize and refine executable student policies during learning that then run on CPUs at deployment.
AI.motivation: Prior work using LLMs to construct executable programs through environment interaction mainly treats LLMs as optimizers and overlooks their ability to transfer knowledge across system levels.
AI.method: The authors formalize Program Distillation (PD), introduce PDBench with 27 discrete- and continuous-control tasks with fixed initial policies, build PDMetaHarness as a model-harness-independent meta-system for monitoring and guiding learning, and add style distillation for interpretable stylistic control.
AI.result: On PDBench, the strongest model reaches a normalized mean score of 0.728, outperforming PPO (0.656) and Jev-like decision models (0.239) while running solely on CPUs with lower inference cost; performance is largely driven by the first learning breakthrough, and structural modifications yield larger gains than parameter modifications despite a slightly lower success rate.
AI.conclusion: Program Distillation provides an analytical framework and practical approach for distilling slow System 2 LLM reasoning into fast, low-cost System 0 executable programs.

title: Ultra-CAN: A Lightweight Blind ISAC Receiver for Chaos-Based Telemetry and Local-Seed Ranging in the Internet of Drones
comment: 14 pages, 6 figures, 9 tables. Submitted to IEEE Internet of Things Journal
summary: The Internet of Drones (IoD) needs secure telemetry and proximity sensing within the SWaP-C constraints. We show that a single blind neural receiver driven by one chaos-based waveform performs both functions without a separate radar transceiver. In telemetry mode it decodes a peer's burst blindly; in radar mode it regenerates the per-burst chaotic reference locally and ranges the echoes of its own transmission. Ultra-CAN pairs a shared $64$-dimensional representation with two ultra-light backbones, an attention-pooled Conv1D network and a multi-head QKV network ($27.6$k--$44.2$k parameters), feeding communication and sensing heads. Both ship as int8 TensorFlow Lite Micro firmware; the Conv1D receiver decides a burst in $16.9$ ms on a $240$ MHz microcontroller with $24.2$ KiB of activations, a measured energy of $2.2$-$3.4$ mJ per burst, and float-equivalent decisions, sustaining up to $59$ bit/s of telemetry or a $7.4$ Hz range track. The two variants rank first and second among learned demodulators in four aerial swarm scenarios, with a pooled BER down to $4.6 \times 10^{-4}$ on the single-echo link ($2.4 \times 10^{-3}$ with three echoes). Its sensing head identifies true obstacles in $66.8\%$ of peer-laden bursts (vs $42\%$ matched filtering, $44\%$ OFDM-ISAC, $48\%$ peak-picker ceiling). A peer-exclusion gate cuts peer reports from $4.4\%$ to $0.02\%$ of answered bursts, answering $23.5\%$ of total bursts ($75\%$ on the exact tap) with $0.70$ m/s velocity tracking. In-domain refitting recovers telemetry BER by up to three orders of magnitude under 3GPP channels, jamming-aware training restores the link, and frequency agility adds a $6$--$9$ dB margin against partial-band jamming.

AI.tldr: Ultra-CAN is a lightweight blind neural ISAC receiver for the Internet of Drones that uses a single chaos-based waveform to perform both peer telemetry decoding and local-seed radar ranging on a microcontroller.
AI.motivation: The Internet of Drones requires secure telemetry and proximity sensing within strict SWaP-C constraints without carrying a separate radar transceiver.
AI.method: Ultra-CAN pairs a shared 64-dimensional representation with two compact backbones, an attention-pooled Conv1D network and a multi-head QKV network (27.6k to 44.2k parameters), feeding communication and sensing heads, deployed as int8 TensorFlow Lite Micro firmware with a peer-exclusion gate.
AI.result: On a 240 MHz microcontroller, the Conv1D receiver processes a burst in 16.9 ms using 24.2 KiB of activations and 2.2-3.4 mJ per burst, sustaining up to 59 bit/s telemetry or a 7.4 Hz range track; the two variants rank first and second among learned demodulators across four aerial swarm scenarios (pooled BER down to 4.6e-4 single-echo and 2.4e-3 three-echo), while the sensing head detects true obstacles in 66.8% of peer-laden bursts (vs. 42% matched filtering, 44% OFDM-ISAC, and 48% peak-picker ceiling) with 0.70 m/s velocity tracking.
AI.conclusion: Ultra-CAN demonstrates that a single chaos-driven neural receiver can deliver both reliable telemetry and obstacle ranging within microcontroller SWaP-C budgets for drone swarms.

title: LLM Trading Agents Earn Beta, Not Alpha: A Look-Ahead-Free Benchmark
comment: 23 pages, 10 figures, 15 tables. Code, frozen markets and leaderboard: this https URL. Original empirical study: a backtest benchmark for LLM trading agents and measurements from 91 runs of six models
summary: Large language model (LLM) trading agents now trade stocks for their users, and benchmarks rank models by their agents' returns. Yet a single run's return says little about skill. In our study, two runs of the same model that differed only in the random seed ended 5.2 points apart on average, so telling skill from luck takes many backtests across markets, models and seeds. However, live arenas trade each day only once, and backtests either use the few months after a model's training cutoff or run on years the model may remember, often with news joined to prices by calendar date. In this paper, we present rta-bench-1, a backtest over three US markets (a rally, a bear market and a crash). It shows each headline only after its publication minute, plays each period blind and named, and checks every run for look-ahead. It also splits each return into factor exposure and alpha and scores every decision against random choices of the same day and sector. In 91 runs of six models from four vendors, no alpha was significant, market and style exposure accounted for a median 78% of the return, and the decisions did no better than random stocks of the same sector. The agents bought the stocks with the most positive news, yet in ablations they earned as much without their headlines. Still, the agents carried out rules reliably, since a single cash rule in the prompt cut a GPT-based agent's share in stocks by 30.3 points in all six pairs. Builders should therefore supply the edge themselves and report exposures and alpha, and benchmarks should replay news by publication time.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces rta-bench-1, a look-ahead-free trading benchmark, and finds that LLM trading agents earn market and style beta rather than statistically significant alpha.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM trading benchmarks suffer from single-run variance (5.2 points average difference between seeds), look-ahead bias from training cutoffs or calendar-date news joins, and lack of factor decomposition.
AI.method: rta-bench-1 evaluates agents across three US market regimes (rally, bear market, crash), releasing each headline only after its publication minute, running periods blind and named, checking for look-ahead, decomposing returns into factor exposure and alpha, and comparing against random same-day, same-sector choices.
AI.result: Across 91 runs of six models from four vendors, no alpha was significant, market and style exposure explained a median 78% of returns, and decisions performed no better than random same-sector stocks; agents bought stocks with the most positive news yet earned as much without headlines in ablations, though a single cash rule in the prompt reliably cut a GPT-based agent's stock share by 30.3 points across all six pairs.
AI.conclusion: Builders should supply trading edge themselves and report factor exposures and alpha, while benchmarks should replay news by exact publication time.

title: Continuation-Guided LLM Evolution of Program Policies and Goal Compilers in Craftax
summary: Coding agents can synthesize and optimize code-based policies from simulator feedback, allowing the resulting program to act with zero inference model calls. But for long horizon tasks, two challenges arise: local improvements can hurt final success and switching to a new objective requires another expensive synthesis run. We propose a framework that first develops competence by refining the policy through a feedback cascade, moving from episode returns to hierarchical goals and belief updates which can be scored densely from simulator. In the Craftax game, a partially observed and procedurally generated environment, refinements via episode level feedback stall at <1% final-level arrival, whereas with the feedback cascade the optimized policy reaches the final stage 50% of time (28% final boss defeats). Furthermore, to make this competence reusable towards new goals, we factor the previous controller into an environment interpreter $I$ (models, memory, skills) and a rule program $p_0$, and we show that coding agents can optimize a reusable goal compiler $C_{\theta}$ that maps structured tasks $g$ into new rule programs $p_g$. Across five independent compiler searches trained only on short tasks, the resulting compilers successfully transfer zero-shot to longer tasks without any task-specific tuning nor inference-time LLM calls: continuation-scored feedback and a fixed machine with an editable program together turn a single-task competent policy into a reusable one. Code at: this https URL

AI.tldr: This paper combines a dense feedback cascade with a factored goal compiler to evolve program policies in Craftax that reach the final stage 50% of the time and transfer zero-shot to longer tasks without inference-time LLM calls.
AI.motivation: Synthesizing code-based policies from simulator feedback struggles on long horizons because local improvements can hurt final success and switching to a new objective requires another expensive synthesis run.
AI.method: The framework first refines a policy using a feedback cascade from episode returns to hierarchical goals and belief updates scored densely by the simulator, then factors the controller into an environment interpreter I and a rule program p_0 and optimizes a reusable goal compiler C_theta that maps structured tasks g to new rule programs p_g.
AI.result: In Craftax, episode-level feedback stalls at under 1% final-level arrival, whereas the feedback cascade reaches the final stage 50% of the time with 28% final boss defeats; across five independent compiler searches trained only on short tasks, the resulting goal compilers transfer zero-shot to longer tasks without task-specific tuning or inference-time LLM calls.
AI.conclusion: Continuation-scored feedback paired with a fixed interpreter and editable rule program turns a single-task competent policy into a reusable multi-task controller.

title: Evidence-Conditioned Completion and Synthesis of Electronic Health Records
summary: Patient information can guide electronic health record (EHR) generation, but how its amount shapes predictive utility and disclosure risk remains poorly characterized. Here we present EHRDiB, which unifies visit completion and synthesis by distinguishing original missingness from withheld inputs and combining a shared multimodal representation with an evidence-conditioned latent diffusion bridge. We compared EHRDiB with three completion and eight synthesis methods on MIMIC-IV and numerical and discretized Duke Health representations. Evaluation covered downstream predictive utility, generative diversity, and distributional fidelity for both tasks, and disclosure risk for synthesis. EHRDiB achieved the smallest utility gaps from real-data-trained classifiers in seven of eight completion comparisons. In synthesis, AUPRC gaps were 45.2% smaller for ten MIMIC-IV principal-diagnosis targets and 53.3% smaller for numerical Duke Health data relative to the best comparator. Synthesis with calibrated thresholding yielded the lowest marginal distribution error across all three datasets, with Coverage above 0.95 for both output rules. Across twelve evidence-fraction intervals in MIMIC-IV synthesis, membership-inference AUROC increased from 0.516 to 0.598 as the mean target evidence fraction rose from 0.20 to 0.50; utility gaps narrowed relative to the lowest evidence configuration but did not decrease monotonically. Our study provides a unified framework and empirical foundation for EHR generation that considers both its utility for clinical analysis and its information disclosure risk.

AI.tldr: EHRDiB unifies electronic health record visit completion and synthesis via an evidence-conditioned latent diffusion bridge, improving downstream utility while quantifying disclosure risk across evidence levels.
AI.motivation: Patient information can guide EHR generation, but how the amount of conditioning evidence affects downstream predictive utility and membership-inference disclosure risk remains poorly characterized.
AI.method: EHRDiB distinguishes original missingness from withheld inputs and combines a shared multimodal representation with an evidence-conditioned latent diffusion bridge, evaluated against three completion and eight synthesis baselines on MIMIC-IV and numerical and discretized Duke Health datasets.
AI.result: EHRDiB achieves the smallest utility gaps from real-data-trained classifiers in seven of eight completion comparisons and reduces AUPRC gaps in synthesis by 45.2% on ten MIMIC-IV principal-diagnosis targets and 53.3% on numerical Duke Health data relative to the best comparator, with Coverage above 0.95; in MIMIC-IV synthesis, membership-inference AUROC rises from 0.516 to 0.598 as mean target evidence fraction increases from 0.20 to 0.50.
AI.conclusion: EHRDiB provides a unified framework and empirical foundation for balancing clinical utility and information disclosure risk in evidence-conditioned EHR generation.

title: Behavioral Assurance for Socially Deployed AI Agents
summary: AI agents are increasingly deployed in socially consequential settings, yet existing evaluations provide limited assurance that they behave consistently with their intended characteristics across diverse interactions. We introduce an evaluation framework for measuring the behavioral consistency of socially deployed AI agents. The framework operationalizes agent behavior along five measurable axes and uses a standardized evaluation battery spanning six socially salient interaction settings to assess behavioral differentiation, consistency, and drift. Controlled persona configurations serve as experimental anchors, enabling systematic testing of whether intended behavioral differences persist across contexts rather than appearing only as stylistic variation. Preliminary analyses demonstrate measurable differentiation across configurations and suggest associations between behavioral profiles and interaction outcomes. By shifting the focus from persona design to behavioral assurance, this work provides a foundation for evaluating whether socially deployed AI agents behave as intended, consistently and measurably, across the situations in which users encounter them.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a behavioral assurance evaluation framework for socially deployed AI agents that measures behavioral differentiation, consistency, and drift across six interaction settings.
AI.motivation: AI agents are increasingly deployed in socially consequential roles, yet existing evaluations offer limited assurance that they behave consistently with intended characteristics rather than exhibiting mere stylistic variation.
AI.method: The framework operationalizes agent behavior along five measurable axes and uses a standardized evaluation battery across six socially salient interaction settings, using controlled persona configurations as experimental anchors.
AI.result: Preliminary analyses show measurable differentiation across persona configurations and suggest associations between behavioral profiles and interaction outcomes.
AI.conclusion: Shifting focus from persona design to behavioral assurance provides a foundation for systematically testing whether socially deployed AI agents behave consistently as intended.

title: A Hierarchical Statistical Framework for Evaluating Agent Reliability
summary: Agents operating in complex scenarios often face uncertainty due to incomplete information about the environment they operate in, ambiguous user queries, complex business rules and the inherently stochastic dynamics of the governing policy. Several new benchmarks have been proposed to evaluate LLM-based agents on complex tasks in multi-tool environments, including settings with policy constraints and varying levels of intent ambiguity. These conditions make it important to evaluate agentic systems systematically and quantify their performance under different conditions to assess their reliability in production. This need is evident in the recently introduced Thinkingbox benchmark, where even the strongest models struggle to perform consistently across diverse business scenarios. This paper presents a statistical framework for evaluating uncertainty and reliability in agentic systems. We define a hierarchy of scenarios, instances, and samples to assess model performance and variability systematically. We apply this framework to common metrics found in the literature: mean pass rate, $pass@k$, and $passhat^k$, with uncertainty estimates for each metric. Aggregating metrics at different levels of the hierarchy reveals different structures and properties of the policy model; we connect this hierarchical aggregation with the known process of \emph{coarse-graining} as intended in the physics and statistical literature. We independently derive exact finite-sample expressions for the sampling variances of the unbiased $pass@k$ and $passhatk$ estimators; related results also appear in recent submissions. Our central contribution is a constructive derivation of hierarchical uncertainty propagation, making explicit its correspondence with coarse-graining and separating execution noise from task heterogeneity.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a hierarchical statistical framework for evaluating uncertainty and reliability in LLM-based agents across scenarios, instances, and samples, connecting metric aggregation to coarse-graining.
AI.motivation: Agents in complex multi-tool environments face incomplete information, ambiguous queries, and stochastic policies, making systematic uncertainty quantification necessary to assess production reliability.
AI.method: The authors define a hierarchy of scenarios, instances, and samples, apply it to mean pass rate, pass@k, and passhat^k with uncertainty estimates, and derive exact finite-sample expressions for the sampling variances of unbiased pass@k and passhat^k estimators while connecting hierarchical aggregation to coarse-graining.
AI.result: The constructive derivation of hierarchical uncertainty propagation explicitly links it to coarse-graining and separates execution noise from task heterogeneity.
AI.conclusion: The framework enables principled reliability assessment of agentic systems by decomposing variance across execution stochasticity and task-level differences.

title: Data-Driven Heuristic-Guided Business Process Redesign
summary: Business process redesign (BPR) has a long-standing catalog of best-practice redesign heuristics, yet, applying them remains a mostly manual task that requires extensive domain knowledge. Despite recent advances using Large Language Models (LLMs) for conversational process model redesign, limitations remain. For example, redesign is user-driven instead of data-driven and is not guided by best practices such as the redesign heuristics. Moreover, only one change can be handled at a time. To address these limitations, given an event log and a BPMN model, we present the DH-BPR framework to realize data-driven heuristic-guided BPR using LLMs. To design DH-BPR, we first conducted an analysis of which redesign heuristics can be automatically detected and applied given information contained in an event log such as the fraction of cases that bypass an activity. Based on this, DH-BPR detects and validates heuristic candidates through a combination of rule-based techniques and an LLM. After that, DH-BPR jointly designs and records an application plan for valid candidates, before finally yielding a redesigned BPMN model and an updated resource model (the way resources execute the process). Evaluation based on simulation using a synthetic benchmark and two real-world event logs shows that the framework's redesign reduces the mean case completion time by up to 61.5%.

AI.tldr: DH-BPR is an LLM-assisted framework for data-driven, heuristic-guided business process redesign that automatically detects, validates, and applies redesign heuristics from event logs and BPMN models.
AI.motivation: Applying best-practice business process redesign heuristics remains largely manual, and existing LLM-based process redesign is user-driven rather than data-driven, lacks heuristic guidance, and handles only one change at a time.
AI.method: Given an event log and a BPMN model, DH-BPR identifies automatable heuristics from log statistics (such as activity bypass rates), detects and validates candidates using rule-based techniques and an LLM, jointly plans their application, and outputs a redesigned BPMN model and updated resource model.
AI.result: Simulation evaluations on a synthetic benchmark and two real-world event logs show that DH-BPR reduces mean case completion time by up to 61.5%.
AI.conclusion: Combining event-log analytics, rule-based validation, and LLM planning enables automated, multi-change business process redesign grounded in established heuristics.

title: When AI Agents Should Repair, Replan, or Abandon: A Threshold Theory of Plan Commitment
summary: AI agents often discover mid-execution that their plan is broken, for example when an action fails or a tool is withdrawn. Deployed systems use conventions such as retry loops or "always replan," and a recent benchmark finds no fixed strategy dominates. This paper derives the optimal policy. In the model, a disruption destroys the causal support of part of a plan; repair is a partial reset that preserves the plan's structure, replanning is a full reset, and changing a plan is costly because others have conditioned on it. The optimal policy is a threshold in effective disruption depth: repair shallow damage, replan after deep damage, and abandon the goal when even a fresh plan is not worth its cost. Depth depends on plan structure. In expectation, a single broken action forces 1+R(G)/n actions to be revalidated, where R(G) counts the pairs of actions joined by a dependency path; to first order, a fully serial plan switches to replanning at raw damage about w times smaller than a plan of w parallel chains. A closed-form stability-price threshold determines when a worse repaired plan should be kept over a better fresh one. As language-model planners push replanning costs toward zero, the stability price becomes the only force sustaining plan commitment. Under repeated disruptions, revision frictions make commitment hysteresis optimal: the agent keeps executing a plan it would never choose fresh, and each repair adds patch debt until the debt outweighs repair's cost advantage and the agent rebuilds. A value-of-diagnosis result states when measuring damage is worth its compute and shows that "always replan" is optimal when damage is predictably deep and replanning is the better fallback. A separately implemented numerical checker tests each proposition (zero violations; 1.6 million static-model evaluations), and the model's regime map reproduces that benchmark's regime flips qualitatively.

AI.tldr: This paper derives the optimal threshold policy for when an AI agent should repair, replan, or abandon a disrupted plan based on effective disruption depth and stability price.
AI.motivation: Deployed agents rely on ad hoc conventions like retry loops or always replanning when plans break mid-execution, and prior benchmarks show no fixed strategy dominates.
AI.method: The authors model plan disruptions as destroying causal support in a dependency graph, where repair is a partial reset, replanning is a full reset, and plan changes incur a stability price because others condition on the plan; they derive closed-form thresholds and verify every proposition with a numerical checker over 1.6 million static-model evaluations.
AI.result: The optimal policy repairs shallow damage, replans after deep damage, and abandons when a fresh plan is not worth its cost, with a single broken action forcing 1+R(G)/n revalidations in expectation; under repeated disruptions, revision frictions create commitment hysteresis and patch debt, and the model's regime map qualitatively reproduces benchmark regime flips with zero checker violations.
AI.conclusion: The threshold theory explains when plan commitment and diagnosis are optimal and shows that stability price becomes the sole force sustaining commitment as LLM replanning costs approach zero.

title: Read Before You Fit: Text-Derived Constraints for Discovering Differential Equations from Noisy Biological Data
summary: Large language models are increasingly used for scientific equation discovery. However, most existing methods are strongly data-driven and assume sufficiently clean and representative observations. This assumption is problematic in biological systems, where individual-level measurements are often sparse, noisy, heterogeneous, and expensive to obtain. While the underlying mechanisms are extensively described in scientific text, they are not explicitly used for the LLM based modeling of such systems. We introduce P2C, an agentic framework that translates textual descriptions of biological systems into a typed set of formal constraints, and use these constraints to restrict candidate ordinary differential equation (ODE) structures before numerical fitting. P2C consists of five stages: Text2Constraint extraction, ODE discovery, symbolic verification, parameter fitting, and model scoring. We evaluate P2C on four published ODE systems of acute inflammation and immune regulation, under clean and noisy observations. By progressively degrading the numerical evidence, we isolate when textual domain knowledge contributes beyond regression alone. Across the four systems, adding Text2Constraint reduces the worst form error from 1.397 to 0.499 on clean data and from 13.096 to 1.095 for data perturbed with Gaussian noise of $\sigma=0.1$; P2C also achieves lower form error and trajectory error than several LLM-based baselines over the tested noise range.

AI.tldr: P2C is an agentic framework that extracts formal constraints from scientific text to restrict candidate ODE structures before numerical fitting on noisy biological data.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based scientific equation discovery methods are strongly data-driven and struggle with sparse, noisy, heterogeneous biological measurements, ignoring mechanistic knowledge already documented in scientific text.
AI.method: P2C operates in five stages: Text2Constraint extraction from textual descriptions into typed formal constraints, ODE discovery, symbolic verification, parameter fitting, and model scoring, evaluated on four published acute inflammation and immune regulation ODE systems under clean and noisy data.
AI.result: Adding Text2Constraint reduces worst form error across the four systems from 1.397 to 0.499 on clean data and from 13.096 to 1.095 under Gaussian noise of sigma=0.1, achieving lower form and trajectory error than several LLM-based baselines.
AI.conclusion: Grounding LLM equation discovery in text-derived formal constraints substantially improves robustness to noise in biological dynamical system modeling.

title: Lossless First-Action Menus for Linear-Reward Planning
summary: We study sequential decision making where an agent reserves a minimum menu of initial actions before multi-objective trade-offs are revealed, followed by unrestricted continuation planning once linear reward weights arrive. We prove that a menu preserves the unrestricted optimal return across all linear scalarizations if and only if its reachable continuations cover all vertices of the full feature polytope. This geometric equivalence yields an output-sensitive algorithm that is fixed-parameter tractable in the vertex count, combining scalar backward induction with oracle-based facet identification. On explicitly layered graphs with unit feature increments, menu verification is coNP-complete and synthesis is complete for the second existential level of the polynomial hierarchy, even under additive loss strictly below one. In fixed dimensions two and higher, verification is polynomial whereas synthesis remains NP-complete, while one-dimensional instances admit polynomial-time solutions.

AI.tldr: This paper characterizes lossless first-action menus for linear-reward planning, proving an exact equivalence to covering all vertices of the feature polytope and establishing the complexity of menu verification and synthesis.
AI.motivation: An agent may need to reserve a minimal menu of initial actions before multi-objective linear reward weights are revealed, while still guaranteeing unrestricted optimal return afterward.
