AI.method: The authors prove that a menu preserves optimal return across all linear scalarizations if and only if its reachable continuations cover all vertices of the full feature polytope, yielding an output-sensitive fixed-parameter tractable algorithm combining scalar backward induction with oracle-based facet identification.
AI.result: On explicitly layered graphs with unit feature increments, menu verification is coNP-complete and synthesis is complete for the second existential level of the polynomial hierarchy even under additive loss below one; in fixed dimensions two and higher, verification is polynomial while synthesis remains NP-complete, and one-dimensional instances are solvable in polynomial time.
AI.conclusion: The geometric vertex-coverage equivalence provides both an exact algorithmic approach and a tight complexity characterization for lossless first-action menu synthesis.

title: MAPS: A Multimodal Agentic Framework for POI Data Production Based on Crowdsourced Street-view Imagery
comment: Accepted for presentation at the 33rd ACM SIGKDD Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining (KDD 2027), Cycle 1
summary: Point-of-interest (POI) databases support location-based services, yet urban changes quickly make their records stale and manual maintenance is costly. Crowdsourced street-view images provide timely visual evidence, but converting them into database actions requires separating multiple POIs and irrelevant text in each image, then resolving incomplete observations against ambiguous records. We study Street-view Image-based POI Data Production and propose MAPS, the first framework to integrate structured POI extraction with database maintenance from such imagery. MAPS contains two cascaded modules. SPICE progressively adapts a lightweight vision-language model to reconstruct and filter text, group entries belonging to the same POI, and classify their semantics and completeness. RIMA retrieves candidate records, performs evidence-grounded POI matching and attribute-level reasoning, and selectively acquires complementary visual, geospatial, or external-source evidence when necessary. In human-reviewed full-task evaluation, MAPS outperforms the strongest baseline by 21.8\%. MAPS has also been deployed in Kuaishou's large-scale POI production pipeline, reducing average processing time by 76.9\% relative to manual annotation. These results demonstrate the effectiveness and practical value of MAPS for scalable POI maintenance.

AI.tldr: MAPS is a multimodal agentic framework for street-view-based POI data production that combines lightweight VLM text extraction with evidence-grounded database matching and reasoning.
AI.motivation: Urban changes quickly make point-of-interest (POI) databases stale, and extracting actionable database updates from crowdsourced street-view imagery requires separating multiple POIs and irrelevant text while resolving incomplete observations against ambiguous records.
AI.method: MAPS cascades two modules: SPICE progressively adapts a lightweight VLM to reconstruct and filter text, group entries per POI, and classify semantics and completeness, while RIMA retrieves candidate records, performs evidence-grounded matching and attribute reasoning, and selectively acquires complementary visual, geospatial, or external evidence.
AI.result: In human-reviewed full-task evaluation, MAPS outperforms the strongest baseline by 21.8%, and in Kuaishou's large-scale POI production pipeline it reduces average processing time by 76.9% compared to manual annotation.
AI.conclusion: MAPS demonstrates that cascading specialized VLM extraction with evidence-grounded agentic reasoning enables scalable, accurate POI database maintenance from street-view imagery.

title: Asking the right question is key to AI discovery in a chain of hypotheses
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) scientists pursue discovery through a chain of hypotheses, fitting candidate models to existing observations and often choosing experiments where those models disagree most. Yet when early data miss a narrow feature, model selection favors simple curves that agree across the unmea- sured gap, so disagreement-guided search has no reason to look where the new phenomenon lies. When we tested two frontier AI scientists, Claude Sonnet 5.5 and GPT-6.1-Sol, across 32 closed-loop trials with a narrow peak omitted from the starting data, both sampled inside the peak region less often than random search. Surprisingly, the agent that followed model disagreement more closely missed the peak in all 32 trials, whereas discovery succeeded when experiments probed the unmeasured gap early and followed up across the anomaly. Asking the right question, rather than testing only where current models disagree, is therefore key to AI discovery in a chain of hypotheses.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that disagreement-guided active learning causes frontier AI scientists to miss narrow unmeasured phenomena, whereas probing unmeasured gaps early enables discovery.
AI.motivation: AI scientists often select experiments where candidate models disagree most, but when early data miss a narrow feature, model selection favors simple curves that agree across the unmeasured gap.
AI.method: The authors test two frontier AI scientists, Claude Sonnet 5.5 and GPT-6.1-Sol, across 32 closed-loop trials where a narrow peak is omitted from the initial data.
AI.result: Both agents sampled inside the peak region less often than random search, and the agent that followed model disagreement more closely missed the peak in all 32 trials, whereas discovery succeeded when experiments probed the unmeasured gap early and followed up across the anomaly.
AI.conclusion: Asking the right question by exploring unmeasured regions, rather than testing only where current models disagree, is critical for AI-driven scientific discovery.

title: When Facts Change, Which Decisions Break? Dependency-Aware Context Graphs for Agents
summary: When an observed fact changes, an agent must identify and repair the decisions that depend on it while preserving unaffected outputs. We investigate the reliability-cost trade-off of field-level dependency graphs extracted from actual agent read traces. A controlled benchmark spans three executable workflow domains and four successive updates, with independent imperative and expression-based references. Across 120 workflows, two models and two repeated runs, we compare full recomputation, rolling summary memory, lexical retrieval, trace-extracted dependencies and verified dependency upper bounds. Trace-derived graphs reduce reviewed decisions and estimated total cost, but omitted alternative supports and missing repair context can reduce complete-plan correctness. Paired ablations isolate the effects of edge deletion, spurious edges, transitive propagation and context scope. An exploratory enhancement supplies the existing record ID/field directory during extraction without revealing unread values or reference edges. We evaluate this enhancement on 60 fresh workflows with two repeats per model. On this fresh set, the directory-aware graph matches observed full-context complete-plan correctness for gpt-6.1-sol (100%) with an estimated 4.0% total-cost reduction, but reaches only 84.8% versus 99.6% for gpt-6-luna. The results distinguish potential dependency impact from actual decision invalidity and show why selective repair must be evaluated with both executable correctness and full memory-processing cost. The evidence concerns explicit procedural workflows; broad real-world agent-memory generalization remains untested.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates field-level dependency graphs extracted from agent read traces for selective decision repair when facts change, finding that trace-derived graphs cut cost but can miss alternative supports unless augmented with a record directory.
AI.motivation: When an observed fact changes, agents must identify and repair dependent decisions without recomputing unaffected outputs, but the reliability-cost trade-off of trace-extracted dependency graphs is unclear.
AI.method: Across 120 workflows in three executable domains with four successive updates, the authors compare full recomputation, rolling summary memory, lexical retrieval, trace-extracted dependencies, and verified upper bounds, plus an exploratory directory-aware enhancement evaluated on 60 fresh workflows.
AI.result: Trace-derived graphs reduce reviewed decisions and estimated cost but can lower complete-plan correctness due to omitted alternative supports and missing repair context; on the 60 fresh workflows, the directory-aware graph matches full-context correctness for gpt-6.1-sol (100%) with a 4.0% estimated cost reduction, but reaches 84.8% versus 99.6% for gpt-6-luna.
AI.conclusion: Selective repair must be evaluated on both executable correctness and full memory-processing cost, and trace-based dependency extraction benefits from structural directory cues though broad agent-memory generalization remains untested.

title: Interactive Structured Environment Scaling for Large Language Model Agentic Reasoning
summary: Reinforcement learning via environmental interaction is a cornerstone post-training paradigm for evolving large language models into autonomous agents capable of multi-turn tool use and exploration. Because the environment defines what the policy observes and how actions are verified, its structure directly bounds the capabilities an agent can acquire. Yet existing structured and retrieval environments rely on upstream pre-filtering---extracting a compact subgraph around the gold answer or retrieving fixed passages before the policy acts. We show that such pre-filtering introduces a fundamental measurement confound: because per-question subgraphs enclose ground-truth paths, they compress the candidate space by orders of magnitude and leak answer locations via local topology, allowing a question-blind degree heuristic to surface gold answers far above chance. To restore path selection, candidate pruning, and optimal stopping as genuine policy decisions, we propose RISE (Interactive Structured Environment), which transitions structured reinforcement learning from static subgraphs to full-scale interactive databases along two coupled axes. First, Decision-Space Scaling exposes the unpruned knowledge graph via a five-stage graph-agnostic typed intent adapter under a bounded call budget and a multiplicative grounding reward gate. Second, Learning-Frontier Scaling overcomes within-group variance collapse under group-normalized objectives by uniting model-independent structural tier progression with a self-evolving competence-frontier bandit. Across nineteen benchmarks and three model backbones, RISE substantially advances in-domain and unseen-schema knowledge-graph reasoning, transfers zero-shot to open-domain passage retrieval, and significantly enhances out-of-domain mathematical and logical deduction.

AI.tldr: RISE transitions structured LLM reinforcement learning from pre-filtered subgraphs to full-scale interactive databases via decision-space scaling and learning-frontier scaling.
AI.motivation: Existing structured and retrieval RL environments pre-filter compact subgraphs around gold answers, which leaks answer locations via local topology and lets question-blind degree heuristics score far above chance.
AI.method: RISE exposes unpruned knowledge graphs through a five-stage graph-agnostic typed intent adapter with a bounded call budget and multiplicative grounding reward gate (Decision-Space Scaling), and pairs model-independent structural tier progression with a self-evolving competence-frontier bandit to prevent within-group variance collapse (Learning-Frontier Scaling).
AI.result: Across nineteen benchmarks and three model backbones, RISE substantially improves in-domain and unseen-schema knowledge-graph reasoning, transfers zero-shot to open-domain passage retrieval, and enhances out-of-domain mathematical and logical deduction.
AI.conclusion: Removing subgraph pre-filtering and scaling both the decision space and learning frontier restores genuine policy decisions in structured agentic RL.

title: Autonomous Multi-modal Agents for ITOps Observability
summary: ITOps observability products must integrate data from different tools and systems. We present ITOps Observability Studio, a multi-modal multi-agent system that orchestrates observability workflows through collaborative AI agents. Its three-tier architecture features inter-agent communication, specialized LLM-powered agents for data access, schema operations and visualization, and unified tool integration. The system supports natural language to GraphQL translation, GraphQL schema generation, schema mapping, trace data lifecycle management and multi-tool workflows for reliability engineering. Its agents are instrumented with agent analytics, so that their model and tool calls can be traced. We evaluate each agent on its own benchmark, scored against gold answers where they exist and by a model judge for schema mapping and chart quality. Query generation on a public benchmark and routing work well with a current open model, and the data lifecycle management agent solves most of its scenarios. The evaluation exposed defects that only appear when prompts, parsers and serving stacks are tested together, and we report them together with their fixes.

AI.tldr: ITOps Observability Studio is a three-tier multi-modal multi-agent system that orchestrates observability workflows including natural-language-to-GraphQL translation, schema mapping, and trace data lifecycle management.
AI.motivation: ITOps observability products must integrate heterogeneous data across tools and systems, requiring coordinated workflows for querying, schema operations, visualization, and reliability engineering.
AI.method: The system uses a three-tier architecture with inter-agent communication, specialized LLM-powered agents for data access, schema operations, and visualization, unified tool integration, and agent analytics tracing model and tool calls, evaluated per agent against gold answers or model judges.
AI.result: Query generation on a public benchmark and routing perform well with a current open model, the data lifecycle management agent solves most scenarios, and joint evaluation uncovered and fixed defects that only emerge when prompts, parsers, and serving stacks interact.
AI.conclusion: Instrumenting specialized multi-agent observability systems and testing prompts, parsers, and serving stacks together is essential for reliable ITOps automation.

title: GEM-MM: Reducing VLM Hallucination with Entropy-Guided Preference Alignment
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) are routinely aligned with offline pairwise RLHF objectives, but multimodal preference data is scarce and treats every response token as equally informative. Under a small preference budget, pair construction becomes nearly irrelevant: standard DPO-style, image-conditional, and self-improvement objectives all perform within 1.1 points on MM-RLHF metrics and 0.5 points on hallucination rates, matching the SFT baseline. We call this entropy-blind preference optimization: the learning signal ignores policy uncertainty, which in chain-of-thought VLMs concentrates on specific fork tokens where visual claims are made. We introduce GEM-MM, extending entropy-guided preference modeling to VLMs. It samples on-policy candidates, rewards high-entropy reasoning forks, penalizes uncertain final answers, and updates the model via group-normalized policy gradients. On a 3000-prompt MM-RLHF budget with Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct, GEM-MM achieves the best entropy-depth preference score (61.7% vs. 57.3-58.4% baselines) and implicit-reward accuracy (41.4%). Crucially, it reduces AMBER hallucination from 23.4-24.0 to 20.6 and CHAIR from 5.0-5.1 to 4.6 at matched caption coverage. It also ranks best on all three HallusionBench granularities, with a conservative operating point raising the near-chosen rate to 62.4%. An off-the-shelf multimodal reward model ranks GEM-MM first, and two such models independently confirm our main ablations (p < 0.001). We report confidence intervals, paired significance tests, metric-reward functional overlaps, and document a collapse mode when exceeding the fair budget. Code and evaluation harness: this https URL

AI.tldr: GEM-MM reduces VLM hallucination under small preference budgets by sampling on-policy candidates, rewarding high-entropy reasoning forks, and penalizing uncertain final answers via group-normalized policy gradients.
AI.motivation: Standard offline pairwise RLHF treats all tokens equally and becomes entropy-blind under small multimodal preference budgets, where DPO-style and self-improvement baselines perform within 1.1 points of SFT on MM-RLHF.
AI.method: GEM-MM extends entropy-guided preference modeling to VLMs by sampling on-policy candidates, rewarding high-entropy reasoning forks where visual claims occur, penalizing uncertain final answers, and updating via group-normalized policy gradients.
AI.result: On a 3000-prompt MM-RLHF budget with Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct, GEM-MM achieves the best entropy-depth preference score (61.7% vs. 57.3-58.4% baselines) and implicit-reward accuracy (41.4%), reduces AMBER hallucination from 23.4-24.0 to 20.6 and CHAIR from 5.0-5.1 to 4.6 at matched coverage, and ranks best on all three HallusionBench granularities (62.4% near-chosen rate at a conservative operating point), confirmed by two multimodal reward models (p < 0.001).
AI.conclusion: Targeting policy uncertainty at reasoning forks and final answers makes preference alignment substantially more effective at reducing VLM hallucinations under limited budgets.

title: Towards Agentic Scientific Discovery in Distributed Systems
summary: We investigate when adaptive tool selection helps identify a shared equation across clients with different input coverage. Query-ATLAS (query-conditioned Agentic Tool-based Learning for Aggregating Symbolic Equations) uses an LLM to guide symbolic search from client errors and previous proposals in a simulated distributed system. A four-architecture comparison reveals task-dependent opportunities: relative to fixed PySR-LLM, validation acceptances rise from 3/12 to 7/12 on CRK3 and from 11/12 to 12/12 on oscillator2, while MatSci3 favors the fixed workflow. Across 72 settings in a post-hoc six-task subset of eight development tasks, Query-ATLAS achieves 64 validation and 64 in-distribution passes, versus 62 and 59 for the fixed workflow; both pass 47/60 eligible out-of-distribution tests. The fixed workflow retains lower median errors and cost. Broader query coverage emerges as a promising benefit, motivating task-aware tool selection and client-aware fitting for scientific agents.

AI.tldr: Query-ATLAS uses an LLM for adaptive tool selection in distributed symbolic equation discovery, improving validation acceptances on some tasks while a fixed PySR-LLM workflow retains lower median error and cost.
AI.motivation: It is unclear when adaptive LLM-guided tool selection outperforms fixed symbolic regression workflows when aggregating a shared equation across distributed clients with differing input coverage.
AI.method: Query-ATLAS guides symbolic search using client errors and prior proposals in a simulated distributed system, compared against a fixed PySR-LLM workflow across four architectures and 72 settings on a six-task subset of eight development tasks.
AI.result: Relative to fixed PySR-LLM, validation acceptances rise from 3/12 to 7/12 on CRK3 and 11/12 to 12/12 on oscillator2 while MatSci3 favors the fixed workflow; across the 72 settings, Query-ATLAS achieves 64 validation and 64 in-distribution passes (vs. 62 and 59 for fixed), both pass 47/60 out-of-distribution tests, and the fixed workflow retains lower median errors and cost.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive tool selection offers task-dependent benefits and broader query coverage, motivating task-aware tool selection and client-aware fitting for distributed scientific agents.

title: The Frontier Must Grow - Self-proposed, interpreter-labelled training roughly doubles a 4B model's accuracy on a fresh exam as its verified frontier grows
summary: A model can learn from problems it poses itself when an executable oracle supplies the answers. Qwen3-4B proposed Lua 5.1 programs; those it predicted wrong at least once in four samples joined a pool labelled by the interpreter, each round adding twice as many programs as the last (300, 900, 2100 in total), and each round trained a fresh adapter from the base on the pool. On the original exam the procedure met its registered criterion, an item-level test of each adapter against its predecessor. On a 2340-item exam drawn afterwards, accuracy rose from 8.3% to 16.7%; that follow-up's registered criteria were not met because round 1 gained nothing, while rounds 2 and 3 added 5.0 and 2.9 points on average, both intervals above zero. One fit on the same amount of base-proposed frontier data reached 14.6%, so the rounds' 2.1-point advantage is inconclusive. Three earlier registered series met no per-lineage criterion, and the same loop showed no gain on repository tasks or for a 27B agent in those configurations.

AI.tldr: Self-proposed Lua 5.1 programs labelled by an interpreter roughly double Qwen3-4B's accuracy on a fresh exam from 8.3% to 16.7%, though gains are inconsistent across series and configurations.
AI.motivation: A model can learn from self-posed problems when an executable oracle supplies ground-truth labels, but the reliability and limits of this self-play frontier growth need controlled testing.
AI.method: Qwen3-4B proposes Lua 5.1 programs, adds those it gets wrong at least once in four samples to an interpreter-labelled pool (doubling additions per round to 300, 900, and 2100 total), and trains a fresh adapter from the base model each round.
AI.result: On the original exam the procedure met its registered item-level criterion, and on a 2340-item follow-up exam accuracy rose from 8.3% to 16.7% (rounds 2 and 3 adding 5.0 and 2.9 points, round 1 gaining nothing), though a single fit on base-proposed data reached 14.6% (making the 2.1-point round advantage inconclusive) and three earlier series plus repository and 27B-agent tests showed no gain.
AI.conclusion: Interpreter-labelled self-proposed problems can substantially boost small-model coding accuracy in targeted settings, but multi-round advantages over single-batch frontier data and broader generalization remain fragile.

title: When Valid Decisions Are Not Enough: Evaluating Structural Constraints in Knowledge-Guided Generative Systems
summary: Knowledge-guided generative systems use explicit domain constraints to improve decision consistency and alignment with human-created solutions. However, locally valid decisions do not necessarily preserve contextual relationships in human decision-making. This paper examines when structural constraints improve or degrade agreement with human reference solutions. We introduce HARMONIX, an experimental framework using automated musical harmonization as a controlled testbed for knowledge-guided decision-making. Four configurations share the same Viterbi-based optimization mechanism: a baseline, repetition constraints, functional constraints, and their combination. Experiments cover 19,745 records and 143,634 motif pairs across training and validation partitions. Combined constraints improve reference root-interval agreement by approximately five percentage points in stable structural contexts but reduce it by nearly nine percentage points in contexts involving transposition tracking. These opposing effects are consistent across both partitions, while overall exact chord agreement changes only marginally. Contexts are identified retrospectively using reference annotations; no adaptive constraint-selection mechanism is evaluated. The findings demonstrate that interpretable constraints can introduce systematic context-specific failures concealed by aggregate accuracy metrics. They highlight the need to evaluate relationships between decisions and the contextual applicability of constraints in knowledge-guided generative systems.

AI.tldr: Using HARMONIX for musical harmonization, this paper shows that explicit structural constraints can improve local agreement in stable contexts while degrading performance in contexts requiring transposition tracking.
AI.motivation: Knowledge-guided generative systems use domain constraints to improve consistency, but locally valid decisions may fail to preserve broader contextual relationships in human-created solutions.
AI.method: The authors introduce HARMONIX, evaluating four Viterbi-based harmonization configurations (baseline, repetition constraints, functional constraints, and combined) across 19,745 records and 143,634 motif pairs.
AI.result: Combined constraints improve reference root-interval agreement by about 5 percentage points in stable structural contexts but reduce it by nearly 9 percentage points in contexts involving transposition tracking, while overall exact chord agreement changes only marginally.
AI.conclusion: Aggregate accuracy metrics can conceal systematic context-specific failures introduced by interpretable domain constraints, underscoring the need for context-aware constraint evaluation.

title: A Matrix with Steps: An Episodic and Procedural Memory Method for Tool-Using Agents and Robots
summary: Agents that call tools and robots that execute tasks are challenged by two shortcomings: they repeat what failed before, and they learn from runs that they only believe succeeded. We describe the construction of a memory that addresses both, built for a production agent platform. Every run is recorded as an episode, and only an outcome confirmed by an external check, a test, a tool result or a person counts; the agent's own claim never does. What is learned from episodes is kept in a memory with two parts: an associative matrix, written with the delta rule, which finds the procedure that applies to a situation; and a section of ordered, addressable step records that answers what comes after a given step, where a step is a goal of the agent, not a motion. Because the matrix sums its associations, it keeps no order and cannot return or delete a single one; it serves as the finder, and order, outcome counts and deletion live in the records. We describe how execution outcomes are stored, how episodes are recalled and used for solving tasks, and the file format that stores the memory. In simulation, a robot that judged its own success and stopped when it believed it was done reported $96\%$ of its tasks as done and solved $35\%$; with external verification it solved $79%$. In a store of $100000$ synthetic episodes ($457$MB on disk), the oldest episode was still found first, no episode from another person's memory was returned, and a success vouched for only by the model was never recalled; a lookup took $16$ms on a laptop and $40$ms on a server node (median). Task outcomes were measured up to about $10000$ confirmed records, where the exact records solved every revisit at the first attempt.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a two-part episodic and procedural memory for tool-using agents and robots that stores only externally verified outcomes, improving simulated robot task success from 35% to 79%.
AI.motivation: Tool-using agents and robots often repeat past failures and learn from runs they only mistakenly believe succeeded.
AI.method: Every run is recorded as an episode, accepting only outcomes confirmed by external checks (tests, tool results, or humans); learned knowledge is split into an associative matrix updated with the delta rule to locate applicable procedures and ordered, addressable step records storing goal sequences, outcome counts, and deletions.
AI.result: In simulation, a self-judging robot reported 96% completion but solved only 35% of tasks, whereas external verification raised solved tasks to 79%; in a 100,000-episode synthetic store (457 MB), median lookup took 16 ms on a laptop and 40 ms on a server with zero cross-user leakage or unverified recall, and 10,000 confirmed records solved every revisit on the first attempt.
AI.conclusion: Pairing externally verified episode logging with an associative finder and ordered step records prevents false-success learning and enables fast, reliable procedural recall.

title: Deploying a Control-Logic LLM Assistant in Air-Gapped Power Plants: Lessons in Source Authority and Bounded Retrieval
comment: Extended version of a paper accepted at IAAI-27 (AAAI 2027). 8 pages, 2 figures, 3 tables
summary: Deploying Large Language Model (LLM) assistants in industrial operational technology environments poses constraints largely absent from cloud applications: site policies restrict engineering and operational data from leaving the plant, on-premises compute is limited, and incorrect causal attribution can mislead incident response. We report lessons from deploying a control-logic evidence layer that underpins a broader on-premises operator assistance system at two gas power plants. Two prototypes revealed where generative models added avoidable uncertainty and cost. The first used a Vision Language Model (VLM) to reconstruct control topology from PDF printouts routinely exchanged by engineers. Across the full 6,979-page document, extraction reached 0.51 connection precision and required 3.1 hours on 4xH200 GPUs; consultation with controls engineers then revealed a native structured export from the authoring system. The second used an LLM tool-calling agent to plan repeatedly over eight predefined graph operations. In a controlled benchmark of 40 template-generated questions, replacing this agent with explicit execution plans reduced mean token use by 20x and median latency by 3x, with identical retrieved node sets across repeated runs. The deployed design ingests the authoritative export into a versioned knowledge graph, executes bounded graph operations in fixed software, and confines the local LLM to fallback intent classification and evidence-grounded explanation. At one site, the graph contains 221K nodes across seven controllers. Our experience suggests a practical division of labor for high-consequence AI: LLMs interpret natural-language requests and explain results, while deterministic software constructs and retrieves technical evidence grounded in authoritative sources. Abstention, entity disambiguation, graph versioning, and read-only integration provide additional safeguards.

AI.tldr: Deploying a control-logic LLM assistant in two air-gapped gas power plants shows that deterministic software should ingest authoritative exports into a versioned knowledge graph while confining the local LLM to intent classification and explanation.
AI.motivation: Industrial operational technology environments enforce strict data isolation, limited on-premises compute, and high stakes where incorrect causal attribution can mislead incident response.
AI.method: After a VLM PDF-extraction prototype yielded only 0.51 connection precision in 3.1 hours on 4xH200 GPUs and an LLM tool-calling agent proved costly and nondeterministic, the deployed system ingests native structured exports into a versioned knowledge graph (221K nodes at one site), runs bounded graph operations in fixed software, and restricts the local LLM to fallback intent classification and evidence-grounded explanation.
AI.result: Replacing the tool-calling agent with explicit execution plans on 40 template-generated questions cut mean token use by 20x and median latency by 3x while returning identical node sets across repeated runs.
AI.conclusion: High-consequence industrial AI benefits from a strict division of labor where deterministic software handles authoritative evidence retrieval and LLMs handle natural-language interpretation and explanation.

title: A Structural Framework for Succession: Continuation, Recognition, and Realization
summary: Succession asks whether an entity encountered later is the same entity that entered an arrangement earlier. For an artificial system that is fine-tuned, distilled, or copied, it has to be answered. We look for a mathematical structure weak enough to cover any such case and strong enough to support general theorems, so that results follow from the structure's conditions rather than from a particular pipeline or criterion. Succession is modeled on state/modification graphs with relational lifts that compose along paths. Within this framework we separate four questions that are often conflated: which continuations a representation admits, which descendants are compatible with a modification, which are recognized as continuing the identity, and which are realized. The framework allows one to address systematically questions of symmetry, computational complexity, recoverability, and robustness to partial realization, and we establish what the structure settles in each case before any particular criterion of identity is chosen.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a general mathematical framework for succession on state/modification graphs with relational lifts, separating representation continuation, modification compatibility, identity recognition, and realization.
AI.motivation: Assessing whether an artificial system that is fine-tuned, distilled, or copied is the same entity that entered an earlier arrangement requires a pipeline-independent mathematical structure.
AI.method: The authors model succession using state/modification graphs with relational lifts that compose along paths, formally distinguishing four conflated questions: admissible continuations, compatible descendants, recognized identity, and realized identity.
AI.result: The framework establishes general results on symmetry, computational complexity, recoverability, and robustness to partial realization before any specific identity criterion is chosen.
AI.conclusion: Separating continuation, compatibility, recognition, and realization provides a rigorous foundation for reasoning about entity identity across model modifications.

title: FinVerify: A Verification Framework for Financial Agents
comment: 15 pages, 2 figures. Accepted to the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Who Verifies the Agents? Toward Reliable Agent Development
summary: Financial agents produce numerical claims that can be wrong even when their calculations execute correctly, due to mismatched reporting periods, unsupported sources, incompatible units, or incorrect financial definitions. We introduce FinVerify, an evidence-grounded framework for verifying financial agents' numerical claims. Based on an analysis of 190 incorrect trajectories from the Agent Finance Reasoning dataset, we define five error categories--temporal integrity, source fidelity, comparability, accounting integrity, and financial-model fidelity--and operationalize them as verification protocols. An LLM structures claims and supporting evidence, while deterministic validators check financial requirements; when authoritative formulas are available, Z3 checks consistency with grounded inputs. FinVerify accepts only if all applicable checks pass, rejects proven violations, and abstains when evidence is insufficient. We evaluate the framework against a Direct baseline and an LLM judge across five fixed-candidate benchmarks. On Agent Finance Reasoning, accepted-claim precision increases from 56.4% for the LLM judge to 76.7% at 81.2% coverage. On XBRLFiling, FinVerify achieves 99.8% accepted-claim precision and 97.0% decision accuracy; on FinanceBench-67, it reaches 87.9% accepted-claim precision versus 69.7% for the judge. Improvements are smaller on FinQA and TAT-QA, where authoritative evidence is limited. These results suggest that explicit, evidence-backed verification can improve financial-agent reliability while exposing trade-offs between correctness, false rejection, and abstention.

AI.tldr: FinVerify is an evidence-grounded verification framework for financial agents that combines LLM claim structuring with deterministic financial validators and Z3 consistency checks to substantially boost accepted-claim precision.
AI.motivation: Financial agents can produce wrong numerical claims despite correct arithmetic due to mismatched reporting periods, unsupported sources, incompatible units, or incorrect financial definitions.
AI.method: Based on 190 incorrect trajectories from Agent Finance Reasoning, FinVerify defines five error categories (temporal integrity, source fidelity, comparability, accounting integrity, financial-model fidelity), uses an LLM to structure claims and evidence, and applies deterministic validators plus Z3 checks to accept, reject, or abstain.
AI.result: On Agent Finance Reasoning, FinVerify raises accepted-claim precision from 56.4% (LLM judge) to 76.7% at 81.2% coverage; it achieves 99.8% precision and 97.0% accuracy on XBRLFiling, and 87.9% precision vs. 69.7% for the judge on FinanceBench-67, with smaller gains on FinQA and TAT-QA where authoritative evidence is limited.
AI.conclusion: Explicit, evidence-backed verification with abstention improves financial-agent reliability while clarifying trade-offs between precision, false rejection, and abstention.

title: The Logic Chain Breaking Point: A Controlled-Variable Benchmark for Reasoning Degradation in Open-Weight Language Models
summary: We introduce The Logic Chain Breaking Point, a controlled-variable benchmark for deductive reasoning in open-weight language models. It spans three phases: (i) pure modus-ponens chain scaling, (ii) distractor resilience with a fixed core chain, and (iii) contradiction detection under primacy versus recency placement. Independent variables follow a powers-of-two sequence $v \in \{1,2,4,8,16,32,64,128\}$, with ground truth known by construction. We evaluate sixteen open-weight models across instruction-tuned and reasoning-tuned panels, including a small-model suite and a larger local-model extension. All models are evaluated with greedy decoding under model-appropriate context and output budgets, while context- and length-limited trials are quarantined from the valid accuracy denominator. Our results reveal a sharply non-monotonic difficulty surface: pure deductive chains up to $L=128$ remain near saturation for most models, and distractor noise causes only model-specific degradation at high $D$, while the inconsistent premise condition has the lowest accuracy. Instruction-tuned models, including larger 24B--27B baselines, score essentially zero on inconsistent premise sets, while reasoning-tuned models recover only partially and remain below reliable accuracy. Within this benchmark, inconsistent premise sets are associated with the strongest degradation under the benchmark's abstention-based scoring rule.

AI.tldr: The Logic Chain Breaking Point benchmark evaluates 16 open-weight language models across deductive chain length, distractors, and premise contradictions, finding that inconsistent premises cause the steepest accuracy collapse.
AI.motivation: Existing reasoning evaluations often confound deductive chain length, distractor noise, and premise contradictions, obscuring where open-weight models actually break down.
AI.method: The benchmark varies independent variables in powers of two from 1 to 128 across three phases (pure modus-ponens scaling, distractor resilience, and contradiction detection under primacy vs. recency placement), evaluating 16 open-weight instruction-tuned and reasoning-tuned models with greedy decoding and abstention-based scoring.
AI.result: Pure deductive chains up to L=128 remain near saturation for most models and distractors cause model-specific drops only at high D, whereas inconsistent premise sets yield near-zero accuracy for instruction-tuned models (including 24B-27B baselines) and only partial, unreliable recovery for reasoning-tuned models.
AI.conclusion: Contradictory premises, rather than raw deductive depth or distractors, represent the primary failure mode for current open-weight language models on controlled logic chains.

title: Agent-Guided Configuration Tuning for SMT Solvers
summary: SMT solvers expose many configuration choices that determine how well their existing algorithms perform on a workload. We present, to our knowledge, the first workflow that uses general-purpose LLM agents to tune SMT solver configurations. Agents read solver documentation, source code, and persistent experiment records to propose option changes, and a deterministic harness measures each proposal, validates the returned models, and selects changes separately for each competition Division. Over roughly nine weeks, our tuning campaign recorded 4,545 proposals for cvc5 across 13 Divisions and 36 logics. We evaluate the tuned configurations on the 2026 and 2025 SMT-COMP ModelValidation benchmarks under a 24-second cutoff. On problems not used for training, they validate more problems than official cvc5 in ten of the 13 Divisions in 2026 and in eight in 2025, with geometric-mean gains of 7.8% and 6.8% across Divisions. On the complete official selections, which include training problems, the tuned floating-point counts exceed those of every individual competition participant in both years. Further studies show how configuration changes make existing algorithms effective by changing access to strategies, scheduling, and option compatibility, and how benchmark families trade off against one another. The agents' experiment traces contain hypothesis-based proposals in every tuning group, and 64.3% of the extracted hypotheses draw on prior measurements. These results show that agent-guided tuning can specialize a mature SMT solver and that accumulated experimental evidence informs sustained search.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an LLM-agent workflow that tunes cvc5 SMT solver configurations over 4,545 proposals, outperforming official cvc5 on most SMT-COMP ModelValidation divisions.
AI.motivation: SMT solvers expose numerous configuration options that strongly affect workload performance, yet tuning them manually across logics and divisions requires deep expertise.
AI.method: General-purpose LLM agents read solver documentation, source code, and persistent experiment records to propose option changes, while a deterministic harness measures performance, validates returned models, and selects configurations per competition division across 13 divisions and 36 logics over nine weeks.
AI.result: Evaluated on 2026 and 2025 SMT-COMP ModelValidation benchmarks under a 24-second cutoff, the tuned configurations validate more unseen problems than official cvc5 in 10 of 13 divisions (2026) and 8 of 13 (2025) with geometric-mean gains of 7.8% and 6.8%, and exceed every individual participant's floating-point counts on the full official selections; 64.3% of extracted agent hypotheses draw on prior measurements.
AI.conclusion: Agent-guided configuration search grounded in deterministic validation and persistent experiment traces can effectively specialize mature SMT solvers.

title: EVIDENT: Evaluating Evidence Grounding in GUI Agents
summary: GUI agents are increasingly evaluated by whether they complete web tasks, but surface success can hide a critical failure: the final answer may not be supported by evidence observed during navigation. We introduce EVIDENT, an evidence-driven benchmark for evaluating whether GUI agents ground their decisions in observable web evidence. EVIDENT contains 220 real-world English and Korean tasks spanning semantic grounding, contextual inference, and visual grounding, each paired with human-curated evidence metadata specifying what must be verified. We further separate surface task completion from evidence-grounded success using three metrics: TSR, ESR, and GSR, which respectively measure outcome success, required evidence observation, and claim-level evidence support. Experiments on commercial and open-source GUI agents reveal substantial gaps between surface success and evidence-grounded success, especially in contextual and visual tasks. These results show that current evaluations can overestimate agent reliability and highlight the need to assess not only whether agents answer, but whether they verify.

AI.tldr: EVIDENT is a 220-task English and Korean benchmark for GUI agents that separates surface task completion from evidence-grounded success, revealing large gaps on contextual and visual grounding tasks.
AI.motivation: Standard GUI agent evaluations measure only whether a web task is completed, hiding cases where the final answer is unsupported by evidence actually observed during navigation.
AI.method: EVIDENT pairs 220 real-world English and Korean tasks across semantic grounding, contextual inference, and visual grounding with human-curated evidence metadata, introducing three metrics: TSR (outcome success), ESR (required evidence observation), and GSR (claim-level evidence support).
AI.result: Experiments on commercial and open-source GUI agents reveal substantial gaps between surface task success and evidence-grounded success, particularly in contextual inference and visual grounding tasks.
AI.conclusion: Evaluating whether GUI agents observe and verify supporting evidence, rather than only checking final answers, is essential for accurately assessing agent reliability.

title: VAHBench: A Harness Benchmark for Agentic Long-Video Generation
summary: AI agents are commonly used for everyday information retrieval and coding. We ask whether they can also interpret human requests and turn them into complete videos. We introduce VAHBench, a benchmark that tests this ability through five short-drama briefs specifying story, characters, dialogue and duration. Agents plan and carry out production using shared generation tools. Evaluation combines video completeness and basic quality with checks of production reliability and reporting accuracy. Across 240 runs covering 48 configurations of general-purpose and video-specific agents, higher quality scores do not necessarily mean more complete delivery. Missing episodes, repeated footage and static filler reveal gaps between producing a video file and fulfilling the brief. Added composition tools help some agents but do not consistently improve performance. VAHBench measures how well agents translate user intent into finished video content and helps identify where that process breaks down.

AI.tldr: VAHBench benchmarks agentic long-video generation across five short-drama briefs and 240 runs, finding that higher visual quality scores do not guarantee complete brief fulfillment.
AI.motivation: While AI agents are widely used for retrieval and coding, it remains unclear how reliably they can plan and execute end-to-end long-video production from human briefs.
AI.method: VAHBench evaluates general-purpose and video-specific agents across 48 configurations (240 runs) on five short-drama briefs specifying story, characters, dialogue, and duration, scoring video completeness, basic quality, production reliability, and reporting accuracy.
AI.result: Higher quality scores do not necessarily correspond to more complete delivery, as agents frequently exhibit missing episodes, repeated footage, and static filler; adding composition tools helps some agents but does not consistently improve overall performance.
AI.conclusion: VAHBench exposes critical reliability and completeness gaps between generating video files and faithfully fulfilling multi-element user briefs.

title: ToolGraph as a Q-Function for Test-Time Scaling of Tool-Use Agents
comment: 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). Workshop: From Pretrained Representations to Acting Agents (PTA)
summary: Tool-use agents must chain interdependent calls, yet which outputs satisfy which later inputs in a deployed catalog is not something a general-purpose language model reliably infers from tool descriptions alone. We compile that structure once into a reusable external representation. ToolGraph is a directed, weighted dependency graph over a tool catalog: parameter matching and interventional probes, which execute a candidate chain with and without its proposed predecessor, propose edges whose evidence is combined into an edge confidence. Prior work uses such graphs to retrieve tools, search for tool paths, or score the next call. We ask instead whether the same structure can supply a \emph{multi-step} value by composing graph paths into a goal-conditioned action value \(Q(s,a,g)\). We study three estimators (dynamic programming over entity sets, a GraphSAGE estimator distilled from it, and an LLM scorer conditioned on graph evidence) plus a verbalizer that returns action--goal feedback to the agent, which keeps final action selection. Across two tool-use benchmarks and three backbones, we compare value ranking against personalized-PageRank retrieval over the identical graph, and against direct and reflective agents. Composition pays off only when the estimator also reads the concrete state: the LLM estimator improves on PageRank in every benchmark--backbone setting, by \(8.3\) points on average, while the two purely structural estimators fall below it, because a value defined over tool types cannot separate a correct tool called with a wrong argument. Graph construction is a one-time cost; we report it separately rather than assume it amortized away (at our scale it is comparable to request-time cost) and sweep four knobs controlling how much graph evidence to expose against success and tokens.

AI.tldr: ToolGraph compiles tool-catalog dependencies into a directed weighted graph and shows that an LLM-based Q-value estimator conditioned on graph evidence and concrete state outperforms PageRank retrieval by 8.3 points on average.
AI.motivation: Tool-use agents struggle to infer which tool outputs satisfy which later inputs from descriptions alone, and prior graph methods only retrieve tools or score the next call without modeling multi-step value.
AI.method: ToolGraph builds a dependency graph via parameter matching and interventional probes, then evaluates three Q(s,a,g) estimators (dynamic programming over entity sets, distilled GraphSAGE, and an LLM scorer conditioned on graph evidence) with a verbalizer returning feedback to the agent across two benchmarks and three backbones.
AI.result: The LLM estimator outperforms personalized-PageRank retrieval in every benchmark-backbone setting by an average of 8.3 points, whereas the two purely structural estimators fall below PageRank because tool-type values cannot distinguish correct tools called with wrong arguments.
AI.conclusion: Composing tool-dependency graphs into multi-step action values improves test-time tool-use scaling only when the value estimator also inspects the concrete execution state.

title: Dynamic Shaping: Acquiring Interfaces and Constructing Execution over Frozen Pretrained Components
comment: 12 pages, 2 figures. Code and complete evidence: this https URL
summary: We introduce Dynamic Shaping, a method for constructing executable neural arrangements through acquired response and partial-derivative interfaces over frozen pretrained components. The method learns local descriptions of available computation, ranks component rebindings using task-gradient alignment, transports the current interface across a rebinding, and retains changes through behavioral feedback. Continuous interface acquisition uses proximal policy optimization; the source coefficients remain fixed. We derive an exact identity relating transport error in component responses and partials to changes in action logits and their sensitivities. A pixels-only ViZDoom Basic study evaluates first task acquisition without a competent reference controller, demonstrations or intact response targets. Across three initializations and 100 shared held-out game seeds, initial arrangements succeed on 86/300 controller/episode pairs; joint interface-and-binding construction succeeds on 295/300. Fixed-binding interface acquisition also reaches 295/300. Each policy executes four source fragments, with 110 acquired interface values and fixed random visual and action projections. The artifact includes all candidate trials, interventions and costs; all 1,200 recorded initial/retained outcomes replay exactly. The contribution is an explicit profile, rebind, transport and retain procedure and a reproducible reference-free acquisition case over frozen pretrained computation.

AI.tldr: Dynamic Shaping constructs executable neural policies over frozen pretrained components by acquiring response and partial-derivative interfaces, ranking rebindings by gradient alignment, and transporting interfaces with PPO.
AI.motivation: Building executable neural arrangements from frozen pretrained components without a competent reference controller, demonstrations, or intact response targets requires a principled way to acquire interfaces and rebind computation.
AI.method: The method learns local response and partial-derivative descriptions, ranks component rebindings via task-gradient alignment, transports interfaces across rebindings using an exact error-to-logit identity, and retains changes via PPO with fixed source coefficients, evaluated on pixels-only ViZDoom Basic.
AI.result: Across three initializations and 100 held-out game seeds (300 pairs), initial arrangements succeed on 86/300 pairs, while both joint interface-and-binding construction and fixed-binding interface acquisition reach 295/300 using four source fragments and 110 acquired interface values, with all 1,200 recorded outcomes replaying exactly.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic Shaping provides a reproducible, reference-free procedure for composing executable policies over frozen pretrained computation.

title: BiGSyn: A Bi-Level Heterogeneous Graph Contrastive Learning Framework for Interpretable Drug Synergy Prediction
comment: 2026 IEEE International Conference on Data Mining (ICDM 2026)
summary: Drug combination therapy has become a mainstream of modern medicine, with the potential to enhance efficacy, reduce toxicity, and overcome drug resistance. However, identifying synergistic drug combinations remains challenging, as it requires modeling complex interactions across multiple biological scales---from atom-level molecular structures to entity-level relations in biological networks. Existing approaches typically model these levels in isolation, overlooking complementary signals and long-range dependencies. To address these limitations, we propose BiGSyn, a Bi-level heterogeneous Graph contrastive learning framework for drug Synergy prediction. Specifically, BiGSyn leverages heterogeneous graph transformers to extract high-order dependencies from molecular graphs and biological networks, and introduces a bi-level contrastive learning objective to bridge the cross-level semantic gap. Extensive experiments on two benchmark datasets show that BiGSyn consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. Moreover, its attention mechanism highlights key molecular substructures and biological interactions driving synergy, providing interpretable insights.

AI.tldr: BiGSyn is a bi-level heterogeneous graph contrastive learning framework for drug synergy prediction that models both atom-level molecular structures and entity-level biological networks.
AI.motivation: Identifying synergistic drug combinations requires capturing multi-scale interactions from molecular structures to biological networks, which existing methods typically model in isolation.
AI.method: BiGSyn uses heterogeneous graph transformers to extract high-order dependencies from molecular graphs and biological networks and applies a bi-level contrastive learning objective to bridge the cross-level semantic gap.
AI.result: Across two benchmark datasets, BiGSyn consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, and its attention mechanism highlights key molecular substructures and biological interactions driving synergy.
AI.conclusion: Bridging molecular and biological-network representations via bi-level contrastive learning improves both predictive accuracy and interpretability in drug synergy prediction.

title: AdMem: Expectation-Grounded Procedural Memory for Long-Horizon Task-Solving Agents
comment: 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). Workshop: Agents in the Wild: Safety, Security, and Beyond
summary: An agent that carries memory across tasks is only as good as the entries it keeps. We begin from an observation that is easy to reproduce and uncomfortable for the field: naively accumulating cross-task experience can make an agent \emph{worse} than one with no memory at all. On AgentBoard, a workflow-induction memory solves fewer tasks than a memoryless ReAct agent in seven of eight domains, and a per-step procedural store with no surrounding structure loses half of ReAct's completions on Jericho. We argue that the missing ingredients are per-action credit assignment and an explicit life cycle for stored entries, and present AdMem, which supplies both. Before each action the actor commits to an expected outcome; a concurrently running critic scores the realized outcome against that expectation and writes a procedural entry carrying a binary reward and a reflection, so credit lands on the action that earned it and no environment reward is required. Each entry then carries a scalar utility, updated online under a noisy-OR reward model, that ranks retrieval jointly with context similarity and drives eviction and merging, giving the store a forgetting and consolidation policy instead of unbounded growth. Across 707 tasks in eight AgentBoard domains AdMem solves 441 against 388 for ReAct and 312 for the workflow-induction baseline --- a pooled gain significant under a two-sided Fisher exact test, concentrated in the domains that supply transferable cross-task structure. All memory stays human-readable text, which is what makes the failures above diagnosable --- and, as we discuss, also makes the store an auditable but attackable surface.

AI.tldr: AdMem is an expectation-grounded procedural memory with per-action credit assignment and utility-based eviction that solves 441 of 707 AgentBoard tasks, outperforming ReAct (388) and workflow-induction baselines (312).
AI.motivation: Naively accumulating cross-task agent memory can degrade performance below a memoryless agent because entries lack per-action credit assignment and an explicit life-cycle policy.
AI.method: Before each action the actor states an expected outcome, a concurrent critic scores the realized outcome to write a human-readable procedural entry with a binary reward and reflection without requiring environment rewards, and a scalar utility updated under a noisy-OR model guides retrieval, merging, and eviction.
AI.result: Across 707 tasks in eight AgentBoard domains, AdMem solves 441 tasks versus 388 for ReAct and 312 for workflow induction (statistically significant under a two-sided Fisher exact test), with gains concentrated in domains with transferable cross-task structure.
AI.conclusion: Per-action expectation-grounded credit assignment and utility-driven forgetting turn cross-task memory into a reliable performance gain while keeping entries auditable.

title: GEAR$^2$: Pruned Experts Live On through Gated Reuse of Activated Experts and a Missing-Mass Residual
summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) Large Language Models (LLMs) activate only a few experts per token while generally keeping all the experts in GPU memory for high efficiency. Expert pruning reduces this GPU memory footprint cost, yet discards the contribution of pruned experts. Existing remedies either rely on static substitutes, merge experts at the cost of altering their functions, or require costly recovery training. In this paper, we find that the functionalities of pruned experts can be efficiently reconstructed from the activated remaining experts. We propose GEAR (Gated Expert Activation Reuse), which reuses the scaled outputs of reliable activated experts without any training or additional expert computation. In addition, we propose GEAR$^2$ to further recover what reuse cannot express with an ultra-lightweight residual. On five MoE LLMs from 16B to 106B parameters with 25% and 50% of experts pruned, GEAR improves over its training-free counterparts in nearly every setting (up to 4 pp.) in terms of accuracy, and GEAR$^2$ outperforms baseline approaches (up to 2.75 pp.) in every setting on nine zero-shot benchmarks, with larger advantages (up to 2.72 pp. higher) under more aggressive pruning (up to 50%).

AI.tldr: GEAR and GEAR^2 reconstruct the outputs of pruned experts in MoE LLMs from remaining activated experts, improving accuracy by up to 4 percentage points training-free and 2.75 percentage points with a lightweight residual.
AI.motivation: Expert pruning reduces the GPU memory footprint of Mixture-of-Experts LLMs, but existing remedies either discard pruned experts' contributions, distort functions by merging, or require costly recovery training.
AI.method: GEAR (Gated Expert Activation Reuse) reuses scaled outputs of reliable activated experts without training or extra expert computation, and GEAR^2 adds an ultra-lightweight residual to recover what reuse cannot express.
AI.result: Across five MoE LLMs (16B to 106B parameters) at 25% and 50% expert pruning on nine zero-shot benchmarks, GEAR improves over training-free baselines in nearly every setting (up to 4 pp.), and GEAR^2 outperforms all baselines in every setting (up to 2.75 pp., with larger gains up to 2.72 pp. at 50% pruning).
AI.conclusion: Functionalities of pruned MoE experts can be effectively reconstructed from activated experts, enabling high-accuracy memory reduction with minimal or no training.

title: UbiHearo: Bringing Scenario-Aware Sound Guidance to DHH Users with Mobile Agents
summary: For Deaf and Hard-of-Hearing (DHH) users, effective sound awareness goes beyond detecting \emph{what} sound occurs; it requires understanding \emph{what it means}, \emph{how urgent it is}, and \emph{what to do}. However, existing mobile assistants largely reduce acoustic scenes to isolated labels or generic alerts, failing to provide contextual guidance when the same sound implies different risks across scenarios. We present \sysname, a mobile hearing assistant agent that closes the sensing--reasoning--action loop for \textit{scenario-aware} and \textit{personalized} DHH assistance. \sysname adopts a \textit{neuro-symbolic} design that transforms continuous acoustic and physical context streams into structured intermediate representations (IRs) for controllable reasoning and guidance. It introduces three key mechanisms. \textit{First}, a perception-thresholded sensing mechanism enables energy-efficient always-on awareness by activating processing only for perceptually meaningful events while preserving safety-critical cues through deterministic overrides. \textit{Second}, a staged neuro-symbolic reasoning framework performs promptless scenario understanding by conditioning an on-device audio-language model on structured IRs instead of user-authored context descriptions. \textit{Third}, a bounded human-in-the-loop personalization mechanism adapts user-specific guidance through lightweight on-device decision-boundary updates while preserving population-aligned reasoning. We evaluate \sysname on smartphones and in-vehicle systems across diverse scenarios. It achieves favorable accuracy--latency--energy tradeoffs and personalized guidance.

AI.tldr: UbiHearo is a neuro-symbolic mobile hearing assistant for Deaf and Hard-of-Hearing users that converts acoustic and physical context streams into structured intermediate representations for scenario-aware, personalized sound guidance.
AI.motivation: Existing mobile assistants reduce acoustic scenes to isolated labels or generic alerts, failing to convey urgency or actionable guidance when the same sound carries different risks across scenarios.
AI.method: UbiHearo combines perception-thresholded sensing with deterministic overrides for safety-critical cues, staged neuro-symbolic reasoning conditioning an on-device audio-language model on structured intermediate representations without user-authored prompts, and bounded human-in-the-loop personalization via lightweight on-device decision-boundary updates.
AI.result: Evaluations on smartphones and in-vehicle systems across diverse scenarios show favorable accuracy-latency-energy trade-offs and effective personalized guidance.
AI.conclusion: Grounding on-device audio-language models in structured neuro-symbolic representations enables energy-efficient, scenario-aware, and personalized sound guidance for DHH users.

title: VIVID: A Visual Harness for Agentic Video Editing
summary: Video editing requires agents to make editing decisions grounded in audiovisual observations and precise temporal localization, and to evaluate their effects in rendered outputs. General-purpose coding agents possess strong comprehension, reasoning, and code execution capabilities, while media interaction and evidence management mechanisms tailored to video tasks can further unlock their editing potential. We introduce VIVID, a visual harness that supports multiple native coding agents in video post-production without additional model training. VIVID provides tools for on-demand video inspection, audio analysis, and transcription, and preserves observations alongside their corresponding media versions and temporal coordinates. Agents can actively retrieve these observations as they reason, perform edits using their native coding and shell tools, and inspect rendered outputs to guide subsequent revisions. On AgenticVBench, comprising 100 tasks across Assembly, Repair, Sequencing, and Repurpose, Codex with VIVID achieves an average score of 58.6%, an improvement of 20.2 percentage points over native Codex. The same harness also integrates with Claude Code and OpenCode, achieving average scores of 55.1% and 37.1%, respectively, both substantially exceeding their native baselines. These results highlight VIVID's potential as a reusable visual harness for extending the capabilities of general-purpose coding agents to video editing.

AI.tldr: VIVID is a visual harness that equips general-purpose coding agents with on-demand video inspection, audio analysis, and transcription tools, boosting Codex's score on AgenticVBench by 20.2 percentage points.
AI.motivation: General-purpose coding agents have strong reasoning and shell execution skills, but lack tailored media interaction and evidence-management tools needed for audiovisual video editing.
AI.method: VIVID provides on-demand video inspection, audio analysis, and transcription tools that preserve observations alongside media versions and temporal coordinates, enabling coding agents to edit with native tools and inspect rendered outputs without additional training.
AI.result: On AgenticVBench (100 tasks across Assembly, Repair, Sequencing, and Repurpose), Codex with VIVID achieves 58.6% average score (+20.2 pp. over native Codex), while Claude Code and OpenCode with VIVID reach 55.1% and 37.1%, both substantially exceeding their native baselines.
AI.conclusion: A reusable visual harness for audiovisual inspection and temporal evidence tracking unlocks video post-production capabilities in off-the-shelf coding agents.

title: AgentFaultBench: State-Verified Evaluation of Tool-Fault Recovery
comment: 63 pages, 7 figures, including appendices. Submitted to the NAACL 2027 Industry Track
summary: Does recovery advice help an agent finish a task after a tool fails? AgentFaultBench evaluates LangGraph and CrewAI agents performing specified tasks in an isolated GitLab installation. We inject tool errors and check both the resulting files and issues and the required reads, verification and final response. The prompt supplies the expected issue and report text, so the task tests execution rather than content generation. In the primary comparison of 1,944 planned runs, advice changes success by -8.33, 0.00 and +1.06 percentage points relative to a neutral reminder; missing outcomes leave the latter two comparisons inconclusive. Later experiments test a revised recovery policy. GPT-4o mini improves, while Sol and Claude already complete the recoverable cases. In a separate 624-run study on six related tasks not previously used by that policy, the guided condition records 161 correct final states and one unknown outcome in 192 planned runs, versus 142/192 with neutral feedback. The gain lies between +9.90 and +10.42 pp when missing outcomes are included. Removing issue IDs gives 47/48 successes versus 46/48 with IDs; other execution information remains. A second checker agrees on 1,879 observed primary outcomes and 241 constructed test cases. No human validation was collected. The findings support testing advice against explicit recovery controls rather than assuming it helps.

AI.tldr: AgentFaultBench evaluates tool-fault recovery in LangGraph and CrewAI agents on an isolated GitLab setup, showing that recovery advice does not consistently help by default and must be tested against neutral controls.
AI.motivation: It is often assumed that providing recovery advice helps agents finish tasks after tool failures, but this has not been rigorously tested with state-verified execution controls.
AI.method: AgentFaultBench injects tool errors into GitLab tasks with fixed expected outputs, verifies final states and required reads, and compares recovery advice against neutral reminders across 1,944 primary runs and a 624-run follow-up study with a revised policy.
AI.result: In the primary comparison, advice changes success by -8.33, 0.00, and +1.06 percentage points relative to a neutral reminder; with a revised policy on six related tasks, guided recovery achieves 161/192 correct final states (1 unknown) vs. 142/192 for neutral feedback (+9.90 to +10.42 pp.), with a second checker agreeing on 1,879 primary outcomes and 241 test cases.
AI.conclusion: Tool-fault recovery advice can hurt or have no effect unless carefully designed and validated against explicit neutral-feedback controls.

title: PEETS: Preference-aware Embeddings with Explicit Tree Structure for Auxiliary Product Bundling
summary: Auxiliary products such as flight protection and flexible-change services are recommended alongside primary travel purchases. This setting creates a granularity ambiguity: SKUs within one product type share semantics but differ in price and coverage, while rejecting one offer does not imply disinterest in the entire type. We present \textbf{PEETS} (\textbf{P}reference-aware \textbf{E}mbeddings with \textbf{E}xplicit \textbf{T}ree \textbf{S}tructure), a training-time framework for auxiliary product bundling. PEETS regularizes an existing click--conversion predictor through two conditional comparisons. Hierarchical Contrastive Loss uses the pair's common ancestor as a reference; Negative Contrastive Loss conditions structural sampling and comparison shifts on logged rejection events. Both act on shared SKU representations during training. This separates catalog relatedness from individual preference supervision and leaves the predictive serving path intact. PEETS achieves 78.20\% AUC, exceeding TWIN V2 by 0.90 percentage points and the matched base model by 1.15 points. In a 14-day online evaluation, gross auxiliary GMV per exposed user-day improves by 8.20\% over Policies, 3.06\% over Base, and 0.84\% over TWIN V2, with all three user-bootstrap 95\% intervals above zero. Bundling rate is 0.51 points below Policies. The cancellation interval's upper limit exceeds the prespecified margin. PEETS adds no auxiliary-loss computation to serving and records 42.1~ms p95 latency, compared with 42.0~ms for Base.

AI.tldr: PEETS regularizes auxiliary product bundling models during training using hierarchical and rejection-conditioned contrastive losses, improving AUC to 78.20% and online gross auxiliary GMV without adding serving latency.
AI.motivation: Auxiliary travel products share semantics within a product type while differing in price and coverage, so rejecting one SKU does not mean disinterest in the whole type.
AI.method: PEETS applies Hierarchical Contrastive Loss (using common ancestors as references) and Negative Contrastive Loss (conditioned on logged rejection events) to shared SKU representations during training, leaving the serving path unchanged.
AI.result: PEETS reaches 78.20% AUC (+0.90 pp. over TWIN V2, +1.15 pp. over matched base) and in a 14-day online test increases gross auxiliary GMV per exposed user-day by 8.20% over Policies, 3.06% over Base, and 0.84% over TWIN V2, while maintaining 42.1 ms p95 latency (vs. 42.0 ms for Base), though bundling rate is 0.51 points below Policies and cancellation intervals exceed the prespecified margin.
AI.conclusion: Training-time tree-structured and rejection-aware contrastive regularization improves auxiliary bundling revenue and offline discrimination at zero serving-latency cost.

title: Routing Beyond Task Categories: A Cost-Aware LAB-Bench Study
comment: 21 pages, 3 figures. Reproduction archive at this https URL
summary: We tested whether features of biology questions or of a model's first answer can improve accuracy within an inference budget. In a LAB-Bench pilot, we compared a category router with one that adds six structural features. Neither reached the primary 80% accuracy target on development. At the 50% and 60% secondary targets, both chose Haiku for all 120 held-out questions and scored 71/120. We then froze a new comparison before collecting responses on 144 additional questions. Semantic routing scored 86/144. A policy that could defer after reading Haiku's answer scored 87/144. Both stayed within the inference budget of USD 0.678 per 1,000 queries. Against a 95% Haiku and 5% GPT mixture, the accuracy gains were 0.66 percentage points for semantic routing and 1.35 points for deferral. The paired 95% intervals were [-0.28,2.25] and [-0.14,3.47] points. A simple rule that escalated Haiku nonanswers scored 92/144 at USD 0.710 per 1,000 queries, above the budget. A retrospective nonanswer rule with a calibration-selected escalation probability gave an expected 85.63/144. At the learned deferral policy's observed inference cost, post hoc interpolation gave an expected 86.14/144. In a later development check, Astra and Gemini each scored 30/40. The best tested policy in each router family matched that score. The pair covered 33/40 in hindsight. The routers missed the 32/40 criterion, so the proposed 120-question evaluation did not start.

AI.tldr: This cost-aware LAB-Bench study tests feature-based and deferral routing on biology questions, finding that semantic routing and post-answer deferral yield small, statistically inconclusive gains over a fixed Haiku-GPT mixture within budget.
AI.motivation: Routing queries or deferring after a cheap model's first answer could improve biology QA accuracy under strict inference budgets, but its actual cost-accuracy trade-off requires controlled evaluation.
AI.method: In a LAB-Bench pilot and a frozen 144-question comparison within a USD 0.678 per 1,000 queries budget, the authors compare category routing, structural-feature routing, semantic routing, and post-Haiku-answer deferral against a 95% Haiku / 5% GPT mixture.
AI.result: On the 144 questions, semantic routing scores 86/144 (+0.66 pp., 95% CI [-0.28, 2.25]) and deferral scores 87/144 (+1.35 pp., 95% CI [-0.14, 3.47]) within budget, while escalating Haiku nonanswers reaches 92/144 at USD 0.710 per 1,000 queries (over budget); in a later 40-question check, Astra and Gemini each score 30/40 and routers miss the 32/40 criterion.
AI.conclusion: Under tight inference budgets on LAB-Bench, learned routing and deferral policies offer only marginal, inconclusive accuracy gains over simple model mixtures.

title: GainCtrl: Predicting Remaining Gains for Efficient LLM Agent Execution
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are widely used to power agents that interact with tools and environments to solve complex tasks. Repeated attempts improve the quality of tool-using agents, but continued execution incurs additional costs even when it is unlikely to improve the best result ultimately returned. This raises the question of when to stop an attempt to reduce execution cost while preserving task-level Best-of-N quality. To address this question, we introduce GainCtrl, a gain-based execution controller for LLMs. In GainCtrl, a lightweight CPU predictor uses interaction histories to estimate expected positive gains over retained scores, which are then used to guide stopping decisions with calibrated thresholds to limit the loss in mean Best-of-N task quality. We evaluate the controller through trajectory replay across three environments and three LLM actors. Comparisons of interpolated quality-cost Pareto frontiers show that GainCtrl generally uses fewer tokens than baselines at matched target quality. Fixed policies also achieve quality close to that of full execution while substantially reducing token consumption. The predictor runs at millisecond latency on a single CPU thread, supporting repeated monitoring without access to LLM internals.

AI.tldr: GainCtrl is a lightweight CPU execution controller that predicts remaining positive gains from interaction histories to stop redundant Best-of-N agent attempts early, reducing token consumption at matched task quality.
AI.motivation: Repeated agent attempts improve Best-of-N quality, but continuing execution when further attempts are unlikely to beat the current best result wastes tokens and compute.
AI.method: GainCtrl trains a lightweight CPU predictor (running at millisecond latency on a single thread without LLM internal access) to estimate expected positive gains over retained scores from interaction histories, using calibrated thresholds to trigger early stopping.
AI.result: Trajectory replay across three environments and three LLM actors shows that GainCtrl uses fewer tokens than baselines at matched target quality on interpolated quality-cost Pareto frontiers, and fixed policies preserve near-full quality with substantial token savings.
AI.conclusion: Predicting remaining Best-of-N gains on-the-fly enables practical, model-agnostic token savings for tool-using agents.

title: EEGProbe: Do Vision-Language Models Really Understand EEG? A Benchmark for Signal-Grounded EEG Signals Evaluation
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) have shown strong multimodal capabilities across scientific and biomedical domains, yet their ability to understand electroencephalography (EEG) signals remains unclear. We introduce EEGProbe, a signal-grounded benchmark for evaluating whether general-purpose VLMs can extract and reason from minimally processed, channel-wise EEG without task-specific feature engineering or EEG-specific adaptation. EEGProbe contains 620 EEG-centered questions across 13 subtasks and three capability categories: EEG Signal Classification, EEG Cross-modal Alignment, and EEG Neurophysiological Reasoning. To reduce shortcut-based answering, EEGProbe preserves the temporal structure of the recordings where possible, minimizes benchmark-induced processing, and applies signal-necessity testing followed by expert verification. We evaluate 11 representative open- and closed-source VLMs under a unified zero-shot protocol. The strongest model, GPT-5.6 Sol, achieves an overall score of only 41.63\%, with cross-modal EEG alignment emerging as a major bottleneck.
