We further examine model behavior from a neurophysiological perspective and analyze how temporal, spectral, spatial, and physiological EEG structure relates to model successes and failures. Inference-time neurophysiological guidance can reshape model predictions by helping models recognize the neurophysiological patterns present in the input and connect them with relevant neurological knowledge, narrowing the gap between general multimodal competence and EEG understanding. EEGProbe provides a testbed for current VLMs and a basis for developing future multimodal models that can interpret EEG evidence more reliably. The EEGProbe benchmark will be publicly available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: EEGProbe benchmarks 11 VLMs on 620 signal-grounded EEG questions across 13 subtasks, finding that the strongest model scores only 41.63% zero-shot and that cross-modal EEG alignment is a major bottleneck.
AI.motivation: While VLMs perform well on many biomedical tasks, it remains unclear whether they can actually interpret minimally processed, channel-wise EEG signals without task-specific adaptation.
AI.method: EEGProbe preserves temporal recording structure, applies signal-necessity testing and expert verification across three capability categories (Signal Classification, Cross-modal Alignment, Neurophysiological Reasoning), and evaluates 11 open- and closed-source VLMs under a unified zero-shot protocol, also testing inference-time neurophysiological guidance.
AI.result: The strongest tested model, GPT-5.6 Sol, achieves only 41.63% overall zero-shot accuracy, with cross-modal alignment emerging as a primary bottleneck; inference-time neurophysiological guidance helps models recognize patterns and connect them to neurological knowledge, narrowing the performance gap.
AI.conclusion: Current general-purpose VLMs struggle with raw EEG interpretation, and EEGProbe provides a signal-grounded testbed for advancing multimodal neurophysiological reasoning.

title: Regularizing Treatment Leakage for LLM-based Uplift Estimation
summary: Uplift modeling estimates the conditional average treatment effect (CATE) and supports industrial decisions such as promotional pricing. When large language models (LLMs) encode product text, treatment-revealing content can introduce shortcuts that do not transfer to deployment. We propose \emph{LLM-based Uplift Leakage Regularization} (\textsc{LULR}), which uses a CLUB-based penalty on the causal head's trainable shared representation while keeping the LLM encoder frozen. Controlled proxy experiments show a positive ranking-score interaction and higher scores than the tested weight-decay configuration; treatment-dependent evaluation limits their interpretation to exploratory model behavior. Structured-only comparisons provide reference performance, without establishing a general advantage over tree-based estimators. On a million-record industrial pricing RCT, \textsc{LULR} improves offline $\text{lift@}0.3$ in $4/5$ seeds, although the difference is not statistically significant and estimated policy values are near-tied. A separate one-week online A/B experiment records $5.45\%$ higher sales volume and $1.91\%$ higher GMV than the control arm. These aggregate results provide short-term business evidence for the complete deployed pricing policy; they do not isolate the regularizer's contribution.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes LULR, a regularization method for LLM-based uplift modeling that penalizes treatment leakage in the causal head, and evaluates it on proxy tasks and an industrial pricing RCT.
AI.motivation: When LLMs encode product text for CATE estimation, treatment-revealing content can create shortcuts that fail to transfer at deployment.
AI.method: LULR applies a CLUB-based penalty to the causal head's trainable shared representation while keeping the LLM encoder frozen.
AI.result: LULR improves offline lift@0.3 in 4/5 seeds on a million-record pricing RCT (not statistically significant, near-tied policy values), while a separate one-week online A/B test shows 5.45% higher sales volume and 1.91% higher GMV for the full deployed policy.
AI.conclusion: LULR mitigates treatment leakage in frozen-LLM uplift models, though the online gains reflect the complete deployed policy rather than isolating the regularizer's effect.

title: ForeSay: Tell the Future in Words, Branch the Details in Noise for Precipitation Nowcasting
summary: Precipitation nowcasting involves two distinct scales of uncertainty: macroscopic storm evolution and fine-scale local convective variations. Current generative ensemble methods entangle both scales within independent random noise draws. This coupling causes two practical limitations: every ensemble member must execute the full sampling trajectory from scratch, so an N-member ensemble costs N times a single forecast; moreover, divergent trajectories spatially misalign heavy-rain echoes across members, causing standard pixel-wise averaging to blur critical high-intensity extremes. We present ForeSay, a generative nowcasting framework that decouples macroscopic evolution prediction from local stochastic detail generation. Given historical radar frames, a vision-language model first predicts a textual scenario of future storm dynamics to condition a Rectified Flow generator. Guided by this shared macroscopic prior, ensemble members share early trunk sampling steps to establish the storm trajectory and branch with fresh noise only in later steps to explore local convective details. Because members then differ mainly in local details, self-anchored support-consensus decoding replaces pixel averaging with discrete support voting to preserve sharp heavy-rain cores. Across six datasets, ForeSay achieves the best CSI at the highest precipitation thresholds, with relative improvements over the strongest baseline on each dataset ranging from over 10% to 84%. Our 8-member ensemble retains the forecasting skill and diversity of eight independently sampled runs while reducing computational cost from 8x to 5.2x that of a single forecast.

AI.tldr: ForeSay is a generative precipitation nowcasting framework that decouples macroscopic storm evolution from local convective details, improving extreme-rain CSI while reducing ensemble sampling cost.
AI.motivation: Existing generative ensemble nowcasting methods entangle macroscopic storm trajectories and fine-scale details in independent noise draws, causing N-times sampling cost and blurred heavy-rain extremes under pixel averaging.
AI.method: A vision-language model first predicts a textual future storm scenario to condition a Rectified Flow generator; ensemble members share early trunk sampling steps, branch with fresh noise only in later steps, and use self-anchored support-consensus decoding instead of pixel averaging.
AI.result: Across six datasets, ForeSay achieves the best CSI at the highest precipitation thresholds with relative gains over the strongest baselines from over 10% to 84%, while an 8-member ensemble cuts cost from 8x to 5.2x a single forecast.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling macroscopic priors from local stochastic branching preserves sharp heavy-rain cores and reduces ensemble inference cost.

title: LynnReal-Hand: Unlocking World Interaction with Hand Control
summary: Interactive video world models enable exploration through text and camera controls, yet direct object interaction requires finer control. Hands provide a natural interface, but translating continuous hand movements into coherent visual responses remains challenging because of complex hand-object dynamics and demanding real-time computation. To address these challenges, we introduce LynnReal-Hand, a hand-controlled video world model that unifies precise interaction modeling with efficient streaming generation. We curate 100K interaction clips spanning diverse real and synthetic environments and develop hand-aware supervision to improve fine-grained hand motions and object interactions. Building on this foundation, we learn a causal flow map for few-step generation and introduce region-aware score distillation that combines complementary video and image priors to refine interaction dynamics and visual appearance. To further reduce inference latency, we propose Ultra-Fast-VAE, a compact video decoder that preserves high reconstruction fidelity with substantially lower computational cost. Extensive evaluations on HandBench demonstrate superior hand-following accuracy and visual quality compared with existing approaches. Our full-sequence model achieves an FVD of 181.67 and a MANO Dice score of 93.02, while the three-step causal model maintains a MANO Dice score of 92.49. For real-time interaction, 540p streaming on a single H200 reaches 18.03 FPS with 741ms latency and an optimized peak GPU memory footprint of only 34.89GB. We will release the datasets, model weights, and the full training and inference code to support research on hand-controlled video world models.

AI.tldr: LynnReal-Hand is a hand-controlled video world model that unifies fine-grained hand-object interaction modeling with real-time streaming generation.
AI.motivation: Translating continuous hand movements into coherent visual responses in interactive video world models is difficult due to complex hand-object dynamics and high real-time computation costs.
AI.method: The authors curate 100K interaction clips with hand-aware supervision, learn a causal flow map with region-aware score distillation combining video and image priors for few-step generation, and introduce Ultra-Fast-VAE for fast decoding.
AI.result: On HandBench, the full-sequence model reaches 181.67 FVD and 93.02 MANO Dice (92.49 for the 3-step causal model), and 540p streaming on a single H200 runs at 18.03 FPS with 741 ms latency and 34.89 GB peak GPU memory.
AI.conclusion: LynnReal-Hand enables accurate, real-time hand-controlled world interaction and will release its dataset, weights, and code.

title: Lost in the Hallway: Benchmarking Persistent Spatial Memory Across Revisits
summary: Persistent spatial understanding is essential for embodied agents to operate reliably in environments they repeatedly encounter. It requires recognizing revisited places despite viewpoint changes, distinguishing them from similar-looking rooms, and updating memories as environments change. Yet existing evaluations often leave physical place identity across separated visits implicit. We introduce ReSpaceBench, a benchmark comprising 3,244 questions across 590 synthetic and real-home scenes, organized into 9 tasks spanning room association, persistent state tracking, and downstream reasoning. Controlled walkthroughs define visits by physical room entry and deliberately include same-type room distractors and cross-session object changes. Our evaluation of 32 models and 3 agentic video-understanding frameworks reveals substantial limitations: the strongest evaluated zero-shot model achieves 50.5% overall accuracy and 52.2% on a 450-question subset, compared with 90.1% for human annotators. The evaluated agentic frameworks offer no overall improvement over direct inference with the same base model. Analysis of agent execution traces reveals evidence omissions and incorrect cross-visit room associations as major failure modes, suggesting that iterative evidence seeking alone does not ensure consistent spatial memory. Further analyses expose a gap between recognizing familiar rooms and identifying the correct visited room, while annotation-guided sampling highlights the importance of preserving intervening visits and transitions. We also provide RS-30K, a separate training dataset from synthetic sources with no template, scene, route, or video overlap with the benchmark. Fine-tuning Qwen3-VL-8B raises overall accuracy from 35.5% to 60.4%, with the largest gains in association and improvements extending to real-life scenes.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces ReSpaceBench and RS-30K to evaluate and improve persistent spatial memory across room revisits in embodied and video-understanding models.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations often leave physical place identity across separated visits implicit, failing to test whether agents can distinguish similar-looking rooms and track cross-session state changes.
AI.method: ReSpaceBench provides 3,244 questions across 590 synthetic and real-home scenes in 9 tasks with same-type room distractors and object changes; the authors also curate RS-30K for synthetic training without benchmark overlap.
AI.result: Across 32 models and 3 agentic frameworks, the strongest zero-shot model reaches 50.5% overall accuracy (52.2% on a 450-question subset) versus 90.1% for humans, agentic frameworks give no overall gain, and fine-tuning Qwen3-VL-8B on RS-30K raises accuracy from 35.5% to 60.4%.
AI.conclusion: Current models and iterative evidence-seeking frameworks struggle with persistent cross-visit spatial memory, which targeted synthetic training can partially improve.

title: DuoFlow: Towards Synchronized Speech and Motion Generation with Fine-Grained Control
summary: An embodied speaker's expressiveness depends not only on what is said, but also on how the voice sounds and how the body moves. However, existing joint speech-motion generation models are largely driven implicitly by transcript semantics or intermediate speech representations, offering little explicit control over motion hierarchy, body parts, or vocal style. To bridge this gap, we construct MotionSpeech, a structured benchmark for controllable joint speech-motion generation that includes transcripts, voice-style descriptions, and motion conditions at two hierarchical levels. Building on this benchmark, we propose DuoFlow, a dual-stream latent flow transformer that jointly denoises speech and motion under a shared noise level and a unified second-based temporal coordinate. Modality-specific residual connectors inject structured conditions into the corresponding streams, layer-wise bidirectional cross-modal attention coordinates their generation, and a monotonic phoneme pathway combines normalized progress anchors with CTC supervision to strengthen speech temporal modeling. DuoFlow provides a unified interface for fine-grained motion and vocal-style control and demonstrates the ability to synthesize high-quality, synchronized, and instruction-consistent speech-motion sequences.

AI.tldr: The authors introduce the MotionSpeech benchmark and DuoFlow, a dual-stream latent flow transformer for controllable, synchronized joint speech and motion generation.
AI.motivation: Existing joint speech-motion models are driven implicitly by transcripts or intermediate speech features, lacking explicit control over motion hierarchy, body parts, and vocal style.
AI.method: DuoFlow jointly denoises speech and motion under a shared noise level and second-based temporal coordinate, using modality-specific residual connectors, layer-wise bidirectional cross-modal attention, and a monotonic phoneme pathway with normalized progress anchors and CTC supervision.
AI.result: DuoFlow synthesizes high-quality, synchronized, and instruction-consistent speech-motion sequences with fine-grained control over motion and vocal style on MotionSpeech.
AI.conclusion: Explicit dual-stream conditioning and shared temporal alignment provide a unified interface for controllable embodied speech-motion generation.

title: BLIP-Live: Balancing Timeliness & Firing Precision in Proactive Streaming Video Agents
summary: Streaming video understanding is becoming increasingly important for real-world interactive systems. Such systems must be proactive for natural and useful human interaction: they should respond as soon as sufficient evidence becomes available while avoiding premature, redundant, or incorrect responses. We present BLIP-Live, a framework unifying data, metrics, harness, and training around a shared formulation of proactivity as effective causal response decisions balancing the two competing objectives of responding vs silence. First, we construct BLIP-Live-780K dataset containing human annotations of proactive response content and timing, which defines this desired behavior. We then propose PAUC-F, a metric to effectively measure our desired proactive behavior. PAUC-F combines existing response timeliness metrics with firing precision to reward early useful responses without rewarding excessive firing. With our desired behavior defined and measurable, we finally investigate model-agnostic inference harnesses that draw out proactive streaming capabilities of offline vision language models (VLMs), together with training pipelines that learn to further improve their proactive responsiveness. Across both settings, we find that combinations of sliding visual windows, online interaction memory, and structured response outputs consistently yield strongest proactive performance. Our experiments result in two models, with our BLIP-Live-Qwen model achieving state-of-the-art performance across four proactive streaming benchmarks, with gains up to 44% over baselines and outperforming multiple closed API models. Our code and data will be released publicly.

AI.tldr: BLIP-Live is a framework for proactive streaming video agents that unifies dataset construction, evaluation metrics, inference harnesses, and training to balance response timeliness and firing precision.
AI.motivation: Proactive streaming video agents must respond as soon as sufficient evidence appears without firing prematurely, redundantly, or inaccurately.
AI.method: The authors build the BLIP-Live-780K dataset, propose the PAUC-F metric combining timeliness and firing precision, and evaluate model-agnostic inference harnesses (sliding visual windows, online interaction memory, structured outputs) alongside training pipelines.
AI.result: BLIP-Live-Qwen achieves state-of-the-art performance across four proactive streaming benchmarks, with gains up to 44% over baselines and outperforming multiple closed API models.
AI.conclusion: Formulating proactivity as causal response-versus-silence decisions with aligned data, metrics, and memory harnesses substantially improves streaming video agents.

title: Reference Forcing: Long Video Generation with Region-Guided Drift Correction
comment: 17 pages, 12 figures, 3 tables. Project page: this https URL
summary: Long video generation should keep the subject and background consistent while supporting rich, natural motion. However, autoregressive models are often distilled with distribution matching distillation (DMD) over short windows, which does not train them to keep this consistency over long ranges. As a result, the subject and background can drift over time. Methods that manage the key-value (KV) cache retain or retrieve history to reduce drift. Yet this history may itself have drifted. We propose Reference Forcing, which uses the initial frames as an appearance reference. We first build a teacher that uses attention masks to force each region of a new frame to attend to the same region in the initial frames. The teacher finds these regions with off-the-shelf segmentation models. We then distill this behavior into a separate attention path of the student, which needs no external models at inference. We further introduce value correction, which corrects drifted values in the KV cache toward the matching values of drift-free initial frames. Experiments show that Reference Forcing achieves state-of-the-art subject and background consistency among long-video methods on different base models, and its advantage grows with video length. Ablations show both components are needed to gain consistency without losing motion. More visualizations and code are available at this https URL

AI.tldr: Reference Forcing is a long-video generation method that reduces subject and background drift by distilling region-guided attention to initial frames and correcting drifted KV cache values.
AI.motivation: Autoregressive video models distilled over short windows suffer from subject and background drift over long horizons, and KV-cache history methods can still retrieve already-drifted frames.
AI.method: A teacher uses segmentation masks to force each region to attend to the corresponding region in drift-free initial frames, which is distilled into a student attention path needing no external segmentation at inference, paired with KV-cache value correction toward initial frames.
AI.result: Reference Forcing achieves state-of-the-art subject and background consistency across different base models with widening gains at longer lengths, and ablations confirm both components are needed to preserve motion.
AI.conclusion: Anchoring both attention and KV-cache values to initial frames effectively mitigates long-range drift in autoregressive video generation.

title: Wildfire-SSR: Geolocation-Aware Multimodal Fusion for Structure-Level Wildfire Risk Assessment
summary: Structure-level wildfire vulnerability assessment is critical for reducing losses in wildland-urban interface communities, yet existing methods often fail to combine parcel-scale ignition pathways with community-scale geographic coverage. This study introduces Wildfire-SSR (Satellite and Street-view for wildfire Risk), a geolocation-aware multimodal framework that integrates macro-scale satellite context with micro-scale street-view evidence. A Vision-Language Model extracts wildfire-relevant building and site attributes from pre-event street-view panoramas and converts them into structured semantic text. These features are spatially aligned with satellite imagery through a decoupled cross-attention fusion decoder, while a frozen satellite-pretrained DINOv3 encoder captures overhead visual context. Alternative geolocation embedding strategies are evaluated to anchor text-derived features within each satellite patch. The framework is tested on approximately 37,000 structures affected by the 2025 Eaton and Palisades fires in Los Angeles, using wildfire risk labels derived from relative post-event damage patterns to better represent inherent structural vulnerability. Rotary Positional Embedding provides the strongest spatial grounding, achieving a building localization F1 score of 0.6735 and a harmonic mean F1 score of 0.2476 for five-class pixel-level risk classification, outperforming unimodal baselines and an unanchored multimodal configuration. The model also shows a conservative bias in higher-risk classes, reducing severe-risk underestimation, and completes end-to-end assessment of the study area in 37 minutes on a single GPU. Wildfire-SSR reframes cross-view fusion as localized semantic alignment and provides a scalable tool for mitigation prioritization, resilience planning, and insurance-oriented wildfire risk assessment.

AI.tldr: Wildfire-SSR is a geolocation-aware multimodal framework that fuses street-view VLM attributes with satellite imagery for structure-level wildfire risk assessment.
AI.motivation: Existing wildfire vulnerability methods struggle to combine parcel-scale ignition details with community-scale geographic coverage.
AI.method: A VLM extracts building and site attributes from pre-event street-view panoramas as structured text, which is spatially aligned with frozen DINOv3 satellite features via a decoupled cross-attention fusion decoder using Rotary Positional Embedding.
AI.result: Tested on about 37,000 structures from the 2025 Eaton and Palisades fires, Wildfire-SSR achieves 0.6735 building localization F1 and 0.2476 harmonic mean F1 for five-class risk classification, outperforming unimodal and unanchored baselines in 37 minutes on one GPU.
AI.conclusion: Reframing cross-view fusion as localized semantic alignment enables scalable structure-level wildfire risk assessment for mitigation and resilience planning.

title: When Do Histology Foundation Models Need Geometric Test-Time Augmentation?
summary: Test-time augmentation (TTA) aggregates model predictions across multiple transformed views of an input during inference. Because histology images lack a canonical orientation, $D_4$ TTA---pooling across the 8 rotations and reflections of a square---is a standard default in computational pathology. However, the rise of self-supervised histology foundation models (FMs) with inherent rotational invariance calls its continued utility into question. We benchmark 9 histology FMs and 6 general-purpose models across four patch-level and two whole-slide image (WSI) datasets. We find that $D_4$ TTA remains a reliable post hoc improvement, but benefits diminish from $+1.98$ percentage points (pp) for general-purpose backbones to $+0.50$ pp for histology FMs on TCGA-UT, and shrink further for the largest models. To eliminate computational overhead, our experiments demonstrate that entropy routing---applying TTA selectively to uncertain predictions---recovers most of the gain while augmenting only ${\sim}13\%$ of samples. Finally, we show that patch-level TTA improvements do not transfer to slide-level multiple instance learning (MIL). Code: this https URL

AI.tldr: This study benchmarks D4 geometric test-time augmentation (TTA) across histology foundation models and proposes entropy routing to cut its computational overhead.
AI.motivation: While D4 TTA is standard in computational pathology, self-supervised histology foundation models with built-in rotational invariance may no longer need it.
AI.method: The authors evaluate 9 histology foundation models and 6 general-purpose models across four patch-level and two whole-slide image datasets, and test entropy routing to apply TTA only to uncertain predictions.
AI.result: D4 TTA still helps, but gains drop from +1.98 pp for general-purpose backbones to +0.50 pp for histology FMs on TCGA-UT; entropy routing recovers most gains while augmenting only ~13% of samples, and patch-level TTA gains do not transfer to slide-level MIL.
AI.conclusion: Selective entropy-routed TTA preserves accuracy gains at low cost for patch-level tasks, whereas slide-level MIL does not benefit from patch-level TTA.

title: FaceJev: Direct Visual Decisions for Face Forgery Detection
summary: Face forgery detection methods often perform well on seen manipulations but generalize poorly to unseen ones. Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) can recognize facial parts and assess their visual plausibility. Existing MLLM-based methods typically express these judgments through textual explanations, but seldom treat individual part decisions as explicit learning targets. We present FaceJev, an MLLM-based method for face forgery detection through direct visual decisions. Following the Jev formulation, FaceJev answers eight independent questions about facial parts using a shared image encoding and reads anomaly probabilities from the native answer logits. A face is classified as forged if any part is predicted to be abnormal, directly linking the detection result to the part decisions. We construct PartForensics, a dataset of approximately 160k images with binary anomaly targets for the eight facial parts, to supervise these decisions. We further propose FS-GRPO, which optimizes each part decision through an exact reward comparison with its alternative, using both detection and part rewards. FaceJev outperforms the strongest baseline by 7.25 percentage points on unseen manipulations. Extensive ablation studies validate our design choices and the effectiveness of the main components.

AI.tldr: FaceJev is an MLLM-based face forgery detector that predicts binary anomaly probabilities for eight facial parts directly from native answer logits.
AI.motivation: Face forgery detectors generalize poorly to unseen manipulations, and existing MLLM approaches rely on textual explanations rather than treating individual part decisions as explicit learning targets.
AI.method: FaceJev answers eight independent facial-part questions from a shared image encoding, reads anomaly probabilities from native logits, classifies a face as forged if any part is abnormal, and trains on the 160k-image PartForensics dataset using FS-GRPO.
AI.result: FaceJev outperforms the strongest baseline by 7.25 percentage points on unseen manipulations, with ablations confirming the effectiveness of its components.
AI.conclusion: Direct part-level visual decisions supervised with exact-comparison RL substantially improve generalization in face forgery detection.

title: ViRA: Toward Ultra-High-Resolution Visual Agents via Cross-Input Relative Policy Optimization
comment: 74 pages, 11 figures, 26 tables. Code: this https URL
summary: Visual agents answer questions about ultra-high-resolution photos by zooming into the relevant regions. However, existing agents often answer from common sense instead of reading the evidence. Reinforcement learning (RL) on the final answer cannot correct this, because a guess earns the same reward as reading. We propose Cross-Input Relative Policy Optimization (CrossRPO), which trains agents on contrast sets. A contrast set asks one question about several versions of an image that differ only in a small region with the evidence and have different answers, so only reading the evidence solves the whole set. CrossRPO rewards solving the whole set, and we prove that it does not reinforce a set answered from common sense. We build contrast sets for training (ViRA-Train) and evaluation (ViRA-Bench) by editing one small object in images of 21 to 120 megapixels, and we photograph further sets with real changes (ViRA-Bench-Real) to exclude editing traces. We train two Visual Reasoning Agents, ViRA-9B and ViRA-27B, with CrossRPO on only about 3,500 items of ViRA-Train each. CrossRPO achieves 63.3% set accuracy on ViRA-Bench at the maximum resolution, against 59.3% for GRPO. ViRA-9B is the most accurate open model of its size on all benchmarks, and ViRA-27B outperforms Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6-Luna, both at their highest thinking level, on most benchmarks.

AI.tldr: CrossRPO trains ultra-high-resolution visual reasoning agents on contrast sets so they must read local visual evidence rather than guess from common sense.
AI.motivation: Existing visual agents often answer ultra-high-resolution questions from common sense, and standard RL on final answers cannot prevent guessing.
AI.method: CrossRPO rewards solving an entire contrast set of image variants that differ only in a small evidence region; the authors build ViRA-Train, ViRA-Bench (21-120 MP), and ViRA-Bench-Real, and train ViRA-9B and ViRA-27B on ~3,500 items each.
AI.result: CrossRPO reaches 63.3% set accuracy on ViRA-Bench at maximum resolution versus 59.3% for GRPO; ViRA-9B leads open models of its size, and ViRA-27B outperforms Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6-Luna on most benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Contrast-set policy optimization provably avoids reinforcing common-sense guesses and yields strong ultra-high-resolution visual agents.

title: RoboACE: Adversarial Co-Evolution for Robot Self-Improvement
summary: Robot agents can improve reusable skills, planning procedures, and recovery strategies from execution feedback, yet a fixed practice source leaves the search for new weaknesses unchanged. Useful practice depends on the agent's current capabilities, so the procedure that chooses practice must also be revisable. We present RoboACE (Robot Adversarial Co-Evolution), a framework that jointly evolves curriculum and execution harnesses around frozen foundation models. The curriculum harness uses accumulated capability evidence to propose informative challenges, while the execution harness responds with reusable revisions that expand execution capabilities. Alternating updates hold one side fixed as the other changes, and admitted challenges form fixed snapshots for comparing execution revisions. Starting from a compact set of LIBERO practice conditions, the resulting frozen deployment outperforms the evaluated controllers and agent systems across four LIBERO-family panels. On LIBERO-PRO, it reaches 74.0% success, exceeding the initial deployment by 15.0 percentage points and direct execution by its VLA controller by 13.5 points. Case studies document changes to evidence-guided practice selection, drawer-skill grounding, and controller intervention.

AI.tldr: RoboACE is an adversarial co-evolution framework that jointly updates curriculum and execution harnesses around frozen foundation models for robot self-improvement.
AI.motivation: Robot agents using fixed practice sources cannot adaptively target new weaknesses as their capabilities evolve.
AI.method: RoboACE alternates between updating a curriculum harness that proposes informative challenges from capability evidence and an execution harness that adds reusable revisions, using admitted challenges as fixed snapshots for comparison.
AI.result: Starting from compact LIBERO conditions, RoboACE outperforms evaluated controllers and agent systems across four LIBERO-family panels, reaching 74.0% success on LIBERO-PRO (+15.0 pp over initial deployment, +13.5 pp over direct VLA execution).
AI.conclusion: Co-evolving practice selection alongside execution harnesses enables frozen robot foundation models to self-improve effectively.

title: A Survey of Image-to-Code Generation for Software Engineering
summary: A large fraction of software intent is expressed visually before it is implemented. A designer hands a screenshot or a Figma mockup to a front-end engineer, an architect sketches a UML diagram or a flowchart, and a bug report ships with a picture of what went wrong. Turning such visual artifacts directly into executable software has therefore become an active problem at the intersection of computer vision and software engineering. The present survey organizes the literature on image-to-code generation for software engineering, defined as the family of methods whose input contains a visual modality and whose output is software an engineer would otherwise write by hand. We deliberately scope the survey to software-engineering code, namely user-interface and front-end code, code recovered from software diagrams such as UML and flowcharts, program repair and test code driven by visual signals, and general software-code targets, and we exclude adjacent code-generation domains whose home communities lie elsewhere, such as chart plotting scripts, vector-graphics programs, hardware description languages, and robot policies. Rather than cataloguing systems in isolation, we introduce a unified processing pipeline of visual understanding, component recognition, layout reasoning, code planning, code generation, and verification, and organize the survey around its stages. We trace five overlapping eras from rule-based reverse engineering to agentic generation, survey each pipeline stage and each software-engineering task in depth grounded in what individual systems actually do, consolidate the datasets, benchmarks, and metrics, and lay out the open challenges of design-system generalization, long-horizon and interactive generation, cross-framework deployment, accessibility, hallucinated components, and unreliable evaluation.

AI.tldr: This survey organizes the literature on image-to-code generation for software engineering around a unified six-stage processing pipeline and five historical eras.
AI.motivation: Visual artifacts such as UI mockups, UML diagrams, and bug screenshots are central to software engineering, yet prior work is often catalogued in isolation without a shared structural view.
AI.method: The authors define a unified pipeline (visual understanding, component recognition, layout reasoning, code planning, code generation, verification), trace five eras from rule-based reverse engineering to agentic generation, and consolidate datasets, benchmarks, and metrics.
AI.result: The survey maps each pipeline stage and software-engineering task (UI/front-end, diagrams, visual program repair/testing) and identifies open challenges including design-system generalization, long-horizon generation, accessibility, hallucinated components, and unreliable evaluation.
AI.conclusion: Framing image-to-code generation as an end-to-end pipeline clarifies current capabilities and key bottlenecks for future software-engineering research.

title: Robustness as a Transferable Skill: Cross-Task Adversarial Defense for Vision-Language-Action Policies
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies are vulnerable to adversarial visual perturbations, while defenses often require task-specific adversarial fine-tuning. We investigate whether robustness learned on source manipulation tasks can protect independently specialized target policies without target-side adversarial training. We first show that even a single source defense update improves robustness on held-out tasks, establishing cross-task defense reuse independently of multi-source aggregation. To combine source updates, we introduce Source-Norm Transferable Robustness Vector (SN-TRV), which retains the direction of their mean while calibrating its magnitude using source-update norms. The resulting update is applied to the target visual encoder without target adversarial data, target-side gradient optimization, or additional inference modules. Evaluations across three VLA backbones, fixed and adaptive attacks, and different source defense recipes show improved robustness over naive averaging and identify limits in attack coverage. Physical PiPER trials increase average success under printed adversarial patches from 20.3% to 45.8%.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that adversarial robustness can transfer across manipulation tasks for VLA policies and proposes SN-TRV to combine source defense updates without target-side adversarial training.
AI.motivation: Vision-Language-Action policies are vulnerable to adversarial visual perturbations, and existing defenses typically require expensive task-specific adversarial fine-tuning.
AI.method: SN-TRV averages source defense update directions and calibrates the magnitude using source-update norms, applying the update to the target visual encoder with no target adversarial data, gradient optimization, or extra inference modules.
AI.result: Across three VLA backbones and fixed/adaptive attacks, SN-TRV outperforms naive averaging, and in physical PiPER trials it raises average success under printed adversarial patches from 20.3% to 45.8%.
AI.conclusion: Adversarial robustness can be reused as a transferable skill across VLA tasks, though attack coverage remains a limiting factor.

title: RouteDiff: Low-Dose CT Denoising via Fidelity-Refinement Routing and Hypergraph State Regulation
comment: 16 pages, 10 figures, 7 tables. Submitted to Knowledge-Based Systems
summary: Diffusion models have become a strong prior for low-dose computed tomography (LDCT) restoration. However, existing samplers apply one structure-detail trade-off to the whole image, set the restoration emphasis of each step by the timestep, and derive each next state recursively from the current one, carrying its errors forward. We propose RouteDiff, a state-aware dual-route diffusion framework that routes detail to where it can be trusted, regulates each reverse step by the state it has reached, and re-enters the trajectory from an anchored estimate. Fidelity-Refinement Routing (FRR) equips one shared U-Net with a conservative fidelity route and a detail-oriented refinement route, fuses them pixel-wise with a confidence map, and exposes their disagreement as route evidence. Hypergraph State Regulation (HSR) organizes the current features and this evidence into a state hypergraph, whose soft hyperedges group scattered regions in the same state. Its readout yields an ordered stage judgment that modulates the bottleneck, and its incidence guides feature interaction in the skip connections. Estimate-Anchored Re-entry (EAR) re-projects a route-aware anchor onto the trajectory at a fixed step and hands the new state back to HSR to be judged again. With the ten network evaluations of its baseline, RouteDiff achieves the best peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) and structural similarity index (SSIM) on four datasets with inserted, real and simulated noise (40.95 dB and 95.13% on Mayo 2020; 45.18 dB and 97.23% on Mayo 2016). It also generalizes to unseen doses of real scans and yields the highest Dice (80.92%) in downstream segmentation.

AI.tldr: RouteDiff is a state-aware dual-route diffusion framework for low-dose CT denoising that routes detail by local confidence and regulates reverse steps via a state hypergraph.
AI.motivation: Existing diffusion samplers for LDCT apply a single structure-detail trade-off globally, schedule emphasis by timestep, and propagate errors recursively across steps.
AI.method: RouteDiff combines Fidelity-Refinement Routing (a shared U-Net with conservative and detail routes fused by a confidence map), Hypergraph State Regulation (grouping features and route disagreement into a state hypergraph), and Estimate-Anchored Re-entry.
AI.result: Using 10 network evaluations, RouteDiff achieves top PSNR and SSIM on four datasets (40.95 dB / 95.13% on Mayo 2020; 45.18 dB / 97.23% on Mayo 2016), generalizes to unseen doses, and reaches 80.92% Dice in downstream segmentation.
AI.conclusion: State-aware routing and hypergraph regulation improve LDCT restoration quality and downstream clinical utility without increasing evaluation steps.

title: Personalized and Adaptive Federated Learning for Canine Cardiomegaly Keypoint Prediction
summary: In the field of medical imaging, limited data and cross-institutional heterogeneity remain major challenges for training robust deep learning models. Federated learning (FL) has emerged as a promising approach that enables collaborative training across institutions while preserving data privacy by keeping datasets local. In this work, we propose a structure-aware personalized and adaptive federated learning framework, PAFL, for automatic vertebral heart score (VHS) estimation and cardiomegaly classification from canine thoracic X-rays. Our method treats the task as anatomical keypoint prediction followed by geometry-based VHS computation, introducing implicit structural consistency and improving interpretability. To address cross-institutional heterogeneity, we adopt a parameter-decomposed architecture that separates shared feature representations from client-specific adaptation modules. Furthermore, we introduce an adaptive, quality-aware aggregation strategy that dynamically weights client contributions based on both dataset size and model quality, thereby enhancing robustness to non-IID data distributions. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed PAFL framework improves models' predictive performance compared to isolated training and to conventional and existing personalized federated learning (PFL) methods. Our results demonstrate the potential of integrating structure-aware modeling with PFL for reliable and interpretable medical image analysis.

AI.tldr: PAFL is a structure-aware personalized and adaptive federated learning framework for canine vertebral heart score estimation and cardiomegaly classification from thoracic X-rays.
AI.motivation: Medical imaging models face limited data and cross-institutional heterogeneity, which standard federated learning struggles to handle under non-IID distributions.
AI.method: PAFL predicts anatomical keypoints for geometry-based VHS computation, uses a parameter-decomposed architecture separating shared representations from client-specific adapters, and weights client aggregation by dataset size and model quality.
AI.result: PAFL outperforms isolated training, conventional FL, and existing personalized FL baselines in predictive performance.
AI.conclusion: Combining structure-aware keypoint modeling with quality-aware personalized FL yields more reliable and interpretable veterinary X-ray analysis.

title: Accelerating Variational Cone-Beam CT Reconstruction with Learned Warm Starts
summary: Variational reconstruction provides a rigorous framework for cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) by combining an explicit acquisition model with image priors. However, iterative optimization remains computationally demanding, particularly under severe noise and sparse-view conditions. Although learning-based methods achieve high reconstruction quality, they often replace the original variational formulation with learned optimization schemes or nonlinear equilibrium models. We propose a neural network-guided warm-start framework that accelerates variational reconstruction while preserving its original formulation. Projection data are first reconstructed using the Feldkamp-Davis-Kress (FDK) algorithm, and the resulting image is refined by an image-domain neural network. The network output is used solely to initialize the subsequent model-based optimization, leaving the forward model, data-fidelity term, regularization, and optimization scheme unchanged. A pre-regularization step further improves compatibility with the variational priors. Experiments on pelvic CT images from the SynthRAD2025 challenge show a more than threefold reduction in reconstruction time while maintaining comparable image quality.

AI.tldr: This paper accelerates variational cone-beam CT reconstruction by using an image-domain neural network to warm-start the optimization while keeping the variational formulation intact.
AI.motivation: Variational CBCT reconstruction is computationally slow under severe noise and sparse views, whereas learning-based methods often replace the explicit variational model.
AI.method: Projection data are reconstructed with FDK, refined by an image-domain neural network with a pre-regularization step, and used solely to initialize the unchanged model-based variational optimization.
AI.result: On pelvic CT images from SynthRAD2025, the warm-start framework reduces reconstruction time by more than threefold while maintaining comparable image quality.
AI.conclusion: Learned warm starts offer a practical way to speed up variational CBCT reconstruction without sacrificing model-based guarantees.

title: Foundation Model Fine-Tuning with Attention-based Multi-View Fusion for Multi-Task Cardiac Function Assessment
comment: 9 pages, 1 figure. Original pre-peer-review manuscript. Accepted for publication in the MICCAI 2026 Satellite Events (Workshops and Challenges) proceedings. The accepted version includes methodological revisions and is available at this https URL
summary: In cardio-oncology, left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) is the standard biomarker for monitoring cardiac function during cancer therapy. However, its estimation from echocardiography is highly operator dependent, and clinically meaningful declines are often detected only after myocardial injury has progressed, motivating automated methods for standardized assessment and earlier detection of LV dysfunction. To address this need, we propose a multi-task framework integrating cardiac cycle-based temporal standardization, multi-view spatiotemporal feature extraction, and joint optimization for LVEF estimation and LV dysfunction classification. Apical four- and two-chamber echocardiographic sequences are temporally standardized by sampling a clip over an estimated cardiac cycle before being processed by the EchoPrime foundation model, which is fine-tuned end-to-end within the proposed architecture. View-specific features are fused through an attention-based aggregation module to generate a patient-level embedding, from which two task-specific prediction heads estimate continuous LVEF and binary LV dysfunction. To broaden the LVEF distribution encountered during training, samples from the MIMIC-IV-ECHO dataset are incorporated using a balanced sampling strategy. Evaluated on the EchoRisk-MICCAI Challenge, our method achieves an MAE of 4.003 for LVEF estimation (Task 1) and an AUC of 0.764 for LV dysfunction detection (Task 2) on the validation set, demonstrating the effectiveness of foundation model fine-tuning with attention-based multi-view fusion for automated cardiac function assessment in cardio-oncology.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a multi-task framework that fine-tunes the EchoPrime foundation model with attention-based multi-view fusion for LVEF estimation and LV dysfunction detection.
AI.motivation: Echocardiographic LVEF estimation is operator-dependent and often detects myocardial injury late in cardio-oncology.
AI.method: Apical four- and two-chamber clips are temporally standardized over a cardiac cycle, encoded by end-to-end fine-tuned EchoPrime, fused via attention into a patient-level embedding, and trained with balanced MIMIC-IV-ECHO sampling.
AI.result: On the EchoRisk-MICCAI Challenge validation set, the method achieves an MAE of 4.003 for LVEF estimation and an AUC of 0.764 for LV dysfunction detection.
AI.conclusion: Temporal standardization and attention-based multi-view fusion of a fine-tuned echo foundation model support automated cardiac function assessment.

title: Technical Report of Auriga's 1:10 Scale Autonomous Vehicle Robot
comment: 62 pages, 32 figures, 11 tables, 1 algorithm. Technical report of Team Auriga's 2025 1:10 scale autonomous vehicle platform (Robotics and Intelligent Automation Laboratory, Shahid Beheshti University)
summary: This report presents the design and implementation of Auriga Robotics' 1:10 scale autonomous vehicle, developed at Shahid Beheshti University's Robotics and Intelligent Automation Laboratory. The platform integrates a custom mechanical chassis, a distributed embedded system based on ESP32 microcontrollers, and a Jetson Orin NX module for high-level perception and control. The embedded layer manages sensor interfacing, real-time data acquisition, and actuator control, while the Jetson handles environment perception through deep-learning--based lane, sign, and traffic light detection, as well as decision-making and trajectory control. System communication is achieved via structured UART links, ensuring synchronized operation between perception and control subsystems. The vehicle's software stack incorporates ROS, modular firmware design, and multiple control algorithms---Stanley, PID, and Pure Pursuit---to achieve stable autonomous navigation in structured driving scenarios. The overall system demonstrates robust performance and reliability in urban-like environments, serving as a modular research platform for future autonomous driving studies.

AI.tldr: This technical report describes the hardware and ROS-based software architecture of Auriga Robotics' 1:10 scale autonomous vehicle platform.
AI.motivation: A modular, low-cost research platform is needed to integrate embedded real-time control with deep-learning perception for autonomous driving studies.
AI.method: The vehicle combines a custom chassis, ESP32 microcontrollers for sensor/actuator control, and a Jetson Orin NX for deep-learning lane, sign, and traffic light detection, communicating over UART and running ROS with Stanley, PID, and Pure Pursuit controllers.
AI.result: The integrated system demonstrates reliable autonomous navigation in structured, urban-like driving scenarios.
AI.conclusion: Auriga's 1:10 scale vehicle provides a modular testbed for future autonomous driving research.

title: Lasso: Towards Sustainable AI-Generated Media Detection with Intel QAT On-Chip Compression
summary: Synthetic text, images, and video are rising. Software-only detectors are power-hungry, too slow, and costly, and do not scale with demand. When software cannot scale, historically hardware often comes to the rescue. We perform the first reverse engineering of a compression accelerator--Intel QuickAssist Technology (QAT) microarchitecture and--find different amount of time on each, a novel data structure-dependent property. Using this information, we then build Lasso, a low-cost, high-performance detector for AI-generated content that turns the accelerator into a measuring instrument. For text detection, Lasso achieves 100% accuracy on original DetectRL text and retains 92% average accuracy after paraphrasing, compared with 78% for Binoculars and 55% for DetectGPT. Across original, paraphrased, and perturbed text, it achieves 82% average accuracy, outperforming all five baselines. With topic, length, and formatting matched, accuracy reaches 95% for instruction-tuned generators, including when the tested generator is unseen. On RAID, accuracy averages 82% when trained on one generator and tested on another, and 74% across eight held-out domains. Detection takes 0.74 microseconds, a speedup of at least 83,784x across five baselines. At the same time, Lasso consumes over 99% less energy per document than both Binoculars and DetectGPT. At the same time, Lasso detects AI-generated videos, software code, and images with 67.5%, 70% and 78% accuracy, respectively, with low latency and power opening avenues for practical real time and edge device detection of multimodality AI artifacts for the first time. No other compared technique supports detection across all four modalities: text, video, images, and code.

AI.tldr: Lasso is a hardware-accelerated AI-generated media detector that repurposes Intel QAT on-chip compression timing differences to detect synthetic text, video, images, and code.
AI.motivation: Software-only AI-content detectors are too slow, power-hungry, and costly to scale with rising synthetic media.
AI.method: By reverse-engineering Intel QuickAssist Technology (QAT) microarchitecture, the authors exploit data-structure-dependent compression timing as a measurement signal for AI-generated content.
AI.result: Lasso reaches 100% accuracy on original DetectRL text and 92% after paraphrasing (vs. 78% Binoculars, 55% DetectGPT), runs in 0.74 microseconds (at least 83,784x faster) with over 99% less energy per document, and detects AI video, code, and images at 67.5%, 70%, and 78% accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Turning commodity compression accelerators into measurement instruments enables ultra-fast, low-energy, multimodal AI-artifact detection.

title: Learned Regularization for Sparse-View CT: Accuracy, Lesion Detectability and Distribution Shift of a Plug-and-Play Prior against Tuned Total Variation
comment: 62 pages, 22 figures, and 30 tables. Preprint (not peer-reviewed); also available on Zenodo: this https URL. Code and stored results are available at: this https URL
summary: Learned image priors are often proposed to replace hand-crafted regularizers in sparse-view computed tomography (CT), yet they are usually judged by PSNR on data resembling their training set. We evaluate one noise-conditioned DnCNN denoiser used as a Plug-and-Play prior against filtered back-projection (FBP), Tikhonov and total-variation (TV) regularization, with every method tuned on validation data and all differences paired. On synthetic 28x28 digit images, the prior beats box-constrained TV by about 3.4 dB at moderate noise (sigma = 0.05, 20 angles), but the advantage shrinks at low noise and reverses under distribution shift: an MNIST-trained prior is 3.1 dB (Fashion-MNIST) and 4.3-4.6 dB (Shepp-Logan phantom) below TV, whereas a Fashion-MNIST-trained prior beats TV by 2.2 dB on Fashion-MNIST, consistent with prior mismatch rather than a failure of PnP itself. In a lesion-insertion test the prior detects lesions worse than TV in distribution despite its higher PSNR, and under mismatch it produces more lesion-like false blobs than box-constrained TV for seven of eight lesion types. On real LoDoPaB-CT slices (patient-disjoint split; 30, 60 and 120 angles; three dose levels; 40 test patients), the prior does not consistently outperform a well-tuned TV in PSNR (-0.93 to +0.33 dB) and has lower SSIM in eight of nine conditions. Its lesion-detection AUC is higher than this TV's in all nine conditions (significant in six) but never significantly higher than that of Hann-filtered FBP, which the PSNR-tuned TV falls below in detection in all nine conditions (seven significant). On non-anatomical phantoms its PSNR falls below TV in all six conditions. PSNR and lesion detectability thus rank the methods differently. Our conclusions concern one small denoiser, and the CT analysis was developed after seeing results, without pre-specified primary comparisons.

AI.tldr: This study evaluates a noise-conditioned DnCNN Plug-and-Play (PnP) prior against tuned total variation (TV) and FBP in sparse-view CT across accuracy, lesion detectability, and distribution shift.
AI.motivation: Learned CT priors are typically judged by in-distribution PSNR, leaving their behavior under distribution shift and on clinical lesion detectability unclear.
AI.method: The authors compare a DnCNN PnP prior against FBP, Tikhonov, and box-constrained TV on synthetic 28x28 digits, non-anatomical phantoms, and 40 test patients from LoDoPaB-CT across multiple angles and doses.
AI.result: The prior beats TV by ~3.4 dB on in-distribution digits but drops 3.1-4.6 dB below TV under distribution shift and detects inserted lesions worse than TV in distribution; on LoDoPaB-CT it does not consistently beat TV in PSNR (-0.93 to +0.33 dB), has lower SSIM in 8/9 conditions, and never significantly beats Hann-filtered FBP in lesion-detection AUC.
AI.conclusion: PSNR and lesion detectability rank reconstruction methods differently, and a small learned PnP prior is vulnerable to distribution shift and false lesion-like artifacts.

title: VLN-Flash: Parallel Action Decoding with Adaptive Execution for Vision-and-Language Navigation
summary: When a vision-and-language navigation policy generates an action sequence autoregressively, the robot waits for a chain of dependent predictions. A small discrete action vocabulary makes it possible to score all short-horizon plans in parallel. We introduce VLN-Flash, a training-free decoder that evaluates the complete action-prefix tree in a single forward pass. Branch-specific attention and matched token positions preserve the original policy's conditional action distribution for each prefix in exact arithmetic. We use the score margin between the stepwise-greedy prefix and its strongest alternative at each depth to decide how many actions to execute. The robot then executes the plan with the highest joint score at the chosen depth before observing again. On matched inputs, VLN-Flash achieves a nearly $3\times$ speedup in action decoding over native autoregression on Uni-NaVid and StreamVLN. Compared with the native autoregressive decoders, it improves success rate and success weighted by path length (SPL) on R2R-CE and RxR-CE, with success gains up to 2.7 percentage points. On a Unitree GO2, VLN-Flash improves navigation success and cuts the mean wait between actions by about 160 ms after subtracting network transmission time.

AI.tldr: VLN-Flash is a training-free parallel action decoder with adaptive execution depth that accelerates vision-and-language navigation policies while improving navigation success.
AI.motivation: Autoregressive action-sequence decoding forces VLN robots to wait through dependent token predictions, slowing down execution.
AI.method: VLN-Flash evaluates the full short-horizon action-prefix tree in one forward pass using branch-specific attention and matched token positions, and uses the score margin between the greedy prefix and its strongest alternative to choose execution depth.
AI.result: VLN-Flash achieves nearly 3x decoding speedup on Uni-NaVid and StreamVLN, improves success rate by up to 2.7 pp on R2R-CE and RxR-CE, and cuts mean inter-action wait by ~160 ms on a Unitree GO2 robot.
AI.conclusion: Exact parallel prefix-tree evaluation with margin-based adaptive execution speeds up discrete VLN policies without retraining.

title: HongguoTrending: A Longitudinal, Multimodal Archive of Trending Videos and Topics on a Leading Micro-Drama Platform
summary: Micro-dramas (duanju) are reshaping digital production and consumption, yet a lack of longitudinal data connecting series to their platform visibility persists, limiting our understanding of the emerging medium. We introduce HongguoTrending, a longitudinal, multimodal dataset of hourly snapshots from seven trending lists of Hongguo, China's largest micro-drama platform. Collected through a two-stage asynchronous pipeline, the archive links 63,200 ranking entries across 632 web list-hours and 157 client hours (889 distinct series) to metadata, cover images, sampled episode videos, and audience engagement metrics. Exploratory analyses show distinct turnover rates between web and mobile trending lists, production-driven mainstream values alongside kinship-centered synopses, genre-specific cover palettes, and strong associations between user sharing and next-day rank gains. Accessible via a RESTful API, this dataset supports empirical research on algorithmic gatekeeping, popularity dynamics, and multimodal digital culture.

AI.tldr: HongguoTrending is a longitudinal, multimodal archive of hourly trending lists, metadata, cover images, and sampled episode videos from China's largest micro-drama platform.
AI.motivation: Research on micro-dramas (duanju) is limited by the lack of longitudinal datasets linking series to platform visibility and engagement.
AI.method: Collected via a two-stage asynchronous pipeline, the dataset links 63,200 ranking entries across 632 web list-hours and 157 client hours (889 distinct series) to metadata, covers, video samples, and engagement metrics, exposed via a RESTful API.
AI.result: Exploratory analyses reveal distinct web versus mobile list turnover, mainstream values alongside kinship-centered synopses, genre-specific cover palettes, and strong links between user sharing and next-day rank gains.
AI.conclusion: HongguoTrending provides an empirical foundation for studying algorithmic gatekeeping, popularity dynamics, and multimodal digital culture in micro-dramas.

title: XLSAR-Bench: Towards Extremely Large SAR Imagery Understanding of MLLMs
summary: The rapid development of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) has highlighted the need for comprehensive benchmarks to assess their capabilities and limitations in remote sensing (RS). However, evaluating MLLMs in large-size synthetic aperture radar (SAR) scenarios remains challenging, as understanding complete scenes requires both global semantic interpretation and fine-grained target perception. Existing SAR benchmarks predominantly rely on small image patches, limiting their ability to assess these capabilities jointly. To address these limitations, we present XLSAR-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating the perception and reasoning capabilities of MLLMs in large-scene SAR imagery. XLSAR-Bench comprises 405 images with an average size of 7153$\times$7153 pixels, ten tasks spanning visual question answering, visual grounding, and detailed image captioning, with all evaluation samples meticulously annotated manually, assisted by a semi-automatic captioner. Experimental results from general-purpose and domain-specific MLLMs reveal persistent challenges in understanding large SAR scenes and accurately perceiving small targets. We have open-sourced XLSAR-Bench to support further research in developing more powerful MLLMs for complete large SAR scenes.

AI.tldr: XLSAR-Bench is an open-source benchmark for evaluating MLLMs on global semantic understanding and small-target perception in extremely large SAR imagery.
AI.motivation: Existing SAR benchmarks use small image patches, failing to test whether MLLMs can jointly interpret large scenes and perceive fine-grained targets.
AI.method: XLSAR-Bench contains 405 images averaging 7153x7153 pixels across ten tasks covering VQA, visual grounding, and detailed captioning, manually annotated with semi-automatic captioner assistance.
AI.result: Evaluations of general-purpose and domain-specific MLLMs show persistent difficulties in understanding large SAR scenes and accurately localizing small targets.
AI.conclusion: XLSAR-Bench establishes a challenging testbed for advancing MLLM capabilities on full-scale synthetic aperture radar imagery.

title: Pixel-KWS: Rendered-Glyph Representations for Orthographically Robust Open-Vocabulary Keyword Spotting
summary: Open-vocabulary keyword spotting (KWS) allows users to enroll arbitrary keywords at inference time. However, character and phoneme-based text encoders rely on fixed symbol vocabularies learned during training, limiting their ability to handle unseen or visually similar symbols such as homoglyphs, l33tspeak substitutions, and accented characters. We propose PIXEL-KWS, an open-vocabulary KWS framework that represents characters through rendered glyphs rather than learned embedding lookups. We render each character as a grayscale image and encode it with a lightweight CNN, enabling the text encoder to generalize from visual form rather than a fixed vocabulary. On LibriPhrase, PIXEL-KWS and its matched character-based counterpart achieve 9.57% and 9.55% EER on LibriPhrase-hard, 0.43% and 0.41% EER on LibriPhrase-easy, outperforming all published baselines without pre-training or synthetic data. PIXEL-KWS provides substantially greater robustness to both homoglyph and l33tspeak symbol-level perturbations. These results highlight glyph-based representations as a simple and effective approach for robust open-vocabulary KWS in practical settings.

AI.tldr: PIXEL-KWS is an open-vocabulary keyword spotting framework that encodes keywords as rendered glyph images rather than fixed character or phoneme embeddings.
AI.motivation: Fixed symbol vocabularies in character- and phoneme-based KWS encoders fail on unseen or visually similar perturbations such as homoglyphs, l33tspeak, and accented characters.
AI.method: Each character is rendered as a grayscale glyph image and encoded with a lightweight CNN, allowing the text encoder to generalize from visual form.
AI.result: On LibriPhrase without pre-training or synthetic data, PIXEL-KWS achieves 9.57% EER on LibriPhrase-hard and 0.43% on LibriPhrase-easy, matching its character-based counterpart, beating published baselines, and showing much stronger robustness to homoglyphs and l33tspeak.
AI.conclusion: Rendered-glyph representations offer a simple, effective path to orthographically robust open-vocabulary KWS.

title: Semantics First, Pixels Later: Mission-Driven Event Streams for Drone Video over Bandwidth-Starved Links
comment: 20 pages, 3 figures; includes the supplementary material as an appendix; a demonstration video is attached as an ancillary file
summary: A surveillance drone on a bandwidth-starved link cannot send the video its operator would need, yet the operator's questions are often not about pixels: did three people converge, when, and where? We study what should cross a link of 1 Mbps down to 1 kbps instead, and in what order. BPS, a behavior-primitive stream, sends semantics first and pixels later: it runs a detector and a tracker onboard and sends short records (25 bytes on average) of multi-frame events selected by a mission card of 16-125 bytes, ahead of positions and pictures. We measure it by what a ground-side language model answers from it, under a preregistered protocol with a held-out set, against H.265 read by the vision fine-tune of the same model, H.265 on which the ground runs our own perception, a stream of quantized tracks, and onboard captions. On the development set (84% of questions about convergence, mostly one location) the event stream answers 74.3% of questions at 0.13 kbps. A reader that receives nothing answers 57.4%, and the video reader 59.6% at 100 kbps and 64.7% on the source frames. When the ground instead runs our perception on the video, video matches the stream at 100 kbps, about 800 times the stream's rate, and falls behind at 64 kbps and below. A track stream matches it at 96 times the bytes and loses 0.03 at 17 times. On held-out data the result is weaker: with events taken from annotated tracks, an oracle, the stream beats H.265 at 100 kbps (+0.13), but with onboard perception it does not (+0.01 [-0.04, +0.06]) and is no better than receiving nothing. Sent alone through emulated links the event records answer 0.739 at 1 Mbps and still 0.724 at 0.3 kbps; an every-frame track stream holds down to 1 kbps and video with ground-side perception down to about 100 kbps. On a Jetson Orin Nano the unchanged pipeline runs at 4.5 fps and misses most events.

AI.tldr: BPS is a mission-driven behavior-primitive stream for drone surveillance over bandwidth-starved links that transmits compact semantic events ahead of positions and video.
AI.motivation: Drones on 1 kbps-1 Mbps links cannot stream full video, even though operators often only need answers to specific event-level questions.
AI.method: BPS runs onboard detection and tracking to send 25-byte multi-frame event records selected by a 16-125 byte mission card before positions and pixels, evaluated by a ground-side LLM against H.265 video, quantized tracks, and onboard captions.
AI.result: On the development set, BPS answers 74.3% of questions at 0.13 kbps (matching ground-side perception on H.265 at 100 kbps, ~800x higher rate), though on held-out data onboard perception does not beat H.265 at 100 kbps (+0.01) or receiving nothing, and runs at 4.5 fps on Jetson Orin Nano.
AI.conclusion: Semantic-first streaming can drastically cut bandwidth when onboard perception is accurate, but real-time onboard perception errors currently limit held-out generalization.

title: Cache or Denoise Less? Residual Reuse in a Flow-Matching World Action Model
comment: Honorable Mention at the CoRL 2026 Workshop on Efficient Foundation Models for Real-Time Embodied AI (EEAI). Code and data available at this https URL
summary: Flow-matching robot policies generate each action chunk through repeated network evaluations, one per denoising step. Cross-cycle caches such as C$^3$ache reuse computation from earlier replanning calls, but whether they beat simply taking fewer steps is unclear. We compare the two in Fast-WAM, a 6B-parameter world action model, on LIBERO-Goal. Two uncached steps keep the success of ten: on all 500 initial states they are non-inferior within two percentage points, for one checkpoint and noise seed. Under PyTorch's default compile mode, they also cut a replanning call on an RTX A6000 from 202 to 92 ms. This leaves little room for caching. A cache that keeps two fresh steps cannot be faster than two uncached steps: every call still encodes the images, runs the video expert and computes those two steps. Caching the first of two steps, refreshed every fourth call, saves at most 11--14% of a call by our cost model. Cached policies are also fragile. Their losses tracked the share of the flow path the cached steps cover: under Fast-WAM's current time shift, C$^3$ache's eight cached steps cover 80% of the path instead of 44%, and the cached policy succeeds on 63% of states against 95% uncached. Resampling the noise on every call cost caches covering 60% or more of the path 14--40 points. These results argue for fewer-step baselines and for testing reuse under the deployed sampler and noise settings. We release our evaluation harness, logs and a checklist.

AI.tldr: This paper compares cross-cycle feature caching against simply taking fewer denoising steps in Fast-WAM, a 6B-parameter flow-matching robot policy.
AI.motivation: Cross-cycle caches like C3ache reuse earlier replanning computations, but it is unclear whether they outperform reducing the number of uncached denoising steps.
AI.method: The authors evaluate Fast-WAM on LIBERO-Goal across 500 initial states, comparing 2 uncached steps against 10 steps and against C3ache under deployed time-shift and noise-resampling settings.
AI.result: Two uncached steps match 10-step success within 2 pp and cut replanning latency on an RTX A6000 from 202 ms to 92 ms; caching 1 of 2 steps saves at most 11-14%, while C3ache's 8 cached steps drop success from 95% to 63% under Fast-WAM's time shift.
AI.conclusion: Fewer-step uncached baselines are faster, simpler, and more reliable than cross-cycle caching, which should always be tested under the deployed sampler and noise settings.

title: JEPA4R: Embodied JEPA World Models with 4D Point Planning
comment: Code: this https URL, Website: this https URL
summary: Joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA) world models predict future embeddings instead of pixels and plan in latent space. Two challenges remain: 2D images leave the metric geometry that manipulation acts on implicit and entangled with appearance, and what these models imagine stays hidden, as they are mostly judged in simulation by short-horizon latent planning. We present JEPA4R, a JEPA world model that observes single-depth-camera point clouds, predicts and plans in their latent space, and acts through a policy head on its frozen latents; we call this 4D point planning. A decoder on the frozen world model shows what it imagines as 4D point clouds, with a mean point error within 1.1 cm over 200 steps. Under the policy-learning protocols of OGBench and CortexBench, JEPA4R leads pixel JEPA models on OGBench Cube-Single, Cube-Double, Cube-Triple and Scene, and ranks first on MetaWorld and Adroit Relocate with 98.4% and 88.0%, above the runner-up, R3M, at 96.0% and 65.3%. Trained only in a digital twin, JEPA4R and its policy heads run zero-shot on the real arm with both a gripper and a dexterous hand.

AI.tldr: JEPA4R is an embodied JEPA world model that predicts and plans in 4D point-cloud latent space from single-depth-camera observations.
AI.motivation: 2D-image JEPA world models leave 3D metric geometry implicit and entangled with appearance, while their imagined rollouts remain hidden.
AI.method: JEPA4R encodes single-depth-camera point clouds, predicts and plans in latent space, acts via a policy head on frozen latents, and uses a point-cloud decoder to visualize imagined 4D rollouts.
AI.result: The decoder reconstructs imagined 4D point clouds within 1.1 cm mean point error over 200 steps; JEPA4R leads pixel JEPA on OGBench tasks, ranks first on MetaWorld (98.4%) and Adroit Relocate (88.0%) ahead of R3M (96.0%, 65.3%), and transfers zero-shot to a real arm.
AI.conclusion: Grounding JEPA world models in 4D point-cloud latents improves metric manipulation accuracy, interpretability, and sim-to-real transfer.

title: Lao Siji: Adapting openpilot to Closed-Loop End-to-End Driving in Neural Reconstruction
summary: We present Lao Siji, an end-to-end driving policy that ranks third in the 2026 NVIDIA AlpaSim E2E Driving Challenge, ahead of most entries built on foundation models. Instead of training from scratch on a general-purpose vision backbone, we adapt openpilot, an open-source L2 production model. We freeze its vision encoder and fine-tune the policy layers with an ego-state adapter and a route memory. On closed-loop rollouts in neural-reconstructed scenes, we supervise the policy with a privileged map teacher for lateral self-correction and a body-extent loss for road and obstacle clearance, while distilling the base model's remaining outputs to retain car following. Ablations show that self-correction samples carry the gain, while the clearance loss substitutes for them where no teacher exists. Longitudinal safety instead rests on the base model's lead-vehicle estimate behind a rule-based speed layer. Longer training, imitating human logs, and human-log speed targets yield either no measurable gain or adverse effects. Without further training, Lao Siji also places among the leaders on HUGSIM and Odyssey. The final training takes only one GPU-hour and shifts the weights by 3.9% from the shipped model. Code will be released after review.

AI.tldr: Lao Siji adapts the open-source openpilot L2 driving model with closed-loop neural-reconstruction fine-tuning to place third in the 2026 NVIDIA AlpaSim E2E Driving Challenge.
AI.motivation: Rather than training an end-to-end driving policy from scratch on a general vision backbone, adapting an existing production L2 model may offer a stronger, more data-efficient starting point.
AI.method: With openpilot's vision encoder frozen, the policy layers are fine-tuned with an ego-state adapter and route memory on closed-loop neural-reconstructed rollouts using a privileged map teacher for lateral self-correction, a body-extent clearance loss, and base-model distillation.
AI.result: Training takes 1 GPU-hour, shifts weights by 3.9%, ranks third on AlpaSim ahead of most foundation-model entries, and places among the leaders on HUGSIM and Odyssey without further training.
AI.conclusion: Lightweight closed-loop fine-tuning of a production L2 driving model with self-correction and clearance supervision is highly effective and generalizes across simulators.

title: PlanDiv: Test-Time Scaling with Latent Plans for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Test-time scaling improves vision-language-action (VLA) policies by drawing several action candidates and executing the best one. We find that its returns diminish quickly when the candidates are resampled from one decoder: they differ by noise rather than by plan, and for each of three resampling sources, going from four to eight candidates adds only 0.06-0.07 to the average number of completed tasks on CALVIN. We introduce PlanDiv, an action head that makes the candidates differ by plan: a lightweight planner proposes K latent plan hypotheses, a shared masked-diffusion executor decodes one action chunk per plan from a single backbone pass, and the policy executes the chunk that its own likelihood ranks highest. The plans are learned from demonstrations alone, without plan labels or rewards. With the backbone, data and training recipe held fixed, eight plan-conditioned candidates raise five-task chain success on CALVIN ABC$\rightarrow$D from 56.9% to 69.9%, while eight candidates from autoregressive, plan-free or same-plan resampling reach at most 64.9%. The same-plan baseline is PlanDiv's own checkpoint with the plan held fixed, so this gap comes from the plans, not from drawing more samples. On LIBERO-Long, four plans remove 40% of single-candidate failures, against at most 21% for matched resampling. On a real Franka arm the gain appears where a task admits more than one solution: PlanDiv is on par with a single-output OpenVLA-OFT+ baseline on a one-solution task and succeeds in 51 of 54 trials against 40 of 54 on two tasks with two solutions.

AI.tldr: PlanDiv is a test-time scaling action head for VLA models that generates diverse latent plan hypotheses rather than resampling noisy candidates from a single decoder.
AI.motivation: Resampling multiple candidates from one VLA decoder yields diminishing returns because candidates differ by noise rather than by high-level plan.
AI.method: A lightweight planner proposes K latent plan hypotheses learned from demonstrations without plan labels, a shared masked-diffusion executor decodes one chunk per plan in a single backbone pass, and the policy executes the highest-likelihood chunk.
AI.result: With 8 candidates, PlanDiv raises CALVIN ABC->D five-task chain success from 56.9% to 69.9% (vs. at most 64.9% for resampling), cuts LIBERO-Long single-candidate failures by 40% with 4 plans, and succeeds in 51/54 real Franka trials on multi-solution tasks (vs. 40/54 for OpenVLA-OFT+).
AI.conclusion: Conditioning test-time scaling on diverse latent plans unlocks substantial gains on multi-modal manipulation tasks.

title: Prompt Re-Specification and Target-Mask Availability in Mask-Conditioned Visual Reinforcement Learning for Moving-Platform Landing
summary: Visual reinforcement learning (RL) policies that land a drone on a moving platform can fail when the landing pad looks different from the one used in training.
