Using binary target masks as the visual input removes most pixel-level appearance information while preserving the spatial representation of the target, and lets a text prompt specify the target. In simulation, we test whether a frozen (fixed-weight) mask-based DrQ-v2 policy can handle a new pad when only the prompt of its fine-tuned SAM 3 detector changes. A banana-themed pad lowered landing success from 75.6% to 12.0%, and SAM 3 rarely detected it under the original prompt. A revised prompt, chosen after testing several candidates, restored success to 68.4% with no weight updates. In a separate experiment with a policy trained on ground-truth masks, filling in masks that were missing while the pad was visible helped landing far more than the tested mask-centroid and area corrections. Tracking the pad over time supplied masks more often and also kept producing them after the pad was confirmed absent from the rendered image, but it did not establish a reliable improvement in landing success. Whether a usable mask reaches the policy at all thus appears to be an important limiting factor for this approach.

AI.tldr: This study examines prompt re-specification and target-mask availability for frozen mask-conditioned DrQ-v2 RL policies landing a drone on visually novel moving platforms.
AI.motivation: Mask-conditioned visual RL policies can fail when a landing pad's appearance changes and the upstream detector fails to produce a usable target mask.
AI.method: In simulation, the authors test prompt re-specification for a fine-tuned SAM 3 detector driving a frozen DrQ-v2 policy on a banana-themed pad, and separately test mask-filling, centroid/area corrections, and temporal tracking on ground-truth masks.
AI.result: The novel pad drops landing success from 75.6% to 12.0%, and revising the SAM 3 prompt restores success to 68.4% with no weight updates; filling missing masks helps far more than geometric corrections, while temporal tracking supplies masks even when the pad is absent without reliably improving success.
AI.conclusion: Ensuring a usable target mask reaches the frozen policy—via prompt adaptation or missing-mask recovery—is a primary bottleneck for mask-conditioned landing.

title: Sequential Semantic-Non-Semantic Watermarking: Robustness Against UnMarker Attacks
comment: 13 pages, 16 figures. Preprint based on this http URL. thesis research
summary: Advancements in artificial intelligence (AI) have accelerated digital content generation and intensified concerns around fraud, misuse, counterfeiting, and content provenance. Defensive image watermarking provides a practical mechanism for identifying and tracing digital content, but recent watermark-removal attacks challenge its robustness. This study investigates Sequential Semantic Non-Semantic Watermarking (SSNSW), which combines HiDDeN and StegaStamp as complementary non-semantic and semantic watermarking schemes. Using 50 images from MS-COCO and CelebA-HQ, both embedding orders are evaluated, followed by UnMarker's non-semantic and semantic attacks applied individually and sequentially. Results show that both watermarks remain highly decodable after dual embedding, with only limited embedding-order effects. Under individual attacks, one watermark generally remains strongly decodable: StegaStamp under the non-semantic attack and HiDDeN under the semantic attack. Sequential attacks are therefore required to substantially reduce both watermark signals, while attack order has a limited and configuration-dependent effect. The semantic attack also shows a broader effect across the two watermark types than the non-semantic attack. LPIPS remains relatively low in several settings, although qualitative inspection reveals noticeable distortions, particularly in selected facial images, indicating that LPIPS should not be used alone to assess visual quality. Overall, the findings show that combining complementary watermark types can increase robustness against single-stage removal attacks and motivate broader multi-layer watermarking, stronger perceptual evaluation, and further study of sequential watermark-removal strategies.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates Sequential Semantic Non-Semantic Watermarking (SSNSW), combining HiDDeN and StegaStamp, against individual and sequential UnMarker removal attacks.
AI.motivation: Recent watermark-removal attacks challenge single-scheme image watermarks, motivating layered defenses that combine complementary mechanisms.
AI.method: Both embedding orders of HiDDeN (non-semantic) and StegaStamp (semantic) are tested on 50 MS-COCO and CelebA-HQ images under UnMarker's non-semantic and semantic attacks applied individually and sequentially.
AI.result: Dual-embedded watermarks remain highly decodable; under single attacks one watermark survives (StegaStamp under non-semantic, HiDDeN under semantic), so sequential attacks are needed to substantially degrade both, while LPIPS misses noticeable facial distortions.
AI.conclusion: Combining semantic and non-semantic watermarks improves resilience to single-stage removal, highlighting the need for stronger perceptual metrics alongside multi-layer watermarking.

title: Streaming across viewing conditions - The effect of viewing distance and display luminance on video quality
summary: The visibility of streamed video distortions is affected by the user's display and viewing conditions, such as their display's luminance or the viewing distance. Distortions become less visible at lower luminance levels or farther viewing distances. However, most image and video quality metrics assume fixed optimal display and viewing conditions, making them insensitive to the viewing conditions. In this work, we demonstrate how existing metrics can be adapted to account for both factors and compare such an adaptation with the metrics that natively model viewing conditions. First, we collected a new video quality dataset, HDR-VDC, which contains streaming distortions in 4K HDR videos. The dataset consists of 12 4K and 4 FHD HDR source video content, each distorted with AV1 encoding and Lanczos upscaling from a lower resolution. The quality loss due to the distortions was measured at two viewing distances, corresponding to 60 and 120 pixels per visual degree, and two display mean luminance levels, varying by a factor of 8 in terms of luminance. Next, we developed a pre-processing framework that lets us adapt many quality metrics so that they can evaluate content across the viewing distances and luminance levels. The framework employs a display model and perceptually uniform encoding, PU21, to account for the effect of display luminance, and perspective projection scaling (PPS) to account for the effect of viewing distance. We used the framework to compare the performance of 35 state-of-the-art metrics. This allowed us to identify a selection of existing quality metrics that can be effectively adapted to account for the viewing conditions.

AI.tldr: This work introduces the HDR-VDC dataset and a pre-processing framework (PU21 and perspective projection scaling) to adapt 35 existing video quality metrics for varying display luminance and viewing distance.
AI.motivation: Most image and video quality metrics assume fixed optimal viewing conditions, ignoring how lower display luminance or farther viewing distances reduce distortion visibility.
AI.method: The authors collect HDR-VDC (12 4K and 4 FHD HDR videos with AV1 and Lanczos distortions measured at 60/120 ppd and an 8x luminance ratio) and apply PU21 luminance encoding plus perspective projection scaling (PPS) to adapt 35 state-of-the-art metrics.
AI.result: The framework enables benchmarking of 35 metrics across viewing conditions and identifies a subset of existing metrics that can be effectively adapted to account for luminance and viewing distance.
AI.conclusion: Display- and distance-aware pre-processing makes standard video quality metrics sensitive to real-world streaming viewing conditions.

title: Beyond AUC: Do Mammography Risk Models Predict When Cancer Occurs?
comment: 7 pages, 2 figures, 1 table. Submitted to ISBI 2027
summary: Longitudinal deep learning models for mammography-based breast cancer risk prediction output either per-year cumulative risks or a discrete distribution over the year of diagnosis, from which cumulative risks F1,...,F5 are derived. These models are evaluated almost exclusively with year-wise AUCs and the concordance index. We show that these metrics are largely insensitive to when cancer occurs: they can be high even for a model that carries no information about the year of diagnosis. We re-evaluate two recent longitudinal models (OA-BreaCR, LMV-Net) on CSAW-CC with a 5-year horizon using timing metrics computed on cancer cases only. Despite C-indices up to 0.75, neither orders cancer cases by time to diagnosis significantly better than chance (c_time 0.51 and 0.55, both 95% CIs covering 0.5). Weighted absolute timing error favours a constant "year 3" prediction over both models, so we use c_time as the primary timing metric. For Mirai's additive-hazard head, also used by LMV-Net, we analyse how per-year increments passed through a ReLU can collapse under severe class imbalance. We also propose a breast-level, two-stage model that separates whether from when. It matches LMV-Net in discrimination (C-index 0.745 vs. 0.746) but orders cancer cases better (c_time 0.58 vs. 0.51, paired 95% CI of the difference 0.01-0.13), on par with Mirai's published weights (0.57).

AI.tldr: This paper shows that standard AUC and C-index metrics miss whether mammography risk models predict when cancer occurs, and proposes a two-stage model that separates whether from when.
AI.motivation: Longitudinal breast cancer risk models are evaluated almost exclusively with year-wise AUCs and C-index, which can remain high even when a model carries no timing information.
AI.method: The authors re-evaluate OA-BreaCR and LMV-Net on CSAW-CC using a cancer-only timing concordance metric (c_time), analyze ReLU hazard collapse under class imbalance, and propose a breast-level two-stage model separating occurrence from timing.
AI.result: Despite C-indices up to 0.75, OA-BreaCR and LMV-Net achieve c_time of 0.51 and 0.55 (95% CIs covering 0.5); the proposed two-stage model matches LMV-Net's C-index (0.745 vs. 0.746) while improving c_time (0.58 vs. 0.51), on par with Mirai (0.57).
AI.conclusion: Evaluating longitudinal risk models with timing-specific metrics is essential, and decoupling occurrence from timing improves time-to-diagnosis ordering.

title: Sidewalk Stewards: A Visual Analytics Approach for Interactive Topology Repair of Sidewalk Networks
summary: Accurate pedestrian network data is foundational to urban accessibility, routing, and infrastructure planning, yet such data remains scarce and difficult to produce at scale. Automated extraction pipelines have made significant strides by leveraging computer vision to derive sidewalk networks from aerial imagery, and have seen real-world adoption by municipalities seeking cost-effective inventory solutions. Yet, these pipelines consistently produce topological errors (e.g., disconnected components, dangling edges, missed connections, malformed intersections) that undermine the utility of the extracted networks for routing and accessibility analysis. Correcting these errors requires situated human judgment that global automated repair strategies cannot replicate, yet practitioners currently lack dedicated tools to support this work efficiently. We present Sidewalk Stewards, a visual analytics system that bridges the gap between automated extraction and a deployment-ready pedestrian network. Sidewalk Stewards detects candidate topology errors, supports interactive user-guided correction through coordinated spatial views, and provides real-time quality feedback as edits are applied. We evaluate Sidewalk Stewards through a comparative user study, case studies across cities, and a quantitative evaluation. Compared with conventional workflows, the system facilitates error identification and enables faster and more complete correction. The case studies illustrate the workflow across different urban contexts, and the quantitative evaluation shows that a small number of user corrections can enhance multiple sidewalk quality metrics. Sidewalk Stewards is available at this http URL.

AI.tldr: Sidewalk Stewards is a visual analytics system for interactive topology repair of automatically extracted sidewalk networks.
AI.motivation: Computer-vision pipelines extract sidewalk networks at scale but consistently leave topological errors such as disconnected components and malformed intersections that require situated human judgment to fix.
AI.method: Sidewalk Stewards detects candidate topology errors, supports interactive correction through coordinated spatial views, and provides real-time quality feedback during editing.
AI.result: A comparative user study, city case studies, and quantitative evaluation show faster, more complete error correction than conventional workflows, with a small number of edits improving multiple sidewalk quality metrics.
AI.conclusion: Human-in-the-loop visual analytics bridges the gap between automated aerial extraction and deployment-ready pedestrian networks.

title: AsymEEF: Bimanual Manipulation with Asymmetric End Effectors
summary: Teleoperated demonstrations are costly to collect and rarely reusable across end-effectors with different kinematics and action spaces. This burden grows in bimanual manipulation, where each end-effector pair may require new data. We present AsymEEF, a framework for executable cross-end-effector demonstration generation and unified bimanual policy learning. Given a small source dataset, AsymEEF transfers demonstrations to heterogeneous combinations of two-, three-, and five-fingered end-effectors without additional teleoperation. Kinematic teacher anchors provide geometric supervision, while sparse real-world X-Calib anchors correct discrepancies in grasp execution. A shared encoder maps wrist poses and actuator states to a morphology-agnostic latent space, and a morphology-conditioned decoder reconstructs target commands. Generated trajectories undergo replay filtering for task-level executability. The representation also supports a unified bimanual visuomotor policy trained across multiple pairs. Across four simulated and six real-world tasks, AsymEEF improves replay success over adapted transfer baselines, achieves a mean replay-valid expansion gain of 16.6 times in simulation, and is evaluated through downstream policy training on real robots. Project website: this https URL.

AI.tldr: AsymEEF is a framework that transfers teleoperated demonstrations across asymmetric two-, three-, and five-fingered bimanual end-effectors and trains a unified visuomotor policy.
AI.motivation: Collecting teleoperated demonstrations for every bimanual end-effector pair is costly and rarely reusable across differing kinematics and action spaces.
AI.method: AsymEEF uses kinematic teacher anchors and sparse real-world X-Calib anchors, maps wrist poses and actuator states to a morphology-agnostic latent space with a morphology-conditioned decoder, and filters trajectories via replay for executability.
AI.result: Across four simulated and six real-world tasks, AsymEEF outperforms adapted transfer baselines in replay success, achieves a 16.6x mean replay-valid expansion gain in simulation, and supports unified downstream real-robot policy training.
AI.conclusion: Morphology-agnostic latent transfer with replay filtering enables scalable bimanual policy learning across heterogeneous end-effectors.

title: Vision-Language Grounded Semantic Navigation for Autonomous Mobile Robots
summary: Language-guided navigation enables mobile robots to interpret natural language commands and navigate toward user-specified targets in unstructured environments. However, integrating open-vocabulary visual perception with classical robotics pipelines for mapping and navigation remains a challenging problem. In this work, we present a complete ROS2-based system that combines frontier-based exploration, open-vocabulary object detection using Grounding DINO, depth-based 3D localization, and semantic mapping to enable end-to-end vision-language grounded navigation in simulation. The system accepts natural language commands such as ``go to the yellow box,'' detects candidate objects from RGB images using text prompts, estimates their positions in the world frame, and generates navigation goals executed by the Nav2 stack. In a Gazebo-based indoor environment with a TurtleBot3 robot, the system autonomously explored the room, detected three of the five target objects, and successfully executed both natural language navigation commands tested, without task-specific training. The results indicate that open-vocabulary grounding models can be integrated into classical navigation pipelines, though performance is limited by detection uncertainty, depth-based localization error, and incomplete exploration coverage. These findings highlight both the feasibility and current limitations of deploying vision-language grounded navigation systems using lightweight, CPU-only architectures.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a CPU-only ROS2 system integrating Grounding DINO, depth-based 3D localization, frontier exploration, and Nav2 for open-vocabulary semantic navigation.
AI.motivation: Integrating open-vocabulary visual perception with classical robotics mapping and navigation pipelines remains challenging without task-specific training.
AI.method: The ROS2 pipeline combines frontier-based exploration, Grounding DINO object detection from RGB prompts, depth-based 3D localization, semantic mapping, and Nav2 goal execution.
AI.result: In Gazebo with a TurtleBot3, the system autonomously explored an indoor room, detected 3 of 5 target objects, and executed both tested natural-language navigation commands without task-specific training.
AI.conclusion: Open-vocabulary grounding can be integrated into classical CPU-only ROS2 navigation, though detection uncertainty, depth error, and exploration coverage remain limiting factors.

title: OrthoMark: Place Recognition with Point-Anchored Orthographic Height Mark
summary: LiDAR place recognition provides the loop closures of Simultaneous Localization and Mapping(SLAM). Perspective from Z-axis, a gravity-aligned scan is an orthographic map of the scene, and a revisit from another position and heading moves this map rigidly in the plane, a motion that a polar Fourier spectrum ignores and phase correlation recovers. Along the vertical, the heights of the returns describe the structures, but which heights are observed depends on the range, because the sensor's vertical field of view cuts nearby structures low; height thus misleads a global key, yet is decisive once two scans are aligned and compared cell by cell where they overlap. We present \method, a training-free method built on one principle: two LiDAR scans can only be compared through features computed from the same geometric surfaces in both scans. \method retrieves candidates with a translation- and rotation-invariant polar spectrum of the bird's-eye view (BEV), 1.9,KB per keyframe, and verifies each candidate by estimating its planar pose through phase correlation and scoring it with \emph{point-anchored height columns}: every BEV cell keeps a 16-bit mask of the heights of its own returns; within a session, the score is weighted by the expected overlap of the two scans' sensing ranges, computed from their distance. We show that this vertical link pays off in verification but hurts in retrieval, where what a height slice contains depends on the range to the structure. For single robot, \method has the highest AP of the training-free methods without 3D registration on the KITTI development sequences; across robots, on all multi-robot sequences, it matches or exceeds RING++ at 1/350 of its descriptor size and closes more inter-robot loops than the learned BEVPlace++ on all tests.

AI.tldr: OrthoMark is a training-free LiDAR place recognition method that retrieves candidates with a polar BEV Fourier spectrum and verifies them via phase correlation and range-weighted point-anchored height columns.
AI.motivation: Height information in LiDAR scans depends on sensor range due to vertical field-of-view clipping, which misleads global retrieval keys even though it is decisive once two scans are aligned.
AI.method: OrthoMark retrieves candidates using a translation- and rotation-invariant polar BEV spectrum (1.9 KB/keyframe) and verifies them by estimating planar pose via phase correlation and scoring 16-bit point-anchored height columns weighted by expected range overlap.
AI.result: On KITTI, OrthoMark achieves the highest AP among training-free methods without 3D registration; on multi-robot sequences, it matches or exceeds RING++ at 1/350 of its descriptor size and closes more inter-robot loops than learned BEVPlace++.
AI.conclusion: Separating range-invariant BEV retrieval from surface-aligned height verification yields compact, accurate, training-free LiDAR place recognition.

title: Selective Sensor Acquisition for Multimodal Place Recognition
summary: Multimodal Place Recognition (PR) can improve robustness, but most systems rigidly read and process every sensor for every query, even when the primary sensor is sufficient, with implications for energy consumption, second sensor update rate, and domain-specific considerations such as passive stealth. We introduce selective, controllable sensor acquisition, where a user specifies a desired second sensor usage rate and the system acquires the additional sensor only when the primary sensor's estimated performance is sufficiently poor. An online threshold adjustment achieves the requested usage rate by adapting to recent primary sensor performance, directing additional sensing towards queries where fusion is most likely to help without calibration specific to sensor modality, PR method, or environment. The approach requires only a PR method that produces a match score and applies to both single-frame and sequence-based PR. Our system, across multiple datasets, PR descriptors, and sensor combinations, recovers 55% of the available PR performance gain while using the second sensor on only 25% of queries, and 81% while using it on 50%. We further analyse alternative acquisition decision mechanisms and usage-rate control methods, and examine performance when the second sensor is stronger than, comparable to, or weaker than the primary sensor.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces selective, controllable sensor acquisition for multimodal place recognition, activating a secondary sensor only when primary-sensor performance is estimated to be poor.
AI.motivation: Standard multimodal place recognition rigidly queries every sensor for all frames, wasting energy, bandwidth, and stealth when the primary sensor alone suffices.
AI.method: Given a user-specified second-sensor usage rate, an online threshold adapts to recent primary-sensor match scores to trigger secondary sensing without modality-, method-, or environment-specific calibration.
AI.result: Across multiple datasets, descriptors, and sensor pairs, the method recovers 55% of available PR performance gain using the second sensor on 25% of queries, and 81% using it on 50% of queries.
AI.conclusion: Online score-based thresholding enables plug-and-play, budget-controlled multimodal sensor fusion for place recognition.

title: Robotic Reward Models in the Foundation-Model Era
summary: Robotic reward models (RRMs) use foundation models to replace per-task reward engineering with reusable, task-conditioned evaluation. Yet under one name, their outputs answer different questions, from whether a task succeeded to which execution is better. This survey organizes 114 methods into five semantic families by the question their native outputs answer: Outcome, Absolute Progress, Relative, Temporal Value, and Hybrid. Within this taxonomy, we review how model design determines what an evaluator can judge, how raw experience becomes supervision, and how existing evaluation practice tests the result. The review exposes a gap: agreement with demonstration order and downstream policy gains do not show whether a reward tracks task fulfillment. We therefore introduce RRM-Bench-1K, 1,117 real-robot videos of closed-loop executions with task-state and camera-evidence labels, and four contrast suites that separate the credited condition from its usual cues. A unified study of 27 evaluators shows that the strongest final scores rank whole executions well enough for selection and filtering. Dense credit, however, follows the progression of an execution more closely than its task state, and no evaluator signals when the decisive view is missing. How much fidelity a reward model needs therefore depends on the decision it drives. We outline directions from real-failure supervision to metrics that separate task state from chronology, and open-source RRM-Hub, a toolbox in which 14 existing RRMs can be readily applied and new evaluators tested on the same capabilities.

AI.tldr: This survey classifies 114 robotic reward models into five semantic families and introduces RRM-Bench-1K and RRM-Hub to evaluate whether rewards track true task fulfillment.
AI.motivation: Existing robotic reward models answer different questions under one name, and agreement with demonstration order or policy gains does not prove a reward tracks actual task state.
AI.method: The authors group 114 methods into Outcome, Absolute Progress, Relative, Temporal Value, and Hybrid families, release RRM-Bench-1K (1,117 real-robot videos with task-state and camera-evidence labels plus four contrast suites), and benchmark 27 evaluators in RRM-Hub.
AI.result: Strongest final scores rank whole executions well for selection and filtering, but dense credit tracks execution progression rather than task state, and no evaluator signals when the decisive camera view is missing.
AI.conclusion: Reward-model fidelity requirements depend on the downstream decision, motivating real-failure supervision and metrics that separate task state from chronology.

title: CivilBench: Benchmarking Vision-Language Models for Multimodal Information Integration in Civil Engineering
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs), is increasingly applied in civil and structural engineering for disaster assessment, structural analysis, and engineering decision support. However, the extent to which current VLMs possess the reasoning capabilities required for reliable engineering judgments remains unclear. In this work, we introduce CivilBench, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating VLMs in civil engineering and disaster-related scenarios. CivilBench covers three major task families: Sequential Reasoning, Image-based Structural Understanding, and Open-world Understanding, encompassing numerical reasoning, structural damage assessment, risk inference, causal analysis, and repair planning. The benchmark is constructed through a systematic pipeline of domain-specific data collection, engineering-oriented captioning, expert annotation, question design, and quality verification. Evaluation of representative state-of-the-art VLMs reveals substantial limitations in domain-specific reasoning, with Sequential Reasoning emerging as a major bottleneck, particularly when models must infer numerical relationships from sparse structured observations. Further experiments show that numerical priors and external knowledge can alleviate these limitations, although their effectiveness depends on the model's ability to reliably interpret and use the available evidence. CivilBench provides a capability-oriented testbed for identifying reasoning limitations and evaluating progress toward reliable AI-assisted engineering decision-making. The benchmark will be publicly available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces CivilBench, a multimodal benchmark for evaluating vision-language models (VLMs) on civil engineering and disaster-related reasoning, finding that current VLMs struggle significantly with domain-specific sequential reasoning.
AI.motivation: While LLMs and VLMs are increasingly applied to civil and structural engineering tasks, it remains unclear whether they possess the reasoning capabilities needed for reliable engineering judgments.
AI.method: The authors construct CivilBench via domain-specific data collection, engineering-oriented captioning, expert annotation, question design, and quality verification across three task families: Sequential Reasoning, Image-based Structural Understanding, and Open-world Understanding.
AI.result: Evaluations of representative state-of-the-art VLMs reveal substantial limitations in domain-specific reasoning, with Sequential Reasoning (especially inferring numerical relationships from sparse structured observations) acting as a major bottleneck; numerical priors and external knowledge help, depending on the model's ability to interpret the evidence.
AI.conclusion: CivilBench provides a capability-oriented testbed for diagnosing reasoning bottlenecks and advancing AI-assisted engineering decision-making.

title: Scribble Once, Segment the Sequence: Bidirectional Temporal Consistency for Weakly Supervised Segmentation in Echocardiography Sequences
summary: Temporal medical image segmentation relies on pixel-wise annotations, which are prohibitively expensive for long image sequences. Existing weakly-supervised methods reduce the annotation burden per frame but still require repeated annotations across the sequence. Furthermore, sparse supervision can result in temporally unstable representations. Addressing both challenges requires a model that can leverage strong spatial priors from large-scale pretraining while minimizing reliance on dense annotations. Frozen 2D vision foundation models provide a promising basis for this by offering transferable spatial representations with low trainable parameters. However, their lack of explicit temporal modeling limits their ability to propagate reliable information across anatomical sequences. To address this, we present a weakly-supervised framework for temporal segmentation from a single scribble-annotated frame, with all remaining frames left unlabeled. The framework combines parameter-efficient adaptation of DINOv3 encoders present in the mean-teacher architecture. Furthermore, a set of complementary losses, including a temporal loss helps generate reliable segmentation priors for the unlabeled frames. This formulation decouples annotation costs from sequence length while retaining the transferable spatial knowledge of the pretrained encoder. Extensive experiments on the publicly available CAMUS and CardiacNet datasets demonstrate that our approach outperforms other scribble-supervised methods. These results show that accurate and temporally consistent segmentation can be achieved from extremely sparse supervision, substantially reducing annotation requirements for temporal echocardiographic segmentation and providing a practical framework for scalable clinical deployment.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a weakly-supervised temporal segmentation framework for echocardiography sequences that requires only a single scribble-annotated frame, outperforming existing scribble-supervised baselines on CAMUS and CardiacNet.
AI.motivation: Temporal medical image segmentation typically requires expensive pixel-wise annotations across long sequences, while existing weakly-supervised methods still need repeated per-frame annotations and can suffer from temporal instability.
AI.method: The framework combines parameter-efficient adaptation of frozen DINOv3 encoders within a mean-teacher architecture, using complementary losses including a temporal loss to propagate reliable segmentation priors to unlabeled frames.
AI.result: Experiments on the CAMUS and CardiacNet datasets show that the proposed method outperforms other scribble-supervised approaches while decoupling annotation cost from sequence length.
AI.conclusion: Accurate and temporally consistent echocardiographic segmentation can be achieved from extremely sparse supervision, offering a practical path toward scalable clinical deployment.

title: Investigating the Benefit of Transfer Learning from the Locus Coeruleus for Substantia Nigra Pars Compacta Segmentation
comment: 5 pages, 3 figures, 1 table. Submitted to IEEE ISBI 2027
summary: The substantia nigra pars compacta (SNpc) is a small midbrain nucleus that degenerates early in Parkinson's disease (PD). T1-weighted FLASH MRI enables its visualization and may support early detection of neurodegeneration. However, manual segmentation is difficult and time-consuming, and deep learning models often suffer from the limited availability of labeled data. Transfer learning (TL) may help by adapting pre-trained models to small datasets. We investigate whether TL from a model trained on the locus coeruleus (LC), a nucleus with a similar appearance in this sequence, improves SNpc segmentation. Several TL strategies were evaluated using a 3D U-Net. With as few as 5-14 labeled subjects, TL and training from scratch achieved similar performance, reaching a Dice similarity coefficient of up to 0.77, close to reported inter-rater agreement. No TL strategy differed significantly from training from scratch, suggesting that initialization from the LC offers no significant benefit for SNpc segmentation.

AI.tldr: This study investigates whether transfer learning from a model trained on the locus coeruleus (LC) improves 3D U-Net segmentation of the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNpc) in T1-weighted FLASH MRI, finding no significant benefit over training from scratch.
AI.motivation: Manual segmentation of the SNpc for early Parkinson's disease detection is difficult and time-consuming, and deep learning models are hindered by limited labeled data.
AI.method: The authors evaluate several transfer learning strategies using a 3D U-Net initialized from a model pre-trained on the LC, a midbrain nucleus with similar appearance in T1-weighted FLASH MRI, across 5 to 14 labeled subjects.
AI.result: Both transfer learning and training from scratch achieve similar performance, reaching a Dice similarity coefficient of up to 0.77 (close to reported inter-rater agreement), with no statistically significant difference between any transfer learning strategy and training from scratch.
AI.conclusion: Initializing a 3D U-Net from an LC-trained model does not provide a significant advantage for SNpc segmentation.

title: Rotation-Invariant Machine Learning for Highly Symmetric Molecular Configurations
comment: NeurReps 2026 Extended Abstract Track (NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Symmetry and Geometry in Neural Representations)
summary: Atomistic machine learning can approximate expensive quantum mechanical calculations at a fraction of their computational cost, but accuracy depends strongly on how the three-dimensional atomic environments are represented. Invariant representations enable fast computation but can fail to distinguish geometrically distinct configurations, especially in highly symmetric environments. We introduce a lightweight benchmark to evaluate expressivity on $n$-fold symmetric configurations, and use it to expose degeneracies in both invariant and equivariant architectures. Guided by these results, we construct a new invariant basis for HIP-HOP which resolves most of the identified failures. On a methane simulation dataset, the extended basis achieves the lowest error among the HIP-HOP variants and has similar accuracy to EquiformerV3 while running $3.2\times$ faster at inference. These results show that carefully constructed invariant representations can mitigate key expressivity limitations while balancing accuracy and computational efficiency.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a benchmark to expose expressivity degeneracies in invariant and equivariant atomistic models on n-fold symmetric configurations, and proposes an extended invariant basis for HIP-HOP that matches EquiformerV3 accuracy on methane at 3.2x faster inference.
AI.motivation: Invariant atomic representations enable fast computation for approximating quantum mechanical calculations, but they can fail to distinguish geometrically distinct configurations, particularly in highly symmetric environments.
AI.method: The authors design a lightweight benchmark for n-fold symmetric configurations to diagnose degeneracies, and use these insights to construct a new extended invariant basis for HIP-HOP.
AI.result: On a methane simulation dataset, the extended HIP-HOP basis achieves the lowest error among HIP-HOP variants and matches the accuracy of EquiformerV3 while running 3.2x faster at inference.
AI.conclusion: Carefully designed invariant representations can overcome key expressivity limitations while maintaining a favorable balance between accuracy and computational efficiency.

title: GHySSeg: Real-Time Geometric Ground and Road Segmentation for Hybrid Solid-State LiDAR
comment: 14 pages, 8 figures, 3 tables. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Intelligent Transportation Systems. This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible. HySoLiD-Drive dataset: this https URL
summary: Hybrid solid-state LiDAR sensors are making their way into production vehicles, yet the data they produce differs structurally from that of the established spinning mechanical sensors behind today's autonomous-driving datasets: it is ring-free, dense, cluttered, and concentrated in a frontal field of view. The classical geometric methods that autonomous vehicles rely on for drivable space computation and navigation assume the ordered ring-and-column structure of a 360-degree spinning LiDAR and degrade or fail on this data, while learned alternatives are computationally heavy, hard to certify, and trained almost exclusively on spinning-LiDAR data. We demonstrate that the same dense, per-curve geometry is instead an opportunity to close the divide between the industry's preferred sensors and autonomous-driving research. We present GHySSeg, a purely geometric method that segments ground and drivable road from a single hybrid solid-state LiDAR frame by tracing each scan curve and reading two geometric signatures, a step in height and a fold-back in range, with no training and no graphics processing unit. To evaluate it, we release HySoLiD-Drive, the first public benchmark dedicated to ground and road segmentation on an automotive hybrid solid-state LiDAR, comprising 100 manually labeled and 7000 unlabeled frames recorded by two vehicles in real driving. On this benchmark, GHySSeg surpasses both geometric and learned state-of-the-art baselines across ground and road segmentation, reaching an intersection-over-union of 0.907 for road and 0.896 for ground at over 0.96 precision, while running in real time at about 22 milliseconds per frame on a single core.

AI.tldr: This paper presents GHySSeg, a training-free geometric method for real-time ground and road segmentation on hybrid solid-state LiDAR, along with the HySoLiD-Drive benchmark, achieving 0.907 road IoU and 0.896 ground IoU at 22 ms per frame on a single CPU core.
AI.motivation: Hybrid solid-state LiDAR produces ring-free, dense, cluttered, frontal-FOV data that breaks classical geometric methods designed for 360-degree spinning LiDARs, while learned alternatives are heavy, hard to certify, and trained on spinning-LiDAR data.
AI.method: GHySSeg traces each scan curve in a single hybrid solid-state LiDAR frame and detects two geometric signatures, a step in height and a fold-back in range, without requiring training or a GPU; the authors also release HySoLiD-Drive (100 labeled and 7000 unlabeled frames from two vehicles).
AI.result: On HySoLiD-Drive, GHySSeg outperforms both geometric and learned state-of-the-art baselines, achieving 0.907 IoU for road and 0.896 IoU for ground at over 0.96 precision while running at about 22 ms per frame on a single core.
AI.conclusion: Exploiting per-curve geometry enables accurate, real-time, and certifiable drivable-space segmentation for automotive hybrid solid-state LiDARs without deep learning overhead.

title: How Much Does Saliency Accuracy Matter for Saliency-Guided 360-degree Image Compression?
comment: 8 pages, 7 figures, 1 table. Accepted at the 2027 IEEE/SICE International Symposium on System Integration (SII 2027)
summary: Saliency-guided coding allocates bits to the regions viewers are most likely to attend, but accurate 360-degree saliency prediction is computationally expensive, an obstacle for low-latency immersive streaming applications such as robot teleoperation. We quantify how much saliency-prediction accuracy actually translates into compression gain. Building on a saliency-guided rate-distortion-optimized (RDO) learned codec, modified so that the training-time latent mask is driven by ground-truth saliency, which yields a single, predictor-agnostic codec, we evaluate saliency predictors spanning two orders of magnitude in compute on both the learned codec and H.265/HEVC. The results show that higher saliency-prediction accuracy yields diminishing compression gains: a lightweight predictor fast enough for live use (52 frames per second) captures 65% of the ground-truth oracle's bit-rate saving, a 3.3x heavier one reaches 74%, and a further 38x increase in compute adds no measurable benefit, on either codec. Therefore, lightweight predictors might also be a practical choice for latency-constrained 360-degree streaming.

AI.tldr: This paper quantifies how saliency-prediction accuracy affects bit-rate savings in saliency-guided 360-degree image compression, showing diminishing returns where a 52 FPS lightweight predictor captures 65% of oracle savings.
AI.motivation: Accurate 360-degree saliency prediction is computationally expensive, creating a bottleneck for low-latency immersive streaming applications such as robot teleoperation.
AI.method: The authors modify a saliency-guided rate-distortion-optimized (RDO) learned codec to use ground-truth saliency during training for a predictor-agnostic model, and evaluate saliency predictors spanning two orders of magnitude in compute on both the learned codec and H.265/HEVC.
AI.result: A lightweight 52 FPS predictor captures 65% of the ground-truth oracle's bit-rate saving, a 3.3x heavier predictor reaches 74%, and a further 38x compute increase yields no measurable benefit on either codec.
AI.conclusion: Lightweight saliency predictors are a practical choice for latency-constrained 360-degree streaming because higher prediction accuracy yields diminishing compression gains.

title: Averaged-Cost Control with Shared Feedback under Model Uncertainty
summary: This paper studies the shared-feedback design problem for finite-horizon averaged-cost control under model uncertainty represented by a joint law over the model parameter and initial state. One feedback map is shared across all realizations and uses only time and the current state as online inputs. We develop two methods: the nonlinear adjoint method combines forward closed-loop solves, backward adjoints, and joint-law policy gradients, while the linear moment method gives exact cost and gradient formulas for a homogeneous linear-quadratic design model by propagating conditional second moments. Numerical studies compare averaged and nominal designs for time-dependent neural feedback and static linear feedback in nonlinear Van der Pol and Stuart-Landau systems; the static gains are designed from oscillator linearizations and evaluated on the original nonlinear systems. Averaged design has lower cost in most comparisons.

AI.tldr: This paper develops nonlinear adjoint and linear moment methods for finite-horizon averaged-cost control with shared feedback under model and initial-state uncertainty, showing lower cost than nominal designs in oscillator benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Designing a single shared feedback map that performs well across a joint law of uncertain model parameters and initial states using only time and current state is challenging for finite-horizon control.
AI.method: The authors propose a nonlinear adjoint method combining forward closed-loop solves, backward adjoints, and joint-law policy gradients, alongside a linear moment method that propagates conditional second moments for exact cost and gradient formulas in homogeneous linear-quadratic models.
AI.result: Numerical studies on nonlinear Van der Pol and Stuart-Landau systems compare averaged and nominal designs for time-dependent neural feedback and static linear feedback, showing that the averaged design achieves lower cost in most comparisons.
AI.conclusion: Both proposed methods effectively synthesize shared feedback controllers under uncertainty, outperforming nominal designs across nonlinear oscillator tests.

title: Refinement vs. Replanning: Inference Compute Allocation in Robot Policies
comment: NeurIPS 2026 Workshop: Post-Training Adaptation of Robot Foundation Models
summary: A frozen chunked robot policy can spend deployment-time inference compute in two coupled ways: more work within each policy call to refine a predicted action chunk, or more frequent policy calls to replan from fresh observations. We study this allocation without updating model weights. Our evaluation procedure reports success with both nominal compute rate and complete attempt cost, selects comparisons on discovery tasks, and tests prespecified comparisons on held-out tasks. Comparisons added after inspecting the held-out results only summarize observed patterns. We demonstrate the procedure with one frozen SmolVLA checkpoint in synchronous LIBERO simulation, using denoising count as the refinement control and fixing chunk length at K=50. Arithmetic and latency characterize cost differently: at d=10, 82.1% of counted arithmetic is independent of denoising, whereas a descriptive affine fit to fixed-input host time assigns 17.7% to its intercept. At h=2, d=2 succeeds on 139/160 attempts versus 122/160 for d=5 (+10.6 percentage points; task-conditional 95% interval: +4.4 to +16.9), while using 5.9% less arithmetic per control step. Executing h=5 rather than h=2 at d=2 yields 138/160 versus 139/160 successes and 60.7% lower arithmetic per attempt; equivalence is not established. The case study shows why deployment adaptation must evaluate generation effort and feedback frequency jointly; it does not define a universal setting.

AI.tldr: This paper studies deployment-time inference compute allocation between action-chunk refinement and replanning frequency in a frozen SmolVLA robot policy on LIBERO, finding that frequent replanning with fewer denoising steps outperforms heavier refinement.
AI.motivation: A frozen chunked robot policy can spend inference compute either on refining each action chunk or on replanning more frequently from fresh observations, but the trade-off between these two coupled choices is not well understood.
AI.method: Using a frozen SmolVLA checkpoint in synchronous LIBERO simulation (chunk length K=50), the authors vary denoising count d and replanning horizon h, reporting success rates alongside both counted arithmetic and host latency.
AI.result: At h=2, d=2 achieves 139/160 successes versus 122/160 for d=5 (+10.6 percentage points, 95% CI +4.4 to +16.9) with 5.9% less arithmetic per step; at d=2, h=5 yields 138/160 successes with 60.7% lower arithmetic per attempt, while at d=10, 82.1% of counted arithmetic is independent of denoising.
AI.conclusion: Deployment adaptation must evaluate generation effort and feedback frequency jointly rather than relying on a single universal setting.

title: Certify, Then Select: Viability-Aware Runtime Steering of Frozen Diffusion Policies
summary: Diffusion policies, which generate short action sequences by denoising random noise, are a leading way to learn robot skills from demonstrations. Once deployed, they meet constraints the demonstrations never contained, and retraining for each is impractical. A safety filter edits the policy's action to satisfy them, but the edit ignores the task, and a large edit can leave the policy where it cannot continue. We propose CAST (Certified Action Selection at Test time): draw a few action chunks from the frozen policy, certify each with a barrier condition, and execute the certified chunk that a learned value ensemble ranks highest. We prove that a certified step is safe whatever the critic does; that, whenever a certified sample exists, the executed chunk stays within log N nats of the policy conditioned on feasibility, while a safety-filter projection can be singular to it; and that an exact closed-loop identity splits the gain of ranking into availability, spread and the critic's target. Certifying the next chunk is not enough: a generative controller can have safe actions available now and none later. We characterise the safe control authority of a frozen policy under finite sampling, and CAST-V preserves it through a policy-conditioned viability, estimated with a model under a finite-sample guarantee or learned from the controller's own logs (CAST-VL). On robomimic manipulation, a planar quadrotor, a MuJoCo humanoid and a unicycle, with frozen policies, CAST raises joint task-and-constraint success above the output filter in nearly every setting; certifying before ranking is decisive where a filter's edit is large, and viability removes most dead ends that one-step certification cannot see. Project page: this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes CAST and viability-aware CAST-V/CAST-VL to steer frozen diffusion policies at test time by certifying sampled action chunks with barrier conditions before ranking them, outperforming safety filters across manipulation and locomotion tasks.
AI.motivation: Safety filters edit a frozen diffusion policy's actions to satisfy new deployment constraints without considering the task, which can leave the policy in states where it cannot continue.
AI.method: CAST draws action chunks from the frozen policy, certifies each with a barrier condition, and executes the certified chunk ranked highest by a learned value ensemble; CAST-V and CAST-VL extend this by preserving policy-conditioned viability estimated via a model or controller logs.
AI.result: On robomimic manipulation, a planar quadrotor, a MuJoCo humanoid, and a unicycle, CAST improves joint task-and-constraint success over output filters in nearly every setting, with viability removing most dead ends missed by one-step certification.
AI.conclusion: Certifying sampled chunks before value-based selection, combined with viability awareness, enables safe and task-effective runtime steering of frozen diffusion policies.

title: SPARC: Evidence-guided adaptive model composition for materials discovery
comment: 52 pages, 5 figures; main text with Supplementary Information
summary: Closed-loop experimentation requires more than selecting the next experiment. It must also determine which existing measurements and model-derived relationships are sufficiently supported to influence that decision. Here we introduce SPARC (Sparse Predictive Aggregation of Regression Components), a framework that continually revises this support as experimental evidence accumulates. Competing model families are evaluated through out-of-fold predictions, so that each model is tested on observations not used in its corresponding fit. Sparse posterior composition assigns model influence according to predictive contributions supported by the out-of-fold evidence, retaining complementary contributions from several model families. Candidate-dependent predictive dispersion and residual variability define trust, which modulates exploration alongside the predicted response. Independent diagnostics also prioritize existing measurements for prospective verification, with model-derived trust reported alongside them. Across eight published materials datasets, SPARC achieved higher $R^2$ than the corresponding literature-reported values in six, with relative gains of up to 77% without the density-functional-theory- or experiment-derived descriptors used by several published pipelines. In an automated alkaline oxygen-evolution-reaction campaign, 8 of 11 SPARC-selected experiments reached overpotentials below 300 mV, with a best value of 242 mV, compared with 18 of 125 initial experiments. Measurements prioritized for verification before repetition subsequently deviated by 76 mV on average, compared with 27 mV for matched controls. SPARC therefore turns experimental evidence into a basis for revising model influence, directing exploration and identifying measurements that warrant verification.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces SPARC, an evidence-guided adaptive model composition framework for closed-loop materials discovery that outperforms literature R^2 on six of eight datasets and accelerates an alkaline OER campaign.
AI.motivation: Closed-loop experimentation needs to determine not only which experiment to run next, but also which existing measurements and model-derived relationships are sufficiently supported by evidence to guide that decision.
AI.method: SPARC evaluates competing model families via out-of-fold predictions, assigns sparse posterior weights based on predictive contributions, modulates exploration using candidate-dependent predictive dispersion and residual variability as trust, and flags existing measurements for verification.
AI.result: SPARC achieves higher R^2 than literature values on six of eight materials datasets (up to 77% relative gain without DFT or experimental descriptors); in an alkaline OER campaign, 8 of 11 SPARC-selected experiments reached overpotentials below 300 mV (best 242 mV) versus 18 of 125 initial experiments, and flagged measurements deviated by 76 mV on average versus 27 mV for controls.
AI.conclusion: SPARC turns accumulating experimental evidence into a principled basis for revising model influence, guiding exploration, and identifying unreliable measurements.

title: TokenFormer V2: Breaking the Resolution-Complexity Dilemma in Unified Recommendation
summary: Industrial recommendation faces a resolution--complexity dilemma: dense interactions make detailed modeling of long behavior histories expensive, while compact history summaries restrict the evidence available to prediction. A unified backbone must preserve rich behavioral details within strict serving budgets. We introduce \textbf{TokenFormer V2}, a unified architecture that explicitly decouples \emph{representation resolution} from \emph{interaction density}. Its group-wise token layout jointly encodes behavior segments with non-sequential context, expands interaction ranges via hierarchical group merging, and coordinates distributed groups through \emph{NS Fusion} and \emph{Global Sync} modules. Through this \emph{local--global decomposition} paradigm, computation is concentrated on structured interactions while preserving fine-grained evidence, ensuring that every encoded event remains directly accessible to the \emph{Full-Resolution Readout} module. On the Tencent Advertising Algorithm Competition 2026 (TAAC 2026) benchmark, TokenFormer V2 achieves top-ranking accuracy among unified recommendation baselines while using \textbf{5.1$\times$ fewer FLOPs} than leading baselines, sustaining its advantage across long histories and imbalanced behavior domains. Furthermore, in billion-parameter evaluations on WeChat Channels advertising, it consistently outperforms state-of-the-art industrial baselines, yielding up to a \textbf{+0.07 pp} overall AUC gain. In live online A/B testing against the production model, TokenFormer V2 delivers a statistically significant \textbf{2.33\% increase in GMV}. These results establish TokenFormer V2 as a battle-tested blueprint for scalable, full-resolution behavior modeling in industrial recommendation.

AI.tldr: This paper presents TokenFormer V2, a unified recommendation architecture that decouples representation resolution from interaction density, achieving top accuracy on TAAC 2026 with 5.1x fewer FLOPs and +2.33% GMV in live A/B testing.
AI.motivation: Industrial recommendation systems face a resolution-complexity dilemma where dense interactions over long behavior histories are too expensive, while compact summaries lose fine-grained behavioral evidence.
AI.method: TokenFormer V2 uses a group-wise token layout with non-sequential context, hierarchical group merging, NS Fusion and Global Sync modules for local-global decomposition, and a Full-Resolution Readout module that keeps every encoded event directly accessible.
AI.result: On TAAC 2026, TokenFormer V2 achieves top-ranking accuracy with 5.1x fewer FLOPs than leading baselines; in billion-parameter WeChat Channels evaluations, it gains up to +0.07 pp overall AUC, and in live online A/B testing it delivers a statistically significant 2.33% increase in GMV.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling representation resolution from interaction density provides a scalable blueprint for full-resolution behavior modeling in industrial recommendation.

title: Using machine learning approaches to classify false-positives generated by static analysis tools - An empirical study using small datasets
summary: Static Code Analysis (SCA) tools are vital for software development to reduce the cost and time required for manual code reviews. It was established in our previous study that the best tools reported in the software engineering community return high false-positive and false-negative rates when used for code analysis. Several approaches have been taken in existing studies to identify false-positive alarms generated by SCA tools, in helping to enhance the utility of these tools. However, existing studies reveal several limitations, chiefly among which is the tendency to focus on a limited number of alarm types or failing to evaluate a large breadth of Machine-Learning (ML) techniques comprehensively. This study has addressed this opportunity. We identified the best Code Representation Learning (CRL) techniques and ML algorithms for identifying false-positives, where results show that performance outcomes vary based on the characteristics of the training datasets and the goal of the model building. Given the evidence established in this study, we recommend further investigations targeting specific configurations of advanced CRLs and ML Algorithms, including simple ML models.

AI.tldr: This empirical study evaluates a broad range of code representation learning (CRL) techniques and machine learning algorithms for classifying false-positive alarms from static code analysis tools on small datasets.
AI.motivation: Static code analysis tools produce high false-positive and false-negative rates, and prior ML-based filtering studies have focused on limited alarm types or narrow sets of ML techniques.
AI.method: The authors systematically evaluate multiple CRL techniques and ML algorithms on small datasets to identify effective combinations for false-positive classification.
AI.result: Classification performance varies depending on the characteristics of the training datasets and the specific modeling goal, with no single universal configuration dominating all settings.
AI.conclusion: Future work should investigate targeted configurations of advanced CRLs and ML algorithms, including simple ML models, tailored to dataset characteristics.

title: A predictive, per-engine energy roofline of the Apple Neural Engine
comment: 40 pages, 5 figures, 36 tables (including a 28-table supplement as appendices). Accepted to ACM Transactions on Architecture and Code Optimization (TACO). Code and data: this https URL
summary: The Apple Neural Engine (ANE) is in over a billion devices, but is characterized indirectly via CoreML. Using a CoreML-free fused-graph dispatch path, we measure the ANE, along with the Apple GPU and CPU on the same device, with per-engine energy accounting. The consumer-available roofline does not predict the ANE in practice. A critical correction is that the ANE sees two effective memory bandwidths: a slow activation path and a fast weight-stream path. Two roofline ridges follow, and the weight-stream ridge is below that of the GPU. The ANE single-operand compute peak decreases instead of plateauing. Its weight stream is byte-bound in fp16 but limited by the dequantizer's element rate in int8. As a result, int8 compression saves energy at unchanged throughput and an int4 lookup-table stream raises throughput and efficiency at a cost of 2.55 points of ImageNet top-1. The corrected roofline identifies the lower-energy ANE paths and bounds it from below. A constructed device map reproduces across four unique ANE generations. Results show that operators should be placed by arithmetic intensity and fused for optimal performance.

AI.tldr: This paper measures the Apple Neural Engine (ANE) via a CoreML-free fused-graph path and derives a corrected two-ridge energy roofline that explains its distinct activation and weight-stream memory bandwidths.
AI.motivation: Although the ANE is present in over a billion devices, it has only been characterized indirectly through CoreML, and standard consumer rooflines fail to predict its actual performance and energy behavior.
AI.method: Using a CoreML-free fused-graph dispatch path, the authors measure per-engine energy and throughput across the ANE, GPU, and CPU, constructing a corrected roofline and device map across four ANE generations.
AI.result: The ANE exhibits two effective memory bandwidths (a slow activation path and a fast weight-stream path below the GPU ridge), with fp16 weight streams byte-bound, int8 limited by dequantizer element rate (saving energy at unchanged throughput), and int4 lookup-table streams raising throughput and efficiency at a 2.55-point ImageNet top-1 cost.
AI.conclusion: The corrected per-engine roofline bounds ANE energy from below and shows that operators should be placed by arithmetic intensity and fused for optimal efficiency.

title: ST-GAT: A Leakage-Free Spatio-Temporal Graph Attention Framework for Robust Network Intrusion Detection
summary: Intrusion detection systems are a central defence in modern networks. Deep learning models report strong anomaly-detection results, but evaluations on standard benchmarks such as CSE-CIC-IDS-2018 are often inflated by two methodological problems: temporal leakage from overlapping sliding windows, and contamination from preprocessing fitted before the train/test split. Per-flow classifiers also ignore the spatio-temporal dependencies across sequences of network flows. We propose a Spatio-Temporal Graph Attention Network (ST-GAT) that represents traffic as a sequence of graph snapshots. It builds k-Nearest Neighbour (k-NN) edges within each window, applies multi-head Graph Attention Network (GAT) layers for spatial aggregation, and uses a Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM) network with temporal attention for sequence modelling. To prevent leakage, we use non-overlapping temporal windows (stride equal to window length) and fit all preprocessing on the training split only. We compare three class-imbalance strategies: inverse class-frequency weighting, dynamic balanced sampling, and few-shot metric prototyping. Across three random seeds, ST-GAT with inverse class weighting reached a Macro-F1 of 96.65% (+/- 0.87) and an accuracy of 99.14%. This is 14.3 percentage points higher in Macro-F1 than a per-flow Random Forest baseline (82.34%). Balanced sampling reduced Macro-F1 by 2.3 points (to 94.37%) relative to loss weighting. This suggests that aggressive resampling of small, noisy minority classes can hurt detection in heavily imbalanced traffic.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes ST-GAT, a leakage-free spatio-temporal graph attention framework for network intrusion detection that reaches 96.65% Macro-F1 on CSE-CIC-IDS-2018, outperforming a per-flow Random Forest by 14.3 percentage points.
AI.motivation: Prior deep learning evaluations on intrusion detection benchmarks like CSE-CIC-IDS-2018 are often inflated by temporal leakage from overlapping windows and preprocessing fitted before train/test splitting, while per-flow models ignore spatio-temporal flow dependencies.
AI.method: ST-GAT builds k-NN graph snapshots over non-overlapping temporal windows, fits all preprocessing strictly on the training split, applies multi-head GAT layers for spatial aggregation and a BiLSTM with temporal attention for sequence modeling, and compares three class-imbalance strategies.
AI.result: Across three seeds on CSE-CIC-IDS-2018, ST-GAT with inverse class-frequency weighting achieves 96.65% (+/- 0.87) Macro-F1 and 99.14% accuracy, beating a per-flow Random Forest (82.34% Macro-F1) by 14.3 pp, whereas dynamic balanced sampling drops Macro-F1 by 2.3 pp to 94.37%.
AI.conclusion: Preventing temporal and preprocessing leakage while modeling spatio-temporal flow graphs enables robust intrusion detection, and loss weighting is preferable to aggressive minority-class resampling.

title: ANCHOR: A Port-Hamiltonian Model for Forecasting Team Dynamics in Human-in-the-Loop Systems
summary: Cyber-physical-human systems close a loop around people by sensing human behavior, predict it and act on it. Human teams are a natural target, because collaboration breaks down in ways that a timely prompt could prevent. Collaborative mixed reality makes this loop practical, since each headset senses who speaks, where its wearer looks and who stands together, and it can deliver a light prompt. In this loop, the headsets are sensors, the prompts are actuators and the team is the plant. Closing the loop needs a plant model that is small enough to learn from few teams, safe to iterate and readable by a designer. We propose ANCHOR, which models a team as a ball in an energy bowl. The bottom of the bowl is where the team rests, and it is set by the team's recent behavior, its own history and other teams. Formally, ANCHOR is a switched port-Hamiltonian system with 52 parameters, and each part stands for a testable claim from team psychology. Because of this structure, for any fitted parameters, a forecast moves away from rest only when task progress or a prompt pushes it, and prompts of bounded size that are spaced in time move it a bounded distance. On \nGroups{} four-person teams held out from training, a team that drifts from its usual behavior returns most of the way within half a minute. After 32 s, about 24% of the deviation remains, and ANCHOR predicted 30%. Forecasts are clearly better when the resting point blends its three sources than when it uses one. ANCHOR matches the accuracy of a black-box baseline with about 40,000 parameters. It anticipates conversation collapse with an AUROC of 0.85. In simulation under assumed prompt effects, it removes 2.2 times as much breakdown time per prompt as periodic prompting.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces ANCHOR, a 52-parameter switched port-Hamiltonian model of human team dynamics that matches a 40,000-parameter black-box baseline and predicts conversation collapse with 0.85 AUROC.
AI.motivation: Closing a human-in-the-loop mixed-reality prompting loop around teams requires a plant model that is small enough to learn from few teams, safe to iterate, and interpretable to designers.
AI.method: ANCHOR models a team as a ball in an energy bowl whose resting point blends recent behavior, team history, and other teams, formulated as a 52-parameter switched port-Hamiltonian system with bounded prompt-response guarantees.
AI.result: On held-out four-person teams, ANCHOR predicts 30% remaining deviation at 32 s (versus 24% observed), matches a ~40,000-parameter black-box baseline in accuracy, anticipates conversation collapse with 0.85 AUROC, and removes 2.2x as much breakdown time per prompt as periodic prompting in simulation.
AI.conclusion: Physics-inspired port-Hamiltonian structure enables data-efficient, interpretable, and safe forecasting for human-in-the-loop team interventions.

title: Generalization Testing of Grid Foundation Models for Power Flow and Optimal Power Flow
summary: There is growing interest in foundation models (FMs) for power grids, particularly for power flow and optimal power flow. Their usefulness depends on generalization accuracy, which existing works test on their own benchmarks. We propose a three-axis framework to test their generalization limits: changed admittance matrices of training grids, load levels, and unseen grids. We test GENCO, LUMINA and GridSFM against the DC baseline, alongside their reported limitations, and discuss theoretical reasons for their failures. Experiments reveal that adding a line degrades all FMs more than removing one, and longer lines eventually make LUMINA and fine-tuned GENCO worse than DC. All three degrade beyond their training load range, where the loading-voltage curve steepens. On unseen grids, LUMINA degrades sharply even inside its training range, and GridSFM fails on the grid farthest from it. Thus, beyond training conditions, FMs behave more like meta-models requiring test-time fine-tuning data and compute.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a three-axis generalization testing framework for power-grid foundation models (GENCO, LUMINA, GridSFM), showing they degrade beyond training load ranges and on unseen grids, behaving like meta-models needing test-time fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Grid foundation models for power flow and optimal power flow are typically evaluated only on their own benchmarks, leaving their generalization limits under topology, load, and grid changes unclear.
AI.method: The authors evaluate GENCO, LUMINA, and GridSFM against a DC baseline across three axes: modified admittance matrices of training grids, out-of-range load levels, and unseen grids.
AI.result: Adding a transmission line degrades all foundation models more than removing one, longer lines make LUMINA and fine-tuned GENCO worse than DC, all three degrade beyond their training load range, LUMINA drops sharply on unseen grids even in-range, and GridSFM fails on the farthest unseen grid.
AI.conclusion: Beyond their training distributions, current grid foundation models act more like meta-models that require test-time fine-tuning data and compute.

title: Continuous Lower-Limb Joint-Angle Estimation from sEMG and IMU: The Conditional Value of Cross-Activity and Cross-Subject Data under Update-Matched Controls
comment: 8 pages, 5 figures, 3 tables. Submitted to IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L)
summary: Intent-driven exoskeleton control needs a continuous, causal estimate of the wearer's joint kinematics and an answer to a second question: whose data should train the estimator for a new user? Borrowing the user's recordings of other activities, or other users' recordings of the same activity, is usually evaluated as "more data" versus "less data," which confounds the information a source carries with the optimizer updates it adds and hides negative transfer behind averages. We separate these effects for hip, knee, and ankle angle estimation from high-density sEMG and an IMU across six locomotion activities on all ten participants of a public dataset. A compact residual causal TCN-GRU decoder is frozen, and an update-matched replay control prices every added source against the same number of updates on the user's own data. A user's own other activities raise $R^2$ from 0.722 to 0.788, of which +0.048 is information beyond replay; stair descent is a reliably harmful donor and sit-stand-walk a reliably beneficial one. Other users' same-activity data help while the user has only the target activity ($G_\mathrm{T} = +0.053$) and half as much once own other-activity data exist ($G_\mathrm{W} = +0.028$); at full calibration, donor value collapses after one to two target records. Per-target gains from the two sources correlate, and leave-one-participant-out gates recover most of the cross-subject value only at low calibration. Data value is hierarchical, state-dependent, and directional; the bottleneck is deciding, without test labels, when to transfer.

AI.tldr: This paper isolates information value from optimizer-update effects in sEMG/IMU lower-limb joint-angle estimation using update-matched replay controls, showing that data transfer value is hierarchical, state-dependent, and directional.
AI.motivation: Evaluating cross-activity or cross-subject data by simply adding more data confounds information content with extra optimizer updates and hides negative transfer behind averages.
AI.method: Using a frozen residual causal TCN-GRU decoder on six locomotion activities across ten participants, the authors compare adding a user's other activities or other users' same-activity data against update-matched replay on the user's own data.
AI.result: A user's own other activities raise R^2 from 0.722 to 0.788 (+0.048 beyond replay), with sit-stand-walk beneficial and stair descent harmful; other users' same-activity data help when only target-activity data exist (G_T = +0.053) and half as much when own other-activity data exist (G_W = +0.028), collapsing after one to two target records at full calibration.
AI.conclusion: Transfer value in continuous joint-angle estimation is hierarchical and directional, making label-free detection of when to transfer the primary bottleneck.

title: Physics-Informed Causal Reasoning for Nonstationary Robot Dynamics
comment: 22 pages, 6 figures. Project page: this https URL
summary: Reasoning about what an action will cause requires internalizing how a system behaves. As conditions seldom stay fixed, this must often happen within a few interactions. Yet systems that look identical in a snapshot can respond differently to the same action, depending on physical conditions the snapshot hides. Context-based models capture this separation by summarizing recent transitions into a latent context, but do not specify how that context should change the equations of motion. Physics-informed neural networks build those equations into the model, but describe only a single system and cannot recognize when it has changed. We present Physics-Informed Causal Reasoning (PICR), which bridges the two. Only a context, re-inferred from recent interactions, is updated; it conditions a fixed physics-informed network that determines the robot's inertia and potential energy, so the robot adapts to new physical conditions from its own experience without retraining or a hand-specified robot model. On a Franka Panda arm in NVIDIA Isaac Sim, PICR predicts motion under changing and unseen payloads, reducing error on the latter by 1.6-3.8x over baselines, and extends to counterfactual queries under alternative torques. Our analysis shows that the context, inferred solely from interaction, encodes payload physical properties, tracks their changes, and governs the arm's response. The gravity and inertia terms induced by the context further demonstrate its physical validity, each agreeing with the simulator at the level of individual Lagrangian components.

AI.tldr: This paper presents Physics-Informed Causal Reasoning (PICR), which conditions a fixed physics-informed network on a latent context inferred from recent interactions to adapt to nonstationary robot dynamics, reducing unseen-payload error by 1.6-3.8x.
AI.motivation: Context-based models do not specify how latent context alters equations of motion, while physics-informed neural networks describe only a single fixed system and cannot adapt when physical conditions change.
AI.method: PICR infers a latent context solely from recent interaction transitions and uses it to condition a fixed physics-informed network representing the robot's inertia and potential energy without retraining or a hand-specified model.
AI.result: On a Franka Panda arm in NVIDIA Isaac Sim under changing and unseen payloads, PICR reduces motion prediction error on unseen payloads by 1.6-3.8x over baselines, supports counterfactual torque queries, and recovers gravity and inertia terms agreeing with the simulator's Lagrangian components.
AI.conclusion: Conditioning a physics-informed network on interaction-inferred context enables rapid, physically valid adaptation to nonstationary dynamics.

title: Delay-Aware Reinforcement Learning for O-RAN Control under Stochastic Reward Feedback
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) is increasingly employed for real-time control in Open Radio Access Networks (O-RANs). However, the asynchronous nature of O-RAN feedback introduces stochastic delays between actions and their observable rewards, leading to misaligned credit assignment and unstable training. This letter formulates the O-RAN control problem as a Markov decision process (MDP) with delayed and stochastic rewards, where the true reward corresponding to an action is received after an unknown delay. To address this, we propose a delay-aware deep RL framework that integrates a long short-term memory (LSTM)-based delay predictor and a temporal reward realignment module within an off-policy learning pipeline. Using empirical delay traces collected from the Open AI Cellular (OAIC) testbed, we demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves faster convergence and significantly reduces latency violations and packet drops compared to conventional RL methods that ignore feedback delay. The results confirm that reward-delay compensation is critical for reliable AI-driven O-RAN control.

AI.tldr: This letter proposes a delay-aware deep RL framework for O-RAN control with stochastic reward feedback, combining an LSTM delay predictor and temporal reward realignment to improve convergence and reduce latency violations and packet drops.
AI.motivation: Asynchronous feedback in Open Radio Access Networks introduces stochastic delays between actions and observable rewards, causing misaligned credit assignment and unstable RL training.
AI.method: The authors formulate O-RAN control as an MDP with delayed stochastic rewards and integrate an LSTM-based delay predictor with a temporal reward realignment module into an off-policy deep RL pipeline.
AI.result: Evaluated on empirical delay traces from the Open AI Cellular (OAIC) testbed, the framework achieves faster convergence and significantly fewer latency violations and packet drops than conventional RL baselines that ignore feedback delay.
AI.conclusion: Compensating for stochastic reward delays is essential for reliable AI-driven real-time control in O-RANs.

title: Enforcing Ellipsoidal Constraints in Neural Networks with a Polynomial Safety Layer
summary: Often the output of a learned mapping must satisfy prescribed constraints. In the control of autonomous systems, for example, the chosen action must keep the system within a collision-free region. We consider the case in which a proposed output is corrected by projection onto a safety ellipsoid. Computing this projection amounts to solving a quadratically constrained quadratic program (QCQP). We construct a neural-network safety layer by unrolling a feasibility-preserving polynomial penalty iteration. The unrolled structure allows the loss gradient to propagate from the feasible output through the safety layer to the network parameters during training. We show how to choose the layer parameters so that every iterate is feasible and give a computable bound on its distance to the exact projection at any prescribed depth.
