We illustrate the method by training a LiDAR-based policy to control an unmanned aerial vehicle. A privileged model predictive control expert uses the map and the measured vehicle state to generate the training data. In the simulated narrow mazes, the filtered policy avoided wall contact at every tested stage of training, including at initialization, when every unfiltered flight hit a wall. A representative build of the learned policy and its safety layer for an Arm Cortex-M4F microcontroller occupies about 36 KiB of flash, with a RAM budget below 5 KiB.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a polynomial safety layer that unrolls a feasibility-preserving iteration to project neural network outputs onto safety ellipsoids, achieving zero wall collisions in simulated UAV maze navigation within 36 KiB flash and 5 KiB RAM.
AI.motivation: Learned control policies for autonomous systems must satisfy hard safety constraints, such as collision avoidance, which requires differentiable projection onto safety sets like ellipsoids (a QCQP).
AI.method: The authors unroll a feasibility-preserving polynomial penalty iteration into a differentiable neural-network safety layer, providing parameter selection rules for iterate feasibility and computable bounds on distance to the exact projection.
AI.result: Trained with a privileged MPC expert on LiDAR-based UAV navigation in narrow mazes, the filtered policy avoids wall contact at every training stage including initialization (where all unfiltered flights crash), and fits in ~36 KiB flash and <5 KiB RAM on an Arm Cortex-M4F.
AI.conclusion: Unrolling a feasibility-preserving polynomial iteration yields a lightweight, end-to-end trainable safety layer suitable for resource-constrained microcontrollers.

title: Predicting, Fast and Slow: SSD Already Knows Which Guess Is Wrong
summary: Heimdall, a learned controller, calls slow on 52% of an SSD's reads when 30% are slow. Uncertainty estimators, the remedy prescribed for its wrong guesses, cannot find them: nine of them do no better than a coin. The drive can. On one trace, 2% of the reads of 4 to 8 KiB that found less than 4 KiB outstanding while the drive was answering came back slow, and Heimdall called 96% of them slow. A 4,096-entry table of how the drive's recent reads came back, untrained and 21 ns a decision, ranks the wrong guesses at a median AUROC of 0.68 on 57 held-out traces, where the nine sit at 0.46 to 0.52, and it predicts slow reads better than Heimdall itself.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that a 4,096-entry untrained history table of recent SSD read outcomes (21 ns per decision) detects wrong slow-read predictions by the Heimdall learned controller at 0.68 median AUROC, outperforming nine uncertainty estimators.
AI.motivation: The Heimdall learned SSD controller misclassifies many fast reads as slow (calling 52% slow when 30% are slow), and standard uncertainty estimators fail to identify these wrong guesses.
AI.method: The authors use an untrained 4,096-entry table tracking how the drive's recent reads returned, taking 21 ns per decision, and compare it against nine uncertainty estimators across 57 held-out traces.
AI.result: On 57 held-out traces, the history table ranks Heimdall's wrong guesses at a median AUROC of 0.68 versus 0.46 to 0.52 for the nine uncertainty estimators, and predicts slow reads better than Heimdall itself.
AI.conclusion: Simple drive-level read-outcome history tables provide a fast, effective alternative to uncertainty estimation for catching wrong predictions in learned storage controllers.

title: Equilibrium measures for anisotropic exponential interaction energies with applications to transformers
summary: We study the minimization of anisotropic exponential interaction energies over probability measures on the sphere, motivated by mean-field models of self-attention in transformer architectures. For every symmetric positive definite interaction matrix, we relate the minimizer to a corresponding anisotropic Brownian motion and use the Feynman--Kac formula and elliptic regularity theory to show that it admits a smooth, strictly positive density on the sphere. We further show that it is the only stationary measure with full support for the dynamics considered. We use the stochastic viewpoint to derive an algorithm for sampling from the minimizer. In dimension two, we also propose a numerical scheme for approximating its density based on a Mathieu series expansion.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes equilibrium measures for anisotropic exponential interaction energies on the sphere, motivated by transformer self-attention, proving smooth positive density and uniqueness and proposing sampling and 2D numerical approximation schemes.
AI.motivation: Mean-field models of self-attention in transformers lead to minimizing anisotropic exponential interaction energies over probability measures on the sphere, whose equilibrium properties need rigorous characterization.
AI.method: For any symmetric positive definite interaction matrix, the authors connect the energy minimizer to anisotropic Brownian motion using the Feynman-Kac formula and elliptic regularity theory, and derive a stochastic sampling algorithm plus a 2D Mathieu series approximation.
AI.result: The authors prove that the minimizer admits a smooth, strictly positive density on the sphere and is the unique stationary measure with full support for the associated dynamics.
AI.conclusion: The stochastic and analytic characterization provides both theoretical uniqueness guarantees and practical numerical tools for studying mean-field self-attention equilibria.

title: NAP-Wave: A Neural Adaptive Plane-Wave Architecture for High-Frequency Helmholtz Problems
summary: Training neural networks to simulate highly oscillatory wavefields presents optimization challenges, often hindered by spectral bias and poorly conditioned physics-based loss landscapes. To address these challenges and enhance convergence, we propose NAP-Wave, a joint neural architecture and training strategy that expands the target scattered wavefield in an adaptive neural plane-wave basis. The basis functions are extracted from all hidden layers and modulated by trainable plane-wave carriers, embedding the high-frequency oscillatory physics directly into the network's trial space. NAP-Wave is trained on a physics-informed loss built from the Lippmann-Schwinger integral equation, so no differentiation of the network with respect to its input is required. We develop a decoupled optimization strategy in which Adam updates the parameters of the neural plane-wave basis, while the linear combination coefficients are computed exactly by a least-squares (LS) solver. We couple this with an adaptive-depth training strategy in which the network starts shallow and grows progressively layer-by-layer. At each growth step, we avoid the loss spikes typical of dynamic network growth using the LS-computed coefficients, the warm-started parameters, and the preservation of the first- and second-order optimizer moments of the previous stage. Ablation studies confirm that the plane-wave basis, the exact coefficient solve, and the progressive schedule independently accelerate convergence and improve accuracy. Validated on exact-solution benchmarks, NAP-Wave achieves relative L2 errors of order 1%. On highly heterogeneous geophysical benchmarks, it achieves relative errors of 5%, 9%, and 10%, significantly outperforming published PINN methods in both accuracy and convergence time. To ensure reproducibility, the code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes NAP-Wave, a neural adaptive plane-wave architecture trained with a Lippmann-Schwinger physics-informed loss, decoupled Adam/least-squares optimization, and progressive depth growth, achieving 1% error on exact benchmarks and 5-10% on geophysical benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Neural networks simulating high-frequency oscillatory wavefields suffer from spectral bias and poorly conditioned physics-informed loss landscapes.
AI.method: NAP-Wave extracts basis functions from all hidden layers modulated by trainable plane-wave carriers, trains on a Lippmann-Schwinger integral loss (avoiding input differentiation), alternates Adam basis updates with exact least-squares coefficient solves, and grows network depth progressively with warm-started moments.
AI.result: NAP-Wave achieves relative L2 errors of ~1% on exact-solution benchmarks and 5%, 9%, and 10% on heterogeneous geophysical benchmarks, significantly outperforming published PINN methods in accuracy and convergence time.
AI.conclusion: Embedding oscillatory plane-wave physics with exact least-squares solves and progressive growth overcomes spectral bias in high-frequency Helmholtz problems.

title: Attacker Diversity Reduction in Adaptive LLM Red Teaming
summary: Reinforcement learning can make automated red-teaming more successful while narrowing the attacks it produces. Co-training an attacker and a defender with group-relative policy optimization (GRPO) has been reported to reduce attacker diversity. This experiment reproduces attack diversity reduction using three runs with a Qwen2.5-14B attacker and a Phi-4-mini defender trained by direct preference optimization (DPO). The attacker receives a success-only reward and uses a length-unbiased loss, bounded updates, warm-up and ratio clipping. The attacker is evaluated on 26 AdvBench behaviors. Training ended after 12 rounds, following a decision based on development checkpoints, so the reported intervals are nominal. Attack Diversity Retention (ADR) compares the within-behavior of the trained attacker spread with the untrained attacker. In order for an attack diversity to be consider as having been reduced, a criterion requires the ADR to be below a 0.75 target with a 95% confidence interval together with continued attacker effectiveness. Therefore, if an attacker narrows its attack vector by 25% consistently its considered less diverse. After 24 attacker and 12 defender LORA-based updates, ADR for the three runs were 0.63, 0.61 and 0.63, respectively. Each run met the criterion at round 12; the earlier checks at rounds 4 and 8 fell short. Despite attacks being less diverse, attack success continued to improve as the attacker was updated after each training run.

AI.tldr: This paper reproduces attacker diversity reduction in adaptive LLM red teaming using a Qwen2.5-14B attacker and DPO-trained Phi-4-mini defender, finding that Attack Diversity Retention drops to 0.61-0.63 after 12 rounds while attack success continues rising.
AI.motivation: Reinforcement learning can make automated LLM red-teaming more successful while narrowing the diversity of generated attacks, a phenomenon previously reported under GRPO co-training.
AI.method: Across three runs on 26 AdvBench behaviors, the authors train a Qwen2.5-14B attacker (success-only reward, length-unbiased loss, bounded updates) against a DPO-trained Phi-4-mini defender for 12 rounds (24 attacker and 12 defender LoRA updates) and measure Attack Diversity Retention (ADR).
AI.result: All three runs meet the diversity-reduction criterion (ADR < 0.75 with 95% CI) at round 12 with ADRs of 0.63, 0.61, and 0.63 (whereas rounds 4 and 8 did not), while attack success continues to improve.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive red-teaming with success-only RL rewards consistently narrows attacker diversity by over 25% even as attack effectiveness increases.

title: Set-based State Estimation for Unknown Dynamical Systems from Noisy Output Data with Probabilistic Guarantees
summary: We develop a methodology for set-based state estimation from noisy input-output trajectories, without a predefined model structure for the unknown state dynamics or access to training state measurements. We derive a bound on the state set diameter that depends on the sensor map and leverage it as a surrogate to formulate a tractable linear program balancing state set tightness against output trajectory coverage. Combining this certificate with deterministic or probabilistically certified measurement noise sets and leveraging the results from scenario optimization with relaxation, we provide joint a posteriori probabilistic guarantees for state inclusion and state set diameter. Numerical simulations corroborate our developed theoretical guarantees.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a model-free set-based state estimation method from noisy input-output trajectories, formulating a tractable linear program with joint a posteriori probabilistic guarantees on state inclusion and set diameter.
AI.motivation: State estimation for unknown dynamical systems without a predefined model structure or training state measurements requires balancing state-set tightness against output trajectory coverage under noise.
AI.method: The authors derive a sensor-map-dependent bound on the state set diameter as a surrogate for a tractable linear program, combining it with deterministic or probabilistically certified noise sets and scenario optimization with relaxation.
AI.result: Theoretical analysis establishes joint a posteriori probabilistic guarantees for both state inclusion and state set diameter, which are corroborated by numerical simulations.
AI.conclusion: The proposed linear programming and scenario-optimization framework enables certified set-based state estimation for unknown systems directly from noisy output data.

title: Found, but Not Fixed : From Software Vulnerability Discovery to Fixes with Iterative LLM Pipelines
summary: Software vulnerabilities persist as a critical threat despite the deployment of sophisticated detection tools and AI assistants. While detection has advanced, the subsequent code repair phase remains a primary bottleneck; manual intervention is inherently slow, costly, and prone to introducing secondary regressions and issues. In this paper, we investigate whether an iterative, LLM-based pipeline can provide a robust solution for the automated repair of vulnerable functions in real-world code. We propose a generalized framework that leverages the reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) through a multi-stage feedback loop. We benchmark this approach against state-of-the-art models, including GPT-4o, GPT-5.1, and Gemini 3 Flash, demonstrating that such a pipeline can achieve high-quality code repair. To support the broader security community, we provide our evaluation framework, fine-tuned weights, and comprehensive experimental dataset on our website: this https URL

AI.tldr: This paper investigates an iterative, multi-stage LLM feedback pipeline for automated repair of software vulnerabilities in real-world code, benchmarking against GPT-4o, GPT-5.1, and Gemini 3 Flash.
AI.motivation: While vulnerability detection has advanced, automated code repair remains a bottleneck because manual fixing is slow, costly, and prone to introducing regressions.
AI.method: The authors propose a generalized iterative LLM pipeline that leverages reasoning through a multi-stage feedback loop for repairing vulnerable functions, and benchmark it against GPT-4o, GPT-5.1, and Gemini 3 Flash.
AI.result: The experiments demonstrate that the iterative pipeline achieves high-quality automated code repair, and the authors release their evaluation framework, fine-tuned weights, and dataset.
AI.conclusion: Multi-stage iterative feedback loops enable LLMs to perform reliable automated vulnerability repair in real-world software.

title: Relax-and-Sparsify Approximation Algorithms for Sparse Ridge Regression
summary: This paper studies sparse ridge regression in the low-rank, high-dimensional setting that often arises when data collection is expensive. By exploiting the low-rank structure, we develop approximation algorithms within a relax-and-sparsify framework: solve a convex relaxation and then sparsify its solution to satisfy the original sparsity constraint. Specifically, we establish a tight rank-dependent sparsity bound for the convex relaxation by decomposing its support into two parts. This decomposition in turn motivates two approximation strategies, parameter reduction and binary redistribution, each exploiting a different part. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets show that the binary redistribution algorithms outperform the benchmarks in most instances.

AI.tldr: This paper develops relax-and-sparsify approximation algorithms for low-rank, high-dimensional sparse ridge regression, establishing a tight rank-dependent sparsity bound and showing that binary redistribution outperforms benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Sparse ridge regression frequently arises in low-rank, high-dimensional regimes where data collection is expensive, requiring principled approximation algorithms.
AI.method: The authors solve a convex relaxation and sparsify its solution to meet the sparsity constraint, deriving a tight rank-dependent sparsity bound by decomposing the support into two parts and proposing parameter reduction and binary redistribution strategies.
AI.result: Experiments on synthetic and real datasets show that the binary redistribution algorithms outperform existing benchmarks in most instances.
AI.conclusion: Exploiting low-rank support decomposition within a relax-and-sparsify framework yields effective approximation algorithms for sparse ridge regression.

title: Where the Error Lives: Separating Lid-Edge and Body-Induced Error in Neural Pressure Prediction for 3D Cavity Flow
summary: Can a pressure surrogate score much better globally without better resolving the pressure around immersed bodies? We test this in a three-dimensional lid-driven cavity with an unregularized lid and centered pressure at native $128^3$ resolution. On 60 cases from 12 unseen geometries, with predictions sealed before the CFD truth existed, adding a body-free, Reynolds-conditioned reference correction to the same frozen $64^3$ surrogate lifted to $128^3$ lowers the mean full-volume relative $L_2$ error from 20.6% to 7.5%. In the post hoc regional analysis, the lid-edge junction occupies 1.5% of the fluid but holds 69% of the truth pressure energy and 95% of the uncorrected surrogate's squared error. Interior error changes by just +0.16% relative, and object-local peak error and recall change little on average. Retrospective ablations locate the learned term's contribution in the interior and near the bodies; rebasing on the reference lowers global error further with little change in cohort-mean near-body metrics. Reference-relative body-response error remains about 25% in the interior near-body band. Grid-refinement, lid-regularization and convergence checks delimit the numerical scope. In this benchmark, a large global gain chiefly reflects correction of a shared boundary field, not better resolution of the body response. We recommend reporting regional truth-energy and model-error shares alongside near-body and reference-relative body-response errors.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that a large global L2 error reduction (20.6% to 7.5%) in 3D cavity-flow neural pressure prediction comes almost entirely from correcting a shared lid-edge boundary field rather than improving pressure resolution around immersed bodies.
AI.motivation: It is unclear whether global error improvements in neural pressure surrogates reflect better resolution of immersed-body pressure or merely better fitting of shared boundary features.
AI.method: Testing a frozen 64^3 surrogate lifted to 128^3 on 60 cases across 12 unseen geometries with a body-free, Reynolds-conditioned reference correction, the authors perform post hoc regional energy and error decompositions.
AI.result: The reference correction lowers mean full-volume relative L2 error from 20.6% to 7.5%, but the lid-edge junction (1.5% of fluid volume) holds 69% of truth pressure energy and 95% of uncorrected squared error; interior error changes by only +0.16% relative, and reference-relative near-body error remains ~25%.
AI.conclusion: Benchmarks for neural PDE surrogates should report regional truth-energy and error shares alongside near-body and reference-relative metrics to avoid mistaking boundary corrections for body-response accuracy.

title: PIRanNN: Random-Feature Pricing and Calibration under Jump-Diffusion and Stochastic-Volatility Models
comment: 29 pages, 4 figures, 14 tables. Code: this https URL
summary: We study a random-feature method for pricing and calibrating European options under jump-diffusion (Merton, Kou) and stochastic-volatility (Heston, SABR) models. The network has one hidden layer with a probit activation and fixed random inner weights, so fitting it to the pricing equation, the payoff and the boundary conditions is a single regularised least-squares problem, with no iterative training. For Merton and Kou the jump integral of each feature is explicit, so no quadrature is needed. One factorisation of the least-squares matrix gives the price at every state and time, its Greeks, and the exact derivatives of the prices with respect to the model parameters for gradient-based calibration. For the jump models, subtracting the Black-Scholes price removes the payoff kink and reduces the pricing error by about two orders of magnitude. The method is then about as accurate as a standard Crank-Nicolson finite-difference scheme at the same run time, although a finite-difference scheme that also subtracts the Black-Scholes price is about two orders of magnitude more accurate still. On the test problems of a recent physics-informed neural network study, the method matches that network's accuracy in seconds instead of about half an hour. The calibration experiments show that a solver can fit the quotes and still return wrong parameters when its pricing error is not small compared with the effect of the parameters on the prices: without the subtraction the solver misses the jump parameters by up to 50%, and with it they are recovered to within 3%. For Heston and SABR, used as an applicability study with boundary conditions that need no reference prices, pricing errors are about one percent and the calibrated parameters are within about 15% of the true values.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes PIRanNN, a single-hidden-layer random-feature network solved via regularized least squares for European option pricing and calibration, matching PINN accuracy in seconds instead of half an hour.
AI.motivation: Physics-informed neural networks for option pricing and calibration require slow iterative training, and calibration can fail when pricing errors are not small relative to parameter sensitivities.
AI.method: PIRanNN uses fixed random inner weights with probit activations so fitting the PDE, payoff, and boundary conditions reduces to one regularized least-squares solve (with explicit jump integrals for Merton/Kou and Black-Scholes subtraction to remove payoff kinks).
AI.result: Black-Scholes subtraction reduces jump-model pricing error by ~2 orders of magnitude, matching Crank-Nicolson accuracy at similar runtime and PINN accuracy in seconds instead of ~30 minutes; calibration recovers jump parameters within 3% (versus 50% error without subtraction), and Heston/SABR calibration achieves ~1% pricing error and ~15% parameter error.
AI.conclusion: Random-feature least squares with Black-Scholes subtraction provides fast, accurate option pricing and reliable gradient-based calibration.

title: IANN: A Unified Framework for Equivariant InterAtomic Neural Networks with User-Friendly Implementation
comment: 31 pages, 7 figures, 4 tables; Supplementary Information included (49 figures, 11 tables). IANN is MIT-licensed. Code: this https URL - Documentation: this https URL - Curated DFT databases: this https URL - Foundation models: this https URL
summary: Machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) now approach density functional theory (DFT) accuracy at a fraction of its cost, but the practical benefit is limited by software fragmentation: each state-of-the-art architecture is released as a separate codebase, with its own data format, configuration system, training loop and molecular-dynamics interface. Comparing two architectures on the same dataset, or moving a trained model into a production simulation, therefore requires substantial re-engineering. We introduce IANN (InterAtomic Neural Network), an open-source PyTorch framework that reimplements equivariant graph neural networks - PaiNN, NequIP, MACE, Allegro, EquiformerV2, EquiformerV3 and UMA - behind a unified data object, a unified trainer and a single deployment route, so that the architecture is a one-word change in a configuration dictionary. Forces, stresses and virials are obtained for every architecture from one analytic differentiation of the energy with respect to the edge vectors of the atomic graph, exact under periodic boundary conditions. Distributed training is configured automatically from the SLURM, PBS or MPI environment, so the same script runs unchanged from a workstation to a multi-node GPU allocation. Self-describing checkpoints serve directly as ASE calculators, as ensembles reporting uncertainties, or as TorchScript models run inside LAMMPS through bundled C++ pair styles with single- and multi-GPU inference. Trained on a common dataset of millions of structures, the architectures can be compared under identical conditions. We further release PaiNN foundation models trained on 41.9 million curated DFT structures from MPtrj, Alexandria, OMat24, MatPES, OC20, OC22, OC25, MPr2SCAN and MatPESr2SCAN, spanning the PBE, RPBE and r2SCAN functionals. Additionally, IANN provides an agent interface to facilitate integration with autonomous agents.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces IANN, an open-source PyTorch framework that unifies seven equivariant interatomic neural network architectures under one data/training/LAMMPS deployment pipeline, and releases PaiNN foundation models trained on 41.9M DFT structures.
AI.motivation: Software fragmentation across machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) forces substantial re-engineering when comparing architectures or deploying models to production molecular dynamics.
AI.method: IANN reimplements PaiNN, NequIP, MACE, Allegro, EquiformerV2, EquiformerV3, and UMA behind a unified data object, trainer, analytic periodic differentiation for forces/stresses/virials, automatic SLURM/PBS/MPI distribution, and ASE/LAMMPS deployment, plus an agent interface.
AI.result: The authors demonstrate unified training and deployment and release PaiNN foundation models trained on 41.9 million curated DFT structures across nine datasets (MPtrj, Alexandria, OMat24, MatPES, OC20, OC22, OC25, MPr2SCAN, MatPESr2SCAN).
AI.conclusion: IANN eliminates engineering friction for benchmarking equivariant MLIPs under identical conditions and deploying them into production simulations.

title: Hermitian Positive Definite Neural Networks for Matrix-CFAR Geometric Signal Detection in Nonhomogeneous Clutter
summary: Matrix information geometry (MIG) detectors exploit the Riemannian geometry of Hermitian positive definite (HPD) matrices to achieve robust object detection in nonhomogeneous clutter. The matrix constant false alarm rate (matrix-CFAR) method is a representative MIG detector that relies on the geometric structures with respect to specific metrics. In most cases, computing representative HPD covariance matrices requires numerical methods, typically involving computationally intensive iterative optimization algorithms. Although explicit formulas are available for certain cases, such as the log-Euclidean (LE) mean, they are generally unavailable for many other matrix means and medians. To address this challenge, we propose integrating the Hermitian positive definite neural network (HPDNet) into the matrix-CFAR framework, replacing conventional numerical optimization procedures with a learned, geometry-preserving mapping that directly estimates representative HPD covariance matrices from data. In the simulations, the framework is evaluated for MIG detectors using both means and medians associated with the affine-invariant Riemannian metric, the LE metric, and the Bures--Wasserstein metric, on both simulated compound-Gaussian clutter and real IPIX sea clutter. In both cases, the HPDNet is trained solely on simulated data to assess its applicability to the study of real data. The results show a significant reduction of computational cost in testing, while maintaining detection performance and robustness.

AI.tldr: This paper integrates Hermitian Positive Definite Neural Networks (HPDNet) into matrix-CFAR geometric signal detectors to replace iterative optimization, reducing test-time computation while preserving detection performance on simulated and IPIX sea clutter.
AI.motivation: Computing representative HPD covariance matrices in matrix information geometry (MIG) detectors typically requires computationally intensive iterative optimization for metrics lacking closed-form means or medians.
AI.method: The authors train HPDNet solely on simulated data to learn a geometry-preserving mapping that directly estimates representative HPD covariance matrices for affine-invariant Riemannian, log-Euclidean, and Bures-Wasserstein means and medians.
AI.result: Evaluations on simulated compound-Gaussian clutter and real IPIX sea clutter show that HPDNet significantly reduces test-time computational cost while maintaining detection performance and robustness.
AI.conclusion: Learned geometry-preserving mappings enable fast, robust matrix-CFAR detection without iterative Riemannian optimization at test time.

title: ProTTS: End-to-End Prominence-aware Natural and Controllable Text-to-Speech via Automatic Word Stress Discovery
summary: Natural speech conveys meaning not only through words, but also through the prominence on a few words. Yet most text-to-speech (TTS) systems remain prominence-unaware, existing prominence-aware TTS require external stress annotations, while unsupervised stress detectors operate in isolation, disconnected from synthesis. This creates a fundamental gap no existing system can automatically discover where stress should be placed, realize it as natural-sounding prosody, and offer user control over emphasis placement, all within a single model. To circumvent this, we propose ProTTS, a unified framework where stress detection emerges from the TTS model itself and, in turn, guides it to synthesize more natural and controllable speech. We incorporate a clustering head into the variance adaptor of FastSpeech_2 that discovers word stress directly from aggregated prosodic features. The discovered stress then drives emphasis variance predictors that modify pitch, energy, and duration for stressed words. The framework is trained end-to-end: TTS reconstruction and clustering losses jointly shape a stress-discriminative feature space without requiring stress labels at any stage. At inference, the same architecture also supports user-controllable emphasis by accepting a custom stress mask. We evaluate ProTTS on ISLE (non-native), LibriTTS, VCTK (native training), and three evaluation benchmarks (Tatoeba, TinyStress-15k, EmphAssess). Listeners prefer ProTTS over the baseline with a MOS of 3.96 vs. 3.12 and 83.5% preference rate. For stress detection, ProTTS achieves 0.839/0.861 F1 on ISLE (German/Italian L2), outperforming unsupervised (0.70) and supervised (0.82) baselines, and 0.933 F1 in zero-shot transfer to Tatoeba.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes ProTTS, an end-to-end TTS framework that automatically discovers word stress via a clustering head in FastSpeech 2, achieving 3.96 MOS (83.5% preference) and 0.839/0.861 F1 on ISLE stress detection.
AI.motivation: Existing TTS systems are either prominence-unaware or require external stress annotations, while unsupervised stress detectors operate separately from speech synthesis.
AI.method: ProTTS adds a clustering head to FastSpeech 2's variance adaptor to discover word stress from prosodic features, feeding emphasis variance predictors for pitch, energy, and duration, trained end-to-end with reconstruction and clustering losses and supporting custom stress masks at inference.
AI.result: Evaluated on ISLE, LibriTTS, VCTK, Tatoeba, TinyStress-15k, and EmphAssess, ProTTS achieves 3.96 MOS versus 3.12 for the baseline (83.5% preference), 0.839/0.861 F1 on ISLE (beating unsupervised 0.70 and supervised 0.82 baselines), and 0.933 F1 zero-shot on Tatoeba.
AI.conclusion: Jointly learning word stress discovery and emphasis-aware synthesis in a single end-to-end model yields more natural, controllable TTS without stress labels.

title: Local Order Matters: A Lightweight CPU-Trainable CNN for Website Fingerprinting on Defended Tor Traffic
comment: 5 pages, 1 figure. Conference paper submitted to the 11th International Conference on Computer and Information Processing Technology (ISCIPT 2026)
summary: Website fingerprinting (WF) attacks let a passive adversary infer which site a Tor user visits from the encrypted cell sequence. On undefended traffic, hand-crafted-feature attacks are already near-ceiling, so deep learning offers only a marginal advantage there. We show that the decisive regime is defended traffic: against the FRONT padding defense, which injects dummy cells that corrupt the volume and count features feature attacks rely on, a compact 95,103-parameter 1-D convolutional network trained on the raw cell-direction sequence, on CPU only, stays robust while three implemented direction-only feature baselines degrade. On the closed-world WFlib FRONT set (95 sites), our model reaches 54.2% top-1 accuracy versus 38.5% for the strongest implemented feature baseline (k-FP-style RF), a gain of 15.7 percentage points (3 seeds; seed-0 paired-bootstrap 95% CI [+14.5, +17.0] pp on per-trace correctness, excluding zero). On undefended traffic the CNN reaches 94.1% versus 92.3% for k-FP-style RF. A controlled order-ablation permutes only nonzero traffic cells within each trace, preserving direction counts, retained length, and trailing zero-padding positions while destroying traffic order. This collapses the CNN below every feature baseline (from 54.2% to 7.6%, a 46.6 pp drop), showing that the model depends strongly on order-derived information under FRONT.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that a 95,103-parameter CPU-trainable 1-D CNN on raw cell-direction sequences reaches 54.2% accuracy on FRONT-defended Tor traffic (15.7 pp over k-FP RF), and collapses to 7.6% when cell order is permuted.
AI.motivation: While hand-crafted feature attacks are near-ceiling on undefended Tor traffic, padding defenses like FRONT corrupt volume and count features, degrading feature-based website fingerprinting.
AI.method: The authors train a compact 95,103-parameter 1-D CNN on CPU using raw cell-direction sequences, compare against three direction-only feature baselines on WFlib FRONT (95 sites), and run a controlled order-permutation ablation on nonzero cells.
AI.result: On WFlib FRONT, the CNN achieves 54.2% top-1 accuracy versus 38.5% for k-FP-style RF (+15.7 pp; 95% CI [+14.5, +17.0] pp) and 94.1% versus 92.3% on undefended traffic; permuting nonzero cell order collapses CNN accuracy from 54.2% to 7.6% (-46.6 pp).
AI.conclusion: Local cell-direction order is the decisive signal exploited by compact sequence models under FRONT padding, whereas count-based features fail.

title: Conversing with a Conversational Agent: A Real Conversation, Not a Simulated One
summary: The claim that interactions with artificial conversational agents merely simulate human conversation rests on a philosophical distinction between reproducing the observable features of an activity and actually performing it. Although this distinction is appropriate for certain physical phenomena, its application to linguistic and symbolic activities is far less straightforward. This article argues that conversations with large language model (LLM)-based agents are genuine conversational activities rather than mere simulations, without thereby attributing consciousness, subjective understanding, or human intentionality to artificial systems. Drawing on the distinction between subjective and objective simulation, the article first examines the limitations of defining conversation exclusively through the intrinsic properties of its participants. It then develops a relational and semiotic account of conversational activity, informed by linguistic pragmatics, Lacan's Conversing with a Conversational Agent theory of the mirror, Baudrillard's concept of the simulacrum, Simondon's philosophy of individuation, and Peirce's semiotics. These perspectives make it possible to distinguish the reality of conversational interaction from the appearance of artificial subjectivity and from the epistemic validity of the meanings produced. The argument culminates in the concept of Hybrid Semiotic Fabrication, which characterizes meaning-making as a distributed process involving human participants, artificial intelligence, corpora, and technical arrangements. Recognizing the reality of human-AI conversation therefore entails neither anthropomorphizing artificial agents nor granting their outputs epistemic authority. Rather, it requires a more precise account of the relational, semiotic, and normative conditions under which conversational meaning is produced and justified.

AI.tldr: This philosophical article argues that human interactions with LLM-based conversational agents are genuine conversational activities rather than mere simulations, introducing the concept of Hybrid Semiotic Fabrication.
AI.motivation: The common claim that human-AI dialogue merely simulates conversation relies on a distinction between reproducing observable features and performing an activity, which is problematic for linguistic and symbolic practices.
AI.method: Drawing on linguistic pragmatics, Lacan, Baudrillard, Simondon, and Peirce's semiotics, the author critiques participant-intrinsic definitions of conversation and develops a relational, semiotic account of distributed meaning-making.
AI.result: The analysis distinguishes the reality of conversational interaction from artificial subjectivity and epistemic validity, framing meaning-making as Hybrid Semiotic Fabrication across humans, AI, corpora, and technical arrangements.
AI.conclusion: Recognizing human-AI conversation as real does not anthropomorphize AI or grant it epistemic authority, but clarifies the relational and normative conditions of meaning production.

title: Accelerate Bench: Evaluating Agents for Application-Level Program Optimization
comment: 49 pages, 8 figures. Work by Bowen Liu was done during an internship at Tencent Hy Team. Yuhan Li is Project Lead; Nuo Chen is corresponding author (chennuo26@gmail.com). Project page: this https URL
summary: Application optimization requires coding agents to discover useful changes and coordinate them across a complete program while preserving the required computation. We introduce Accelerate Bench, a benchmark of 32 CPU optimization tasks adapted from scientific applications and supercomputing competitions. Each task provides a working program and specifies the workload, correctness requirements, timing boundaries, and permitted edits, leaving agents to choose where and how to optimize. Public testing supports iterative development, and a separate verifier scores the final submission. On benchmark version 1.1, we evaluate 16 coding agents, each pairing a model with a harness. Their Score@1 ranges from 25.5% to 67.4%. Most of their programs are correct, and the size of the speedup separates them: the two leading agents are at least 2x faster on 22 or more of the 32 tasks, while the other fourteen reach 2x on 8 to 17 and leave 125 of their 412 correct outcomes below 1.25x. Controlled replays show why coordination across an application matters: identical source code runs between 0.29x and 2.12x depending only on build and runtime settings, and one code change is worth 1.01x or 6.4x depending on another. Accelerate Bench pairs executable workloads with agents' programs and trajectories to evaluate both their gains and the process behind them.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Accelerate Bench, a benchmark of 32 CPU program optimization tasks, evaluating 16 coding agents (Score@1 from 25.5% to 67.4%) and showing that build settings and cross-change interactions strongly govern speedups.
AI.motivation: Application-level program optimization requires coding agents to discover and coordinate multiple changes across an entire program while preserving correctness.
AI.method: Accelerate Bench provides 32 scientific and supercomputing CPU optimization tasks with workloads, correctness checks, timing boundaries, and permitted edits, evaluated via a separate verifier on benchmark v1.1.
AI.result: Across 16 coding agents, Score@1 ranges from 25.5% to 67.4%; the top two agents achieve >=2x speedup on 22+ of 32 tasks, while the other 14 reach 2x on 8-17 tasks; controlled replays show identical code varies from 0.29x to 2.12x by build/runtime settings, and one change can yield 1.01x or 6.4x depending on another.
AI.conclusion: Pairing executable workloads with agent trajectories in Accelerate Bench reveals that cross-application coordination separates top optimization agents from the rest.

title: Which AI Use Cases Deserve a Pilot? A Risk and Value Framework for Funding, Scoping, and Scaling AI
comment: 18 pages. All results use synthetic data. A companion Python package reproduces the tables
summary: A composite score can rank AI use cases while leaving the permitted operating scope and the evidence required for expansion unspecified. We treat the unit of decision as a use case at a proposed scope (authority, human mediation, limits, volume, environment, population) and define three decisions: screen the scope, fund the experiment, and authorize expansion only when residual risk is acceptable and evidence of incremental net value applies at that scope. A risk track (R1-R4) is implemented as an explicit decision table with vetoes and documented precedence, and a value track follows four evidence stages with each transition needing its own evidence. Funding uses expected value of perfect information as an upper bound and the value of sample information for the specific experiment. A quantified expected-loss check, required where policy says so, computes the containment an expansion needs and credits a control only on evidence measured at the proposed scope; in a synthetic scenario the highest-value control design fails that test while a smaller scope passes. A reproducible Python package with 279 passing tests demonstrates the framework on synthetic refund, reconciliation and knowledge-assistant use cases, including a synthetic matched-scope fixture and a transferability stress test (value evidence is simulated, not realized), and compares it with a public AWS sample. Thresholds and appetite are prototype policy requiring field validation.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a risk-and-value decision framework for screening, funding, and scaling AI use cases at a specified operating scope, demonstrated via a Python package with 279 passing tests on synthetic cases.
AI.motivation: Composite scores can rank AI use cases without specifying the permitted operating scope or the evidence required to justify expansion.
AI.method: The framework treats a use case at a proposed scope as the decision unit, combining an R1-R4 risk decision table with vetoes, a four-stage value track using EVPI and value of sample information, and a quantified expected-loss check.
AI.result: A reproducible Python package with 279 passing tests demonstrates the framework on synthetic refund, reconciliation, and knowledge-assistant cases (plus an AWS sample comparison), showing that a high-value control design can fail the expected-loss test at a large scope while passing at a smaller scope.
AI.conclusion: Scoping AI decisions with explicit risk vetoes and scope-matched value evidence prevents premature scaling, though prototype thresholds require field validation.

title: Multi-LLM Agentic AI at the Edge: Joint Agent Scheduling and Resource Allocation
summary: In this paper, an edge-enabled multi-large language model (LLM) agentic AI architecture is proposed, where one supervisor AI agent and multiple worker AI agents cooperatively execute users' requests at the edge. The supervisor AI agent decouples the user request into a series of sub-tasks and dynamically dispatches them to LLM-equipped worker AI agents via two agentic workflows, i.e., parallel and serial workflows, with a two-level retry mechanism to enhance execution reliability. To prolong the service duration of worker AI agents, the energy minimization problems are formulated by jointly considering AI agent selection and resource allocation, subject to task execution latency and quality of service (QoS) constraints. A resource allocation scheme based on alternating optimization (AO) is proposed. Specifically, for the parallel workflow, the scheme decouples the original problem into bandwidth allocation, retrieval selection and AI agent selection sub-problems, which are iteratively solved by the proposed successive convex approximation (SCA), Lagrangian relaxation (LR), and Gale-Shapley (GS) or LLM-based algorithms, respectively. For the serial workflow, the problem is similarly decoupled into service time allocation, retrieval selection and AI agent selection sub-problems; the optimal service time allocation is obtained via Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions, while the latter two sub-problems are addressed by extending the proposed algorithms to the serial scenario. Simulation results show that the proposed resource allocation scheme can reduce system energy consumption compared with other benchmarks, while experiments on a multi-LLM agentic AI system based on Qwen and Llama demonstrate improved task execution success rates.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an edge-enabled multi-LLM agentic AI architecture with parallel and serial workflows, using alternating optimization to jointly schedule agents and allocate resources, reducing energy consumption and improving task success.
AI.motivation: Deploying cooperative multi-LLM agents at the edge requires minimizing worker agent energy consumption while meeting task latency and QoS constraints across sequential and parallel workflows.
AI.method: A supervisor agent decomposes requests into sub-tasks dispatched to LLM worker agents with a two-level retry mechanism; an alternating optimization scheme decouples bandwidth/service-time allocation, retrieval selection, and agent selection using SCA, Lagrangian relaxation, KKT conditions, and Gale-Shapley/LLM algorithms.
AI.result: Simulations show reduced system energy consumption compared to benchmarks, and experiments on a Qwen- and Llama-based multi-LLM system demonstrate improved task execution success rates.
AI.conclusion: Joint agent scheduling and resource allocation enables energy-efficient, reliable multi-LLM agentic execution at the edge.

title: Advancing Cognitive Pairwise Comparisons for Human-Centric Artificial Intelligence and Data Science: A Human-in-the-Loop Framework
comment: 33 pages, 19 tables, 8 figures; interactive web demos available at this https URL ; source code and datasets at this https URL ; archived at this https URL ; earlier preprint version available at SSRN 4048692 (this http URL or this https URL)
summary: Human-centric artificial intelligence and data science (HCAD) systems increasingly involve human-in-the-loop (HITL) interventions to overcome the limitations of fully automated machine learning algorithms, such as automation bias and the inability to incorporate tacit domain knowledge, and continuously improve predictive performance. Data transformations, feature selection, feature weighting, and model selection usually require laborious human involvement across iterations of artificial intelligence and data science (AI&DS) pipelines, making development a challenging and time-consuming process. The Cognitive Pairwise Comparison (CPC) framework is proposed as a human-centric methodology to elicit preferences and priorities in a structured format. To establish essential facets of human-centricity, this research advances the CPC methodology so that user preference elicitation can be systematically quantified in these challenging AI&DS tasks. To demonstrate the usability and validity of these facets, this study presents several applications within movie recommender systems using the MovieLens dataset. It exemplifies how the extended CPC framework can facilitate interactions between human judgments and data across supervised learning, dimensionality reduction, and unsupervised learning algorithms.

AI.tldr: This paper extends the Cognitive Pairwise Comparison (CPC) human-in-the-loop framework to quantify user preference elicitation across supervised learning, dimensionality reduction, and unsupervised learning in MovieLens recommender systems.
AI.motivation: Fully automated machine learning pipelines suffer from automation bias and cannot easily incorporate tacit domain knowledge, while manual feature and model iteration is laborious.
AI.method: The authors advance the CPC methodology to systematically structure and quantify human-in-the-loop preference elicitation for data transformations, feature selection/weighting, and model selection.
AI.result: Applications on the MovieLens dataset demonstrate how the extended CPC framework facilitates human-data interaction across supervised learning, dimensionality reduction, and unsupervised learning tasks.
AI.conclusion: Structured cognitive pairwise comparisons provide a practical human-centric mechanism for integrating domain preferences into AI and data science pipelines.

title: Razavi-Bench: Tracking AI Progress in Analog Circuit Reasoning
comment: 6 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables. Project page: this https URL ; code and data: this https URL
summary: We propose Razavi-Bench, a benchmark built from the 50 questions in Razavi's two Analog Design Experiments With AI articles and graded by GPT-6 Luna against reference answers and rubrics, and use it to track how fast AI models improve at analog circuit analysis. Across 73 multimodal large language models released between May 2024 and November 2026, the top score rose from 28.83% to 98.33% in 30 months, mostly before the reference answers were published. The leading models now answer almost every textbook question correctly; the hardest questions show a circuit that resembles a textbook one but works differently, or ask about behavior the obvious analysis misses. Within two and a half years, a set of questions that exposed the limits of AI models has become one they answer almost perfectly.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Razavi-Bench, a 50-question analog circuit reasoning benchmark, showing that top multimodal LLM scores rose from 28.83% to 98.33% across 73 models released between May 2024 and November 2026.
AI.motivation: Tracking how rapidly AI models improve on specialized engineering reasoning requires a consistent benchmark of challenging analog circuit analysis problems.
AI.method: Razavi-Bench compiles 50 questions from Razavi's two Analog Design Experiments With AI articles and grades 73 multimodal LLMs (released May 2024 to November 2026) using GPT-6 Luna against reference answers and rubrics.
AI.result: Over 30 months, the top model score increased from 28.83% to 98.33% (mostly before reference answers were published), with leading models answering nearly all textbook questions correctly and only failing on deceptive circuits that deviate from standard textbook operation.
AI.conclusion: Within two and a half years, multimodal LLMs progressed from struggling on analog circuit analysis to near-perfect performance on Razavi-Bench.

title: Hilbert States for Decision-Making under Partial Observability
summary: Decision-making under partial observability can be fundamentally limited by information, even with known dynamics: distinct physical states can induce the same observation history while favoring different actions. We study three questions: when is full-state optimality unattainable, what information exactly preserves the best observation-based decision, and how does finite-data learning affect reliability? First, we characterize decision ambiguity through conditional action preferences. We give a zero-regret criterion, a positive lower bound for conflicting uniquely optimal actions on positive-probability regions with uniformly positive cost gaps, and an exact binary-action regret formula. This also shows why physical-state ambiguity alone need not cause decision loss. Second, for two actions and squared terminal-goal costs in the plane, we derive an exact inner-product representation of conditional expected cost differences using three conditional moment contrasts and a goal-dependent feature. This Hilbert state preserves observation-optimal actions without hidden-state reconstruction. Under nondegenerate history and goal variation, its three-dimensional form is minimal among exact bilinear cost-contrast representations. Third, we relate finite-data state errors to excess decision regret via goal-projected errors, action margins, and goal geometry. Physics-based simulations verify information-limited regret, exact action preservation, and the role of second moments. Held-out real-SAR experiments demonstrate feasible goal-conditioned decisions from masked images, while finite-data evaluations reveal goal-dependent reliability. Together, these results separate irreducible information loss, exact representation sufficiency, and learning-induced excess regret.

AI.tldr: This paper characterizes information-limited decision regret under partial observability, derives a minimal 3D Hilbert state that preserves observation-optimal actions for planar goal-conditioned tasks, and links finite-data errors to excess regret.
AI.motivation: Under partial observability, distinct physical states can produce identical observation histories while favoring different actions, making it unclear when full-state optimality is unattainable and what minimal state suffices for optimal decisions.
AI.method: The authors establish a zero-regret criterion and binary-action regret formula, derive an exact 3D inner-product (Hilbert state) representation using three conditional moment contrasts for two-action planar terminal-goal costs, and bound finite-data excess regret via goal geometry.
AI.result: Physics-based simulations verify information-limited regret, exact action preservation, and the role of second moments, while held-out real-SAR experiments demonstrate feasible goal-conditioned decisions from masked images.
AI.conclusion: The Hilbert state framework separates irreducible information loss, exact representation sufficiency, and finite-data excess regret without requiring hidden-state reconstruction.

title: GRACE: Parallel Best-of-N Multi-Agent Analysis of Closed-Form Questions over Dataframes with Guardrail Selection and Adaptive Retry
comment: Accepted at the 5th Italian Conference on Big Data and Data Science (ITADATA 2026). To appear in CEUR Workshop Proceedings
summary: LLM agents answer closed-form questions over a tabular dataframe by writing and executing Python, almost always as a single rollout: one interpretation, one script, one result, accepted without comparison. The few pipelines that produce several candidates reconcile them by answer-agreement voting, which needs a single comparable scalar and always returns one, even when every candidate is wrong. We present GRACE (Generative, Ranked, Adaptive Code Ensemble), a production-oriented pipeline that instead runs parallel best-of-N selection specialised to dataframe code. N agents run concurrently under a strict, machine-checkable output contract, diversified by persona hints, per-retry rotation, and a two-regime temperature schedule. Rather than vote, GRACE judges the executed artefacts: a pairwise tournament pre-filters the pool and a domain-specialised guardrail either selects the best candidate or, when none is defensible, rejects the whole pool and abstains with a diagnosis (an option voting structurally lacks), which in turn drives an adaptive retry with per-agent feedback. On InfiAgent-DABench (DAEval, M = 246), using Qwen3.6-35B-A3B as the backbone, GRACE raises answer match from 39% for a single-rollout baseline to 71% (+32 pp, 1.8x), recovering 53% of previously wrong answers. On the same DAEval task, the smaller dense Qwen3.5-9B lifts answer match from 38% to 63% (+25 pp, 1.7x). A controlled 3 x 3 study that sweeps the number of parallel agents against the retry budget finds, on the 35B backbone, the two levers largely substitutable: once either one is generous, the other adds little, identifying a cheap operating point for deployment. The same directional pattern replicates on the independent DataBench benchmark, again on the Qwen3.6-35B-A3B backbone, where answer match rises by 15 percentage points (from 70% to 85%) across 400 sampled questions.

AI.tldr: GRACE is a parallel best-of-N multi-agent pipeline for closed-form dataframe questions that replaces scalar voting with pairwise tournament pre-filtering, domain-specialized guardrail selection or abstention, and adaptive retry with per-agent feedback.
AI.motivation: Single-rollout LLM agents accept one script without comparison, while answer-agreement voting requires a single comparable scalar and always returns an answer even when all candidates are wrong.
AI.method: GRACE runs N concurrent agents under a machine-checkable output contract diversified by persona hints, per-retry rotation, and a two-regime temperature schedule, then uses a pairwise tournament and a guardrail to select the best executed artifact or abstain with a diagnosis that guides adaptive retries.
AI.result: On InfiAgent-DABench (DAEval, M=246), GRACE lifts answer match from 39% to 71% with Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and from 38% to 63% with Qwen3.5-9B, and on 400 sampled DataBench questions it improves Qwen3.6-35B-A3B from 70% to 85%.
AI.conclusion: Judging executed artifacts with abstention-capable guardrails and adaptive retries substantially outperforms single-rollout baselines and reveals that parallel agents and retry budgets are largely substitutable at deployment.

title: Hivemind: A Federated Protocol for AI-Mediated Tacit Knowledge Sharing in Organisations
summary: This paper presents Hivemind, a federated protocol that enables AI agents to exchange tacit knowledge on behalf of their users, asynchronously and without requiring any direct human interaction. Individual AI memory systems capture the decisions, reasoning, and contextual knowledge that surface during AI-assisted work. Hivemind creates the shared space in which this captured knowledge can flow between individuals across team and departmental boundaries, addressing a structural gap that neither centralised knowledge repositories nor existing AI tooling closes, even where partial solutions such as expert-finding systems exist. The paper evaluates centralised versus decentralised design approaches, proposes a federated architecture grounded in Nonaka and Takeuchi's (1995) Socialisation, Externalisation, Combination and Internalisation (SECI) model, and demonstrates a proof-of-concept implementation using Design Science Research (DSR) methodology. Measuring the enterprise benefit of federated tacit expertise sharing remains an open task for future work.

AI.tldr: Hivemind is a federated protocol that allows AI agents to asynchronously exchange tacit knowledge captured in individual AI memory systems across organizational boundaries without direct human interaction.
AI.motivation: Centralized knowledge repositories and existing AI tooling fail to transfer the decisions, reasoning, and contextual knowledge that surface during individual AI-assisted work across teams and departments.
AI.method: The paper evaluates centralized versus decentralized designs, proposes a federated architecture grounded in Nonaka and Takeuchi's SECI model, and builds a proof-of-concept using Design Science Research methodology.
AI.result: The authors demonstrate a working proof-of-concept implementation of the federated protocol, while noting that measuring the enterprise benefit of federated tacit expertise sharing remains open for future work.
AI.conclusion: Hivemind provides an architectural blueprint for turning individual AI memory systems into a shared organizational knowledge layer.

title: K2-Horizon: A Frontier Fleet of Open Source Language Models
summary: We present K2-Horizon, a fleet of six fully open language models, from a 0.9B dense model to a 375B-A23B MoE, built for general-purpose reasoning and agentic work across math and science, software engineering, deep research, office automation, and beyond. The models lead or are competitive with strong open models of their size on agentic and coding benchmarks. On the modeling side, to strengthen reasoning, we introduce Mixture-of-Value Attention (MoVA), applying MoE to attention value projections, and softplus attention gating, a more flexible, theoretically motivated gate. Our 36B-A4B model uses both and nearly matches a 32B dense model trained on the same data, with one-seventh the active parameters. We also introduce Uno, lossless diffusion adapters that speed up decoding by up to 2.2x without a separate draft model. Our release follows the LLM360 definition of open source for transparency and reproducibility: the full development history, including intermediate checkpoints from every training stage, pre-training data, training logs, and all training, evaluation, and infrastructure code, notably our production-scale xLLM framework for dense and MoE training and the RL360 reinforcement-learning stack. Beyond the data itself, we release and document in detail every pipeline that built it, the part of model development that open releases most rarely disclose. These pipelines produced roughly 10T synthetic pre-training tokens, showing that synthetic data can be a major ingredient of pre-training at scale. Four of the models share one 22T-token pre-training corpus and recipe, revealing consistent scaling behavior and enabling controlled studies of scale and sparsity. All artifacts are available at this https URL

AI.tldr: K2-Horizon is a fleet of six fully open-source language models from 0.9B dense to 375B-A23B MoE that introduces Mixture-of-Value Attention, softplus attention gating, and Uno diffusion adapters for fast, transparent reasoning and agentic work.
AI.motivation: Open model releases rarely disclose the data-generation pipelines and full training history needed for transparency, reproducibility, and controlled scaling studies.
AI.method: The models combine Mixture-of-Value Attention, softplus attention gating, and Uno lossless diffusion adapters, trained with the xLLM and RL360 frameworks on a 22T-token corpus that includes roughly 10T synthetic tokens, with all checkpoints, logs, and data pipelines released.
AI.result: The 36B-A4B model nearly matches a 32B dense model trained on the same data with one-seventh the active parameters, Uno speeds up decoding by up to 2.2x without a draft model, and the fleet leads or matches strong open models on agentic and coding benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: K2-Horizon demonstrates that full-stack open-source releases, including synthetic data pipelines and intermediate checkpoints, can achieve frontier agentic performance and consistent scaling behavior.

title: SWE-OPD: On-Policy Distillation for Agentic Coding
summary: In this work, we study on-policy distillation (OPD) for transferring agentic coding capabilities from a large teacher model to a smaller student model. Prior work has focused primarily on reasoning and short-horizon agentic tasks. We present SWE-OPD, a minimal OPD study for software engineering, where the student interacts with executable repositories and the teacher supervises the prefixes visited by the student. Across three teacher--student pairs, two training sources, and three SWE benchmarks, we find that on-policy supervision transfers coding capability: supervision from Qwen3.6-27B increases the SWE-bench Pro resolve rate of Qwen3.5-9B from 35.9% to 39.4%. Refreshing trajectories is not strictly required either, as an offline variant with cached teacher scores still improves over the student baselines while cutting end-to-end GPU-hours by 59.4%--72.6% and halving peak GPU allocation, at benchmark-dependent accuracy. Furthermore, we extend the offline variant to corss-tokenizer scenarios: distilling GLM-4.5-Air from DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 raises its SWE-bench Pro and Multilingual resolve rate from 35.8% to 39.7% and from 41.8% to 46.2%, around 4% and 4.6% improvement, respectively. We also find that a decreasing loss, however, does not necessarily indicate improved agent performance: under top-$K$ reverse-KL loss, one student exhibits severe repetition despite a decreasing loss. We identify a support-mass gradient term as a potential mechanism underlying this failure.

AI.tldr: SWE-OPD applies on-policy distillation and an offline cached-score variant to transfer agentic coding capabilities from large teachers to smaller students, including across different tokenizers.
AI.motivation: Prior on-policy distillation work focused on reasoning and short-horizon tasks rather than long-horizon software engineering where agents interact with executable repositories.
AI.method: The student interacts with executable repositories while the teacher supervises visited prefixes; an offline variant reuses cached teacher scores to avoid trajectory refreshes and extends to cross-tokenizer distillation.
AI.result: On-policy supervision from Qwen3.6-27B raises Qwen3.5-9B's SWE-bench Pro resolve rate from 35.9% to 39.4%, the offline variant cuts GPU-hours by 59.4% to 72.6% and halves peak GPU allocation, and cross-tokenizer distillation from DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 lifts GLM-4.5-Air from 35.8% to 39.7% on SWE-bench Pro and 41.8% to 46.2% on Multilingual.
AI.conclusion: On-policy and cached-score distillation effectively transfer agentic coding skills, though decreasing top-K reverse-KL loss can still induce repetition via a support-mass gradient term.

title: System 1 agents: a method for local, reliable and fast agentic AI
comment: 18 pages, 5 figures, 9 tables. Code and data: this https URL
summary: Agentic artificial intelligence could automate analyses of sensitive clinical data, but current agents depend on large language models (LLMs). Cloud LLMs expose patient data. Local LLMs hallucinate, and an invented value in a tool call propagates through every later step. Here we present a method to build System 1 agents: local agents that call tools without generating text. A deterministic compiler turns each tool's schema and the request into multiple-choice questions whose options come from the request and the schema, then a one-pass decision model answers them. On 1,952 requests to 157 biomedical tools, the best System 1 agent chose the right tool, or correctly declined, for 97.0% of requests, significantly ahead of all 18 local LLM-agent settings (best 95.2%). The System 1 agent filled 97.0% of 6,056 stated argument values. No System 1 call contained invented content, against 5.5-19.7% of LLM calls. The System 1 Agents framework is freely available as open-source software at this https URL.

AI.tldr: System 1 agents are local, non-generative tool-calling agents that compile tool schemas and user requests into multiple-choice questions answered in one pass, eliminating hallucinated arguments.
AI.motivation: Cloud LLMs expose sensitive clinical data, while local LLMs hallucinate invented values in tool calls that propagate through downstream steps.
AI.method: A deterministic compiler converts each tool's schema and the request into multiple-choice questions whose options come strictly from the request and schema, and a one-pass decision model selects the answers without generating free text.
AI.result: Across 1,952 requests to 157 biomedical tools, the best System 1 agent achieved 97.0% tool-selection accuracy (beating all 18 local LLM-agent settings, best 95.2%), filled 97.0% of 6,056 stated argument values, and produced zero invented content compared to 5.5% to 19.7% for LLM calls.
AI.conclusion: Framing tool calling as deterministic multiple-choice selection enables fast, private, and hallucination-free local clinical agents.

title: Sage S2.1 Flash Technical Report
summary: We introduce Sage S1.5 Flash, a 320-billion-parameter general-purpose mixture-of-experts model designed to reason over scientific evidence and act in interactive environments. Sage Sci-Perception uses dedicated encoders for molecular graphs and biological sequences and represents spectra as ordered patches of measurements. Modality-specific projectors map these representations into the input space of a shared backbone, which processes them alongside text and images. To develop the model's agent capabilities, we construct verifiable environments for tool use, search, and coding, as well as specialized workflows involving machine learning experiments and scientific software. Task completion is checked against execution results, changes in environment state, or submitted artifacts. We evaluate Sage S1.5 Flash on 33 benchmarks across seven domains. In the primary comparison against five baselines, it ranks first on OfficeQA Pro (72.2), MLE-bench Lite (90.3 HumanRank), Harvey LAB, and SpreadsheetBench~2, and second on OSWorld-Verified (85.2), WebArena-Verified (67.6), and DeepResearch Bench~II (54.2). These results show particular strengths in using documentary evidence, producing verifiable workbooks, and carrying out machine learning tasks, alongside competitive performance in desktop and browser workflows that require the model to act on visual feedback.

AI.tldr: Sage S2.1 Flash (introduced as Sage S1.5 Flash in the abstract) is a 320B-parameter MoE model with modality-specific scientific encoders trained in verifiable interactive environments for scientific reasoning and agentic workflows.
AI.motivation: General-purpose models need both specialized scientific perception for molecules, sequences, and spectra and verifiable interactive training to act reliably in scientific and office software environments.
AI.method: Sage Sci-Perception uses dedicated encoders for molecular graphs, biological sequences, and ordered spectral patches mapped into a shared MoE backbone, trained in verifiable environments for tool use, search, coding, and ML workflows checked against execution results.
AI.result: Across 33 benchmarks, it ranks first on OfficeQA Pro (72.2), MLE-bench Lite (90.3 HumanRank), Harvey LAB, and SpreadsheetBench 2, and second on OSWorld-Verified (85.2), WebArena-Verified (67.6), and DeepResearch Bench II (54.2).
AI.conclusion: Combining domain-specific scientific encoders with execution-verified agentic environments yields strong performance across documentary reasoning, scientific workflows, and GUI/browser tasks.

title: Counting What Matters: Reducing Redundant Object Detections in Overlapping UAV Mapping Imagery for Disaster Response
comment: 9 pages, 6 figure, IEEE International Symposium on Safety, Security, and Rescue Robotics, SSRR 2026, Incheon, Korea, November 02-04, 2026
summary: UAV mapping flights enable rapid aerial reconnaissance of large-scale incident sites in civil protection. However, the image overlap required for orthophoto generation causes every physical object to be detected multiple times across images, while dynamic objects may be omitted from or duplicated in the resulting orthomosaic. Analysis based on the orthophoto alone is therefore structurally insufficient. We address this by detecting objects on the individual images and merging redundant detections across them. This task lies between multi-object tracking and re-identification, as mapping flights form temporally ordered but sparsely sampled sequences with object reappearances across flight strips. We fine-tune YOLO detectors on a new domain-specific nadir dataset from real civil protection operations, roughly doubling mAP50 over the previous system, and propose re-identification approaches based on 3D positions from sparse reconstruction, DINOv3 appearance embeddings, and their combination via constrained greedy clustering. %On four manually annotated real-world mapping flights, the combined weighted multi-pass approach achieves the best trade-off between association accuracy and count error. On four manually annotated real-world mapping flights, an association-only evaluation using ground-truth detections shows that the combined weighted multi-pass approach provides the best trade-off between association quality and count error. It is integrated into the open-source web application ARGUS and visualized as verifiable, correctable object groups for first responders. this https URL

AI.tldr: This paper reduces duplicate object detections in overlapping UAV disaster-response imagery by fine-tuning YOLO on nadir civil-protection data and clustering detections using 3D sparse reconstruction and DINOv3 embeddings.
AI.motivation: Overlapping UAV mapping images cause physical objects to be detected multiple times, while orthophotos omit or duplicate dynamic objects.
AI.method: The authors fine-tune YOLO detectors on a domain-specific nadir dataset and merge redundant detections across images via constrained greedy clustering over 3D positions from sparse reconstruction and DINOv3 appearance embeddings, integrated into the open-source ARGUS web app.
AI.result: Fine-tuning roughly doubles mAP50 over the previous system, and on four manually annotated real-world mapping flights using ground-truth detections, the combined weighted multi-pass clustering achieves the best trade-off between association accuracy and count error.
AI.conclusion: Combining geometric 3D reconstruction with DINOv3 appearance features enables accurate, verifiable object counting for first responders in overlapping UAV imagery.

title: Conflict-Aware Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation in Aligned Action Spaces for Cross-Game Generalization
summary: Zero-shot cross-game generalization aims to consolidate accessible source-game experts into a single vision-language model (VLM) that controls unseen games from raw pixels without target-game parameter updates. While multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) mitigates offline exposure bias and single-game reinforcement learning (RL) overfitting, scaling it to autoregressive VLMs faces two bottlenecks. First, token-to-action misalignment from subword length bias distorts discrete action probabilities and uncertainty margins. Second, multi-teacher policy conflict arises as source teachers under incompatible dynamics issue contradictory closed-loop corrections, causing negative transfer. We propose CAMOPD (Conflict-Aware Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation), a post-training framework that resolves multi-teacher policy conflict within an aligned semantic action space. CAMOPD first uses complete-action alignment to normalize command completion likelihoods over each game's legal action set, forming a calibrated categorical policy that provides reliable uncertainty margins for selective on-policy retention and visual specialist probes that can be evaluated across source games. To resolve policy conflict without target-game data, conflict-aware multi-teacher consolidation cross-evaluates these specialists across source games to capture both visual identifiability and inter-teacher compatibility, upweighting compatible teachers while suppressing conflicting corrections. On GameWorld's temporal and directional transfer suites with Qwen3.5-4B, CAMOPD achieves 26/30 (86.7%) and 24/30 (80.0%) Task-1 zero-shot success on unseen GeoDash and Doodle Jump, outperforming prompting, weight-merging, and multi-task baselines.

AI.tldr: CAMOPD is a conflict-aware multi-teacher on-policy distillation framework that aligns token-to-action spaces and suppresses contradictory teacher corrections to enable zero-shot cross-game generalization in VLMs.
AI.motivation: Scaling multi-teacher on-policy distillation to autoregressive VLMs suffers from subword length bias distorting action probabilities and from conflicting corrections issued by teachers trained under incompatible game dynamics.
AI.method: CAMOPD normalizes command completion likelihoods over each game's legal action set for calibrated uncertainty margins and cross-evaluates visual specialist probes across source games to upweight compatible teachers and suppress conflicting ones.
AI.result: With Qwen3.5-4B on GameWorld's transfer suites, CAMOPD reaches 26/30 (86.7%) and 24/30 (80.0%) Task-1 zero-shot success on unseen GeoDash and Doodle Jump, outperforming prompting, weight-merging, and multi-task baselines.
AI.conclusion: Action-space calibration and compatibility-weighted teacher consolidation prevent negative transfer and unlock zero-shot cross-game control from raw pixels.

title: Inference Equivalence and Quotient Coding
summary: Incomplete observations can admit multiple physical interpretations without making every task conclusion ambiguous. Recovering all compatible scenes is often unnecessary, whereas indiscriminate compression may change which claims are justified. We ask which distinctions among observation-compatible interpretation sets must be retained to preserve every valid conclusion of a specified task. We first define inference validity as truth across all physically compatible states and characterize it, under a closedness condition, by distances to physically realizable falsifying measurements. For a finite semantic claim family ordered by specificity, the Exact Inference Frontier forms the unique minimal antichain generating all valid claims. We then define inference equivalence between compatibility sets and construct a canonical quotient code from their frontiers. Among deterministic codes admitting exact inference decoding, it induces the coarsest partition, minimizing the number of distinguishable code values rather than storage or computation. Finally, we characterize inference errors from learned compatibility sets, derive conditions for exact inference preservation despite set errors, and evaluate an asymmetric learning surrogate under distribution shifts. On a registered finite bank, 145 compatibility sets yield 31 quotient codes with unchanged valid-claim sets. Across geometry, mechanism, and joint shifts, learned estimates exhibit different accuracy-specificity trade-offs. On 1,962 official HRSID test images, 1,913 distinct candidate sets induce only 36 seven-claim inference signatures, while a visual 3-NN baseline achieves 87.31% precision on issued claims.

AI.tldr: This paper formalizes inference equivalence for incomplete observations and constructs a canonical quotient code from Exact Inference Frontiers that minimally preserves all valid task claims.
AI.motivation: Recovering every physically compatible scene from incomplete observations is often unnecessary, whereas indiscriminate compression can alter which task conclusions are justified.
AI.method: The authors define inference validity via distances to falsifying measurements, characterize valid claims via the minimal antichain Exact Inference Frontier, construct the coarsest deterministic quotient code from frontiers, and analyze learned compatibility sets with an asymmetric learning surrogate.
