AI.result: On a registered finite bank, 145 compatibility sets collapse to 31 quotient codes with unchanged valid-claim sets, and on 1,962 HRSID test images, 1,913 candidate sets induce 36 seven-claim inference signatures while a visual 3-NN baseline achieves 87.31% precision on issued claims.
AI.conclusion: Quotient coding over inference frontiers provides a principled way to compress observations while guaranteeing exact preservation of valid task conclusions.

title: InclusionMed: Benchmarking AI for Inclusive Healthcare
comment: 31 pages, 8 figures, 10 tables. Project website: this https URL
summary: Advancing medical AI for inclusive healthcare requires evaluation across diverse healthcare roles, tasks, and care settings, but benchmark coverage remains uneven. We introduce InclusionMed, an open medical AI evaluation initiative for inclusive healthcare. The InclusionMed Atlas organizes benchmarks across three healthcare roles and three AI capabilities. For the first release, we selected four public benchmarks from 388 candidates through structured audits and independent reproduction. With InclusionMed-DxFiles, our private diagnostic reasoning benchmark, the Atlas contains five benchmarks covering three of its nine role--capability cells. We evaluated frontier large language models on the Atlas and aggregated their results into the InclusionMed Index, with overall scores ranging from 17.5 to 49.1 out of 100. The Index also reports scores by healthcare role and AI capability, showing that a model's rank varied with the role or capability considered. A within-benchmark analysis using task-level tags showed that the ten highest-ranked models in the Index all scored higher on patient communication than on clinical decision-making. Models with similar Index scores also differed substantially in estimated inference cost. These findings highlight the need for evaluation covering more diverse healthcare needs and for context-specific model selection. Through open collaboration and community contributions, InclusionMed seeks to ensure that diverse healthcare needs worldwide shape how medical AI progress is defined and measured.

AI.tldr: InclusionMed is an open medical AI evaluation initiative and Atlas organizing five benchmarks across healthcare roles and AI capabilities, revealing that frontier LLMs vary widely by role and cost.
AI.motivation: Existing medical AI benchmarks have uneven coverage across diverse healthcare roles, tasks, and care settings.
AI.method: The authors audit 388 candidate benchmarks to select four public ones alongside their private InclusionMed-DxFiles diagnostic benchmark, mapping them onto a 3x3 role-capability matrix and aggregating frontier LLM scores into the InclusionMed Index.
AI.result: Frontier LLMs score between 17.5 and 49.1 out of 100 on the InclusionMed Index, with rankings shifting by role and capability; the top ten models all score higher on patient communication than clinical decision-making while differing substantially in estimated inference cost.
AI.conclusion: Evaluating medical AI across diverse roles and capabilities exposes systematic gaps in clinical decision-making and underscores the need for context-specific model selection.

title: How Developer Personality Shapes the Use of AI Coding Assistants
summary: Developers differ in personality traits that shape how they approach software development tasks, yet AI coding assistants either behave uniformly or offer personalization features whose fit with individual developers must be found through trial and error. This is because it remains unclear how personality shapes developers' experiences with AI assistants, and thus which traits personalization should account for. In other words, we provide tools with no underlying theory on what works when and why. We take a first step towards such a theory with a systematic scoping review on how users' personality relates to their perception of LLM-based tools. We identified twelve studies through general search engines, major Software Engineering (SE) venues, AI tooling, and snowballing. They all reported associations between personality and perceptions, particularly perceived usefulness, yet none addressed this in a SE context. Building on these findings, we conducted an exploratory two-wave survey with 29 and 11 developers, collecting first empirical evidence of how developers' personality (measured using the Big Five Model) relates to the perception of AI coding assistants. Higher Extraversion was associated with more positive private-use experiences in both waves, while Agreeableness was associated with negative professional experiences in the first wave and positive ones in the second. These results provide first indications that the personality effects found in the literature extend to developers. Although further studies with bigger samples are needed to build a theory, our work takes the first step towards an empirical grounded theory of developer personality and AI personalization traits.

AI.tldr: A scoping review of 12 studies and an exploratory two-wave developer survey (N=29 and N=11) provide initial empirical evidence linking Big Five personality traits to perceptions of AI coding assistants.
AI.motivation: AI coding assistants behave uniformly or rely on trial-and-error personalization because there is no underlying theory of how developer personality shapes assistant experiences.
AI.method: The authors conduct a systematic scoping review of LLM-tool personality studies and run an exploratory two-wave survey measuring developers' Big Five traits alongside their private and professional experiences with AI coding assistants.
AI.result: All 12 reviewed studies link personality to perceived usefulness outside software engineering; in the developer survey, higher Extraversion associates with more positive private-use experiences across both waves, while Agreeableness shifts from negative to positive associations with professional experiences across waves.
AI.conclusion: Personality effects observed in general LLM tools extend to software developers, laying groundwork for an empirically grounded theory of personalized AI coding assistants.

title: CAE-Bench: Benchmarking AI Agents for Reusable CAE Solver Development
comment: 18 pages, 6 figures, 8 tables. Zhiyu Zhou and Tianyou Liu contributed equally
summary: We developed CAE-Bench, a benchmark to evaluate AI agents on Computer-Aided Engineering (CAE) solver development. A CAE solver is more than a PDE solver; it must be able to generalize across various inputs, such as different boundary conditions, geometries, and material properties. CAE-Bench evaluates the generalizability of AI-developed CAE solvers by providing the same task, such as a heat transfer problem, multiple cases, with each case specifying an input. The AI agent develops a solver for a fixed task using only a few public cases, and the resulting solver is then tested on held-out cases, i.e., cases it has never seen before. We evaluate 12 models across a range of reasoning settings on 80 computational tasks. Our experiments show that even if a solver developed by an AI agent performs well on the public cases, it may even get 0 score on held-out cases. For tasks such as fluid dynamics problems, even the solver developed by GPT-6 Astra performs poorly on held-out cases. A data format and an SDK for task registration are provided, so the researcher can use the benchmark on their own infrastructure. We hope that CAE-Bench will help the community to develop AI agents that can develop reusable CAE solvers that generalize to various inputs.

AI.tldr: CAE-Bench is an 80-task benchmark evaluating whether AI agents can develop reusable Computer-Aided Engineering solvers that generalize from a few public cases to held-out geometries, boundary conditions, and materials.
AI.motivation: A practical CAE solver must generalize across unseen inputs rather than overfitting to a single PDE instance, a capability existing benchmarks do not test.
AI.method: Agents build a solver for each fixed task using only a few public cases and are evaluated on unseen held-out cases; the authors test 12 models across reasoning settings on 80 tasks and release the data format and task-registration SDK.
AI.result: Solvers that perform well on public cases frequently score 0 on held-out cases, and even GPT-6 Astra performs poorly on held-out cases for tasks such as fluid dynamics.
AI.conclusion: CAE-Bench exposes a major generalization gap in AI-generated scientific solvers and provides infrastructure to drive progress toward reusable CAE software.

title: Turing Agent: Agentic Formal Verification for Mathematical Research
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are rapidly advancing mathematical discovery, moving beyond benchmark-level problem solving to tackle frontier research problems. This progress is ushering mathematics into an era of proof abundance, raising a fundamental challenge: how can we ensure the correctness of the ever-growing volume of AI-generated proofs and transform them into trustworthy, machine-verified mathematical knowledge? We introduce Turing Agent, an agent harness designed to orchestrate end-to-end formal verification of research-level mathematics. Its wo-scale architecture integrates theorem formalization and proof formalization agents, empowered by structured proof decomposition, parallel verification, accumulated proof experience, and selective semantic review. Leveraging our collaborations with theoretical computer science (TCS) researchers, we focus our evaluation on TCS, a particularly demanding domain characterized by intricate quantification, complex dependencies, and stringent semantic requirements. Against direct generation and general-purpose coding harnesses, including Codex CLI and Claude Code, Turing Agent achieves approximately 57-62% faithful formalization success on Formal TCS Bench and 83% overall pass@1 on a TCS-focused subset of RLMEval, using GLM-5.3 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro. Notably, Turing Agent, built on DeepSeek, successfully completes the formal verification of three previously unresolved TCS tasks from OpenAI's October 2026 collection. One particularly challenging TCS problem required about a hundred formally verified auxiliary claims. Moreover, by actively exploring and refining the formalization process, Turing Agent can uncover simpler alternative proofs, expose unnecessary dependencies in original proofs, and generate reusable mathematical knowledge as a byproduct of verification.

AI.tldr: Turing Agent is a two-scale agent harness for end-to-end formal verification of research-level mathematics, achieving 57-62% faithful formalization on Formal TCS Bench and verifying three previously unresolved TCS tasks.
AI.motivation: As LLMs generate increasingly abundant mathematical proofs, ensuring their correctness requires transforming them into machine-verified formal proofs, which general-purpose coding harnesses struggle to do for complex research mathematics.
AI.method: Turing Agent pairs theorem formalization and proof formalization agents with structured proof decomposition, parallel verification, accumulated proof experience, and selective semantic review.
AI.result: Using GLM-5.3 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Turing Agent achieves 57-62% faithful formalization on Formal TCS Bench and 83% pass@1 on a TCS subset of RLMEval (beating direct generation, Codex CLI, and Claude Code), and verifies three unresolved TCS tasks from OpenAI's October 2026 collection.
AI.conclusion: Specialized hierarchical formalization harnesses can verify frontier theoretical computer science proofs and uncover simpler alternative proofs and unnecessary dependencies.

title: Share your Screen and Talk to Gemini: How Young Learners Interact with Multimodal GenAI While Solving Scratch Tasks
comment: accepted for: The 21th WiPSCE Conference on Primary and Secondary Computing Education Research (WiPSCE 27)
summary: Children using Scratch to learn programming can struggle with text-heavy, lengthy explanations and hints during debugging. Verbal interactions based on screen sharing or camera data may be an interesting alternative for supporting learners. We therefore explore the quality, use, and perceptions of fifth- and sixth-graders' verbal interactions with a GenAI tutor. The goal is to investigate the quality and use of the multimodal GenAI tutor in the given context. First of all, a pilot study of eight tasks conducted without students helped inform the process of the tutor's classroom evaluation. The classroom study was realized after fifth- and sixth-graders had participated in six Scratch classroom lessons. Then 23 students were introduced to the tutor, worked on the eight tasks with the GenAI tutor, and completed a questionnaire. The analysis of the pilot and classroom study shows that the tutor's responses were intelligible and actionable, and no single turn revealed a complete solution. However, the tutor missed existing errors in 61.5% of 603 error-related classroom turns, compared to 15.7% in the pilot study. Children's voice prompts were brief and mostly responded to the tutor. Although a video had explained that responses could be incorrect, 39.1% of the children trusted the tutor's answers to always be correct. These findings have implications for educators and learners using multimodal GenAI tutors, as they need to be aware that an intelligible and human-like voice does not ensure correct support. For developers, our results suggest that screen sharing alone does not ensure responses that match the program state.

AI.tldr: A classroom study with 23 fifth- and sixth-graders using a screen-sharing verbal GenAI tutor for Scratch finds that the tutor missed 61.5% of program errors and 39.1% of students trusted it to always be correct.
AI.motivation: Young learners debugging Scratch struggle with lengthy text hints, making verbal multimodal tutors appealing, yet their real-world classroom reliability and student trust are poorly understood.
AI.method: Following an eight-task pilot without students, 23 fifth- and sixth-graders completed six Scratch lessons and then solved eight tasks using a verbal screen-sharing GenAI tutor, followed by a questionnaire.
AI.result: The tutor gave intelligible, actionable responses without revealing full solutions, but missed existing errors in 61.5% of 603 error-related classroom turns (versus 15.7% in the pilot), and 39.1% of students believed its answers were always correct despite an introductory warning video.
AI.conclusion: Screen sharing alone does not guarantee accurate program-state tracking in multimodal tutors, and human-like voice fluency risks fostering over-trust among young learners.

title: Benchleaking Is Accelerating: Benchmark contamination has worsened sharply in the past month -- from post-training down to pre-training base models
summary: Benchmark contamination is not new, but recent model releases show it in a sharper form. We use the term benchleaking for the case in which a benchmark's own test examples enter training data, so that a score reflects recall rather than capability. This differs from benchmaxxing, which optimizes toward a benchmark without seeing its test set. We document two escalations over the past month. First, in post-training, the traces have become explicit: recent audits show an agent stating hidden test requirements it was never given in 23% of its attempts, where its predecessor did so in none, and continuing to follow them after the task is changed to contradict them (Schaeffer and Räuker, 2026; Lo and Lo, 2026). Second, the problem has reached pre-training. Using few-shot continuation on 20 benchmarks across four public base models, we find that some base models write out other test examples---complete questions, options, and answers---that appear nowhere in their input. For the recently released ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base, 96% of HumanEval problems leak with their reference implementations and 85% of OpenBookQA questions leak with their answers, against 9% and none for DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base. To quantify what a reported score owes to such examples, we define an Anti-Hack score: the benchmark score recomputed with every leaked example marked wrong and the number of examples unchanged. Averaged over the suite, it costs DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base 1.5 points and Hy3-preview-Base 1.3, against 5.0 for MiMo-V2.5-Base and 16.6 for ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base. Open base models are the foundation of much downstream research, so benchleaking now affects more than leaderboard rankings. We call for decontamination reports and contamination-adjusted scores to become standard practice.

AI.tldr: This paper documents accelerating benchmark contamination ("benchleaking") from post-training down to pre-training base models and proposes an Anti-Hack score that penalizes leaked examples.
AI.motivation: Test examples entering training data ("benchleaking") inflate benchmark scores via recall rather than capability, distorting both leaderboard rankings and downstream research built on open base models.
AI.method: The authors audit post-training traces and run few-shot continuations across 20 benchmarks on four public base models, defining an Anti-Hack score that marks every leaked example wrong while keeping the denominator fixed.
AI.result: Post-training audits show an agent stating unprovided hidden test requirements in 23% of attempts; in pre-training, ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base leaks 96% of HumanEval and 85% of OpenBookQA (versus 9% and 0% for DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base), costing ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base 16.6 Anti-Hack points versus 1.5 for DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base.
AI.conclusion: Because benchleaking now compromises open base models, decontamination reports and contamination-adjusted metrics like Anti-Hack should become standard evaluation practice.

title: VisualArtifactSpec 1.0: Evaluating Visual Artifacts under Task Specifications
comment: 24 pages. Project page: this https URL
summary: Visual artifact tasks test agents' ability to translate task specifications and source materials into outputs that meet practical needs. Evaluation across artifact families helps distinguish broadly applicable authoring capabilities from strengths confined to a particular medium. We introduce VisualArtifactSpec 1.0 (VAS), a benchmark of 211 creation and modification tasks spanning presentations, static graphics, animations and videos, and web interfaces. Each task specifies authoring objectives, source materials, constraints, and deliverables. Existing benchmarks provide limited support for systematically evaluating how authoring choices suit different audiences, purposes, and media across artifact families. VAS evaluates two aspects separately: Task Fulfillment verifies explicit requirements and applicable functionality, while Artifact Performance assesses Content, Organization, Visuals, and Delivery. Task-specific rating anchors instantiate shared criteria for the intended audience, purpose, and medium, with judgments grounded in source materials and artifact inspection records. We evaluate nine model-harness configurations on all 211 tasks. Overall scores range from 42.12 to 70.52, with Artifact Performance accounting for 73.4% of the gap between the highest- and lowest-scoring configurations.

AI.tldr: VisualArtifactSpec 1.0 (VAS) is a 211-task benchmark evaluating how well agents translate specifications and source materials into presentations, static graphics, animations/videos, and web interfaces.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks lack systematic evaluation of how authoring choices suit different audiences, purposes, and media across visual artifact families.
AI.method: VAS separates evaluation into Task Fulfillment (explicit requirements and functionality) and Artifact Performance (Content, Organization, Visuals, and Delivery) using task-specific rating anchors grounded in source materials and inspection records.
AI.result: Across nine model-harness configurations on all 211 tasks, overall scores range from 42.12 to 70.52, with Artifact Performance explaining 73.4% of the gap between the top and bottom configurations.
AI.conclusion: Separating requirement fulfillment from audience- and medium-aware artifact quality reveals that design and delivery quality drive most performance differences among visual authoring agents.

title: Shaping AI's Beliefs Before It Generates: Human Sense of Agency in Creative AI
comment: The Proactive Co-Creator (PaCC) can be accessed at this https URL. Accepted at Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026) Creative AI Track
summary: AI systems for creative media generation expand human capabilities yet risk diminishing human agency. A core problem is anchoring, where the user's thinking becomes anchored to a polished, generated artifact, shifting the user's role from active authoring to reactive editing. We propose pre-generation belief controls that can empower creators to inspect, revise, and steer the AI's interpretation before any media is generated, so that the initial anchor is set by the human. We formalize four design principles and instantiate them in the Proactive Co-Creator (PaCC), a system for early-stage conceptual ideation and prototyping that proactively surfaces its assumptions and uncertainty through clarifications, belief graphs, and media attributes, inviting users to shape the AI's beliefs before generating the final outcome. Using PaCC as a design probe in a small-scale, single-arm exploratory user study, we observed that participants reported directionally positive sense of agency and process control relative to their familiar prompt-based AI tools, noting that surfaced assumptions helped them think through details they had overlooked, whereas their feelings about ownership and authorship diverged

AI.tldr: Proactive Co-Creator (PaCC) introduces pre-generation belief controls—clarifications, belief graphs, and media attributes—so creators steer AI assumptions before media generation, improving perceived agency in an exploratory study.
AI.motivation: Polished AI-generated media anchors users' thinking early, shifting their role from active authoring to reactive editing and diminishing human sense of agency.
AI.method: The authors formalize four design principles and instantiate them in PaCC, which surfaces its assumptions and uncertainty before generating final media, evaluated in a small-scale, single-arm exploratory user study.
AI.result: Participants reported directionally positive sense of agency and process control compared to familiar prompt-based tools, noting that surfaced assumptions helped them catch overlooked details, while feelings of ownership and authorship diverged.
AI.conclusion: Exposing and letting users edit AI beliefs prior to generation shifts creative anchoring back to the human, though questions of authorship remain nuanced.

title: Harness Leverage Across Model Size: A Ladder of Five Local Agent Harnesses from 0.75B to 4.7B
summary: A harness turns a model into a system that completes tasks: it builds the prompt, exposes tools and decides when work is done. Harness comparisons hold the model fixed. Model comparisons hold the harness fixed. We vary both: five shipped harnesses, 18 artifact-producing tasks, four locally deployable open-weight models from 0.75B to 4.7B and a 35.5B anchor, with one deterministic checker scoring all 360 ladder cells. The completion-controlling harness, Mingbird, has the highest mean at every size. Of four pre-registered paired contrasts, two survive Holm correction, at 0.75B and 4.7B. Thirteen of sixteen paired intervals exclude zero under the deployment reading, with leads from 0.075 over the strongest rival to 0.819 over the weakest. The completion gate is not the carrier: disabling all six executable checks moves the mean by +0.080, +0.117, +0.003 and -0.004, every interval including zero, and only at 1.9B does disabling it create empty runs. Removing one repeat-blocking rule alone costs 0.411 at 0.75B and leaves eight of eighteen tasks with no artifact. The harness effect is a progress effect: it decides whether a run leaves anything on disk. Of 357 usable cells, 127 leave none of their declared artifacts and 85 of those exit normally, so a scorer that reads exit status credits work that was never written. Whether the effect grows or shrinks with size, four rungs cannot settle: a floor arm produces a rise, a ceiling a decline, and a cross-family rung a peak.

AI.tldr: Evaluating five agent harnesses across four local models (0.75B to 4.7B) and a 35.5B anchor on 18 tasks shows that the completion-controlling harness Mingbird leads at every size by preventing empty runs.
AI.motivation: Standard evaluations vary either the model or the harness in isolation, leaving unclear how harness leverage behaves across local model sizes.
AI.method: The authors test five shipped harnesses across 18 artifact-producing tasks and five model sizes (360 ladder cells) using a deterministic checker, alongside ablations disabling completion checks and repeat-blocking rules.
AI.result: Mingbird achieves the highest mean at every size (leads of 0.075 to 0.819); disabling all six executable checks barely changes means, whereas removing one repeat-blocking rule drops 0.75B performance by 0.411, and 85 of 127 empty-artifact cells still exit normally.
AI.conclusion: Harness gains come primarily from ensuring runs actually write artifacts to disk rather than from exit-status checks, and exit status alone is an unreliable proxy for task completion.

title: Learning to Reason with Predictive Gains for Generative Recommendation
summary: Reasoning-enhanced generative recommendation (GR) has attracted increasing attention for leveraging the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) to improve next-item prediction. However, existing methods primarily optimize reasoning through Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with rule-based rewards determined by final recommendation performance, which faces two key limitations: (i) unmeasured predictive contributions within reasoning, where the predictive contributions of individual reasoning steps are not directly reflected in optimization signals, and (ii) weakly discriminative learning signals within groups, where different reasoning trajectories within the group often receive indistinguishable rewards, limiting effective policy optimization. In this paper, we propose GainReason, a simple yet effective training framework that optimizes reasoning through Predictive Gain (PG). Specifically, PG measures changes in target Semantic ID (SID) log-likelihood induced by individual reasoning sentences, providing contribution-aware and discriminative rewards. We further theoretically establish the alignment between expected PG and the recommendation ranking objective. Building on this signal, we develop PG-based Reasoning Optimization (PGRO) to optimize reasoning generation with sentence-level rewards, supported by a custom causal attention mechanism for efficient PG computation. Additionally, an auxiliary PG-based Reasoning Utilization (PGRU) task adaptively strengthens reasoning-conditioned prediction to complement PGRO. Extensive experiments on three public benchmarks demonstrate that GainReason consistently outperforms competitive baselines and achieves substantial performance gains from reasoning.

AI.tldr: GainReason improves reasoning-enhanced generative recommendation by using Predictive Gain—the change in target Semantic ID log-likelihood per reasoning sentence—as a dense, contribution-aware reward.
AI.motivation: Existing GRPO-based generative recommendation methods rely on sparse outcome rewards, leaving individual reasoning steps unmeasured and producing weakly discriminative signals within trajectory groups.
AI.method: GainReason computes sentence-level Predictive Gain via a custom causal attention mechanism, proves its alignment with the recommendation ranking objective, and combines PG-based Reasoning Optimization (PGRO) with an auxiliary PG-based Reasoning Utilization (PGRU) task.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on three public benchmarks show that GainReason consistently outperforms competitive baselines and delivers substantial gains from reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Sentence-level Predictive Gain provides a theoretically grounded, discriminative reward signal that overcomes the credit-assignment limits of outcome-only GRPO in generative recommendation.

title: Subprocess-Constrained Markov Decision Processes
comment: To appear at NeurIPS '26. Code available at this https URL
summary: Constrained Markov decision processes (CMDPs) typically bound expected cumulative cost from an initial state. Such a guarantee can be insufficient when a policy must remain feasible after every history it may encounter. We introduce \emph{subprocess-constrained MDPs} (S-CMDPs), which require the expected discounted cost of each continuation, conditional on any reachable history, to satisfy a bound determined by the current state. This stronger requirement changes the structure and complexity of the problem: we show that stationary policies can be strictly suboptimal, and finding even an approximately optimal stationary policy is NP-hard. We adapt a recently introduced value-set iteration framework to show that history-dependent policies surprisingly overcome both obstacles. Our polynomial-time algorithm represents such a policy implicitly: its expected reward is within $\epsilon$ of the optimal feasible value, it violates each subprocess cost bound by at most $\delta$, and its action distribution can be computed in polynomial time for any given history.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces subprocess-constrained MDPs (S-CMDPs), proves stationary policies are suboptimal and NP-hard to approximate, and gives a polynomial-time algorithm for near-optimal history-dependent policies.
AI.motivation: Standard CMDPs only bound expected cumulative cost from the initial state, which is insufficient when a policy must remain feasible after every reachable history.
AI.method: The authors formalize S-CMDPs requiring every continuation's expected discounted cost to satisfy a state-dependent bound, prove hardness for stationary policies, and adapt a value-set iteration framework to implicitly represent history-dependent policies.
AI.result: The proposed polynomial-time algorithm computes an action distribution for any history whose expected reward is within epsilon of optimal and whose subprocess cost violations are at most delta.
AI.conclusion: History-dependent policies via value-set iteration bypass the suboptimality and NP-hardness of stationary policies in history-feasible constrained MDPs.

title: Generative AI and the Crisis of Higher Education Assessments: Examining 'AI-Proofing' Strategies for College-Level Assessments
summary: Higher education is confronting an academic-integrity challenge unlike any in its history. Students can now outsource homework, take-home assignments, and online examinations to large language models (LLMs) that complete them in seconds. Existing research on evaluating LLM performance on academic assessments has focused largely on standardized examinations, or on questions from college-level courses drawn from a single discipline. Far less is known about how LLMs perform on college-level assessment questions spanning multiple disciplines, that instructors have purposely designed to be AI-resistant, and about which features of such questions, if any, meaningfully constrain LLM performance. We address this gap by collecting 75 questions from authentic college coursework assessments, spanning 17 disciplines, which were contributed by 37 faculty members from ten U.S. universities and one U.K. university. Of these, 61 questions were intentionally designed by faculty members to be 'LLM-proof', while the remaining 14 questions were sourced from online courses. We then (i) evaluate three state-of-the-art LLMs' ability to correctly answer these questions with and without supplementary course materials; (ii) identify five strategies, through thematic analysis, that faculty used to make their questions harder for LLMs to solve; and (iii) test whether these strategies impact LLMs' ability to answer the questions accurately. Our experimental results show that the best-performing model scored approximately 83% without supplementary course materials and 85% with them, and we observed noteworthy differences across models, answer formats, and instructor tweaking strategies. We discuss implications for assessment design, academic-integrity policy, and the broader ethics of deploying LLMs in educational settings.

AI.tldr: Testing three frontier LLMs on 75 authentic college assessment questions across 17 disciplines (61 designed to be LLM-proof) shows the best model scores ~83% without and 85% with course materials.
AI.motivation: Prior evaluations of LLM academic integrity focused on standardized exams or single disciplines, leaving unclear how well intentionally AI-resistant college coursework questions hold up across disciplines.
AI.method: The authors collect 75 coursework questions from 37 faculty across 11 US/UK universities, evaluate three state-of-the-art LLMs with and without supplementary materials, and thematically identify five faculty AI-proofing strategies to test their impact.
AI.result: The best-performing LLM achieves approximately 83% accuracy without supplementary materials and 85% with them, with notable differences across models, answer formats, and instructor tweaking strategies.
AI.conclusion: Even intentionally AI-resistant college assessments are largely solvable by current LLMs, underscoring the need to rethink assessment design and academic-integrity policies.

title: Safe Resemblance, Silent Propagation: Limits of Text-Similarity Guardrails for AI Agent Safety
summary: When AI agents relay information to one another, an output can preserve an injected instruction's effect on downstream agents even after its wording changes, yet legitimate quotation and template reuse can produce high textual overlap with the source, so text-similarity guardrails that attempt to flag the former risk conflating these two cases. We test this distinction using DonkeyRail, a public classifier combining BLEU, ROUGE-L, and METEOR features, deployed in a controlled three-agent email relay, defining a behavioral measure in which an output counts as functional (the injected procedure induces fresh computations in two subsequent agents) independent of the detector's score, alongside legitimate controls that explicitly authorize quotation and reuse. At its default threshold the classifier misses 8 of 19 functional outputs while flagging 70 of 192 legitimate replies, with every completed quotation and template-reuse reply triggering a false alert; calibrating for low false positives on one template set does not transfer, as the recalibrated threshold detects only one functional output and still produces 15 false alerts on new templates. We also identify an operating-point error in all 21 published classifier configurations, where ROC interpolation replaces direct threshold application, and show formally that high AUC against a surface-level text criterion provides no distribution-free guarantee of high AUC against the behavioral target, while the existing evaluation labels lack the joint observations needed to estimate the gap. An authorization analysis further shows that identical visible transcripts can require different safety decisions depending on the governing policy, a distinction no observation-only classifier can resolve. These results argue for behavioral and policy-grounded evaluation over text-similarity guardrails.

AI.tldr: Evaluating the text-similarity guardrail DonkeyRail in a three-agent email relay shows high false positives on legitimate quotation/reuse and false negatives on paraphrased prompt injections, arguing for behavioral, policy-grounded evaluation.
AI.motivation: Text-similarity guardrails risk conflating paraphrased prompt injections that retain downstream effect with legitimate quotation and template reuse that share high surface overlap.
AI.method: The authors test DonkeyRail (BLEU, ROUGE-L, METEOR) in a controlled three-agent email relay using a behavioral ground-truth measure of functional injection alongside authorized quotation/reuse controls, and analyze ROC operating points and authorization policies.
AI.result: At its default threshold DonkeyRail misses 8 of 19 functional injections while flagging 70 of 192 legitimate replies (including every completed quotation/reuse reply), recalibration fails to transfer (catching 1 functional output with 15 false alerts), and all 21 published configurations suffer from an ROC-interpolation operating-point error.
AI.conclusion: Surface text-similarity guardrails cannot reliably separate malicious propagation from authorized reuse, and observation-only classifiers cannot resolve policy-dependent authorization.

title: SciResearch-Eval: Evaluating Scientific Judgment in Autonomous Experimental Agents
comment: 28 pages, 7 figures. Code and leaderboard: this https URL
summary: We introduce SciResearch-Eval, an interactive benchmark of scientific judgment built on a standard laboratory problem: measuring a material's thermal properties by heating it and fitting a heat-conduction simulator. An agent designs its own experiments, uses a supplied simulator that may be under-resolved or physically wrong, and reports each property with a 95% interval. To our knowledge it is the first benchmark to combine agent-designed experiments, a deliberately flawed simulator, and proper scoring of calibrated intervals against exact ground truth. On a held-out split (93 tasks, 9 models, 2,511 episodes), models handle procedural traps. When the simulator is missing physics, most report wrong values while stating they are 95% sure: their ranges contain the truth in 20-62% of cases, against 94% for GPT-6 Astra and 99% for Claude Fable 5.2. At default effort the failing Claude 5.5 models rarely diagnose the missing physics (Opus in 35% of episodes, against 66% for Astra), and even when they do, their ranges often miss; Astra and Fable design experiments in which the flawed simulator is accurate, such as gentle heating, which keeps Astra calibrated even when it does not name the cause. Asking for wider intervals does not help; stating the strategy improves interval scores 1.6-2.5-fold, replicated on a pre-registered fresh split, but coverage barely moves. A pre-registered effort ablation shows that the correction is latent in the Claude 5.5 models: at maximum effort Opus improves more than tenfold and is no longer detectably behind Astra at default, but only with 13-31 times more reasoning; older and open-weight models gain nothing. Fable 5.2 is the most accurate model at default effort (interval score 1.9 times better than Astra's) but writes 6 times as many tokens, and at Astra's token count it falls short. We release the environment, graders and harness.

AI.tldr: SciResearch-Eval benchmarks scientific judgment by having agents design heating experiments with a deliberately flawed simulator and report calibrated 95% intervals, exposing severe overconfidence in most models except GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.2.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks rarely test whether autonomous experimental agents can design informative experiments and maintain calibrated uncertainty when their supplied physical simulator is under-resolved or wrong.
AI.method: Agents design heating experiments to measure thermal properties using a potentially flawed heat-conduction simulator and report 95% intervals scored against exact ground truth across 93 held-out tasks and 9 models (2,511 episodes).
AI.result: Most models achieve only 20-62% coverage while claiming 95% confidence, whereas GPT-6 Astra reaches 94% and Claude Fable 5.2 reaches 99% (1.9x better interval score than Astra, though using 6x more tokens); maximum reasoning effort lifts Claude 5.5 Opus over tenfold at 13-31x more reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Frontier models differ sharply in their ability to design experiments around flawed simulators and calibrate uncertainty, with latent capability in some models unlocked only by heavy reasoning budgets.

title: Minimum cores in lattice graphs: zonotope structure and quartic growth
summary: A core of a graph is a nonempty vertex set in which every member has at least as many neighbours inside the set as outside. We study the minimum size $c_{m,n}$ of a finite core in the graph on $\Z^m$ joining points at sup-norm distance at most $n$. The local majority condition imposes a global geometric constraint: the convex hull of every core has an explicit lattice zonotope $H_n^{(m)}$ as a Minkowski summand. In the plane, this zonotope has width asymptotic to $6\zeta(3)n^3/\pi^2$. We prove that all its lattice points form a core and construct a shell with $O(n^4)$ points. Together with a packing argument, this gives $c_{2,n}=\Theta(n^4)$ and coordinate widths $\Theta(n^3)$ for every minimum core. We determine $c_{2,1}=12$ and $c_{2,2}=96$ by analytic arguments and prove uniqueness up to translation in both cases. Explicit forced-set and deficit certificates determine further minima within the prescribed zonotope hull. We distinguish these restricted results from global optimality and state the remaining geometric conjectures. We also give a direct reduction from \textsc{Clique} showing that the core problem is NP-complete on general finite graphs, which settles a conjecture of Hassanpour in the terms in which it was posed.

AI.tldr: This paper proves that minimum cores in n-neighborhood lattice graphs on Z^2 have quartic size Theta(n^4) with explicit zonotope structure, determines c_{2,1}=12 and c_{2,2}=96, and proves core NP-completeness on general finite graphs.
AI.motivation: A graph core requires every vertex to have at least as many neighbors inside the set as outside, but its minimum size growth and geometric structure in lattice graphs and complexity on general graphs were open.
AI.method: The authors show the convex hull of any core contains an explicit lattice zonotope H_n^(m) as a Minkowski summand, construct an O(n^4) shell, use packing and certificate arguments for exact small cases, and reduce from Clique for general graphs.
AI.result: In Z^2, minimum core size grows as c_{2,n} = Theta(n^4) with coordinate widths Theta(n^3), c_{2,1}=12 and c_{2,2}=96 uniquely up to translation, and the core problem is NP-complete on general finite graphs, settling Hassanpour's conjecture.
AI.conclusion: Local majority conditions on lattice graphs enforce rigid global zonotope geometry, resolving both the asymptotic growth in 2D and the general-graph complexity.

title: Brain AI Scientist: An Evidence-Based Multi-Agent System for Translational Neuroimaging in Precision Psychiatry
summary: Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI) has revealed widespread brain-network alterations in psychiatric disorders, yet translating these findings into individualized clinical decision support remains challenging. Here we introduce Brain AI Scientist, an autonomous multi-agent framework that integrates patient-specific fMRI, clinical information, and scientific evidence through retrieval, verification, and prioritization. Guided by Research Domain Criteria and evidence-based medicine, it builds traceable chains linking phenotypes, anatomical abnormalities, biomarkers, mechanisms, interventions, and validation strategies. In a representative autism case, Brain AI Scientist generated 37 anatomical hypotheses, retained 26 after literature verification, and derived 65 evidence-supported biomarkers from 90 unique publications to generate patient-specific treatment and validation guidance. Across 17 autism spectrum disorder cases, it outperformed GPT-3.5 baselines with and without fMRI impression in evidence grounding, personalization, clinical actionability, and biomarker-treatment reasoning. Brain AI Scientist therefore provides an auditable framework for translating patient-specific neuroimaging into individualized clinical decision support for precision psychiatry.

AI.tldr: Brain AI Scientist is an evidence-based multi-agent framework that integrates patient rs-fMRI, clinical data, and literature verification to generate auditable treatment and validation guidance in precision psychiatry.
AI.motivation: Translating resting-state fMRI findings into individualized clinical decision support for psychiatric disorders remains difficult due to fragmented evidence and lack of traceable reasoning.
AI.method: Guided by Research Domain Criteria and evidence-based medicine, Brain AI Scientist retrieves, verifies, and prioritizes literature to build traceable chains from phenotypes and anatomical abnormalities to biomarkers, mechanisms, and interventions.
AI.result: In an autism case it generated 37 anatomical hypotheses, retained 26 after verification, and derived 65 biomarkers from 90 publications; across 17 ASD cases it outperformed GPT-3.5 baselines (with and without fMRI impression) in evidence grounding, personalization, actionability, and biomarker-treatment reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Auditable multi-agent evidence synthesis provides a structured path to translate patient-specific neuroimaging into precision psychiatry decision support.

title: Swarm Shepherd: Securing Multi-Agent Ecosystems Against Persistent Latent Compromise
comment: The Fortieth Annual Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems
summary: Agentic ecosystems are emerging as a new platform layer in which agents maintain persistent memory, retrieve from shared knowledge bases, execute through tool interfaces, and coordinate through shared states. These capabilities create a security problem that per-turn defenses miss: compromise can accumulate across sessions, agents, and system layers before visible failure. We define this threat as Agentic Sleeper, a system-level adversary that first behaves legitimately, gains routing trust, and later activates across memory, agent logic, and infrastructure. We formulate defense as inference under partial observability and propose Swarm Shepherd, a system-level defense framework centered on an inference filter for early warning, paired with a backward trace-back module for entry attribution. Our analysis yields a two-scale deployment rule that balances longer event histories against broader agent coverage. Across LangGraph, CrewAI, and AutoGen, Agentic Sleeper drift begins 2.7--8.9$\times$ faster than natural baselines, propagates across agents on most topologies, and evades per-turn and stateful defenses above 80\%. Swarm Shepherd warns at least three sessions before visible degradation (2.6 sessions when failure is scored by the benchmark's own task grader), while trace-back reaches 0.69 top-1 accuracy and 0.72 macro-F1 over 24 variants. The two-scale deployment rule is empirically confirmed, and in live end-to-end runs on LangGraph and AutoGen the posterior-guided defense stack drives cross-agent propagation below the self-sustaining regime, which removing only the visibly compromised agent does not achieve.

AI.tldr: Swarm Shepherd defends multi-agent ecosystems against persistent latent compromise ("Agentic Sleeper") using an inference filter for early warning and backward trace-back for entry attribution, halting cross-agent propagation.
AI.motivation: Persistent memory, shared knowledge bases, and inter-agent coordination allow adversaries to gain routing trust legitimately and later trigger cascading compromise that per-turn defenses miss.
AI.method: Formulating defense as inference under partial observability, Swarm Shepherd pairs an inference filter for early warning with a backward trace-back module and derives a two-scale deployment rule balancing history length against agent coverage.
AI.result: Across LangGraph, CrewAI, and AutoGen, Agentic Sleeper evades per-turn and stateful defenses over 80% of the time, while Swarm Shepherd warns at least 3 sessions before visible degradation (2.6 sessions by task grader), reaches 0.69 top-1 accuracy and 0.72 macro-F1 on trace-back, and suppresses propagation in live runs.
AI.conclusion: System-level partial-observability inference and trace-back stop persistent multi-agent compromises that simply removing a visibly compromised agent fails to contain.

title: Max-Min Throughput in RSMA-Aided SWIPT for Sustainable Internet of Underground Things: A Deep Reinforcement Learning Approach
summary: Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV)-enabled wireless-powered underground sensor networks (WPUSNs) allow underground devices (UDs) to harvest radio-frequency energy from a UAV via wireless energy transfer (WET) techniques, enabling sustainable Internet of underground things (IoUT) applications. This paper integrates rate-splitting multiple access (RSMA)-aided simultaneous wireless information and power transfer (SWIPT) into UAV-enabled WPUSNs to deliver information and energy to UDs. Within this framework, we investigate a max-min fairness problem that jointly optimizes the UAV transmit power, power allocation and message splitting, power-splitting ratios, and time allocation, aiming to maximize the minimum uplink throughput across UDs subject to per-UD downlink throughput requirements and a UAV energy-consumption constraint. To address this non-convex problem under dynamic underground environments, we develop an off-policy deep reinforcement learning approach based on the primal-dual truncated quantile critics (PD-TQC), where a TQC-based reward critic evaluates the fairness objective, cost critics estimate constraint costs, and an actor learns the resource-control policy with adaptive dual-variable updates. Simulations using in-situ soil volumetric water content measurements from a center-pivot irrigation farm demonstrate that PD-TQC achieves the highest annual average minimum uplink throughput compared with four benchmarks while satisfying the per-frame constraints in over 96% of the evaluated frames, and that this throughput advantage is preserved under different Rician factors, numbers of UDs, and downlink throughput thresholds.

AI.tldr: This paper integrates RSMA-aided SWIPT into UAV-enabled wireless-powered underground sensor networks and uses primal-dual truncated quantile critics (PD-TQC) to maximize minimum uplink throughput under constraints.
AI.motivation: Sustainable underground sensor networks require joint optimization of UAV transmit power, message splitting, power-splitting, and time allocation under dynamic soil conditions, which is non-convex and challenging for classical solvers.
AI.method: The authors formulate a max-min fairness problem subject to downlink throughput and UAV energy constraints and solve it with an off-policy DRL algorithm, PD-TQC, combining a TQC reward critic, cost critics, and adaptive dual-variable updates.
AI.result: Simulations using in-situ soil volumetric water content measurements show PD-TQC achieves the highest annual average minimum uplink throughput among four benchmarks while satisfying per-frame constraints in over 96% of frames across varying Rician factors, device counts, and thresholds.
AI.conclusion: Primal-dual quantile DRL effectively manages non-convex resource allocation in RSMA-SWIPT underground networks under realistic, time-varying soil channels.

title: First-order smoothed exact-penalty methods for equality-constrained regularized nonconvex optimization
summary: We consider regularized nonconvex optimization over a closed convex set $\mathcal{X} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$, which involves a convex nonsmooth regularizer $r$ in the objective and $n$ smooth equality constraints. To find a near-KKT point of the problem, we propose a prox-linear first-order method, named as SEPi-Prox, based on a smoothed exact-penalty formulation. At each outer iteration of SEPi-Prox, a strongly convex prox-linear subproblem is formed and solved inexactly to a sufficient accuracy. Under a local non-singularity condition that is weaker than some other commonly used regularity conditions or constraint qualifications, SEPi-Prox finds an $\epsilon$-KKT point within $O(\epsilon^{-2})$ first-order oracle calls, matching the lower bound for unconstrained smooth nonconvex optimization. We employ Nesterov's accelerated proximal-gradient method (APG) and a dual cutting-plane method (DCP) for the prox-linear subproblems. Let $\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{FO}}$ and $\mathcal{C}_r$ denote the numbers of arithmetic operations of evaluating one first-order oracle and one proximal mapping of $r$ over $\mathcal{X}$, respectively. Then SEPi-Prox requires $\widetilde{O}(\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{FO}}\epsilon^{-2} + (dn + \mathcal{C}_r)\epsilon^{-5/2})$ and $\widetilde{O}((\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{FO}} + dn^2 + n\mathcal{C}_r + n^{3.373})\epsilon^{-2})$ total arithmetic operations to produce an $\epsilon$-KKT point, respectively by using APG and DCP as the subsolver. The latter result is preferable when $n$ is small and nearly matches the optimal dependence on $\epsilon$. Numerical experiments on instances of the multi-class Neyman-Pearson classification demonstrate the efficiency of SEPi-Prox with both subsolvers.

AI.tldr: SEPi-Prox is a first-order smoothed exact-penalty prox-linear method for equality-constrained regularized nonconvex optimization that achieves O(epsilon^-2) first-order oracle complexity under a weak local non-singularity condition.
AI.motivation: Finding near-KKT points in nonconvex optimization with nonsmooth regularizers and smooth equality constraints typically requires strong constraint qualifications or higher-order oracle complexity.
AI.method: SEPi-Prox forms strongly convex prox-linear subproblems from a smoothed exact-penalty formulation and solves them inexactly using either Nesterov's accelerated proximal-gradient (APG) method or a dual cutting-plane (DCP) method.
AI.result: Under a weak local non-singularity condition, SEPi-Prox reaches an epsilon-KKT point in O(epsilon^-2) first-order oracle calls, with total arithmetic complexity O~(C_FO epsilon^-2 + (dn + C_r) epsilon^-5/2) for APG and O~((C_FO + dn^2 + n C_r + n^3.373) epsilon^-2) for DCP, verified on multi-class Neyman-Pearson classification.
AI.conclusion: SEPi-Prox matches the unconstrained smooth nonconvex lower bound in oracle complexity while offering a dual cutting-plane option that is nearly optimal in epsilon when the number of constraints n is small.

title: Dynamic Spatio-Temporal Graph Attention Networks with Nested Clustered Optimization for Multi-Asset Portfolios
comment: 10 pages, 7 figures, 2 tables. Replication package and dataset available at this https URL
summary: Nested Clustered Optimization (NCO) insulates asset allocation from Markowitz covariance ill-conditioning. However, classical tree clustering relies on static pairwise Pearson correlation, failing to capture time-varying, asymmetric downside risk contagion across multi-asset markets. We propose a unified deep graph machine learning architecture: Dynamic Spatio-Temporal Graph Attention Networks with Nested Clustered Optimization (ST-GAT-NCO) for multi-asset tactical allocation. The framework extracts temporal momentum and downside risk dynamics via causal dilated 1D-convolutions, then deploys a multi-head Graph Attention Network (GAT) over dynamic market topologies to learn latent spatial node representations. These learned embeddings define an angular metric distance space that guides two-stage downside NCO optimization under institutional constraints and turnover smoothing. Evaluated over a 73-month non-anticipative walk-forward out-of-sample window (January 2020 to January 2026) across 13 global asset classes net of 10 bps transaction costs, ST-GAT-NCO achieves a 5.32% CAGR and 37.06% cumulative net return, delivering an excess Sharpe ratio of 0.30 and a Sortino ratio of 0.48. This substantially outperforms classical Minimum Variance (3.68% CAGR, 0.08 Sharpe), Hierarchical Risk Parity (2.65% CAGR), and Plain Symmetric NCO (4.11% CAGR, 0.15 Sharpe), while restricting maximum drawdown to -13.07% (versus -19.44% for Equal-Weight and -16.36% for Downside NCO) under a controlled one-way turnover of 15.31%/month. Regime analysis confirms active capital preservation across the 2020 COVID-19 crash, 2022 monetary tightening, and 2023-2026 disinflation rallies.

AI.tldr: ST-GAT-NCO combines causal dilated 1D-convolutions, dynamic multi-head Graph Attention Networks, and two-stage downside Nested Clustered Optimization to outperform classical portfolio allocation methods over a 73-month out-of-sample test.
AI.motivation: Classical Nested Clustered Optimization relies on static pairwise Pearson correlations, missing time-varying, asymmetric downside risk contagion across multi-asset markets.
AI.method: The framework extracts temporal momentum and downside risk via causal dilated 1D-convolutions, learns latent spatial embeddings with a dynamic GAT, and uses their angular metric distances to guide two-stage downside NCO under institutional constraints and turnover smoothing.
AI.result: Over a 73-month walk-forward test (Jan 2020–Jan 2026) across 13 asset classes net of 10 bps costs, ST-GAT-NCO achieves 5.32% CAGR, 37.06% cumulative net return, 0.30 excess Sharpe, 0.48 Sortino, and -13.07% max drawdown at 15.31%/month turnover, beating Minimum Variance, HRP, and Plain NCO.
AI.conclusion: Learning dynamic, downside-aware market topologies with spatio-temporal GATs substantially improves risk-adjusted returns and drawdown control in clustered portfolio optimization.

title: CoSyDelay: Cognitive Symbolic Regression for Traffic Delay Estimation
summary: Trustworthy estimation of traffic delays at signalized intersections is critical for modern transportation systems, as it supports proactive traffic control for congestion mitigation. Existing analytical methods often rely on idealized assumptions that limit their accuracy under complex traffic conditions, whereas data-driven methods may achieve strong estimation performance but usually lack transparent structures, which reduces confidence in their practical application. To address these limitations, we propose CoSyDelay, a cognitive symbolic regression (SR) framework for automatically deriving explicit and physically consistent empirical delay estimation expressions (DEEs). Specifically, CoSyDelay decomposes intersection-level delay estimation into turning-movement-level subproblems, thereby reducing the complexity of the symbolic search. During DEE learning, CoSyDelay constructs domain-informed symbolic inputs from traffic variables. Large language models (LLMs) are employed as symbolic search operators to iteratively generate and refine candidate expression structures, whose movement-specific coefficients are subsequently calibrated using approach-level delay labels. A composite fitness function evaluates the learned DEEs jointly in terms of estimation accuracy and compliance with specified traffic-delay principles. Experimental results on multiple signalized intersections demonstrate that the resulting expressions achieve competitive estimation performance while maintaining physical consistency, thereby supporting trustworthy delay estimation. Source code and datasets are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: CoSyDelay is a cognitive symbolic regression framework that uses LLMs as evolutionary operators to derive explicit, physically consistent traffic delay estimation expressions at signalized intersections.
AI.motivation: Analytical traffic delay models rely on idealized assumptions that hurt accuracy in complex traffic, whereas black-box data-driven models lack transparency for practical deployment.
AI.method: CoSyDelay decomposes intersection delay into turning-movement subproblems, constructs domain-informed symbolic inputs, uses LLMs to iteratively propose and refine expression structures, calibrates coefficients with approach-level labels, and scores candidates on both accuracy and physical consistency.
AI.result: Experiments across multiple signalized intersections show the derived expressions achieve competitive estimation accuracy while preserving physical consistency with traffic-delay principles.
AI.conclusion: Combining turning-movement decomposition with LLM-guided symbolic search produces transparent, trustworthy traffic delay formulas without sacrificing predictive accuracy.

title: Discovering Programmatic Policies from Reinforcement Learning-Based Traffic Signal Controllers
summary: Traffic signal control (TSC) is critical for mitigating urban congestion. Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) has achieved strong performance by learning adaptive policies from traffic observations, but learned neural controllers are often opaque, structurally complex, and difficult to generalize across scenarios. We propose PPL-TSC, a programmatic policy learning framework that distills compact and human-readable TSC policies from DRL teachers. PPL-TSC formulates policy learning as an evolutionary search over phase utility functions (PUFs), which score candidate signal phases and select the highest-utility phase for execution. Each generation consists of four steps: policy generation, policy review, policy calibration, and policy evaluation. In the generation step, a large language model (LLM) acts as a semantics-aware evolutionary operator to propose and refine candidate PUFs. Generated PUFs are screened through explicit checks for syntactic validity, mathematical soundness, and consistency with TSC principles, with invalid ones repaired through iterative feedback. Valid PUFs are then calibrated to improve behavioral fidelity to the DRL teacher, and evaluated using a joint score combining teacher fidelity and traffic-control performance to select candidates for the next generation. Extensive experiments across diverse traffic scenarios and representative DRL-based controllers show that PPL-TSC produces compact and human-readable policies, achieves competitive performance for most teacher families, improves transfer generalization, and substantially reduces computational cost. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: PPL-TSC distills compact, human-readable programmatic traffic signal control policies from DRL teachers using LLM-driven evolutionary search over phase utility functions.
AI.motivation: Deep reinforcement learning traffic signal controllers achieve strong performance but are opaque, complex, and hard to generalize across traffic scenarios.
AI.method: Each generation of PPL-TSC uses an LLM to propose and refine phase utility functions, screens and repairs them for syntax, math, and domain consistency, calibrates them for fidelity to the DRL teacher, and selects candidates by a joint fidelity-and-performance score.
AI.result: Across diverse traffic scenarios and DRL teacher families, PPL-TSC produces compact, readable policies that match most teachers, improve transfer generalization, and substantially lower computational cost.
AI.conclusion: Evolutionary programmatic distillation with LLMs bridges the gap between high-performing black-box DRL controllers and interpretable, generalizable traffic signal policies.

title: Towards GPROF V08: A Machine-Learning Framework for Simulating Passive Microwave Observations of Precipitation
summary: Spatially resolved precipitation retrievals based on convolutional neural networks (CNNs) can improve precipitation estimates from passive microwave (PMW) observations and will be used to implement the next operational PMW retrieval algorithm for the Global Precipitation Measurement (GPM) mission. However, the conventional radiative transfer simulations used to extend the retrieval algorithm to the various sensors of the GPM constellation do not provide the spatial coverage required to train CNN-based retrievals. To address this, we introduce a machine-learning-based simulation framework that enables the training of the CNN-based GPROF-NN 3D retrieval algorithm for the full GPM constellation. At the core of this framework is Satformer, a new neural-network architecture that can translate PMW observations between any pair of GPM sensors. The resulting synthetic observations exhibit lower errors than conventional radiative transfer simulations and lead to more accurate precipitation retrievals when used to train GPROF-NN precipitation retrievals. We further demonstrate the applicability of the framework to new instruments by developing GPROF-NN retrievals for the Microwave Imager aboard the Weather System Follow-on Microwave satellite. While GPROF-NN retrievals based on the new simulation framework achieve lower instantaneous retrieval errors and higher correlations compared to independent reference data than conventional retrievals, residual simulation errors can introduce systematic biases in the resulting retrievals. The proposed simulation framework provides a key component for extending GPROF-NN to the full GPM constellation as part of the upcoming operational GPROF V08 retrieval algorithm. The results demonstrate the potential of machine-learning-based simulations to support spatially resolved precipitation retrievals across heterogeneous satellite constellations.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Satformer, an ML sensor-translation architecture that simulates passive microwave observations across the GPM satellite constellation to train GPROF-NN 3D precipitation retrievals for GPROF V08.
AI.motivation: Conventional radiative transfer simulations lack the spatial coverage needed to train CNN-based precipitation retrievals across all sensors in the Global Precipitation Measurement (GPM) constellation.
AI.method: Satformer translates passive microwave observations between any pair of GPM sensors to generate synthetic training data for the GPROF-NN 3D retrieval algorithm, including adaptation to new instruments such as the WSF-M Microwave Imager.
AI.result: Satformer-generated observations have lower errors than conventional radiative transfer simulations and yield GPROF-NN retrievals with lower instantaneous errors and higher correlations against independent reference data, though residual simulation errors can introduce systematic biases.
AI.conclusion: ML-based inter-sensor simulation enables spatially resolved CNN precipitation retrievals across heterogeneous satellite constellations for the upcoming operational GPROF V08.

title: Practice Is Not Free: Measuring the Embodied Cost of Reset-Free Robot Practice
comment: 16 pages, 6 figures. Code, data, logs and videos: this https URL
summary: When a robot practices without human resets, every attempt still costs wall-clock time, actuator wear, and sometimes a person's attention, yet the schedulers that decide what to practice next treat attempts as free. We present an open, low-cost testbed for measuring these costs: a self-built SO-101 arm runs two demonstration-trained ACT policies that reset each other, with a vision-based success detector and a ledger that records the time, joint travel, and human interventions of every attempt. We formulate cost-aware practice scheduling, in which task selection is rewarded by measured competence gain net of embodied cost, and specify in advance the comparison that will test it. Its first two conditions, run on hardware for 51 minutes of robot time, show that a fixed retry limit did not reduce the share of execution time lost to failures (36%, against 27% for a feasibility rule; not significant) and saved no robot time. The logs suggest why: failures showed no sign of clustering, so a retry right after a failure was as likely to succeed as any other attempt. The ledger also shows that most of the retry rule's extra human time came from cubes knocked out of reach rather than from the rule itself, and a cost-aware rule replayed on the logs recovers the sensible choice without a hand-set limit. We also report lessons from building the system, including a coverage effect in which concentrating demonstrations in a smaller workspace raised success there from 8/20 to 10/10.

AI.tldr: An open, low-cost SO-101 robot testbed logs time, joint travel, and human interventions during reset-free practice, showing that a fixed retry limit does not save robot time because failures do not cluster.
AI.motivation: Reset-free robot practice schedulers treat attempts as free, ignoring real embodied costs in wall-clock time, actuator wear, and human attention.
AI.method: Two demonstration-trained ACT policies reset each other on an SO-101 arm with a vision success detector and cost ledger; the authors formulate cost-aware practice scheduling and run 51 minutes of hardware trials comparing a fixed retry limit against a feasibility rule.
AI.result: The fixed retry limit lost 36% of execution time to failures versus 27% for the feasibility rule (not significant) because failures did not cluster, while extra human time stemmed mainly from out-of-reach cubes; replaying a cost-aware rule on the logs recovers the sensible choice without a hand-set limit.
AI.conclusion: Measuring embodied costs directly reveals that unclustered failures undermine simple retry heuristics and motivates cost-aware practice scheduling.

title: U-HamGNN: a universal model for magnetic Hamiltonians conditioned on spin and Hubbard U
summary: The electronic structure of a magnetic crystal depends jointly on its spin configuration and the on-site Hubbard correction U, requiring a separate DFT+U calculation for each combination. We introduce U-HamGNN, an equivariant network that takes these two inputs directly and predicts spin-resolved Hamiltonians across diverse crystal chemistries. A spectral-hybrid optimizer that weights each update direction by how consistently the gradient points along it reaches 8% lower Hamiltonian error than Muon and 26% lower than AdamW in a ten-epoch benchmark. The predicted bands reproduce U-dependent gap opening and altermagnetic spin splitting within the trained window and beyond it; exchange couplings and magnetic-order calls derived from the Hamiltonian agree with DFT+U on a calibration set. This universal model provides a new tool for magnetic research.

AI.tldr: U-HamGNN is a universal equivariant neural network that predicts spin-resolved magnetic Hamiltonians conditioned directly on spin configuration and Hubbard U, trained with a spectral-hybrid optimizer.
AI.motivation: Electronic structure in magnetic crystals depends jointly on spin configuration and on-site Hubbard U, normally requiring a separate DFT+U calculation for every combination.
AI.method: U-HamGNN takes spin configuration and U as direct inputs to predict spin-resolved Hamiltonians across crystal chemistries, trained with a spectral-hybrid optimizer that weights update directions by gradient consistency.
AI.result: On a ten-epoch benchmark, the optimizer achieves 8% lower Hamiltonian error than Muon and 26% lower than AdamW; predicted bands reproduce U-dependent gap opening and altermagnetic spin splitting within and beyond the trained window, and derived exchange couplings and magnetic-order calls agree with DFT+U.
AI.conclusion: Conditioning equivariant Hamiltonian models on spin and Hubbard U provides a fast, generalizable surrogate for costly DFT+U magnetic calculations.

title: SWAN-Rx: Efficient and Bandwidth-Scalable Neural Reception for MIMO-OFDM
comment: This work has been submitted to IEEE for possible publication
summary: We present a Scalable Windowed Axial-attention Neural Receiver (SWAN-Rx) for multiple-input multiple-output orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (MIMO-OFDM) systems. The receiver improves reception accuracy and reduces forward-pass computation while supporting frozen-weight reuse across bandwidth allocations and channel conditions. It combines a common resource-element representation of received observations and pilot context with alternating time-axis and local frequency-axis attention. Shared parameters and relative positional information permit soft detection across allocation lengths without inference-time parameter updates. At fixed subcarrier spacing, model configuration, and symbol count, bounded frequency neighborhoods give linear growth of forward-pass computation with bandwidth. Evaluations compatible with the 5G New Radio physical layer reuse weights trained on four physical resource blocks (PRBs) at up to 273 PRBs and on unseen channels. At the training bandwidth, SWAN-Rx achieves lower pre- and post-decoding bit error rates than the implemented three-step neural receiver (NRX) and DeepRx-MIMO baselines, with 16.9% and 39.7% fewer parameters and 56.3% and 35.7% fewer forward-pass operations, respectively. The same weights achieve lower pre-decoding error rates than these baselines throughout the evaluated bandwidth-extrapolation and 16-PRB channel-transfer tests, with an estimated 0.4-0.9 dB signal-to-noise ratio reduction relative to NRX at a pre-decoding error rate of $10^{-2}$ in the 16-PRB tests.

AI.tldr: SWAN-Rx is a scalable windowed axial-attention neural receiver for MIMO-OFDM that extrapolates frozen weights trained on 4 PRBs up to 273 PRBs with linear bandwidth complexity and lower bit error rates than baselines.
AI.motivation: Neural receivers for MIMO-OFDM need to scale efficiently across varying bandwidth allocations and channel conditions without retraining or inference-time parameter updates.
AI.method: SWAN-Rx represents received observations and pilot context in a common resource-element space and applies alternating time-axis and local frequency-axis attention with shared parameters and relative positional information.
AI.result: At the 4-PRB training bandwidth, SWAN-Rx beats NRX and DeepRx-MIMO in bit error rate with 16.9% and 39.7% fewer parameters and 56.3% and 35.7% fewer forward-pass operations, and maintains lower pre-decoding error rates up to 273 PRBs and on 16-PRB unseen channels (0.4-0.9 dB SNR gain over NRX at 10^-2 BER).
AI.conclusion: Bounded frequency-neighborhood axial attention enables bandwidth-scalable, zero-shot-transferable neural reception compatible with 5G NR physical layers.

title: Kolmogorov-Arnold Lookup Table Demappers for Amplitude Phase-Shift Keying over Nonlinear Satellite Links
summary: Next-generation high-throughput satellites increasingly demodulate and decode on board, so the per-symbol cost of the receiver constrains payload power and throughput. Soft demappers for nonlinear satellite links must therefore produce accurate bit log-likelihood ratios (LLRs) at low cost. We introduce a KAN-LUT demapper, a two-layer Kolmogorov--Arnold network (KAN) whose learned univariate edge functions are stored as 128-entry lookup tables (LUTs), so that inference needs only table reads, linear interpolation, and additions. We bound the LLR error introduced by the tables and evaluate the demapper on amplitude phase-shift keying (APSK) links with low-density parity-check (LDPC) coding and a nonlinear traveling-wave-tube amplifier. For 16-, 32-, and 64-APSK, KAN-LUT stays within 0.2 dB of a per-cluster Gaussian log-MAP (LogMAP-CG) demapper, while its cost relative to LogMAP-CG falls from 87% to 27% as the order grows. It matches or slightly exceeds multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) at about one fifth of their cost, remains competitive under operating-point mismatch, and needs only tens of kilobytes of tables. KAN-LUT is therefore a low-cost candidate demapper for regenerative payloads.

AI.tldr: KAN-LUT is a two-layer Kolmogorov-Arnold network whose univariate edge functions are stored as 128-entry lookup tables, offering low-cost soft demapping for nonlinear APSK satellite links within 0.2 dB of LogMAP-CG.
AI.motivation: On-board demodulation in high-throughput satellites requires accurate bit log-likelihood ratios over nonlinear links at minimal payload power and compute cost.
AI.method: The authors train a two-layer KAN, quantize its learned univariate edge functions into 128-entry lookup tables so inference uses only table reads, linear interpolation, and additions, and bound the resulting LLR error.
AI.result: On LDPC-coded 16-, 32-, and 64-APSK links with a nonlinear TWT amplifier, KAN-LUT stays within 0.2 dB of LogMAP-CG while cutting relative cost from 87% to 27% as order grows, matches or beats MLPs at ~20% of their cost, and requires only tens of kilobytes of tables.
AI.conclusion: Lookup-table KANs provide a compact, low-power soft demapper well suited for regenerative satellite payloads.

title: High-Throughput Serving of Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe with Regime-Aware Megakernels and Kernel Fusion
summary: Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe ranks first among open-weight models on the Hugging Face Open ASR leaderboards. Serving it efficiently takes more than fast operators: continuous batching changes the amount and mix of work at every iteration, and the best fusion granularity changes with it. We present a serving engine that, for every pass, chooses between persistent megakernels and chains of fused kernels at crossovers measured offline. On an H100 SXM GPU, throughput of our accuracy-preserving serving peaks at 4,345x real time, 1.39x the peak of tuned vLLM, and is up to 4.39x faster at low concurrency; on B200 it peaks at 6,367x, 1.64x vLLM at the highest concurrency we measured. Word error rate (WER) is 1.91 to 1.93% against 1.88 to 1.93% for vLLM. Within a 400 ms budget for p95 end-to-end completion time, it serves 8x as many concurrent requests. Choosing per pass beats either level alone: 23% higher throughput than always using megakernels at 128 concurrent requests, and 9% higher than always using fused kernels at 8. Opt-in switches, including greedy MoE layer skipping, add 13 to 16% throughput on B200 for offline jobs that can accept higher WER.

AI.tldr: A regime-aware serving engine for Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe dynamically switches per pass between persistent megakernels and fused kernel chains, achieving up to 1.64x vLLM throughput while preserving WER.
AI.motivation: Continuous batching alters workload size and mix every iteration, so a single static kernel-fusion granularity cannot maximize serving throughput across concurrency regimes.
AI.method: For every pass, the engine selects between persistent megakernels and chains of fused kernels using offline-measured crossover points, with opt-in greedy MoE layer skipping for offline jobs.
AI.result: On H100 SXM it peaks at 4,345x real time (1.39x tuned vLLM, up to 4.39x at low concurrency) and on B200 at 6,367x (1.64x vLLM), maintaining 1.91-1.93% WER (versus 1.88-1.93% for vLLM) and serving 8x more concurrent requests within a 400 ms p95 budget; per-pass switching beats always-megakernel by 23% at 128 concurrency and always-fused by 9% at 8.
AI.conclusion: Regime-aware per-pass kernel selection substantially boosts ASR serving throughput and latency-bounded concurrency without sacrificing transcription accuracy.

title: Washout-free synchronization, parameter estimation and uncertainty quantification of echo state networks
summary: Echo state networks (ESNs) forecast chaotic systems for several Lyapunov times. Like all recurrent networks, ESNs require a washout before forecasting, i.e., a phase in which the full state drives the network until the reservoir state synchronizes with the system. At deployment, however, sensors measure only part of the state, with noise and at a lower sampling rate than the training data. We propose a washout-free deployment of ESNs via ensemble data assimilation. In closed loop, the ESN is a Markovian dynamical system; hence, a sequential filter can correct its reservoir state whenever data are available. The filter synchronizes an ensemble of reservoir states, drawn from the training data, with the system, and quantifies the forecast uncertainty.
