We extend the method to parametric ESNs, to infer physical parameters, and to parallel ESNs with localization, to forecast high-dimensional systems. We test the method on the Lorenz-63 and Lorenz-96 systems. First, the filter synchronizes the ESN with a fraction of the data of a washout. Second, the filter deploys one full-state ESN from a subset of its components, which a washout cannot do. Third, the filter estimates a forcing that is not in the training data, and the estimated forcing lengthens the forecast. Fourth, localization synchronizes a parallel ESN with eight times fewer members than the global filter. Fifth, the ensemble spread signals, without the true state, when the ESN synchronizes and when the filter fails. This work enables the deployment of ESNs from partial, sparse and noisy observations.

AI.tldr: Ensemble data assimilation enables washout-free deployment of echo state networks from partial, sparse, and noisy observations while simultaneously estimating unknown physical parameters and quantifying forecast uncertainty.
AI.motivation: Echo state networks normally require a full-state washout phase before forecasting, which fails at deployment when sensors only observe a noisy, downsampled subset of state variables.
AI.method: Treating the closed-loop ESN as a Markovian dynamical system, a sequential ensemble filter updates reservoir states from incoming observations, extending to parametric ESNs for forcing estimation and localized parallel ESNs for high-dimensional systems.
AI.result: Tested on Lorenz-63 and Lorenz-96, the filter synchronizes with a fraction of washout data, deploys full-state ESNs from partial components, estimates unseen forcings to lengthen forecasts, reduces ensemble size 8x via localization, and signals synchronization or failure through ensemble spread.
AI.conclusion: Sequential ensemble data assimilation removes the full-state washout bottleneck and adds parameter inference and uncertainty quantification to ESN forecasting.

title: A plug-in energy-balance freezing module for transformer frost nowcasting without leaf-sensor inputs
comment: 45 pages main text + 19 pages supplementary material
summary: Frost protection requires local warnings where leaf-sensor inputs are unavailable. In the frost literature we surveyed, physics entered machine-learning models through inputs, numerical-model coupling, or losses, rather than model structure. We develop a transformer-compatible module that embeds leaf energy-balance physics in freezing-probability forecasts: an energy-balance temperature reference and a learned residual predict leaf temperature, which drives a multiplicative gate imposing a temperature-dependent probability cap. We mathematically prove conditional monotonicity and an alarm boundary, and test whether placing the same information in the output pathway or in attention yields different benefits. We evaluated 12 hourly leads at 19 Korean stations over five frost seasons, with and without leaf-sensor inputs. In the 2025-2026 hold-out season without these inputs, our time-token transformer (PET-E) achieved a lead-mean critical success index (CSI) of 0.516 versus 0.478 for fixed-configuration, joint-lead LightGBM, with significant gains at all 12 leads, and the fraction of alarms at observed leaf temperatures of at least 2 degrees C fell from 0.087 to 0.051 relative to the unmodified backbone. Across the hold-out and a retrospective 2024-2025 evaluation, the module reduced Brier scores and warm-surface alarm fractions in both the time-token transformer and iTransformer, with no significant CSI decrease at any lead. At held-out stations without static or leaf-sensor inputs, both module-equipped backbones exceeded LightGBM at all 12 leads (CSI 0.468 and 0.467 versus 0.437). In the time-token backbone, the temperature pathway reduced this alarm fraction in all four settings, whereas the attention prior increased CSI in three. These findings link an explicit temperature-dependent probability cap to improved forecasts and distinguish output-side from attention-based embedding.

AI.tldr: A plug-in leaf energy-balance module embeds a physics-based temperature cap into transformer frost nowcasting without leaf-sensor inputs, improving critical success index and cutting warm-surface false alarms.
AI.motivation: Local frost warnings are needed where leaf-sensor inputs are unavailable, and prior ML frost models incorporated physics via inputs, coupling, or losses rather than model architecture.
AI.method: An energy-balance temperature reference plus a learned residual predicts leaf temperature, which drives a multiplicative gate imposing a proved conditionally monotonic temperature-dependent probability cap in output or attention pathways.
AI.result: Across 19 Korean stations over five frost seasons (12 hourly leads) without leaf sensors, the time-token transformer (PET-E) reaches 0.516 lead-mean CSI versus 0.478 for LightGBM, cuts alarms at >=2 degrees C from 0.087 to 0.051, and beats LightGBM at all 12 leads on held-out stations (0.468/0.467 vs 0.437).
AI.conclusion: Embedding an explicit energy-balance probability cap directly into transformer pathways improves frost nowcasting calibration and generalization without leaf sensors.

authors: José Arce y de la Borbolla
title: Cleanly-DINO: Efficiently Learning Visual Task Spaces for Robotics
comment: 11 pages, 5 figures, accepted at COMPOGEN Workshop CoRL 2026, Austin, USA
summary: Learning manipulation tasks from few demonstrations requires abstractions that capture the changes relevant to task completion, such as object poses in rigid-body manipulation. However, tasks such as cleaning are defined by changes in visual state rather than object pose, making the choice of task representation less clear. In this work, we propose Cleanly-DINO to learn visual task spaces from few demonstrations. Given a mask of a task-relevant region and frozen ViT features, Cleanly-DINO fits a projection to isolate a task space and fit a progression metric to it. We train the model on diverse cleaning examples and evaluate its ability to localize incomplete task regions and transfer across visual domains. We also study its utility for robot learning by using it as an observation encoder and reward signal in a reinforcement learning setting. Finally, we deploy our fitted model within a real-world robotic wiping pipeline to evaluate its use in guiding task execution.

AI.tldr: Cleanly-DINO learns visual task spaces and progression metrics from few demonstrations using masked frozen ViT features, enabling cross-domain localization, RL reward shaping, and real-world robotic wiping.
AI.motivation: Non-rigid-body tasks like cleaning are defined by visual state changes rather than object poses, making standard pose-based task representations unsuitable for few-shot robot learning.
AI.method: Given a task-relevant region mask and frozen ViT features, Cleanly-DINO fits a projection to isolate a visual task space and learns a progression metric on top of it, used both as an observation encoder and reward signal.
AI.result: Evaluated on diverse cleaning examples, Cleanly-DINO localizes incomplete task regions, transfers across visual domains, supports reinforcement learning, and guides task execution in a real-world robotic wiping pipeline.
AI.conclusion: Projecting frozen ViT features into a masked visual task space offers a data-efficient representation for visual-change manipulation tasks like robotic cleaning.
